frames.concerns: Injury, pain and a heart attack are central plot points; the medical and rehab framing (Sakuragi's months of rehab, TV Tropes) differs from the church's prayer-based healing; members decide for themselves.

frames.aligns: Teshuvah (return) in Mitsui; respect for a teacher; effort (hishtadlut). Pirkei Avot 4:1 on the strong person as one who conquers his impulse fits Sakuragi's growth and Santos's reading that a boy must "conquer himself."
frames.concerns: Many Haredi homes restrict secular media; nivul peh (crude speech) and insults in English versions; comic violence.

frames.aligns: Teshuvah, mentorship, community; kind speech is the weak point.
Dignity of the outsider; repair (tikkun) of a broken team.
Tawba (repentance) in Mitsui; sabr (patience) in loss; ihsan in practice; brotherhood.
frames.concerns: Profanity; fighting played for laughs; romantic chasing and locker-room partial nudity in the anime (lowering the gaze, 24:30-31). Scholars differ on images and entertainment.

frames.aligns: Svadharma: each player finds his role (Sakuragi as rebounder); disciplined action (karma yoga); the teacher (guru) who transforms students.
frames.concerns: Rajasic anger and pride are strong early.

frames.aligns: Anzai as the "White-Haired Buddha": calm, compassion and patience after suffering; impermanence of each tournament; right effort.
frames.concerns: The story runs on craving to win and on anger in early volumes; ego is softened but not let go. Lay observance days exclude entertainment.

frames.aligns: Haumai (ego) overcome: Rukawa learns to pass, Sakuragi learns basics; chardi kala after defeat; seva to the team.
Unity and cooperation; transformation of character; excellence as service.
frames.concerns: Fighting and coarse language against the "chaste and holy life" (to verify wording).

frames.aligns: Makoto (sincerity) of effort; gratitude to the mentor; harmony (wa); the film's shrine prayer is treated respectfully (Plugged In).
Self-knowledge and personal growth; community. "Harm none" is broken by the brawls, which the story moves past.
"Be competent" (The Way to Happiness); group dynamic; no psychiatric content.
Second chances for a delinquent; emotional openness among boys (crying, apology); the film's grief story and respected female manager (Common Sense Media).
frames.concerns: Women largely in support roles; the colorist "Gorilla" nickname; comic violence and playing through injury (AAP guidance on youth sports injury, from general knowledge; to verify).

frames.aligns: Human effort, practice and reason transform people; no supernatural help; failure as learning (film: "losing will be an asset," Common Sense Media).
Discipline, respect for a wise elder, duty to team and school, hard work over shortcuts, personal responsibility, redemption through effort.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; mild language and comic fighting.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of the "punk" and the dropout; interdependent web of a team.
Self-development and earned respect; Sakuragi's self-confident "genius" persona; no false piety. TST tenets on correcting mistakes fit Mitsui's arc.
frames.concerns: The story subordinates the self to the team and honors humility; the Church of Satan's individualism sits uneasily. (Range: TST closer to A; Church of Satan closer to C.)

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Early chapters celebrate answering insult with fists and headbutts (v1-2; TV Tropes); the gym fight (v7-8) answers honor with violence. But the story moves disputes onto the court, and Mitsui's change includes a vow not to fight (Wikipedia).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Discipline and basics under Anzai and Akagi; delinquent freedom is shown as a dead end (Mitsui, v8).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Loyalty goes to team and school, and to Sakuragi's band of friends (Mito's "Sakuragi Legion"); families mostly offstage in the manga.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Senpai-kohai, captain and coach are deferred to; but Sakuragi, a beginner, earns a starting role, and Anzai leads gently.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No faith shapes choices; practice and strategy win. School club traditions keep it from the far end.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Hard work and endurance are central; so are Sakuragi's flamboyant self-expression and love of the game.

folkways.japan: The furyō delinquent style, senpai-kohai deference, school club teams, head-shaving as an apology (ch. 133) and the third-years' last tournament are Japanese school norms shown as setting. The "Gorilla" nickname reflects 1990s Japanese colorism, as Common Sense Media notes. The story's own message (second chances, team over self) is less hierarchical than the Confucian cluster's placement; Confucian ties with Orthodox Europe by distance.

delivery.evidence: ANN's Kimlinger calls it "a fun read" without depth early; Common Sense Media stresses teamwork and humility.
delivery.note: Lessons arrive through games and character turns, and rival teams' approaches are treated with respect.

personified.ideology: Bitterness and gang life, then repentance
Patient faith in players; never give up
Lone talent
Win by any means

entry.dominant: Communitarianism, Classical virtue ethics, Pragmatism; Might makes right and Nihilism critiqued.

entry.heading: The Climber (Kokou no Hito)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A life is worth living when you give all your strength to something, but no one can live entirely alone. The rope that ties climbers together, and in the end a family, is what brings a person back down the mountain.

frames.aligns: The ending favors marriage, a child and life over a deadly goal; isolation is shown as a wound; lust is resisted.
frames.concerns: Reckless risk to life (CCC 2288-2290 on care for health and life); Takemura's rope cut and the suicide-attempt backstory (CCC 2280-2283); Yumi's arc.

frames.aligns: Ascetic endurance, struggle with the passions ("Worldly desires", ch. 42), solitude that ends in communion with others.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses makes the sexual scenes and dark imagery a concern; despair shown at length.

frames.aligns: Perseverance; resisting temptation; family at the end.
frames.concerns: Sexual content (Philippians 4:8); despair without reference to God. Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Depicts sin and despair without endorsing them; redemption through love and belonging.
frames.concerns: No source of hope beyond human ties; sexual content.

frames.aligns: Clear cost of obsession; family restored.
frames.concerns: Hallucinations and dark visions; sexual temptation scenes. Little occult content.

frames.aligns: Common grace lets families value the craft; human pride ("Sinful pride", ch. 101) is shown failing.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 on lascivious pictures for the Yumi chapters; WLC Q136 on risking life needlessly.

frames.aligns: Vocation in marriage and work at the end; human limits exposed.
frames.concerns: Sexual content; despair. LCMS and WELS families tend to be more cautious than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Discipline, perseverance, growth toward love of others.
frames.concerns: Sexual content; holiness churches more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: Judged by framing: obsession and isolation are shown as costly; love and belonging win.
Humility before creation; community and family at the end.
frames.concerns: Individual glory and competition are the engine of the story; worldly media in general. Conservative groups avoid it; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Family as the place of belonging; marriage and a child redeem a lonely life.
frames.concerns: Sexual content; risk to life. Members vary in strictness.

frames.aligns: Mental-health honesty; loneliness taken seriously; critique of media sensationalism.
frames.concerns: Treatment of women (ANN; MAL); untreated depression.

frames.aligns: Perseverance, temperance at the end, family.
frames.concerns: "By beholding we become changed": the despair, sexual scenes and death imagery. Health message runs against reckless risk.
Sexual content (Galatians 5:19-21); reckless risk to life, which members are taught to respect as sacred. Little spiritism.
Long dwelling on fear, despair, illness and death.

frames.aligns: Choosing life and family at the end (Deuteronomy 30:19).
frames.concerns: Needless danger is forbidden (Deuteronomy 4:15, ushmartem); suicide-adjacent scenes; tzniut makes the sexual chapters a concern. Many Haredi homes avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Patience (sabr) and endurance; family at the end.
frames.concerns: Throwing oneself into destruction (Qur'an 2:195) and the prohibition of suicide (4:29) for the risk and the rope cut; lowering the gaze (24:30-31) for the sexual chapters.

frames.aligns: Tapas (discipline) and detachment; a householder stage that follows a seeker's stage.
frames.concerns: Some families apply the Gita's tamasic category to the despair and lust.

frames.aligns: Craving and attachment (to summits, to recognition) cause suffering; chapter titles use karma, rebirth, worldly desires, liberation.
frames.concerns: Lust scenes; risk to life. Right mindfulness of what feeds the mind.

frames.aligns: Honest work, endurance; ego (haumai) and lust shown as struggles.
frames.concerns: Lust scenes; ego as the hero's fuel for much of the story.

frames.aligns: Service and unity, solitude overcome by love; work as worship.
frames.concerns: Sexual content against a "chaste and holy life".

frames.aligns: Reverence and fear before mountains; sincerity (makoto); purity motifs; ancestors and family.
frames.concerns: Death on mountains as impurity; little to raise in message.

frames.aligns: Respect for nature's power; harm none, including oneself.
Survival across the dynamics, from self to family; taking care of oneself (Way to Happiness).
frames.concerns: Self-destructive risk; depression shown without the Church's frame.

frames.aligns: Honest look at depression and isolation; critique of sensational media.
frames.concerns: Women characters (ANN's Dee; MAL); unclear stance on toxic masculinity; untreated mental illness; suicide-adjacent scenes need safe-messaging context.

frames.aligns: Meaning made in a finite life by effort and human bonds; nature's indifference faced honestly.
Discipline, endurance, self-reliance, marriage and fatherhood as the answer to drift.
frames.concerns: Sexual content; long despair; gratuitous risk.

frames.aligns: Free search for meaning; interdependence (the rope); worth of every person.
Individualism, self-mastery and rejection of social conformity in most of the story (Church of Satan).
frames.concerns: Ends by choosing belonging over the solitary self; self-destructive risk runs against self-preservation.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Mori climbs for himself, not to answer insults; rivals' pride and Niimi's fight to clear his father's name (ch. 55, 81) are shown as costly.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Solo climbing against warnings and club rules (ch. 10-14, 21-24); freedom from others is the hero's goal for most of the story.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Little civic life; the ending places worth in a wife and child (ch. 129 "Mountains or family"; final chapter).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Mentors (Onishi, Adachi) are respected for care, not rank; the K2 team's leaders are not revered.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No faith practice; Buddhist words as metaphor; reverence for mountains.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Climbing as self-expression and meaning, balanced by bare survival, poverty and frostbite.

folkways.japan: Pressure to fit in at school and work, the outsider who cannot read the group, a teacher as moral guide, and taking the wife's family surname in marriage (mukoyōshi-style naming) are Japanese social norms in the setting rather than the story's message.

delivery.evidence: ANN's Dee: unclear whether it critiques or endorses toxic masculinity. Reviewers praise visual metaphor; none call it preachy.
delivery.note: The message comes through visual metaphor, interior monologue and consequences rather than speeches.

personified.ideology: Solitary self-reliance
Trust and mentorship
Success at any cost
Belonging and family

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Expressive individualism (critiqued), Stoicism, Classical virtue ethics.

entry.heading: The Flowers of Evil
entry.label: From summaries

frames.aligns: Sin is shown as enslaving, not freeing; guilt, confession (the note in ch. 8) and a long reckoning lead toward reconciliation. Evil is not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7). Baudelaire, a poet steeped in Catholic ideas of sin, is the frame (from general knowledge; to verify).
frames.concerns: Nakamura's nihilism is voiced with sympathy and never answered in faith; the planned suicide (CCC 2280-2283); sexual content involving minors, including an assault (CCC 2521-2524).

frames.aligns: A clear picture of the passions (lust, pride, despair) growing from one act. Repentance-like turning in the second half.
frames.concerns: No spiritual answer; the passions are explored at length with no ascetic remedy. Nepsis (guarding the senses) makes the voyeurism, assault and suicide plan a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: Sin's consequences are shown honestly; confession and a changed life later.
frames.concerns: No gospel hope; nihilism voiced sympathetically; vulgar language. Under Philippians 4:8 the sexual content and suicide plan are a heavy concern. Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: A realistic fallen world in which hidden sin grows and is exposed; restoration through honesty. Many in this tradition distinguish depicting sin from endorsing it.
frames.concerns: No gospel answer; Nakamura's contempt for everyone as "shitbugs" is never refuted. Explicitness involving minors is high even for families who engage culture.

frames.aligns: No occult or demonic content; a vivid picture of bondage to shame.
frames.concerns: No spiritual deliverance offered; a dark, oppressive atmosphere. Holiness standards make the sexual content a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: Total depravity has a strong echo: Nakamura's claim that everyone hides perversion; the "respectable" Saeki is no exception. Common grace lets adults value serious art.
frames.concerns: No grace named. WLC Q139 makes the sexual imagery a heavy concern; the suicide plan as self-murder (WLC Q136).

frames.aligns: Law at work: guilt crushes Kasuga until he confesses and is accepted (Saeki, later Tokiwa).
frames.concerns: No gospel offered. Conscience decides; LCMS and WELS families are typically more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Growth toward a changed life in the second half; friends who reach out.
frames.concerns: No grace named; holiness churches would weigh the sexual content and suicide plan heavily, the UMC less so.

frames.aligns: Serious literary treatment of sin, shame and reconciliation in the line of Baudelaire and confessional fiction; judged by framing.
frames.concerns: Nihilism unanswered; content with minors. Practice ranges widely.

frames.aligns: The cost of secrecy and the value of confession and community; no violence made heroic.
frames.concerns: Separation from worldly media makes the explicitness a heavy concern; Old Order groups would avoid it, MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Repentance and a changed life; family repair (Nakamura's mother).
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth asks for media that invites the Spirit; sexual content with minors, vulgar language and the suicide plan put it outside youth guidance.

frames.aligns: Compassion for outcasts (Nakamura); honest treatment of shame, consent and mental health; restoration over punishment.
frames.concerns: A boy's sexual assault is little addressed afterward (to verify); the suicide plan against safe-messaging norms. Significant for younger readers.

frames.aligns: Hidden sin brings ruin; a later turn to a healthier life.
frames.concerns: No hope beyond human ties. Fundamental Belief 22 and "by beholding we become changed" make the sexual content and despair a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: Immorality and theft are shown as harmful.
frames.concerns: No hope in God's Kingdom; jw.org counsel on entertainment featuring immorality makes the sexual content a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: Love and acceptance (Saeki, Tokiwa) help Kasuga out of self-condemnation.
frames.concerns: Shame, despair and the suicide plan dwelt on at length; members guard thought ("Stand porter at the door of thought," Science and Health 392).

frames.aligns: Teshuvah has an echo: confession, facing those he wronged, and a changed life. Choosing life over death at the festival.
frames.concerns: Tzniut and nivul peh make the sexual content and language a heavy concern; many Haredi homes avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Teshuvah; dignity of the outcast; choosing life.
frames.concerns: Degrading sexual content involving minors and vulgar speech concern Jewish values of modesty and dignity.

frames.aligns: Honest about shame, coercion and mental health; repair of relationships.
frames.concerns: The suicide plan; sexual content with minors; Significant for younger readers.

frames.aligns: Wrongdoing is exposed and leads to loss; later repentance-like change.
frames.concerns: Lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) makes the voyeurism, underwear theft and sexual content a heavy concern; despair of mercy (Qur'an 39:53) is voiced and not answered in faith.

frames.aligns: Karma-like consequences from one act; the turn from tamasic confusion toward clarity and creative work.
frames.concerns: Tamasic content under Gita 17; views vary by community.

frames.aligns: Close to teaching on craving, attachment and a constructed self: Kasuga's idealized self-image and idealized Saeki both fall apart ("I am an empty person"), and peace comes from acceptance.
frames.concerns: Right mindfulness of what feeds the mind makes the sexual and suicide scenes a depiction concern, Significant for younger readers.

frames.aligns: Lust, ego and attachment shown as destructive; humility and honest work later.
frames.concerns: Lust shown on the page is a depiction concern; no spiritual answer.

frames.aligns: Sexual wrongdoing and despair shown as damaging; reconciliation and service later.
frames.concerns: Shoghi Effendi's call to a "chaste and holy life" makes the sexual content a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) over false appearances is the story's core contrast; purification after a hometown "impurity" when Kasuga leaves and later returns. The festival is a matsuri (from general knowledge; to verify whether a shrine is shown).
frames.concerns: Disrupting a festival float is an act some families may weigh as disrespect toward a community and kami celebration.

frames.aligns: Personal responsibility; harm shown as harm (the Rede). No witches or pagans stereotyped.
Survival chosen over death; honesty about one's own overts (wrong acts) and their effects.
frames.concerns: Depression framed as psychological; any push toward psychiatric help would run against the church's stance. No content code for fiction.

frames.aligns: Serious treatment of shame, puberty and mental health; no glamorized fan service; the outcast given dignity.
frames.concerns: Voyeurism and theft of girls' underwear; a boy's sexual assault whose aftermath gets little attention (to verify); the suicide plan, which safe-messaging guidelines advise care with.

frames.aligns: This-life focus; self-knowledge, honesty, friendship and creative work as what makes life livable; critique of empty conformity without nihilism winning.
frames.concerns: Cruelty and the suicide plan are a depiction concern, Significant for minors.

frames.aligns: Shows where a loss of restraint leads; the later turn to responsibility, school and a steady relationship.
frames.concerns: Rebellion against family and community is voiced sympathetically; the good, the true and the beautiful are often degraded on the page.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of an outcast; honest search for meaning; reconciliation.
frames.concerns: Age-appropriateness makes it older-teen or adult reading.

frames.aligns: Rebellion against hypocrisy and conformity, with Baudelaire (who wrote "Litanies of Satan," from general knowledge; to verify) as the patron text; self-determination in the end.
frames.concerns: Coercion of others and a sexual assault go against the Eleven Rules' consent principles; the girls' stolen clothing is a violation of others.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Nakamura's attack on Kasuga's father (vol. 6) and Saeki's arson (vol. 5) are not celebrated; the later beach fight (vol. 11) ends in reconciliation, not victory.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The first arc celebrates breaking free of small-town conformity ("the other side of the mountain"); the festival plan is stopped (ch. 33) and the second arc values chosen, ordinary freedom.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Families are distant and the school hushes the case (vol. 6); help comes from friends (Tokiwa, Kinoshita) more than kin, though Nakamura's mother offers her peace (vol. 10-11).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: No elder or leader is held up for deference; teachers and parents are marginal.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No faith or custom guides anyone; Baudelaire and literature take that place.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Finding one's true self and writing it (Tokiwa's novel, Kasuga's writing, vol. 8-11) is the story's resolution.

folkways.japan: The pressure to be "normal," the closed middle-school class, a school handling a scandal internally and a family moving away to escape shame (vol. 6) reflect Japanese norms of group harmony and face; the story criticizes these more than it endorses them.

delivery.evidence: Reviewers praise that "everything is established through the natural flow of the aesthetics and scenes, not by anything being told to us" (Creamer).
delivery.note: The series gives each of its three teenagers' views a sympathetic voice and lets consequences, not statements, carry its verdicts.

personified.ideology: Nihilistic contempt for conformity; escape to "the other side"
Respectable goodness and social conformity
Literature and creative work as a way to live
Romantic self-image as a Baudelairean outsider

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Nihilism (voiced, then moved past), Expressive individualism (explored), with secular humanism and a Dharmic echo in the recovery arc.

series.title: Homunculus
series.adult_reason: Homunculus: deep entry scores 9; likely Mature 18+ (publisher rating unconfirmed)

entry.heading: Homunculus
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: The series does not hold up a model of a good life. It shows people hiding guilt and trauma behind masks (money, rank, surgery, lies), and asks whether a person who has no self underneath the mask can be healed at all. Its answer, as summaries read it, is bleak: Nakoshi's search for himself ends in self-mutilation, a woman's death and a world in which every face is his own.

frames.aligns: Lies, vanity and the refusal to know oneself lead to ruin; the kumicho's confession and act of reparation echo contrition and penance.
frames.concerns: Sexual use of a minor framed ambiguously; mutilation of the body (CCC 2297); no hope beyond the self; evil sometimes made fascinating, against Inter Mirifica 7. Sexual content and nudity are a heavy depiction concern (CCC 2521-2525).

frames.aligns: A study of the passions (vanity, lust, self-love) and a soul without a true face; their cost is shown.
frames.concerns: No repentance or grace in the tradition's sense; the self dissolves rather than being healed. Watchfulness over the senses (nepsis) makes the sexual imagery and body horror a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: Sin's consequences (lies, lust, self-harm) are not hidden.
frames.concerns: No hope in Christ; a minor's sexual exploitation not clearly condemned; skull drilling as a path to "truth". Under Philippians 4:8 the sexual content, gore and suicide are a heavy concern. Congregations are self-governing, so views vary.

frames.aligns: A picture of a fallen self that cannot remake itself; masks and lies exposed. Many in this tradition distinguish depicting sin from endorsing it.
frames.concerns: No gospel answer; the Yukari scene; the series' open verdict. Explicitness is high even for families who "engage" culture.

frames.aligns: Shows a man opening himself to unseen forces and being destroyed by it.
frames.concerns: ESP and a "sixth sense" gained by drilling the skull may be read as an "open door"; no spiritual answer; sexual content. Holiness standards make it a heavy depiction concern.

frames.aligns: The heart's deceitfulness (Jeremiah 17:9) has a strong echo: the homunculi may be Nakoshi's own projections. Common grace lets adults value serious art.
frames.concerns: No grace; the Yukari scene; self-mutilation. WLC Q139 makes the sexual imagery a heavy concern; suicide as self-murder (WLC Q136), treated pastorally.

frames.aligns: A man curved in on himself (incurvatus in se), shown to his ruin.
frames.concerns: No word of forgiveness. Conscience-based; LCMS and WELS families are typically far more cautious than ELCA about the content.

frames.aligns: The kumicho's turn from violence; Ito's reconciliation with his father.
frames.concerns: No grace named; sexual exploitation of a minor. Holiness churches avoid it; UMC families would see it as adult reading.

frames.aligns: Works judged by how they frame good and evil; the story shows vanity and lies destroying a man.
frames.concerns: The Yukari scene's framing; no hope offered. Content puts it firmly in adult literary reading.

frames.aligns: Violence leads to ruin; the yakuza boss leaves violence behind.
frames.concerns: A world with no community to catch anyone; mutilation and sexual content. Old Order groups would avoid it; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Repentance and restitution (the kumicho); a father-son reconciliation.
frames.concerns: Sexual exploitation of a minor; self-mutilation; no hope beyond the self. For the Strength of Youth asks for media that invites the Spirit; this falls outside youth guidance.

frames.aligns: Trauma taken seriously; a sympathetic arc for a gender-questioning character (Ito, per Looper); homelessness shown humanely.
frames.concerns: A minor's sexual exploitation framed ambiguously; women as objects of the hero's need; suicide shown.

frames.aligns: Unhealthy, self-destroying living shown as destroying.
frames.concerns: No hope; sexual content; body horror. "By beholding we become changed" and Fundamental Belief 22 make it a heavy concern; health teaching weighs the self-mutilation.

frames.aligns: Immorality and violence shown as harmful.
frames.concerns: Psychic "sixth sense" content may be weighed as spiritism; sexual immorality (Galatians 5:19-21); violence (Psalm 11:5).

frames.aligns: Nakoshi's visions may be his own thought; the story sees mind as shaping experience.
frames.concerns: Trauma, disease and mutilation presented as the deepest reality; surgery as the path to insight. "Stand porter at the door of thought" (Science and Health 392) makes dwelling on it a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: The body is not ours to damage; teshuvah echoed in the kumicho's confession.
frames.concerns: Self-wounding (chavalah); sexual exploitation of a minor; no moral verdict. Tzniut and nivul peh make it a heavy concern; many Haredi homes avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Teshuvah; the dignity of the homeless.
frames.concerns: Self-mutilation; the Yukari scene; no verdict. Degrading sexual content is a concern under modesty values.

frames.aligns: Harm to the vulnerable shown as harm; Ito's self-acceptance.
frames.concerns: Exploitation of a minor framed ambiguously; women as objects.

frames.aligns: Lying and vanity lead to ruin; repentance (the kumicho).
frames.concerns: Changing God's creation (Qur'an 4:119, cited on cosmetic surgery) is a theme the story explores without a verdict; self-harm; sexual content with a minor. Lowering the gaze (24:30-31) makes it a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: Karma-like return: each "cure" lands on Nakoshi's own body.
frames.concerns: No path to release; self-harm; sexual content. Tamasic content under Gita 17. Views vary.

frames.aligns: Close to teaching on no-self and clinging: Nakoshi grasps after a fixed self and ends trapped in a world of his own face; masks of ego; suffering born of craving.
frames.concerns: No path out of suffering; the ending is dissolution, not liberation. Right mindfulness of what feeds the mind makes the sexual and gore content a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: The five vices (lust, ego, attachment) shown as destructive; haumai (ego) as the root problem.
frames.concerns: No spiritual answer; lust on the page.
Sexual content with a minor; no spiritual answer. The call to a "chaste and holy life" makes it a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) and its absence: a man built on lies.
frames.concerns: Bodily impurity (kegare): blood, death and mutilation. No shrines or kami mocked.

frames.aligns: Self-knowledge as a theme; no witches or pagans stereotyped; "homunculus" as alchemical image.
frames.concerns: The Rede ("harm none") is broken repeatedly, against Yukari and Nanako.

frames.aligns: Trauma images that bind a person until confronted echo the church's own teaching on past trauma (my own framing); survival of self.
frames.concerns: Ito's psychoanalytic and medical framing, and brain surgery as the path to insight, run against the church's stance on psychiatry and brain intervention.

frames.aligns: Sympathetic gender-identity arc for Ito (Looper; MAL review); trauma, homelessness and appearance culture taken seriously.
frames.concerns: Sexual activity between an adult and a 17-year-old framed as "rescue" rather than clearly as abuse; reviewers call it a rape scene; women as objects of the protagonist's need; suicide by hanging.

frames.aligns: Ito's skeptical, scientific frame; the placebo reveal; critique of pseudoscience (trepanation as insight) can be read in.
frames.concerns: Unethical human experiments are the premise and not clearly condemned; cruelty to the vulnerable.

frames.aligns: Shows the emptiness of a life of money, vanity and lies.
frames.concerns: No stable family, faith or duty offered; exploitation of a minor; mutilation. Content that degrades the good, true and beautiful.

frames.aligns: Free search for identity; Ito's self-acceptance; dignity of the homeless.
frames.concerns: The worth and dignity of Yukari and Nanako are violated; adult reading only.

frames.aligns: Self-determination and the rejection of social masks; skepticism toward the supernatural.
frames.concerns: Harm to a minor and unwanted sexual advances, which the Eleven Rules condemn, are framed ambiguously.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: The yakuza code of finger-cutting is shown as guilt in disguise; the boss's last cut is atonement, not honor, and he leaves the gang (Japanese Wikipedia; JP v4-6 likely).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Institutions (hospital, gang, family) fail; Nakoshi lives outside all rules in his car; the story neither celebrates order nor endorses his freedom.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Families harm (Ito's father, Yukari's parents) though Ito reconciles with his father; the homeless park is the nearest thing to community (Ita-san).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Rank (banker, doctor, yakuza boss) is shown as a mask over trauma; no elder is held up for deference.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No religion; the frame is scientific and psychoanalytic (Ito's experiments, placebo reveal).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: The story is about the self and its expression (surgery, identity, Ito's transition), set among the homeless struggling to survive.

folkways.japan: Yakuza finger-cutting (yubitsume), compensated dating and burusera shops, heavy education pressure, appearance culture and the homeless of Shinjuku are Japanese context the story uses as setting; it criticizes more than endorses them.

delivery.evidence: MAL reviewers call it "overexplained and pretentious" and "pseudo-philosophical"; Ito explains psychoanalytic theory on the page.
delivery.note: Ideas about trauma and the self are spelled out in dialogue, but the story never settles whether Nakoshi's visions are real.

personified.ideology: Scientific skepticism about the mind and the occult
A self made of surface: money, surgery, lies
Atonement through confession and self-punishment

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Postmodernism (identity as surface), Naturalism, Nihilism (explored).

series.title: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure Part 6: Stone Ocean
series.romaji: JoJo no Kimyou na Bouken: Stone Ocean
series.native: ジョジョの奇妙な冒険 ストーンオーシャン

entry.heading: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure Part 6: Stone Ocean
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is chosen, not fated: loyalty to family and friends, courage under unjust power, and sacrifice for the weak are worth more than the peace of a destiny imposed from above, and hope in an unknown future is part of being human.

frames.aligns: Evil is not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7): Pucci's scheme fails and his "Heaven" is shown as false. The story sides with free will against fate, close to CCC 1730-1742; Jolyne's death for Emporio echoes John 15:13. Concern for prisoners and the falsely accused echoes the works of mercy (Matthew 25:36). Pucci keeps a confession secret (ch. 127-129).
frames.concerns: A priest as the main villain who misuses Scripture (Christ "fated" to the cross, ch. 143) and gives God-like love to DIO (ch. 94). Fatalism differs from Providence, which works with free creatures (CCC 302-308). Masturbation reference (ch. 1), sexual subtext with a minor, gore; reincarnation-like ending (CCC 1013).

frames.aligns: Freedom (autexousion) and synergy over fate; a counterfeit "Heaven" exposed; self-sacrificial love.
frames.concerns: A cleric turned servant of a demonic figure; Christ's passion recast as blind fate (ch. 143); a universe remade without God; guarding the senses (nepsis) weighs the gore and the sexual material.

frames.aligns: Evil is clearly framed as evil and defeated; a religious leader whose faith is false (Matthew 7:15-20); self-sacrifice; justice for the falsely accused.
frames.concerns: Phil 4:8 test: constant gore, a masturbation reference (ch. 1), sexual subtext, strong language. A priest-villain misusing Scripture. Soul liberty: each family decides.

frames.aligns: Engaging culture: a story that rejects a counterfeit heaven built by a false shepherd and honors self-giving love (ch. 155). Depicts without endorsing.
frames.concerns: Pucci's "happiness" is peace without God; the story offers no gospel alternative, only human hope. Sexual material and gore (Romans 14 conscience).

frames.aligns: Clear good and evil; a demonic figure's plan defeated.
frames.concerns: Souls pulled from bodies, a baby born from absorbed souls (ch. 76-77, 95), devotion to a vampire "as God" (ch. 94), "the 14 phrases" recited from DIO's notebook (ch. 95): many would see an "open door" to spiritual darkness.

frames.aligns: A rich talking point: Pucci's "gravity" is impersonal fatalism, while the Westminster Confession (3.1) says God's decree does no "violence... to the will of the creatures." Common grace lets families value the craft.
frames.concerns: Westminster Larger Catechism Q139 on lascivious material (ch. 1, the DIO-Pucci flashback); gore; a pastor figure using Scripture to justify murder.

frames.aligns: Bondage of the will is about sin, not blind fate; the story sides with grace-like gifts (sacrifice, friendship). Vocation of a father (Jotaro).
frames.concerns: A priest villain; Christ's cross called "fate" (ch. 143) rather than a free self-giving; sexual material. LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Prevenient grace and free response fit the story's rejection of fate; social holiness: the falsely imprisoned and abused.
frames.concerns: Gore, language, sexual material; holiness churches more cautious than UMC (General Rules on diversions).

frames.aligns: Imaginative fiction judged by framing (Lewis's tradition): a counterfeit heaven (compare The Great Divorce) defeated by love. Article 17 cautions against despair from a misused doctrine of predestination, which is Pucci's path.
frames.concerns: Clergy as villain; gore and sexual material.

frames.aligns: Exposure of a church official who serves another master; suffering of prisoners; Jolyne's sacrifice.
frames.concerns: Violence is the heroes' main tool, ending with Pucci beaten to death as he begs (ch. 158) (Matthew 5:39). Conservative groups avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Moral agency is central to the plan of salvation (2 Nephi 2:27), and the story defends agency against a forced, fore-known fate; family across generations; sacrifice.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth: the masturbation reference, sexual subtext and gore do not invite the Spirit for many families; a resetting universe.

frames.aligns: Critique of the carceral state and of racist violence (ch. 128); a female lead; a clergyman who abuses pastoral power is exposed.
frames.concerns: Graphic violence; the slur in the manga; Anasui's femicide treated lightly as backstory.

frames.aligns: Free will and the great controversy between good and evil; a false "heaven" exposed.
frames.concerns: The state of the dead: souls taken out as discs, a ghost room, and the dead returning in a new universe conflict with Fundamental Belief 26; "by beholding we become changed" weighs the gore and sexual material.

frames.aligns: A religious leader who uses God's name for evil is condemned.
frames.concerns: Spiritism-like content (souls extracted, the dead returning), constant violence (Psalm 11:5), sexual material; jw.org counsel on entertainment weighs these heavily. Jesus is said to die on a "cross" (ch. 143).

frames.aligns: Fear is overcome; Pucci's "gravity" as a mental law resisted.
frames.concerns: Fear, decay and death shown as overwhelming and real; body horror; time and matter as all-powerful.

frames.aligns: "All is foreseen, yet freedom is given" (Avot 3:15) and Rambam on free will (Hilchot Teshuvah 5) fit the heroes' stand; racism and lynching condemned.
frames.concerns: Tzniut and nivul peh: the masturbation reference, strip search, sexual subtext, language; gore. Many Haredi homes avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Free will against fate; justice for the wrongly imprisoned; racism condemned.
frames.concerns: Sexual material and gore; Christian clergy as villain is not a Jewish concern in itself. No antisemitic tropes reported.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam echoes in the critique of prisons and racism; a woman as hero.
frames.concerns: Violence; the slur in the manga. No antisemitic tropes reported.

frames.aligns: Pucci's love of DIO "as I love God" (ch. 94) is a form of shirk, and he is defeated; justice for the oppressed; mercy and sacrifice.
frames.concerns: Qadar (divine decree) is a pillar of faith, but Pucci's version removes human responsibility; he says Jesus was put on the cross (ch. 143), which Qur'an 4:157-158 denies (said by a villain); lowering the gaze (24:30-31) for the sexual material; gore.

frames.aligns: Cyclical time and a universe that ends and begins again echo the kalpas; karma: Pucci's actions return to him; the Gita's call to act rightly whatever the outcome (2.47).
frames.concerns: Tamasic content (gore, cruelty); the "reset" is achieved by a villain, not dharma.

frames.aligns: Craving and attachment drive Pucci; release from fear comes not from knowing the future but from compassion and right action; cycles of time.
frames.concerns: Non-harm (first precept) against constant killing; the final killing of a begging enemy.

frames.aligns: Hukam (divine order) is accepted in Sikh teaching, but through humility, not ego; Pucci shows haumai (ego) disguised as acceptance. Defending the weak.
frames.concerns: Violence and sexual material; a vision of the divine will imposed by force.

frames.aligns: Free will and the unity of humankind: racist violence (ch. 128) is shown as evil; a false religious leader is exposed.
frames.concerns: Constant violence; sexual material ("chaste and holy life").

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) in the heroes; gratitude (Emporio's debt to Jolyne and Weather, ch. 157); renewal after the reset.
frames.concerns: Death, blood and corpses (kegare) are constant.

frames.aligns: Cycles of time and rebirth; a moon-timed ritual (the new moon at Cape Canaveral) framed as power, not evil in itself; the self-directed will.
Self-determinism against an imposed fate; personal responsibility. The Way to Happiness: "Do not murder."
frames.concerns: Memories and abilities ripped out as discs; constant killing by heroes and villains.

frames.aligns: First female JoJo, refusing an editor's request to make her male (Wikipedia); critique of the carceral state (Anime Feminist); racist violence condemned; a trans inmate shown respectfully (TV Tropes YMMV).
frames.concerns: Anasui's dismemberment of his girlfriend treated as quirky backstory while he courts Jolyne; the "queer" slur (manga); DIO-Pucci subtext with a 16-year-old; Anime Feminist notes Jolyne starts as "the least in control of her own power."

frames.aligns: Human choice and solidarity beat a cosmic plan; the religious villain's "Heaven" is false; hope without guarantees.
frames.concerns: The supernatural is central as fiction; heavy violence.

frames.aligns: Father-daughter love and duty (Jotaro, Jolyne); loyalty, sacrifice and courage; evil punished.
frames.concerns: A priest as villain; heroes are convicts; masturbation reference and sexual subtext; strong language.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth (prisoners, outsiders); free search for meaning; religion used for harm critiqued.
A religious authority who claims to know what is best for all humanity is defeated; individual will and self-determination win.
frames.concerns: Proportional retaliation (Church of Satan) and compassion (Satanic Temple Tenet 1) would read the final killing differently; the DIO-Pucci material involving a minor (Eleven Rules on children).

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Wrongs are settled personally, not by courts: Ermes's revenge for her sister (likely ch. 51-57), Weather's vow against Pucci (ch. 133-137), Emporio's debt (ch. 157). Courts are rigged (ch. 1-8).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Prison order is oppressive and the villain's ideal is total order of fate; freedom of choice is the story's prize.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Bloodline and father-daughter loyalty drive the plot (ch. 11, 75, 154); a found family of inmates; the civic institutions fail.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Guards' and the chaplain's authority are abused; a child, Emporio, wins.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Religious authority is the villain's; the heroes choose for themselves. A bloodline legacy remains honored.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival in prison comes first; Jolyne's style and self-possession lean toward self-expression.

folkways.japan: The Joestar "bloodline" and inherited duty, and the gratitude and debt Emporio feels (on), reflect Japanese norms. A Catholic priest as a stylish villain fits a Japanese pop-culture habit of borrowing Christian imagery without Christian doctrine, which matches Araki's statement that the priesthood was only a facade. The idea of a universe that cycles and returns to its origin, which Araki named, has echoes in Buddhist ideas of time (from general knowledge; to verify; no source links Araki to it).

delivery.evidence: TV Tropes calls Pucci the franchise's most well-intentioned villain; ANN's writers say the story answers his fate with hope and choice.
delivery.note: The villain argues his theology of fate in long speeches, and the story answers him through the heroes' choices and sacrifices rather than counter-sermons.

personified.ideology: Accepting a known fate is happiness; God's will as irresistible "gravity"
Will and hope against fate; sacrifice for others
Choice and justice can change fate
Victim of racism and fate who answers with vengeance

entry.dominant: Existentialism (affirmed), Classical virtue ethics (affirmed), Collectivism/authoritarianism and Stoic-style fatalism (critiqued through Pucci), Christian (explored through a villain), Critical theory and Feminism (explored).

entry.heading: Kagurabachi
entry.label: From summaries

content.framing: Mixed: revenge killing of villains endorsed early; atrocities and torture condemned; war violence shown with consequences

frames.aligns: Evil (trafficking, torture, a hidden massacre) is framed as evil; filial piety; atonement and self-sacrifice (Samura); protecting the innocent.
frames.concerns: Private vengeance as the hero's goal; killing by a vigilante without lawful authority (CCC 2302 on anger and revenge); gore not always serving understanding (Inter Mirifica 7).

frames.aligns: Repentance for past sins (Samura, the Sword Saint); a son honoring his father; truth over a national myth.
frames.concerns: Nepsis (guarding the senses) and constant dismemberment; anger nursed as a motive.

frames.aligns: Clear villains; human trafficking condemned; sacrifice for others.
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 test for gore and torture; revenge as motive; no source of forgiveness. Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Depicts the cost of violence; a hero who rescues the enslaved; exposure of a lie told by the powerful.
frames.concerns: Romans 14 conscience on graphic violence; the hero is admired as a killer; vengeance never surrendered to God.

frames.aligns: Clear good and evil; deliverance of captives.
frames.concerns: Sorcery as a normal power system and "cursed" blades may be read as an "open door"; graphic violence. Views range widely.

frames.aligns: Common grace in a well-made work; total depravity in the Seitei War cover-up and the Sword Saint's fall; the state's sins exposed.
frames.concerns: Sixth commandment (WLC Q135-136): private revenge and needless killing; vengeance not left to the magistrate.

frames.aligns: Two kingdoms: the corrupt Kamunabi and a dictator show the abuse of the sword; vocation as a craftsman (reforging Enten).
frames.concerns: Private vengeance outside lawful office; LCMS and WELS families weigh gore more than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Social concern for trafficking victims; sanctification-like change in Chihiro (first smile, protecting others).
frames.concerns: Holiness churches cautious about violence-as-entertainment; revenge as the starting virtue.

frames.aligns: Good and evil framed clearly; a literary revenge tragedy that questions its own premise (Kunishige's blades, ch. 58, 72).
frames.concerns: Gore for younger readers; vengeance framed sympathetically.

frames.aligns: Exposure of war crimes and war myths; costs of violence shown.
frames.concerns: The hero kills, and violence is the story's answer and its pleasure (Matthew 5:39, 44); vengeance is the premise. Conservative groups avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Family bonds central; a father reunited with a daughter; sacrifice.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth: graphic violence and torture may not "invite the Spirit"; revenge motive.

frames.aligns: Critique of nationalism and a state cover-up; trafficking condemned; the "enemy" humanized (ch. 72).
frames.concerns: Female characters as plot devices (ComicBook.com; ANN); vigilante killing; gore.

frames.aligns: Life valued in the rescue plots; war crimes exposed.
frames.concerns: "By beholding we become changed" (2 Corinthians 3:18) applied to constant dismemberment; Fundamental Belief 22 on entertainment; revenge as theme. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Exposure of nationalist war myths; rescue of captives.
frames.concerns: jw.org's question whether entertainment features what God hates, especially violence (Psalm 11:5): it is the series' main content; sorcery may be read as spiritism. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Love and family ties outlast loss.
frames.concerns: Fear, gore, torture and grief dwelt on as real and powerful; "Stand porter at the door of thought" (Science and Health 392). (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Kibbud av (honoring a father); trafficking condemned; truth about a hidden massacre.
frames.concerns: Lo tikom (Leviticus 19:18, no revenge) against the premise; constant violence; many Haredi homes restrict such media. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Honoring a parent; justice for captives; memory over myth.
frames.concerns: Revenge outside law; graphic violence. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam in undoing harm the blades caused; critique of dehumanizing "savages" rhetoric (ch. 72).
frames.concerns: Violence for younger readers; vigilante justice. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Justice for the oppressed; protecting captives and children; condemnation of trafficking.
frames.concerns: Qisas belongs to lawful authority, and forgiveness is praised when one could take revenge (Qur'an 42:40, 5:45); mutilation and torture; sorcery (sihr) as a normal power.

frames.aligns: Dharma of a warrior who protects the weak; karma of the blades' past; a teacher-student bond (Shiba).
frames.concerns: Tamasic qualities (rage, gore) per Gita ch. 17; revenge as motive rather than duty.

frames.aligns: Hatred shown as suffering ("base expression is anguish"); the cycle of revenge (Yura, Samura, the Sword Saint) explored; a Buddhist temple setting.
frames.concerns: First precept and the killing that drives the plot; what the gore feeds the mind.

frames.aligns: Saint-soldier ideal: the sword (kirpan) to protect the oppressed; trafficking condemned.
frames.concerns: Krodh (anger) as the hero's fuel, one of the five vices. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Unity, exposure of prejudice against a foreign people (ch. 72).
frames.concerns: Strong commitment to non-violence and forgiveness; revenge and constant killing. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto); the sword and smithing as a sacred craft tradition; gratitude to a father.
frames.concerns: Blood and death as impurity (kegare); a temple used as a battlefield. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: No stereotyping of witches or pagans; sorcery is neutral.
frames.concerns: "Harm none" against a revenge plot; the threefold return echoed in the cycle of vengeance. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness precepts "do not murder" and protecting children appear in the rescue plots.
frames.concerns: The hero murders in revenge; little else to raise. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Critique of nationalism, war myths and dehumanizing language ("bloodthirsty savages"); trafficking and abuse condemned; state power distrusted.
frames.concerns: Weak female roles (ComicBook.com; ANN's Moore); vigilante killing as heroism; graphic violence for under-14s (ScreenWise).

frames.aligns: Truth over official myth; human dignity of the "enemy"; the costs of violence.
frames.concerns: Revenge as the motor; gore; a world solved by stronger weapons.

frames.aligns: Filial duty; a craftsman's heritage; mentorship; courage; men protecting the vulnerable.
frames.concerns: Graphic violence; distrust of every institution; a state turned dictatorship.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of the "enemy" (ch. 72); justice for trafficked people.
frames.concerns: Violence and revenge as the answer; female roles. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Self-reliance; retribution against those who harm you (Satanic Statements: "vengeance instead of turning the other cheek"); defiance of a corrupt authority; protecting children (Eleven Rules).
frames.concerns: Torture and harm to children by villains (condemned in the story); The Satanic Temple's tenets on compassion and justice weigh against cruelty. (from general knowledge; to verify)

Dignity vs honor.evidence: The father's murder must be answered personally (ch. 1-2); the Kamunabi and courts are bypassed; payback killings of villains (ch. 8, 17-18).

Order vs freedom.evidence: The hero acts outside the law, but against criminals and a tyrant; order itself is not rejected, only corrupt order (vol. 10; ch. 111).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Family and found family first: avenging a father, Samura and Iori, the uncle twist (vol. 12). Rescuing strangers (Yuu's sister, Char) adds a civic strand.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Master-apprentice and clan hierarchies (Sazanami head, Sword Saint) exist but are often abusive; the mentor Shiba is close and informal.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Inherited craft and a father's legacy guide the hero; no religion; the national myth is debunked by evidence (ch. 72).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival, strength and protection come first; little room for leisure or self-expression in a world at war.

folkways.japan: Sword-smithing as an inherited craft, master-apprentice loyalty, yakuza underworld codes and the remembered war are Japanese settings and genre conventions (with, as Hokazono says, a "Hollywood version of Japan"); the story's own message lies in filial loyalty turned to protecting others and in facing the truth about the war.

delivery.evidence: Reviewers focus on art, pacing and memes; none opened calls it preachy. Ch. 72 gives the "invaders" a human face.
delivery.note: Questions about revenge, war memory and a father's responsibility are carried by plot reveals and fights rather than speeches.

personified.ideology: Filial revenge turning into protection
Atonement by eliminating all who misused the blades
Exposing a national lie by violence
Might makes right; rule by one strongman

entry.dominant: Might makes right (critiqued), Classical virtue ethics, Traditionalism (filial and craft), Critical theory (war memory and state power).

series.title: Jujutsu Kaisen 0
series.romaji: Jujutsu Kaisen 0: Tokyo Toritsu Jujutsu Koutou Senmon Gakkou
series.native: 呪術廻戦 0 東京都立呪術高等専門学校

entry.heading: Jujutsu Kaisen 0 (Gege Akutami)
entry.label: From summaries

frames.aligns: Love that lets go; a despairing teen comes to value his life; friends and a mentor who protect him; a false religious leader exposed.
frames.concerns: Sorcery and a spirit-bond are the hero's power (CCC 2115-2117 on spiritism, judged here by framing); Yuta offers his soul to a curse; past suicide attempt.

frames.aligns: Grief, remembrance of the dead and their release; struggle against a deceiver.
frames.concerns: Spirits of the dead bound to the living and used in battle treat spiritual reality as a tool; guarding the senses against the gore.

frames.aligns: Courage, loyalty, a bullied boy finding friends; a cult leader's fraud exposed.
frames.concerns: Spirit contact and vows to a curse (Deuteronomy 18:10-12); suicide content. Congregations differ on fantasy magic.

frames.aligns: A clear deceiver (fake monk) defeated; sacrificial love; trauma turned to service ("a curse... that can save people," Plugged In).
frames.concerns: Occult mechanics; a dead girl's spirit as the hero's weapon. Range is wide on fantasy magic.

frames.aligns: Evil is real and must be fought; a false religion exposed.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": a spirit of the dead attached to a boy, a vow of his soul to it, curses summoned and absorbed are the story's engine.

frames.aligns: Common grace: love, loyalty and courage shine in a dark world; religious hypocrisy judged.
frames.concerns: Occult framework; suicide (WLC Q136, handled pastorally).

frames.aligns: Law and gospel shapes: Yuta's guilt binds him; release comes from the truth being told and accepted.
frames.concerns: Occult themes (Large Catechism on sorcery); LCMS and WELS stricter than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Grace-like turning: a boy who wanted to die chooses to live for others; social holiness in a found community.
frames.concerns: Occult; holiness churches more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: Grief, remembrance and letting the dead rest; sacrifice; a fantasy tradition with Anglican roots.
frames.concerns: Occult system; a false religious group. Episcopal families generally less concerned than ACNA families.

frames.aligns: Mutual care; a gentle protagonist; release of grasping love.
frames.concerns: Violence as the heroes' calling and climax (Matthew 5:39); occult themes. Conservative groups avoid most popular media.

frames.aligns: Covenant-like promise and faithfulness; family-like loyalty; hope after death (Rika passes on in peace).
frames.concerns: Spirits of the dead bound to the living and used as weapons; suicide content.

frames.aligns: Bullying, trauma and healing; a found community; critique of an elite that would execute a troubled teen; supremacy defeated.
frames.concerns: Suicide content for younger readers; childhood-engagement framing.
Spiritualism is rejected; here the dead persist as a conscious spirit bound to the living, the reverse of the Adventist teaching that the dead sleep.

frames.aligns: Love among friends; a false religion exposed.
frames.concerns: Spiritism and contact with the dead are the core of the story; fighting as the hero's calling.

frames.aligns: The twist that Yuta's own thought (refusal to let go) made the curse fits the teaching that thought shapes experience; love heals.
frames.concerns: Death and evil spirits shown as real and overwhelming.

frames.aligns: Pikuach nefesh: protecting life; mourning that ends and lets the dead rest.
frames.concerns: Necromancy-like bond with the dead (Deuteronomy 18:11) is the hero's power; suicide content. Many Haredi homes restrict such media.

frames.aligns: Saving life; healthy mourning; a hateful supremacist defeated.
frames.concerns: Bond with the dead as a craft; suicide content.

frames.aligns: Human dignity against supremacy ("monkeys"); healing from trauma; tikkun olam through service.
Protecting the weak; patience (sabr); a false religious leader who takes people's money is defeated.
frames.concerns: Sihr and binding with a spirit of the dead are the hero's craft; offering one's soul to a spirit; suicide content.

frames.aligns: Duty to protect; release of an attached soul so it can move on; karma-like justice for Geto.
frames.concerns: Sacred-adjacent imagery (monk robes, mudras) used for spectacle; gore.

frames.aligns: The central twist is about attachment: clinging to the dead creates suffering, and release brings peace. Compassion for all beings answers Geto's hatred.
frames.concerns: A man in monk's robes runs a fraudulent group (critiqued, but the image is borrowed); violence and the first precept.

frames.aligns: Courage to defend others; ego and hatred (Geto) defeated; seva-like service.
Unity and the oneness of humanity against Geto's supremacy; service.
frames.concerns: Strong commitment to non-violence; spirit contact; suicide content.

frames.aligns: Onryo (vengeful spirits) and their pacification are deep Shinto themes; Sugawara no Michizane, feared as an onryo and later honored as Tenjin, is invoked as Yuta's ancestor; Rika is "purified" and freed.
frames.concerns: A revered kami-figure used as a power source in a battle story.

frames.aligns: Bonds with spirits shown with responsibility; consent and release of a spirit; a cult leader's abuse of power condemned.
frames.concerns: "Harm none" set against lethal guarding; a vow of one's soul.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness: help others, do not murder; the murderer is defeated.
frames.concerns: Trauma and suicide themes, which the Church reads apart from psychiatry.

frames.aligns: A bullied, sensitive boy as hero; women as strong as men (Common Sense Media); supremacy and an elite that would execute a troubled teen are critiqued; trauma turned to care.
frames.concerns: Suicide content and safe messaging; romanticized child engagement.

frames.aligns: Meaning comes from relationships and chosen purpose; a teen chooses life; human dignity against supremacy; magic clearly fiction.
frames.concerns: Suicide and grief content for younger readers.

frames.aligns: Duty, sacrifice, loyalty, a faithful promise, good mentors; a clear villain whose ideology is condemned.
frames.concerns: The institution (higher-ups) is cold; fan affection for Geto.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of every person against Geto's supremacy; healing community.
Compassion and bodily autonomy; a fraudulent religious leader exposed (Satanic Temple Tenets 1 and 5); no divine command.
frames.concerns: Self-sacrifice for others over self-interest; harm to children in backstory.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Rika's revenge on bullies (ch. 0-1) is shown as the curse's danger, not as justice; Yuta fights to protect friends, not to answer insults (ch. 0-4).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Gojo bends the higher-ups' order to save Yuta (ch. 0-1), while the class trains under discipline (ch. 0-2).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Yuta's bond to one person (Rika) is loosened into care for his class and for strangers; Geto's in-group loyalty to sorcerers is condemned (ch. 0-3 to 0-4).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Geto's ranking of sorcerers over "monkeys" is the villain's creed (Plugged In); teacher authority is warm but real.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Japanese spirit lore (onryo, Michizane) is used respectfully as story physics, but organized religion appears as Geto's fraud.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival under threat dominates, but the ending's message is to live a full life (Rika's last wish, ch. 0-4).

folkways.japan: The school class, senpai-teacher bonds and the shonen sword-training montage reflect Japanese school norms; the onryo figure of Sugawara no Michizane and the idea of pacifying a vengeful spirit come from Japanese religious history rather than the story's own message.

delivery.evidence: Reviewers praise Geto's presence but Otaku USA wanted more time for him; Beneath the Tangles calls his introduction muddied.
delivery.note: The love-as-curse theme is stated once in a line by Gojo and then shown through plot, while Geto's ideology gets little room in this volume.

personified.ideology: Sorcerers are superior; non-sorcerers should be exterminated
Love that releases; live to protect others
Possessive love that will not let go
Raise and protect the next generation

entry.dominant: Pagan/occult (Japanese folk religion and Shinto), Existentialism, Communitarianism, Dharmic (attachment and release), Might makes right (critiqued, through Geto's supremacy). Labels are this entry's framing unless a source is named.

series.title: Toilet-Bound Hanako-kun
series.native: 地縛少年 花子くん

entry.heading: Toilet-Bound Hanako-kun
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life treasures the people you have now, faces guilt and fate honestly, and refuses easy wishes that make someone else pay the price.

frames.aligns: Wishes that cost others are shown as evil; guilt for a grave sin is real, and Hanako seeks to atone through service (ch. 3); self-giving love (Tsukasa for Amane, the friends for Aoi).
frames.concerns: The hero is a spirit of the dead who grants wishes, and summoning him is the premise (spiritism and divination, CCC 2115-2117); salvation by "doing your duties" rather than grace.

frames.aligns: Repentance and the weight of sin (Hanako's hidden guilt, ch. 27, 57); compassion for the dead.
frames.concerns: Contact with spirits of the dead and wish bargains with spirits, which the tradition reads as demonic.

frames.aligns: Clear warning about bargains ("be careful what you wish for"); loyalty and sacrifice.
frames.concerns: Summoning rituals and spirit contact (Deuteronomy 18:10-12) are the story's engine; the ghost hero is likeable. Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: A story about guilt, sacrifice and refusing to let another die in your place; mercy toward the lost.
frames.concerns: The occult premise (summoning, wishes, exorcism) presented as everyday reality, not as fantasy magic.

frames.aligns: Exorcism exists and evil spirits are real; courage to rescue friends.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": a summoning chant children can copy, spirits as friends and guides, exorcists shown as harsh (Teru). Views range by church.

frames.aligns: Human sin shown plainly (fratricide, cruelty, selfish wishes); consequences follow; no easy escape from guilt.
frames.concerns: A world governed by spirits, bargains and a book of fate rather than providence; works-based "erasing" of sin.

frames.aligns: Honesty about sin and its weight; love that sacrifices for a brother.
frames.concerns: Spirit contact and wishes (second commandment, Large Catechism); atonement by works. LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Mercy toward the suffering (Kou and Mitsuba); friends bearing one another's burdens; warning against harming others for gain.
frames.concerns: Occult premise; Wesley's rule on diversions that "cannot be used in the name of the Lord Jesus." Holiness churches stricter than UMC.

frames.aligns: Good and evil judged by framing: selfish wishes and cruelty bring ruin; guilt and love are treated seriously.
frames.concerns: Spirit contact and wish-granting normal and sympathetic. Episcopal and ACNA families differ.

frames.aligns: Self-sacrifice, mercy toward enemies, refusal to buy one's life with another's.
frames.concerns: Occult world; violence and exorcism as tools; worldly entertainment. Conservative groups avoid such media; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Family love across death (twins); service; agency and accountability for sin.
frames.concerns: Spirit contact and occult practice avoided by members; ghost romance. Members vary.

frames.aligns: Empathy for the lonely and bullied; questions of who is sacrificed and why; mercy over purity (Kou versus Teru).
frames.concerns: Nene as a frequent damsel; the forced kiss (ch. 105).

frames.aligns: Loyalty and sacrifice; selfish bargains condemned.
frames.concerns: The dead are unconscious until the resurrection, so a ghost of a dead boy as hero, a land of the dead and spirits that bargain run against teaching on the state of the dead and spiritualism.

frames.aligns: Love and loyalty; truthfulness about guilt.
frames.concerns: Spiritism, summoning and wish-granting by the dead are the series' core and shown sympathetically (Galatians 5:19-21 in jw.org counsel).

frames.aligns: Love outlasts fear; Nene's insistence that she never wished for another to die.
frames.concerns: Death, curses and spirits shown as real powers; spiritualism rejected as error.

frames.aligns: Guilt and teshuvah-like longing for atonement; refusal to save one life by taking another.
frames.concerns: Summoning a ghost of the dead and bargaining with him is the premise (Deuteronomy 18:10-11 forbids the ov and yidoni). Many Haredi homes restrict such media.

frames.aligns: Moral weight of killing a brother (an echo of Cain and Abel); refusing to trade lives.
frames.concerns: Necromancy-like premise, though usually treated as fantasy.

frames.aligns: Repair after harm; the value of each life; empathy for outsiders.
Taking a life is grave (Qur'an 5:32); guilt and seeking forgiveness; loyalty.
frames.concerns: Summoning spirits and wish bargains resemble sihr and jinn contact; ghosts of the dead roaming the world differ from teaching on barzakh.

frames.aligns: Karma and consequence: every wish has a price; restless spirits and the passage of the dead; duty (dharma) as atonement for Hanako.
frames.concerns: Tamasic elements (fear, cruelty) some families weigh.

frames.aligns: Attachment binds the dead to the "near shore" (Teru, ch. 10); craving through wishes brings suffering; compassion for spirits (Kou and Mitsuba).
frames.concerns: The first precept is broken by heroes and villains alike; the story offers no clear path of release yet.

frames.aligns: Selfless service; the five vices shown in Tsukasa (anger, ego) and in selfish wishes (greed, attachment).
frames.concerns: The Gurus rejected magic and superstition; wishes and rituals are the plot.

frames.aligns: Unity across difference (humans and spirits), the soul's continued life, service as atonement.
frames.concerns: Spirit contact and occult practice discouraged; frequent fighting.

frames.aligns: Spirits, yorishiro, the boundary between this world and the next, rumors that shape spirits, purification of the restless dead and respect for the Seven Mysteries' territories are all drawn from the Japanese religious world and treated seriously; sincerity (makoto) is rewarded.
frames.concerns: A human sacrifice rite to separate worlds (ch. 60-71) and a "kannagi" sacrifice (Red House) use sacred categories for horror; ANN notes that treating a person as a yorishiro is dehumanizing (S2 ep. 17). Death as kegare is constant.

frames.aligns: Spirits of place, a living boundary between worlds, wishes and charms that work, and a clear ethic that magic used for selfish ends rebounds.
frames.concerns: The forced kiss; a sacrifice imposed on an unconsenting girl.

frames.aligns: The spirit outlives the body; personal responsibility for harm; "Do not murder" (The Way to Happiness).
frames.concerns: Violence; spirit contact framed as folk religion.

frames.aligns: Empathy for the bullied and lonely; a strong, self-accepting heroine (Anime Feminist); the ethics of sacrificing one person for another taken seriously.
frames.concerns: Nene "often has to be saved by her male friends" (Common Sense Media); body-shaming jokes; a forced kiss (ch. 105); possessive romance (Hanako's jealousy); suicide-adjacent scenes (Mitsuba, Kou).

frames.aligns: The value of finite life ("Make the most of what you have now"), responsibility for harm, refusing to trade lives, defying a written fate.
frames.concerns: Spirits and wishes are real in the story (fiction, but worth naming).

frames.aligns: Loyalty, sacrifice, guilt that leads to duty, consequences for selfish wishes; Teru's sense of order.
frames.concerns: Occult premise some religious conservatives avoid; adults largely absent; Nene seems to live alone.

frames.aligns: Worth of every being, including spirits (Kou's mercy); pluralism; justice for the sacrificed.
Defiance of an imposed fate (Amane changes his written future); suspicion of sacrifice demanded by authority (Severance); compassion (Tenet 1).
frames.concerns: Harm to children (Tsukasa's abuse, a four-year-old trapped in the Red House) is condemned in the Eleven Rules, and the story also condemns it.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Revenge is rarely celebrated; Hanako hides guilt rather than defending a name (ch. 27, 57); Kou answers Mitsuba with mercy, not retribution.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The Mysteries keep balance and rules bind spirits to territories, but the heroes break rules to rescue friends from the far shore (ch. 83-97).

Civic vs kin.evidence: The twin bond and friend group come first emotionally, yet the story condemns saving one's own by sacrificing a stranger (Aoi, ch. 71).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Numbered Mysteries with Hanako as leader, an exorcist clan and a court of Clock Keepers (ch. 108-111); the friends themselves are peers.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Folk religion, rites of the dead and inherited vocations are real and powerful; only cruel rites (sacrifice) are questioned.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Self-acceptance ("You're great just the way you are"), Nene's interests and body defended (Anime Feminist), but much of the plot is about survival against death.

folkways.japan: Hanako-san of the toilet and the Seven Mysteries of a school are real Japanese school legends (ANN folklore feature, citing a 1948 collection and 1990s popularity). Yorishiro, exorcist families, the near and far shores of the dead, Tanabata wishes and the gakuran-and-cape student look (the bankara style, per ANN) are Japanese religious and cultural context, not the story's argument.

delivery.evidence: ANN calls it "a creepy old-fashioned fairy tale"; no review opened calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its warnings about wishes, guilt and sacrifice come through ghost-story plots, and the exorcist and coexistence views are both given reasons.

personified.ideology: Mercy and coexistence with spirits
Spirits must be exorcised; living and dead kept apart
Atonement through duty; ends justify means for the one he loves
Wishes and curiosity without limits

entry.dominant: Pagan / occult (Japanese folk religion), Dharmic (Buddhist afterlife imagery), Existentialism (defying a written fate), Classical virtue ethics (loyalty and sacrifice).

series.title: Gantz
series.adult_reason: Gantz: Dark Horse rates it 18+; deep entry scores 10/10 mature content

entry.heading: Gantz
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is found in caring for particular people (a lover, a little brother, a friend) and protecting them, even in a universe that shows no sign of caring back. Selfishness, cruelty and pleasure-seeking are shown as both common and ugly; altruism is shown as rare and costly.

content.framing: Mixed: sexual assault is shown as vile; fan service and casual sex are not framed critically

frames.aligns: Kato's self-giving love for strangers and his brother (John 15:13); the dignity of victims; remorse after killing (Sakurai, ch. 340); critique of bystander indifference (ch. 1).
frames.concerns: The final reveal denies God and the worth of the soul with no answer from faith; fan service and sexual assault drawn for the reader's eye run against Inter Mirifica 7 (evil not made attractive) and CCC 2523-2525 on modesty and permissiveness.

frames.aligns: Struggle with the passions (lust, wrath, despair) is on every page; Kurono's slow change toward love.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis) makes the constant nudity and gore a heavy concern; holy images of the Buddha shown as monsters; a final cosmology without God, where souls are "nothing special."

frames.aligns: Clear moral contrast between Kato and the Osaka team; sacrifice for others.
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 is the common test, and the nudity, sex scenes and profanity fail it for most families; the denial of God goes unanswered. Each congregation is self-governing, so views vary.

frames.aligns: Many distinguish depicting sin from endorsing it: massacres and sexual predators are shown as vile. Hunger for purpose in a "purposeless" world (Hypercritic) can open faith conversations.
frames.concerns: Fan service is presented for enjoyment, not as sin; the story's hope is human love without God (Romans 1 readings). Some families favor separation from such media.

frames.aligns: Courage, sacrifice, clear evil in the massacres.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": a cosmos ruled by indifferent powers, souls treated as data, and graphic sexual content. Holiness standards make it a strong concern. Views vary between churches.

frames.aligns: Total depravity has a strong echo: bystanders, bullies, the Osaka team and Gantz players show sin in raw form. Common grace allows adults to value serious work by non-Christians.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 lists "lascivious... books, pictures" among sins against the seventh commandment; the explicit sex and nudity weigh heavily. Providence is replaced by indifferent beings.

frames.aligns: Law without gospel: no one can save themselves in the game; Kato's free self-giving reads as a picture of neighbor-love.
frames.concerns: No gospel offered; the beings deny God. Entertainment is adiaphora judged by conscience; LCMS and WELS families are much more cautious than ELCA about the explicitness.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy (Kato); social holiness against bullying and abuse.
frames.concerns: Wesley's rule against diversions that cannot be used "in the name of the Lord Jesus"; holiness churches would avoid the sexual content entirely; UMC families are more open.

frames.aligns: A literary tradition that judges dark works by framing; Gantz frames massacre and predation as evil.
frames.concerns: The final cosmology denies God without challenge; the fan service is not framed as wrong. Episcopal and ACNA families would both treat it as adult reading.

frames.aligns: Kato tries to use capture weapons rather than kill (TV Tropes); remorse after killing (ch. 340).
frames.concerns: Violence shown as the way to survive and win is the central concern (Matthew 5:39); Old Order groups avoid such media entirely; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Family care (Kato and Ayumu); love between Kurono and Tae; agency against an arbitrary game.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth asks for media that invites the Spirit; the 18+ rating, nudity and sex put it far outside youth guidance. Souls called worthless clashes with the plan of salvation.

frames.aligns: Critique of bystander apathy, bullying and abuse; empathy for the giants as a people with families.
frames.concerns: Objectification of women and homophobic jokes (WWAC); sexual violence used as plot.

The dead return as copies and souls reincarnate, against teaching on the state of the dead; Fundamental Belief 22 and "by beholding we become changed" (2 Corinthians 3:18) make the explicit content a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: Love of family, protecting the weak.
frames.concerns: jw.org counsel asks whether entertainment features what God hates: violence (Psalm 11:5) and immorality are central here; reincarnating souls conflict with teaching on death.

frames.aligns: Love as what carries Kurono through.
frames.concerns: The story dwells on fear, death, bodily destruction and sensuality and treats matter as all there is until the soul reveal; members guard thought against these ("Stand porter at the door of thought," Science and Health 392).

frames.aligns: Value of saving a life (the opening rescue); memory of the dead; protecting a younger brother.
frames.concerns: Tzniut and nivul peh make the nudity, sex and profanity a heavy concern; many Haredi homes restrict such media entirely. Denial of God unanswered.

frames.aligns: Saving life; critique of bystanders; dignity of victims.
frames.concerns: Degrading sexual content and stereotyped women; denial of God.

frames.aligns: Bystander ethics; tikkun olam echoes in Kato; empathy for the giants.
frames.concerns: Exploitation and objectification of women; sexual violence as spectacle.

frames.aligns: Patience (sabr) under trial; protecting kin; saving life (Qur'an 5:32).
frames.concerns: "Lowering the gaze" (Qur'an 24:30-31) makes the nudity and sex a heavy concern; denial of God; souls treated as data.

frames.aligns: Souls exist and reincarnate (ch. 370), an echo of rebirth; duty to protect family; craving and violence lead to ruin.
frames.concerns: Souls called meaningless with no dharma or moksha; Buddhist statues as monsters. Many families apply the Gita's tamasic category (ch. 17) to the gore and sex.

frames.aligns: Rebirth of souls (ch. 370); suffering and craving as the human condition; impermanence; Kurono's turn from selfishness toward compassion.
frames.concerns: A thousand-armed Buddha figure is a killer alien (ch. 56-91; to verify); killing as the means of release breaks the first precept; mindfulness of what feeds the mind makes the sex and gore heavy.

frames.aligns: The five vices (lust, anger, greed, attachment, ego) are on display in the Osaka team and Nishi and lead to ruin; Kato's courage for others echoes the saint-soldier ideal.
frames.concerns: Lust is shown so often and so explicitly that it reads as appealing; denial of God.

frames.aligns: Service and sacrifice (Kato); the world's peoples facing a common threat.
