frames.concerns: Shoghi Effendi's call to a "chaste and holy life" warns against degrading art; constant conflict; denial of God.

frames.aligns: Yokai-themed aliens in the Osaka arc draw on folklore; sincerity in Kato.
frames.concerns: Blood and death as kegare (impurity) are pervasive; temple statues shown as monsters (a Buddhist site, but often shared ground in Japan). No doctrine on fiction.

frames.aligns: Respect for life and the giants' families; no stereotyped witches.
frames.concerns: The Rede ("harm none") against constant killing; sexual exploitation without consent.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness precepts: "Do not murder," "Safeguard and improve your environment"; massacres condemned.
frames.concerns: Glorified killing in places; no content code for fiction.

frames.aligns: Critique of bystander apathy, bullying, abuse and media spectacle; empathy for the "alien" as a people.
frames.concerns: Objectification of women, sexual assault as plot, homophobic and fat-phobic jokes (WWAC; THEM Anime). Consent and representation make the explicitness a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: Meaning made by people in an indifferent universe (Hypercritic; Grimoire of Horror: "our apparent insignificancy does not diminish our value"); no God needed for love or courage.
frames.concerns: Cruelty and exploitation shown for shock; the reveal also asserts souls exist, which a naturalist would reject.

frames.aligns: Courage, protective masculinity, loyalty, duty to a younger brother; critique of decadence (Osaka team).
frames.concerns: Media that degrades the good, the true and the beautiful; sexual content; contempt for institutions.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of every person, including the giants; justice for abuse victims.
frames.concerns: Objectification and sexual violence; age-appropriateness makes this adult reading.

frames.aligns: Art that challenges authority: Gantz is an arbitrary master, and the beings' God-denial matches Church of Satan non-theism; individuals make their own meaning.
frames.concerns: The Eleven Rules condemn harm to children and unwanted sexual advances, both of which appear (Kato's brother; sexual assaults).

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Revenge and status drive several characters (Sakurai's revenge killings, v10; Nishi's school massacre, vol. 26) but are shown as ugly; Kurono and Kato fight for others, not for face.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Gantz's order is arbitrary and the state is absent (Shinjuku, ch. 119-124); survival is left to individuals and small teams.

Civic vs kin.evidence: The deepest loyalties are particular: Kato and his brother, Kurono and Tae. Kato's rescue of a stranger (ch. 1) is the civic counterweight.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Teams sort by points and experience, but leadership is earned (Kurono) rather than inherited; the Osaka team's self-styled leader is shown as hollow (TV Tropes).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Religion appears as monsters (temple statues) or helpless prayer; the final cosmology is technological and God-denying (ch. 369-370).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival is the whole game; security and staying alive come first, with little room for self-expression.

folkways.japan: Bystander shame in public (the subway scene), school bullying, salaryman and part-time workers among the Osaka team, and yokai folklore in the Osaka arc reflect contemporary Japanese settings more than a message aimed at readers elsewhere. The cluster match is loose (distance above 4 for all clusters), because the story's values are mostly defined by an extreme survival setting.

delivery.evidence: Santos (ANN) says its killing dilemma sends "mixed messages"; a MAL reviewer calls the final arc unsubtle. No review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Most of its themes come through events, but the final arc states its cosmology through a long lecture by the beings behind Gantz.

personified.ideology: Altruism and nonviolence where possible
Meaning found through love and loyalty

personified.character: The beings behind Gantz (Room of Truth)
personified.ideology: Materialism; no God; souls without worth
Cynical self-interest

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Nihilism, Naturalism, Secular humanism, Absurdism.

entry.heading: The Quintessential Quintuplets (Negi Haruba)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is built by honest effort, loyalty to family and the willingness to grow; love means choosing one person for life while keeping faith with everyone else you love.

content.framing: Endorsed (romance, ending in marriage); Neutral (fan-service gags)

frames.aligns: Diligent work and study; family loyalty; forgiveness between sisters; romance resolved in one lifelong marriage (ch. 122).
frames.concerns: Fan service of teens in vol. 1 and innuendo (CCC 2521-2524 on modesty and purity of heart); kisses without consent treated as romantic; deception among sisters (ch. 74). Evil is not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7), but some wrongs go unaddressed (Nino's drugging).

frames.aligns: Humility and growth, love shown in service (Yotsuba), reconciliation in the family.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis) against the early fan service and suggestive gags; romantic competition among sisters.

frames.aligns: Hard work, keeping a promise, one marriage as the goal; sibling loyalty.
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 test on vol. 1 fan service and innuendo; kisses without consent; Nino's drugging played for laughs. Soul liberty leaves the call to families.

frames.aligns: Depicts rather than endorses most wrongs; apology and forgiveness (ch. 86); faithful choice of one spouse.
frames.concerns: Fan service of minors; romantic "conquest" framing of the harem; consent in the festival kisses (ch. 102-108). Engage-or-separate views differ by family.

frames.aligns: Joy, restoration of broken sister relationships, perseverance.
frames.concerns: Holiness standards on modesty; romance as rivalry. No occult content, so the "open door" concern is low.

frames.aligns: Common grace in diligence and family love; vocation (teacher, baker, actress).
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 on "lascivious... pictures" applies to vol. 1 fan service; deception and the sleeping-pill gag.

frames.aligns: Vocation and daily work; Fourth Commandment (honoring parents) tested and partly repaired; marriage ending.
frames.concerns: Sixth Commandment ("sexually pure and decent life") against the fan service and innuendo; confessional (LCMS, WELS) families more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Diligence, mutual help in study, a small community of support.
frames.concerns: Wesley's rule on books that do not "tend to the knowledge or love of God"; holiness churches would avoid the fan service; UMC families vary.

frames.aligns: Judged by framing: growth, apology, sibling loyalty and a faithful marriage.
frames.concerns: Fan service of high school girls and consent in the kisses.

frames.aligns: Family loyalty, humility in Yotsuba, simple work at the end (bakery).
frames.concerns: Separation from worldly media; fan service and romantic display of teens; the franchise's commercial side. MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Education, family, marriage as the goal; developing talents (careers).
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth on entertainment that invites the Spirit; modesty and chastity in thought; kisses without consent.

frames.aligns: Sisters grow into their own careers; class difference bridged; apology and reconciliation.
frames.concerns: Sexualization of minors in early art; girls defined by competition for one boy (Anime Feminist); consent in the kisses.

frames.aligns: Diligence, family, temperance in Futaro's frugal life.
frames.concerns: Fundamental Belief 22 on entertainment "of the highest quality"; "by beholding we become changed" weighs on fan service and romantic obsession.
jw.org counsel against entertainment featuring immorality; dating as recreation rather than with marriage in view; drugging and sensual gags.

frames.aligns: Fear and failure overcome through effort and love; Yotsuba's self-condemnation healed.
frames.concerns: Dwelling on rivalry, jealousy and sensual images as mental influences.

frames.aligns: Torah-like value on learning (study as the plot); kibbud av va'em tested and repaired; marriage as the goal.
frames.concerns: Tzniut: mixed-sex teen intimacy (sleepovers, kisses), fan service; many families would not keep it at home.
Modesty and the sexualization of teens; families apply values case by case.

frames.aligns: Growth, self-chosen careers, repairing family relationships (a form of tikkun).
frames.concerns: Consent in the kisses; girls framed as prizes; informed autonomy leaves it to families.

frames.aligns: Seeking knowledge, honoring family, marriage as the outcome; Futaro's restraint for much of the story.
frames.concerns: Lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) and modest dress; unchaperoned teen intimacy and kisses; fan service; images of the body.

frames.aligns: Vidya (learning) as a path; duty to family (dharma); a single marriage with family blessing.
frames.concerns: Some families apply the Gita's rajasic and tamasic categories to romantic and sensual media; brahmacharya for students.

frames.aligns: Effort, letting go of jealousy, compassion among sisters; Yotsuba lets go of her past self (ch. 108).
frames.concerns: Craving and attachment in romantic rivalry; sensual imagery as feed for the mind.

frames.aligns: Kirat karni (honest work), seva in helping others learn, humility.
frames.concerns: Kaam (lust) and moh (attachment) played for comedy; ego in the rivalry.

frames.aligns: Education, unity of a family, work as worship, marriage.
frames.concerns: The call to a "chaste and holy life" against the fan service and casual kissing.

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto), gratitude, honoring a deceased mother, a respectful Fushimi Inari visit (ch. 80).
Self-discovery, each sister following her own path; "harm none" in reconciliation.
frames.concerns: Consent in the kisses and the drugging gag run against harm none for some families.

frames.aligns: Competence, study and work ethic; communication repairs relationships.
frames.concerns: The Way to Happiness precepts on decency and honesty (disguises, drugging).

frames.aligns: Each sister gets her own career and voice; class difference bridged; the sisters "grow beyond their initial stereotypes" (Popverse).
frames.concerns: Harem framing of girls as interchangeable brides (Anime Feminist); kisses "without the recipient's consent" (CSM film); fan service of minors (ANN's Beckett: "off-putting").

frames.aligns: Meaning from effort, learning and relationships; no supernatural framing.
frames.concerns: Critical thinking about how the genre presents girls and consent.

frames.aligns: Diligence, family loyalty, respect for parents slowly restored, monogamous marriage and a wedding as the goal; Haruba rejected a harem ending.
frames.concerns: Fan service and innuendo in early volumes; casual kissing; deception.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of each sister, each honored in the ending (Haruba: not to "discard the four"); reconciliation.
frames.concerns: Age-appropriateness; consent; girls framed as rivals.

frames.aligns: Self-made success (Futaro), individual choice of career; vital existence.
frames.concerns: Concern for children in the Eleven Rules may apply to fan service of minors; the drugging gag.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Wrongs are settled by apology and talk (Ichika to Miku, ch. 86), not by retaliation; Nino's hostility softens rather than being avenged.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Exams, school rules and a parent's conditions (Maruo's threat to fire Futaro if a sister fails) structure life; the sisters push back but end inside family and school order.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Family first: the sisters transfer schools together for Yotsuba; "the five of us" outranks romance; Futaro works to pay family debt.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Peers are equals across wealth lines; tutor-pupil and parent-child roles matter; Ichika as oldest sister has a mild lead role.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Secular school life; traditional marriage ending; shrine visit and grave visits as custom.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Futaro's struggle out of poverty (survival) beside the sisters' self-chosen careers and open confessions (self-expression).

folkways.japan: Exam-centered school life, the class trip to Kyoto and Fushimi Inari, monthly grave visits, family debt as shared obligation, the stepfamily formalities and the shōnen-magazine harem romance convention are Japanese norms that frame the story rather than form its message.

delivery.evidence: The Guardian's Phil Hoad calls the film "stridently sentimental and moralistic"; most reviewers treat it as genre comfort food.
delivery.note: Its lessons on effort, family and fidelity come through exam arcs and sister conflicts, while the harem framing itself goes unexamined.

personified.ideology: Self-improvement through study and work
Self-sacrifice for others
Winning love by any means
Cold, self-interested fatherhood

entry.dominant: Confucian ethics, Classical virtue ethics, Traditionalism, Communitarianism.

entry.heading: Soul Eater
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life faces fear with courage, trusts its partners, and keeps a "sound soul in a sound mind and a sound body" (the DWMA motto and the last chapter's title). Neither absolute order nor madness is the answer; courage and human bonds are.

frames.aligns: Evil framed as evil and defeated; courage, mercy toward Crona, atonement by self-offering (ch. 112). A Catholic blogger links the DWMA motto to body-soul unity (Mage in a Barrel).
frames.concerns: A death god as moral authority; occult magic and soul-eating as play; objectifying fan service of girls played as humor (CCC 2523-2524 on modesty).

frames.aligns: Struggle with the passions (Book of Eibon's sins, v18); madness as a spiritual sickness to be resisted by watchfulness.
frames.concerns: Death made a sympathetic god; souls eaten for power; clerical imagery on a traitor (Justin, ch. 23, 86); nepsis (guarding the senses) weighs the fan service heavily.

frames.aligns: Clear good and evil; courage and loyalty; sins named and resisted (v18).
frames.concerns: Witchcraft and a death god shown as normal and good (Deuteronomy 18:10-12); a pastor-like figure falls (ch. 86); nudity and groping played for laughs. Families decide under soul liberty.

frames.aligns: Depicts sin without endorsing it in the main plot: madness, cruelty and lust are villains' traits; mercy for Crona.
frames.concerns: The occult as setting; fan service endorsed as humor; grace has no source beyond courage and friendship.

frames.aligns: Fear and madness shown as spiritual attacks to be resisted; courage and unity win.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": witches, magic, soul-eating and a death god are the fabric of the world, shown neutrally or positively; the witch hunt ends in friendship (ch. 113).

frames.aligns: Common grace lets families value craft and courage; sin in the heart pictured as madness.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 lists "lascivious ... books, pictures" (the prologues); a death god reigning as moral order; Justin's "We choose the god who suits us" (ch. 86) as a creed.

frames.aligns: Law and gospel echo: no one saves themselves from madness alone; Crona is rescued by Maka's reaching in (ch. 112).
frames.concerns: Occult setting; fan service. LCMS and WELS families tend to be more cautious than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy toward Crona; resisting the seven deadly sins (v18); holiness of mind and body echoes the motto.
frames.concerns: Fan service runs against Wesley's rule on diversions; holiness churches more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: Judged by framing: madness, cruelty and lust are framed as evil; courage and friendship as good; strong Burton-like imaginative world.
frames.concerns: Fan service of minors played as comedy; the death-god pantheon. ACNA families may weigh the occult more.

frames.aligns: Peace with old enemies (truce with witches, ch. 113); mercy toward Crona.
frames.concerns: Fighting and killing evil humans are the heroes' job; soul-harvest as the path to promotion. Old Order groups avoid such media entirely.

frames.aligns: Courage, loyalty, body and spirit as a unity (the motto); redemption for Crona.
frames.concerns: Nudity and sexualized humor (For the Strength of Youth asks for media that invites the Spirit); death god and witches.

frames.aligns: Ending a long war on witches with a truce (ch. 113); compassion for an abused child (Crona); a female lead.
frames.concerns: Objectifying fan service; Yen Press's male pronouns for a character the author calls of "unknown" sex.

frames.aligns: Courage, friendship, temperance of mind and body.
frames.concerns: The dead are unconscious until the resurrection, so a world of visible, edible souls and a reigning Death conflicts with teaching on the state of the dead; spiritism and magic; fan service.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, courage, peace at the end.
frames.concerns: Spiritism, magic and a death god are central (Galatians 5:19-21); fighting and killing as the heroes' work (Psalm 11:5); sexual humor.

frames.aligns: Fear is the real enemy, and courage dispels it (ch. 112-113), close to the teaching that fear is to be mentally overcome.
frames.concerns: Madness, death and evil shown as powerful realities; fear and gore dwelt upon.

frames.aligns: Courage against fear; mercy; consequences for cruelty.
frames.concerns: Tzniut makes the nudity and fan service a strong concern; a death deity and magic (Deuteronomy 18:10-12); many Haredi homes restrict such media.

frames.aligns: Courage, friendship, ending hatred between peoples (ch. 113).
frames.concerns: Modesty values applied by families to the fan service; magic and death-god imagery.

frames.aligns: Compassion for the abused, reconciliation with a hunted group (ch. 113), a girl as hero.
frames.concerns: Objectification of girls; violence as the main tool.

frames.aligns: Courage against fear, patience, mercy and loyalty; evil framed as evil.
frames.concerns: Lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) makes the fan service a strong concern; magic (sihr) and a death god shown as normal; souls eaten.

frames.aligns: Dharma of duty and partnership; a god of death (comparable in role to Yama) who keeps order; balance of body, mind and soul.
frames.concerns: Tamasic qualities (madness, gore) and crude humor; little mockery of the sacred.

frames.aligns: Fear and craving as the roots of madness (Asura is fear made flesh, ch. 108); the sins of the Book of Eibon as mental poisons; balance.
frames.concerns: Killing as the heroes' path, against the first precept; fan service against mindful consumption.

frames.aligns: The five vices (lust, anger, greed, attachment, ego) are shown in the Book of Eibon and in villains; courage of the saint-soldier.
frames.concerns: Lust played as comedy by the heroes; magic and a death god.

frames.aligns: Unity across old enemies (truce with witches, ch. 113); service; courage.
frames.concerns: Fan service against a "chaste and holy life"; fighting as the solution.

frames.aligns: Shinigami and yokai-like figures are familiar in Japanese culture; sincerity, purity of soul and gratitude echo; no disrespect to shrines or kami.
frames.concerns: Blood and death as impurity pervade; the setting is Western and Halloween-styled rather than Shinto.

frames.aligns: Witches are central and are finally reconciled with, and the witch hunt is declared over (ch. 113); Kim is a sympathetic witch.
frames.concerns: For most of the series witches are villains (Medusa, Arachne), the stereotype the tradition objects to; their souls are hunted to make weapons.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness precepts: help others, be worthy of trust; courage against fear.
frames.concerns: Stein, a mad doctor who dissects and experiments, is a hero; madness is described in quasi-clinical terms.

frames.aligns: A girl as lead by design; ending a witch hunt; empathy for an abused, gender-ambiguous character.
frames.concerns: Fan service of women and girls (Anime Feminist calls it "about power"); groping and peeping as jokes; a sexual-assault threat (ch. 75); English pronouns for Crona differ from the author's "unknown."

frames.aligns: The era of gods ends and people "build their own world" (ch. 113); courage, friendship and reason defeat fear.
frames.concerns: Cruelty played as comedy (Stein's experiments; Medusa's abuse is condemned, though).

frames.aligns: Courage, duty, order, loyalty and a clear fight against chaos.
frames.concerns: Crude humor and fan service; family and fathers shown as weak; ending the witch hunt may read as moral relativism to some.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth even of Crona and of witches; free search for truth (Justin's "we choose the god who suits us," ch. 86, read as a warning); reconciliation.
frames.concerns: Objectification; violence as the main solution.

frames.aligns: Asura's charge that Death sets "normal" and "insane" by his own whim (ch. 108) and the end of a god's reign (ch. 113) echo distrust of absolute authority; individual courage and self-definition (Soul names himself, ch. 84).
frames.concerns: The story still sides with an order-god's academy; harm to a child (Crona) by a parent is condemned.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Black☆Star's boasting and his duels with Mifune (ch. 28-31, 49-52) carry an honor ethic, but the story humbles him; Maka's fights are about protecting others, not her name.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The DWMA's order is the good side, but "absolute order" is exposed as the root of the threat (ch. 108), and Kid's reign opens things up (ch. 113).

Civic vs kin.evidence: The school and partners replace failed families (Medusa and Crona, Spirit and Maka); loyalty extends to a whole academy and finally to former enemies (ch. 113).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Meister and weapon are equal partners, paired across genders; Death and the Death Scythes still form a respected rank.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: A supernatural setting, but the gods' era ends and people "build their own world" (ch. 113).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Eccentric self-expression is celebrated (Kid's symmetry, Black☆Star, Excalibur) within a fight for survival against madness.

folkways.japan: The setting is deliberately Western (Nevada-like desert, Gothic and Halloween styling), so fewer values come from Japanese norms than in most shonen. The shinigami (death god) figure, school-as-family structure and senpai-style deference to teachers do reflect Japanese popular culture; these are context, not the story's message.

delivery.evidence: No review found calls it preachy; a MyAnimeList reviewer calls Medusa "one-dimensional" while praising Stein.
delivery.note: Its message about courage over fear is stated in key lines (ch. 60, 112, 113) but mostly carried by fights and gags.

personified.ideology: Courage overcomes fear
Fear and madness; order is arbitrary
Absolute order
Faith in a god alone

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (courage), Pagan / occult (as setting), Communitarianism, Existentialism, Secular humanism.

entry.heading: Grand Blue Dreaming
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is lived with loyal friends who laugh together, push each other past their comfort zones and share the sea; youth is for fun, and embarrassment fades.

content.framing: Endorsed (played for laughs); occasional comic consequences

frames.aligns: Friendship, loyalty, care for a bullied friend, wonder at creation in the diving scenes.
frames.concerns: Drunkenness, which the Catechism calls sinful (CCC 2290), is made attractive rather than shown as harm (Inter Mirifica 7); nudity and lewd gags against modesty (CCC 2521-2524).

frames.aligns: Friendship and joy; drinking is part of feasts in the tradition.
frames.concerns: Drunkenness and the "passions" shown as harmless; guarding the senses (nepsis) makes the constant nudity a concern.

frames.aligns: Loyalty; standing up for the bullied.
frames.concerns: Many Baptists are teetotal (SBC resolutions); alcohol is shown positively throughout; sexual gags and nudity raise purity concerns.

frames.aligns: Found family; courage to try new things.
frames.concerns: Drunkenness and peer pressure shown as fun, not as sin; lewd humor. Views range from moderation to abstinence.
Many abstain from alcohol (AG position paper); the series celebrates drunkenness; holiness and modesty standards conflict with constant nudity.

frames.aligns: Common grace: comedy and friendship can be enjoyed from non-Christian artists.
frames.concerns: Drunkenness (WLC Q139) and "lascivious... pictures" (WLC Q139) shown as jokes.

frames.aligns: Entertainment is adiaphora; moderate drinking is normal in the tradition.
frames.concerns: Drunkenness is sinful and is the main joke; explicit nudity gags. LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, helping a friend in need (ch. 41-44).
frames.concerns: Historic abstinence (General Rules); holiness churches (Nazarene, Wesleyan) would rate this D. The UMC recommends abstinence as a witness.

frames.aligns: A long tradition of comic literature; friendship and generosity.
frames.concerns: Drunkenness sinful; the comedy rarely frames it as harm.

frames.aligns: Community and loyalty; simple love of the sea.
frames.concerns: Many abstain; drunkenness forbidden; modesty and plain living conflict with the series' core jokes. Conservative groups avoid such media; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Friendship, kindness to Aina, family ties.
frames.concerns: Alcohol is not consumed (Word of Wisdom) and is shown positively throughout; For the Strength of Youth warns against "vulgar, immoral" media.

frames.aligns: Empathy for a bullied classmate; inclusive friend group.
frames.concerns: Coerced drinking and stripping raise consent and harm concerns; addiction risk; sexual embarrassment of women.

frames.aligns: Friendship and enjoyment of nature (the ocean).
frames.concerns: Members abstain from alcohol (Fundamental Belief 22); the health message conflicts with binge drinking as comedy; impure content.
Moderate drinking allowed, but drunkenness is a serious sin and is the series' main joke; immorality in entertainment (Galatians 5:19-21).

frames.aligns: Joy, friendship and the beauty of the sea.
frames.concerns: Members abstain from alcohol (Church Manual); dwelling on intoxication and crude humor.

frames.aligns: Friendship and loyalty; care for family (Nanaka and Chisa).
frames.concerns: Drunkenness discouraged outside ritual; tzniut and nivul peh make the nudity and crude humor a significant concern; many Haredi homes restrict such media.
Excess and pressure to drink; modesty values applied by families.

frames.aligns: Inclusive friendship; standing up to bullying.
frames.concerns: Addiction and coercion concerns; consent in the drinking and stripping gags.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, friendship, helping a friend in need.
frames.concerns: Alcohol is forbidden (Qur'an 5:90) and is the center of the club's life; modesty (haya) and lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) make constant nudity a significant concern. Many families would avoid it.

frames.aligns: Friendship and duty to friends; love of nature.
frames.concerns: Many abstain, especially in devotional traditions; excess and crude humor fit the Gita's tamasic category for some families.

frames.aligns: Friendship, letting go of embarrassment, wonder at the sea.
frames.concerns: The fifth precept (refrain from intoxicants) is broken as the main joke; right speech and what feeds the mind.
Intoxicants forbidden for initiated Sikhs and widely discouraged; lust shown as comic; modesty valued.
Alcohol forbidden; the "chaste and holy life" counsel weighs against crude entertainment.

frames.aligns: Sake at festivals is normal; the sea, festivals and seasonal life; no disrespect to shrines or kami reported.
frames.concerns: Little in doctrine; impurity and excess may be discussed by families.

frames.aligns: Joy, nature and the sea; drinking in moderation is part of some rituals.
Male bodies, not only female ones, are the butt of nudity jokes; a bullied girl is defended.
frames.concerns: Anime Feminist flags coerced drinking, alcohol poisoning played for laughs, sexual harassment, incest jokes and the sexualized humiliation of Chisa; ScreenWise notes refusing a drink is portrayed as failure; glamorized drinking for minors.

frames.aligns: Free, irreverent humor; curiosity and courage; real diving knowledge.
frames.concerns: Harm concern about alcohol poisoning and coercion.

frames.aligns: Male camaraderie, loyalty, courage and protecting a friend.
frames.concerns: Drinking glamorized for young readers; public indecency; profanity; little respect for teachers or elders.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of the outsider (Aina); inclusive friendship.
frames.concerns: Coercion and consent; addiction risk; stereotypes in gay-misunderstanding gags.

frames.aligns: Indulgence, irreverence and freedom from shame fit Church of Satan themes; no harm to children or animals reported.
frames.concerns: "Indulgence, not compulsion": forced drinking conflicts with personal choice; Satanic Temple bodily autonomy (Tenet 3).

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Pranks are answered with revenge pranks and contests (ch. 1-2, 23), but nothing is a matter of real honor; humiliation is shrugged off.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Rules, decency and exams are comic obstacles: public nudity (ch. 1, 78), cheating (side story, v2), the professor tricked into an impact test (ch. 33). Group pressure is the only real order.

Civic vs kin.evidence: The club works as a found family; real family (the Kotegawa sisters, their mother in Palau, ch. 50-57) matters but is not ranked above friends.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Seniors can make juniors drink and strip (ch. 1-2), a senpai-kohai pattern; yet seniors also mentor and are friends.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No religion; festivals are social events; university life is secular.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Fun, self-expression and quality of life come first; work (bartending, ch. 14; part-time jobs, ch. 34) is a backdrop.

folkways.japan: The senpai-kohai pressure to drink, nomikai drinking parties, campus festivals with beauty pageants and the summer-by-the-sea setting reflect Japanese university club culture; the forced drinking shown is a recognized social problem in Japan ("aruhara"), so many Japanese readers will read it as exaggeration of a familiar scene rather than as a model.

delivery.evidence: ScreenWise: refusing a drink is "portrayed as a social failure"; Anime Feminist: humor relies on coercion. No review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its message about friendship and letting loose comes through running gags, not stated lessons; the sober view is held by characters who are often the butt of jokes.

personified.ideology: Hedonism and brotherhood through shared excess
Reluctant conformist who learns to enjoy the group
Restraint and seriousness

entry.dominant: Hedonism, Communitarianism, Expressive individualism.

entry.heading: Record of Ragnarok
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is a defiant one: human beings prove their worth by refusing to bow, fighting to the end for the people they love, and earning respect even from those who would destroy them.

frames.aligns: Human dignity defended against those who would destroy it; Adam as a protective father who bears no hatred (Common Sense Media); courage and self-gift. The gods shown are pagan, not the God of the Church.
frames.concerns: Jesus placed as one "sage" among others and silent (ch. 46): Nostra Aetate's respect for other religions does not extend to presenting Christ as one teacher among equals. Eden retold so that the Fall is the gods' injustice, not human sin (CCC 397-409). Many gods shown as real; demons made sympathetic.

Mocking or trivializing holy things is serious in a tradition that venerates images; Christ shown among other "sages"; demons and Satan as real powers given sympathetic backstories; syncretism is the frame of the whole work. Guarding the senses (nepsis) also weighs the gore and fan service.

Other religions' gods shown as real powers (John 14:6); Jesus reduced to a "sage" (Plugged In); Adam recast from "originator of original sin" into the gods' victim, which reverses the Fall; Beelzebub (VIZ: "also known as Satan") as a tragic figure. Fan service and f-words in the anime.

frames.aligns: Human worth and courage; a story some evangelicals could "engage" as a picture of human pride versus pagan gods.
frames.concerns: Same core concerns as Baptist: Christ demoted to one of the sages, Eden rewritten, demons sympathized with. Many families treat this as a Romans 14 conscience issue.

Media as an "open door": Satan, Beelzebub, Hajun (a Buddhist demon), possession, and many gods shown as spiritually real and powerful; Satan possessing those who love (Round 8). Christ shown as a passive onlooker.

frames.aligns: Common grace allows recognizing skill and the theme of human courage.
frames.concerns: Second commandment (Heidelberg Q96-98): many object to any image of Christ, and here he appears in a fighting manga (ch. 46). Other religions shown as real worship; the Fall reframed against WCF 6.

frames.aligns: Entertainment as adiaphora; courage and love for family; the gods' tyranny as a picture of false gods.
frames.concerns: Christ placed among sages; Eden reframed; other religions treated as true. LCMS and WELS families tend to be stricter than ELCA ones.

frames.aligns: Love for family and humanity; Adam's lack of hatred.
frames.concerns: Wesley's General Rules ask whether reading tends to "the knowledge or love of God"; the irreverent treatment of Christ and the Fall cuts against that. Holiness churches more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: A long literary tradition of retold myth (Lewis); courage and sacrifice.
frames.concerns: Unlike Lewis, the retelling places Christ among sages and rewrites Genesis; judged by framing, this is irreverent rather than reverent. Episcopal and ACNA families may differ.

frames.aligns: Humility in some characters; loyalty to community.
frames.concerns: The entire story is violence as spectacle, framed as noble (Matthew 5:39). Christ, the model of nonresistance, appears cheering at a death match (ch. 46). Conservative groups avoid such media; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Adam is honored in LDS teaching (as Michael), and Eve's choice in Eden is viewed positively; the series also shows both as noble and loving. Family and protection of posterity.
frames.concerns: Christ shown as a passive "sage"; many gods real; graphic violence, fan service and anime profanity against For the Strength of Youth's test of what invites the Spirit.

frames.aligns: Human dignity against arbitrary power; a pluralistic cast; underdog defiance.
frames.concerns: Hindu objections to treating Shiva as entertainment; all-male fighters; fan service; real historical killers recast as heroes.

Fundamental Belief 22's test of what is "of the highest quality"; spirits, demons and Satan shown as characters; souls destroyed after death; Christ among sages; gore and fan service ("by beholding we become changed").

jw.org's questions: does it feature what God hates, especially violence (Psalm 11:5) and spiritism and demons (Galatians 5:19-21)? Here violence is the whole format and demons, Satan and many gods are main characters.
Evil, death and fear shown as overwhelming realities; possession and annihilation of souls; much dwelling on violence.

frames.aligns: Adam, a shared ancestor, shown as a loving father; self-defense of one's people.
frames.concerns: Avodah zarah: many gods shown as real powers; Adam and Eve shown near-nude (tzniut); Eden rewritten; fan service; graphic gore. Many Haredi homes would avoid it altogether.

frames.aligns: Defense of humanity; respect for a worthy opponent.
frames.concerns: Idolatry shown as cosmic reality; Genesis rewritten; Jesus shown as "a Jewish philosopher" (character list) is not itself a concern, but the pantheon is. Families apply modesty values to the fan service.

frames.aligns: Human worth and resistance to tyranny; informed autonomy lets families decide.
frames.concerns: Gore; fan service; other faiths' complaints about how their sacred figures are used. No antisemitic tropes reported.

frames.aligns: Courage, defense of family and the oppressed.
frames.concerns: Shirk is the gravest sin, and the cosmos here is full of many gods as real. Adam and Jesus (Isa) are prophets in Islam, and depicting prophets is widely forbidden; Adam is shown nearly nude and fighting. No Islamic figure appears (character list), but the prophet issue remains. Lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) for the fan service.

frames.aligns: Shiva is shown as powerful and honorable; his Tandava dance and Rudra appear; he praises his opponent ("the best match of my life," fan wiki). Dharma-like respect between warriors.
frames.concerns: Shiva as an entertainment fighter in a blood sport, and as one who backs humanity's extinction (Plugged In); 12 other Hindu deities as a cheering section. Rajan Zed of the Universal Society of Hinduism urged Coamix "not to trivialize Lord Shiva and other highly revered Hindu gods and goddesses" (ANN, 2020) and called the anime "highly inappropriate" (The Quint, 2021); Netflix did not release it in India. Families differ: some Hindu fans enjoy the portrayal (from general knowledge; to verify).

frames.aligns: Buddha turns against the gods out of concern for humans (ch. 43); his "Perfect Enlightenment" and Mahapari Nirvana are named; Zerofuku dies at peace (character list).
frames.concerns: The Buddha fighting, taunting, threatening to kill gods and wielding a weapon that requires hatred (Warscythe of Salakaya, ch. 51) contradicts the first precept and the idea of a Buddha free of defilements. A Thai monk (Thairath, 2023) says the test is whether a work distorts Buddhahood itself, not his appearance. Theravada communities have protested past depictions of the Buddha.

frames.aligns: Defending the oppressed against tyranny; humans facing death fearlessly.
frames.concerns: Many gods shown as real (Sikhism teaches one God); the five vices, especially ego (haumai) and anger, are celebrated in fighters on both sides. No Guru is depicted.

frames.aligns: Unity of humanity; Jesus and Buddha shown as figures humanity reveres.
frames.concerns: Jesus and Buddha are Manifestations of God in Bahá'í teaching, and portraying them as characters, one in combat, is a concern; violence as the plot's engine against Bahá'í non-violence.

frames.aligns: Kami and folk gods are familiar figures in Japanese fiction; Susanoo shown as a great swordsman who slays Orochi (character list); Raiden's sumo, a Shinto-linked art, honored.
frames.concerns: Seven Lucky Gods fused and fought (Round 6); Susanoo loses to a human (Round 10); blood and death bring impurity. No objection from Shinto bodies found.

frames.aligns: Polytheistic cosmos taken seriously as a setting; warrior virtues (Heathenry honors them).
frames.concerns: Norse and Greek gods mostly portrayed as arrogant villains (Zeus, Poseidon, Loki, Odin's plot), which some Heathens and Hellenists see as demonizing their gods.

frames.aligns: Human beings asserting their own ability; The Way to Happiness: help others, safeguard family.
frames.concerns: "Do not murder": killing is the format.

frames.aligns: Resistance to unaccountable power; humanity's worth.
frames.concerns: All-male human roster; exaggerated female bodies and Aphrodite gag (Common Sense Media; TV Tropes); real serial killer recast as a hero; tyrants celebrated; trivializing living faiths' figures (Hindu objection).

frames.aligns: Humanity's worth asserted against arbitrary gods; human genius (Tesla's science, Qin's statecraft) can stand against the divine. Gods read as myth.
frames.concerns: Glorified violence and gore; historical killers glamorized.

frames.aligns: Courage, masculinity, honor, protective fathers (Adam), respect for worthy rivals.
frames.concerns: Irreverence toward religion, including Christ and Genesis; fan service; profanity in the anime.

frames.aligns: Pluralism: many traditions side by side; inherent worth of humans against arbitrary judgment.
frames.concerns: Concern about disrespect toward any faith (Hindu complaint); violence as the solution; all-male fighters.

frames.aligns: Rebellion against tyrannical gods, humanity asserting itself (Brunhilde as a rebel figure); religion shown as a source of arbitrary power.
frames.concerns: Satan portrayed as a malevolent possessing force and ancient plotter, a conventional stereotype both Satanist groups dislike; the story still honors self-sacrifice.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Worth is proved in personal combat; insults and pride drive fights (Poseidon's contempt, Round 3; Buddha's taunts, ch. 46). Respect is earned by fighting, not given by rules.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The heroes defy the gods' order (Brunhilde, Buddha, ch. 43); Buddha "defies Zeus's agreements" (fan wiki). The tournament itself has rules, which are bent.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Fighters represent all of humanity, not a clan; Adam fights as father of all humans (ch. 12). Personal loyalties (Brunhilde's sisters, Siegfried) also matter.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Divine hierarchy is attacked, yet greatness and rank among champions are revered; kings and generals are heroes.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Religious traditions are raw material for spectacle, not guides to life; Tesla's science is a match for gods. The gods are still real in the story.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival of the species is the stake, but fighters' self-expression, style and pride are celebrated (Buddha's T-shirts and lollipops).

folkways.japan: The playful use of gods and buddhas as characters reflects a Japanese pop-culture norm (also seen in works like Saint Young Men) in which sacred figures often appear in fiction; the respect for a worthy rival and the prominence of Japanese fighters (Kojiro, Raiden, Okita) also reflect the source culture more than a message aimed at foreign readers.

delivery.evidence: TV Tropes calls the gods "Jerkass Gods," though Heracles, Buddha and Shiva get nuance; sabukaru sees "no blasphemy or ill-intent." No review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The theme of human worth is stated in speeches and commentary, while the gods' side is mostly arrogance with a few respected exceptions.

personified.ideology: Defiance of divine authority; human worth
Divine right to judge and end humanity
Self-chosen awakening; siding with humanity
Protective love of humanity without hatred

entry.dominant: Secular humanism (as human worth against the gods), Might makes right (as the tournament's format), Classical virtue ethics, Pagan/occult (polytheistic setting), Existentialism.

entry.heading: Gachiakuta
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: Nothing and no one is trash. Things and people that others throw away hold value, and a good life repairs, cherishes and protects them instead of discarding them.

frames.aligns: Dignity of every person and the preferential option for the poor; the wasteful rich are judged; a "throwaway culture" is critiqued, close to Pope Francis's phrase (Laudato Si' 22; my own framing). Abuse is shown as evil (Inter Mirifica 7).
frames.concerns: Revenge as the hero's early aim; souls in objects; coarse language; the abuse arc needs care.

frames.aligns: Mercy to the outcast; repentance and healing of rage; care for creation.
frames.concerns: Anger as a passion the hero feeds on; objects with spirit-like power; nepsis makes the gore and abuse flashback a concern.

frames.aligns: False accusation and injustice are condemned; the poor are defended (Proverbs 31:8-9); abuse is evil.
frames.concerns: Revenge motive; Anima as soul-like power; profanity (Ephesians 4:29). Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Worth of the rejected; echoes of "the stone the builders rejected" (Psalm 118:22; my own framing). Depicts sin without endorsing it.
frames.concerns: Revenge; the spiritual meaning of Anima; language.

frames.aligns: Justice for the oppressed; deliverance from bondage (Amo).
frames.concerns: Objects carrying soul-like power and spirit-like monsters may read as an "open door"; a figure called "the Angel" tied to murder (to verify).

frames.aligns: Common grace lets families value a work that exposes oppression; hereditary guilt is shown as unjust (Ezekiel 18:20).
frames.concerns: Objects with souls; revenge; WLC Q139 concerns on coarse speech.

frames.aligns: Two kingdoms: unjust rulers judged; love of neighbor; vocation in the Cleaners' work.
frames.concerns: Revenge; spirit-like objects. LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Social holiness: defending the poor; works of mercy; Rudo's turn from revenge toward protecting others.
frames.concerns: Profanity and violence; holiness churches more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: Justice and mercy; a dystopia in the tradition of moral fantasy; good and evil judged by framing.
Simple living and repair; solidarity with the poor; suspicion of unjust state power and the death penalty.
frames.concerns: Violence as the heroes' main tool; revenge; conservative groups avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Worth of souls (D&C 18:10); found family; service.
frames.concerns: Coarse language and violence; the abuse arc.

frames.aligns: Structural sin made visible: caste, waste, police injustice, trafficking.
frames.concerns: Creator controversy over a racially insensitive video (2026); revenge.

frames.aligns: Care for creation, stewardship, justice for the poor.
frames.concerns: "By beholding we become changed": frequent violence and coarse speech; objects with spirits; Fundamental Belief 22.

frames.aligns: Love of neighbor; condemnation of injustice and abuse.
frames.concerns: Violence (Psalm 11:5); soul-like power in objects close to spiritism; worldly rebellion against rulers.

frames.aligns: Worth of every person; healing of hatred.
frames.concerns: Fear, waste and evil treated as powerful realities; constant violence.

frames.aligns: Justice for the oppressed and for the stranger; false witness condemned (Exodus 20:13); bal tashchit (do not waste) echoed (my own framing).
frames.concerns: Nivul peh (coarse speech); the abuse arc and violence; many Haredi homes restrict such media.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam; dignity of the stranger and the poor; bal tashchit.
Tikkun olam; anti-discrimination; protection of trafficking victims.
Justice ('adl) for the oppressed; condemnation of waste (Qur'an 17:26-27, israf); orphans protected (Rudo, Amo).
frames.concerns: Revenge; objects with soul-like power; coarse language; the abuse arc and lowering the gaze.

frames.aligns: Critique of hereditary caste stigma echoes reformers; seva; respect for objects in use.
frames.concerns: Constant violence (tamasic for some families); anger as a driving force.

frames.aligns: Compassion for all beings; the cycle of harm (Rudo sees Amo as a fellow victim, ANN); craving and waste.
frames.concerns: Anger and revenge as motive; killing in fights.

frames.aligns: Equality against caste (a core Sikh teaching); defense of the oppressed; honest labor.
frames.concerns: Anger (krodh) as the hero's fuel; violence.

frames.aligns: Oneness of humanity; elimination of prejudice; justice.
frames.concerns: Violence as the main path; anger.

frames.aligns: Respect for objects that serve us, close to tsukumogami belief (my own framing); gratitude; impurity of waste.
frames.concerns: Little to raise in message; blood and filth as impurity.

frames.aligns: Animism-like respect for objects and the earth; "harm none" echoed in protecting the weak.
Way to Happiness precepts: be worthy of trust, do not murder, help others.
Anti-classism, critique of policing and capital punishment, trafficking survivors treated with empathy, Black characters (CSM).
frames.concerns: The creator's 2026 video controversy; a grooming storyline some reviewers felt needed more time (A.V. Club).

frames.aligns: Human dignity apart from birth; critique of hereditary guilt and execution; repair and reason.
Thrift, repair, gratitude to a father figure, hard work, loyalty; justice for the falsely accused.
frames.concerns: Class-war framing; authority shown as mostly corrupt; coarse language.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth and dignity of every person; justice and compassion; the interdependent web.
Rebellion against an unjust authority; justice (Satanic Temple Tenet 2); protection of children.
frames.concerns: The story moves from personal vengeance toward duty to a group; Church of Satan readers may prefer the early Rudo.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Worth is inherent, not set by birth or name (ch. 1 framing), but Rudo's drive to make his accusers "regret calling him filthy" (fan wiki) is an honor-style response the story gradually tempers.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The Sphere's order is unjust and the hero rebels against it; the Cleaners keep discipline and training (Workplace Observation arc, ch. 7-11), so order is not rejected outright.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Blood family failed Rudo; a foster father and a chosen guild replace it. Belonging is by choice and work, not lineage.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Hereditary caste is the central evil (ch. 1); tribesfolk and the rich are shown as equal in worth.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No religion is central, but folk ideas (souls in objects) and tribal heritage and street art (Heritage Mural arc, ch. 82-90) are honored.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival on the Ground is a constant pressure, while graffiti, personal style and cherished objects carry identity.

folkways.japan: The idea that well-used objects gain a spirit (tsukumogami) and the feeling of mottainai (regret over waste) are Japanese folk values the story builds on (my own framing); the hip-hop and graffiti look is a global street-culture influence rather than a Japanese norm.

delivery.evidence: Bleeding Cool: elites "comically, sneeringly evil"; Otaku Orbit: "rich people are bad, poor people are oppressed"; A.V. Club: "persistent undercurrents of class disparity."
delivery.note: The anti-waste and anti-caste message is stated openly through Rudo and Regto, while the wealthy are drawn broadly and the Raiders' violent answer gets more nuance.

personified.ideology: Dignity of the discarded; anger at caste injustice
Hereditary caste and contempt for the poor
Revolution by destroying the Sphere
Care and repair of what others throw away

entry.dominant: Critical theory, Communitarianism, Environmentalism, Secular humanism, Pagan/occult (animism).

entry.heading: The Way of the Househusband
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is a quiet, devoted one: you can leave a violent past behind, and caring for your home and spouse deserves the same skill, pride and seriousness as any job.

frames.aligns: Faithful marriage; turning from violence to service; dignity of domestic work; hospitality to former enemies.
frames.concerns: The gang past is comic rather than repented; profanity (CCC 2142-2155 for God's name). Complementarity readers may discuss the reversed roles.

frames.aligns: Love and humility in marriage; renouncing violence; daily labor as service.
frames.concerns: Traditional family roles commonly taught, so the reversal is a talking point; coarse speech; crime past not framed as sin.

frames.aligns: Faithful marriage; leaving a life of crime; hard work.
frames.concerns: Complementarian teaching (BF&M 2000, Article XVIII: the husband provides) sits uneasily with a wife as breadwinner; profanity (Eph 4:29); no repentance language.

frames.aligns: A clear "old life, new life" story; servant-hearted husband; marriage honored.
frames.concerns: Profanity; some complementarian families will discuss the roles; the crime past is a joke source.

frames.aligns: Transformed life; devotion to his wife; holiness of a peaceful life.
frames.concerns: Profanity and coarse jokes against holiness standards; traditional family roles common in practice.

frames.aligns: Common grace: a non-Christian story showing marital love and vocation in daily work.
frames.concerns: Complementarian churches will note the reversal; profanity (WLC Q113 on misuse of God's name).

frames.aligns: Luther's teaching on vocation: changing diapers and cooking as holy callings; faithful marriage.
frames.concerns: LCMS families may discuss the roles; ELCA less so; profanity.

frames.aligns: Practical holiness; "do no harm" in a man who has stopped harming; egalitarian marriage fits most Methodist bodies.
frames.concerns: Profanity; gang culture used for laughs.

frames.aligns: Comic tradition with a moral core; faithful marriage; humble service.
frames.concerns: Profanity; ACNA families may discuss roles.

frames.aligns: Nonviolence chosen over force; simple, humble domestic service; forgiveness of enemies.
frames.concerns: Conservative groups keep traditional roles and avoid such media; slapstick violence and profanity; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Family and marriage central; repentance-like change; neighborliness.
frames.concerns: The Family Proclamation describes fathers as primarily responsible to provide and mothers for nurture, while allowing "individual adaptation"; For the Strength of Youth warns against vulgar language.

frames.aligns: Egalitarian marriage; masculinity without domination; dignity of care work.
frames.concerns: Police profiling and violence played for laughs; Miku's subversion is limited (Feminism in India).

frames.aligns: Strong family; a peaceful, healthy home; leaving violence behind.
frames.concerns: Profanity, smoking and drinking shown; gang culture as comedy.

frames.aligns: Faithful marriage; turning from violence and crime; peaceful neighborliness.
frames.concerns: Husband as head of household is taught; profanity; crime-world imagery.

frames.aligns: Love and goodness overcoming old fear and violence; harmony in the home.
frames.concerns: Dwelling on violent and coarse imagery.

frames.aligns: Shalom bayit (peace in the home); a man devoted to his wife; teshuvah-like change.
frames.concerns: Distinct roles for men and women in family life; nivul peh (coarse speech); some homes limit such media.

frames.aligns: Shalom bayit; egalitarian marriage; leaving violence.
Egalitarian partnership; care work valued; kindness to strangers.
Mercy and affection in marriage (Qur'an 30:21); leaving wrongdoing; hospitality.
frames.concerns: The husband's duty to provide (nafaqa; Qur'an 4:34) is reversed, which families will discuss; profanity; alcohol and tattoos shown; tawbah not framed.

frames.aligns: Grihastha (householder) duty done with devotion; nonviolence (ahimsa) chosen.
frames.concerns: Rajasic gang imagery used for comedy; profanity.

frames.aligns: Renouncing harm (first precept); mindful attention to ordinary tasks; a critic links it to Zen (CBR).
frames.concerns: Right speech (profanity); drinking and smoking minor.

frames.aligns: Grihasth life, honest work (kirat karni) and service (seva); equality of women and men (Guru Nanak).
Equality of women and men is a core principle; unity in the family; peace over violence.
frames.concerns: Profanity; smoking and drinking (alcohol forbidden) shown briefly.

frames.aligns: Harmony in the community, sincerity (makoto), care for the home; no disrespect to shrines reported.
frames.concerns: Little in doctrine; purity themes and tattoos may be discussed.

frames.aligns: Hearth and home honored; nurture as strength; "harm none."
Leaving harmful acts; industry and helping others (The Way to Happiness).
frames.concerns: Smoking and drinking briefly; violence gags.

frames.aligns: Subverts macho norms (Ready Steady Cut; Feminism in India); values care work; a career wife treated as normal.
frames.concerns: Feminism in India: "deconstructing... gender binaries need not necessarily mean a role reversal"; Doing Sociology: Tatsu's masculinity stays largely intact; police profiling and yakuza culture played lightly.

frames.aligns: Reason over violence; a person can change; humor and kindness.
frames.concerns: Little; some may question making organized crime lovable.

frames.aligns: Fidelity, duty, hard work, frugality, respect for in-laws and neighbors; a strong, protective man.
frames.concerns: The breadwinner role is reversed; profanity; organized crime made lovable. Some traditionalists may read it as admiring manly virtue applied to the home.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of every person, including an ex-criminal; equal partnership; neighbors who judge him are proved wrong.
Self-determination: Tatsu chooses his life and ignores others' opinions; "responsibility to the responsible."
frames.concerns: Little; Church of Satan texts value personal choice over conformity, which fits.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Old honor codes are mocked: the yubitsume attempt is stopped by Miku (chapter to verify); challenges to fight are answered with cooking duels. Some face-saving rivalry remains.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Tatsu keeps neighborhood rules, sorts garbage and collects dues (ch. 58); police suspicion is mocked but law is not.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Marriage comes first, but neighbors, the housewives' circle (ch. 16, 34) and the neighborhood association are warmly shown.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: An equal marriage with reversed roles; old aniki-underling deference continues with Masa.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Secular daily life; folktale and Halloween chapters (ch. 33, 39); traditional domestic arts valued.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Frugality and hard work at home, alongside Miku's hobbies and Tatsu's indifference to others' opinions.

folkways.japan: The yakuza clichés (aniki loyalty, yubitsume, full-body tattoos), the stigma of tattoos, the full-time housewife as a social role, neighborhood associations (chōnaikai) and bargain-sale culture are Japanese norms the comedy plays against, rather than the story's own message.

delivery.evidence: Feminism in India says fears it would be "too preachy" do not hold up; reviewers praise deadpan gags, not lessons.
delivery.note: Its message about peace and the dignity of housework comes through repeated gag contrasts; the opposing view (that Tatsu must return to crime) is held by sympathetic foils who are always shown wrong.

personified.ideology: Peaceful domestic devotion; masculine intensity redirected to care
Yakuza loyalty; the boss belongs in the gang
Career woman with a supportive househusband
Judging a man by his past and looks

entry.dominant: Communitarianism, Classical virtue ethics, Progressivism (gender roles), Traditionalism (marriage and domestic craft).

entry.heading: Claymore
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life holds onto its humanity under pressure. You stay loyal to comrades and to the dead, refuse to be used as someone else's weapon, and choose solidarity with other outcasts over power or revenge.

content.framing: Mixed: some shown as threat or horror, some fan service

frames.aligns: Evil (the Organization's use of women as weapons) is exposed and judged; dignity of the exploited; self-giving love among comrades; a priest who overcomes prejudice and a city that shelters outcasts; nuns caring for orphans (sc. 74).
frames.concerns: The black card normalizes mercy killing on request, read against CCC 2277 on euthanasia and 2280-2283 on suicide; revenge as Clare's motive (rejected in CCC 2302); uncensored nudity and sexual threat (CCC 2521-2524).

frames.aligns: The passions shown as monstrous: hunger and pride (Priscilla, Isley) consume the self; watchfulness over one's inner state as the warriors fight awakening.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis) makes the constant body horror and nudity a serious concern; mercy killing; a dead warrior's spirit dwelling in another's body (finale).

frames.aligns: Clear evil exposed; protecting the weak; loyalty and truth against a lying authority.
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 test for the gore and nudity; mercy killing; a fictional polytheistic church (goddess statues) shown as a place of refuge. Each congregation and family decides (soul liberty).

frames.aligns: Beneath the Tangles reads Teresa as a John the Baptist figure who "prepares the way" for Clare and notes "spiritual themes abound"; sin is depicted, not endorsed; the exploiters fall.
frames.concerns: Graphic violence and nudity; mercy killing; a reviewer in this tradition calls it "certainly not for everyone."

frames.aligns: Good and evil are clear; courage and sacrifice.
frames.concerns: The heroines are called "witches" and carry demon flesh, even though Yoma are parasites, not spirits; a spirit of the dead speaking in the finale; media as an "open door" makes the monstrous imagery weigh more. Views vary by church.

frames.aligns: Total depravity has an echo: the monsters are made by human institutions and human hunger. Common grace lets adults value serious art by non-Christians.
frames.concerns: Mercy killing and suicidal sacrifice (WLC Q136); nudity (WLC Q139); a fictional false religion shown sympathetically.

frames.aligns: Two kingdoms: the Organization is a corrupt power that bears the sword for itself; the warriors protect neighbors. Law without gospel: no one is saved by her own strength.
frames.concerns: Mercy killing; nudity and gore (sixth commandment). LCMS and WELS families tend to be more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy and social holiness: care for orphans (Galatea in Rabona), protecting villagers who scorn their protectors.
frames.concerns: Wesley's General Rules on diversions; graphic content; mercy killing. Holiness churches more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: Just cause against a lying power (Article 37 context); a dark fantasy judged by how it frames good and evil, in a tradition that values fantasy (Lewis).
frames.concerns: Mercy killing; nudity; revenge as motive. Episcopal and ACNA families differ mainly on gender, which the series also raises.

frames.aligns: Solidarity among outcasts; mercy to enemies (Clare toward Ophelia).
frames.concerns: Violence is the heroines' calling and only solution (Matthew 5:39); revenge as motive. Conservative groups avoid such media; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Agency against an institution that controls; loyalty, sacrifice and service; reunion with a lost loved one (Teresa, finale).
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth asks for uplifting media; youth guidance warns against the "violent"; nudity; mercy killing. Members vary in strictness.

frames.aligns: Critique of an institution that exploits women and hides the truth; a church that repents of excluding outsiders; care for the vulnerable.
frames.concerns: Anime Feminist's critique that the series fetishizes women's trauma; queer-coded villains; glorified violence.

frames.aligns: Self-sacrifice, truth against deception, care for orphans.
frames.concerns: Teresa's spirit speaking within Clare (finale) conflicts with teaching that the dead are unconscious until the resurrection; "by beholding we become changed" applied to the gore.

frames.aligns: Loyalty and protection; a deceptive power exposed.
frames.concerns: jw.org's question: does it feature what God hates, especially violence (Psalm 11:5)? Here violence is constant; warriors called "witches"; a spirit of the dead speaks.

frames.aligns: Love and loyalty outlast a material power; the warriors keep their true selves.
frames.concerns: Evil, disease-like transformation and fear are shown as real and overwhelming, against the teaching that they are unreal.

frames.aligns: Protection of life; exposure of a deceiving power; memory of the dead (Teresa).
frames.concerns: Tzniut makes the uncensored nudity a significant concern; mercy killing and suicidal sacrifice against the duty to preserve life; revenge (Leviticus 19:18). Many Haredi homes avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Exposure of human experimentation; dignity of the exploited; self-defense against monsters.
frames.concerns: Mercy killing; nudity applied by family modesty values; revenge.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam: freeing the exploited and protecting the vulnerable; critique of a secret, lying power.
frames.concerns: Glorified violence; how women's suffering is shown (Anime Feminist).

frames.aligns: Fighting to stop oppression; patience (sabr) in trials; mercy and forgiveness (Clare and Ophelia).
frames.concerns: Lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) for the uncensored nudity; mercy killing and self-sacrifice against the prohibition of suicide (Qur'an 4:29); goddess statues incidental; revenge.

frames.aligns: Warrior duty (dharma) to protect; craving and rage as the road to monstrousness; loyalty to a teacher (Teresa).
frames.concerns: Revenge as motive; some apply the Gita's tamasic category to the gore.

frames.aligns: Craving (hunger, power) turns people into monsters; compassion for enemies; impermanence.
frames.concerns: Killing as the plot's solution (first precept); revenge as Clare's drive.

frames.aligns: Defending the oppressed (saint-soldier ideal); the five vices (anger, greed, ego) shown in villains as destructive.
Unity of people despite difference (Yagi's stated vision); equality of women and men in strength; service.
frames.concerns: Strong commitment to non-violence; constant combat; nudity against a "chaste and holy life."

frames.aligns: Sincerity and loyalty; purity of heart kept in a body made impure.
frames.concerns: No kami or shrines; blood and death bring impurity (kegare) throughout.

frames.aligns: Feared "Silver-eyed Witches" are the heroes; the MAL feature reads this as a reversal of medieval witch persecution; a church that bans "unnatural" things learns to welcome them.
frames.concerns: "Harm none" and the constant violence; exploitation of women's bodies.

frames.aligns: Exposure of experimentation on people and of a hidden controlling power; "do not harm a person of good will" (The Way to Happiness).
Critique of an institution that uses women's bodies as weapons; women at the center of the action; prejudice overcome (Rabona).
frames.concerns: Anime Feminist argues the series "reproduces exploitation": fetishized trauma, nudity, infantilized women (Priscilla, Miata), queer-coded villains; the "awakening as climax" premise.

frames.aligns: Human bonds and choice over a monstrous body; truth and inquiry (Miria) against a lying authority; the Yoma have a natural, not supernatural, cause.
frames.concerns: Cruelty and exploitation shown at length; mercy killing needs a mental-health conversation.

frames.aligns: Courage, loyalty, sacrifice and honor among comrades; a faith community as refuge; distrust of an unaccountable secret power.
frames.concerns: Gore and nudity; little place for family life; some conservatives may find the gender framing at odds with traditional roles.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of the exploited and feared; justice against a secret power; a community that welcomes those it once excluded.
frames.concerns: Glorified violence; how women's suffering is framed (Anime Feminist).

frames.aligns: Art that challenges authority: women made into tools rebel against a hidden power and win; self-determination over obedience. The Satanic Temple's compassion and justice tenets fit the warriors' mutual care.
frames.concerns: Harm to children (orphans made into weapons, Priscilla's childhood) is shown as evil, as the Eleven Rules also hold; a sympathetic church.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Personal vendetta drives Clare and Ophelia, and Ophelia's ends in ruin (sc. 39-40). The story moves from revenge toward protecting others; warriors' pride in rank is real but not the final value.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The Organization's rules, numbers and executions are the enemy; deserters and rebels are the heroes (v15-v23). The freed warriors choose their own paths at the end.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Blood kin are mostly dead; loyalty goes to a chosen band of comrades (the Ghosts) and to promises to the dead (Teresa), more than to the whole community. Rabona shows a wider civic duty.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: The rank system (1 to 47) is the Organization's tool; the weakest warrior becomes the hero; Miria leads by trust, not rank.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Monsters have a man-made, natural cause; truth comes by investigation (Miria). A fictional faith is treated with respect and its holy city becomes a refuge, but faith does not solve the plot.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival, endurance and protecting comrades come first in a world of constant threat.

folkways.japan: The setting is a European-style fantasy (a Chartres-like cathedral, a Scottish sword name, Catholic-sounding names, per the MAL feature). Group loyalty, endurance and quiet self-sacrifice (Teresa's "faint smile") reflect values common in Japanese shonen storytelling; the medieval Christian look is borrowed scenery rather than a message about Christianity.

delivery.evidence: ANN (Martin): "ultimately more a human story than anything else." No review in the entry calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its themes of humanity and institutional exploitation emerge through plot reveals and characters' choices rather than speeches.

personified.ideology: Loyalty and humanity kept despite a monstrous body
People as weapons; ends justify means
Faith community moving from exclusion to hospitality
Power without restraint, born of trauma

entry.dominant: Communitarianism, Existentialism, Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued), Transhumanism (critiqued), Feminism (explored).

entry.heading: Blood on the Tracks
entry.label: From summaries

frames.aligns: Evil is not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7): the abuse is shown from the victim's side as terror. Parents' duty to respect the child as a person (CCC 2221-2224). The son's late care for his mother echoes honoring parents even when they failed (CCC 2218).
frames.concerns: No hope of grace named; a killing and a suicide plan (CCC 2280-2283); incestuous undertones and a sexual scene with minors (CCC 2521-2524).

frames.aligns: A clear picture of how a passion (possessive love) grows and devours. The son's final care has a cross-bearing quality.
frames.concerns: No spiritual remedy; long exposure to dread, despair and sexual undertones runs against nepsis (guarding the senses).

frames.aligns: Sin's consequences shown honestly; the cover-up does not hold (vol. 9).
frames.concerns: No gospel hope; under Philippians 4:8 the abuse, killing, suicide plan and sexual content are a heavy concern. Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: A realistic fallen family in which hidden sin is exposed; many in this tradition distinguish depicting abuse from endorsing it.
frames.concerns: No redemption in Christ; despair and emptiness are long and unanswered. Sexual content with minors and incestuous undertones are a heavy concern even for families who engage culture.

frames.aligns: No occult or demonic content; a vivid picture of bondage.
frames.concerns: Oppressive atmosphere with no deliverance offered; holiness standards weigh the sexual undertones heavily.

frames.aligns: Depravity even in the most "loving" mother; the fifth commandment's duties run both ways (WLC Q129-130 on superiors' duties). Common grace lets adults value serious art.
frames.concerns: No grace named; Seiichi's killing and suicide plan (WLC Q136); sexual imagery (WLC Q139).

frames.aligns: The fourth commandment shown broken from the parent's side; the law's weight on Seiichi's conscience is crushing.
frames.concerns: No gospel word; conscience decides, with LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Mercy shown late (taking his mother in); harm named as harm.
frames.concerns: Holiness churches would weigh the dread, killing and sexual undertones heavily; the UMC less so.

frames.aligns: Serious literary treatment of sin, guilt and the duties of family, judged by framing.
frames.concerns: Despair long unanswered; content with minors. Practice ranges widely.

frames.aligns: The cost of a family cut off from community; no violence made heroic.
frames.concerns: Separation from worldly media makes the psychological horror a heavy concern; Old Order groups would avoid it, MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Family relationships treated as eternally weighty; harm within the family shown as grave.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth asks for media that invites the Spirit; abuse, a killing, a suicide plan and sexual undertones put it outside youth guidance.

frames.aligns: A careful portrayal of child abuse from the victim's view; the mother's own unloved childhood; attention to mental health and the vulnerable.
frames.concerns: Suicide planning against safe-messaging norms; sexual content between minors. Significant for younger readers.

frames.aligns: Harm in the home shown as ruinous; the late care has a healing note.
frames.concerns: Fundamental Belief 22 and "by beholding we become changed" make the sustained dread and despair a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: Violence and immorality are shown as harmful.
frames.concerns: Violence (Psalm 11:5) and sexual content; no hope of God's Kingdom.

frames.aligns: A son who stops seeing himself only through his mother's fear.
frames.concerns: Fear, madness and despair dwelt on at length; members guard thought ("Stand porter at the door of thought," Science and Health 392).

frames.aligns: Kibbud av va-em (honoring parents) is tested to its limit; the son's care at the end echoes it, while halakhic sources also limit a child's duties toward a harmful parent (from general knowledge; to verify). Choosing life when the police call comes.
frames.concerns: Tzniut makes the incestuous undertones and sexual scene a heavy concern; many Haredi homes avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Honor of parents and the dignity of the child; teshuvah has only a partial echo.
frames.concerns: Sexual content involving minors; long despair.

frames.aligns: Honest about abuse and mental health; attention to the vulnerable.
frames.concerns: Suicide planning and sexual content with minors; Significant for younger readers.

frames.aligns: Harm and injustice in the family are exposed; the son's care for his aging mother echoes kindness to parents in old age (Qur'an 17:23-24).
frames.concerns: Suicide is forbidden and despair of mercy (Qur'an 39:53) is voiced without a faith answer; modesty (haya) makes the sexual undertones a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: Karma-like "tracks" passing from one generation to the next; the late turn to duty toward a parent.
frames.concerns: Tamasic content under Gita 17; views vary by community.

frames.aligns: Close to teaching on craving and attachment: Seiko's clinging destroys what she clings to; Seiichi's self proves "fragile and easy to shatter" (Oshimi, AniFem); release comes from seeing and letting go.
frames.concerns: Right mindfulness of what feeds the mind makes the sustained dread and the killing a depiction concern, Significant for younger readers.

frames.aligns: Attachment (moh) and anger shown as destructive; the late acceptance echoes hukam.
Family unity valued, and its breakdown shown as tragic; suicide shown as a path not taken.
frames.concerns: Shoghi Effendi's call to a "chaste and holy life" makes the sexual undertones a concern; despair long unanswered.

frames.aligns: Ancestral and family bonds taken with full seriousness; the hill and the mountain as places of memory.
frames.concerns: Death and impurity (kegare) are pervasive; no shrine or kami involved.

frames.aligns: Harm shown as harm (the Rede); personal responsibility and the wheel of life to death.
frames.concerns: Little hope language; harm to a child.

frames.aligns: "Honor and help your parents" tested and finally lived out; survival chosen over self-destruction.
frames.concerns: Seiko's condition is framed as psychiatric (Wikipedia), which runs against the church's stance on psychiatry. No content code for fiction.

frames.aligns: Takes child abuse, intergenerational trauma and mental health seriously and from the victim's side; refuses easy monsters.
frames.concerns: Incestuous undertones and a sexual scene between 14-year-olds; suicide planning shown at length, which safe-messaging guidelines advise care with.

frames.aligns: This-life focus; understanding causes (the mother's own unloved childhood) rather than blame; a self rebuilt without supernatural help.
frames.concerns: Cruelty and the suicide plan are a depiction concern, Significant for minors.

frames.aligns: A sober picture of what happens when a family turns inward without support; the son's duty to care for his mother is honored at the end.
frames.concerns: Respect for parents is tested by a portrait of a parent as abuser; despair and the good, the true and the beautiful often degraded on the page.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of the child and of the broken mother; honest search for meaning in suffering.
frames.concerns: Age-appropriateness makes it older-teen or adult reading.

frames.aligns: Self-ownership against a smothering authority ("I Belong to Me," ch. 75); harm to children condemned in the Eleven Rules, as the story condemns it.
frames.concerns: The son's ritual killing of a third party; the late return to filial care is less in line with self-determination.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Seiichi's violence (vol. 12) is not celebrated; outside institutions (police, court) handle the harm.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The story values the child's freedom from the mother's control ("I Belong to Me," ch. 75) without praising lawlessness.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Kin closeness is shown as suffocating (vols. 1-9), yet the ending honors care for one's mother (vol. 17).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: No parent or elder is held up for deference; parental authority is the problem.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No faith or custom guides anyone; understanding comes through memory and psychology.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Becoming one's own person is the central need, tempered by the plain survival of the adult arc.

folkways.japan: The absent salaryman father, the mother alone in the home, tension with in-laws, keeping family trouble hidden, and the late duty of a child to care for an aging parent reflect Japanese family norms of the 1990s and the current public debate about "toxic parents" (毒親); the story examines these norms rather than endorsing them.

delivery.evidence: The Beat says it avoids demonizing, treating mother and son as products of a failing family; Oshimi avoided "an obvious monster parent."
delivery.note: The series shows the abuse entirely through the son's perception and lets consequences and the mother's revealed past, not statements, carry its judgments.

personified.ideology: Possessive maternal love as control
Conflict-avoidant family normalcy
Escape through outside love and honesty
Self-ownership against enmeshment

entry.dominant: Existentialism (the self that must be claimed), a Dharmic echo of attachment and inherited harm, and Confucian filial duty explored under strain; Nihilism voiced in the adult arc and moved past.

entry.heading: Bloom Into You
entry.label: From summaries
