entry.life_message: A good life is lived as your true self, not as the person others expect, and real love lets the other person change and grow rather than freezing them in place.

frames.aligns: Truthfulness and refusing to live a lie; healing from grief; respect for each person; kindness in rejection (Sayaka).
frames.concerns: The central romance is same-sex and is presented as the good life, culminating in premarital sex (ch. 44), against CCC 2357-2359 and chastity teaching (CCC 2337-2359). The Catechism also calls for respect and sensitivity toward persons (CCC 2358).

frames.aligns: Humility and honesty about the self; grief and memory of the dead (Mio); repentance-like change in Touko (ch. 34-35).
frames.concerns: Traditional teaching on marriage and sexuality; romance and physical intimacy offered as the story's goal. Guarding the senses (nepsis) weighs on the kissing and ch. 44.
Same-sex romance affirmed as the central good (BF&M 2000, Article XVIII; usually a significant concern); premarital sex (ch. 44). Views vary by congregation under soul liberty.

frames.aligns: Being honest about who you are; patience; care for a hurting friend.
frames.concerns: Most churches hold traditional sexual ethics, against the affirmed romance and ch. 44; some affirming congregations would read it differently. Beneath the Tangles writers differ: one argues Christians need not avoid yuri as a category and should judge by personal temptation; another, writing from personal experience of same-sex attraction, recommends Bloom Into You for empathy yet stopped watching the genre.

frames.aligns: No occult or spiritual-warfare content, so the "open door" concern is absent. Honesty and growth.
frames.concerns: Traditional teaching on sexuality (AG position papers) against the affirmed romance and ch. 44; holiness and modesty standards.

frames.aligns: Common grace: well-made art by non-Christians may be valued; honest depiction of grief and self-deception.
frames.concerns: Conservative churches (PCA, OPC) hold traditional teaching on marriage; PC(USA) is affirming. WLC Q139 lists lascivious books and pictures among sins against the seventh commandment, relevant to ch. 44.

frames.aligns: Entertainment as adiaphora, judged by love and conscience; honesty; "put the best construction on everything" in how the friends treat each other.
frames.concerns: LCMS and WELS hold traditional teaching on marriage and chastity; ELCA is affirming.

frames.aligns: Love that seeks the other's good; honesty; care for the lonely.
frames.concerns: UMC affirming since 2024; Global Methodist, Wesleyan and Nazarene traditional on sexuality and chastity.

frames.aligns: A literary tradition that judges works by moral vision; honesty, grief and growth.
frames.concerns: The Episcopal Church allows same-sex marriage; ACNA holds traditional teaching. Premarital sex is a concern across the range.

frames.aligns: No violence; humility, honesty, community work (the play).
frames.concerns: Conservative groups hold traditional teaching on marriage and avoid most popular media; romance and intimacy as the story's goal. MC USA families vary and some are moving toward affirming.

frames.aligns: Honesty (Article of Faith 13); kindness; developing talents (acting).
frames.concerns: Traditional teaching ("The Family: A Proclamation to the World") and the law of chastity against the affirmed romance and ch. 44.

frames.aligns: Affirms same-sex love and a lasting relationship; an adult queer couple as role models; honesty and dignity.
frames.concerns: Touko's kisses without asking (Bauman's "predatory lesbian" critique); teens isolated from adult support (Friedman).
Marriage between one man and one woman (General Conference statements); same-sex romance usually a significant concern; premarital sex (ch. 44).

frames.aligns: No violence or spiritism; honesty and loyalty.
frames.concerns: jw.org counsel against entertainment featuring immorality (Galatians 5:19-21); homosexual acts considered sinful; premarital sex framed positively.

frames.aligns: Thought shapes experience: Touko's freedom from a false self-image; love over fear.
frames.concerns: Purity and marriage valued; premarital sex (ch. 44). Less public teaching on same-sex relationships (to verify).

frames.aligns: Memory of the dead; honesty ("keep far from falsehood," Exodus 23:7); kind speech in rejection.
frames.concerns: Same-sex acts forbidden (Leviticus 18:22); tzniut and the kissing and ch. 44; many Haredi homes restrict such media.

frames.aligns: Dignity of each person (CJLS 2006 permitted same-sex commitment ceremonies; views vary by congregation); honesty; grief processed in community.
frames.concerns: Teen sexual activity (ch. 44); modesty values applied by families.

frames.aligns: LGBTQ inclusion; informed autonomy; honesty and dignity.
frames.concerns: Consent in Touko's kisses; teen sexual activity worth discussing.

frames.aligns: Truthfulness, patience (sabr), loyalty to friends, kindness in refusing someone.
frames.concerns: Traditional teaching on sexuality; same-sex romance and premarital intimacy (ch. 44) as the central good; lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) applies to the kissing.

frames.aligns: Svadharma: living one's own nature rather than another's (Bhagavad Gita 3.35 echoes Touko's arc); duty to family memory; art (theatre) evoking rasa.
frames.concerns: Views on same-sex relationships vary, with traditional views common; teen sexual activity.

frames.aligns: Letting go of a fixed self (Touko's mask); impermanence and grief; compassion in rejection; right speech in honest confession.
frames.concerns: Third precept (avoid harmful sexual conduct): many traditions accept same-sex relationships, views vary by teacher and culture; attachment as a theme.

frames.aligns: Truthful living; equality and dignity; the vice of ego (haumai) behind Touko's facade.
frames.concerns: Sex within marriage; Akal Takht opposed same-sex marriage (2005), though diaspora views vary.

frames.aligns: Rejection of prejudice; honesty; independent search for truth; unity among friends.
frames.concerns: Teaching reserves sexual relations for marriage between a man and a woman; a "chaste and holy life" (Shoghi Effendi).

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) as the story's core value: Touko gives up a false face; respect for the dead (Mio's grave).
frames.concerns: Little to raise; no doctrine on same-sex relationships (practice varies, to verify).

frames.aligns: Love and sexuality as positive between consenting partners; largely LGBTQ-affirming; becoming one's true self.
frames.concerns: Consent in Touko's early kisses ("harm none").
Little in the message; The Way to Happiness asks faithfulness to one's sexual partner, which the couple shows.

frames.aligns: Positive, lasting same-sex romance; adult queer couple; a character who never feels attraction treated with respect (Maki); critique of conformity.
frames.concerns: Touko's kisses without permission (Bauman, ANN; Friedman, Okazu); aro/ace readers may feel Yuu's arc closed that reading (Kaiser, Anime Feminist); teen sexual activity and age-appropriateness.

frames.aligns: Meaning made through honest relationships; identity chosen rather than imposed; no supernatural claims.
frames.concerns: Consent and the lack of adult support (Friedman).

frames.aligns: Duty to a shared project, respect for senpai and teachers, perseverance, loyalty.
frames.concerns: Same-sex romance presented to teen readers as the ideal, a concern for many when presented to children; premarital teen sex (ch. 44); relationship kept from parents.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth and dignity; welcoming LGBTQ people; free search for truth and meaning.
Individualism and self-determination; rejection of imposed identity; bodily autonomy (Satanic Temple Tenet 3); LGBTQ-affirming.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Conflicts are settled by honest talk; no one defends their name. Rejection is handled with grace (Sayaka, ch. 38) and the "perfect senpai" image is something Touko learns to drop (ch. 34-35).

Order vs freedom.evidence: School rules and the council are respected, but the story celebrates personal choice over expectation (Touko's freedom from Mio's role; Yuu's own pace in love).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Friends and the council matter as much as family; Yuu confides in her sister Rei (ch. 33) but not her parents; Touko's arc loosens her family's hold on her identity.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Senpai-kohai roles frame the cast, but the story undoes Touko's senpai pedestal and makes the couple equals.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No religious frame; inherited scripts of romance (shoujo manga) and family roles are questioned. The revived play tradition is honored as a shared project, not as custom.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Self-expression, tolerance and being oneself are the highest goods; the epilogue has Touko still acting by her own choice (ch. 45).

folkways.japan: The senpai-kohai structure, the student council, keeping up appearances (tatemae versus honne) and the "Class S" school-girl romance tradition are Japanese settings and genre conventions; the story's own message pushes against appearances in favor of honesty.

delivery.evidence: Friedman calls it "intriguing, rather than entertaining"; Bauman calls it "not as original as we like to think." No reviewer found calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Views on masks, romance and its absence get fair voices, but no character in the main manga voices a traditional objection to same-sex love.

personified.ideology: Becoming who others expect
Authentic feeling over scripted romance
A life without romantic attraction
Lasting same-sex partnership

entry.dominant: Expressive individualism, Existentialism, Progressivism, Secular humanism.

entry.heading: BLAME!
entry.label: From summaries

frames.aligns: Evil is not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7); human life is treated as worth saving; mercy and self-giving for the next generation.
frames.concerns: The self as transferable data, against the unity of body and soul (CCC 362-365); a child engineered from two women's genes, read against Church teaching on reproductive technology (Donum Vitae; from general knowledge; to verify); the mercy killing (Log 36), read against CCC 2277.

frames.aligns: Endurance through a fallen, disordered world; hope carried by a child.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis) makes the constant body horror itself a concern; the self reduced to data clashes with the tradition's view of the body as part of the person who will be raised.

frames.aligns: Good and evil distinct; perseverance; protecting the helpless.
frames.concerns: No God in the story's world; mind-uploading; the gore under Philippians 4:8. Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Depicts a broken world without endorsing its cruelty; hope in a new life.
frames.concerns: Secular, godless setting; self as data; gore.

frames.aligns: No occult or demonic content reported; clear threat from a hostile power.
frames.concerns: Grotesque imagery as an "open door" concern for some families; a cult's role in the catastrophe; the godless setting.

frames.aligns: Common grace allows valuing serious art by non-Christians; a world wrecked by human folly (the Order's retrovirus) echoes the fall.
frames.concerns: Human remaking of human nature (cloning, gene engineering, uploads); gore.

frames.aligns: Vocation and endurance; a broken order (Safeguard) that no longer serves its neighbor.
frames.concerns: Godless setting; self as data. LCMS and WELS families tend to be more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Mercy and protection of the vulnerable.
frames.concerns: Diversions that do not "tend to the knowledge or love of God" (General Rules); gore. Holiness churches more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: Judged by framing, in a tradition open to dark imaginative fiction.
frames.concerns: Self as data; reproductive engineering; gore.

frames.aligns: Care for a child and the vulnerable; humility of a silent hero.
frames.concerns: Violence is Killy's only tool from start to finish (Matthew 5:39); separation from worldly media.

frames.aligns: Hope through a new generation; persistence; service to humanity.
frames.concerns: The body as a sacred, eternal part of the soul conflicts with bodies treated as disposable shells; gore and horror under For the Strength of Youth.

frames.aligns: Critique of a system that kills people for lacking the right "credentials"; women in leading roles.
frames.concerns: Little in message; violence as the only answer.
"By beholding we become changed" applied to constant gore and body horror; the self as data versus the unity of the person and the state of the dead (from general knowledge; to verify).

frames.aligns: Protecting the helpless; no spiritism reported.
frames.concerns: Violence is constant and the hero's calling (Psalm 11:5).

frames.aligns: Persistence and hope outlast a hostile world.
frames.concerns: Decay, injury and fear are shown as overwhelming realities; body horror is a mental influence the tradition guards against.

frames.aligns: Saving life (pikuach nefesh echo); hope through a child.
frames.concerns: Gore and grotesque images; reproductive engineering outside marriage; many Haredi homes restrict such media.

frames.aligns: Value of human life; a world repaired through a new generation.
frames.concerns: Gore; ethics of cloning and engineered reproduction discussed by families.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam echo: one person working to repair a broken world; critique of dehumanizing systems.
frames.concerns: Little in message; violence as the only tool.
Gore; images of grotesque beings; human creation of life by technology and reproduction outside marriage; a godless world.

frames.aligns: Duty pursued without attachment to reward (Killy's quest); renewal after destruction.
frames.concerns: Some families apply the Gita's tamasic category to the gore and gloom.

frames.aligns: Impermanence and the unstable self (Cibo's many bodies) echo non-self teaching; compassion in the mercy scene.
frames.concerns: Killing is constant, against the first precept; the bleak tone.

frames.aligns: Courage to protect the defenseless; ego and lust for power (Silicon Life) shown as destructive.
Service to humanity as a whole; science applied to restore life.
frames.concerns: Strong commitment to non-violence; constant combat.

frames.aligns: Ending renewal in water and plants (fan wiki, Log 65).
frames.concerns: A world of pollution and decay with no kami, purity or gratitude; blood and death as impurity.

frames.aligns: No negative portrayal of witches or pagans; the ending returns life to nature (Log 65).
frames.concerns: Nature almost entirely erased by the City.

frames.aligns: Persistence; a person's identity surviving the loss of bodies has a loose echo of teaching on the spiritual being apart from the body.
Women as scientists and leaders; a two-woman genetic family as the story's hope; critique of systems that exclude people.
frames.concerns: Graphic violence; exaggerated female designs in the film (Common Sense Media).

frames.aligns: No supernatural answers; science, reason and persistence are the tools; human life valued in an indifferent universe.
frames.concerns: Bleak tone; the mercy killing calls for discussion.

frames.aligns: Duty, endurance, protection of the young; a warning about technology and bureaucracy out of human control.
frames.concerns: Little family, faith or tradition on the page; the engineered two-mother child.

frames.aligns: Worth and dignity of the excluded; free search for meaning.
A lone individual defies a vast, faceless authority; science and the material world are all there is; harm to a child (Log 1) is shown as horror.
frames.concerns: Killy's self-effacing service to humanity rather than self-interest.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: No vendettas or honor codes; Killy fights to survive and to complete his quest, not to defend a name.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The existing order (the Safeguard) is murderous, but the goal is to restore a legitimate order through the Netsphere, not to escape all order (Wikipedia).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Family is nearly absent; the quest serves humanity at large. The two-mother child is the only kin bond at the end (Log 64).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Hierarchies exist (Safeguard levels, the Authority, Toha's Mensab) but are neither celebrated nor attacked as such.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: A wholly technological world: no religion practiced, problems solved by science, genetics and weapons.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival is everything; Yokogao: "only survival is on your mind."

folkways.japan: The near-wordless restraint, a hero who never explains himself, and the secular, technological outlook fit common Japanese seinen science fiction conventions; the Western influences Nihei names (Giger, Moebius, Blade Runner) shape the look more than any value message.

delivery.evidence: Story told "mostly... with his art, and only spartan amounts of dialog" (SelfAwarePatterns); "mystery without explanation can become the entire point" (Yokogao).
delivery.note: The near-wordless storytelling leaves almost every idea implicit, so readers supply most of the meaning themselves.

personified.ideology: Silent persistence on behalf of humanity
Science and self-remaking
Automated rule enforcement without purpose
Power and evolution through violence

entry.dominant: Transhumanism (explored, not endorsed), Existentialism, Nihilism and Absurdism (as mood), Naturalism.

entry.heading: Call of the Night (Yofukashi no Uta)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is one you choose for yourself. Freedom, honesty about your feelings and real connection matter more than fitting in, and love means staying with someone even when it costs you.

frames.aligns: Love matures from desire into faithful, patient commitment (ch. 200); revenge given up (Anko); manipulation (Kiku) shown as destructive.
frames.concerns: An adult-aged being in a sexualized dynamic with a minor; truancy and night wandering without parental care treated as liberation; Mahiru choosing death with Kiku (CCC 2280-2283); lewd humor (CCC 2525 on permissiveness).

frames.aligns: Loneliness healed by communion with others; Kiku's centuries of craving read as unchecked passion.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis): constant sexual teasing and the feeding-as-sex image. Vampires as sympathetic beings of the night. Little framing of the youth's flight from home as a problem.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, honesty, a faithful love that waits years; revenge abandoned (Romans 12:19).
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 test for the lewd jokes and fan service; honoring parents and authority (Ephesians 6:1) set aside; the adult-minor coding. Families decide by conscience; views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Honest portrait of teen loneliness and depression (ANN); faithful love in the ending; forgiveness of enemies (Anko).
frames.concerns: Depicting is not endorsing, but the night-life and truancy are presented as good; sexualized adult-minor dynamic; no spiritual answer to emptiness.

frames.aligns: Rejection of revenge; loyalty to friends.
frames.concerns: Vampires and blood-drinking as an "open door" theme, presented sympathetically and romantically; sexual teasing. Views range between churches.

frames.aligns: Human emptiness without purpose is honestly shown; common grace lets families value well-made art by non-Christians.
frames.concerns: Westminster Larger Catechism Q139 lists "lascivious... books, pictures" among sins against the seventh commandment; fifth-commandment duties of children and parents largely absent.

frames.aligns: Love as self-giving at the end; vocation (Ko works and studies by the epilogue).
frames.concerns: Fourth Commandment: parents and school as God's ordered gifts are absent or escaped. LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Care for the lonely; transformation over time.
frames.concerns: Wesley's caution about diversions; lewd humor; holiness churches more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: A literary vampire tale judged by framing: manipulation and revenge fail; faithful love endures.
frames.concerns: The adult-minor coding and truancy shown approvingly. Episcopal and ACNA families may differ.
Separation from the world: nightlife, sexual humor and a youth leaving community structures are the opposite of the ideal. Conservative groups avoid such media; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Lasting love and faithfulness across years (ch. 200); friendship.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth: entertainment should invite the Spirit; constant sexual innuendo, night wandering and an adult-minor romance work against chastity and family guidance. Members vary in strictness.

frames.aligns: Compassion for depressed and outsider youth; aromantic and queer characters treated with care (ANN); revenge renounced.
frames.concerns: Power imbalance in the adult-minor dynamic; vulnerable children unprotected by adults (Ko, Mahiru).
"By beholding we become changed": sexual teasing and nightlife; vampires and immortality conflict with teaching on the state of the dead.
Supernatural blood-drinking beings presented as attractive; immorality and lewd talk (Galatians 5:19-21); the sacredness of blood (Acts 15:29) inverted into play.

frames.aligns: Love outlasting fear; healing from isolation.
frames.concerns: Depression, insomnia, death and predatory desire shown as powerful realities; sensual focus.
Tzniut and nivul peh: constant sexual talk and fan service; a youth leaving Torah-like structure of home and school; blood consumption is a strong taboo. Many Haredi homes would not admit it.

frames.aligns: Honest look at loneliness; repair of relationships; revenge renounced.
frames.concerns: Adult-minor coding; truancy; modesty values applied by families.

frames.aligns: Informed autonomy and respect for difference (aromantic, queer characters); healing from isolation.
frames.concerns: Power imbalance and consent questions in the adult-minor dynamic; an unsupervised child.

frames.aligns: Loyalty to friends, forgiveness over revenge, patient love.
frames.concerns: Lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) for fan service; lewd talk; zina-adjacent framing of feeding; blood prohibited (Qur'an 5:3); obedience to parents and seeking knowledge set aside.

frames.aligns: Self-discovery and love as devotion over time; Kiku's craving for an endless life read through attachment.
frames.concerns: The Gita's tamasic qualities (night, inertia, intoxication, indulgence) are made attractive; the student stage (brahmacharya) abandoned.

frames.aligns: Clear view of suffering, loneliness and craving; Kiku's 500 years of grasping at love and humanity shows tanha; impermanence in the time-skip ending.
frames.concerns: Sensual craving made attractive; intoxicants shown casually (fifth precept); a teen's death with his lover.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, courage, letting go of anger (Anko).
frames.concerns: Lust (kaam) as constant humor and theme; intoxicants (Nazuna's beer, Anko's smoking) against the Rehat Maryada's rule on tobacco and alcohol.

frames.aligns: Unity across difference; love that serves.
frames.concerns: Shoghi Effendi's call to a "chaste and holy life"; alcohol and casual sexual talk; education set aside.

frames.aligns: Night, seasons and the city treated with sincere wonder; makoto (sincerity) in Ko's honest feelings; no disrespect to shrines or kami reported.
frames.concerns: Blood and death as impurity; teen truancy against social harmony norms.

frames.aligns: Respect for night, nature and outsiders; vampires and supernatural beings portrayed without stereotype; consent-centered love in the end.
frames.concerns: "Harm none": feeding on a minor and Kiku's manipulation raise harm questions.

frames.aligns: Way to Happiness precepts: be worthy of trust, fulfill obligations (Ko keeps his promises).
frames.concerns: Precepts to honor parents, avoid promiscuity and avoid harmful drugs and alcohol; the absent schooling.

frames.aligns: Mental-health honesty; aromantic, queer and gender-nonconforming characters; a critique of overwork and of pressure to conform.
frames.concerns: Consent and power: an adult-aged vampire drawn as a teenager, a 14-year-old "willing victim" (ICv2), and a camera ANN calls "leery" and "intrusive"; Kiku's grooming-like control of a teenager is framed as harmful, but Nazuna's dynamic with Ko is framed as romance.

frames.aligns: Meaning found by choice and relationship, not supernatural rule; revenge replaced by understanding; depression treated seriously.
frames.concerns: Child welfare: no adult intervenes for a truant, sleepless 14-year-old; sexual coding with a minor.

frames.aligns: Faithful love in the end; Ko trains to be strong and protective (EpicStream).
frames.concerns: The family, school and community order are absent or escaped; night culture glamorized; sexualized adult-minor dynamic; alcohol and smoking casual.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of outsiders and of every kind of love (aromantic Seri); free search for meaning.
frames.concerns: Power and consent in the adult-minor dynamic; an unprotected child.

frames.aligns: Liberty, self-determination and rejection of conformity are celebrated; nonconforming identities accepted (Satanic Temple Tenets 3 and 5 on bodily autonomy and freedom).
frames.concerns: The Eleven Rules of the Earth forbid harming little children; the sexual coding of a 14-year-old raises that concern.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Anko's personal revenge is the series' main honor-style drive, and the story has her give it up (Japanese Wikipedia; ANN). Insults and slights are handled with jokes and talk, not combat.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Leaving school, curfew and home routine is presented as liberation (ANN TWIA; Japanese Wikipedia); the night is a space without rules.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Birth families are weak or absent (Ko's mother, Mahiru's parents); loyalty goes to chosen friends and a found community of night people.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Nazuna and Ko on near-equal footing (Amemiya interview); vampire society is loose, without strong ranks; adults earn no deference by position.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No religion or inherited custom guides life; choices are personal.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Self-expression, tolerance of difference and quality of life (sleep, pleasure, honest feeling) are the story's goods (Aftermath).

folkways.japan: School refusal (futoko), late-night convenience-store culture, hostess work and long working hours are Japanese social context; Ko's escape reads partly as a response to Japanese school conformity and group pressure, which the story critiques by showing a kinder world outside it.

delivery.evidence: ANN's This Week in Anime says the show "makes a pseudo-moral argument in favor of truancy"; reviewers otherwise praise its quiet, introspective tone.
delivery.note: Its case for freedom and honest feeling comes through mood and character arcs rather than speeches, while school and parents are mostly absent rather than argued against.

personified.ideology: Freedom and self-discovery outside school norms
Carefree pleasure learning commitment
Revenge as justice
Possessive love as salvation

entry.dominant: Expressive individualism, Existentialism, Hedonism (explored, then tempered).

entry.heading: Fire Force
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is the hero's life: you keep hope against despair, protect people even when they call you a devil, and treat your team as a family. Faith is honored when it is sincere and serves people; institutions that use faith to control people are exposed.

content.framing: Neutral to Endorsed (as comedy); questioned in ch. 280

frames.aligns: Evil (the Evangelist, Rekka) is framed as evil; hope over despair; the sincere nun and prayers for the dead are shown with respect.
frames.concerns: A church modeled on Catholic rites is revealed as founded for evil; a human becomes a creator and fashions Death. The Lure gags make sexual humiliation comic, against Inter Mirifica 7 (evil not made attractive) and CCC 2521-2524 on modesty.

frames.aligns: Prayer for the departed; the struggle against despair.
frames.concerns: Church imagery used for an evil institution; the hero as world-creator; guarding the senses (nepsis) makes the fan service the larger concern.

frames.aligns: Clear good and evil; protecting others; the exposure of religious hypocrisy.
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 applied to the fan-service gags; a human taking God's place in the finale (Isaiah 45:7, 18). Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Hope against despair; hypocrisy and false teachers exposed (Matthew 7:15); sincere faith honored in Iris.
frames.concerns: Faith valued "regardless of the god it's directed to" (Drunken Anime Blog's summary); a human creator-savior; fan service.

frames.aligns: Spiritual warfare imagery: an apocalyptic being and its cult are defeated.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": fire-spirit powers, an otherworld (Adolla), communion with an evil being for power ("Grace"), and a hero who becomes god are shown positively or neutrally. Fan service against holiness standards.

frames.aligns: Total depravity echoed in human cruelty; idolatry of a false church exposed; common grace lets families value the craft.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 ("lascivious... pictures") for the Lure gags; a human creator-god against the Creator-creature distinction.

frames.aligns: Exposing a church that controls through fear echoes Reformation critique; vocation of the firefighter as service.
frames.concerns: A human creator in the finale; fan service (LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA).

frames.aligns: Works of mercy (prayers and care for victims); social holiness against corrupt power.
frames.concerns: Wesley's rule against "diversions" that cannot be used "in the name of the Lord Jesus" applies most to the Lure gags; holiness churches more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: Judged by framing: institutional corruption is critiqued while personal faith is honored, in a tradition at home with fantasy.
frames.concerns: Fan service; the creator-hero finale as theology.

frames.aligns: Suspicion of a state church allied with empire matches Anabaptist history; mutual aid in the companies.
frames.concerns: Violence as the heroes' main tool (Matthew 5:39); fan service; conservative groups avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Exposure of a corrupted church that keeps truth hidden; family reunion (Shinra, Sho and their mother join hands in the finale); hope.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth asks for media that invites the Spirit; the Lure gags; a human remaking creation.

frames.aligns: Critique of institutional religion that serves power; care for victims; sincere faith not mocked.
frames.concerns: Treatment of women in fan service (ANN; CBR); fatalism preached by a church.

frames.aligns: Exposure of a church-state alliance can echo Adventist reading of Revelation (from general knowledge; to verify).
frames.concerns: The dead are unconscious until the resurrection, so souls passing to another realm and a human reviving the dead conflict with teaching; fan service against FB 22.

frames.aligns: Exposure of a corrupt religious establishment may resonate with Witness teaching on false religion (from general knowledge; to verify).
frames.concerns: Spiritism and magic (fire powers, Adolla, communion with a being), violence (Psalm 11:5) and immorality-as-comedy are the jw.org tests.

frames.aligns: Thought shapes reality in the story (Adolla as collective imagination; the hero remakes the world by imagining it); fear of death reduced at the end.
frames.concerns: Fear, fire and death shown as overwhelming forces through most of the series.

frames.aligns: Exposure of idolatry and false prophets; protection of life.
frames.concerns: A human as creator; tzniut makes the fan service a major concern; many Haredi homes restrict such media.

frames.aligns: Exposure of a manipulative cult; protection of life; family reunion.
frames.concerns: Fan service; a human creator figure.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam echoes in rebuilding a burnt world; critique of institutions that oppress.
frames.concerns: Treatment of women in the gags.

frames.aligns: Hope over despair; justice against oppressors; exposure of false religious leaders.
frames.concerns: A human becomes creator and makes Death, against tawhid; lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) weighs heavily with the Lure gags.

frames.aligns: Fire as sacred, cosmic destruction and re-creation, a hero acting from duty; deities are not mocked.
frames.concerns: Some families apply the tamasic category to the gags and horror.

frames.aligns: Adolla as a collective mind shaped by human despair or hope (fan wiki: "collective unconscious"); death feared less at the end.
frames.concerns: Killing is routine; right speech and what feeds the mind weigh on the gags.

frames.aligns: Courage in defense of the oppressed; ego and cruelty condemned in villains.
frames.concerns: Lust shown as comedy (one of the five vices).

frames.aligns: Religion that divides and controls is critiqued; service and unity of former rivals; the faith has no clergy, which matches the critique of a priestly class (from general knowledge; to verify).
frames.concerns: The "chaste and holy life" counsel weighs on the gags.

frames.aligns: Purification prayer for the dead echoes Shinto rites (TV Tropes); sun and fire imagery.
frames.concerns: The name Amaterasu is given to a power plant with a person trapped inside; sun worship shown as a cover for evil.

frames.aligns: Fire and sun as powerful symbols; no witch stereotypes.
frames.concerns: The sun-worshipping religion is the corrupt one, though the story blames its founders, not sun reverence.

frames.aligns: Way to Happiness precepts: do not murder, help others; villains who harm are condemned.
Critique of church-state-corporate power; found family; a non-powered leader (Obi).
frames.concerns: Repeated sexual-humiliation gags (ANN: "offensively awful"; CBR; Anime Feminist); a woman's arc made secondary (CBR).

frames.aligns: Religion used for control is exposed; Benimaru's view that people should act rightly for their own sake; hope as a human choice.
frames.concerns: The finale resolves through a supernatural creator-hero; fan service as exploitation.

frames.aligns: Heroism, duty, loyalty, team as family, protecting the weak.
frames.concerns: Established religion portrayed as founded on a lie; fan service.

frames.aligns: Free search for meaning; worth of every person (even Infernals get a prayer); critique of dogma used for control.
frames.concerns: Treatment of women in the gags; violence.

frames.aligns: A hero branded "devil" is the true protector; established religion is exposed as a tool of control; rebellion against authority is justified (Company 8 as outlaws).
frames.concerns: The story ends in self-sacrifice for the group and a benevolent new god figure.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Shinra seeks recognition as a hero after being called a devil; Benimaru's Asakusa values personal pride (from general knowledge; to verify); Tamaki answers public shaming by fighting on (ch. 280).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Disciplined companies with captains, but the heroes defy corrupt orders and become outlaws (ch. about 175-197).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Team as family (Ohkubo); the Kusakabe brothers and their mother join hands to win the finale; the epilogue serves the whole world.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Ranks exist, but Obi, a non-powered captain, leads by care; the church hierarchy is exposed.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: The inherited state religion is shown as founded on a lie; personal faith is respected; the resolution is supernatural.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Hope and choosing one's own path (ch. 280) weigh against a world built around fatalism.

folkways.japan: The firefighter company as family, senpai-captain respect and the fan-service gag conventions of weekly shonen magazines reflect Japanese manga norms. The church's Western Christian look is an outside model used as setting, which reviewers outside Japan read as close to real Catholicism (Geeks Under Grace; Drunken Anime Blog).

delivery.evidence: Drunken Anime Blog finds the church "at times good and at times bad"; TV Tropes calls Hibana's atheism a straw portrayal.
delivery.note: The series lets sincere believers, skeptics and fanatics each speak, but the church's leadership and its fanatic priest are drawn as plain villains.

personified.ideology: Hope and heroism; faith has worth whatever its object
Sincere personal faith
Religious fanaticism
Despair and contempt for hope

entry.dominant: Communitarianism, Classical virtue ethics, Nihilism (critiqued), Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued), Pantheist/New Age.

entry.heading: Look Back
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is spent making things with and for other people. Talent and rivalry are not enough; art is worth the grind because of who it is shared with. Loss cannot be undone, but it can be carried forward into work.

frames.aligns: Evil (the attack) is shown but not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7); envy (a capital sin) is overcome by friendship; work and gifts used for others echo John Paul II's Letter to Artists.
frames.concerns: No hope of resurrection or prayer for the dead is shown; the "what if" timeline offers no frame beyond human memory.

frames.aligns: Struggle with a passion (envy, pride) turned to love; memory of the dead; watchfulness is not much tested, since the content is restrained.
frames.concerns: No prayer or hope beyond memory; the dead friend's voice may raise questions about contact with the departed.

frames.aligns: Hard work, friendship, grief handled honestly; evil clearly condemned. Philippians 4:8 is easily met by most of the book.
frames.concerns: No faith or hope of heaven; the alternate timeline may confuse younger readers. Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Many will see "redeeming" themes: gifts used for others, loss carried into faithful work. Depicts evil without endorsing it.
frames.concerns: The story's comfort is human memory, not God.

frames.aligns: Clear good and evil; perseverance; no occult practice.
frames.concerns: A dead friend's voice and a message crossing between worlds, left ambiguous, may be weighed as spirit contact by some churches.

frames.aligns: Common grace: excellent art by a non-Christian about vocation and loss. Providence questions raised honestly.
frames.concerns: No providence or God in the story's answer; random evil is unexplained.

frames.aligns: Vocation: ordinary work done for others, a Lutheran theme. Adiaphora: little content to weigh.
frames.concerns: No gospel hope; LCMS and WELS families may want to discuss the afterlife scene's ambiguity.

frames.aligns: Diligence and use of one's gifts; mercy and friendship to a lonely classmate.
frames.concerns: Holiness churches may still apply Wesley's test of whether a book tends to the love of God; the story is silent on God.

frames.aligns: A literary tradition that values imagination will read the "what if" timeline as a legitimate fiction about grief; evil is plainly evil; vocation and love are honored.
Humility, community care, quiet faithfulness to work.
frames.concerns: The rescue is a violent act framed as heroic, though defensive; conservative groups avoid popular media in general.

frames.aligns: Developing talents (parable of the talents), friendship, family members in the background; little to conflict with For the Strength of Youth.
frames.concerns: The bath scene in the film (PG-13); no hope of reunion stated.

frames.aligns: Attention to a vulnerable school refuser; violence against artists mourned; the church's own debates on mental-health stigma echoed in the edits.
frames.concerns: The original version's link between psychosis and violence (since revised).

frames.aligns: Diligence, friendship, temperate content; "by beholding we become changed" is not strongly tested.
frames.concerns: The dead are unconscious until the resurrection, so Kyomoto's voice speaking after death may need framing as memory or imagination.

frames.aligns: Love of friends, hard work, no occult practice shown.
frames.concerns: Spirit contact with the dead is a concern if the voice is read literally; violence against students, though condemned.

frames.aligns: Love and good outlast evil; Fujino's thought turns from despair to purpose.
frames.concerns: Death, fear and senseless evil are shown as real and final.

frames.aligns: Mourning and memory of the dead (zikaron); diligence; condemnation of violence. Little immodesty in the manga.
frames.concerns: Haredi homes restrict secular media in general; the film's bath scene and nude sketches raise tzniut questions for the film.

frames.aligns: Memory, mourning and returning to life and work; violence condemned.
Repair through creative work; empathy for a socially anxious child; attention to stigma (the edits).
Patience in loss (sabr), diligence, loyalty to a friend; violence condemned.
frames.concerns: Debates on images of living beings apply to manga in general; the film's bath scene for families who lower the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31).

frames.aligns: Devotion to one's art (svadharma), friendship, acceptance of loss; sattvic in tone for most of the book.
Impermanence, attachment and grief; envy dissolved into friendship; right effort; no glamor in the violence. The ending reads as acceptance.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; some may note the story's focus on striving and ego early on.

frames.aligns: Honest labor (kirat karni), service to others, ego (haumai) humbled; violence condemned.
Arts as worship when done in service; work done in a spirit of service; friendship across difference.
frames.concerns: The rescue is a violent act; tradition's strong commitment to non-violence.

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) and gratitude; memory of the dead kept at the workspace; craft as devotion.
frames.concerns: Death and violence as impurity, though condemned.

frames.aligns: "Harm none": violence is plainly wrong; creativity honored; memory of the dead.
The Way to Happiness precepts: be industrious, be competent, do not murder.
frames.concerns: The edits removed references to mental illness after advice that included psychiatrists (Pixiv); the Church's opposition to psychiatry gives this debate a different reading.

frames.aligns: Sympathetic portrayal of a school refuser with anxiety (Common Sense Media); two girls as creators; grief handled seriously.
frames.concerns: The original attacker coded as psychotic was criticized as stigmatizing and was revised; some readers found the art-school killings too close to the KyoAni victims (CBR).

frames.aligns: Meaning made by humans in a world without guarantees; art and friendship as what lasts; afterlife left open.
Diligence, discipline, craft, loyalty to a friend; evil not excused.
frames.concerns: Family is in the background; some may raise the decision to edit the work after public pressure.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of a lonely child; interdependence; justice for the stigmatized raised by the edits.
Self-made excellence through will and practice; the protection of the vulnerable (Satanic Temple Tenet 1).
frames.concerns: The story moves from self-centered ambition to devotion to another person, the opposite of Church of Satan individualism.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: No one defends personal honor; the attacker's claim that his work was stolen (a grievance answered with violence) is the act the story condemns (Cartoon Brew; CBR). Fujino's competitive pride is shown as a flaw she grows out of.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Characters pick their own paths: Kyomoto chooses art school over a serialization, Fujino goes on alone (Wikipedia). The story honors both choices while showing their cost.

Civic vs kin.evidence: The central bond is a friendship, not family; Fujino's family fades into the background (TV Tropes). Loyalty is personal rather than to clan or community.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Two partners with complementary skills (WWAC); a teacher and Jump editors appear but are not revered. Early rivalry ranks the girls, then gives way to partnership.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No religion beyond a funeral; meaning comes from work and memory. The voice after death is left ambiguous (TV Tropes).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Art as a calling and self-expression, but also as unglamorous labor ("the hardest thing about drawing is drawing itself," WWAC 2021).

folkways.japan: The manga industry's contest and serialization system, school refusal (futoko), and the quiet, group-mourning response to the Kyoto Animation attack are Japanese context rather than the story's argument. Diligent practice as the path to mastery is a familiar Japanese ideal that the story treats as true.

delivery.evidence: Polygon praised its subtlety (via Wikipedia); ANN calls the wordless final scene affecting; no reviewer found calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The message is carried by images and silence, and Fujino's despair ("I hate drawing") gets a fair hearing before the ending answers it.

personified.ideology: Art as ambition, then art for another
Art as devotion and a way out of isolation
Grievance and entitlement (art "stolen" from him)

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Secular humanism, Classical virtue ethics, Stoicism.

series.title: Wotakoi: Love is Hard for Otaku

entry.heading: Wotakoi: Love Is Hard for Otaku (Fujita)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is shared with people who accept the whole of you, hobbies included; you need not hide what you love, and those who love you should let you open up at your own pace.

content.framing: Neutral to Endorsed (social drinking as normal adult life); occasional comic consequences

frames.aligns: Faithful, patient love; a long courtship that ends in marriage and a child (Hanako and Kabakura, JP vol. 7-9); dignity of the outsider; friendship.
frames.concerns: BL fantasy talk and breast gags as humor (CCC 2521-2524 on modesty); drinking to cope (CCC 2290 permits moderation, not drunkenness); premarital status of the leads unaddressed.

frames.aligns: Gentle, faithful love; humility; marriage and children as the senior couple's path.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis) for gags and BL fantasies; hobbies as the center of life. Alcohol is permitted in Orthodoxy; drunkenness is condemned.

frames.aligns: Kindness, loyalty, apology after fights, marriage before a child.
frames.concerns: Many Baptists abstain from alcohol (SBC resolutions), and here drinking is the normal social glue; smoking; breast jokes and BL fantasies against Philippians 4:8.

frames.aligns: "Accept one another" (Romans 15:7) is close to the story's core; patient love; reconciliation.
frames.concerns: Social drinking as normal; same-sex fantasy talk as humor; no faith in the characters' lives. Engage-or-separate views differ by family.

frames.aligns: Joy, warmth, friendship, kindness to the anxious (Kou).
frames.concerns: Many abstain from alcohol (AG position); holiness standards on modesty and worldly amusements; BL fandom. No occult content.

frames.aligns: Common grace: honest work, faithful love and marriage shown well by a non-Christian author.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 on lascivious books and pictures applies mainly to the breast gags and BL fantasy talk; drunkenness (Hanako) is sinful by WLC Q139, though it is played as a joke.

frames.aligns: Vocation in daily work and friendship; entertainment as adiaphora; marriage honored.
frames.concerns: Hanako's drunkenness; the gags. LCMS and WELS families weigh these more than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Kindness, inclusion of the shy, faithful love.
frames.concerns: Historic abstinence (General Rules; holiness churches ask members to abstain; UMC recommends abstinence as a witness) against a story where drinking is constant; diversions that do not "tend to the knowledge or love of God."

frames.aligns: A gentle, well-told comedy whose good is clearly good; marriage and family; moderate drinking normal in the tradition.
frames.concerns: Drunkenness as a gag; breast jokes. Episcopal and ACNA families differ on the leads' unmarried status and same-sex teasing.

frames.aligns: Simple friendship, forgiveness, peaceable couples, faithful marriage.
frames.concerns: Separation from worldly media makes a secular hobby comedy a concern for Old Order families; many abstain from alcohol; consumer hobby culture. MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Faithful love, marriage and a child; kindness; honest work.
frames.concerns: Word of Wisdom: alcohol and tobacco are shown as normal and pleasant; law of chastity as to the leads is unaddressed; breast gags and BL fantasy talk.

frames.aligns: Welcome of people who feel they must hide who they are; women's hobbies taken seriously; a gender-nonconforming woman (Kou) accepted.

frames.concerns: Alcohol and tobacco, which members abstain from (Fundamental Belief 22 and the health message), are shown as normal; entertainment centered on hobbies and romance.

frames.aligns: Honesty, kindness, a long courtship ending in marriage (senior couple).
frames.concerns: Drunkenness played as a joke (Hanako); BL fantasy talk; worldly entertainment as identity. No violence or spiritism.

frames.aligns: Love and acceptance dispel fear: Narumi's anxiety about being outed eases through Hirotaka's support.
frames.concerns: Members abstain from alcohol and tobacco (Church Manual), shown here as normal; dwelling on anxiety.

frames.aligns: Kindness, loyalty, marriage and children for the senior couple.
frames.concerns: Tzniut: mixed-sex dating and office flirting, breast gags, BL fantasy talk; nivul peh in the couples' insults. Many Haredi homes would not have the series; Modern Orthodox families are selective.

frames.aligns: Dignity of people who feel they must hide; family formed through marriage; kind speech after fights.
frames.concerns: Modesty in the gags; insults between partners; drinking.

frames.aligns: Dignity and inclusion of the judged; informed choices about hobbies; healthy adult relationships.
Kindness, loyalty, marriage before children, honest work.
frames.concerns: Alcohol is forbidden (Qur'an 5:90) and is constant here; unchaperoned dating; lowering the gaze (24:30-31) for the breast gags; BL fantasy talk.

frames.aligns: Grihastha (householder) life arriving through marriage; friendship; diligence.
frames.concerns: Many devotional families abstain from alcohol; some apply the Gita's tamasic category (ch. 17) to intoxication and idle entertainment.

frames.aligns: Patience, compassion for the anxious, letting others move at their own pace.
frames.concerns: Fifth precept (no intoxicants) against routine drinking; attachment to collecting and fandom.

frames.aligns: Seva-like kindness among friends, honest work, faithful marriage.
frames.concerns: Tobacco is one of the four kurehits and alcohol is rejected; both are normal here. Kaam (lust) in the gags; moh (attachment) to possessions.

frames.aligns: Unity, kindness, inclusion of the judged, marriage.
frames.concerns: Alcohol is forbidden and shown as normal; the call to a "chaste and holy life" for the gags and unaddressed premarital status.

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto), harmony in the group, gratitude; drinking among friends fits Japanese social custom.
"Harm none" in accepting friends; self-expression through cosplay; no stereotyping of pagans.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; insults between partners.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness: be worthy of trust, be faithful to one's partner, help others; problems solved by communication.
Anti-stigma message, women's geek hobbies taken seriously (Moore), a gender-nonconforming woman accepted, consent-minded pacing ("watching over someone as they move at their own pace," Fujita).
frames.concerns: "Out-of-place boob comments" (Moore); unhealthy insults in the senior couple (McNulty); drinking as coping.

frames.aligns: Meaning from friendship, love and chosen pleasures; reason and communication solve problems; no supernatural claims.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; responsible drinking is the main talking point.

frames.aligns: Long faithful courtship, marriage before a child, diligent work, loyalty among friends.
frames.concerns: Adults whose identity centers on hobbies and consumer fandom; BL fandom; drinking and smoking as normal; the leads' unmarried relationship has no stated endpoint.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of the judged; free search for one's own interests; acceptance of difference.
Indulgence in chosen pleasures without guilt, refusal to conform to office norms, loyalty to those who earn it (Church of Satan); compassion (Satanic Temple Tenet 1).
frames.concerns: Narumi's long self-concealment reads as yielding to herd judgment.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Worth is inherent; the story asks for acceptance, not for anyone to defend reputation. Narumi's fear of losing face at work is the problem to overcome (JP vol. 11), not a value.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Office rules are followed, but the story sides with people's freedom to live their hobbies openly.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Care flows through a chosen circle of coworkers and friends more than family; families are mostly offstage.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Senpai give advice and juniors listen (Anime Corner), but the friends treat each other as equals and tease freely across rank.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Secular daily life; customs appear only as seasonal events (Christmas). Marriage is valued for the senior couple.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Self-expression and quality of life (hobbies, cosplay, fandom) are the central values; work is a steady background.

folkways.japan: After-work drinking with coworkers (nomikai), senpai-kohai relations, the pressure to keep private hobbies out of the workplace, and the special stigma on adult and female otaku are Japanese norms that frame the story. Fujita presents the shift toward openness as a generational change in Japan (Kodansha 2025).

delivery.evidence: Fujita rates the mix "comedy 8, romance 1.5, seriousness 0.5" (Anime Corner); critics call it breezy and genuine.
delivery.note: Its anti-stigma theme emerges through gags and small arcs, and the non-otaku Naoya is drawn as kindly as the otaku.

personified.ideology: Hiding one's hobbies to fit social norms
Unashamed self-acceptance; love by patience
Guarding a respectable image while secretly a fan
The accepting non-otaku

entry.dominant: Expressive individualism, Communitarianism, Consumerism, Secular humanism.

entry.heading: Yotsuba&!
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is lived with open eyes in ordinary days: curiosity, play, honesty and the kindness of family, friends and neighbors make each day worth enjoying. Family is made by love and care, not only by blood.

frames.aligns: Care for an orphan as a work of mercy; joy and gratitude for creation's ordinary goods; honesty (CCC 2482); honoring elders (CCC 2214-2220). Nothing evil is made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7).
frames.concerns: No mother or marriage in the home, against the ideal of a family of father and mother; Torako's smoking.

frames.aligns: Childlike simplicity and wonder ("become like children," Matthew 18:3); hospitality; respect for elders. Nothing to guard the senses against.
frames.concerns: Buddhist temple custom (nio statue, ch. 69) and Bon Festival shown in passing.

frames.aligns: Passes the Philippians 4:8 test easily: "lovely," "pure," "of good report." Honesty and obedience to a father (Ephesians 6:1). Caring for orphans (James 1:27).
frames.concerns: Halloween and Buddhist customs appear briefly; no church or faith life. Families decide by soul liberty.

frames.aligns: Wonder at creation; adoption; honesty; neighbor love. Depicts no sin to endorse. A Beneath the Tangles commenter called it "entirely free of adult cynicism," and the editors discussed it for their recommendations list.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; the father is a single parent with no faith practice.

frames.aligns: Joy, wonder and a loving father.
frames.concerns: Halloween (ch. 81), a temple guardian statue used to scare away a "lying bug" (ch. 69) and festival masks (ch. 55) are folk-spiritual items some churches weigh more heavily.

frames.aligns: Common grace: a non-Christian author's good art showing the goodness of ordinary life. Adoption is a central doctrine (Westminster Confession ch. 12).
frames.concerns: Very little; Halloween and temple customs in passing.

frames.aligns: Daily bread and vocation: Luther's explanation of the Fourth Petition fits a story of ordinary gifts. Fatherhood as a vocation.
Works of mercy (care for an orphan); kindness; simple joys. Wesley's test of books that "tend to the knowledge or love of God" may be met by its gratitude, though it has no explicit faith.
frames.concerns: Holiness churches may note Torako's smoking and Halloween.

frames.aligns: Imagination and wonder in the tradition of fairy tales and childhood literature; a gentle world where good is plain.
Simple living, community, nonviolence, humility, hard work and helping (ch. 30).
frames.concerns: Old Order groups avoid most popular media regardless of content; urban consumer settings (electronics store, ch. 67-68).

frames.aligns: Family as central; love and teaching of children; honesty; meets the "virtuous, lovely, or of good report" test (Article of Faith 13) and For the Strength of Youth's test of media that invites the Spirit.
frames.concerns: The family has no mother and no marriage, against the Family Proclamation's ideal; members respond with compassion to single-parent homes.

frames.aligns: A non-traditional family shown as whole; care for the vulnerable; welcome of a child from abroad.
frames.concerns: A reported spanking; Fuuka teased about her legs.

frames.aligns: Wholesome fare that meets Fundamental Belief 22's "highest quality" test; nature study (cicadas, frogs, stars, ch. 6, 13, 32).
frames.concerns: Halloween and Christmas customs; coffee, smoking by a side character (health message).

frames.aligns: Love of family, honesty, kindness, care of a child.
frames.concerns: Halloween (ch. 81), Christmas (ch. 106), the Bon Festival (ch. 18) and other religious festivals are celebrations Witnesses do not keep; temple custom (ch. 69).

frames.aligns: Joy, goodness and love dominate; fear never wins.
frames.concerns: Yotsuba's fever (ch. 45) is treated in ordinary medical ways (from general knowledge; to verify).

frames.aligns: Care for an orphan is a great mitzvah; honoring elders; honesty; kind speech. Tzniut is not strained.
frames.concerns: Christmas, Halloween and temple customs; the home has no mother. Many Haredi homes restrict secular media in general.

frames.aligns: Raising an orphan; respect for elders; honesty; joy in daily life.
Inclusion of a non-traditional family; welcome of a child from abroad; kindness.

Caring for an orphan is highly praised (the Prophet: "I and the one who looks after an orphan will be like this in Paradise," Sahih al-Bukhari; from general knowledge; to verify). Honesty, respect for elders, neighborliness.
frames.concerns: Islamic kafala care keeps the child's own lineage, and Qur'an 33:4-5 is read to forbid renaming an adopted child as one's own; Yotsuba takes the Koiwai name. Christmas, Halloween, Bon Festival; dogs and a smoking side character.

frames.aligns: Sattvic in tone (Gita ch. 17): calm, joyful, kind. Seva to a child; respect for elders; festivals as family life.
Present-moment awareness, simple joy, kindness to all beings; the Bon Festival (ch. 18) and a temple visit (ch. 69) shown respectfully. MyAnimeList tags it "Iyashikei" (healing).
frames.concerns: Temple guardian used to frighten a child into honesty may be read as folk custom, not teaching.

frames.aligns: Seva, honest living (kirat karni), sharing, respect for elders.
frames.concerns: Tobacco is forbidden to Sikhs (a kurahit), so Torako's smoking and Yotsuba thinking it "cool" are talking points.

frames.aligns: Service, kindness, unity across peoples (a child from abroad welcomed); art that uplifts.
Festivals, a shrine, seasonal life, gratitude, sincerity (makoto) and purity of heart in a child; Bon and danjiri-style festivals (ch. 18, 55) treated warmly.
Delight in nature and the seasons; harm none; no stereotypes.
The Way to Happiness precepts: honor parents, be industrious, be truthful, help others.
A loving non-traditional family; gender-nonconforming characters shown neutrally (Miura, Torako); curiosity-led learning.
frames.concerns: A reported spanking, against AAP guidance on corporal punishment; Fuuka teased about her legs; online sexualized fan art of the child character (not in the book); smoking near a child.

frames.aligns: Curiosity, empirical wonder at the natural world, kindness without any supernatural framework; human bonds as the source of meaning.
frames.concerns: The nio statue lesson uses fear and folk belief to teach honesty (ch. 69).

frames.aligns: Manners (ch. 2), honesty, discipline, respect for elders, neighborliness, tradition and festivals: the good, the true and the beautiful in daily life.
frames.concerns: No mother or marriage in the home; little faith.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of every person; welcome of a child from abroad; free search for meaning through wonder.
Curiosity, self-directed play, enjoyment of life's pleasures; no harm to children or animals in the message.
frames.concerns: A reported spanking conflicts with the Satanic Temple's opposition to corporal punishment of children (from general knowledge; to verify); deference to adults and custom.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: No insult is answered with force; "revenge" is a water-pistol game (ch. 9), and quarrels with Yanda end in laughter. Disputes are settled by adults explaining.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Yotsuba roams the neighborhood and learns by trying things (ch. 1, 37, 47), but rules on honesty and safety are enforced (ch. 37, 69).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Family is formed by care rather than blood (ch. 6-7, 105); neighbors and strangers treat her as one of their own.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Respect for elders and manners are taught (ch. 2, 44, 89), but adults play with Yotsuba almost as equals.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Festivals and customs are enjoyed as culture (ch. 18, 55, 81, 106), not faith; daily life is practical and secular.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Quality of life, play, wonder and acceptance of difference are the highest goods; work stays in the background.

folkways.japan: Gift and souvenir customs (ch. 14-15), greetings, Respect for the Aged Day (ch. 44), the Bon Festival (ch. 18), neighborhood matsuri and young children running errands alone (ch. 47) reflect ordinary Japanese norms. Readers elsewhere may see the child's independence as riskier than Japanese readers would.

delivery.evidence: Santos (ANN): "sincere storytelling" evoking "the sweet, simple joys of childhood"; Tennekoon (Solrad): "never saccharine." No source calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The series shows its values through everyday episodes and almost never states them, and no character argues for an opposing worldview.

personified.ideology: Wonder and enjoying each ordinary day
Family made by love and present, hands-on fatherhood
Petty adult self-interest

entry.dominant: Communitarianism, Classical virtue ethics, Confucian ethics, Dharmic (Buddhist mindfulness), Traditionalism. All are mild; the series argues for nothing loudly.

entry.heading: Ajin: Demi-Human
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life holds on to particular human bonds and keeps trying to do right in a cruel world, even when cold calculation says to walk away. Treating people (or immortals) as tools, whether by a state lab or a terrorist, is shown as monstrous.

content.framing: Shown with consequences; terror and torture condemned
Neutral (as a game mechanic) and shown with consequences (trauma)

frames.aligns: Human dignity against treating persons as lab material (CCC 2295, experiments on persons); terrorism condemned (CCC 2297); Kei's growth from calculation toward self-giving; justice without execution (Sato imprisoned).
frames.concerns: Self-killing used casually as a tactic, against the gift of life (CCC 2280-2281, though Ajin do not die); Kei's "weighing lives" (ch. 43) is a consequentialism the Church rejects (Veritatis Splendor 75-80); gore that may exceed what the story needs (Inter Mirifica 7).

frames.aligns: Evil framed as evil on both sides; Kaito's self-sacrificing friendship.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis) makes the steady gore and torture a heavy concern; no transcendent horizon; death made trivial by "resets."

frames.aligns: Clear moral lines against terror and torture; Kei restrains himself under torture (ch. 7).
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 is the common test; graphic torture and dismemberment fail it for many families. Each congregation is self-governing, so views vary.

frames.aligns: Depicting sin is not endorsing it: Sato and the labs are shown as monstrous. Human worth and image-bearing raised by the "are they human?" question.
frames.concerns: Self-interest as the hero's default; no gospel or faith element; gore.

frames.aligns: Courage and spiritual-warfare-like clarity about evil.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": torture, gore and repeated self-killing. Holiness standards make it a strong concern for many.

frames.aligns: Total depravity echoed in state, crowds and terrorist alike; common grace in Nakano and Kaito; the magistrate's sword restrains Sato (Romans 13) even though the state is also corrupt.
frames.concerns: Providence absent; WLC Q136 on the sixth commandment includes self-harm and cruelty; graphic torture.

frames.aligns: Vocation: Kei still wants to be a doctor to save people (epilogue); law exposes everyone.
frames.concerns: No gospel; utilitarian calculation by hero and state. Entertainment is adiaphora; LCMS and WELS families more cautious about gore.

frames.aligns: Social holiness: critique of state cruelty and corporate greed (ch. 19).
frames.concerns: Wesley's rule against diversions that cannot be used "in the name of the Lord Jesus"; holiness churches would avoid the gore; UMC families more open.

frames.aligns: A literary tradition that weighs framing; Ajin frames torture and terror as evil and shows a cold hero changing.
frames.concerns: Gore and torture; no transcendence. Treated as older-teen or adult reading.

frames.aligns: Kei refuses violence under torture (ch. 7); Sato is captured, not killed; Nakano's conscience.
frames.concerns: Violence is the means of every solution (Matthew 5:39); Old Order groups avoid such media; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Agency against coercion by the state; friendship and family; the worth of souls against lab exploitation (D&C 18:10).
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth asks for media that invites the Spirit; graphic violence and torture weigh heavily; self-killing as tactic.

frames.aligns: Critique of state abuse of a minority, corporate greed and fear-driven crowds; empathy for the oppressed.
frames.concerns: Gore; few women; the oppressed minority's main voice is a terrorist.

frames.aligns: Care for the body violated by experimenters; Kei's medical calling.
frames.concerns: Fundamental Belief 22 and "by beholding we become changed" (2 Corinthians 3:18) make the torture and gore a heavy concern; resurrection made mechanical.

frames.aligns: Neutrality toward political violence; protecting others.
frames.concerns: jw.org counsel asks whether entertainment features what God hates; violence (Psalm 11:5) is the main content. Spiritism absent.

frames.aligns: Love and loyalty sustain Kei and Kaito.
frames.concerns: The story dwells on bodily destruction and fear; "Stand porter at the door of thought" (Science and Health 392).

frames.aligns: Pikuach nefesh and the value of saving life; condemnation of human experimentation (post-Shoah ethics); bystanders who risk to help (Kaito).
frames.concerns: Bodily mutilation and kavod ha-met concerns; lashon hara-free but gore-heavy; many Haredi homes restrict such media.

frames.aligns: Bystander duty (Leviticus 19:16); dignity of the persecuted; Nuremberg Code echo in the labs.
frames.concerns: Gore; the oppressed minority's leader is a mass murderer.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam; critique of state persecution and of fear politics.
Sanctity of life (Qur'an 5:32); justice against oppressors; loyalty.
frames.concerns: Self-killing even as tactic jars with the prohibition on harming oneself (Qur'an 4:29); graphic violence. Little modesty concern.

frames.aligns: Dharma of the healer (Kei's medical aim); ahimsa breached by both state and terrorist and both lose.
frames.concerns: Tamasic content (Gita 17) in gore; identity after "death" treated physically.

frames.aligns: Suffering from craving (Sato's craving for the "game"); compassion in Nakano; no-self questions in the decapitation rule.
frames.concerns: Killing and self-killing break the first precept; mindfulness of what feeds the mind.

frames.aligns: Saint-soldier ideal in Nakano and Kaito; fighting oppression; humility after loss.
Justice and the unity of humanity against prejudice.
frames.concerns: Constant violence; no spiritual horizon; Shoghi Effendi's warnings on degrading art.

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) in Nakano; harmony restored at the end.
frames.concerns: Blood and death (kegare) everywhere. No doctrine on fiction.

frames.aligns: Autonomy and bodily integrity against state control; condemnation of harm.
frames.concerns: The Rede ("harm none") against constant killing.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness: "Do not murder," "Do not do anything illegal"; critique of coercive pharmaceutical research.
Critique of state abuse, dehumanization of a minority, corporate profit over life (ch. 19), and media-fed panic (TV Tropes).
frames.concerns: Few women with agency; the oppressed group's leader is a terrorist, which some may read as delegitimizing minority resistance (my own framing; no source found).

frames.aligns: Human dignity without religion; reason and empathy defeat both the lab and the terrorist; Kei's medical calling; "human resilience" wins (Brown).
Rule of law against terror; loyalty, duty and courage (Kaito, Nakano); Sato defeated.
frames.concerns: The state is shown as abusive; little family warmth; gore.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth and dignity of every person, including Ajin; justice and compassion.
Kei's rational self-interest and refusal to be anyone's tool echo Church of Satan individualism; the state's control is resisted.
frames.concerns: The Eleven Rules condemn harming non-consenting others; Sato's sport killing breaks them.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Persons have worth the state must not violate (the labs are condemned); Sato's game-driven violence is not honor but play; Kei avoids fights for face.

Order vs freedom.evidence: State control is the main abuse (TV Tropes), but Sato's lawless "revolution" is condemned and ends in imprisonment (v17).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Kei's loyalties are personal (sister, Kaito, ch. 7); Nakano argues for strangers (ch. 43) and Kei finally fights for the public (ch. 48).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Teams form by skill, not rank; Tosaki's bureaucratic authority is shown as compromised.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Science, tactics and reason drive everything; religion is absent.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival, capture and security dominate; little room for self-expression.

folkways.japan: Ministry-led bureaucracy, a public that defers to official panic, the salaryman-style Tosaki, and school-and-career pressure on Kei (studying medicine) reflect contemporary Japanese settings more than a message aimed at readers elsewhere. The cluster match is loose (all distances above 3), because the story's values are shaped by an extreme survival plot.

delivery.evidence: Reviewers praise "complex morally gray protagonists" (Diabolical Plots) and Evil Versus Evil framing (TV Tropes); no review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Kei states his utilitarian logic aloud (ch. 43) and Nakano answers him, but most themes come through plot and tactics rather than speeches.

personified.ideology: Utilitarian self-interest; weighing lives
Life as a game; terrorism as liberation
Empathy and moral duty to strangers
State utilitarianism for the greater good

entry.dominant: Utilitarianism, Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued), Might makes right (critiqued), Critical theory, Secular humanism.

series.title: JoJo’s Bizarre Adventure: Part 8—JoJolion
series.romaji: JoJo no Kimyou na Bouken: JoJolion
series.native: ジョジョの奇妙な冒険 ジョジョリオン

entry.heading: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure Part 8: JoJolion
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is found in the people who choose you: identity is built from love, debt and loyalty, not only from blood or memory; healing has a price, and greed for a shortcut destroys families, while sacrifice for others breaks curses.

frames.aligns: Evil is not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7): the fruit trade and the child-sacrifice are shown as crimes and end in death. Josefumi gives his life for a friend (John 15:13, ch. 53); Mitsuba risks her life for her unborn child (ch. 82). Adoption and the family as the place of love.
frames.concerns: A curse cured by an "equivalent exchange" that kills another person (ch. 108) differs from redemption by grace; superstition (the "evil eye" ward, CCC 2111); uncensored nudity and a mind-controlled assault (CCC 2523); suicide attempt (CCC 2280-2283 counsels compassion).

frames.aligns: Ancestral sin and healing echo Orthodox talk of the ancestral curse and the need for healing; sacrificial love (ch. 53).
frames.concerns: Healing by bargain, not by grace; a sacrifice under a shrine (ch. 64); superstition; nepsis (guarding the senses) weighs the nudity and gore.

frames.aligns: Greed punished (1 Timothy 6:10, the fruit trade); a father's and a friend's love; sins have consequences.
frames.concerns: Phil 4:8 test: gore, adult nudity, an attempted assault, a suicide attempt. Superstition and curse-transfer by sacrifice. Soul liberty: each family decides.

frames.aligns: Engaging culture: a story where shortcuts to healing ruin families and self-giving love saves (ch. 53, 108). Depicts without endorsing.
frames.concerns: No gospel answer to the curse, only exchange and sacrifice; nudity and gore (Romans 14 conscience).

frames.aligns: A curse broken; good and evil clear.
frames.concerns: Generational curses taken literally, a child buried as a sacrifice under a shrine (ch. 64), "evil eye" rituals (ch. 23), a supernatural "calamity" that hunts people (ch. 84-104): many would see an "open door."

frames.aligns: Common grace lets families value the craft; Araki's question of inherited sin is a strong talking point. Idolatry of wealth and health judged.
frames.concerns: Westminster Larger Catechism Q139 (lascivious pictures): the uncensored nudity; superstition; gore.

frames.aligns: Vocation of father and mother shown in love and in failure; sin bound up with family.
frames.concerns: A curse broken by a trade, not a gift; nudity and gore. LCMS and WELS more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Social holiness: a cure sold only to the rich (ch. 50) is condemned; love of neighbor in Josefumi and Josuke.
frames.concerns: Gore, nudity, suicide attempt; holiness churches more cautious (General Rules on diversions).

frames.aligns: Judged by framing: greed and murder lead to ruin; love redeems. Imaginative depth (Lewis tradition).
Wealth and worldly power shown as corrupting; self-giving love.
frames.concerns: Violence is the heroes' tool; a child causes a man's death by a trick (ch. 42); separation from the world weighs the whole.

frames.aligns: Families across generations; adoption; Mitsuba's sacrifice for her unborn child (ch. 82); agency in choosing who to be (Josuke).
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth: uncensored nudity, an attempted assault, gore.

frames.aligns: A cure sold only to the rich and a hospital that hides abuse are critiqued; disaster survivors; found family.
frames.concerns: Graphic violence; the attempted assault used as a plot twist; a suicide attempt told briefly.

frames.aligns: Health and healing valued; greed condemned.
frames.concerns: Curses, a shrine sacrifice and supernatural calamity; "by beholding we become changed" weighs the gore and nudity; Fundamental Belief 22 on entertainment.
Spiritism-like curse ritual and sacrifice (ch. 64), constant violence (Psalm 11:5), nudity; jw.org counsel weighs these heavily.

frames.aligns: A disease belief ("curse") passed down and finally broken; fear overcome.
frames.concerns: Disease, stone and body decay treated as overwhelmingly real; medicine and a hospital central; body horror.

frames.aligns: Ezekiel 18:20 (the son does not bear the father's iniquity) is a strong talking point against the curse's logic; murder for one's own child is condemned.
frames.concerns: Tzniut: uncensored nudity, a mind-controlled assault; a child sacrifice; superstition (darkhei ha-Emori). Many Haredi homes avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Inherited sin questioned; family loyalty and its limits; greed condemned.
frames.concerns: Nudity and gore; no antisemitic tropes reported.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam echoes: unequal access to healing, disaster recovery.
frames.concerns: Violence; the assault plot device. No antisemitic tropes reported.

frames.aligns: Each soul bears its own burden (Qur'an 6:164), set against a family curse; greed and murder punished; a mother's love for her unborn child.
frames.concerns: Lowering the gaze (24:30-31): uncensored nudity; superstition and a sacrifice to transfer a curse; gore.

frames.aligns: Karma: actions return (Jobin, Kaato, Toru); equivalent exchange as a karmic law; family duty (dharma).
frames.concerns: Tamasic content (gore, cruelty); a sacrifice to pass suffering to another.

frames.aligns: Craving (tanha) for a cure, wealth and status drives the villains; impermanence and memory (Toru: only "dreams and memories" remain, ch. 104); identity as a bundle without a fixed self (Josuke).
frames.concerns: First precept against the constant killing; a child killed for another's sake.

frames.aligns: Greed (lobh) and attachment (moh) shown as destructive; selfless service in Josefumi.
frames.concerns: Superstition the Gurus rejected (ritual wards, curses); violence; nudity.

frames.aligns: Unity of a family across difference; justice for those harmed by greed.
frames.concerns: Violence; nudity ("chaste and holy life"); superstition.

frames.aligns: Araki names the curse as kegare (impurity) passed from ancestors, and the story is about its cleansing; gratitude and sincerity (Josefumi's debt, ch. 50); renewal after disaster.
frames.concerns: A child buried beneath a shrine as a sacrifice (ch. 64) misuses a sacred place; blood and death (kegare) are constant.

frames.aligns: Land, plants and cycles of healing; the cost of power acknowledged (a kind of threefold return).
frames.concerns: "Harm none" against curse-transfer by sacrifice and constant violence; folk magic shown as superstition.
