frames.aligns: Personal responsibility; criminals in a hospital exposed.
frames.concerns: Memory loss and identity rewritten; constant killing; a plastic surgeon villain (ch. 77-82).

frames.aligns: Critique of cures sold to the rich; disaster survivors; a female co-lead and narrator; found family.
frames.concerns: The attempted assault under mind control; uncensored nudity; gender-crossing shown only as a superstitious ward; a suicide attempt told briefly.

frames.aligns: Identity built by choice and relationships; superstition and the curse shown as harmful; natural disaster without divine meaning (Toru: calamity makes "no distinction between right or wrong," ch. 104).
frames.concerns: Heavy violence; supernatural powers central as fiction.

frames.aligns: Family, inheritance, adoption, duty and sacrifice; greed and crime punished; a patriarch's household.
frames.concerns: Uncensored nudity; family elders who are criminals; gender-crossing ward; gore.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth (an amnesiac outsider taken in); justice in access to healing; free search for identity.
Self-determination: Josuke chooses who he is; superstition broken.
frames.concerns: Eleven Rules on harm to children: a child buried alive (ch. 64) and a child put at risk by the curse; heavy violence.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Family pride ("The Higashikata Family always wins," Tsurugi, ch. 91) and personal revenge (Ojiro, Kaato) are present, but pride leads Jobin to ruin (ch. 97).

Order vs freedom.evidence: The patriarch's rules (ch. 7) and family rituals constrain; Josuke and Yasuho act on their own; no state authority helps.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Kin and adopted kin come first; parents kill for children (ch. 64, 88); the story honors family love but condemns harming outsiders for it.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: A patriarch and an eldest son's rank (ch. 95) beside an adopted outsider's equal place (ch. 110).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: An inherited curse, rituals and ancestors' sins frame the story; superstition is questioned and medicine is distrusted.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Health, survival and the family business come first; quirky style and self-discovery lean toward expression.

folkways.japan: The household headed by a father with an eldest son's special rank, the idea of a family name to protect (Norisuke hiding Kaato's crime, ch. 58), kegare as an inherited impurity, and on (a debt of gratitude, Josefumi to Holy, ch. 50) reflect Japanese norms. The post-3/11 setting reflects Araki's own home region (Asahi Shimbun 2011).

delivery.evidence: CBR calls the final villain "an enigma"; a student review says "the villain sucks"; Araki calls JoJo "an ode to humanity."
delivery.note: Themes of curse, identity and the cost of healing come through plot and imagery, while the villains' views are stated briefly and left thin.

personified.ideology: Identity made from bonds and debts, not memory or blood
The strong survive, the weak are destroyed; family pride
Rock Human supremacy; calamity without right or wrong
Family first, even through murder

entry.dominant: Existentialism (identity, affirmed), Communitarianism (found family, affirmed), Classical virtue ethics (affirmed), Confucian ethics (explored through inherited sin and filial duty), with Might makes right, Utilitarianism and Consumerism critiqued.

entry.heading: Noragami: Stray God
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is one you choose, not one you were made for: you can turn from a violent past, take responsibility for the people bound to you, and keep faith with the ties (en) that make you real to others.

frames.aligns: Sin has real effects on others; confession, repentance and restoration (v3); a master who suffers for his servant; evil (Father) framed as evil. A Catholic blogger reads the blight as sin darkening the soul (Mage in a Barrel).
frames.concerns: Many gods shown as real and heroic; spirits of the dead bound and named by gods, read against CCC 2115-2117 on spiritism; light fan service.

frames.aligns: Repentance, the passions growing into monstrous form (Yukine's corruption), healing through community.
frames.concerns: Gods and spirit-binding shown as real; evil spirits taken as real in the tradition, so ayakashi and Izanami's underworld weigh more; syncretic religious world.

frames.aligns: Clear evil in Father; repentance and forgiveness; sacrifice for another.
frames.concerns: The heroes are gods of another religion, shown as real (John 14:6); spirits of the dead and underworld journeys (Deuteronomy 18:10-12). Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Beneath the Tangles reads Yato's sacrifice for Yukine as a reflection of Christ's and Yukine's arc as "sinner to saint."
frames.concerns: Exclusive claims of Christ against a polytheistic world; spirit contact; fan service.

frames.aligns: Real spiritual warfare and temptation; Beneath the Tangles reads Nora and Father as pictures of how evil blinds and traps.
frames.concerns: Other gods, spirit-binding of the dead, possession and an underworld are the whole frame and are shown as good or neutral; media as an "open door."

frames.aligns: Sin is serious and affects others; the creature cannot cleanse itself (Yukine needs others). Common grace lets families value good art by non-Christians.
frames.concerns: Other religions as false worship, here shown as real; Heaven's courts as a picture of divine authority are arbitrary.

frames.aligns: Law and gospel echoes: the sin is exposed, confessed and forgiven. A god bearing a servant's sin.
frames.concerns: Other gods shown as real (Large Catechism on the First Commandment). LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Growth in holiness: Yukine changes from spoiled to faithful. Works of mercy for outcasts (Ebisu's strays).
frames.concerns: Occult and spirit motifs; polytheism. Holiness churches more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: Fantasy in a tradition of myth-making (C.S. Lewis); repentance and costly love.
frames.concerns: Other gods shown as real; spiritism motifs. Episcopal and ACNA families differ little on this.
Polytheism and spirits; sword-fighting as the hero's job; conservative groups avoid most such media.

frames.aligns: Agency: Yato chooses who he will be; family ties and repentance; service.
frames.concerns: Other gods; spirits of the dead bound to service; fan service. Members vary.

frames.aligns: Empathy for outcasts and strays; critique of harsh authority; abuse named as evil; gender-role reversals (Flis 2018).
frames.concerns: Fan service; Hiyori's shrinking role debated by fans; the 2015 soundtrack's misuse of the Islamic call to prayer (anime only).

frames.aligns: Repentance and changed life; love for others.
frames.concerns: The dead are unconscious until the resurrection, so spirits of the dead serving as shinki (the core premise) conflicts with teaching on the state of the dead; spiritism.
Spiritism and other gods are the premise; worship of false gods presented positively (Galatians 5:19-21).
Evil, sin, death and fear shown as powerful realities; spirits and sorcery as real.

frames.aligns: Repentance (teshuvah) and responsibility for others; abuse condemned.
frames.concerns: Avodah zarah: other gods are the heroes and are worshipped approvingly; necromancy-like binding of the dead (Deuteronomy 18:10-11); bath scenes and tzniut.

frames.aligns: Teshuvah; protecting the vulnerable; critique of unjust courts.
frames.concerns: Other gods presented as real; modesty values applied by families.

frames.aligns: Repentance, justice for outcasts, informed choice.
frames.concerns: Polytheism as fiction; light fan service.

frames.aligns: Repentance (tawba), responsibility for one's deeds, loyalty, care for the weak.
frames.concerns: Shirk: many gods are real and are the heroes; magic and spirit-binding; bath scenes (Qur'an 24:30-31). The anime's second soundtrack misused the adhan and was recalled with an apology (ANN, 2015).

frames.aligns: Many deities, reincarnation of gods (Ebisu reborn, ch. 38), karma-like consequences (the blight), duty of master and servant.
frames.concerns: Few message conflicts; some families may dislike comic treatment of deities.

frames.aligns: Bishamonten and other Buddhist-derived deities; attachment to past and memory (Yato, Yukine); impermanence; rebirth; compassion for strays.
frames.concerns: Bishamonten recast as a woman and a sword-wielding war god (ANN feature notes the liberty); killing as a solution.

frames.aligns: Seva and loyalty; the five vices (anger, greed, lust) shown in Yukine and condemned; repentance.
frames.concerns: The Gurus rejected magic and superstition; many gods shown as real.
Spiritualism discouraged; violence as the heroes' tool.

frames.aligns: Kami in daily life; five-yen offerings (go-en, "ties"); a hand-made shrine (ch. 26); ablution as purification of kegare; sincerity (makoto) and gratitude; Tenjin, Ebisu and Izanami drawn from myth (ANN feature).
frames.concerns: Comic, even mocking treatment of gods; Amaterasu, the ancestral kami of Ise, shown as a remote and severe ruler who executes gods (ch. 35, 70-72). Shrine-minded families may note this; most Japanese readers accept it (from general knowledge; to verify).

frames.aligns: Respectful polytheism; spirits and gods part of the world; no demonizing of pagan gods.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; spirit-binding of the dead may give some pause.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness precepts: help others, be trustworthy, do not murder (Yato turns from killing).
Critique of arbitrary authority; abuse named; gender-role reversals and a female war god (Flis 2018); empathy for strays.
frames.concerns: Fan service; Hiyori's shrinking role; Father's non-consensual kiss; the dated slur in the English vol. 1 (Manga Librarian).

frames.aligns: Meaning comes from relationships and choices; a made being rejects his maker's purpose; abuse and its effects taken seriously.
frames.concerns: Gods and spirits are real in the story (read as fiction); suicide themes need care.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, responsibility, repentance, keeping one's word, protecting others.
frames.concerns: Irreverent tone toward authority and gods; gender-role reversals; rebellion against Heaven vindicated.

frames.aligns: Worth of every being, even strays and outcasts; pluralism; justice against harsh courts.
Rebellion against an arbitrary Heaven; a created being who refuses his maker's will; compassion and justice (Satanic Temple Tenets 1 and 2).
frames.concerns: Loyalty and self-sacrifice prized over self-interest.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Bishamon's long vendetta against Yato is shown as a mistake she lets go once she learns the truth (fan wiki); Yato answers insults with comedy more than revenge. Loyalty to one's household carries some honor weight.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The god-shinki household keeps rules and names, and sin must be purified (v3); but Heaven's order is challenged and Yato's defiance is vindicated (ch. 70-72).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Chosen family is central: Yato, Yukine and Hiyori; Kofuku and Daikoku; Bishamon's shinki "family." Heaven, the civic order, is distant and harsh.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Gods name and own shinki, and Heaven ranks gods; Yato treats Yukine more as a partner, and Heaven's classism is played for comedy (ANN feature).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Kami, shrines, offerings, purification and the underworld are real within the story and treated warmly (ch. 5, 26, 30-35).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Yato's struggle to exist and be remembered (survival) sits beside his choice to remake himself and Hiyori's freedom from gender expectations (self-expression).

folkways.japan: Shrine offerings, ties (en), purification of impurity (kegare), master-retainer household loyalty and the casual, affectionate humor toward kami are Japanese religious and social norms the story takes for granted; readers from other cultures may see them as setting more than message.

delivery.evidence: Kotaku praises its arcs about letting go of the past; no review opened calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its message about choosing who you become is carried by plot and character arcs, with comedy keeping speeches short.

personified.ideology: Redemption by choice, not by origin
A maker owns and uses what he makes
Order kept by swift judgment
Control the dangerous for the common good

entry.dominant: Pagan/occult (Shinto folk), Existentialism, Classical virtue ethics, Communitarianism, Dharmic.

series.title: That Time I Got Reincarnated as a Slime
series.native: 転生したらスライムだった件

entry.heading: That Time I Got Reincarnated as a Slime
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is building a home where very different people can live together in peace, through friendship, hard work and fair dealing, protected by a ruler strong enough to deter anyone who would destroy it.

content.frequency: Frequent in the war arcs; low in nation-building stretches
content.framing: Shown with consequences (attack on Tempest); largely endorsed (Rimuru's retaliation)

frames.aligns: Hospitality to the stranger and outsider; forgiveness of enemies (orcs, lizardmen); care for orphaned children; the common good as Rimuru's goal.
frames.concerns: Killing soldiers to harvest souls treats persons as means; the just-war limits on non-combatants and the fleeing (CCC 2309-2314) are not observed. Inter Mirifica 7 asks that evil not be made attractive, and the massacre is shown as Rimuru's triumph. Demon summoning, though fantasy, is judged by framing (CCC 2115-2117). The only church is corrupt.

frames.aligns: Hospitality and reconciliation between peoples; humility of the early Rimuru.
frames.concerns: Watchfulness (nepsis) weighs the demonic: the hero takes the title "Demon Lord" and binds a demon to his service from the bodies of the slain. Vengeance and the harvest of souls are shown without repentance. Reincarnation contradicts the tradition's teaching on death and judgment.

frames.aligns: Kindness, hard work, fair dealing, building a peaceful community.
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 test: the massacre and the demonic titles and servants. Vengeance is shown as justified (Romans 12:19). Reincarnation premise (Hebrews 9:27). Soul liberty: each family decides.

frames.aligns: Love for outsiders; Beneath the Tangles finds a reflection on hunger for God in Rimuru's eating. Depicting sin is not endorsing it, for many families.
frames.concerns: Here the story does largely endorse its hero's mass killing; demonic imagery treated lightly; the corrupt church as the only faith.

frames.aligns: Courage, friendship, care for the weak.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": the hero is a Demon Lord, summons and names demons who serve him, harvests souls and revives the dead by a sacrificial process, all presented positively. Views vary by church.

frames.aligns: Common grace: good order, labor and craft (Kuyper's vocation and culture-building echoes in Tempest).
frames.concerns: Mass killing presented as just retribution without lawful authority's restraint; the Westminster teaching on the sixth commandment; reincarnation; corrupt church.

frames.aligns: Vocation: Rimuru's practical service as a "boss"; two kingdoms echoed in a ruler who protects his people.
frames.concerns: The sword used for revenge and power gain rather than lawful defense; demonic powers made friendly. LCMS and WELS families tend to be more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy, social holiness, education of orphaned children.
frames.concerns: Vengeance and the harvest of souls without repentance; demon servants. Holiness churches are more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: Imaginative fantasy tradition (Lewis); reconciliation of peoples.
frames.concerns: Just-war limits (Article 37 permits lawful war, not soul harvesting); evil framed as good at the turning point.

frames.aligns: Peaceful community-building and hospitality in the early chapters; Tempest's citizens are "martial pacifists."
frames.concerns: Violence shown as heroic is the central concern, and here the peaceful nation's survival is credited to overwhelming force and a massacre (Matthew 5:39, 44). Conservative groups avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Industry, education, building Zion-like community, family-like bonds.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth asks whether media invites the Spirit: a hero who becomes a Demon Lord, summons demons and kills thousands. Members vary in strictness.

frames.aligns: Welcome for the outsider and the "monstrous"; opposition to binding summoned people like slaves.
frames.concerns: Rule by one strong man; collective punishment of conscripts; fan service; colonial "civilizing" echo (Oliveros).

frames.aligns: Healthy community, hard work, care for the young.
frames.concerns: The dead are unconscious until the resurrection, so harvesting souls, preserving them (Shuna) and reviving them by a Demon Lord's power conflicts with teaching on the state of the dead; demon summoning.

frames.aligns: Peace between peoples, honesty in trade.
frames.concerns: jw.org's questions on violence (Psalm 11:5) and spiritism (Galatians 5:19-21): demons, magic, summoning and soul harvesting are central; the hero's title is Demon Lord.

frames.aligns: Love, harmony and cooperation outlast hostility; Rimuru's good will toward all.
frames.concerns: Evil, death and fear are shown as powerful and real, and death is undone by a magical power gained through killing, against the teaching that these are not part of God's creation.

frames.aligns: Hospitality to strangers; honest commerce; communal responsibility.
frames.concerns: Killing beyond what self-defense requires (the law of the pursuer, rodef, ends when the threat ends); demonic and necromantic themes; fan service and tzniut. Many Haredi homes restrict such media.

frames.aligns: Welcoming the stranger; building a just society; tikkun olam echoes.
frames.concerns: Mass killing framed as justified; resurrection through killing.

frames.aligns: Inclusion of outsiders; opposition to slavery-like binding; diversity.
Justice for the wronged, protection of one's people, generosity and fair trade.
frames.concerns: Islamic rules of war forbid killing those who flee or surrender and limit retaliation (Qur'an 2:190, "do not transgress"); magic and summoning jinn-like demons; the hero's title; fan service and lowering the gaze (24:30-31).

frames.aligns: Rebirth premise; a king (raja) protecting his subjects as dharma; respect for many kinds of beings.
frames.concerns: Killing to gain power (asuric conduct in Gita ch. 16 terms) rather than for dharma; a Demon Lord as hero.

frames.aligns: Rebirth premise; kindness, non-discrimination toward all beings; letting go of grudges toward former enemies.
frames.concerns: Killing thousands to bring back loved ones is attachment and craving in Buddhist terms; first precept; no karmic consequence.

frames.aligns: Defense of the oppressed; service (seva); equal treatment of all peoples.
frames.concerns: The response turns to anger (krodh) and ego (ahankar), two of the five vices, presented as admirable.

frames.aligns: Unity of diverse peoples is the series' strongest ideal: many species in one federation, a summit of monsters and humans.
frames.concerns: Commitment to peace and consultation: Tempest's peace rests on a massacre and one ruler's will.

frames.aligns: Spirits and non-human beings respected; harmony (wa) of the community; festivals (Tempest Revival Festival, ch. 69).
frames.concerns: Death and blood bring impurity (kegare); the harvest of souls.

frames.aligns: Magic, spirits and many kinds of beings treated with respect; no stereotyping of witches.
frames.concerns: "Harm none": the massacre and magic used for power gain.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness: be industrious, help others, keep promises.
frames.concerns: "Do not murder" precept against the massacre.

frames.aligns: Inclusion of outsiders and different species; opposition to slavery-like summoning (praised by Anime Feminist).
frames.concerns: Autocracy and rule by strength (Cserkits); collective punishment; colonial echo (Oliveros); the ch. 1 sexual joke (Anime Feminist); fan service around Shion and Milim.

frames.aligns: Reason, education, problem-solving, cooperation across differences; reincarnation and magic read as fiction.
frames.concerns: Using people as means; cruelty in the slow killing (ANN); no accountability for the ruler.

frames.aligns: Order, loyalty, a strong protective leader, defense of one's nation, hard work, commerce.
frames.concerns: The massacre goes beyond just-war limits; the corrupt church as the only religion; fan service and gender ambiguity for some families.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of every being, monster or human; justice for the exploited; free search for truth.
frames.concerns: Worth of the Falmuth soldiers ignored; autocracy; fan service.

frames.aligns: Self-determination, retaliation against aggressors and rejection of a corrupt church fit Church of Satan texts (the Eleven Rules say to destroy one who will not stop bothering you); rebellious "demon" hero.
frames.concerns: The Satanic Temple's Tenets on compassion and justice weigh against killing conscripts.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Attacks on Tempest are answered personally and overwhelmingly: the Falmuth massacre (ch. 64-66) and Clayman's death after he strikes Milim and insults Rimuru (ch. 78 onward). Early on, Rimuru forgives defeated foes.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Rimuru's rules shape Tempest (a ban on attacking humans before Falmuth, likely; to verify), with ranks and assigned duties; species may keep their ways under him.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Equal kindness to every citizen is the stated ideal (TV Tropes), but the turning point puts Rimuru's own people above thousands of outsiders (ANN: "sacrificing strangers to save those close to you").

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Named followers form a ranked court; Rimuru's word is final; followers revere him (Diablo, Shion).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Modern knowledge, engineering and planning drive progress; the one religious institution is corrupt.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Security comes first in the war arcs, but food, festivals, baths, tolerance and quality of life are the rewards of the nation.

folkways.japan: Rimuru as an idealized company boss, a loyal inner circle, consensus-minded management and the pleasure taken in food and bath culture reflect Japanese workplace and everyday norms; many readers outside Japan may read these as setting rather than message.

delivery.evidence: ANN's Eisenbeis says the show asks viewers to side with Rimuru and fails; TV Tropes notes a "Strawman Has a Point" reading of Falmuth.
delivery.note: Its ideals of coexistence and benevolent rule are shown through Rimuru's choices and his followers' praise more than through speeches.

personified.ideology: Benevolent rule backed by overwhelming power

personified.character: King Edmaris and the Falmuth army
personified.ideology: Human supremacy and fear of monsters
Domination through manipulation
Nihilism: destroy the world to remake it

lenses.label: Might makes right
lenses.stance: Explored (rejected as a creed by villains, practiced by the hero)

entry.dominant: Collectivism/authoritarianism, Communitarianism, Pragmatism, Utilitarianism, Might makes right.

entry.heading: Rent-A-Girlfriend (Reiji Miyajima)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life means loving someone sincerely and showing up for them, even when the relationship started as a paid act. Lies told for others can hide a truth, but they have to be faced in the end.

content.framing: Neutral to played for comedy (fan service and Kazuya's lust); Explored (paid intimacy)
Mixed: deception is sustained and partly excused, then exposed

content.frequency: Pervasive (premise) and recurring outside the book

frames.aligns: Self-giving love in the film project; honor for grandparents; sincere love sought, not just bought.
frames.concerns: Long deception of family (CCC 2482-2486 on lying); lust and masturbation as comedy (CCC 2351-2352); explicit fantasy (ch. 218); fan service (CCC 2521-2524 on modesty). Inter Mirifica 7: are the wrongs made attractive?

frames.aligns: Care for the dying and the dead (Sayuri); Kazuya's slow repentance.
frames.concerns: Nepsis (guarding the senses) against frequent fan service and the ch. 218 fantasy; deception of elders.

frames.aligns: Hard work and sacrifice for another; grandparents honored.
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 test on fan service and sexual humor; lying to parents (Ephesians 6:1-3); paid intimacy. Soul liberty leaves the call to families.

frames.aligns: Depicts Kazuya's failings as failings; grace-like care (Beneath the Tangles reads Chizuru's kindness as a picture of undeserved grace).
frames.concerns: Lust as running gag; deception sustained for comedy; the commodified "girlfriend." Engage-or-separate views differ.

frames.aligns: Restoration of broken people (Chizuru's grief, Kazuya's growth).
frames.concerns: Holiness standards on modesty and sexual thoughts; worldliness of the rental world. Little occult content, so the "open door" concern is low.

frames.aligns: Common grace in sacrificial work and family love; vocation (Chizuru's acting).
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 lists "lascivious... pictures" and "lascivious... books": fan service and ch. 218; ninth-commandment concerns about the lie (WLC Q145).

frames.aligns: Vocation and daily work; care for the neighbor (the dying grandmother).
frames.concerns: Sixth Commandment ("sexually pure and decent life") against the fan service and gags; Eighth Commandment on false witness; LCMS and WELS more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy for the dying; perseverance.
frames.concerns: Wesley's rule against books that do not "tend to the knowledge or love of God"; holiness churches avoid the sexual comedy; UMC families vary.

frames.aligns: Judged by framing: Kazuya's flaws are exposed and he grows; self-giving love in the film arc.
frames.concerns: Fan service and sexual humor; how long the lie goes unexamined.

frames.aligns: Care for elders; simple sacrificial work.
frames.concerns: Separation from worldly media; sexualized content; a premise built on paid romance and display; the franchise. MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Family, grandparents, marriage hoped for; developing talents (acting).
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth on entertainment that invites the Spirit; law of chastity and its counsel on sexual thoughts and masturbation, both played for comedy; honesty in the temple standards.

frames.aligns: Loneliness treated with compassion; women's own goals honored (Chizuru's career, ch. 380).
frames.concerns: Male entitlement played for laughs (ANN's Silverman); the dignity of workers in a rating-based companionship trade.
Fundamental Belief 22 on entertainment "of the highest quality"; "by beholding we become changed" weighs on fan service and sexual fantasy.

frames.aligns: Honest work; family loyalty in the end.
frames.concerns: jw.org counsel against entertainment featuring immorality and "uncleanness" (Galatians 5:19-21); dating not aimed at marriage; deception.

frames.aligns: Grief and loneliness answered by love and effort; Chizuru learns to accept help.
frames.concerns: Dwelling on lust, jealousy and deceit as mental influences.

frames.aligns: Kibbud av va'em in the wish to comfort grandparents; chesed in the film project.
frames.concerns: Tzniut and shmirat einayim against the fan service; lying to parents (midvar sheker tirchak); sexual humor (nivul peh). Many families would not keep it at home.

frames.aligns: Chesed, family devotion, mourning and remembering the dead.
frames.concerns: Modesty; the long deception; sexual humor. Families apply values case by case.

frames.aligns: Compassion for loneliness; growth; women's autonomy.
frames.concerns: Consent and objectification in the fan service; informed autonomy leaves it to families.

frames.aligns: Honor of elders; marriage as the hoped-for end; care for the dying.
frames.concerns: Lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) against frequent fan service; unchaperoned dating and kissing; images of the body; lying to family.

frames.aligns: Duty to elders (dharma); devotion and sacrifice for another's dream.
frames.concerns: Some apply the Gita's rajasic and tamasic categories to sensual media; kama outside dharma; satya (truth) broken.

frames.aligns: A clear look at craving, attachment and loneliness; compassion for the dying; letting go (Chizuru's grief).
frames.concerns: Right speech (the long lie); sensual imagery as feed for the mind.

frames.aligns: Seva in the film project; kirat karni (Chizuru works for her dream).
frames.concerns: Kaam (lust) played for comedy; moh (attachment) and ego in rivalry; deception.
The call to a "chaste and holy life" against the sexual comedy; truthfulness as "the foundation of all human virtues" (to verify wording).

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) as the story's goal; gratitude to elders; mourning Sayuri.
frames.concerns: Little doctrinal concern; insincerity of the rental act.

frames.aligns: Self-discovery; love freely chosen; Chizuru's right to say "not now."
frames.concerns: Harm-none questions on deceiving the dying and on Ruka's blackmail.

frames.aligns: Competence and work ethic (the film); communication repairing relationships.
frames.concerns: The Way to Happiness precepts on honesty and on being worthy of trust.

frames.aligns: Chizuru's agency and career first (Anime Feminist: "her own agency"); the ch. 380 debate on whether kindness obligates a woman; loneliness without shame.
frames.concerns: Kazuya's early sexism and entitlement (ANN's Silverman; Kotaku's Colbert); male-gaze fan service; stigma around companionship work; slapstick violence by women as a joke.

frames.aligns: Meaning made through human relationships and creative work; no supernatural framing; candor about loneliness.
frames.concerns: Critical thinking about paid intimacy and how the genre shows women.

frames.aligns: Respect for grandparents; one-woman devotion; marriage hoped for; hard work as proof of love.
frames.concerns: Lying to elders; casual sexual humor and fan service; commodified romance; a heroine who puts career before marriage (ch. 380), which some traditional readers would read as a cost.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of rental workers as "real people" (Miyajima, Kodansha interview); compassion for the lonely.
frames.concerns: Objectification in fan service; consent in Ruka's blackmail.

frames.aligns: Self-directed choices (Chizuru's career); candor about desire; no religious guilt.
frames.concerns: Ruka's blackmail and Mami's manipulation; the Eleven Rules' stress on honest dealing.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: The lie exists to save face before family and friends (ch. 1-3); but disputes are settled by talk, not retaliation, and Kazuya's apology (ep. 1) and confessions (ch. 174, 380) are prized.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The rental contract (no sex, star ratings; Anime Feminist) frames the job; adults otherwise choose their own work, dates and living arrangements (cohabitation, ch. 256-261).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Grandmothers drive the plot; the film is made for Sayuri (ch. 146-152); Chizuru says she loves Kazuya's family (ch. 380).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Peers interact as equals; elders are respected but deceived; a father's blow (ch. 55) is not endorsed.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Secular urban life, app dating, crowdfunding; tradition appears as family expectation, not as a guide.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Chizuru works to fund her dream; acting, film-making and romance as self-fulfillment are the celebrated goals.

folkways.japan: The real rental-companion industry, family pressure to show a partner, the family-run shop, deference to grandparents, a father's physical discipline (ch. 55; TV Tropes notes it reads differently in Japan) and the shōnen-magazine harem convention are Japanese settings and norms that frame the story rather than form its message.

delivery.evidence: Reviewers debate whether it critiques or indulges Kazuya; Aftermath calls it "narrative purgatory"; Anime Feminist says Chizuru is "treated with due respect."
delivery.note: Its ideas about loneliness, paid intimacy and honesty come through situation comedy and long arcs, and the story rarely states a verdict outright.

personified.ideology: Sincere devotion as the answer to loneliness
Self-reliance and career before romance
Pursue your dream; lies that protect a truth
Manipulative self-interest in love

lenses.label: Feminism
lenses.stance: Explored (by critics and the ch. 380 debate)

entry.dominant: Consumerism, Expressive individualism, Pragmatism.

entry.heading: Ao Haru Ride (Blue Spring Ride)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life means being honest about who you are and what you feel, even when it costs you friends or safety. Grief and fear of loss must be faced, not hidden, and real friends are the ones who see you clearly.

content.framing: Shown with consequences (healed through honesty and connection)

frames.aligns: Truthfulness; mercy for the grieving; reconciliation of a broken family (honor of parents, CCC 2214-2220); a teacher who keeps a proper boundary.
frames.concerns: Romance led by feeling rather than ordered toward marriage; the forceful kiss and pin-down left unexamined (chastity, CCC 2337-2359).

frames.aligns: Repentance as turning around: Futaba leaves pretense, Kou leaves his coldness; healing through communion with others.
frames.concerns: Passions stirred by romance; guarding the senses (nepsis) applied to the kissing and pinning scenes.

frames.aligns: Honesty, standing up for the bullied, reconciliation with father and brother (Ephesians 6:1-4).
frames.concerns: Teen dating with no aim at marriage; a forceful kiss. Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Beneath the Tangles reads it as a picture of God moving us out of comfort zones (Twwk) and of the fall and the gathered church (Gaheret). Friendship as defending others "out of love and compassion and justice" (Twwk).
frames.concerns: Romance outside a faith frame; the forceful kiss.

frames.aligns: Restoration of the broken-hearted; joy and community among misfits.
frames.concerns: Holiness standards on dating and physical affection. No occult content.

frames.aligns: Common grace allows a well-made story by non-Christians; honesty and confession of fault.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 on what stirs desire, applied to the kissing and pinning scenes.

frames.aligns: Entertainment as adiaphora; forgiveness and reconciliation in family; vocation of a teacher who keeps his duty.
frames.concerns: The Sixth Commandment and the forceful kiss; LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy: friends carrying a grieving boy; inclusion of the bullied girl (v1).
frames.concerns: Holiness churches more cautious about dating content than UMC.

frames.aligns: Judged by framing: honesty and mercy win; a literary tradition that reads romance generously.
frames.concerns: The forceful kiss; Episcopal and ACNA families differ mainly on dating norms.

frames.aligns: Humility, peaceable friendship, forgiveness, care for the grieving.
frames.concerns: Separation from worldly media makes popular romance a concern for conservative groups; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Family repair; service; honesty; a teacher's restraint.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth counsels against steady dating in early teens; the forceful kiss.

frames.aligns: Welcome of outsiders; grief and mental health taken seriously; female friendship and its pressures explored.
frames.concerns: Consent: the forceful kiss and pin-down are not challenged; heteronormativity (Hopper, ANN).

frames.aligns: Kindness, family reconciliation, care for the sick.
frames.concerns: Fundamental Belief 22 on entertainment "of the highest quality"; romance-centered media weighed by families.
Dating as teens with no marriage aim runs against jw.org counsel on dating; the forceful kiss. No spiritism.

frames.aligns: Love and honest affection heal grief and fear; Kou is freed from his false belief that love only hurts.
frames.concerns: Dwelling on illness and death in flashback.

frames.aligns: Honoring parents, comforting mourners, a teacher who keeps a boundary.
frames.concerns: Tzniut: mixed-sex teen romance, kissing and touching are the premise; many Haredi homes restrict such media.

frames.aligns: Comforting mourners; family repair; dignity of the excluded.
frames.concerns: Sexual ethics for teens; consent in the forceful kiss.

frames.aligns: Emotional honesty, inclusion, mourning taken seriously, family repair.
frames.concerns: Consent in the forceful kiss; left to family values.

frames.aligns: Patience (sabr) in grief, honesty, mercy, family ties restored (silat al-rahim).
frames.concerns: The premise is unchaperoned teen romance; lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) for kissing and touching scenes.

frames.aligns: Family dharma restored; seva among friends; acceptance of death and moving on.
frames.concerns: Teen romance against brahmacharya for students; some families judge by sattvic and rajasic qualities.

frames.aligns: Grief and clinging (Kou to guilt, Yui to Kou) shown as suffering that ends with letting go; right speech in honest apology.
frames.concerns: Third precept read differently by communities; little else.

frames.aligns: Honest living, seva, acceptance of loss (hukam), family reconciliation.
frames.concerns: Kaam (lust) among the five vices; teen romance as premise.

frames.aligns: Truthfulness, unity among friends, service, family harmony.
frames.concerns: The call to a "chaste and holy life"; parental consent to marriage is central, and parents are mostly absent from the romance.

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) is the story's core virtue; a shrine framing the story's start and end; harmony restored in the group.
Authenticity and self-acceptance; no stereotyping of pagans.
frames.concerns: Consent in the forceful kiss ("harm none").

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness: honor and help your parents; be worthy of trust; problems solved by communication.
Anti-bullying, emotional honesty, grief and mental health taken seriously, female friendship explored.
frames.concerns: Consent: forceful kiss (ch. 21) and pin-down treated as romance; heteronormativity (Hopper); Kou's "cold and cruel" swings (Hopper). Common Sense-style age guidance not available.

frames.aligns: Meaning built from honest relationships; grief faced in this life; no supernatural framing.
frames.concerns: Grief resolved mainly through love and friends, without counseling.

frames.aligns: Honesty, loyalty, a teacher who respects his role, family repaired after divorce.
frames.concerns: Teen romance without a marriage frame; divorce's damage shown but not argued; consent questions.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of the outcast (the bullied classmate); compassion for the grieving; free search for one's true self.
frames.concerns: Consent in the forceful kiss; heteronormativity.

frames.aligns: Self-honesty over social pretense; individual authenticity against the clique.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; the story's focus on reconciling with family and dutiful restraint sits apart from Church of Satan individualism.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: No defense of honor; conflicts are resolved by talking and apology (Silverman praises the communication).

Order vs freedom.evidence: The story celebrates breaking from clique rules to be oneself (v1), while teachers' boundaries are respected (Yoichi and Shuko, v7).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Chosen friends carry most of the emotional weight, but repairing family (Kou with brother and father, likely v4; the Tanaka name, v13) is a goal.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Peer friendships are flat; a senpai-kohai or teacher line is kept but not revered.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Secular everyday life; the shrine is a setting, not a faith.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Self-expression, emotional honesty and acceptance of others are the highest goods.

folkways.japan: The pressure to fit in with a girls' group, school-trip and festival rituals, and teacher-student formality reflect Japanese school norms; the story's push toward speaking one's mind is set against those norms rather than taken from them.

delivery.evidence: Reviewers praise realism; Hopper (ANN) calls its high school personas "spot on." No review opened calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its message about honesty is spoken in Futaba's narration and confrontations but mostly shown through slow character change.

personified.ideology: Authenticity over conformity
Self-protection by closing off from love
Conformity and exclusion
Duty and restraint

entry.dominant: Expressive individualism, Classical virtue ethics, Communitarianism, Secular humanism.

entry.heading: Mashle: Magic and Muscles
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is a quiet one: protect your family, be kind, work hard, enjoy simple pleasures (cream puffs), and judge people by what they do, not by the gifts they were born with.

content.framing: Neutral (mostly slapstick); shown with consequences in late arcs

frames.aligns: Dignity of every human life against a state that culls the "unfit"; adoptive fatherhood; humility; forgiveness of the enemy. Fantasy magic as setting is "often tolerated, and judged by how it is framed."
frames.concerns: Wand magic is everywhere (CCC 2115-2117 forbid real magic, not its depiction); "gift from God" used by elites to rank people.

frames.aligns: Humility against pride; a villain's attempt at self-deification fails (ch. 155), the opposite of theosis by grace; mercy to the enemy.
frames.concerns: Sorcery is condemned in the tradition and magic is the world's norm; gods summoned as spells (Poseidon). Watchfulness (nepsis) may weigh the constant magic imagery.

frames.aligns: Humble hero, hard work, honoring a father (Ephesians 6:1-2), every person valued.
frames.concerns: Deuteronomy 18:10-12 makes many families cautious about wands, spells and potions, even played for laughs; Harry Potter parody may echo earlier Harry Potter debates.

frames.aligns: Worth not earned by gifts; the outsider accepted; forgiveness; humility (Mash declines the title). Depicts magic as fantasy without spirit contact.
frames.concerns: Spells and wand magic; "God's chosen" title tied to power; villain seeking godhood.

frames.aligns: A hero with no magic who wins by faithfulness and effort; pride brought low.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": constant spellcasting and summoned "gods," though no demons or spirit contact; views vary widely.

frames.aligns: Common grace in a comic fantasy; human pride and self-deification exposed (ch. 155); dignity of the weak.
frames.concerns: Occult practice is forbidden, though fantasy is judged by framing; "Divine Visionary" uses sacred language for a political title.

frames.aligns: Worth not earned (an echo of grace, not works); vocation as ordinary work (Mash's bakery dream, ch. 162).
frames.concerns: Magic as setting; LCMS and WELS families tend to be more cautious.

frames.aligns: Care for the excluded, social holiness, humility.
frames.concerns: Occult forbidden, fantasy generally accepted; holiness churches more cautious.

frames.aligns: Fantasy judged by framing, in a tradition that loves imaginative literature; justice for the outcast.
Humility, simple living, forgiveness of enemies, distrust of state coercion.
frames.concerns: Violence (mostly slapstick) is still the hero's main tool; conservative groups avoid most popular media.

frames.aligns: Family as central; adoption honored; work and self-reliance; fantasy commonly enjoyed.
Clear critique of structural discrimination and state violence against the "unfit"; inclusion of the outsider.
Health and physical discipline, family, humility.
frames.concerns: Spiritualism is strongly rejected; magic here is spells, not spirits of the dead, so the concern is lighter than in spirit-heavy series.

frames.aligns: Love of family, kindness, humility, rejection of pride.
frames.concerns: jw.org counsel firmly rejects magic in entertainment; spells, potions and summoned gods fill the setting, even if the hero has none.

frames.aligns: Goodness and love outlast a power-hungry villain; worth is not material status.
frames.concerns: Magic and "animal magnetism" type powers treated as real forces in the story.

frames.aligns: Every person created in God's image; honoring parents (Exodus 20:12); humility.
frames.concerns: Sorcery forbidden (Deuteronomy 18:10-11); Haredi families often avoid fantasy magic, Modern Orthodox more accepting.

frames.aligns: Dignity of every person; justice for the persecuted; memory of persecution resonates.
frames.concerns: Sorcery forbidden in practice, fantasy accepted.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam; protecting the vulnerable; anti-discrimination.
Honoring parents, care for an orphan (adoption-like guardianship praised), humility, rejecting pride by birth (Qur'an 49:13).
frames.concerns: Sihr is forbidden and magic is the world's norm, though not shown as devil-sourced; a man seeking godhood; "gift from God" used for status.

frames.aligns: Devotion to a parent; dharma of protecting family; humility.
frames.concerns: Birth-based ranking is satirized, which some families may relate to debates on caste; most modern Hindu teachers reject untouchability.

frames.aligns: Rejects worth by birth, echoing the Buddha's teaching that one is noble by deeds, not birth (Vasala Sutta); contentment; forgiveness.
Equality of all people and rejection of caste are core Sikh teachings; humility; family; honest work (Mash's bakery).
frames.concerns: The Gurus rejected magic, though here it is fiction.

frames.aligns: Abolition of prejudice and the oneness of humanity; unity ending in harmony.
Sincerity (makoto), gratitude, family. No disrespect to kami or shrines.
Magic is not equated with evil; many mages are kind friends.
frames.concerns: Magic-users as an oppressive caste may read as a stereotype of mages; magic used to harm is common.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness precepts: honor parents, help others, be industrious.
A sharp satire of eugenics and state discrimination; inclusion; adoption and single fatherhood (Common Sense Media).
frames.concerns: Male-led cast and a one-note female lead (Anime Feminist); police violence played as comedy; a non-binary reveal used as a twist (TV Tropes).

frames.aligns: Worth from human capacity and kindness, not inherited status; reason over dogma ("gift from God" questioned).
Family, hard work, self-reliance, humility, father and son loyalty. Reason (libertarian) praises its critique of "government-imposed discrimination."
frames.concerns: Authorities and nobles mostly corrupt; some may question mocking hierarchy.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth and dignity of every person; justice and equity.
Defiance of an unjust authority; justice (Satanic Temple Tenet 2); individual merit over inherited rank; self-reliance.
frames.concerns: The ending's "power of everyone" (ch. 158) and humility lean communal.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Mash ignores insults and wants peace, but answers threats to his family with force ("Threaten my family again, and I'll kill you," ch. 1).

Order vs freedom.evidence: The state's rules on who may live are the early evil; Mash defies the magic police and the trial (ch. 1, 40-41). He just wants to be left alone.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Protecting his father drives the plot (ch. 1), but the ending extends acceptance to all, with friends and former rivals as an expanded family (ch. 158, 162).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Birth-based caste and bloodline nobility are mocked and dissolved; Mash declines the elite title (ch. 161-162).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Inherited status and "gift from God" claims are questioned; worth comes from effort and ingenuity. Family loyalty stays.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Hard training is honored, but the goal is a peaceful life, tolerance of difference and simple pleasures (bakery dream, ch. 162).

folkways.japan: The school setting, senpai-kohai deference among students and the devoted-child relationship to a parent reflect Japanese norms; the Hogwarts-style academy is a parody of a British setting rather than a message about it.

delivery.evidence: Reason calls it absurdist comedy with a point about discrimination; Anime Feminist calls the villain cop cartoonishly corrupt. No review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The anti-discrimination message rides under deadpan gags, with early villains cartoonish and later opponents given reasons and redemption.

personified.ideology: Worth by deeds, not birth
Only I have worth; self-deification
The strong may take from the weak
Law and order; the magicless as a threat

entry.dominant: Libertarianism (anti-state-discrimination reading), Classical virtue ethics, Critical theory (caste satire), Secular humanism, Communitarianism.

entry.heading: Nana
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is found in honest, loyal bonds with the people you choose, more than in romance, fame or getting what you want; the story shows that running from loneliness through sex, drugs or dependence on another person costs a great deal, and it does not say whether a happy ending is possible.

frames.aligns: Sin is not made attractive in its results (Inter Mirifica 7): adultery, drugs and exploitation bring suffering; Hachi keeps her child; self-giving friendship; care for the grieving.
frames.concerns: Sex outside marriage presented as normal (CCC 2353); an adult's relationship with a minor; a hurried marriage without free, full consent; no hope beyond human ties.

frames.aligns: The passions shown as enslaving (Ren's addiction, Nana's jealousy); love for a friend in grief.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis): frequent sexual content and drug use; no repentance shaped by faith.

frames.aligns: Consequences of sin are real (Galatians 6:7): pregnancy, addiction, broken trust; a child is welcomed.
frames.concerns: Fornication and adultery normalized; drug and alcohol culture; no gospel frame. Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Depicts sin without endorsing hard drugs or betrayal; longing for love and home that many evangelicals read as a longing for God.
frames.concerns: Sex outside marriage is the norm; Christianity has no place; Takumi's control is left unresolved.

frames.aligns: Consequences of drugs and sexual sin are shown.
frames.concerns: Holiness standards: sexual immorality, drunkenness and worldliness fill the setting; media as an "open door" to that influence. Views range widely between churches.

frames.aligns: A sober picture of human depravity and its fruit; common grace lets families value true observation by a non-Christian artist.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 lists "lascivious ... books, pictures" among sins against the seventh commandment; sex outside marriage routine.

frames.aligns: The law shown working: sin brings its own wages; forgiveness between friends. Entertainment as adiaphora, judged by conscience.
frames.concerns: Sexual immorality as the norm; no gospel. LCMS and WELS families tend to be more cautious than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy among friends; consequences of addiction; care for the grieving.
frames.concerns: Wesley's General Rules on diversions and books; sexual content and drunkenness. Holiness churches stricter than UMC.

frames.aligns: Judged by its framing, the story is an honest tragedy: betrayal and addiction wound; friendship is the good.
frames.concerns: Sex outside marriage normalized; an adult with a minor; the marriage question left open. Practice ranges from progressive to conservative.

frames.aligns: Community and mutual care in the chosen family; humility and forgiveness.
frames.concerns: Separation from the world: the rock and fame world is exactly what the tradition avoids; sexual and drug content. Conservative groups avoid such media; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Family and children valued; Hachi keeps her baby; loyalty and service among friends.
frames.concerns: Law of chastity broken throughout; Word of Wisdom (alcohol, tobacco, drugs); For the Strength of Youth asks for media that invites the Spirit.

frames.aligns: Compassion for flawed women; exposure of industry and tabloid exploitation; harm to a minor named as harm by critics.
frames.concerns: Takumi's control and Shin's exploitation are not clearly condemned within the story so far; possible queerbaiting (Anime Feminist).

frames.aligns: Health message echoed: drugs, alcohol and tobacco shown to destroy.
frames.concerns: Fundamental Belief 22 on choosing entertainment; "by beholding we become changed"; sexual content throughout. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Consequences of immorality and drugs are shown.
frames.concerns: jw.org asks whether entertainment features what God hates: immorality (Galatians 5:19-21) is the setting's norm. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Love and friendship as healing forces.
frames.concerns: "Stand porter at the door of thought": grief, fear, addiction and sin dwelt on at length. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Pikuach nefesh echoes: drugs destroy life; a child is kept; loyalty and comfort of mourners.
frames.concerns: Tzniut: sexual content and immodesty throughout; adultery and relations outside marriage normalized; many Haredi homes restrict such media altogether. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Respect for life (the child kept); comforting mourners; consequences of drugs and betrayal.
frames.concerns: Relations outside marriage normalized; an adult with a minor; modesty values applied by families. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Honest picture of young adults' choices; compassion; critique of exploitation; informed autonomy.
frames.concerns: Exploitation of a minor (Shin); a controlling marriage; drug culture. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Patience in grief (sabr); loyalty; intoxicants shown to destroy (Qur'an 5:90); a child is kept.
frames.concerns: Zina normalized throughout; alcohol and drugs part of daily life; lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) and immodest dress; music industry setting.

frames.aligns: Attachment and desire (kama) shown leading to suffering; loyalty in friendship; grief honored.
frames.concerns: Dharma of householder life broken (adultery, a forced-feeling marriage); tamasic habits (intoxicants).

frames.aligns: Craving and attachment as the root of suffering, shown again and again; impermanence (the group's breakup, Ren's death); compassion among friends.
frames.concerns: Fifth precept (intoxicants) and third precept (sexual misconduct) broken throughout; little path out of suffering offered.

frames.aligns: The five vices (lust, attachment, ego) shown causing harm, not admired; seva-like care among friends.
frames.concerns: Intoxicants and tobacco prohibited (Rehat Maryada) yet routine; sex outside marriage. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Unity and friendship valued; drugs shown as destructive.
frames.concerns: A "chaste and holy life" and abstinence from alcohol and drugs are core; both are absent. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) in friendship; mourning and remembrance (seaside memorial, v21 flash-forward).
frames.concerns: Little doctrinal conflict; impurity (kegare) associated with death and drugs is not a theme. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Personal freedom with responsibility; bonds of chosen family; grief honored.
frames.concerns: "Harm none": exploitation of a minor and a controlling partner.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness: "Do not take harmful drugs" and "Be faithful to your sexual partner"; the story shows the cost of breaking both.
frames.concerns: Drug use and infidelity are pervasive; panic attacks and grief handled without the Church's frame. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Complex, flawed women given inner lives; critique of tabloids and industry exploitation; female friendship as central (Anime Feminist, 2025; Little White Lies on the film).
frames.concerns: Grooming and sex work of a 15-year-old (Anime Feminist); Takumi's abuse not yet clearly judged; possible queerbaiting (Anime Feminist, 2020). Common Sense Media: 17+.

frames.aligns: Meaning built through human bonds; honest picture of grief, addiction and consequences without supernatural framing.
frames.concerns: Exploitation of a minor; drug glamour in the band scene; grief handled without professional help.

frames.aligns: Shows the costs of hedonism, broken families and an absent mother; Hachi chooses the child and marriage; Nobu's offer of family duty (v8 review).
frames.concerns: The good, the true and the beautiful versus a world of casual sex and drugs presented as normal; marriage shown mostly as failing.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of flawed people; justice for the exploited; free search for meaning.
frames.concerns: Harm to a minor; coercive relationship; age-appropriateness. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Indulgence and self-expression without shame (Church of Satan); Nana's self-made independence; skepticism toward authority.
frames.concerns: Harm to a child (Shin) violates the Eleven Rules; addiction is compulsion, not indulgence. (from general knowledge; to verify)

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Public shame (tabloid exposés, v10-17) is a threat the characters fear, but the story sides with private worth and forgiveness rather than defending reputation.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Band life, moving to Tokyo alone and living by choice are celebrated; label control and probation (v18-19) are obstacles.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Loyalty to a chosen family (apartment 707, the band) comes before rules and the public; birth family is mostly broken (v16-17).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: The label hierarchy and a husband's control are shown, not celebrated; friends treat each other as equals.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No religious frame; marriage and motherhood appear as personal choices, not duties of tradition.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Music, fashion and personal fulfillment are the characters' goals; money and security matter but are secondary (Web Japan on work and money struggles).

folkways.japan: The pressure of tabloid scandal, the norm of marrying quickly after a pregnancy (dekichatta-kon, "shotgun marriage") and senpai-kohai deference inside bands and labels reflect Japanese norms of the 2000s more than the story's own message (from general knowledge; to verify).

delivery.evidence: The Mary Sue: "very realistic, with little room for romantic tropes"; Web Japan: "about the realities of life." No reviewer found calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The series shows the results of its characters' choices through events and inner narration rather than stating morals, and it leaves most judgments to the reader.

personified.ideology: Independence and self-made ambition
Romantic dependence and the wish for an ordinary home
Career-first pragmatism and control
Practical responsibility and blunt honesty

entry.dominant: Expressive individualism, Existentialism, Feminism, Secular humanism, Dharmic (Buddhist, by echo).

series.title: Boy's Abyss
series.adult_reason: Boy's Abyss: VIZ rates it Mature; Publishers Weekly notes explicit sex, incl. a minor with adults; deep entry scores 9

entry.heading: Boy's Abyss
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: The series presents a good life as one where a young person breaks free of the adults and the town that use him, faces the truth about his family and chooses to keep living on his own terms. VIZ's blurb puts the problem plainly: "Self-serving adults and broken dreams push a teenager toward the abyss."

content.framing: Mixed: abuse shown as harm and punished, but often drawn as charged romance
Shown with consequences, with a romanticized legend

frames.aligns: Exposes adults who abuse authority over a child; the abusing teacher faces arrest; the son is freed by truth; the story ends in life, not death (Inter Mirifica 7 allows depicting evil to show it).
frames.concerns: Suicide romanticized through the legend; adult-minor sex drawn with allure; no repentance or forgiveness named. Explicit sex involving minors is a grave depiction concern (CCC 2521-2524; 2389 on abuse by those responsible for the young).

frames.aligns: Shows the passions (lust, despair, possessiveness) and their wreckage clearly.
frames.concerns: Despair answered only by private escape, with no repentance or spiritual father. Watchfulness over the senses (nepsis) makes explicit sexual images of minors a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: Shows the emptiness of a life without hope and the consequences of sin.
frames.concerns: No hope in Christ; adult-minor sex shown with allure; a romantic suicide legend. Under Philippians 4:8, the sexual content is a heavy concern; congregations are self-governing, so views vary.

frames.aligns: A realistic picture of broken homes and of adults who prey on the vulnerable. Many distinguish depicting sin from endorsing it.
frames.concerns: No gospel answer; abuse partly drawn as romance; explicitness too high even for families who "engage" culture.

frames.aligns: No occult content; adults' manipulation shown as destructive.
frames.concerns: A romantic folk legend of death; no spiritual answer. Holiness standards make the sexual content a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: Total depravity has an echo: nearly every adult is compromised. Common grace lets adults weigh serious art by non-Christians.
frames.concerns: Sin without grace. WLC Q139 ("lascivious... books, pictures") makes the sexual imagery a heavy concern; suicide as self-murder (WLC Q136), treated pastorally.

frames.aligns: Law without gospel: the adults' guilt is exposed, with no word of forgiveness.
frames.concerns: No gospel offered. LCMS and WELS families are typically more cautious than ELCA about the explicitness.

frames.aligns: Social holiness in who failed this boy; friends who push him to leave.
frames.concerns: No grace named. Holiness churches (Nazarene, Wesleyan) are far more cautious than UMC about the sexual content and suicide scenes.

frames.aligns: Literary seriousness about abuse of trust; good and evil framed by consequences (the teacher's arrest, Gen's surrender).
frames.concerns: Abuse partly romanticized; a fairy-tale suicide legend. Episcopal and ACNA families may differ on how much adult fiction they allow.

frames.aligns: Violence leads only to ruin; the evils of a community ruled by one powerful family.
frames.concerns: No caring community appears; escape is individual. Separation from worldly media makes the explicitness a heavy concern; Old Order groups would avoid it, MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Family as what matters most, shown by its betrayal; truth-telling and a new start.
frames.concerns: No plan of salvation; adult-minor sex; a romantic suicide legend. For the Strength of Youth puts the sexual content and suicide outside youth guidance.

frames.aligns: Clear about abuse of power by adults, the burden on young caregivers and a male victim of women abusers.
frames.concerns: Abuse partly drawn as romance; Gen's assault on Chako unaddressed; Gen's gender-identity reveal criticized by readers as poorly handled (TV Tropes). Suicide scenes against safe-messaging norms.

frames.aligns: The cost of broken homes is shown, not admired.
frames.concerns: No hope beyond escape. Fundamental Belief 22 and "by beholding we become changed" make the sexual content and despair a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: Immorality and violence lead to harm.
frames.concerns: Sexual immorality involving minors drawn with allure; a death legend romanticized; no hope in God's Kingdom. jw.org counsel on entertainment that features immorality makes it a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: Truth (the confrontation with his mother) frees Reiji; life is chosen.
frames.concerns: Despair, sickness and death presented as reality and dwelt on. "Stand porter at the door of thought" (Science and Health 392) makes the content a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: Choosing life over death at the end; exposure of those who abuse power over the young.
frames.concerns: Tzniut and nivul peh make the sexual content a heavy concern; many Haredi homes avoid such media entirely. No teshuvah by the main abusers is reported.

frames.aligns: Choosing life; the dignity of a young person exploited by adults.
frames.concerns: Degrading sexual content involving minors conflicts with Jewish values of modesty and dignity.

frames.aligns: Honest about exploitation and abuse of power; compassion for the victims.
frames.concerns: Abuse partly romanticized; suicide content is a depiction concern, especially for younger readers.

frames.aligns: Family duty shown by its betrayal; patience under hardship.
frames.concerns: Sex outside marriage, with minors, drawn with allure; despair of mercy (Qur'an 39:53) answered only by escape; suicide legend romanticized. Lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) makes the content a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: Karma-like chains across a family; parental dharma shown by its failure.
frames.concerns: Suicide romanticized in the legend; tamasic content (Gita 17); views vary by community.

frames.aligns: Craving and clinging (Nagi's death wish, Shibasawa's obsession, Yuko's possessiveness) drive the suffering; release comes through seeing clearly and letting go.
frames.concerns: No path beyond suffering named. Right mindfulness of what feeds the mind makes the sexual and suicide content a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: The five vices (lust, anger, attachment, ego) shown as destructive; attachment (moh) as the root of the trap.
frames.concerns: Lust shown on the page, involving minors. No spiritual answer.

frames.aligns: Sexual harm and family breakdown shown as damaging; truthfulness valued.
frames.concerns: Shoghi Effendi's call to a "chaste and holy life" makes the sexual content a heavy concern; no spiritual answer.

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) reached at last in the confrontation; ordinary life by the river at the end.
frames.concerns: A ravine of death romanticized as a lovers' place; death and blood as kegare may weigh with some families. No shrines or kami mocked.

frames.aligns: Personal responsibility; harm shown as harm (the Rede).
Survival chosen over death; destructive personal influences (the mother, the teacher) shown as such.
frames.concerns: No content code for fiction; any push toward psychiatric help would run against the church's stance.

frames.aligns: Exposes adult abuse of minors, burden on young carers, male victims of women abusers.
frames.concerns: Adult-minor sex drawn as romance as well as abuse; an attempted rape never addressed; a gender-identity reveal readers criticized as poorly handled; suicide method and legend against safe-messaging guidelines.

frames.aligns: This-life focus; freedom through truth and leaving harmful ties; no magical rescue.
frames.concerns: Cruelty and exploitation of minors on the page; romanticized suicide legend.

frames.aligns: Shows the cost of broken families, absent fathers and adults without restraint; consequences for the teacher and the killer.
frames.concerns: Content that degrades the good, the true and the beautiful; adults' sexual use of minors drawn with allure.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth and dignity of an exploited young person; justice against abusers.
frames.concerns: Abuse partly romanticized; age-appropriateness makes it adult reading.

frames.aligns: Self-determination: Reiji breaks free of those who use him; no afterlife; truth over illusion.
frames.concerns: Harm to children (the Eleven Rules condemn it) shown repeatedly, sometimes with allure.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: No revenge is celebrated; Gen's killing of Yuko ends in his surrender (vol. 14) and the story's resolution is a conversation, not vengeance (vol. 18).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Mother, teacher and the Minegishi family all restrain Reiji, and the story celebrates breaking free (TV Tropes: leaving home as the route to growth; vol. 18).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Kin ties are the trap: Yuko's hold, the brother, the grandmother as burden. Release comes through police (Gen's surrender) and leaving the family (vol. 14, 18).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Teacher-student and parent-child hierarchies are abused; the story sides with the young against rank.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Religion is absent; the local legend of the Lover's Abyss is the only "tradition," and it leads toward death.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: The ending is a modest working life, but its value is choosing one's own path apart from family duty.

folkways.japan: The young family caregiver (yangu kearā), the closed rural town, filial duty to a parent and the idol industry's control over young women are Japanese context; the story criticizes these more than it endorses them.

delivery.evidence: VIZ's blurb blames "self-serving adults"; ANN says it does not glorify suicide; CBR calls the suicide legend's framing "incredibly controversial."
delivery.note: The story shows its verdict through consequences rather than speeches, but its abusers are drawn with allure as well as blame.

personified.ideology: Romantic escape through dying together
Possessive protection that excuses abuse of power
Family duty as a hold over a child
Art that uses real people as material

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Nihilism (explored and critiqued), Expressive individualism (escape from family), Critical theory (power of adults over the young).

entry.heading: Made in Abyss
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life follows its longing into the unknown, whatever the cost. Wonder, curiosity and love are worth suffering and even death; the world itself is indifferent, and value is something people choose and pay for.

content.framing: Neutral (often played as comedy); criticized by reviewers

frames.aligns: Bondrewd's use of children as means is shown as evil (CCC 2295 on research on persons); love and loyalty between the children; Prushka's love for her father.
frames.concerns: Mercy killing (Mitty) shown without verdict, against CCC 2276-2279; child nudity framed comically or suggestively runs against Inter Mirifica 7 (evil not made attractive) and CCC 2523-2525 on modesty and the dignity of children.

frames.aligns: Bondrewd as a picture of passion for knowledge without love; compassion of Nanachi.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis) makes the gore and the exposure of children a primary concern; soul-transfer and "value" exchange treat the person as material.

frames.aligns: Clear villainy in Bondrewd; sacrificial love among the children.
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 test fails for the nudity and gore; mercy killing unresolved; longing presented as worth any cost. Each congregation and family decides (soul liberty).

frames.aligns: Story depicts evil without endorsing Bondrewd; Beneath the Tangles engages the mercy-killing question honestly from faith.
frames.concerns: Sexualized framing of children cannot be "redeemed" by context for many; no transcendent hope offered.
Media as an "open door": a mystical, quasi-sacred Abyss, consciousness transfer and curses; holiness standards and child nudity. Views vary between churches.

frames.aligns: Total depravity echoed in Bondrewd's reasoning; common grace lets readers value the craft.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 lists "lascivious... pictures" among sins; child nudity; euthanasia (WLC Q136).

frames.aligns: Law shown in the Abyss's unbending rules; Bondrewd's attempt to master life without grace.
frames.concerns: Child exposure and euthanasia. LCMS and WELS families tend to be stricter than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Compassion, works of mercy (Nanachi caring for Riko).
frames.concerns: Wesley's General Rules on diversions; nudity and gore; holiness churches more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: Judged by framing: Bondrewd condemned, the cost of curiosity shown; strong literary tradition of dark fantasy.
frames.concerns: Child nudity played as comedy; euthanasia without verdict. Range from progressive to conservative.

frames.aligns: Care for the weak, community of the vulnerable, little heroic violence (fighting is mostly defensive).
frames.concerns: Separation from the world makes most of this content unwelcome; children defying elders; graphic suffering. MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Love for a mother, family bonds, sacrifice.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth asks whether media invites the Spirit; child nudity and gore weigh heavily.

frames.aligns: Attention to the vulnerable: orphans, disabled-coded Mitty, exploited children; Bondrewd's abuse of power exposed.
frames.concerns: Representation critiques (Anime Feminist on gender and disability); how children's bodies are drawn.
"By beholding we become changed": graphic suffering and nudity; soul transfer conflicts with teaching on the state of the dead.
Violence (Psalm 11:5), immorality concerns about nudity, curse and mystical elements.
Disease, mutilation and fear are central and real; dwelling on them conflicts with "stand porter at the door of thought."

frames.aligns: Pikuach nefesh echoed in saving Riko's life; abhorrence of experiments on humans.
frames.concerns: Mercy killing is forbidden in halakha; tzniut and child nudity; many Haredi homes would not admit the book.

frames.aligns: Value of every life; condemnation of experimentation.
frames.concerns: Euthanasia without verdict; modesty values applied by families.

frames.aligns: Moral questions on experimentation, disability and death are taken seriously.
frames.concerns: Sexualized framing of children; informed autonomy suggests reading with discussion.

frames.aligns: Condemnation of cruelty and of using people as means; patience under trial (sabr).
frames.concerns: Mercy killing against the prohibition on taking life (Qur'an 4:29; 17:33); nudity and lowering the gaze (24:30-31).

frames.aligns: Karma-like consequences of descent; the soul distinct from the body (Bondrewd's transfers invite discussion).
frames.concerns: Tamasic content (Gita 17): cruelty, degradation; child nudity.

frames.aligns: Suffering, impermanence and craving are the series' engine; compassion (Nanachi, Reg) and the cost of attachment (Riko, Irumyuui, Bondrewd).
frames.concerns: Killing (Mitty) against the first precept, even as mercy; what feeds the mind.

frames.aligns: Bondrewd's ego and attachment (haumai, moh) condemned; seva in Nanachi's care.
Pursuit of knowledge, unity among the children.
frames.concerns: "Chaste and holy life" counsel and the art of children; cruelty.

frames.aligns: Awe before a sacred-feeling natural world; sincerity and gratitude among the children.
frames.concerns: Blood, death and decay as impurity (kegare) are pervasive.

frames.aligns: Awe of nature and the unknown; "harm none" broken by Bondrewd and condemned.
frames.concerns: Harm to children; nudity of minors.

frames.aligns: Way to Happiness precepts: do not harm, care for children; Bondrewd's experiments condemned.
frames.concerns: Bondrewd reads as a psychiatric-style experimenter (the Church's lens); suffering dwelt on.

frames.aligns: Critique of abusive authority and exploitative science; nonbinary-neutral pronouns for Nanachi and Marulk.
frames.concerns: Sexualized framing of children (ANN, Anime Feminist); disability representation (Anime Feminist on Mitty); gender roles (Riko as cook, Reg as protector); age-appropriateness.

frames.aligns: Free inquiry and wonder; ethics of research; mercy and end-of-life choice explored seriously.
frames.concerns: Cruelty and exploitation of children; critics' concerns about sexualized framing.

frames.aligns: Courage, loyalty, sacrifice; monstrous scientist condemned.
frames.concerns: Children defying guardians as the heroic path; euthanasia explored; sexualized depictions of minors; nihilistic tone.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth and dignity violated by Bondrewd and condemned; free search for truth.
frames.concerns: Age-appropriateness; depiction of children's bodies; disability representation.

frames.aligns: Individual will, curiosity and self-chosen fate (Riko); suffering of children condemned in Bondrewd.
frames.concerns: Harm to children is the tradition's main concern (Eleven Rules); critics' charge of sexualized depiction.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Worth is inherent: the story condemns Bondrewd's treatment of children as material (ch. 34-37). Personal vengeance (Faputa, ch. 53-57) is understood but frightening, not celebrated.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Riko and Reg leave the orphanage and Orth's rules to descend (v1-2); the story sides with their choice.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Riko seeks her mother, but the party is a chosen family of friends (Reg, Nanachi), not blood kin.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Whistle ranks matter in Orth and White Whistles hold great power, but the children defy rank; Bondrewd's and Ozen's power is ambiguous or condemned.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No religion guides life; exploration, knowledge and relics drive the world; the Abyss is awesome but not worshipped.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: The story honors longing and self-chosen purpose over survival, even when survival is at stake.

folkways.japan: Strict orphanage discipline, the apprentice-master relation with Ozen and the ranking of explorers echo Japanese institutional hierarchy; the cute "kawaii" art style used for extreme content is a Japanese seinen convention rather than a message of the story.

delivery.evidence: No review opened calls it preachy; ANN notes Bondrewd "sees himself as doing good"; Beneath the Tangles says the mercy killing takes no side.
delivery.note: The series shows rather than argues, leaving euthanasia, experimentation and the worth of longing as open questions.

personified.ideology: Longing and curiosity worth any cost
Progress and knowledge justify using children
Compassion, including mercy killing
Vengeance as love for a mother

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Expressive individualism, Naturalism; Utilitarianism and Transhumanism are critiqued through Bondrewd.

entry.heading: Pandora Hearts
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: Your existence is not a sin. A good life means accepting who you are, facing the truth about the past instead of trying to undo it, and choosing to keep going for the people you love, even when your origin is a lie.

frames.aligns: Evil (Jack's obsession, the cult) is not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7); forgiveness that changes a life (Ada and Vincent, ch. 97); self-giving love (Oscar, Oz).
frames.concerns: Blood contracts and soul transfer as the source of power, judged by framing (CCC 2115-2117); Alice's suicide framed as sacrifice (CCC 2280-2283); reincarnation ending.

frames.aligns: Repentance and forgiveness; Oswald's atonement; the danger of passions (Jack's possessive love) grown unchecked.
