frames.concerns: Contracts sealed with a monster's blood, souls possessing bodies and an Abyss of evil-seeming beings, read through a tradition that treats evil spirits as real. Watchfulness (nepsis) makes the gore and horror a concern.

frames.aligns: Clear exposure of a false religion (the cult); forgiveness; loyalty.
frames.concerns: Pacts with monsters for power and spirit possession (Deuteronomy 18:10-12); reincarnation ending; suicide framed as sacrifice. Each congregation decides.

frames.aligns: Depicts sin without endorsing it; redemption arcs (Vincent); a false prophet (Isla Yura) exposed; sacrificial love.
frames.concerns: Blood contracts and spirit possession as fantasy power; no source of grace beyond people.

frames.aligns: Clear fight against a demonic-seeming realm; forgiveness and deliverance-like moments.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": contracts sealed by drinking a monster's blood, souls entering bodies, a cult worshipping the Abyss. Even framed as fiction, these weigh heavily. Views range by church.

frames.aligns: Total depravity has echoes: no character is innocent, and the past cannot be undone by human effort. Common grace lets families value well-made art by non-Christians.
frames.concerns: Suicide framed as noble (WLC Q136); soul transfer and reincarnation; murky consent in Levi's "experiment."

frames.aligns: Law and gospel echoes: characters cannot erase their own guilt, and acceptance comes from others (Ada to Vincent, Oz to himself through friends).
frames.concerns: Occult-like contracts (Large Catechism, second commandment); reincarnation. LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Change of heart is possible (Vincent, Oswald); works of mercy; friendship across class.
frames.concerns: Blood contracts; suicide framing; dark horror tone. Holiness churches more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: Fantasy in a Carroll-inspired literary frame; judged by how it frames good and evil, and the evil here is clearly framed.
frames.concerns: Suicide framed as sacrifice; reincarnation; occult-like contracts.

frames.aligns: Forgiveness of enemies; humility; violence rarely glorified and usually tragic.
frames.concerns: Conservative groups avoid such media; the horror, beheadings and occult-like contracts are significant concerns. MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Families reunited; the worth of every soul; forgiveness and change.
frames.concerns: Spirit contact and soul transfer; suicide framed as sacrifice; gore.

frames.aligns: Persecution of "Children of Ill Omen" critiqued; exploited orphans; forgiveness and healing of trauma.
frames.concerns: Murky consent in Levi's "experiment"; women's fates often decided by men (Lacie).

frames.aligns: Exposure of a false religion; self-sacrifice; family love.
frames.concerns: The dead are unconscious until the resurrection, so souls living on in other bodies and reincarnation conflict with teaching on the state of the dead; horror and gore.

Spiritism and spirit possession run through the plot, and power comes from drinking blood, which touches the Witness teaching on blood (Acts 15:29) and the counsel against spiritism (Galatians 5:19-21).

frames.aligns: Love outlasts fear; false identity yields to truth.
frames.concerns: Fear, death and evil are shown as real, powerful forces; constant horror.

frames.aligns: Teshuvah-like change (Vincent, Oswald); honoring life; exposing a false cult.
frames.concerns: Necromancy-like soul transfer and blood contracts (Deuteronomy 18:10-11); suicide framed as sacrifice; many Haredi homes restrict such media.

frames.aligns: Teshuvah; memory and the duty to remember the dead; protecting orphans.
frames.concerns: Suicide framing (met with compassion today); occult-like contracts accepted as fantasy.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam echoes in repairing the world's link to the Abyss; critique of persecuting the marked.
frames.concerns: Suicide framing; murky consent in Levi's "experiment."

frames.aligns: Exposure of a false religion; forgiveness; loyalty; the past cannot be undone.
frames.concerns: Sihr-like pacts with spirit-like beings, sealed by drinking blood (blood is forbidden as food, Qur'an 5:3); suicide framed as sacrifice (Qur'an 4:29); reincarnation.

frames.aligns: Karma-like consequences of contracts; rebirth (ch. 104); duty and loyalty.
frames.concerns: Tamasic horror and gore for some families; suicide framing.

frames.aligns: Attachment as the root of suffering: Jack's craving for Lacie and Oswald's clinging to the past cause catastrophe; letting go is the resolution; rebirth (ch. 104).
frames.concerns: Killing and suicide; whether "the self" is affirmed (Oz's "I am") more than released.

frames.aligns: The five vices (attachment and ego in Jack and Isla Yura) are condemned; courage and service.
frames.concerns: Magic and superstition rejected by the Gurus; blood contracts are central.

frames.aligns: Unity, forgiveness, nobility of the soul; the soul progresses.
frames.concerns: Spiritualism discouraged; non-violence ideal versus frequent violence.

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) and gratitude in the heroes; spirits are part of the fantasy world.
frames.concerns: Blood and death bring impurity (kegare); the setting is European, so few Shinto touchpoints.

frames.aligns: Death and rebirth as part of a cycle (ch. 104); no stereotyping of witches or pagans; harm from magic used to harm.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; the cult is a fraud, not a pagan portrayal.

frames.aligns: Precepts against murder and for helping others; the spirit lives many lives (ch. 104).
frames.concerns: Glorified violence is limited, but frequent killing.

frames.aligns: Self-worth against stigma; critique of persecuting the "marked"; trauma treated seriously; exploited children.
frames.concerns: Suicide shown (safe-messaging); Levi's "experiment" and Lacie's lack of choice; Vincent's abuse of Echo.

frames.aligns: Meaning made by people who choose to keep going; forgiveness; facing truth over comforting illusions (Oz and Alice leave the tea-party dream, ch. 104).
frames.concerns: Suicide needs mental-health framing; supernatural rules are fiction.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, duty, master-servant fidelity (Gilbert), protective fatherhood (Oscar), sacrifice.
frames.concerns: Aristocratic and family institutions shown as corrupt; occult themes; suicide portrayal.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth even of those told they are a sin; justice for the marked and exploited; free search for truth.
Rejecting an imposed "sin of existence" and affirming the self; exposing a fraudulent cult; compassion and justice (Satanic Temple Tenets 1-2).
frames.concerns: Self-sacrifice for the world is honored over self-interest.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: House names and duty matter, but Oswald's revenge and Jack's vendetta are shown as destructive; Oz's worth is defended against a family label (ch. 1), not by restoring house honor.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Pandora, the Baskervilles and the dukedoms hide truths and sacrifice individuals (Lacie, ch. 68); the heroes act on their own will.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Chosen family and master-servant bonds (Oz and Gilbert; Oscar as surrogate father, ch. 82) drive the story; blood family is often cruel (Zai; Vincent and Gilbert sold by parents).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: A ducal society with servants; Gilbert's loyal service is honored, while persecution of red-eyed "Children of Ill Omen" is critiqued.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No real-world faith; ceremonies and a cult are shown as tools of manipulation (ch. 1, 52-57); the supernatural is fantasy mechanics.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: The core arc is accepting one's own identity and choosing to exist (ch. 70-104).

folkways.japan: The master-servant devotion (Gilbert to Oz) and the mix of comedy and tragedy reflect Japanese shonen and GFantasy conventions; the Victorian setting and Lewis Carroll motifs are the story's own European frame rather than Japanese norms.

delivery.evidence: No reviewer found calls it preachy. Morrissy (ANN) praises factions that shift "between friend and enemy" and twists that make sense in hindsight.
delivery.note: The message about self-worth emerges through mystery reveals and Oz's choices more than speeches, though key lines state it outright late in the series.

personified.ideology: Self-acceptance: existence is not a sin
Possessive love above the world
Duty to the world above personal love
Religion as fraud promising paradise in the Abyss

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Pagan/occult (fantasy), Secular humanism, Expressive individualism, Dharmic (rebirth and attachment).

entry.heading: Fairy Tail
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is lived among friends who become family. You belong to a group that accepts you as you are, you protect its members at any cost, you forgive former enemies who join you, and you get stronger for the sake of others.

content.framing: Played for laughs (fan service); Condemned (forced stripping)

frames.aligns: Communion of persons; forgiveness and welcome of former enemies (Gajeel, Juvia, Jellal); protecting the weak; evil framed as evil (Inter Mirifica 7). Fantasy magic "judged by how it is framed."
frames.concerns: Fan service treats the body as a gag (CCC 2521-2524 on modesty); heavy drinking without cost (CCC 2290); spirit contracts and a ghost advisor, judged by framing.

frames.aligns: Love within community; repentance of enemies; mercy.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis) makes the constant sexualized art the main concern; demons and spirit contracts shown as friendly powers; the hero is himself a demon (v55).

frames.aligns: Loyalty, forgiveness, discipline within a community (Laxus's expulsion and return). Lorehaven's Burnett sees the guild acting like "a solid biblical local church ought to act."
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 is the common test, and the fan service fails it for many families; drinking; magic as the world's basis. Soul liberty means families decide.

frames.aligns: Burnett (Lorehaven) praises friendship, loving correction ("just as God out of love disciplines his children") and the turn of former enemies toward "repentance." Beneath the Tangles links the guild's unity to Ephesians 4:2-3.
frames.concerns: Burnett: friendship and "getting stronger" become idols; "blatant exploitation, often sexual exploitation, of its own characters for the sake of fanservice"; forgiveness earned by lifelong atonement rather than given.

Media as an "open door": contracts with summoned spirits are the heroine's power, demons are made from books and include the hero, a dead founder advises the living; fan service against holiness standards.

frames.aligns: Common grace lets families enjoy its loyalty and humor; total depravity echoes in how far villains fall; discipline in the guild.
frames.concerns: Westminster Larger Catechism Q139 lists "lascivious... pictures" among sins against the seventh commandment, which covers much of the fan service; friendship as a saving power.

frames.aligns: Entertainment as adiaphora judged by love and conscience; forgiveness of enemies as a picture of grace.
frames.concerns: Fan service and drinking; confessional (LCMS, WELS) families stricter than ELCA ones.

frames.aligns: Social holiness: a community that carries one another's burdens (Makarov: "One person's happiness is everyone's happiness," per Beneath the Tangles).
frames.concerns: Wesley's General Rules on diversions; holiness churches will weigh the fan service and drinking heavily; UMC families more open.

frames.aligns: Imagination as a gift; good and evil clearly framed; friendship in the tradition of Lewis's The Four Loves.
frames.concerns: Fan service; drinking; the guild's disregard for lawful authority.

frames.aligns: Mutual aid, shared life and care in a gathered community echo Anabaptist practice; forgiveness of enemies.
frames.concerns: Violence shown as heroic is the central concern, and fighting is the guild's main answer; separation from worldly media in Old Order groups; fan service.

frames.aligns: Family, belonging, service, forgiveness; a founder's legacy guiding later generations.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth asks for entertainment that invites the Spirit; the fan service and casual drinking (Word of Wisdom) are the main issues.

frames.aligns: Radical welcome of outsiders and former enemies; a chosen family for the abandoned (orphans, runaways, a former slave).
frames.concerns: Sexualized and humiliated women played for laughs (Yukino's forced stripping, torture scenes); harassment joked about.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, care, a community of mutual help.
frames.concerns: "By beholding we become changed" applied to the fan service; the dead appearing and advising the living (Mavis's ghost) conflicts with teaching on the state of the dead; drinking.

jw.org counsel firmly rejects magic and spiritism in entertainment; here they are the basis of every power, including contracts with summoned spirits and a ghost founder; violence as the heroes' way; immodest art.

frames.aligns: Love outlasting hatred; the bonds of friendship as the true power.
frames.concerns: Fear, death and destructive power shown as real; sexualized images; members guard what thought dwells on (Science and Health 392).

frames.aligns: Loyalty, hospitality to the stranger, rescue of captives (Erza's fellow slaves).
frames.concerns: Sorcery (Deuteronomy 18:10-11) as the world's fabric; tzniut makes the fan service a strong concern; mocking speech; many Haredi homes would avoid such media altogether, Modern Orthodox families are selective.

frames.aligns: Community responsibility, teshuvah echoes in former enemies who change, protecting the vulnerable.
frames.concerns: Fan service against modesty values applied by families; drinking played for laughs.

frames.aligns: Inclusive community, tikkun olam echoes in rescuing slaves and the abused.
frames.concerns: Sexualized depiction of women as gags.

frames.aligns: Brotherhood and loyalty (ukhuwwah), forgiveness, rescuing the oppressed.
frames.concerns: Sihr (magic) and spirit contracts are central (Qur'an 2:102); alcohol shown approvingly (5:90); lowering the gaze (24:30-31) makes the fan service a strong concern.

frames.aligns: Duty to one's community, loyalty, protection of the weak, devotion to a teacher-father (Makarov).
frames.concerns: Some families apply the Gita's tamasic category to the fan service and drinking.

frames.aligns: Sangha-like community; compassion toward enemies; Zeref's suffering from attachment and despair.
frames.concerns: Fighting as the main answer (first precept); fan service against right mindfulness of what feeds the mind; drinking (fifth precept).

frames.aligns: Seva-like service and sangat (community); defense of the oppressed.
frames.concerns: Lust (kaam) shown as a harmless gag in the art; heavy drinking (alcohol prohibited for initiated Sikhs).

frames.aligns: Unity, fellowship and service as the source of strength.
frames.concerns: The call to a "chaste and holy life" weighs against the fan service and drinking; fighting as the solution.

frames.aligns: Harmony within the group, sincerity and gratitude; spirits and dragons are familiar from Japanese folk culture; no disrespect to shrines or kami.
Celestial spirits, dragons and nature magic are treated with respect; "harm none" echoes in protecting the weak; no stereotyped witches.
frames.concerns: Little in the message; some will note how spirit contracts are portrayed.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness precepts: help others, be worthy of trust, do not murder (the series avoids killing).
Inclusion and chosen family; second chances; women in combat roles.
frames.concerns: Consent and representation: sexualized women as running gags, forced stripping, sexualized torture, harassment as comedy (Common Sense Media; CBR; Lorehaven).

frames.aligns: Human bonds as the source of meaning; no reliance on gods; forgiveness and growth.
frames.concerns: Problems solved by force and by emotional power-ups rather than reasoning; women's dignity undercut by the art.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, honor, protecting one's own, respect for a fatherly elder, duty to the group.
frames.concerns: Sexualized art and drinking against concern for decency; the guild flouts lawful authority as comedy; family of blood replaced by chosen family.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth and dignity: the guild accepts anyone; justice for the enslaved (Tower of Heaven).
frames.concerns: Objectification of women; fighting as the main tool.

frames.aligns: A guild that defies the Council and lives by its own rules; compassion and justice (Satanic Temple Tenets 1-2); no harm to children condoned.
frames.concerns: Self-sacrifice for the group and deference to a master run against Church of Satan individualism.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: An attack on one member is answered by the whole guild: the Phantom Lord war (ch. 47-69, v6-9) and Natsu storming Sabertooth after Yukino's humiliation (v33-34). Insults to the guild are not left to the Council.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The guild ignores the Magic Council, wrecks property and lives by its own rules; Common Sense Media notes "discord often erupts... even between comrades." Inside, a few rules hold (Laxus's expulsion, v13-16).

Civic vs kin.evidence: The guild is a family and comes first; outsiders are welcomed only by joining. Loyalty is owed to "nakama," not to the realm in general.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: There is a master and an S-class rank, and Makarov is revered, but members argue, fight and joke as equals; the founder Mavis treats all as family.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: The guild honors its founder and its rituals (the guild mark, the farewell sign); no religion guides life; magic is a craft.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Being yourself, partying and tolerance of eccentrics are celebrated; jobs and rent are comic background, not the point.

folkways.japan: The nakama ideal, the master as a father figure and the group's mutual obligations reflect Japanese shonen and workplace norms; the Western-fantasy guild setting and bar culture borrow from European and RPG traditions, so readers may see the values as genre conventions as much as a message aimed at them.

delivery.evidence: CBR says villains fall "with the power of friendship"; Burnett: "this gets said and shown a lot." Silverman (ANN): "cheesy," but the show pulls it off.
delivery.note: The friendship theme is spoken aloud in battle speeches and confirmed by plot wins, while most villains are either redeemed or left thinly motivated.

personified.ideology: Friends as the source of strength
The guild as one family
Strength alone has value; discard the weak
Despair and the curse of endless life

entry.dominant: Communitarianism, Classical virtue ethics, Expressive individualism, Pagan/occult (as fantasy setting), Secular humanism.

entry.heading: Nisekoi: False Love (Naoshi Komi)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: Love is proven by who you become together, not by fate or by a past promise; kindness, honesty about your feelings and loyalty to friends make a good life.

content.framing: Endorsed (romance, ending in marriage); Neutral (fan-service gags)

frames.aligns: Kindness, peacemaking between rivals, faithful choice of one spouse, marriage and a child (ch. 229); Marika freed from a forced marriage (consent to marriage is essential, CCC 1625-1628).
frames.concerns: Yakuza life made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7: evil should not be made attractive); a lie to parents as the premise (CCC 2482-2486); fan service of teens (CCC 2521-2524).

frames.aligns: Humility (Kosaki), reconciliation of rival houses, love shown in patient service.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis) against the bath and beach chapters; casual guns.

frames.aligns: Kindness, one marriage as the goal, loyalty to friends.
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 test on fan service, language (CSM "a lot") and the comic gangster life; deception of parents. Soul liberty leaves the call to families.

frames.aligns: Depicts rather than endorses most wrongs; Beneath the Tangles reads "fake love will become real" as a picture of serving with a cold heart that God warms.
frames.concerns: Gangsters as lovable; slapstick violence; harem "rivals" framing; fan service. Engage-or-separate views differ by family.

frames.aligns: Joy, friendship, a happy faithful ending.
frames.concerns: Holiness standards on modesty and language; no occult content, so the "open door" concern is low.

frames.aligns: Common grace in kindness and loyalty; vocation (public servant, designer, pâtissier).
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 on "lascivious... pictures" applies to the bath chapters; the gang life presented without moral weight; deception.

frames.aligns: Vocation; Fourth Commandment respected in the end; marriage.
frames.concerns: Sixth Commandment on the fan service; Eighth on the long deception; confessional families stricter than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Kindness, peacemaking, a supportive friend group.
frames.concerns: Wesley's rule on books that do not "tend to the knowledge or love of God"; holiness churches would avoid the fan service and gun gags; UMC families vary.

frames.aligns: Judged by framing: growth, honesty about feelings, a faithful marriage, rejection of a forced wedding.
frames.concerns: Fan service of high school characters; comic crime.

frames.aligns: Peacemaking instead of gang war; humility in Kosaki.
frames.concerns: Separation from worldly media; guns and violence as comedy; romance display; franchise commerce. MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Family, marriage and a child as the goal; developing talents (careers); chaste relationship (first kiss before the wedding).
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth on entertainment that invites the Spirit; language; fan service; crime normalized.

frames.aligns: Young people escape parental control (Marika); every girl gets a career; reconciliation.
frames.concerns: Girls framed as rivals; slapstick violence by a girl treated as a joke; a crime family romanticized.
Fundamental Belief 22 on entertainment "of the highest quality"; "by beholding we become changed" weighs on romance obsession, fan service and comic violence.

frames.aligns: Honest feelings in the end, marriage, peacemaking.
frames.concerns: jw.org counsel against violence (Psalm 11:5) and immorality; dating as recreation; gangs and guns as entertainment.

frames.aligns: Fear and confusion yield to honest love; Marika's illness healed.
frames.concerns: Dwelling on violence, jealousy and sensual images as mental influences.

frames.aligns: Marriage as the goal; a forced match rejected; a chaste couple until the wedding.
frames.concerns: Tzniut: mixed-sex teen intimacy and bath scenes; nivul peh (language); many families would not keep it at home.
Modesty and teen fan service; comic crime.

frames.aligns: Autonomy in choosing a partner; repair between rival groups (a kind of tikkun).
frames.concerns: Girls as prizes; slapstick violence; informed autonomy leaves it to families.

frames.aligns: Marriage as the outcome; Raku's restraint; rejection of a marriage without consent (consent is required in Islamic law).
frames.concerns: Lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31); unchaperoned teen romance; bath and beach scenes; drinking gag; gangster life.

frames.aligns: Dharma of family duty balanced with love; a single marriage with family blessing; peace between houses.
frames.concerns: Some families apply the Gita's rajasic and tamasic categories to romantic and violent comedy; brahmacharya for students.

frames.aligns: Letting go of attachment to a past promise; compassion; Kosaki's acceptance.
frames.concerns: Craving and jealousy in the rivalry; violence as humor.

frames.aligns: Seva and humility; honest work; one marriage.
frames.concerns: Kaam and moh played for comedy; krodh (anger) in Chitoge's hitting.

frames.aligns: Unity of rivals, marriage, chastity before marriage.
frames.concerns: The call to a "chaste and holy life" against the fan service; crime as comedy.

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto), festival custom (ch. 42), harmony restored between houses.
Self-discovery, free choice in love, "harm none" in the end.
frames.concerns: Slapstick hitting and forced-marriage plots run against harm none for some families.
The Way to Happiness precepts on honesty (the deception) and on not harming others.

frames.aligns: Free choice over arranged matches (Marika); each girl gets her own career; Tsugumi defies gender expectations.
frames.concerns: Harem framing; female-on-male violence as a joke; organized crime romanticized; OVA fan service (ANN).

frames.aligns: Meaning from relationships and honest choice; the past need not bind the present.
frames.concerns: Critical thinking about genre tropes and violence as humor.

frames.aligns: Monogamous marriage and a child; loyalty; a chaste couple until the wedding; rival families reconciled.
frames.concerns: Crime families as heroes; disrespectful pretense toward parents; language; fan service.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of each girl; consent; reconciliation.
frames.concerns: Age-appropriateness; violence as humor; girls framed as rivals.

frames.aligns: Individual choice over destiny and parental control; vital existence.
frames.concerns: Concern for children in the Eleven Rules may apply to teen fan service.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Gang honor and turf drive the premise, but conflicts are defused by the fake couple and comedy rather than avenged (ch. 1-2).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Parents' arrangements are worked around; Marika's forced wedding is stopped (ch. 191); the friends act on their own choices.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Family and gang loyalty come first; Raku succeeds his father (epilogue); the friend group as chosen kin.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Gang ranks ("young master"), fathers' authority and teacher roles; peers are equals at school.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Secular school life; festival custom and childhood promise as near-fate; traditional marriage ending.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Feelings, confession and personal choice in love; careers in design and baking; no material struggle.

folkways.japan: The yakuza-family comedy, the "young master" hierarchy, exam-year school life, festivals, school trips and the shōnen-magazine harem romance are Japanese conventions that frame the story rather than form its message. Teachers quitting on marriage (ch. 122) is noted by TV Tropes as a Japanese norm that can surprise Western readers.

delivery.evidence: Reviewers call it cliché, light comedy ("packed to the rafters with clichés," UK Anime Network); none call it preachy.
delivery.note: Its view of love emerges through running gags and the final choice, while the gang setting and harem conventions go unexamined.

personified.ideology: Love chosen in the present over a destined promise
Fated, patient love
Parental control over marriage

entry.dominant: Expressive individualism, Traditionalism, Communitarianism.

entry.heading: Delicious in Dungeon
entry.label: From summaries

frames.aligns: Gratitude for food and not wasting creation; hospitality and shared meals; love of a sister; a demon that devours desire is framed as evil and defeated.
frames.concerns: Necromancy-like black magic used sympathetically (CCC 2115-2117), though with consequences; resurrection by magic shown as routine; the cannibalism theme, judged by framing (Inter Mirifica 7).

frames.aligns: Fasting and feasting both take food seriously; the passions (desire, fear of death) are shown as what the demon feeds on.
frames.concerns: Sorcery raising the dead and a wish-granting demon, since evil spirits are taken as real; a demon's dealings with heroes. Watchfulness (nepsis) applies to the body horror.

frames.aligns: Clear evil (the demon) defeated; family loyalty; hard work, thrift and humility.
frames.concerns: Black magic and spirit work shown as tools for good (Deuteronomy 18:10-12); views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Depicts forbidden magic with costs rather than endorsing it; community, hospitality and grace toward enemies; eating as gift.
frames.concerns: Spirituality without God; magic as ordinary craft.

frames.aligns: Clear defeat of a demon; courage and loyalty.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": raising the dead by forbidden magic, a wish-granting demon that speaks to the hero in dreams (ch. 60), souls fused and moved.

frames.aligns: Common grace lets families value well-made art; desire disordered by a demon shows the danger of idols of the heart.
frames.concerns: Occult practice shown in a sympathetic light; Marcille's attempt to override mortality.

frames.aligns: Fantasy as adiaphora judged by love; vocation and daily bread (Small Catechism, Fourth Petition); humility in a reluctant king.
frames.concerns: Black magic shown sympathetically; LCMS and WELS families tend to be more cautious.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy (feeding the hungry, even enemies); care for health and the body.
frames.concerns: Occult elements; holiness churches more cautious.

frames.aligns: Strong fit with the Lewis-Tolkien fantasy tradition Kui herself cites (The Lord of the Rings, per Wikipedia); good and evil judged by framing.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; black magic and a demon pact as plot.

frames.aligns: Simple living, thrift, shared work and meals, suspicion of worldly power; heroes rarely kill people.
frames.concerns: Fantasy magic and popular media (conservative groups avoid); monster killing as a way of life.

frames.aligns: Family rescue, care of the body, service, a demon that feeds on desire defeated.
frames.concerns: Occult and spirit manipulation; drinking in taverns (Word of Wisdom).

frames.aligns: Overcoming prejudice between races; care for outsiders; ethics of consumption (Salon); non-sexualized women.
frames.concerns: Fantasy racism used for comedy at times (orcs as thieves).

frames.aligns: Health, food and nutrition taken seriously; family loyalty.
frames.concerns: Souls moved and raised by magic, against teaching on the state of the dead; eating unclean creatures as the core joke (health message); demon pact.
Magic, spirit manipulation and a demon granting wishes are central (Galatians 5:19-21).

frames.aligns: Love and friendship overcome a demon; healing and care.
frames.concerns: Death, disease, decay and fear shown as real and physical; body horror.

frames.aligns: Honor of life; gratitude for food (blessings before eating); care of family.
frames.concerns: Raising the dead by sorcery (Deuteronomy 18:11); eating non-kosher creatures is the whole premise; cannibalism debate; many Haredi homes avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Gratitude, hospitality (hachnasat orchim), care of the body, overcoming prejudice.
frames.concerns: Necromancy shown sympathetically; kashrut questions raised by the premise.

frames.aligns: Hospitality, curiosity, overcoming prejudice, ethics of eating.
Gratitude for food, no waste (Qur'an 7:31), hospitality, family loyalty; a demon defeated.
frames.concerns: Sihr (sorcery) used sympathetically to raise the dead; eating creatures that are not halal is the premise; drinking in taverns.

frames.aligns: Food as sacred and shared; karma-like consequences of black magic; duty to family.
frames.concerns: Meat-eating of every kind is the premise, which many vegetarian Hindu families weigh (ahimsa); some apply the tamasic category to body horror.

frames.aligns: Gratitude and no waste; impermanence and acceptance of death; desire as what demons feed on.
frames.concerns: Killing animals for food is the premise (first precept); the story affirms desire as part of life rather than releasing it.

frames.aligns: Langar-like shared meals for all; humility; courage defending others.
frames.concerns: Magic and superstition shown as real; meat eating, which Sikh practice debates.

frames.aligns: Unity across races; service; overcoming prejudice; moderation.
Gratitude for food and the lives taken; respect for nature's cycles; Japanese food culture.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; blood and corpses bring kegare, shown matter-of-factly.

frames.aligns: Magic as craft, the cycle of eating and being eaten, respect for nature.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; black magic framed as dangerous.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness: take care of yourself, set a good example, help others.
Overcoming prejudice; non-sexualized women (Anime Feminist); queer and neurodivergent readings welcomed by fans; ethics of consumption (Salon).
frames.concerns: Species stereotypes for jokes (orcs); monarchy restored at the end; Senshi underwear gags.

frames.aligns: Curiosity, empirical study of an ecosystem, practical reason, acceptance of mortality; magic treated like a science.
Self-reliance, thrift, hard work, family loyalty, a reluctant but dutiful king, suspicion of bureaucrats.
frames.concerns: Some concern about occult themes; taboos (cannibalism) questioned.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth across races; interdependent web of existence (the food chain); free search for truth.
Desire and appetite affirmed as part of life; individualism of eccentrics (Laios, Senshi); skepticism of authority.
frames.concerns: The story ends with community and duty above self; the demon that feeds on desire is the villain.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Insults and slights are answered with talk or a meal, not vendetta; Kabru's grievances go into planning, not duels.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Practical rules (food safety, no waste) are honored, but official rules (the ban on black magic, governors, elven oversight) are bent or resisted for good reasons (ch. 27; ch. 31-32).

Civic vs kin.evidence: The quest is a rescue of kin (Falin), but the final feast gathers strangers, rivals and former enemies (Popverse, ch. 97).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Race and lifespan hierarchies are questioned; elves' condescension is criticized (Kabru). The story ends with a monarchy, held reluctantly.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Curiosity, biology and practical reason guide the heroes; magic is treated like a science; no religion is central. Senshi's craft traditions are respected.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Thrift, food and survival come first in every chapter, alongside a strong celebration of eccentric self-expression (Laios, Senshi).

folkways.japan: Gratitude for food and the lives taken ("itadakimasu"), the food-education (shokuiku) framing Kui chose (Automaton), and comic restraint around romance reflect Japanese norms more than a message aimed at readers elsewhere. The dungeon-fantasy frame itself comes from Western tabletop and computer RPGs (Wikipedia).

delivery.evidence: Reviewers praise its "debates about where to draw the line" on eating (SLJ); Geeks Under Grace notes no moralizing. No review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its ideas about eating, mortality and prejudice come through arguments between characters and the plot rather than lectures.

personified.ideology: Eat what you kill, waste nothing, respect the ecosystem
Love that refuses death; overcoming mortality
Short-lived races first; distrust of power
Possessive loyalty, preserving a kingdom by force

entry.dominant: Environmentalism (ecology), Pragmatism, Communitarianism, Secular humanism, Classical virtue ethics.

entry.heading: GTO: Great Teacher Onizuka
entry.label: From summaries

content.framing: Mixed: often comic and endorsed when Onizuka does it; shown with consequences for villains
Played for comedy; abuse shown with consequences

frames.aligns: Care for the lost one (the parable of the lost sheep); rescue from suicide; works of mercy; family reconciliation.
frames.concerns: Sexualized humor around minors and chastity (CCC 2337-2359, 2521-2524); vigilante violence; legitimate authority mocked (CCC 2234-2246). Inter Mirifica 7: evil depicted must not be made attractive.

frames.aligns: Self-emptying love for others; repentance of characters such as Uchiyamada and Urumi.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis): the lewd comedy is the main concern; disrespect for elders and authority.

frames.aligns: Rescue of the bullied and suicidal; loyalty; consequences for abusers.
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 test fails on the lewd humor; violence and lawbreaking framed as heroic. Congregations differ.

frames.aligns: Grace-like refusal to give up on anyone; depiction of sin with real consequences in the darker arcs.
frames.concerns: Lechery toward students is played for laughs; abusive backstories (rape, incest) are heavy.
Holiness standards on modesty and worldliness; Ouija board as a party game (vol. 4) viewed as an "open door" by some.

frames.aligns: Common grace in a flawed hero; human depravity shown in adults and children alike.
frames.concerns: Westminster Larger Catechism Q139 lists "lascivious... books, pictures" against the seventh commandment; lawful authority (WLC Q123-133).

frames.aligns: Simul iustus et peccator echo: a sinner who still serves his neighbor; vocation as teacher.
frames.concerns: Lewd humor; contempt for authority (Fourth Commandment). LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy; care for the outcast and bullied.
frames.concerns: Wesley's General Rules caution against diversions that cannot be "used in the name of the Lord Jesus"; holiness churches more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: Imagination and satire valued; good and evil judged by framing; compassion wins.
frames.concerns: Sexual humor about minors; violence as a teaching tool. Episcopal and ACNA families differ mainly in strictness.

frames.aligns: Care for the weak; refusal of institutional status.
frames.concerns: Violence as the hero's tool is the central concern (Matthew 5:39); worldly media.

frames.aligns: Family reconciliation; ministering to the one.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth: entertainment should invite the Spirit; lewd humor and crude language weigh heavily.

frames.aligns: Advocacy for the bullied and marginalized; critique of systems that sort children by scores.
frames.concerns: Sexism and sexualized minors; Tokiwa's rape trauma handled through a male hero's lesson.
Fundamental Belief 22 on entertainment; "by beholding we become changed" applied to lewd humor and violence. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Love for neighbor; rescue of the suicidal.
frames.concerns: jw.org asks whether entertainment features what God hates: violence (Psalm 11:5) and immorality, both endorsed as comedy here; a Ouija board. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Love and goodness heal broken students.
frames.concerns: Dwelling on lust, fear and violence ("Stand porter at the door of thought," Science and Health 392). (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Pikuach nefesh echo: saving a life overrides rules; care for the orphan-like child.
frames.concerns: Tzniut and nivul peh: lewd images and coarse language; many Haredi homes restrict such media altogether. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Saving life; repairing families; tikkun olam in a broken school.
frames.concerns: Modesty and kind speech; false accusation (lashon hara and motzi shem ra) as the class's origin. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Justice for the bullied; informed questioning of institutions.
frames.concerns: Sexism and minors sexualized; stereotypes of the time. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Mercy, protecting the weak, keeping promises, reconciliation of parents and children.
frames.concerns: Lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) and the lewd humor; suicide attempts read against Qur'an 4:29; violence by a teacher.

frames.aligns: The guru as one who transforms students; seva; dharma of a teacher.
frames.concerns: Rajasic and tamasic content (Gita 17) in lust and anger; disrespect of elders.

frames.aligns: Compassion (karuna) for suffering students; letting go of status and test scores.
frames.concerns: Lust and anger shown as comic strengths; right speech; violence.

frames.aligns: Seva, courage to protect the oppressed, the saint-soldier who defends the weak.
frames.concerns: Lust (kaam) and anger (krodh), two of the five vices, are part of the hero's comic persona. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Education as a sacred task; unity across class and status; service.
frames.concerns: A "chaste and holy life"; violence as method; backbiting and false accusation. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) in the hero; purification-like renewal of troubled students.
frames.concerns: Little doctrinal conflict; impurity themes only in a loose sense. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: "Harm none" echoed in protecting the bullied; nonconformity valued.
frames.concerns: Harm done by the hero's methods; Ouija board as a joke. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness precepts: help others, be a good example, respect others; Onizuka rescues people in crisis.
frames.concerns: Mayu's anxiety supplement and drug use are a minor theme; lawbreaking by the hero. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Anti-bullying, empathy for traumatized youth, critique of test-score culture and authoritarian administration.
frames.concerns: Sexualization of minors played as comedy; "frequently sexist" (Thompson); Tokiwa's rape survivor arc criticized (TV Tropes); consent; a false rape accusation as plot engine.

frames.aligns: Human dignity of every student; reason over rote rule-following; mutual aid.
frames.concerns: Cruelty played for comedy; violence as pedagogy.

frames.aligns: Courage, loyalty, responsibility (Fujisawa's stated theme), protective masculinity, restored families.
frames.concerns: Mockery of authority and institutions; crude sexual humor; delinquent culture glamorized.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth and dignity of every student; justice for the bullied.
frames.concerns: Violence and sexism; consent. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Rebellion against hypocritical authority, individualism, protecting children (Satanic Temple Tenets; Church of Satan's Eleven Rules on children).
frames.concerns: Harm to children in backstories, shown as wrong. (from general knowledge; to verify)

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Disputes are settled personally: fights, dares and a 100-man arm-wrestling match (vol. 15); Onizuka's yankii code of loyalty. Students' grievances go to the hero, not to rules.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Rules, PTA and surveillance (vol. 20) are obstacles; the hero breaks laws for good ends (stolen car, vol. 4).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Loyalty is to one's own class as a found family, but rescues reach outsiders too; birth families reconcile (Anko, Uchiyamada).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Rank and credentials are mocked (Teshigawara's elite pedigree, Uchiyamada); the teacher acts as an older brother.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No religion; tradition plays almost no role; practical results guide action.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Be yourself and live without regrets (Hypercritic); quality of each student's life over test scores, though poverty and debt are present.

folkways.japan: The yankii and bosozoku delinquent culture, the senpai-kohai hierarchy the story mocks, exam pressure and 1990s concern over bullying and enjo kosai are Japanese settings that many readers elsewhere will see as context rather than a message aimed at them.

delivery.evidence: Kimlinger (ANN): works "as both a parody and as the thing it parodies"; Thompson: "approaches true social satire." No review found calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Lessons arrive through Onizuka's speeches at climaxes and through rescues, inside broad comedy that also mocks the uplifting-teacher genre.

personified.ideology: Care and loyalty over rules
Career-minded rule-keeping
School as a business, surveillance and metrics
Elite credentials and perfectionism

entry.dominant: Pragmatism, Classical virtue ethics, Communitarianism, Libertarianism (anti-institutional), Critical theory (of schooling).

entry.heading: Blue Box
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is lived by trying with everything you have, at your sport and in love, so you will not regret it. Honesty with others, and patience in love, matter more than winning.

frames.aligns: Love shown as patient and self-giving; honesty; hard work; good is made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7).
frames.concerns: Teen dating as a goal in itself; a relationship hidden from parents; living under one roof.

frames.aligns: Patience, humility in defeat, care for others.
frames.concerns: Nepsis (watchfulness) asks what romantic daydreaming feeds; leotard shots in the anime.

frames.aligns: Philippians 4:8 fits much of it: honest, kind, pure in conduct.
frames.concerns: Secrecy from parents; sharing a home with a crush. Each family decides (soul liberty).

frames.aligns: Depicts first love without sexual content; honesty with Hina; effort and endurance.
frames.concerns: Romance as the center of a teen's life; secrecy from parents.

frames.aligns: No occult or spiritual content to weigh; clean romance.
frames.concerns: Holiness standards on modesty (leotards) vary by church.

frames.aligns: Common grace: well-crafted art about vocation and diligence.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139's concern with "lascivious" pictures does not fit a story this restrained; teen dating and secrecy are the talking points.

frames.aligns: Adiaphora: a clean story judged by love and conscience; Fourth Commandment respected by the end.
frames.concerns: Secrecy from parents. LCMS and WELS families may be more cautious about teen dating than ELCA ones.

frames.aligns: Holiness of conduct; diligence; kindness to rivals.
frames.concerns: Wesley's question whether a book tends to the love of God: the story has no faith content.

frames.aligns: Framing of good is clear; romance is gentle and honest.
frames.concerns: Little to raise beyond secrecy from parents.

frames.aligns: No violence; humility in defeat; hard work.
frames.concerns: Separation from the world makes popular media itself a concern for Old Order groups; romance-driven plot and competition for glory. MC USA families are much more open.

frames.aligns: Chaste pace; family hospitality; hard work; honesty.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth asks youth to avoid steady, exclusive dating while young; this couple dates exclusively from their teens.

frames.aligns: Female athlete with her own goals; honesty and kindness in romance.
frames.concerns: Hina's role as a rejected rival; secrecy from parents.

frames.aligns: No violence, substances or occult; diligence.
frames.concerns: "By beholding we become changed": romance-centered fiction and daydreaming; Ellen White's warning against fiction that excites the passions.
jw.org counsels dating only when ready to marry; here teen dating is the core message, and a couple is hidden from parents.

frames.aligns: Love, persistence and resilience after loss; little fear or illness to dwell on.

frames.concerns: Tzniut and shomer negiah: physical affection between unmarried teens, a boy and girl sharing a home without marriage, leotard shots. Many Haredi homes restrict such media altogether; Modern Orthodox families may read selectively.

frames.aligns: Kind speech, honesty, respect for parents and hosts.
frames.concerns: Modesty values applied by families; secrecy from parents.

frames.aligns: Informed autonomy; kindness; healthy teen relationships.
Hard work, patience (sabr), honesty, care for a guest.
frames.concerns: Dating outside marriage is the central plot; lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) for leotard and romantic scenes; an unrelated boy and girl sharing a home.

frames.aligns: Effort without attachment to results echoes the Gita's teaching on action; respect for parents and hosts.
frames.concerns: Romance chosen against parental knowledge; some families favor family-guided matches.

frames.aligns: Right effort; impermanence (graduation ends the "box," ch. 250); kindness.
frames.concerns: Romantic craving and attachment are the engine of the plot.

frames.aligns: Hard work (kirat karni), honesty, humility; lust is not glamorized.
frames.concerns: Little in the message; dating before marriage is a family conversation.
"Chaste and holy life" guidance may raise teen dating itself.

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto), effort and gratitude to hosts; seasonal festivals.
"Harm none" in honest rejection; seasons and festivals.
The Way to Happiness: be industrious, be worthy of trust, honor parents.
A girl's athletic goals drive the plot (Anime Feminist); no fan service beyond one shot; honest communication.
frames.concerns: Hina as a rejected "losing heroine" whom some critics see as a plot function (ANN); conventional love-triangle tropes.

frames.aligns: Effort, honesty and choosing your own path; no supernatural claims.
Hard work, modest pacing, respect for elders, a host family's duty.
frames.concerns: Months of secrecy from parents; a father who "turns a blind eye" (ch. 156).

frames.aligns: Worth and dignity of each person, including the rejected Hina.
Self-directed striving and honesty about one's desires.
frames.concerns: Self-sacrifice for a team and deference to parents and seniors sit against Church of Satan individualism.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: No insults are avenged; rivalry is settled in games and honest talk. Taiki's rejection of Hina is framed as fairness, not pride (ch. 77).

Order vs freedom.evidence: School and club discipline is honored (daily practice, captaincy in ch. 156), but the couple's private choices are respected by the adults (ch. 156).

Civic vs kin.evidence: A host family treats an unrelated girl as one of its own; loyalty runs to teams and friends as much as family.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Senpai-kohai and captain roles are respected; the romance crosses the senpai line, with the older girl as the stronger athlete.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No religion; life is guided by personal goals and choice. Festivals appear as setting.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Hard work and discipline are prized, but in service of personal dreams and feelings (not regretting, choosing your love).

folkways.japan: The school-club system, senpai-kohai etiquette, early-morning practice, summer festivals and the Inter-High tournament are Japanese school norms that frame the story; the living-with-a-crush setup is a familiar manga premise rather than a statement about family life.

delivery.evidence: Reviewers praise restraint: "never becomes tacky or prurient" (ANN); "doesn't abuse the shoujo romantic tropes" (SLJ). None call it preachy.
delivery.note: Its messages about effort and honesty come through Taiki's narration and the parallel sports and romance plots rather than speeches.

personified.ideology: Effort and honesty over talent
Discipline and goals before feelings
Wholehearted pursuit of love
Results-focused parental authority

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Existentialism (striving without regret), Communitarianism (team and host family), Expressive individualism (following one's feelings).

series.title: Chained Soldier
series.adult_reason: Chained Soldier: Yen Press rates it 18+ M (Mature); built-in sexual 'reward' scenes, nudity; deep entry scores sexuality 8

entry.heading: Chained Soldier (Mato Seihei no Slave)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is lived in service to your team and the people you love: be diligent, loyal and brave, protect the weak, and keep your promises. Physical pleasure is shown as a fair and fun payoff for hard work.

frames.aligns: Courage, service and protection of the weak; the bureau's abuse of people condemned; a sister sought and reconciled.
frames.concerns: Sexual acts as a reward make lust attractive rather than depicted for understanding (Inter Mirifica 7); the person used as an object (CCC 2525 on permissiveness and modesty).
Guarding the senses (nepsis) makes the constant fan service the main concern; the passions are fed, not fought.
Philippians 4:8 test fails on the sexual reward mechanic; Matthew 5:28 on lust. Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Servant heart (Yuuki), redemption-like truce with humanoid Shuuki.
frames.concerns: Depicting sin versus endorsing it: here sexual contact is endorsed as the payoff. No Christian review found.
Holiness and modesty standards; beings calling themselves gods; lust as an "open door."

frames.aligns: Common grace: real loyalty and courage.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 lists "lascivious... books, pictures" among sins against the seventh commandment; the series is built on them.

frames.aligns: Vocation: Yuuki's faithful housework and duty.
frames.concerns: Sixth Commandment (Small Catechism: "lead a sexually pure and decent life"). LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Works of service; care for the vulnerable humanoid Shuuki.
frames.concerns: Wesley's rule against diversions that cannot be used "in the name of the Lord Jesus." Holiness churches stricter than UMC.

frames.aligns: Clear framing of the monsters and the bureau as wrong; just defense.
frames.concerns: Lust framed as reward; women as prizes. Episcopal and ACNA families differ.
Violence as the hero's calling plus sexualized entertainment throughout; separation from the world.

frames.aligns: Family search and reunion; diligence; service.
frames.concerns: Law of chastity; For the Strength of Youth asks for media that invites the Spirit.

frames.aligns: Justice for the experimented-on humanoid Shuuki; a female-led world.
frames.concerns: Consent played for laughs (Butwhytho); women's bodies centered for a male gaze; a child's cheek-kiss reward.
"By beholding we become changed"; Fundamental Belief 22 on purity in entertainment; the central mechanic is sexual.
Immorality as a running reward; self-styled gods and spirit-like powers; violence (Psalm 11:5).
Dwelling on fear, violence and sensuality.
Tzniut and shmirat einayim (guarding the eyes) make the fan service central; intimacy outside marriage as a reward throughout.

frames.aligns: Protecting life; justice for the wronged; family.
frames.concerns: Modesty values; women as objects of reward.

frames.aligns: Justice for the experimented-on; protecting the vulnerable.
frames.concerns: Consent and objectification; a child in the reward system.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, patience, protecting the weak, fighting only against aggressors.
frames.concerns: Lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) and avoiding nearness to zina (17:32): the sexual content is central and endorsed.

frames.aligns: Dharma of protection; duty to family; mythic underworld setting.
frames.concerns: Kama pursued outside dharma; tamasic content (Gita ch. 17).
Third precept (sexual misconduct); craving fed as reward; killing as the solution.

frames.aligns: Courage to defend others; seva-like service.
frames.concerns: Kaam (lust) is the first of the five vices and here is the reward.

frames.aligns: Service, unity across humans and humanoid Shuuki.
frames.concerns: A "chaste and holy life"; violence as the main path.

frames.aligns: Japanese underworld (Yomi) mythology, peaches and thunder deities used as setting (Takahiro interview).
frames.concerns: Possible irreverence toward kami-like figures (Thunder Gods as villains); impurity themes.

frames.aligns: Mythic setting; consensual pleasure not treated as shameful.
frames.concerns: "Harm none": consent issues (Butwhytho) and power over another's body; a child in the reward system.

frames.aligns: Way to Happiness precepts: help others, be industrious.
Women in command; justice for the experimented-on.
frames.concerns: Anime Feminist: "a vehicle for an awkward, adolescent version of a dominatrix fantasy"; consent treated as "no big deal" (Butwhytho); gender theme underused.

frames.aligns: Human dignity of humanoid Shuuki defended against state experiments; reason and teamwork.
Duty, loyalty, protective courage, respect for rank and family lines.
frames.concerns: Undermines sexual modesty and marriage norms; a gender-reversed society.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of humanoid Shuuki; justice.
frames.concerns: Consent and objectification; a child in the reward system; age-appropriateness.

frames.aligns: Indulgence of desire between consenting adults; challenge to authority (the bureau).
frames.concerns: Harm to children (Nei is 11, though her reward is non-sexual); consent questions.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Kyouka's long revenge for her destroyed village drives her (fan wiki; Wikipedia); squad commanders duel for pride and rank (Six-Squad exchange match, Japanese Wikipedia; chapters to verify).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Military squads, ranks and contracts structure life; desire is freely pursued within that order.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Yuuki's search for his sister Aoba and Nei's for her parents; the Azuma family succession arc; but the squad and protecting the public come first.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Master and slave, commanders and members, a noble family's headship; Kyouka aims to be Supreme Commander.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Myth as backdrop, not belief; a modern state military; no practiced faith.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival against monsters is constant, but pleasure, desire and personal rivalry are celebrated.

folkways.japan: Rank and seniority in the squads, noble family houses (the Azuma banquet), and Kojiki-based underworld imagery reflect Japanese settings and myth; the harem-and-reward format is a convention of Japanese ecchi manga for boys rather than a message aimed at other cultures.

delivery.evidence: Reviews say the gender-politics premise is raised then underused (MyAnimeList review; Anime Feminist); none call it preachy.
delivery.note: Its values come through Yuuki's conduct and the reward mechanic rather than stated lessons, and its gender-reversed society is mostly backdrop.

personified.ideology: Selfless, diligent service
Duty and command fueled by revenge
Revenge for exploitation of Mato
State power over "monstrous" people

entry.dominant: Hedonism, Communitarianism, Classical virtue ethics, Might makes right (as the power system), Pagan / occult (Japanese myth).

entry.heading: ReLIFE
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is not lost when you fall out of society. You can restart it by facing your past honestly, letting others in, and helping the people beside you, even when it hurts.

frames.aligns: Human dignity in work; condemnation of harassment; hope and second chances; chaste romance aimed at lasting love.
frames.concerns: Suicide backstory (handled as tragedy; CCC 2280-2283 and 2282 on diminished responsibility); memory erasure without consent; deception in the premise.

frames.aligns: Repentance as a turning back and starting again; humility; care for the dead (grave visit).
frames.concerns: Memory erasure as a violation of the person; little spiritual frame for the recovery.

frames.aligns: Clear wrong (harassment) and clear good (honesty, friendship). Chaste romance.
frames.concerns: No spiritual source of renewal; deception premise; smoking and drinking played lightly.

frames.aligns: Beneath the Tangles finds "a little show with a big, big heart" and reads it through Luke 10 (Mary and Martha).
frames.concerns: Memory erasure ethics (Beneath the Tangles guest writer: "Love is a relational value"); humanistic hope only.

frames.aligns: Restoration and hope after despair; no occult content.
frames.concerns: Recovery comes through a company program, not spiritual power; suicide backstory.

frames.aligns: Common grace in a well-told story; sin and cruelty in the workplace shown honestly; vocation matters.
frames.concerns: Self-help framing of renewal; memory erasure; WLC Q136 on self-murder (shown as tragedy, not endorsed).

frames.aligns: Vocation: work as service to neighbor; Kaizaki ends serving others (ch. 222). Adiaphora for the content.
frames.concerns: Memory erasure; mild substance use. Confessional families may be stricter.

frames.aligns: Social holiness: justice for the harassed and the shut-in; growth in love.
frames.concerns: Smoking and drinking (traditional Wesleyan caution); memory erasure.

frames.aligns: Story judged by how it frames good and evil: harassment wrong, friendship good.
frames.concerns: Memory erasure accepted by the story; suicide backstory.

frames.aligns: Nonviolent; humility; community care; Kaizaki learns to serve, not dominate.
frames.concerns: Popular media itself (Old Order groups avoid it); worldly school and office settings.

frames.aligns: Self-reliance and work; repentance as change; chaste dating; service.
frames.concerns: Smoking and drinking (Word of Wisdom); suicide backstory.

frames.aligns: Structural sin in labor exploitation and sexism; dignity of the marginalized (NEETs, shut-ins).
frames.concerns: Corporate power over subjects goes largely unquestioned.

frames.aligns: Health and recovery; hope; chaste romance.
frames.concerns: Smoking and drinking (health message); suicide backstory; fiction itself for stricter members.

frames.aligns: No violence, spiritism or immorality; honesty and friendship.
frames.concerns: Christmas celebrations and a birthday on December 25 (Witnesses do not observe these); smoking.

frames.aligns: Hope and the power of changed thinking to change a life.
frames.concerns: Dwelling on despair and suicide; the remedy is a drug.

frames.aligns: Dignity of every person; condemnation of shaming (lashon hara and humiliation); teshuvah-like turning.
frames.concerns: Suicide backstory; deception in the premise; mixed-sex school romance against tzniut for many homes.

frames.aligns: Kind speech; dignity; repair of one's life.
Tikkun olam in fighting workplace injustice; informed autonomy.
Patience (sabr) and hope (never despair of God's mercy, Qur'an 39:53); justice for the wronged.
frames.concerns: Suicide backstory (Qur'an 4:29); alcohol and smoking; mixed-sex dating and Christmas scenes.

frames.aligns: Dharma of work and service; rebirth-like "second life" as a metaphor; respect for elders.
Suffering, attachment and letting go; compassion; impermanence (memories that fade).
frames.concerns: Alcohol and smoking (fifth precept); erasure as a kind of loss.

frames.aligns: Kirat karo (honest work), seva and humility; the five vices not glorified.
frames.concerns: Alcohol and tobacco (prohibited in the Rehat Maryada for initiated Sikhs).

frames.aligns: Work as worship; unity; chaste romance; service.
Sincerity (makoto); honoring the dead (grave visit); New Year customs.
"Harm none" fits the critique of harassment; respect for the dead.
Personal betterment; The Way to Happiness precepts on helping others and being industrious.
frames.concerns: A drug-based "cure" and a treatment program; mental health framed in psychology terms.

frames.aligns: Critique of exploitative labor and workplace sexism; mental health taken seriously; destigmatizes quitting and NEETs.
frames.concerns: Corporate consent problems (memory erasure); the "Christmas cake" joke; adult-teen premise (both leads adults).

frames.aligns: Human renewal through reason, friendship and effort; meaning without the supernatural.
frames.concerns: Memory erasure ethics; science used without consent.

frames.aligns: Work, responsibility, gratitude to mentors, chaste romance leading toward marriage (vol. 15 epilogue).
frames.concerns: Quitting a job and a corporate welfare program as the cure may sit uneasily with self-reliance; TV Tropes notes quitting can read as cowardice in Japan.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of every person, including NEETs and shut-ins; justice at work.
Leaving an abusive group and choosing one's own path (Church of Satan individualism); compassion (Satanic Temple Tenet 1).
frames.concerns: The story ends in service to a company and friends over the self.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Worth is inherent; harassment is wrong. Kaizaki's personal confrontation of the harasser made things worse (Japanese Wikipedia), and the story values listening over answering an insult.

Order vs freedom.evidence: School routine and a group are shown as healing (creator interview), but freedom to quit a harmful job is defended (ch. 92).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Found family among classmates matters more than blood family; Ohga's family loyalty (ch. 165) is shown with sympathy.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Abusive seniority at the company is critiqued; mentors (Saiki, Yoake) are respected for their care, not their rank.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: A science experiment drives the plot; religion is almost absent; holidays are social.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Quality of life and mental health come before enduring a harmful job; the story still values returning to work (ch. 222).

folkways.japan: The black-company setting, the stigma on quitting young (noted by TV Tropes), senpai-kohai bonds at work and school, and the "Christmas cake" joke reflect Japanese norms; the story's own message pushes against the first two.

delivery.evidence: ANN says flashbacks show lessons Arata applies; no review opened calls it preachy. Black company shown only as harmful.
delivery.note: The message comes through Kaizaki's flashbacks and his advice to classmates rather than speeches, though the workplace side has no sympathetic voice.

personified.ideology: Restart is possible; honesty and connection heal
Quiet support and second chances, within company rules
Efficiency over cooperation, then learning connection
Conformity and profit over people

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Communitarianism, Secular humanism, Existentialism, Critical theory (labor).

entry.heading: The Seven Deadly Sins
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is lived in loyal love and friendship, chosen across the lines that clans, races and gods draw. Love and loyalty should outlast curses, prejudice and even the rulers of heaven and hell.

content.framing: Endorsed (played as comedy); critics call it harassment

frames.aligns: Faithful married love, forgiveness of enemies (Hendrickson, Dreyfus, Merlin), self-giving sacrifice (Elaine, Escanor).
frames.concerns: The groping gag makes a sin against dignity attractive and funny (Inter Mirifica 7; CCC 2354-2356 on chastity and respect). A "supreme deity" shown as a tyrant, and the inversion of "sins" and "commandments," read against the tradition's moral names.

frames.aligns: Love and loyalty, repentance of former enemies.
frames.concerns: Demons as heroes and a goddess clan as oppressors can blur the spiritual line the tradition keeps; magic and purgatory imagery. Guarding the senses (nepsis) makes the repeated groping images a concern.

frames.aligns: Clear villains defeated; faithful marriage at the end; friendship and forgiveness.
frames.concerns: Harassment played for laughs (Philippians 4:8); magic and demon heroes; views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Redemption of villains, love that sacrifices, friendship.
frames.concerns: The Supreme Deity cast as a villain; heroes who are literally demons; the harassment gag. Some families "engage" fantasy, others separate (Romans 14).
Media as an "open door": demon heroes, a demon king, curses, magic and purgatory all shown as real, and the highest deity framed as evil. Views range widely.

frames.aligns: Common grace: friendship, loyalty and faithful marriage are honored.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 lists "lascivious... pictures" among sins against the seventh commandment; the gag is lighthearted lechery. A tyrant "god" and inverted moral names.

frames.aligns: Forgiveness offered to the undeserving (Merlin, Hendrickson); vocation as protector and ruler.
frames.concerns: Harassment as comedy; demon heroes. LCMS and WELS families tend to be more cautious than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Forgiveness and transformation of former enemies; love across divisions.
frames.concerns: Lechery as humor; magic. Holiness churches more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: A playful retelling of Arthurian legend (ANN feature), a literary tradition many Anglicans value; love and loyalty win.

frames.concerns: Violence is the heroes' main tool throughout; worldly entertainment and magic. Conservative groups avoid most popular media; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Families formed and continued: marriages and children close the story; loyalty and sacrifice.
frames.concerns: Harassment played for laughs; revealing outfits; magic. For the Strength of Youth asks whether media invites the Spirit.

frames.aligns: Love across racial lines and the defeat of clan hatred; redemption of oppressors.
frames.concerns: Non-consensual touching as comedy; Jericho's arc toward "femininity"; childlike designs on adult characters.
The dead appear (Elaine's ghost in the Capital of the Dead), purgatory, resurrection by magic and reincarnation conflict with teaching on the state of the dead; magic and demon heroes.
Magic, curses, demons and spirits of the dead are central motifs (Galatians 5:19-21); fighting as the heroes' path; lechery.

frames.aligns: Love outlasts curses; forgiveness over hatred.
frames.concerns: Curses, death and evil shown as powerful realities; constant battle.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, marriage, forgiveness of the repentant.
frames.concerns: Tzniut and nivul peh make the groping gag and outfits a concern; magic and many "gods"; many Haredi homes restrict such media altogether.

frames.aligns: Love across divisions; teshuvah-like change in former enemies.
frames.concerns: Harassment as comedy; idol-like gods; families apply modesty values.

frames.aligns: Anti-prejudice message; repair after harm (Merlin told to take responsibility, ch. 337).
frames.concerns: Non-consensual touching as comedy; gender stereotypes.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, marriage and family, forgiveness, fighting oppression.
frames.concerns: Many gods and a tyrant "supreme deity"; magic; the groping gag and revealing outfits ("lowering the gaze," Qur'an 24:30-31).

frames.aligns: Devas and asuras at war, with love crossing the line; reincarnation across many lives (Elizabeth); dharma as protector-king.
frames.concerns: Lechery as comedy; some families apply the Gita's tamasic category.

frames.aligns: The sins as named passions (wrath, envy, greed, sloth, lust, gluttony, pride) that each character works through; rebirth; hatred between clans as the root of suffering.
frames.concerns: Killing is the plot's solution (first precept); craving-driven humor.

frames.aligns: Five vices (lust, anger, greed, attachment, ego) are literally the team's emblems and are partly overcome; courage to defend the oppressed.
frames.concerns: Lust shown as comic and harmless in the hero.

frames.aligns: Unity of peoples: the war ends when clans stop hating one another; love across races.
frames.concerns: Violence as the path; the "chaste and holy life" call applied to the gag.

frames.aligns: Nature spirits, fairy forest, sacred spring (Fountain of Youth) treated with respect; sincerity in friendship.
frames.concerns: Little on message; the gag weighs against sincerity and respect.

frames.aligns: Druids, fairies, nature gods and a sacred forest shown with respect (ANN feature on Celtic roots); love across clans; tyrant gods overthrown.
The Way to Happiness precepts: be faithful to a partner, do not harm a person of good will.
Anti-prejudice and interracial love; forgiveness; strong women fighters.
frames.concerns: Non-consent played for laughs (ANN; Otaku USA; Common Sense Media); Jericho's arc; childlike designs on adult partners; restored monarchy.

frames.aligns: Human (and non-human) bonds over divine rule; rebellion against tyrannical gods; forgiveness.
Loyalty, honor, marriage and children, rightful monarchy restored, knightly ideals from Arthurian legend.
frames.concerns: Lechery as humor; moral names inverted; rulers and fathers as villains.

frames.aligns: Worth and dignity of every clan; free choice in love; redemption.
frames.concerns: Groping undercuts bodily dignity; violence as the main solution.

frames.aligns: Rebellion against a tyrannical supreme deity and a demon king who forbid love; individual choice over clan law; demons humanized.
frames.concerns: The Satanic Temple's Tenet 3 ("One's body is inviolable") against the groping gag; loyalty to a captain over self.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Escanor's pride and personal duels sit beside repeated forgiveness of enemies (Hendrickson, Dreyfus, Merlin, ch. 337); Ban's vendetta-free immortality humor.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The heroes are outlaws who defy the Holy Knights and both clans' laws on love; order is restored only under a just king (vol. 41).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Loyalty to the band, to lovers and to blood brothers (Meliodas and Zeldris) drives the story more than duty to the kingdom at large.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Captain and princess are honored and the monarchy returns, but outcasts from every clan stand as equals in the band.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Magic, gods and curses are real; no faith practice is honored, and the gods are tyrants.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Personal love and choosing one's partner across races are the highest goods; battles for survival frame them.

folkways.japan: The groping gag follows a long-standing shonen comedy convention, and the captain-and-crew loyalty echoes group norms common in Japanese storytelling; readers elsewhere may see both as genre norms more than a message aimed at them.

delivery.evidence: Otaku USA says the series "humanizes its villains"; the Demon King and Supreme Deity get little inner life. No review found calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its themes of love across clan lines and forgiveness come through backstory flashbacks and battle speeches rather than lectures.

personified.ideology: Love defies clan law and divine curse
Rule by fear and clan hatred
Order by force; war to save the kingdom
Knowledge and ambition over loyalty

entry.dominant: Communitarianism (found family), Expressive individualism (love against clan law), Pagan / occult (Celtic fantasy), Traditionalism, Classical virtue ethics.

entry.heading: Solanin
entry.label: From summaries

frames.aligns: Honest work, friendship, a mother's care and grief borne with love; no evil made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7). The dead are remembered.
frames.concerns: Cohabitation outside marriage is normal in the story and unexamined (CCC 2390-2391); no hope beyond this life is voiced; any bed scenes (to verify) under CCC 2521-2524.

frames.aligns: A story of loss that does not make sin attractive; love that endures beyond death through memory.
frames.concerns: No prayer or memory of the dead in the Church's sense; cohabitation; watchfulness (nepsis) over any intimate scenes.

frames.aligns: Hard work, loyalty, honest emotion; no glamorized wrongdoing.
frames.concerns: Cohabitation presented as normal; no gospel hope in grief; language and any intimacy measured against Philippians 4:8. Each congregation decides.

frames.aligns: A realistic look at young-adult aimlessness and loss; many in this tradition would use it to "engage" questions of purpose.
frames.concerns: No answer beyond this life; cohabitation unexamined.

frames.aligns: No occult content; honest grief; friends who carry each other.
frames.concerns: No spiritual answer to death; cohabitation against holiness standards; any intimate scenes.

frames.aligns: Common grace: honest art by a non-Christian about vocation, love and death. Work shown as worth doing.
frames.concerns: Cohabitation; no providence or hope named. WLC Q139 would weigh any lascivious images (to verify whether any exist).

frames.aligns: Vocation: ordinary work and service to others as worthy (Taneda's return to a job); grief honestly expressed. Entertainment is adiaphora, judged by conscience.
frames.concerns: Cohabitation; no gospel. LCMS and WELS families will weigh this more than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Friendship and community carry the grieving; social holiness in caring for one another.
frames.concerns: Cohabitation; drinking (to verify); holiness churches more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: Serious literary treatment of grief and vocation; good and evil framed clearly where they appear (the harassing boss).
frames.concerns: Cohabitation and the absence of faith; families across the Anglican range differ.

frames.aligns: Community care, no violence shown as heroic, simple work and music.
frames.concerns: A worldly life of bands and city jobs; cohabitation; separation from popular media leads Old Order groups to avoid it, MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Family love (Meiko's mother), hard work, the epilogue's marriage and child.
frames.concerns: Cohabitation and sexual intimacy outside marriage presented as normal; no plan of salvation or hope beyond death; any language and drinking against For the Strength of Youth.

frames.aligns: Compassionate, honest picture of young adults' economic insecurity and grief; workplace harassment shown as wrong; a woman who leads her band.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; the death's possible suicide reading deserves care.
Cohabitation; drinking and smoking (to verify); a story with no hope beyond death; "by beholding we become changed" applied to the lifestyle shown.

frames.aligns: No spiritism or occult; no violence admired.
frames.concerns: Cohabitation is treated in Witness literature as immorality (Galatians 5:19-21); no hope in God's Kingdom.

frames.aligns: Love and friendship lift Meiko out of grief; life goes on.
frames.concerns: Death and loss presented as final reality; members "stand porter at the door of thought" about dwelling on grief and accident.

frames.aligns: Honest mourning; the value of work and friendship; a mother's care.
frames.concerns: Cohabitation and intimacy outside marriage against tzniut; language (nivul peh); many Haredi homes avoid secular media entirely.

frames.aligns: Mourning and memory; work and friendship.
frames.concerns: Cohabitation; no religious frame for death.

frames.aligns: Honest picture of young adults finding purpose; harassment shown as wrong; community after loss.
Patience (sabr) in grief; work and family duty.
frames.concerns: Cohabitation and intimacy outside marriage; drinking (to verify); lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) for any intimate scenes; no turn to God in loss. Music is debated among scholars.

frames.aligns: Dharma of work and duty to others; impermanence; love remembered.
frames.concerns: No spiritual frame for death; cohabitation weighed differently by community.

frames.aligns: Impermanence and attachment are the story's quiet subject: youth, dreams and a loved one pass, and Meiko learns to hold them lightly; Wrong Every Time reads it as "impermanent but real" experience.
frames.concerns: Drinking (to verify) against the precepts; mindfulness of what feeds the mind.

frames.aligns: Honest work (kirat karni), friendship and service; grief without despair.
Work as worship, the arts, friendship.
frames.concerns: Cohabitation against a "chaste and holy life"; drinking (to verify).

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) in friendship and grief; ordinary life and seasons; no shrines or kami mocked.
frames.concerns: Death as kegare may weigh with some families.

frames.aligns: Personal responsibility, harm none, honoring the dead through art; no stereotyped pagans.
