Survival through work, friendship and group (the band); a person who recovers and goes on.
frames.concerns: Grief handled without the Church's methods; no content code for fiction.

frames.aligns: A woman who leads her life and band; workplace harassment named; honest about young workers' insecurity and grief.
frames.concerns: The death's possible suicide reading; safe-messaging care if it is drawn that way (to verify).

frames.aligns: This-life meaning through work, art, love and friendship; grief faced without supernatural comfort; Asano says the work comes from "my own real world and real life."
Hard work, a loving mother, loyalty; drifting is shown to have costs; the epilogue's marriage and child.
frames.concerns: Cohabitation as the norm; quitting a job without a plan; the music-industry life.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth, free search for meaning, compassion in grief, a flat circle of friends.
This-life focus, self-determination (Meiko quits and chooses her path), art as self-expression, rejection of a crushing job.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; harassment by the boss is framed as wrong.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: No one answers insult personally; Meiko simply quits the job with the harassing boss (ComicsAlliance). No fights.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Meiko and Taneda quit to choose their own way (VIZ synopsis), but the story also respects steady work (Taneda's return to a job) and her mother's practical advice.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Chosen friends (the band, Ai) matter more than blood family, though Meiko's mother and Taneda's father are shown with warmth (Manga Bookshelf; Japanese Wikipedia).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: A flat circle of friends; bosses and the record label are the only hierarchy and are shown with mixed or critical eyes (ComicsAlliance; TV Tropes).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No religion; cohabitation unremarked; grief handled through music and friends. The epilogue's marriage softens this a little.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Music and self-expression are celebrated (Meiko playing "Solanin"), while the need to pay rent keeps survival in view.

folkways.japan: The pressure to join a company after graduation, the "freeter" life of part-time work, parents in the provinces sending produce, and politeness in hiding a cohabitation from a parent are Japanese context rather than the story's own argument; the story questions the company track more than it endorses it.

delivery.evidence: The Fandom Post: Asano "doesn't offer easy solutions"; ComicsAlliance notes the record executive's sell-out choice gets a fair justification.
delivery.note: The story weighs dream against stability through characters and leaves the verdict largely to the reader.

personified.ideology: Pursuing the dream of music over "proper work"
Practical stability; happiness need not be the hard road
Pride set aside for a career inside the industry

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Secular humanism, Pragmatism, Dharmic (Buddhist) by echo, Expressive individualism (explored).

entry.heading: Assassination Classroom
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life comes from finding your own strength, being seen and believed in by someone, and facing hard things together. Nobody is worthless because a system ranks them low, and anyone, even a killer, can change.

content.frequency: Constant (as premise); bloody only in a few arcs

frames.aligns: Human dignity of the "worthless" students; a teacher who gives his life (John 15:13); a killer's conversion through Aguri's love; mercy to enemies.
frames.concerns: Koro-sensei asks to be killed: read against CCC 2276-2283 on euthanasia and suicide. Adult-on-minor kissing and porn gags played for laughs (CCC 2521-2524 on modesty).

frames.aligns: Repentance (metanoia) of the Reaper; love that changes a person; humility of the teacher.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis) weighs on the fan service. The premise trains children in killing as a game.

frames.aligns: Clear evil in Yanagisawa and Takaoka; second chances; honoring good teachers.
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 test for the sexual gags and the "Bitch-sensei" nickname; killing a teacher as the premise. Soul liberty means families decide.

frames.aligns: Depicts violence without endorsing it on humans; redemption; grace given to those written off. Beneath the Tangles draws a "which master we serve" lesson (Romans 6:15-23) from Terasaka's arc (ch. 44-48).
frames.concerns: Comic sexualization of minors; whether the premise trivializes killing (the concern school-library challengers raised).

frames.aligns: Good and evil clearly drawn; transformation of a life.
frames.concerns: Little occult content; holiness standards weigh the fan service and coarse nickname.

frames.aligns: Common grace: a non-Christian work that honors vocation and teaching; human depravity shown in Yanagisawa and Asano.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 on "lascivious ... pictures" for the fan service; willing death (WLC Q136).

frames.aligns: Vocation: teaching as a calling served with love. Law and gospel echo: the students cannot "earn" worth by rank; worth is given.
frames.concerns: Willing death at the students' hands; fan service. LCMS and WELS families tend to be stricter than ELCA ones.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy, social holiness for the outcast class; prevenient grace in the Reaper's change.
frames.concerns: Wesley's General Rules on "diversions"; holiness churches would weigh the sexual gags more.

frames.aligns: Framing is clear: abusers condemned, love transforms; a strong tradition of judging fiction by its framing (Lewis, Sayers).
frames.concerns: Comic sexual content with minors; the ending's willing death.

frames.aligns: Love of enemies (the Reaper, Takaoka spared); humility; community.
frames.concerns: Training children to kill is the premise, even with harmless weapons; the hero is a former assassin who teaches assassination. Conservative groups avoid most popular media.

frames.aligns: Agency, growth and potential; a teacher who serves; redemption.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth asks for media that invites the Spirit: the porn gags, kissing gags and "Bitch-sensei" weigh here.

frames.aligns: Justice for the marginalized class; a critique of a system that shames the weak; restorative care for the abused.
frames.concerns: Gender gags (Nagisa cross-dressing, Irina's role); comic sexualization of minors.

frames.aligns: Self-sacrifice; caring education (Adventist schooling values); change of character.
frames.concerns: Fundamental Belief 22 on entertainment; "by beholding we become changed" applied to the killing premise and sexual gags. (from general knowledge; to verify)
jw.org's question on violence (Psalm 11:5): killing is the class's goal and training. Immorality in the gags. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Love that heals people; belief in each child's capacity.
frames.concerns: Fear, death and a ticking doomsday are central; dwelling on harm. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Respect for teachers (kavod harav); teshuvah in the Reaper; protecting the weak.
frames.concerns: Tzniut makes the fan service and adult-student kissing a strong concern; killing as a school game; a willing death. Many Haredi homes restrict such media. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Respect for teachers; teshuvah; care for the bullied.
frames.concerns: Modesty values for the gags; the willing death. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam in lifting a written-off class; critique of humiliation; informed choice.
frames.concerns: Gender gags; comic sexual content with minors. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Respect for teachers and parents; repentance (tawba); patience; forgiveness.
frames.concerns: Lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) for the fan service; willing death read against Qur'an 4:29.

frames.aligns: Guru-shishya bond is the heart of the story; dharma of the teacher; karma in the Reaper's change.
frames.concerns: Rajasic or tamasic content (Gita 17) in the violence and gags.

frames.aligns: Compassion; change of a killer (echoes of Angulimala, from general knowledge); acceptance of impermanence and death.
frames.concerns: Killing as the class's aim, against the first precept; sexual gags and right speech.

frames.aligns: Seva of the teacher; the five vices (ego, anger, greed) shown in Asano, Takaoka and Yanagisawa and condemned; courage.
frames.concerns: Lust played for laughs (one of the five vices). (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Education as the key to human potential; unity of a divided class (ch. 143-146 reconciliation).
frames.concerns: Non-violence and a "chaste and holy life": the premise and gags. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto), gratitude to teachers, purification of a stained past.
Growth, harm to children condemned, personal power used well.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; no witch or pagan stereotypes reported.

frames.aligns: Way to Happiness precepts: help and teach others, honor good teachers, do not harm.
Critique of meritocratic sorting and humiliation; anti-bullying; an abusive parent condemned; Nagisa's gender expression read as affirming by some (Anime Rants).
frames.concerns: An adult kissing minors as comedy; Nagisa's cross-dressing as a gag and "toxic masculinity" (Anime Rants); the "Bitch" nickname.

frames.aligns: Education as human flourishing; reason, effort and human relationships; no supernatural answers; a teacher's legacy lives on in students.
frames.concerns: Comic sexualization of minors; the willing death needs a careful talk.

frames.aligns: Discipline, hard work, respect for teachers, earning success; abusers punished; Terasaka's atonement.
frames.concerns: Moms for Liberty and Citizens Defending Freedom objected to killing a teacher as a premise and to sexual content (ANN, 2023); the series mocks school authority (Asano).

frames.aligns: Inherent worth and dignity of every student; justice for the marginalized; free search for each one's path.
frames.concerns: Gender gags; adult-on-minor comedy. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Individual excellence; challenging an unjust authority (Asano's system); compassion (Satanic Temple Tenet 1); self-determined death of a consenting adult.
frames.concerns: Exploitation of children is condemned in the story; a Church of Satan reading may see Koro-sensei's self-sacrifice as against self-preservation. (from general knowledge; to verify)

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Class 3-E answers humiliation by winning fair contests (exams, sports, the school festival), not by revenge. Takaoka's revenge and Kayano's vendetta (ch. 128-133) are shown as destructive. Class pride matters.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Discipline and drills are celebrated (Karasuma), but the rigid, shaming school order is critiqued.

Civic vs kin.evidence: The class, not the family, is the main bond; Nagisa's controlling mother is a problem to overcome (ch. 112-114).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Deep respect for a good teacher, but rejection of rank by test score and of Class A's elite status.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: A secular, science-shaped world; no religion reported; reason and study solve problems.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Each student's talent and self-esteem is the goal (Common Sense Media: "never giving up," "believing in yourself"); epilogue careers fit each person.

folkways.japan: The exam-ranking pressure, the "E class" stigma, the senpai-kohai and teacher-student respect, and the school festival are Japanese school norms. The series critiques the ranking culture from inside it, and readers elsewhere may see the respect for teachers as a setting norm.

delivery.evidence: Matsui calls it "lessons upon lessons"; one MyAnimeList review faults "superficial satire". No review in this entry calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Koro-sensei states each lesson aloud, while the opposing view (Asano's fear-based system) gets a sympathetic backstory but Takaoka is drawn as a plain sadist.

personified.ideology: Personal, caring education; redemption through service
Meritocracy by fear and humiliation
Authoritarian discipline by force
Science and ambition without ethics

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Secular humanism, Communitarianism, Confucian ethics.

entry.heading: Yona of the Dawn
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is one where privilege is turned into service: you face hard truths, grow strong enough to protect others, keep faith with the people who stand by you, and refuse revenge in favor of healing the land.

frames.aligns: Evil (trafficking, drugs, corruption) is shown but not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7); a ruler's duty to the common good and the poor; mercy over vengeance.
frames.concerns: A non-Christian divine order (dragon gods, a god-king, reincarnation) presented as real; the usurper's murder is never fully judged.

frames.aligns: Struggle against the passions of revenge and pride; humility of a princess who learns to serve.
frames.concerns: Dragon gods and reincarnation shown as real; nepsis makes repeated battle imagery a matter to watch.

frames.aligns: Clear wrongs named and opposed; loyalty, courage, care for the poor.
frames.concerns: Divine dragons and rebirth as real (John 14:6); Kusanagi's world has no single God. Each congregation decides.

frames.aligns: Depicts sin without endorsing it; Speculative Faith calls it "thought-provoking entertainment" and finds a "Christian-like" theme in refusing revenge; Beneath the Tangles links Yona's anger to righteous anger (Matthew 21:12-13).
frames.concerns: Myth and reincarnation shown as real; the series has no explicit Christian content.

frames.aligns: Clear good and evil; courage and sacrifice.
frames.concerns: Dragon gods who give powers through blood, an immortal servant of a god-king, and reincarnation, all positive in the story; "open door" concern varies by church.

frames.aligns: Common grace in a non-Christian story; corrupt rulers held to account; honest picture of sin in everyone, including heroes and Su-won.
frames.concerns: Reincarnation and dragon gods; no images of God or Christ are involved.

frames.aligns: Two kingdoms: rulers bear the sword to protect the weak; Su-won as a ruler who protects but is not pure.
frames.concerns: Non-Christian spirituality. LCMS and WELS families are more cautious than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy toward the poor, the sick (Yun as healer) and the trafficked; social holiness.
frames.concerns: Mythic spirituality; Holiness churches more cautious about fantasy violence.

frames.aligns: Fantasy judged by its framing of good and evil, in the tradition of C.S. Lewis; just war when Kouka is invaded.
frames.concerns: Little to raise beyond non-Christian myth.

frames.aligns: Compassion, community care, refusal of revenge, a gentle king (Il) who hated war.
frames.concerns: The story treats Il's pacifism as a failure that left the poor unprotected; the heroine's path is learning to fight and kill. Conservative groups avoid most popular media.

frames.aligns: Service, loyalty, chaste romance, care for the poor, growth through trial.
frames.concerns: Some violence and a revealing dance outfit (ch. 65). Members vary in strictness.

frames.aligns: Justice for the trafficked and the poor; a woman's leadership; structural corruption named.
frames.concerns: Royal legitimacy treated as meaningful; violence as the main tool.

frames.aligns: Care for the poor; temperance (the Nadai drug arc condemns addiction); chaste romance.
frames.concerns: Reincarnation and an immortal soul-bond to a god-king conflict with teaching on the state of the dead; frequent battles.

frames.aligns: Love of neighbor, honesty, opposing exploitation.
frames.concerns: Dragon gods, powers from divine blood, reincarnation and fighting as the heroes' path weigh as spiritism and violence (Psalm 11:5).

frames.aligns: Love and right thinking overcome fear and hatred; Yona chooses healing over revenge.
frames.concerns: Violence, disease (Su-won's illness, later arcs; to verify) and fear shown as powerful realities.

frames.aligns: Justice for the oppressed; honoring a father's memory; opposing trafficking and drug trade.
frames.concerns: Polytheistic gods and a divine king shown as real; tzniut concerns for the dance scene (ch. 65); many Haredi homes restrict such media.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam echoes in repairing a broken kingdom; justice for the poor; memory of the dead.
frames.concerns: Polytheistic myth; modesty applied by families.

frames.aligns: Justice, human dignity, women's leadership, opposing trafficking.
Justice for the oppressed, care for the poor and orphans, fighting only against oppression, forgiveness preferred (Qur'an 42:40).
frames.concerns: Dragon gods and a god-king shown as real (shirk concerns); reincarnation; images of living beings debated; the revealing dance (ch. 65) for lowering the gaze.

frames.aligns: Raja dharma: a ruler's duty to protect the people; rebirth of Hiryuu in Yona; loyal warriors serving a righteous heir.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; some families apply the Gita's tamasic category to battle scenes.

frames.aligns: Letting go of revenge; compassion for suffering villagers; impermanence and Zeno's grief at endless life; rebirth.
frames.concerns: Killing remains the means in war arcs, against the first precept.

frames.aligns: The saint-soldier ideal: courage to defend the oppressed; the five vices (greed, anger, ego) shown in corrupt lords and condemned; service to all.
Service, justice for the poor, equality of women and men shown in Yona's growth.
frames.concerns: Strong commitment to non-violence; war arcs.

frames.aligns: Dragon gods and sacred lineage treated with respect; sincerity (makoto) in Yona; purification of a corrupted land.
Respect for myth, divine beings and nature; "harm none" echoes in protecting villages.
Way to Happiness precepts: be worthy of trust, do not harm a person of good will, safeguard and improve the environment; drug harm condemned (Nadai arc).
A heroine's agency praised by ANN and Anime Feminist; anti-trafficking; care for the poor; plain treatment of menstruation (ch. 128).
frames.concerns: Hak's gruff possessive-seeming style (discussed by Anime Feminist); monarchy and royal blood treated as meaningful; fan service is light.

frames.aligns: Human effort, learning and compassion change the world; free inquiry into what makes a just ruler.
frames.concerns: Divine dragons and destiny as real; fiction, but the plot leans on them.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, duty, honor, courage, legitimate rule, protective masculinity in Hak.
frames.concerns: A pacifist king shown as weak; some families may question a princess as warrior, though the story frames it as duty.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of the poor and outcast (Shin-ah's village, trafficked girls); justice; a free search for what is right.
frames.concerns: Violence as the main solution in war arcs.

frames.aligns: Compassion and justice (Satanic Temple Tenets 1 and 2); a heroine who defies her expected role; protection of children from traffickers.
frames.concerns: Loyalty to a divine lineage and duty over the self are honored; Church of Satan individualism would read the band's devotion skeptically.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Yona chooses not to take revenge on Su-won (Beneath the Tangles; Speculative Faith), and the "cycle of revenge" is criticized (TV Tropes). Loyalty and personal honor still drive Hak (ch. 91, 152).

Order vs freedom.evidence: The band acts outside the law against corrupt officials (ch. 28-53), but the goal is restoring good order, and Yona allies with the crown (ch. 178-179).

Civic vs kin.evidence: A found family is central, yet Yona's duty grows from her own kin to all of Kouka's people, including strangers in Awa and Sensui.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Royal blood, the Hiryuu lineage and retainer loyalty are honored; a princess also cooks, trains and lives with commoners, and rulers are judged by service.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Dragon gods, prophecy and reincarnation are real (ch. 101, 121); Su-won's pragmatic reform is shown as effective but cold.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Hardship, hunger and war shape the band; Yona's arc is also about choosing her own path, and the series does not mock her care for clothes and hair (Anime Feminist).

folkways.japan: The retainer's loyalty to his lord, the mandate-of-heaven idea and a fantasy blend of Korean, Chinese and Japanese court life reflect East Asian historical norms the setting takes for granted; the story's own message is the ruler's duty to serve the people.

delivery.evidence: ANN praises the "political complexity"; Anime Feminist hosts praise villains as "complex individuals who aren't entirely evil." No review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its messages about just rule and service are spoken in Yona's lines and shown through the villages she helps, while Su-won's opposing view gets a fair hearing.

personified.ideology: Rule as service to the people
Strong-state realism; ends justify means
Pacifism at any cost
Greed and exploitation of the weak

entry.heading: Dragon Ball (manga, 1984-1995)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is one of joyful striving: train hard, keep getting stronger, enjoy the fight, protect your friends, forgive rivals and give former enemies a place at the table.

content.frequency: Constant in the second half; frequent in the first
content.framing: Endorsed (fighting as virtue), with deaths shown with consequences
Played for laughs; Roshi's lechery is mocked but rarely punished

frames.aligns: Self-sacrifice for others (Vegeta, ch. 467; Piccolo shielding Gohan); mercy to defeated enemies; conversion of villains; tyrants condemned.
frames.concerns: Lechery and child-nudity gags played as harmless (ch. 2, 4), which Inter Mirifica 7 would see as making wrong attractive; resurrection by wish rather than grace; gods as fighters.

frames.aligns: Repentance and transformation of enemies (Piccolo, Vegeta); self-sacrifice.
frames.concerns: Fighting enjoyed for its own sake (the tradition treats killing as needing repentance, St. Basil canon 13); a "Demon King," a wizard (Babidi) and gods who can be out-powered treat the spiritual lightly; lust gags feed the "passions." Guarding the senses (nepsis) weighs on both halves.

frames.aligns: Courage, perseverance, loyalty, redemption arcs; tyrants defeated.
frames.concerns: Other gods shown as real (John 14:6); harassment gags go unpunished; drinking played for laughs, where many are teetotal. Many families would treat vols. 1-16 as off-limits for children.

frames.aligns: Friendship, teamwork and sacrifice (Beneath the Tangles).
frames.concerns: Beneath the Tangles: the series reinforces Japanese spiritual ideas; "Animism, reincarnation, and the such are part of life" in its world; answers "both yes and no." Movieguide (on the 2014 Battle of Gods film, not the manga) calls the worldview "very strong polytheistic pagan."

Many gods, a Demon King, wizards, magic orbs and an afterlife without one God, presented as the real order of the world; media as an "open door" makes this weigh heavily. Plugged In warns of "dark and disturbing spiritual fascinations."

frames.aligns: Common grace: real goodness (loyalty, sacrifice, mercy) in a non-Christian story.
frames.concerns: False gods as characters; might as the final arbiter; lascivious gags (WLC Q139) shown as comedy.

frames.aligns: Fantasy is usually adiaphora; mercy and forgiveness of enemies.
frames.concerns: Gods surpassed by training reads as salvation by effort; sexual gags (sixth commandment). Confessional (LCMS, WELS) families stricter than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Characters grow toward goodness; love of friends and neighbors.
frames.concerns: Fighting as delight sits poorly with "do no harm"; drinking (historic abstinence); sexual humor.

frames.aligns: Redemption, loyalty, self-sacrifice; myth and fantasy have deep Anglican roots.
frames.concerns: Harassment gags treated as harmless; many gods.

frames.aligns: Mercy to defeated enemies; Goku's refusal to kill when unnecessary.
frames.concerns: Fighting is the story's core pleasure and solution, which nonresistance rejects at the level of message, not just image. Many conservative families avoid such media; Mennonite Church USA families may be more open.

frames.aligns: Family lineage, fathers protecting children, effort and self-improvement; enemies redeemed.
frames.concerns: Lechery shown as funny rather than wrong; drinking (Word of Wisdom); an afterlife unlike the plan of salvation. The Z volumes weigh less on modesty.

The dead walking with halos and returning by wish conflicts with the teaching that the dead sleep unconsciously (Fundamental Belief 26); lust gags; fighting as joy. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Mercy to enemies; protecting the innocent.
frames.concerns: Loving violence (Psalm 11:5) is the story's engine; spiritism and magic (gods, wizards, a living afterlife) are a major concern in jw.org counsel; an immortal-soul afterlife contradicts teaching; immorality as comedy. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Goodness and joy winning over destruction; death not final.
frames.concerns: Fear, destruction and bodily harm as constant mental imagery; strength sought through matter and training; drinking. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Redemption over punishment; multi-species friendships; a woman scientist.
frames.concerns: Sexual harassment as comedy (Roshi); Mr. Popo's design; mockery of a gay-coded villain; violence as the main solution.

frames.aligns: Teshuvah-like turning of former enemies; protecting life; loyalty.
frames.concerns: Gods as characters (avodah zarah in an Orthodox reading); lewd humor (nivul peh) and immodesty (tzniut) in the early volumes. Many Haredi homes avoid such media entirely. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Turning of former enemies; saving life (pikuach nefesh) in the heroes' sacrifices.
frames.concerns: Gods as characters; immodest gags. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Redemption; protecting the world; a woman inventor.
frames.concerns: Harassment gags; Mr. Popo's design, as a stereotype concern. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Discipline, striving, protecting the weak, humility in victory.
frames.concerns: Many gods shown as real powers (shirk imagery); resurrection by wish; drinking. Lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) makes the early nudity a strong depiction concern.

frames.aligns: Righteous fighting to protect the world (dharma); karma-like consequences; rebirth of Buu as Uub; many deities fit a pluralistic view.
frames.concerns: Gods out-powered or joked about may feel disrespectful to some; lechery gags; violence as joy rather than duty (rajasic rather than sattvic).

frames.aligns: King Yama (Enma) judging souls; rebirth of Buu as Uub; Goku's orange dōgi echoes Buddhist monks (Toriyama).
frames.concerns: Endless craving for power and fights (tanha); violence as delight (first precept); lust gags (third precept); drinking (fifth precept).

frames.aligns: Kami (Kami-sama of Earth), sacred places and spirits as a natural part of the world; gratitude and harmony among friends.
frames.concerns: Kami treated with little reverence in places; blood and death without purification. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Defending the oppressed against tyrants; humility in victory; redeemed pride (Vegeta).
frames.concerns: Lust (kaam) played as comedy and anger and ego (krodh, ahankar) as the joy of battle, two of the five vices shown as admirable; drinking. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Unity of former enemies; service to others.
frames.concerns: Degrading humor against a "chaste and holy life"; fighting for pleasure, against the commitment to non-violence; drinking. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Beings basically good and capable of growth; self-improvement through effort; survival of all life (the Spirit Bomb).
frames.concerns: Harassment gags; violence as fun. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Life energy (ki) shared by all living things; many deities treated without contempt.
frames.concerns: Fighting for pleasure against "harm none"; harassment gags. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Bulma as a scientist and leader; redemption over punishment; multinational, multi-species friendships.
frames.concerns: Roshi's harassment as comedy (ScreenWise flags it); Mr. Popo's design; mocking of a gay-coded villain; violence as the main solution (Common Sense Media).

frames.aligns: Human effort, not divine help, decides outcomes; reason and invention (Bulma); gods are characters, not truths.
frames.concerns: Exploitative gags and lack of consent (ch. 2, 4) shown as harmless; violence as fun.

frames.aligns: Effort, honor, loyalty; marriage and children; fathers who protect; tyrants defeated.
frames.concerns: Absent father; mother as comic nag; crude humor. Plugged In compares Z to "video sugar."

frames.aligns: Strength, self-improvement and pride in one's own power; indulgence without guilt (Church of Satan); rebellion against tyrants.
frames.concerns: Unwanted sexual advances are rejected in the Eleven Rules, and the series plays them as jokes. Church of Satan readers may grade higher than The Satanic Temple. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Redemption of former enemies; worth of every being; respect for many traditions.
frames.concerns: Harassment as comedy; Mr. Popo's design; mockery of a gay-coded villain. (from general knowledge; to verify)

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Martial pride and the tournament code of honor run through the series; Vegeta's bloodline pride drives his arc. The story also honors mercy (sparing Frieza) and Vegeta's turn from pride to self-sacrifice (ch. 467).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Goku fights for the joy of it and does not seek command; each arc's hero is stronger but chooses not to rule (Philosophy essay). Gods are bureaucrats and mentors, not lawgivers, and Goku leaves home to train Uub (ch. 517-519).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Goku protects Earth because his friends live there. Former enemies join the circle (Piccolo, Vegeta, Buu). Family is present but often secondary to friends and training.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Tyrants who want to own others are destroyed (Frieza, Cell, Kid Buu). Rank exists among fighters and gods (Kais, Supreme Kai), but strength is earned by training, and rivals are welcomed as equals.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: A Buddhist, Taoist and folk cosmology (King Yama, Kami, halos) is setting, not worship; Toriyama said he did not think deeply about it. Capsule Corp technology and whatever works solve problems (Pragmatic lens).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Joyful striving is the life message: train, enjoy the fight, food and friends. Death is often reversible through the Dragon Balls, so security fears weigh lightly.

folkways.japan: The Jump formula of friendship, effort and victory, the master-and-disciple training model (Roshi, Kami) and the folk cosmology borrowed from Chinese and Japanese Buddhism reflect Japanese boys' manga norms of the 1980s and 1990s rather than the story's own argument.

delivery.evidence: Inferred from the entry's summaries; no review addresses preachiness.
delivery.note: Values of effort and friendship come through comedy and fights with little direct moral commentary.

personified.ideology: Joyful striving and mercy
Pride and bloodline
Cruelty and domination

entry.heading: The Guy She Was Interested In Wasn't a Guy at All
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is lived openly as yourself, among people who share what you love; music is how you find them, and real friends and partners back each other's dreams.

frames.aligns: Honesty and dropping a false front; Joe's self-giving care for his niece; defending the bullied; respect for each person.
frames.concerns: The central romance is same-sex and presented as the good life, ending in cohabitation (ch. 12), against CCC 2357-2359 and teaching on marriage; masculine presentation read by some through the 2024 Dicastery documents on gender. The Catechism also asks respect and sensitivity toward persons (CCC 2358).

frames.aligns: Humility, honesty about the self, sacrificial family care (Joe).
frames.concerns: Traditional teaching on marriage and sexuality; the romance and cohabitation offered as the story's goal.

frames.aligns: Honesty, perseverance, loyal friendship, standing up for the mistreated.

frames.aligns: Being honest about who you are; kindness across cliques; using gifts (music).
frames.concerns: Most churches hold traditional sexual ethics, against the affirmed romance; some affirming congregations read it differently. No Christian review of this series was found.

frames.concerns: Conservative churches (PCA, OPC) hold traditional teaching on marriage; PC(USA) is affirming.

frames.concerns: The Episcopal Church allows same-sex marriage; ACNA holds traditional teaching.

frames.aligns: No violence; humility, honesty, community built around shared work.
frames.concerns: Conservative groups hold traditional teaching on marriage and avoid most popular media, including rock culture; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Honesty (Article of Faith 13); developing talents; family care (Joe).

frames.aligns: Affirms same-sex love and a lasting relationship; dignity of a butch girl; defends the bullied.
frames.concerns: Mitsuki's early deception; teen virality and industry pressure.
Marriage between one man and one woman (General Conference statements); same-sex romance a significant concern; secular music culture.

frames.aligns: No violence or spiritism; honesty and loyalty.
frames.concerns: jw.org counsel against entertainment featuring immorality; homosexual acts considered sinful; same-sex romance framed as ideal.

frames.concerns: Purity and marriage valued; less public teaching on same-sex relationships (to verify).

frames.aligns: Honesty ("keep far from falsehood," Exodus 23:7); kindness; Joe's care for an orphaned-seeming niece.
frames.concerns: Same-sex relationships forbidden (Leviticus 18:22); tzniut and the kiss; cross-dressing questions (Deuteronomy 22:5) may be raised by some about Mitsuki's clothing; many Haredi homes restrict such media.

frames.aligns: Dignity of each person (CJLS 2006 permitted same-sex commitment ceremonies; views vary); honesty; care for family.
frames.concerns: Cohabitation outside marriage; views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: LGBTQ inclusion; informed autonomy; honesty and dignity.
Truthfulness, loyalty, patience (sabr), care for family (Joe).
frames.concerns: Traditional teaching on sexuality; same-sex romance as the central good; lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31); some scholars also object to music and to imitating the other sex's dress.

frames.aligns: Svadharma: living one's own nature (Bhagavad Gita 3.35); duty to family (Joe); music as art evoking rasa.

frames.aligns: Letting go of a false self-image; compassion for the excluded; right speech in honest confrontation.
frames.concerns: Third precept: many traditions accept same-sex relationships, views vary by teacher; attachment to fame and status (the viral video, ch. 8).

frames.aligns: Truthful living; equality and dignity; the vice of ego (haumai) behind hiding and posing.
frames.concerns: Sex and partnership within marriage; Akal Takht opposed same-sex marriage (2005), though diaspora views vary.

frames.aligns: Rejection of prejudice; honesty; unity across social groups.
frames.concerns: Teaching reserves sexual relations for marriage between a man and a woman; a "chaste and holy life."

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto): Mitsuki drops a false face; harmony among friends.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; no doctrine on same-sex relationships (practice varies, to verify).

frames.aligns: Love and self-expression as positive; largely LGBTQ-affirming; becoming one's true self.

frames.concerns: Little in the message; The Way to Happiness asks faithfulness to one's partner, which the couple shows.

frames.aligns: Positive, lasting same-sex romance; a butch girl's gender expression treated with respect; coming out without trauma tropes (Okazu); anti-bullying; low sexualization (Okazu: salaciousness "0").
frames.concerns: The title's "guy" gag and Mitsuki's disguise (vol. 1), which reviewers say the story defuses.

frames.aligns: Meaning through honest relationships, art and community; no supernatural claims.
Hard work and practice; Joe's family sacrifice; loyalty; respect for the principal and school events; no sexual content reported.
frames.concerns: Same-sex romance presented to teen readers as the ideal, a concern for many when presented to children; masculine presentation of a girl celebrated; unmarried cohabitation after the time skip.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth and dignity; welcoming LGBTQ people; community through shared art.
Individualism and self-determination; rejection of imposed conformity; LGBTQ-affirming.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Hurts are settled by direct, honest talk (Aya confronts Mitsuki over the concert ticket, ch. 3). Aya does publicly defend Mitsuki against a disrespectful classmate (ch. 8, likely), a small honor note.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The story celebrates dressing, liking and loving as you choose; rules and school events are friendly backdrops rather than constraints.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Joe's kin sacrifice for his niece is honored (vol. 1-2); friendship across cliques and the music scene matter as much.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Gyaru and "nerd" become equals; senpai-kohai ties (Hime) and the principal appear but carry little weight.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No religious frame; Western rock as chosen culture; careers chosen by interest (music, translation).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Self-expression, tolerance and quality of life are the highest goods, though ch. 12 shows the cost of making a living in music.

folkways.japan: The school trip, school festival, gyaru fashion culture, and hiding one's real tastes to keep group harmony (tatemae versus honne) are Japanese settings; the story's own message favors honne. The imported "prom" is presented as a novelty organized by students (vol. 3).

delivery.evidence: Nippon.com says the same-sex relationship is treated as unremarkable; no reviewer found calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The mocking classmate Narita is redeemed fairly, but no character voices a traditional objection to same-sex love or to Mitsuki's dress.

entry.heading: Deadman Wonderland
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is one you choose to keep living after injustice and loss. You hold on to friends, refuse to become the monster that hurt you, and show mercy instead of taking revenge. People who treat others as entertainment, property or lab material are the real criminals.

content.framing: Condemned (as cruelty for profit and pleasure); shown with consequences
Mixed: some fan service played for comedy, sexual violence condemned
Shown with consequences; suicide finally rejected

frames.aligns: Human dignity of prisoners; injustice and dehumanization exposed; mercy instead of revenge (ch. 57); the death wish finally rejected (CCC 2280-2283).
frames.concerns: Gore that reviewers call the main draw ("red meat for the gorehound's soul," ANN), against Inter Mirifica 7 on not making evil attractive; sexualized depiction of teen girls (CCC 2354, 2521-2524); several suicides; experimentation on a child.

frames.aligns: Mercy and the refusal to kill; grief and repentance (Sorae's apology).

Rebellion against an unjust authority; harm to children condemned (Eleven Rules); compassion and justice (Satanic Temple Tenets 1 and 2).
frames.concerns: Little in the message; the sadists are framed as villains, which fits.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Ganta starts out seeking revenge (ch. 5-6) but ends by refusing it (ch. 57). Disputes are finally settled by exposing evidence to inspectors and courts (ch. 21, 40), not by vendetta. G Ward fighters keep a personal code (Senji).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Escape from an unjust order is heroic (Scar Chain, ch. 13-21). Rules are tools of the powerful (collars, points, Punishment Game). Makina's lawful order is respected, so it is not pure liberty.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Blood families often harm children (ch. 9, 15, 46). The heroes' loyalty goes to a chosen community of friends. The story celebrates protecting everyone in G Ward, not clan.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Rank and authority are mostly abusive (Tamaki, the Undertakers, Kōzuji's gang). Inmates cooperate as equals.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No tradition or faith is shown sincerely; the one monk is a madman (ch. 20). The world is explained through science (nanomachines), and abused science is the villain, judged by secular ethics.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: The setting is pure survival (food, antidote, points). The ending celebrates ordinary wishes ("go to school, play with friends," ch. 57) and Chaplin's self-expression, balancing the two.

folkways.japan: The post-disaster setting reflects Japan's experience of earthquakes and rebuilding. Distrust of a closed, profit-driven institution and the emphasis on group loyalty among friends are common in Japanese shonen. The fan service is a genre convention of the magazine. These are context more than the story's own message.

delivery.evidence: ANN's Kimlinger says it avoids "ponderous moralizing," with only "the occasional swipe at dehumanizing prison conditions and privatized punishment."
delivery.note: Its critique of punishment as spectacle is built into the setting and the crowd scenes; most villains are open sadists, and several get sympathetic backstories.

personified.ideology: Will to live and mercy over revenge
Profit and pleasure from others' suffering
Death as salvation (twisted Buddhism)
Despair and a wish to die

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Critical theory (critique of the prison system), Secular humanism, Communitarianism.

series.title: Golden Kamuy
series.adult_reason: Golden Kamuy: VIZ rates it Mature (18+, VIZ Signature); extreme gore, cannibalism, human-skin horror, crude sexual gags; deep entry scores 9

entry.heading: Golden Kamuy
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is lived by your own hands and promises: survive with skill, respect the animals and land that feed you, keep faith with the dead and the living, and refuse to let greed or other men's wars decide your future.

frames.aligns: Greed condemned by outcome; promise-keeping, care for a widow (James 1:27), stewardship of creation; Ogata's guilt treated as real.
frames.concerns: Atrocity and perversion sometimes made comic, which can make evil attractive or trivial (Inter Mirifica 7); Ogata's suicide (CCC 2280-2283); animist rites shown as true.

frames.aligns: Penance and the weight of sin on Sugimoto and Ogata; greed as a passion that destroys.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis) weighs heavily against constant gore and obscene gags; spirits and kamuy treated as real.

frames.aligns: Greed and lust for power punished; loyalty and promise-keeping.
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 test: gore, crude sexual humor, bestiality gag; animist worship shown positively. Each family decides (soul liberty).

frames.aligns: Depicts sin without endorsing greed or murder; mercy and loyalty in Sugimoto; care for the weak.
frames.concerns: Crude humor and perversion played for laughs; occult elements (seer); a lead cast of killers.

frames.aligns: Clear consequences for greed and violence.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": a seer whose prophecies come true (ch. 122) and kamuy worship shown as true; holiness standards against the crude content.

frames.aligns: Common grace: a non-Christian work that shows human depravity honestly and greed undoing its schemers.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 on lascivious books and pictures applies to the sexual gags; violence often a spectacle.

frames.aligns: Vocation and duty (a soldier's guilt, a hunter's craft); law exposes sin in nearly every character.
frames.concerns: Confessional (LCMS, WELS) families more cautious about the crude content than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy, honesty about guilt, care for the poor and the widow.
frames.concerns: Wesley's General Rules against diversions that cannot be used "in the name of the Lord Jesus"; holiness churches stricter than UMC.

frames.aligns: Good and evil judged by framing; greed and coups fail; strong adventure-literature tradition.
frames.concerns: Comic framing of atrocity; suicide. Episcopal and ACNA families differ more on sexual gags than on the message.

frames.aligns: Distrust of state violence and war; a simple, land-based Ainu life is honored; Asirpa refuses to fund a war.
frames.concerns: Violence is the heroes' everyday tool (Matthew 5:39); worldly entertainment avoided by conservative groups.

frames.aligns: Keeping covenants and promises; family history and identity (Asirpa and Wilk).
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth: crude sexual humor, nudity gags and gore would not invite the Spirit; suicide.

frames.aligns: Attention to an Indigenous people, land and language; critique of militarism and abandoned veterans.
frames.concerns: Ienaga as a trans cannibal villain (Anime Feminist); Ito's critique that the anime softens colonial history.
"By beholding we become changed": gore and crude content; spirits and divination shown as real.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, mercy, rejection of political coups and war.
frames.concerns: jw.org's test: violence (Psalm 11:5), immorality and spiritism (Galatians 5:19-21) all appear, the first constantly.

frames.aligns: Hope and resilience; nature as good.
frames.concerns: Dwelling on fear, gore and disease runs against "Stand porter at the door of thought" (Science and Health 392).

frames.aligns: Kindness to animals' dignity in hunting (echo of tza'ar ba'alei chayim); keeping vows; caring for a widow.
frames.concerns: Nivul peh and tzniut make the crude sexual humor and nudity a concern; suicide; many Haredi homes avoid such media entirely.

frames.aligns: Memory, identity and survival of a minority people; promise-keeping.
frames.concerns: Crude speech and gore applied by family values.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam echoes: protecting land and a people's future; attention to stereotypes.
frames.concerns: Stereotyped trans villain; debate on colonial sanitizing.

frames.aligns: Justice for the wronged, condemnation of greed, kindness to animals in slaughter and use.
frames.concerns: Lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) against nudity and sexual gags; animist worship; suicide (Qur'an 4:29).

frames.aligns: Respect for animals and nature as sacred; dharma of keeping one's word; karma-like consequences for greed.
frames.concerns: Tamasic content (gore, perversion) by the Gita's ch. 17 test.

frames.aligns: Greed (tanha) destroys every faction; impermanence; gratitude for life taken for food.
frames.concerns: Killing as daily survival and plot solution, against the first precept; what the gore feeds the mind.

frames.aligns: The five vices shown and punished (greed in all factions, lust in the villains, ego in Tsurumi); courage to protect the vulnerable.
frames.concerns: Lust and cruelty played as comedy.

frames.aligns: Unity across peoples (Japanese, Ainu, Russian allies); justice for the oppressed.
frames.concerns: Strong non-violence teaching against constant killing; a "chaste and holy life" against the crude content.

frames.aligns: Kamuy-centered animism echoes the kami worldview; gratitude, sincerity, purity of the hunt; respect for spirits of animals.
frames.concerns: Blood and death as impurity, shown constantly.

frames.aligns: Animist reverence for nature and animal spirits presented as wisdom; no stereotyping of shamans or seers.
Way to Happiness precepts: keep promises, do not murder (murderers mostly fall), safeguard the environment.
frames.concerns: Killing as the plot's main tool.

frames.aligns: An Indigenous co-lead, praised by Anime Feminist; strong women; critique of militarism.
frames.concerns: Trans woman as cannibal villain ("very problematically written," Anime Feminist); Ito argues the anime erases Japan's colonial past; gay couple killed off in the live-action series.

frames.aligns: Reason, skill and human bonds; no supernatural rescue; honest about war trauma; ends by choosing land and future over wealth.
frames.concerns: Concern centers on cruelty played for laughs (animal abuse, cannibalism).

frames.aligns: Honor, duty, keeping faith with comrades and widows; respect for an ancestral culture; manliness and self-reliance.
frames.concerns: Crude humor and homoerotic gags; national institutions shown as betraying soldiers; the series sides with no nation-building project.

frames.aligns: Dignity of an Indigenous people; interdependent web of life; justice.
frames.concerns: Stereotyped trans villain; violence as spectacle.

frames.aligns: Individual survival, self-reliance and distrust of authority; Asirpa decides her own path.
frames.concerns: The Eleven Rules oppose harm to animals and children: Anehata's animal abuse and child kidnappings in Sapporo, even as villain acts.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Personal vows, revenge and honor drive the cast: Asirpa seeks her father's killer, Sugimoto keeps his oath to a dead comrade, Hijikata fights for a lost samurai cause. Disputes are settled by force, not courts.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The heroes are outsiders acting on their own; the state and army are shown betraying veterans; would-be new orders (Tsurumi's junta, ch. 31) fail.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Kin and chosen kin first: Asirpa and her father and grandmother, Sugimoto and Umeko, the band of companions.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Military hierarchy is shown as manipulated (Tsurumi); Ainu elders are respected; the core band is fairly flat.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Ainu animism and custom are honored (ch. 11-12, 119, 122), while practical skill and modern change are also valued.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival is the series' core: hunting, cold, food, war.

folkways.japan: The late-Meiji setting, military loyalty, samurai nostalgia (Hijikata) and Japanese views of bears as man-eaters (TV Tropes, Values Dissonance) are Japanese historical context. The Ainu values shown (kamuy, gratitude to animals) belong to an Indigenous culture within Japan, not to mainstream Japanese norms.

delivery.evidence: Reviewers praise its morally gray factions (MAL, ANN); Rika Ito argues it offers a "sanitized Ainu-Japanese relationship"; Anime Feminist flags a "problematically written trans woman."
delivery.note: The story lets nationalist, separatist and Indigenous causes speak through likable characters, but critics question how it handles colonial history and one trans character.

personified.ideology: Ainu tradition renewed by a new generation
Militarist nationalism for abandoned soldiers
Samurai restorationism, Republic of Ezo
Nihilism, denial of guilt

entry.dominant: Pragmatism (survival), Pagan / animist (Ainu), Classical virtue ethics, Environmentalism, Communitarianism.

entry.heading: To Your Eternity (Fumetsu no Anata e)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is made of the people you love and who change you. Pain and loss are the price of connection and the way a person grows. A life without end is only worth living if it is shared, and even the immortal must let others go.

frames.aligns: Self-giving love; grief honored; mercy and forgiveness; human dignity of the weak. Evil is not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7).
frames.concerns: Reincarnation shown as real; the only major church (Bennett) is corrupt; Kahaku's self-destruction framed as atonement (CCC 2280-2283).

frames.aligns: Struggle with the passions (Hayase's possessive "love"); remembrance of the dead; growth through suffering.
frames.concerns: Spirits of the dead and rebirth; a church shown only as a persecutor; nepsis makes the gore and Hayase's scenes a concern.

frames.aligns: Sacrificial love; evil framed as evil; care for orphans and the old (James 1:27).
frames.concerns: Reincarnation and spirits shown as real (Hebrews 9:27); church as villain. Self-governing churches vary.

frames.aligns: TWWK (Beneath the Tangles, via ANN) praises Fushi choosing to keep loving "often at great cost to himself." Depicts sin without endorsing it.
frames.concerns: Non-Christian afterlife; the creator figure is cold; TWWK compares the Observer's look to Satan in The Passion of the Christ.

frames.aligns: Clear good against evil; sacrifice and perseverance.
frames.concerns: Seeing and talking with the dead (Bon), possession-like parasites, a creator-observer who is not the God of Scripture, all shown as real; "open door" concern.

frames.aligns: Total depravity echoes in how power corrupts church and crown; common grace in non-Christian art.
frames.concerns: Rebirth instead of judgment; self-destruction framed as noble (WLC Q136); Hayase's predatory scenes (WLC Q139).

frames.aligns: Theology of the cross echo: love shown through suffering; the church condemned when it seeks power, a theme Lutherans know from their own history.
frames.concerns: Rebirth and spirits; suicide-adjacent scenes. LCMS and WELS more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy; care for the poor and imprisoned (Renril, Jananda); growth in love.
frames.concerns: Self-destruction framed as noble; Hayase's scenes. Holiness churches more cautious.

frames.aligns: Imaginative fiction on death and grief, judged by framing; good and evil clear.
Forgiveness, endurance under persecution (Fushi tortured by a church, like the martyrs' history), community care.
frames.concerns: Defensive war at Renril is heroic; Fushi fights constantly. Conservative groups avoid most popular media.

frames.aligns: Family bonds, care across generations, the value of mortal experience and growth through trial.
frames.concerns: Reincarnation rather than resurrection; self-destruction; Hayase's scenes.

frames.aligns: Critique of religious power, care for prisoners, refugees and the marginalized; fluid gender of the hero.
frames.concerns: Hayase's predatory obsession; Indigenous-coded opening without Indigenous people (Oima's own choice).
The dead are unconscious until the resurrection, so spirits of the dead and rebirth conflict with teaching on the state of the dead.
Spiritism (Bon's sight of the dead), immortal soul imagery, reincarnation, violence (Psalm 11:5).

frames.aligns: Love outlasting death; growth of understanding.
frames.concerns: Death, disease, dementia and fear are shown as real and central; the story dwells on them.

frames.aligns: Mourning and memory of the dead (zikaron); care for the old (Pioran); kindness.
frames.concerns: Self-destruction framed as noble; reincarnation shown as real (gilgul has a place in kabbalah, debated); Hayase's scenes (tzniut).

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam in protecting Renril; critique of persecution for belief; memory.
Patience in loss (sabr), care for parents and the old, mercy.
frames.concerns: Reincarnation (rejected), a creator figure who is not God, self-destruction (Qur'an 4:29); lowering the gaze for some outfits.

frames.aligns: Atman-like continuity across forms and lives; rebirth; duty and devotion; detachment in the ending.
frames.concerns: Little in the message; some families apply the Gita's tamasic test to the gore.

frames.aligns: Impermanence, suffering from attachment, rebirth, compassion; the ending's letting go.
frames.concerns: Killing Nokkers as a solution; some readings ask whether Fushi's clinging to his dead is attachment.

frames.aligns: Service, courage for the oppressed, the five vices (Hayase's lust and attachment, the church's ego) condemned.
frames.concerns: Self-destruction; rebirth framed without a divine name.

frames.aligns: Unity across peoples, service, growth through tests.
frames.concerns: Violence as a frequent solution; self-destruction.

frames.aligns: Respect for spirits, nature and the dead; sincerity and gratitude.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; blood and death as impurity.

frames.aligns: Nature, ancestors, the wheel of death and rebirth; persecution of "heretics" shown as wrong.
Being who outlives bodies; helping others (Way to Happiness).
frames.concerns: Self-destruction; grief and depression shown without therapy framing.

frames.aligns: Fluid gender of the hero; critique of religious and state power; empathy for prisoners, refugees and the bullied.
frames.concerns: Hayase's predatory obsession, called "possibly rapey" (ANN); mostly White or Asian cast (Common Sense Media); Arctic setting without its Indigenous people.

frames.aligns: Meaning made by human bonds; a finite life valued over endless life; critique of dogma and of a perfect "desire-free" future.
Duty, self-sacrifice, care for elders, the old order of family and friendship over technological utopia.
frames.concerns: Religious institution shown as villain; fluid gender; weak bonds of lineage.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of every being, free search for meaning, justice for the persecuted.
Critique of a power-hungry church; Fushi rejects the Beholder's offer of omnipotence and chooses his own path; individual choice (friends end "their own stories").
frames.concerns: Self-sacrifice for others, which Church of Satan texts do not prize.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Fushi fights to protect, not to answer insults; Hayase's vendetta-like pursuit is condemned. Bon's honor is shown as self-giving, not defending his name (vol. 9).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Church, crown, cult and scored society are shown as oppressive (ANN S2 ep. 7; TV Tropes); the hero refuses omnipotence and lets friends choose their own endings (ch. 201).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Chosen family across bloodlines (March, Gugu, Pioran) is celebrated; Hayase's blood-line duty is a dark mirror (fan wiki). Renril's defense shows civic solidarity (vols. 10-12).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Royal and priestly rank is critiqued; a prince earns respect only by sacrifice (Bon).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Folk sacrifice and church dogma are shown as harmful, but spirits and rebirth are real; technology that ends suffering is also questioned.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Early arcs are about survival; the story's goal is a life of chosen bonds and inner growth, and a utopia of satisfied desire is not the answer (Kodansha vol. 20, 24 blurbs).

folkways.japan: Mono no aware (gentle sorrow at impermanence), respect for elders and the dead, and Buddhist rebirth imagery reflect Japanese cultural norms more than an argument made to readers; the story's suspicion of authority is its own theme.

delivery.evidence: ANN's Beckett finds the Church "so comically evil" and Hayase's motives not "well-communicated"; no review calls the series preachy.
delivery.note: Its messages about grief and connection are shown through deaths and Fushi's reactions, with the Beholder and others sometimes stating them aloud.

personified.ideology: Humanity learned through love and loss
Possessive devotion presented as love
Religious authority used for power
Detached observation; "pain promotes growth"

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Dharmic (Hindu/Buddhist), Secular humanism, Classical virtue ethics, Communitarianism.

entry.heading: Girls' Last Tour
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is found in companionship, curiosity and small joys, even when there is no future to build. Memory and record-keeping matter, but letting go matters too.

frames.aligns: Dignity of the person in a ruined world; friendship; reverence for the dead (returning grave goods); war shown as ruin. Evil is not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7).
frames.concerns: No hope beyond death; religion treated as a human comfort and a "fairy tale" by one lead (ch. 10); teen drunkenness.

frames.aligns: Watchfulness over small things; remembrance of the dead; humility before death.
frames.concerns: Mocking a sacred statue and self-deifying joke (ch. 10); no resurrection hope.

frames.aligns: Friendship, sharing the last ration (ch. 2), honesty.
frames.concerns: Underage drunkenness shown warmly (ch. 21 likely); religion dismissed as a fairy tale (ch. 10); nude bath (ch. 3). Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Depicts a fallen world without endorsing its sin; Ecclesiastes-like reflection on vanity and small joys.
frames.concerns: No gospel hope; religion shown only as human comfort.

frames.aligns: No occult practice or demons; love and loyalty.
frames.concerns: A Buddhist paradise temple and statues (ch. 10); Yuuri calls herself a god as a joke. Views vary by church.

frames.aligns: Common grace: beauty and friendship among ruins; a sober view of human sin in war.
frames.concerns: No providence; religion as a human invention; drinking scene.

frames.aligns: Vocation in small daily tasks (eating, washing, writing); honesty about death.
frames.concerns: No word of promise or grace; temple joke. LCMS and WELS families tend to be more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy in miniature: sharing food, honoring the dead.
frames.concerns: Teen drinking shown as sweet; no faith. Holiness churches are more cautious than the UMC.

frames.aligns: A literary tradition (Lewis, Sayers) that values imaginative works on mortality; good and evil framed honestly; war as ruin.
frames.concerns: No hope beyond the end; religion treated lightly.

frames.aligns: Simplicity, sharing, rejection of weapons: Yuuri finally throws her rifle away (vol. 6, WaniKani thread). War is what ended the world. Conservative groups avoid most popular media; MC USA families vary.
Love of records and keeping a journal; memory of those who came before; friendship.
frames.concerns: Drinking (Word of Wisdom); no eternal hope; nude bath. Members vary in strictness.

frames.aligns: Anti-war reading; care for the vulnerable; honest questions about faith.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; the bleak ending may need context for younger readers.

frames.aligns: The dead are "asleep" and unaware, which echoes the quiet ending; sober view of war.
frames.concerns: Drinking; Buddhist paradise imagery; no resurrection hope.

frames.aligns: Peaceful pair, war shown as ruin; no spiritism or magic.
frames.concerns: A temple to other gods and Yuuri's "I am a god" joke (ch. 10); no hope of a restored earth.
Death, cold and decline shown as real and final; dwelling on fear.

frames.aligns: Honoring the dead and returning what belongs to them; preserving memory and books.
frames.concerns: Idol statues and a paradise temple (ch. 10); nude bath (tzniut); drinking by minors. Many Haredi homes restrict such media altogether.

frames.aligns: Memory, books, kindness and respect for the dead.
frames.concerns: Idol temple scene; bleak view of the future.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam in reverse: what a broken world teaches about repair; anti-war reading.
frames.concerns: Little; the ending may need discussion.

frames.aligns: Patience (sabr), sharing food, respect for graves, war as destruction.
frames.concerns: Alcohol shown fondly (ch. 21 likely); statues of gods (ch. 10) and Yuuri's self-deifying joke; nude bath (lowering the gaze, Qur'an 24:30-31).

frames.aligns: Impermanence and detachment; letting go of possessions (vol. 6); sattvic calm.
frames.concerns: Few message conflicts; the paradise temple is treated lightly.

frames.aligns: Impermanence (mono no aware, per ANN); a Pure Land temple (ch. 10); non-attachment as the girls shed possessions; equanimity before death.
frames.concerns: Yuuri's mockery of the statue; drinking (fifth precept).

frames.aligns: Letting go of attachment (moh); sharing; humility; seva-like care for each other.
frames.concerns: No Naam or divine presence; drinking.

frames.aligns: Unity and friendship; war as humanity's ruin.
frames.concerns: Alcohol is forbidden; no faith or progressive revelation; bleak ending.

frames.aligns: Gratitude for food, water and warmth; purity and sincerity of the pair; reverence for the dead.
frames.concerns: Toppling and mocking a statue (ch. 10), even though the temple is Buddhist; Chito's warning of divine punishment is shrugged off.

frames.aligns: Harm none: a gentle pair; seasons, snow, moon and stars as wonders (moonlight scene ch. 21 likely).
Survival and helping each other; no psychiatric themes.
frames.concerns: The tone dwells on decline and loss.

frames.aligns: Anti-war reading, no stereotypes, two capable girls, honest about death.
frames.concerns: Underage drinking; bleak ending for younger readers.

frames.aligns: Meaning made by humans: curiosity, books, art (ch. 32 likely), friendship; religion read as a human comfort (ch. 10).
frames.concerns: Little to raise; some readers find the outlook fatalistic.

frames.aligns: Love of inherited books and culture; memory of grandfather; duty to the dead; war's cost.
frames.concerns: No family, faith or nation to pass on to; the culture ends.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth, free search for meaning, compassion, peace.
No authority, self-reliance, Yuuri's joke that she is a god; no harm to children or animals is endorsed.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: No insults are avenged; quarrels end in slapstick and sharing (ch. 2, 9). Worth is simply assumed.

Order vs freedom.evidence: No rules or authority; the girls choose their own way upward. Old machines keep order without people, which the story treats with curiosity, not reverence.

Civic vs kin.evidence: The pair are each other's only family; yet they return grave goods to strangers (ch. 19-21 likely) and help Kanazawa and Ishii.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Two equals; no ranks. Chito and Yuuri trade roles of leader and follower.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Religion is treated as a human comfort and questioned (ch. 10); books, science and records are prized, then let go (vol. 6).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival is the setting, but the story celebrates music, art, photographs and small joys (ch. 9, 32 likely) over mere survival.

folkways.japan: The tone of mono no aware (gentle sadness at impermanence), the Pure Land temple and the iyashikei ("healing") genre are Japanese conventions; readers from other cultures may take the calm acceptance of death as a message, while Japanese readers may read it as a familiar aesthetic.

delivery.evidence: TCJ: "it does not moralize" beyond "implicit dismay towards war." One MyAnimeList review called the existential tone heavy-handed.
delivery.note: Ideas come through quiet dialogue between Chito and Yuuri, who are given equal weight, and the story rarely states a conclusion.

personified.ideology: Memory and knowledge give life meaning
Live in the present; enjoy what is here
A life's purpose in one project

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Dharmic (Buddhist impermanence), Absurdism, Secular humanism.

entry.heading: Real
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life means facing your real situation, not the one you had or the one others rank you by. It takes daily effort and honest connection with others, and your worth does not depend on your body, your status or your wins.

frames.aligns: Dignity of every human life regardless of ability; pride brought low (Takahashi); Nomiya's guilt moving toward responsibility; evil not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7).
frames.concerns: Profanity; the self-harm scene and despair; hope rests on human effort alone.

frames.aligns: Humility through suffering; struggle against pride and despair, both named passions in the tradition.
frames.concerns: Watchfulness (nepsis) over coarse speech and fights; no spiritual frame for suffering.

frames.aligns: Pride before a fall (Proverbs 16:18); perseverance; the worth of the weak (1 Corinthians 12:22). Views vary by congregation.
frames.concerns: Swearing tested against Philippians 4:8; delinquency and street fights.

frames.aligns: Depicts sin (theft, arrogance, violence) without endorsing it; second chances; the "least of these" honored.
frames.concerns: Language; a purely human source of grace and grit.

frames.aligns: No occult or spiritual content, so the "open door" concern is minimal; perseverance and restoration.
frames.concerns: Language; healing is never expected or sought, which some families may discuss.

frames.aligns: Common grace: a non-Christian work truthful about human pride and frailty. Providence-like turns through suffering.
frames.concerns: Swearing (Philippians 4:8; WLC on corrupt speech); the self-harm scene.

frames.aligns: Vocation: each character finds a useful place on a team; the law exposes Takahashi's pride. Largely adiaphora.
frames.concerns: Little in the message; LCMS and WELS families may weigh the language more.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy and social holiness: the disabled included in community; a change of heart over time.
frames.concerns: Holiness churches may weigh the profanity and fights.

frames.aligns: Honest literary realism about suffering, judged by framing.
Humility, mutual aid, care for the weak; violence leads to jail, not glory (v15).
frames.concerns: Competitive sport and ambition (Togawa's drive to win, pro-wrestling heel culture); conservative groups avoid popular media.

frames.aligns: Agency, effort and growth through trial; family reconciliation (Takahashi's parents).
frames.concerns: Language; For the Strength of Youth asks whether media invites the Spirit.

frames.aligns: Disability justice themes; challenge to pity and to ranking people.
frames.concerns: Male-centered cast and thin women (Anime Feminist); "able-bodied champion" framing.

frames.aligns: Health, discipline, perseverance, care for the sick.
frames.concerns: "By beholding we become changed": swearing, fights and despair; Takahashi's mother's drinking.

frames.aligns: Love of neighbor, family reconciliation, honesty about wrongdoing.
frames.concerns: Fights and pro-wrestling violence (Psalm 11:5); competitive ambition; no spiritism present.

frames.aligns: Persistence, hope and refusal to be defined by limitation.
frames.concerns: The story treats disease, paralysis and bodily limits as fixed facts and centers medical rehabilitation, against the teaching that matter and disease are not ultimately real.

frames.aligns: Pikuach nefesh and the value of every life; teshuvah echoes in Nomiya's guilt and amends.
frames.concerns: Nivul peh (coarse speech); secular content; many Haredi homes restrict such media.

frames.aligns: Dignity of the disabled (inclusion is a stated value in the movement); teshuvah; honoring parents.
Tikkun olam through inclusion; informed autonomy; repair after harm.
Sabr (patience) in trial; humility after arrogance; drinking shown as destructive (Takahashi's mother, Shiratori).
frames.concerns: Language; free mixing and sport culture vary by family.

frames.concerns: Little to raise; some families apply the Gita's tamasic category to coarse speech.

frames.aligns: Suffering, impermanence and clinging to a lost self (Takahashi's identity as a star); compassion over pity; right effort.

Service, unity, the nobility of every person; tests as a means of growth.

frames.concerns: Little to raise; no kami or shrines appear, so the fit is neutral rather than close.

frames.aligns: "Harm none" in the consequences of harm; honoring the body as it is.

frames.aligns: Disability representation praised for realism and for challenging pity (Wikipedia; MAL review).
frames.concerns: Anime Feminist: "over-masculinity," Natsumi as a "characterless means," the "able-bodied champion" trope, ableist moments (v1-3); a karmic framing of disability.

frames.aligns: Meaning built by people through effort and relationship; medicine and rehab shown realistically; no supernatural answers.
frames.concerns: Self-harm scene needs care in discussion.

frames.aligns: Personal responsibility, discipline, hard work, consequences for theft and fighting, family reconciliation.
frames.concerns: Some may note the absence of faith and the coarse language.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth and dignity of every person; challenge to ranking people; justice for disabled people.
frames.concerns: Male-centered cast; ableist moments flagged by Anime Feminist.

frames.aligns: Self-determination and striving against limits (Togawa; Shiratori); rejection of pity; no harm to children or animals celebrated.
frames.concerns: The story also values humbling the ego and serving the team over the self.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Worth is inherent, not won: the series is praised for challenging pity and ranking (MAL review; Wikipedia). Nomiya answering mockery with his fists lands him in jail (v15), so honor-fighting is not celebrated.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Discipline and practice are valued (A-Camp, v12), but individuals choose their own paths; rules are tools, not ideals.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Teams and rehab friends carry as much weight as family; families are broken and partly repaired (Takahashi's parents, v12).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Takahashi's "A to E" ranking is the view the story dismantles (Wikipedia). Coaches are respected but not revered.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No religion; medicine, rehab, classification and training science guide recovery.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Hard work, grit and getting through each day dominate (VIZ vol. 16 blurb), alongside self-realization through sport and tolerance of difference.

folkways.japan: School club culture, senpai-kohai relations, and the shame and self-punishment in Nomiya's head-shaving (Wikipedia) reflect Japanese norms; the story's own message is about personal dignity and acceptance.

delivery.evidence: Reviewers say it resists easy inspiration: "unforgiving, much like life" (Manga Bookshelf); leads "flawed and believable rather than saintly."
delivery.note: Its lessons come through setbacks and character change rather than speeches, though Anime Feminist finds some disability stereotypes.

personified.ideology: Human worth measured by rank and ability
Competitive individual excellence
Guilt turned into responsibility
Refusal to accept limits
