entry.heading: Choujin X
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life means finding your own will instead of living in someone else's shadow, and using whatever you become to protect others. Power drawn from desire is dangerous; it is redeemed by empathy, friendship and honesty about yourself.

frames.aligns: Evil (genocide, tyranny) is shown but not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7); self-giving courage; mercy toward enemies; a father's blessing (ch. 35).
frames.concerns: Drug-made power and opioid dependence (CCC 2291); fan service (CCC 2521-2524); "Behold the Man" used as a chapter title in a secular story.

frames.aligns: Struggle with the passions: powers grow from desire and complexes, a picture of passions made flesh; repentance themes in Batista.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis) makes the body horror and fan service a concern; scripture phrases borrowed for chapter titles; prophecy shown outside any church.

frames.aligns: Clear wrong in genocide and tyranny; friendship and sacrifice; honesty between friends (ch. 43).
frames.concerns: Drug use as the source of power; visions and prophecy shown as real outside Scripture; fan service. Each congregation and family decides (soul liberty).

frames.aligns: Depicts sin without endorsing it; a hero who learns to act on his own conviction and to love enemies (Matthew 5:44).
frames.concerns: Drug-origin powers; fan service; a "Mother" figure whose prophecy justifies mass killing.

frames.aligns: Courage; evil prophecy-driven violence is shown as evil.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": visions, marks passed between bearers, a Tower of Mourning and prophetic calamity presented as real and unrelated to God; body horror.

frames.aligns: Total depravity has an echo: the powers expose what people most desire; common grace lets families value good art by a non-Christian.
frames.concerns: Fan service (WLC Q139); scripture phrases as chapter titles; drug-made powers.

frames.aligns: Two kingdoms: Yamato Mori bears the sword and licenses power to protect the weak; Tokio serves his neighbor.
frames.concerns: Drug content and body horror; LCMS and WELS families tend to be more cautious than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy, care for outcasts (Palma), reconciliation of friends.
frames.concerns: Drug and opium content; fan service. Holiness churches more cautious than the UMC.

frames.aligns: Good and evil judged by framing; a fantasy-adventure frame with moral weight; just war (Article 37) fits the fight against Zora's tower.
frames.concerns: Drug-made power and opioid dependence; borrowed scripture phrases.

frames.aligns: Compassion for enemies; community care; Ely argues against killing Zora (vol. 12).
frames.concerns: Violence as the heroes' main tool throughout (Matthew 5:39); conservative groups avoid such media; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Agency and choosing one's own path; friendship and service; a supportive father (ch. 35).
frames.concerns: Drug use (Word of Wisdom echoes); fan service; body horror. For the Strength of Youth: does this invite the Spirit?

frames.aligns: Attention to the marginalized (unlicensed Choujin, Palma); structural harm from war and drug trade.
frames.concerns: Objectifying designs (SLJ); thin early writing of Ely (ANN).

frames.aligns: Courage, friendship and clear condemnation of mass killing.
frames.concerns: Health message and drug content; body horror and fan service. "By beholding we become changed" (2 Corinthians 3:18); Fundamental Belief 22.

frames.aligns: Love of friends; condemnation of mass killing.
frames.concerns: jw.org's test: violence (Psalm 11:5), immorality and spiritism; visions and marks shown as real; frequent fights.
Fear, disease-like mutation and horror are made vivid and real, against "Stand porter at the door of thought" (Science and Health 392).

frames.aligns: Protecting life; condemnation of genocide; honoring a father (ch. 35).
frames.concerns: Tzniut makes fan service and nudity gags a concern; nivul peh for coarse language (to verify); many Haredi homes avoid such media; prophecy outside Torah framing.

frames.aligns: Protecting life; genocide shown as evil; memory of victims (ch. 27, 49).
frames.concerns: Modesty values applied by families; drug content.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam echoes in protecting the vulnerable; genocide condemned.
Patience, loyalty, protecting the weak; genocide condemned.
frames.concerns: Intoxicants (Qur'an 5:90) and drug-made power central; immodest designs and nudity gags (lowering the gaze, 24:30-31); prophecy outside revelation.

frames.aligns: Dharma of protecting others; the powers as desire (kama) and ego made visible; karma in consequences.
frames.concerns: Some families apply the Gita's tamasic category to body horror and drugs.

frames.aligns: Craving and complexes as the root of monstrous power fits the teaching on tanha; compassion for enemies; impermanence.
frames.concerns: Killing as a frequent solution (first precept); intoxicants (fifth precept).

frames.aligns: Courage to defend the oppressed; ego (haumai) and attachment shown as dangerous in villains.
frames.concerns: Intoxicants (forbidden in the Rehat Maryada) central to the plot; fan service.

frames.aligns: Unity ("humanity is one large family," Ishida's world rule); service.
frames.concerns: Strong teaching against drugs and in favor of nonviolence; Shoghi Effendi's "chaste and holy life" (to verify wording) and the fan service.

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) and gratitude in Tokio; animal-form transformations familiar from folklore.
frames.concerns: Blood and death as impurity, heavily shown; little sacred imagery mocked.

frames.aligns: "Harm none" echoed in protecting others; visions and prophecy not stereotyped; Ely's later chapter titled "Witch" (vol. 15) needs checking.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; check vol. 15 for how a "witch" is portrayed.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness precepts: help others, do not murder (mass killers condemned).
frames.concerns: Drugs as the gateway to power; powers tied to "mental instability" (TV Tropes), a psychiatric framing the Church opposes.

frames.aligns: Critique of war, tyranny and drug economies; outsiders humanized.
frames.concerns: Objectifying female designs (SLJ); Ely as comic relief early (ANN); a 16+ rating; drug use as a power-up.

frames.aligns: Meaning chosen by the self; empathy and reason (Tokio's plans); prophecy shown as dangerous when it justifies killing (ch. 49).
frames.concerns: Body horror and cruelty; drug use framed through fantasy.

frames.aligns: Courage, protective friendship, a father's guidance, condemnation of tyranny.
frames.concerns: A hero who quits school and leaves home (vol. 6); drug-made power; fan service; authority shown as unreliable.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth even of enemies (Palma, Zora, Batista); justice for victims of war.
frames.concerns: Violence as the main solution; objectifying designs.

frames.aligns: A hero who claims his own will instead of serving another; villains who use prophecy to justify harm are exposed; questioning institutions (Yamato Mori).
frames.concerns: Harm to children (a boy killed by Chandra) is condemned in the story, which fits the Satanic Temple Tenets; little else to raise.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Thugs who answer humiliation with revenge are villains (v1); disputes go through licensing and Yamato Mori (vol. 2). Personal rivalry between Tokio and Azuma is settled by an honest talk that turns into a fight (ch. 43).

Order vs freedom.evidence: The licensing system is respected, but Tokio is celebrated for leaving school to follow his own path (vol. 6) and for overriding a task force's plan (vol. 7).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Friends and mentors matter more than family; Yamato Mori protects everyone; Tokio's father supports him (ch. 35). Zora's "children" show kin loyalty turned dangerous.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Ranks and mentors exist (Sandek, Ichiro), but a junior's good plan wins over seniors (vol. 7).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Science and drugs, not ritual, make Choujin; prophecy exists but is shown as dangerous when it justifies killing (ch. 49). Ishida's world has one language and no separate peoples (Manga Passion).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: The story celebrates finding one's own dream and identity (ANN), within a dangerous, war-torn world where safety matters.

folkways.japan: school as the center of teenage life, truancy as a serious offense (vol. 1), senpai-style mentorship and a licensed, orderly hero system reflect Japanese norms; Tokio's break from school is notable partly because it cuts against those norms.

delivery.evidence: Reviews praise sympathetic villains (Batista "a great tragic villain"); TV Tropes calls Queem a "Complete Monster". No review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its ideas about identity and desire are built into the power system and the villains' backstories rather than spoken as lessons.

personified.ideology: Finding one's own will; empathy
Prophecy justifies any cost
Rewrite the past for the greater good
Might makes right

entry.title: Onani Master Kurosawa
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Kurosawa, an isolated and scornful 14-year-old, secretly masturbates every day in an unused school girls' restroom. When he avenges a bullied classmate, Kitahara, by soiling her bullies' gym clothes, she discovers him and blackmails him into targeting other girls. The story turns from dark comedy to a drama about consequences, guilt and redemption.
entry.life_message: It holds up facing one's wrongdoing, opening up to others and changing, rather than hiding in contempt and isolation.

entry.heading: Magi: The Labyrinth of Magic
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is chosen freely rather than handed down by fate or by a ruler. You face your own pain without sinking into hatred, treat every people as equal, and work with friends to build a world without slaves or masters, even if a free world stays messy and cruel.

frames.aligns: Human dignity against slavery and caste; mercy and reconciliation (Aladdin with Kassim and Mogamett); free will. Evil (Al-Thamen, David) is not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7).
frames.concerns: Scripture's Solomon and David reworked, David as monster; Goetic spirit names on heroes' weapons; groping gags (CCC 2521-2523 on modesty).

frames.aligns: Struggle against the passions shown as black rukh; repentance at death (Mogamett).
frames.concerns: Nepsis makes the fan service a concern; demons from a grimoire are taken as real in the tradition; reworked holy kings.

frames.aligns: Clear condemnation of slavery and tyranny; friendship and sacrifice.
frames.concerns: Biblical figures reinvented; occult names; the story's hope rests on human will with no God behind it. Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Beneath the Tangles reads Morgiana's freed life as a picture of grace and gratitude, and sees "subversive goodness in imitation of Christ."
frames.concerns: The same writer says the series distorts biblical material and draws on a grimoire that presents demons positively.

frames.aligns: Freedom from bondage; good defeats a world-devouring evil.
frames.concerns: Spirits named after the 72 demons of the Lesser Key of Solomon serve as the heroes' power source (Beneath the Tangles) — an "open door" concern; magic shown as good.

frames.aligns: Total depravity has an echo in black rukh; common grace lets families value good art.
frames.concerns: The story treats any guided destiny as tyranny, against providence; WLC Q139 on lascivious pictures for the fan service; scripture kings reworked.

frames.aligns: Two kingdoms echo: rulers answer for how they serve; vocation of kings. Mercy toward enemies.
frames.concerns: Bondage of the will versus the story's confidence in human choice; occult names. LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Social holiness: abolition, care for the poor in Balbadd's slums; grace-like reconciliation.
frames.concerns: Fan service and groping; occult names. Holiness churches more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: Judges by framing, in a tradition of fantasy literature; slavery, caste and tyranny framed as evil.
Compassion for enemies; the story says war is "largely unnecessary" (The Fandom Post) and turns to trade over conquest.
frames.concerns: Heroes still win by combat and djinn weapons; popular media is avoided by conservative groups.

frames.aligns: Agency (free will) is the story's central good; families and friendships last; service as leadership.
frames.concerns: Fan service; occult names; scripture figures reworked.

frames.aligns: Structural sin: slavery, caste, empire; the dignity of the poor and of other peoples.
frames.concerns: Groping played for laughs; Common Sense Media's whitewashing concern.
The dead live on in the rukh and speak to the living, against teaching on the state of the dead; magic central.
Magic and spirit power (spiritism, Galatians 5:19-21) are the core of the story; demon names; violence.

frames.aligns: Love and right thinking overcome darkness; hatred is shown as the trap.
frames.concerns: Evil, death and suffering are presented as powerful realities.

frames.aligns: Freedom from slavery (an Exodus theme); justice; memory of the dead.
frames.concerns: David and Solomon, kings of Israel, reworked into a monster and a god-founding rebel; magic; tzniut makes the fan service a concern.

frames.aligns: Exodus echoes in liberation from slavery; justice for the vulnerable.
frames.concerns: Reworked Jewish kings; modesty values applied by families.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam: ending slavery and caste; informed choice.
frames.concerns: David as villain may trouble some; fan service.

frames.aligns: Justice, freedom from slavery, mercy; Sulaiman commanding jinn is a Qur'anic image.
frames.concerns: Depicting prophets is widely forbidden, and Solomon and David appear as characters; the evil god's name "Ill Ilah" echoes Arabic for "the god" (my own observation); groping and fan service against lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31).

frames.aligns: Rajadharma: a king's duty to protect and serve; karma-like consequences of hatred; the life flow returns to its source.
frames.concerns: Fan service; some apply the tamasic category to the darker arcs.

frames.aligns: Interdependence (rukh), compassion for enemies, hatred as the source of suffering.
frames.concerns: Violence as the main way forward; fan service.

frames.aligns: Equality of all peoples, opposition to slavery and caste; ego and greed shown in villains.
frames.concerns: Sinbad's ego-driven plan is partly sympathetic; fan service.

frames.aligns: Unity of humankind and of peoples; removal of prejudice; peace by consultation rather than conquest.
frames.concerns: Violence; fan service against a "chaste and holy life."

frames.aligns: Magic and magicians shown respectfully overall; a life-force flow; "harm none" in the refusal of hatred.
frames.concerns: Magician supremacy is the Magnostadt villainy, not a pagan stereotype.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness precepts: don't harm others, honor others' freedom; spirit-like life force.
Anti-slavery, anti-caste, anti-imperial; the poor have voice.
frames.concerns: Groping as comedy; male-gaze art (ScreenWise); whitewashing in the anime (Common Sense Media).

frames.aligns: Human freedom over fate and gods; self-government; reason and cooperation; the ending removes the god-like system (ch. 351-369).
Courage, duty, honor, marriage, responsibility of rulers, loyalty among friends.
frames.concerns: The story's suspicion of inherited order and fate; monarchy gives way to a republic (ch. 64).

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of every people; justice; free search for truth; refusal of imposed destiny.
Rebellion against a controlling god and imposed fate (Solomon, the ending); individual liberty; compassion and justice (Satanic Temple Tenets 1-2).
frames.concerns: Heroes also prize self-sacrifice and community; groping of non-consenting people.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Revenge is a trap that feeds black rukh (Hakuryuu, Judar, Mogamett); Alibaba and Aladdin reconcile with Kassim and Mogamett. Personal worth is not tied to standing.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Fate, empire, caste and Sinbad's benevolent control all lose; the ending picks "A Cruel But Free Path" (ch. 364).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Found family matters most, but blood families are often harmful (Kassim's father, Gyokuen) and Alibaba puts his people above his royal kin (ch. 64).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Solomon's equality of all species (Wikipedia); abolition of slavery; Balbadd becomes a republic (ch. 64). Kings remain, but rank must be earned by service.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: The god-like Rukh system and its "fate" are ended (ch. 351-369); magic gives way to human choice and trade. Spirituality is present but not traditional faith.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Freedom, tolerance and choosing one's path outrank security; the heroes give up a guaranteed peace for liberty.

folkways.japan: The imperial Kou family (modelled on Chinese dynasties), duty to one's lord, and the senpai-like bonds among Sinbad's generals reflect East Asian norms more than the story's own message, which favors freedom over hierarchy.

delivery.evidence: TV Tropes calls Magnostadt's grievances "partly justified"; fans split on Sinbad. No review in the entry calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Themes of fate, kingship and equality are argued in long speeches and shown through rulers whose plans are given a real hearing before they fail.

personified.ideology: Free will, equality, refusing hatred
Benevolent control over fate
Magician supremacy born of grief
Unification by imperial conquest

entry.heading: Boruto: Naruto Next Generations (Ukyo Kodachi, Masashi Kishimoto and Mikio Ikemoto, 2016-)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is one where you protect the people you love, carry your parents' legacy without being trapped by it, and keep your own sense of who you are even when everyone else sees you wrongly.

frames.aligns: Love within the family, an adopted child welcomed, a father's self-gift (Naruto) and Kurama's sacrifice; evil (child experimentation, possession) is framed as evil.
frames.concerns: Sexualized covers of child characters; possession and a "Karma" curse as fantasy mechanics; an adopted son's possessive love.

frames.aligns: Self-sacrifice for others; honoring parents; truth persisting under false accusation.
frames.concerns: Possession by god-like beings, spirit-like curses and devouring tree-beings read as more than fantasy for many families; guarding the senses (nepsis) about the cover art.

frames.aligns: A son learning to honor his father (Ephesians 6:1-4); faithfulness under false accusation; adoption shown as love.
frames.concerns: Curse marks and possession (Deuteronomy 18:10-12); immodest covers of children; violence.

frames.aligns: Adoption as belonging (Ephesians 1:5 is a common evangelical reading); fathers' sacrifice; perseverance; truth over the crowd.
frames.concerns: Alien "gods" and possession; covers sexualizing 12-year-olds. No Plugged In review exists (searched).

frames.aligns: Courage, protecting family, a hero who will not kill his rival lightly.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": possession by Otsutsuki, the Karma mark, beings that devour people, body-snatching are weighed heavily even in fiction; immodest covers.

frames.aligns: Common grace: real goods (sacrifice, faithfulness, family love) in a non-Christian work. Flawed characters and good intentions gone wrong (Kawaki) fit a realistic view of the heart.
frames.concerns: Lascivious pictures (WLC Q139) for the covers; occult-styled mechanics.

frames.aligns: Vocation: Naruto's duty as father and as Hokage pull against each other; two kingdoms, with fallible rulers.
frames.concerns: Fantasy occult elements (usually adiaphora); cover art.

frames.aligns: Love that seeks the outsider (Kawaki); peace kept by sacrifice; social concern about experimentation on children.
frames.concerns: Cover art; drinking (holiness churches ask members to abstain).

frames.aligns: Fantasy in the Lewis tradition; good and evil clearly framed; reconciliation between rivals.
frames.concerns: Cover art; possession mechanics judged by framing.

frames.aligns: Family, community and protecting the weak.
frames.concerns: Nearly every conflict is settled by combat, and fighting is heroic; worldly media.

frames.aligns: Family as central; adoption; parents' sacrifice for children; the father-son bond restored.
frames.concerns: Immodest covers; possession and curse marks; drinking (Word of Wisdom).

frames.aligns: Care for an abused, trafficked child; criticism of experimentation on children; women in leadership and combat (CSM).
frames.concerns: Gender roles of the adult cast (Anime Feminist); overwork treated as normal; sexualized covers of girls.
Possession and spirits shown as real; violence; "by beholding we become changed." (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Love of family; refusing to give in to hatred.
frames.concerns: Violence as the main action (Psalm 11:5); possession and curse marks as spiritism; loyalty to a military village. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Identity that stays true when others see falsely (the Omnipotence arc fits the idea of true identity behind appearances).
frames.concerns: Fear, possession and body horror as mental imagery. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Honoring parents (Exodus 20:12); responsibility for an orphaned and sold child; truth against false witness.
frames.concerns: Sorcery-like mechanics (Deuteronomy 18); immodest covers against tzniut. Haredi homes would avoid it; Modern Orthodox families are selective. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Family, adoption, the dignity of an abused child.
frames.concerns: Cover art; occult mechanics. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam in protecting the vulnerable; questions of memory and truth.
frames.concerns: Gender roles; cover art. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Care for orphans and the abused (Qur'an 93:9); honoring parents; patience (sabr) under false accusation.
frames.concerns: Lowering the gaze (24:30-31) makes the covers a strong concern; sihr-like curse marks and possession (2:102); drinking.

frames.aligns: Duty to family (dharma); chakra as life energy.
frames.concerns: "Karma" used for a curse brand rather than moral cause and effect may read as careless use of a sacred term.

frames.aligns: Attachment's harm shown in Kawaki's clinging love and Code's devotion; compassion for enemies.
frames.concerns: "Karma" as a curse mark; violence (first precept); drinking (fifth precept).

frames.aligns: Service (seva) and protecting the weak; facing false accusation with courage; overcoming ego (Boruto's early arrogance).
frames.concerns: Lust played lightly (Eida's charm); drinking. (from general knowledge; to verify)
Degrading imagery (covers); drinking; violence. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Ancestors and inherited duty; a sacred tree (Shinju) and kami-like beings; harmony of the village.
frames.concerns: The Divine Tree made into a predator, and god-like beings as parasites, may seem careless to some. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Bonds with animal spirits (Kurama); nature energy.
frames.concerns: Fighting against "harm none"; nature (the tree) as a devouring threat. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Basically good beings who can change (Kawaki, Kashin Koji); survival of family and group.
frames.concerns: Violence; experimentation. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Care for a trafficked, abused child; women in leadership and combat (CSM); critique of a society that turns on one person.
frames.concerns: Sexualized covers of 12-year-olds; traditional adult gender roles and overwork shown uncritically (Anime Feminist); weight pressure on Cho-Cho (CSM).

frames.aligns: People, not gods, save the world: the heroes resist god-like Otsutsuki; science and technology are useful tools.
frames.concerns: Destiny and bloodline themes ("The Singularity of Fate," Two Blue Vortex vol. 4) cut against self-made achievement.

frames.aligns: Family loyalty, honoring parents and teachers, sacrifice, inherited duty, marriage and children as normal.
frames.concerns: Sexualized covers of children; a hero who defies the village's rulers.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of an outcast and an abused child; search for truth against mass deception.
frames.concerns: Gender roles; cover art. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: A hero who rejects the village's false verdict and acts on his own judgment; gods shown as predators.
frames.concerns: Self-sacrifice and loyalty themes cut against Church of Satan individualism; harm to children condemned in both texts. (from general knowledge; to verify)

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Boruto is falsely branded a killer (ch. 79-80) and answers by protecting people, not by revenge; personal rivalry with Kawaki still drives the plot.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Village order and the Hokage are honored (vols. 1-3), but the hero must act outside the law as a fugitive (Two Blue Vortex vols. 1-4).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Family is the core: Boruto and Naruto, Sarada and Sasuke, the adopted Kawaki (ch. 25-27). Kawaki's family-first obsession is shown as dangerous (ch. 77).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Ranks, teachers and the Hokage line are respected; Sarada's goal is to become Hokage.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: A modernizing village with trains and ninja tech (vol. 6); god-like beings are aliens, not gods; inherited eyes and legacy still matter.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Threat and survival dominate from vol. 5 on; Boruto's wish to be himself rather than "the Hokage's son" gives some place to self-expression.

folkways.japan: The overworked father (Anime Feminist links it to Japanese overtime and karoshi), respect for teachers and senpai, and a stay-at-home mother reflect Japanese norms of the 2010s rather than an argument the story makes.

delivery.evidence: TV Tropes lists the "Talk-no-Jutsu return" as a fan dispute; ANN praises its generational theme. No review found calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its points about fathers, legacy and identity come through the plot's twists more than speeches, though rival views are argued mid-fight.

personified.ideology: Honor your legacy but forge your own path
Protect loved ones by any means, even control
Higher beings may harvest lesser ones
Duty to all before time with family

entry.dominant: Communitarianism (family and village), Classical virtue ethics, Transhumanism (critiqued), Confucian ethics. Lens labels are this entry's own framing unless a source is named.

entry.heading: Mob Psycho 100
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is not defined by talent or power. You become a good person by how you treat others, by honest effort and by accepting all of yourself, including the feelings you would rather hide.

content.framing: Condemned (as a way to solve problems); shown with consequences

frames.aligns: Evil is not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7); humility, honesty and mercy toward enemies; worth not tied to talent. Beneath the Tangles links Mob's love and humility to Christ's Passion and Romans 7.
frames.concerns: Psychic powers, exorcism by laymen and spirits treated as real; occult practice is forbidden (CCC 2115-2117), though story magic is judged by framing.

frames.aligns: Struggle with the passions inside oneself (???); humility over pride (Teru).
frames.concerns: Evil spirits are real in the tradition, so possession and lay exorcism played as comedy or action are a serious concern; guarding the senses (nepsis).

frames.aligns: Clear wrong in bullying, scams and cults; repentance and confession (Reigen, ch. 99-100); honoring family.
frames.concerns: Psychics, spirits and exorcism (Deuteronomy 18:10-12); a boy worshipped as a god (shown critically). Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Beneath the Tangles: "Mob's treasure is the treasure of a loving heart"; power and self-satisfaction lose to love and humility. Sin is depicted, not endorsed.
frames.concerns: Spirit contact and possession shown as real; the story's grace has no divine source.

frames.aligns: Clear battle with evil spirits; humility and love win.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": possession, evil spirits, a cult that "manifests" a being through belief (Divine Tree arc), psychic power as a gift, all shown neutrally or positively.

frames.aligns: Common grace lets families value a story about pride, envy and repentance; a sharp picture of the heart's divided will (Romans 7).
frames.concerns: Occult powers framed neutrally; no source of grace beyond human kindness.

frames.aligns: Law and gospel echo: Reigen's confession of his lies frees Mob (The Mary Sue: "the extended hand"). Vocation: ordinary work and effort have worth.
frames.concerns: Occult elements; LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Holiness of heart and life: self-control, kindness, works of mercy to enemies.
frames.concerns: Psychics and spirits; Holiness churches more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: Judged by framing: good and evil are clear and kindness wins; fantasy tradition (C.S. Lewis).
Violence is a last resort (Anime Feminist); Mob refuses to use power on people and talks enemies down; humility and community.
frames.concerns: The heroes still win many fights; conservative groups avoid most popular media and fantasy.

frames.aligns: Honesty, family, self-mastery, service and personal growth.
frames.concerns: Spirit contact and the occult; a smoking, drinking mentor. Members vary in strictness.

frames.aligns: Empathy for the bullied and the marginal; critique of domination and manipulative religion; gentle masculinity (Anime Feminist).
frames.concerns: Reigen's exploitation of a child worker is mostly played for laughs.

frames.aligns: Self-control, humility, honesty, love of enemies.
frames.concerns: The dead are unconscious until the resurrection, so spirits of the dead as real (ghosts, Mogami's mother as an evil spirit, ch. 65; Mogami himself) conflict with teaching on the state of the dead.

frames.aligns: Love, honesty, rejection of violence as a solution.
frames.concerns: Spiritism, exorcism and spirits of the dead are central motifs (Galatians 5:19-21).

frames.aligns: Love outlasts fear; Mob is healed by being known and loved.
frames.concerns: Mental force over matter (psychic power), possession and evil spirits shown as real powers, close to what the tradition calls mesmerism or "animal magnetism."

frames.aligns: Humility, honesty, anger and pride mastered; teshuvah-like change in Teru, Ritsu and Reigen.
frames.concerns: Necromancy and spirits (Deuteronomy 18:10-11); a boy worshipped as a god (critiqued). Many Haredi homes avoid fantasy and secular media altogether, which would make this Significant for them.

frames.aligns: Teshuvah (return), honesty, kind speech; worth not set by gifts.
frames.concerns: Sorcery and spirits as story devices.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam echoes in protecting the weak; empathy; critique of manipulative leaders.
Humility, self-control over anger, honesty, rejecting worship of a human (the Psycho Helmet cult is exposed).
frames.concerns: Jinn are real in Islamic belief, so lay exorcism and psychic power framed as neutral gifts are a concern; sorcery (sihr) by Mogami for money (ch. 62, 65).

frames.aligns: Ego (ahamkara) humbled in Teru; self-mastery; karma-like consequences for Mogami's curse-killings.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; some families apply the Gita's tamasic category to horror.

frames.aligns: Attachment to power and status causes suffering (Teru, Claw); compassion for enemies; accepting all of one's mind (???) rather than suppressing it.
frames.concerns: Fighting still occurs; spirits are common in folk practice and not a concern.

frames.aligns: The five vices, especially ego (haumai) and anger, shown in villains and overcome; honest work; fake mediums exposed.
frames.concerns: The Gurus rejected magic and superstition, and psychic power is real in the story.

frames.aligns: Non-violence and unity; truthfulness; service; independent investigation of truth against blind cult following.
frames.concerns: Spiritualism is discouraged; psychic power and spirits shown as real.

frames.aligns: Spirits are familiar; sincerity (makoto), purity of heart and gratitude in Mob.
frames.concerns: A con man selling exorcisms could read as disrespect to real practice, but no shrine or kami is mocked (to verify).

frames.aligns: No witch stereotyping; spirit world taken as real; "harm none" echoes in Mob's rule against using power on people.
The Way to Happiness precepts: be honest, do not murder, help others, set a good example.
frames.concerns: Spirit possession and psychic power framed outside the church's own teaching; cults shown as manipulation.

frames.aligns: Anime Feminist: a rejection of toxic masculinity; empathy; anti-bullying; critique of authoritarian groups.
frames.concerns: Reigen's exploitation of a child is played as comedy for long stretches; few female leads; the Mogami arc's bullying and torment. Common Sense Media has reviewed only the drama (13+).

frames.aligns: "Your talents aren't what define you; how you treat others and navigate the world are far more important" (The Mary Sue). Fraud is exposed by honesty; cults are mocked; empathy and reason win.
frames.concerns: Psychic powers and spirits are fiction, not offered as fact.

frames.aligns: Hard work, humility, self-control, honesty, family ties, anti-cult and anti-utopian.
frames.concerns: Little shown of duty to nation or faith; adult mentor is a con man; masculine ideals are softened (which some readers praise and others may not).

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of every person, including enemies; free search for truth against cult conformity.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; some cartoon violence.

frames.aligns: Skepticism of cults and leaders who demand worship; reason over superstition; Mob accepts his own desires (???) as part of himself.
frames.concerns: Selflessness, humility and restraint of one's power are the story's ideals.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Mob does not answer insults with force; Teru's pride is broken and he learns he is "just an ordinary person" (ch. 18-19). Worth is inherent, not won.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Imposed orders (Claw, cults, a scheming student council, ch. 20-33) are villains; the ideal is self-restraint freely chosen (Mob's rule on powers) and freedom to be oneself.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Brotherhood with Ritsu matters, but Mob helps strangers and even enemies equally (Minegishi, ch. 87; the Awakening Lab kids).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Espers are not superior; the most powerful boy calls himself ordinary; the mentor is unmasked as a fraud and the apprentice outgrows him (ch. 68-73). Club seniors are kind rather than commanding.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Cults, fake mediums and worship of a boy are mocked (ch. 5-9, 68-73, 91/92-97); choice and honesty guide life. Spirits exist, but no tradition offers the answers.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Accepting one's feelings and desires (??? in ch. 99-100) and tolerance of others are the climax; effort and training (Body Improvement Club) still matter.

folkways.japan: School clubs, senpai-kohai respect, the reserved, conflict-avoiding hero and the urban-legend and exorcist folklore are Japanese settings; the story's own message, which questions group conformity and status, pushes against some of these norms rather than simply reflecting them.

delivery.evidence: /Film: Mob "peel[s] away the villain's layers of self loathing"; villains get backstories. No review in this entry calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Lessons are stated outright in Reigen's and Mob's speeches, while villains' worldviews are given real backstories and are argued with, not mocked.

personified.ideology: Worth comes from kindness and effort, not power
Street-smart pragmatism; self-interest softened by care
Esper superiority and "main character" pride
Misanthropy: people are wicked at heart

lenses.label: Confucian ethics, Traditionalism, Progressivism, Utilitarianism, Postmodernism, Absurdism, Hedonism

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Secular humanism, Pragmatism, Existentialism, with Might makes right and Collectivism / authoritarianism clearly critiqued.

entry.heading: BEASTARS
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life means knowing your own nature, including its dangerous urges, and choosing to master them for the sake of others, while refusing the labels a society hands you. Love and coexistence across a deep divide are possible, but only with honesty, restraint and a cost.

content.framing: Neutral to sympathetic (Haru); shown with consequences (predation as desire)

frames.aligns: Mastery of passions (temperance); murder and the black market framed as evil; mercy to enemies; the story ends in a proposal of marriage.
frames.concerns: Teen sexual activity outside marriage shown sympathetically (CCC 2353); desire fused with consuming another; naturalistic world with no transcendence. Inter Mirifica 7 asks that evil not be made attractive: Riz's romantic framing of murder is the test case.

frames.aligns: Struggle with the passions is the hero's arc; humility; mercy.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis) makes the sexual scenes and gore a concern in themselves; love and devouring blended; no God in the story's world.

frames.aligns: Clear condemnation of murder; self-control (Galatians 5:23); loyal friendship.
frames.concerns: Sex outside marriage among teens without judgment; Plugged In says it is "weighed down by sexual content between teenagers and questionable naturalistic themes." Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Honest picture of a heart at war with itself (Romans 7); restraint and sacrifice; mercy toward a killer.
frames.concerns: Naturalism and humanism (Plugged In); sexual content between teens; a world with no need of grace from outside. Some families "engage" it as culture; others avoid it.
Little occult content, but holiness standards make the sexual scenes and nudity the main concern; a spirit appearance of a dead mother.

frames.aligns: Total depravity has an echo: every carnivore carries a real urge to harm. Common grace lets families value good art by non-Christians.
frames.concerns: Westminster Larger Catechism Q139 lists "lascivious... books, pictures" among sins against the seventh commandment; the story's cure is self-effort, not grace.

frames.aligns: Law-like rules fail to change the heart (school rules, the meat ban); mercy shown to Riz.
frames.concerns: Teen sexual activity; no gospel beyond human effort. LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy; growth in self-mastery; social concern for the marginalized (hybrids, meat addicts).
frames.concerns: Wesley's rule against "diversions" that cannot be used in the name of the Lord; sexual content. Holiness churches more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: Judged by framing: violence and murder condemned, restraint and mercy honored; strong literary tradition of animal fable (Lewis).
frames.concerns: Sexual content among teens; a parent's suicide. Episcopal and ACNA families differ mainly on sexual ethics.

frames.aligns: Restraint of violent urges is the hero's aim; mercy for enemies; community care.
frames.concerns: Fighting becomes Legoshi's main tool in later arcs; sexual content. Conservative groups avoid most popular media.

frames.aligns: Self-mastery; marriage as the hoped-for end (ch. 196); loyalty.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth asks for media that invites the Spirit; teen sexual activity and nudity are the concern.

frames.aligns: Critique of segregation and profiling; empathy for outcasts (hybrids, addicts, Haru).
frames.concerns: Romantic framing of predation; some readers find the gender allegory confused (ANN Hopper: "Patriarchy is not a natural human instinct").

frames.aligns: Self-control; meat-eating as a harm, which echoes the church's health message (from general knowledge; to verify).
frames.concerns: Fundamental Belief 22 and "by beholding we become changed": sexual content, gore and a dead mother's spirit appearing (state of the dead).
jw.org's question whether media features what God hates: violence (Psalm 11:5) and sexual immorality (Galatians 5:19-21) are both recurring; a dead mother's spirit appears.

frames.aligns: Love and self-mastery overcome a supposedly fixed animal nature.
frames.concerns: Fear, appetite and violence are shown as powerful realities; much dwelling on dark thought.

frames.aligns: Yetzer hara (the evil inclination) mastered by effort is close to Legoshi's arc; murder condemned; marriage at the end.
frames.concerns: Tzniut makes nudity and teen sexual scenes a strong concern; many Haredi homes restrict such media altogether; suicide of a parent.

frames.aligns: Conquering the inclination; justice for the vulnerable; critique of prejudice.
frames.concerns: Sexual content among teens; modesty values applied by families.

frames.aligns: Anti-prejudice and anti-profiling message; tikkun olam echoes in Legoshi's work for coexistence.
frames.concerns: Sexual content; whether the species allegory risks implying fixed group natures (a concern ANN's Hopper raises for gender).

frames.aligns: Self-restraint (sabr, mastery of the nafs); justice; forbidding the killing of the innocent; marriage as the goal.
frames.concerns: Lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) makes nudity and sexual scenes a strong concern; sex outside marriage shown without judgment; a parent's suicide (Qur'an 4:29).

frames.aligns: Ahimsa and restraint of appetite fit the meat-ban premise; the Gita's mastery of the senses; dharma by nature versus by choice.
frames.concerns: Sexual content; some families apply the Gita's tamasic category to the gore.

frames.aligns: Craving (tanha) as the root of harm; restraint; compassion even for the killer Riz; the first precept against killing at the center of the world's law.
frames.concerns: The third precept (sexual misconduct) and the sexual scenes; the story often resolves things through combat.

frames.aligns: The five vices (lust, anger, greed, attachment, ego) at work in Riz, Melon and the black market; equality across groups; service.
frames.concerns: Lust is the vice most tied to the hero's arc and is not always framed as a vice; sexual content.

frames.aligns: Unity across divided peoples and the end of prejudice are central Bahá'í aims.
frames.concerns: A "chaste and holy life" makes the sexual content a concern; violence is the hero's path later on.

frames.aligns: Harmony between groups; sincerity (makoto) in Legoshi; respect for festival customs.
frames.concerns: Blood and death as impurity; little else in the message.

frames.aligns: Nature honored and faced honestly; "harm none" echoes in the meat ban and restraint.
The Way to Happiness: do not murder, be temperate, help others.
frames.concerns: Riz's urge-suppressing pills and Gohin's clinical treatment of addicts could be read through the Church's opposition to psychiatric drugs.

frames.aligns: Critique of segregation, profiling and elite power; empathy for outsiders; Haru's sexuality read as agency (ANN Hopper).
frames.concerns: The predator-as-sexual-desire metaphor (AIPT: "disturbingly easy to map onto... sexual assault"); CSM warns the Haru-Legoshi relationship "may send negative messages"; risk of reading group traits as fixed.

frames.aligns: Reason over instinct; individuals defy labels; no supernatural rescue (Plugged In notes the humanism); mercy and justice by human effort.
Self-control, courage, loyal friendship, protective masculinity in Legoshi, a marriage proposal at the end.
frames.concerns: Teen sexual activity without judgment; institutions shown as hollow; Plugged In's "questionable naturalistic themes."

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of every being, including hybrids and a killer; justice across divides; free search for truth.
frames.concerns: Sexual content and violence for younger readers; stereotype concerns in the allegory.

frames.aligns: Embracing one's nature honestly rather than hiding it; bodily autonomy (Louis offers his own leg); defiance of hollow authority.
frames.concerns: Self-denial and fasting as virtue run against Church of Satan indulgence ethics; harm to the vulnerable condemned, which fits the Eleven Rules.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: The story wants disputes settled by law and reform (ch. 193), but Legoshi repeatedly settles things by personal fights (Riz, v11; Melon, v19-22) and Gosha's backstory turns on a personal feud (ch. 189).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Rules and institutions are shown as failing or hypocritical; Legoshi leaves school (ch. 99) and acts on his own conscience. Self-discipline is valued, but as personal choice, not obedience.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Loyalty crosses group lines (Legoshi and Louis, Legoshi and Haru); family secrets (Leano, Gosha) matter, but the goal is a shared society.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: The Beastar elite, the Shishigumi's rank and Louis's early pride are critiqued; the drama club and friendships flatten rank.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No religion; reason and self-knowledge guide characters (Plugged In's "naturalistic"); festival customs appear only as setting.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Being true to oneself, tolerance of difference and choosing whom to love are central; survival pressures (black market, fasting) are obstacles, not ideals.

folkways.japan: The boarding-school setting, the drama club's senpai-kohai ranks and the "herbivore/carnivore" slang for sexually passive and active people (ANN, Rebecca Silverman) are Japanese norms that frame the story; many readers outside Japan will see the slang layer only through notes.

delivery.evidence: MAL reviewer Krunchyman says Itagaki "never pointed the finger"; another (qwyxivi) feels it was made "mostly for the sake of social commentary."
delivery.note: The prejudice and appetite themes are carried by the premise and characters' inner monologues more than by speeches, and villains get sympathetic backstories.

personified.ideology: Self-mastery over instinct; coexistence
Herbivore pride and will to power
Predation as true love; instinct as the real self
Hybrid self-hatred and nihilism

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Classical virtue ethics, Naturalism, Secular humanism, Critical theory.

entry.heading: Akame ga KILL!
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is spent fighting for the weak against a cruel order, even at the cost of your own life and innocence. Killing the wicked is shown as necessary, but never as clean: the killers call it murder and expect to pay for it.

content.framing: Shown with consequences (heroes' killings); Condemned (villains' torture)
Condemned (sexual violence, shown as villains' crimes); Neutral (fan service)

frames.aligns: Evil (torture, abuse of the weak, corrupt power) is never made attractive; concern for the poor village; self-giving love among comrades.
frames.concerns: Private assassination as the main means of justice; the winners torture Honest and execute a child; sexual violence and fan service used for shock (Inter Mirifica 7; CCC 2297-2298 on torture).

frames.aligns: Struggle against the passions is visible in the villains (cruelty, lust, pride).
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis) weighs heavily against the gore and sexual violence; no repentance or grace for most.

frames.aligns: Clear condemnation of oppression and cruelty; courage and sacrifice.
frames.concerns: Vigilante killing as the hero's calling; Philippians 4:8 test fails on many pages; premarital relationship. Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Geeks Under Grace (8.5/10, anime) praises teamwork and compassion and reads Honest as a lying, Satan-like tempter.
frames.concerns: Barham (Geeks Under Grace, via Beneath the Tangles) asks: "Can there be hope for anyone when grace is not allowed into the picture?" Depicts sin; the depiction is heavy.
Little occult content, but a cult leader and alchemy (vol. 14-15, Wild Hunt's Dorothea); the main concern is the sexual and violent content as an "open door."

frames.aligns: Total depravity has an echo: the powerful are corrupt at every level; the heroes confess their own guilt.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 ("lascivious... pictures") applies to fan service and sexual violence; private vengeance in place of the magistrate.

frames.aligns: Two kingdoms: a corrupt government that has forfeited its calling.
frames.concerns: Private killing as heroism; the content load. LCMS and WELS families tend to be stricter than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Social holiness: concern for the poor and exploited.
frames.concerns: Wesley's General Rules would rule out much of the content; killing without grace. Holiness churches more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: Judged by framing: evil is clearly evil; just-war questions about revolution (Article 37).
frames.concerns: Assassination, the torture of Honest and the child's execution are framed as the cost of victory.

frames.aligns: Compassion for the weak; a critique of the empire.
frames.concerns: Violence shown as heroic and necessary is the whole plot (Matthew 5:39).

frames.aligns: Courage, loyalty, protecting the innocent; a married-family ending.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth: sexual violence, fan service and gore do not invite the Spirit; the premarital relationship.

frames.aligns: Systemic injustice named; the poor village; corruption exposed.
frames.concerns: Sexual violence used as a villain marker and shock device; women sexualized; vengeance rather than restorative justice.
"By beholding we become changed" (2 Corinthians 3:18) weighs against the gore and sexual violence; Fundamental Belief 22.

frames.aligns: Corrupt rulers fail; love of comrades.
frames.concerns: Violence (Psalm 11:5) and immorality are central; political revolution as the solution, against Witness neutrality.
Evil, cruelty and death shown as overwhelming and real.

frames.aligns: Justice against oppressors; protecting the weak.
frames.concerns: Tzniut and nivul peh make the fan service and sexual violence a strong concern; many Haredi homes would not have it. Execution without due process.
Sexual violence and gore; torture by the winners.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam echoes in fighting injustice; women in leadership.
frames.concerns: Sexual violence and gore; the child Emperor's execution.

frames.aligns: Resisting oppression (zulm) is a recognized duty; loyalty; the poor village's welfare.
frames.concerns: Lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) weighs against fan service; assassination and torture of captives; premarital relationship.

frames.aligns: Dharma may require fighting an adharmic ruler (Gita); duty and sacrifice; the warrior who fights without hate.
frames.concerns: Tamasic content (Gita 17) in gore and sexual violence; cruelty by the victors.

frames.aligns: Esdeath and Honest as pictures of craving and cruelty; Mage in a Barrel reads a cycle of violence.
frames.concerns: Killing is the plot's solution, against the first precept; little compassion for enemies.

frames.aligns: Resisting tyranny and protecting the weak (the saint-soldier ideal); the five vices shown in the villains and defeated.
frames.concerns: Lust displayed in fan service; torture of the defeated.
Strong commitment to non-violence and a "chaste and holy life"; violence and sexual content central.
Blood and death as impurity throughout; little sacred content either way.

frames.aligns: No stereotyped witches or pagans; resistance to abuse of power.
frames.concerns: "Harm none" sits against the whole method.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness: do not murder, help others; corrupt officials condemned.
frames.concerns: Killing as the solution; drugs used to control people (Kurome).
Sexual violence used as shock and villain shorthand (TV Tropes calls some of it failed shock value); fan service; child victims; vigilante executions. Common Sense Media 15+.

frames.aligns: Critique of tyranny and cruelty; the heroes admit killing is murder.
frames.concerns: Torture of prisoners by the winners; little due process.

frames.aligns: Duty, loyalty, courage, protecting the weak; condemnation of a decadent elite; a family ending.
frames.concerns: Violent overthrow of a monarchy; public execution of a child king; crude content conflicts with "the good, the true and the beautiful."

frames.aligns: Justice for the oppressed; worth of the poor.
frames.concerns: Inherent worth of every person, including enemies and the child Emperor; sexual violence.

frames.aligns: Rebellion against corrupt authority; lex talionis against those who prey on the weak; Satanic Temple Tenet 2 (justice).
frames.concerns: Harm to children (Eleven Rules) is condemned by the story too; Esdeath's social Darwinism is defeated.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Wrongs are answered personally, outside any court: Tatsumi kills Aria himself (ch. 1); revenge drives Seryu, Run and Bols's story; Honest is tortured by those he wronged (ch. 78).

Order vs freedom.evidence: The story celebrates armed resistance to a corrupt state and its police; Seryu's law-and-order "justice" is shown as twisted (ch. 28).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Loyalty to the found family of Night Raid and to sisters (Akame and Kurome) sits alongside fighting for the nation and the poor villages.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Against hereditary nobles and a puppet throne; but military rank and Najenda's command are respected.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Little religion; the one religious movement is a front for manipulation (vols. 6-9); the ancient monarchy and its heirloom weapons are destroyed.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Life is about survival and sacrifice in war; "promise not to die" is the team's creed.

folkways.japan: The pseudo-European fantasy setting, the sister bond and the shonen convention of a team that trains, bonds and dies together are genre norms; the rejection of loyalty to a corrupt throne is more the story's own message than a Japanese norm.

delivery.evidence: ANN (vol. 1) praises "shades of gray"; MAL reviewer calls villains "almost comically evil"; Sportskeeda: anime "became too black and white."
delivery.note: The anti-tyranny message is carried by action and backstories; the Empire's side gets sympathetic Jaegers but cartoonish top villains.

personified.ideology: Social Darwinism, strength as the only law
Corrupt power for its own pleasure
Revolution by any means needed
Loyal service to a state he believes is good

entry.dominant: Might makes right (critiqued), Collectivism / authoritarianism (critiqued), Utilitarianism, Pragmatism, Classical virtue ethics.

series.title: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure Part 1: Phantom Blood
series.romaji: JoJo no Kimyou na Bouken: Phantom Blood
series.native: ジョジョの奇妙な冒険 ファントムブラッド

entry.heading: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure Part 1: Phantom Blood
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is lived as a "gentleman": with courage that knows fear and masters it, loyalty to family and friends, and self-sacrifice for the weak. Being human, with its limits and its death, is better than power gained by giving up one's humanity.

frames.aligns: Evil is not made attractive in the end (Inter Mirifica 7): Dio's pride and wish to "transcend humanity" (ch. 11) end in ruin. George and Jonathan lay down their lives for others (John 15:13). Marriage and a child are the hero's reward. Jonathan mourns his enemy (ch. 42).
frames.concerns: Fans find Dio more attractive than the hero (2016 poll, Otaku USA). A crucifix shown as powerless against Dio (TV Tropes). Vampires and a prophecy (CCC 2115-2117 forbids divination; fiction is judged by framing). Gore and animal cruelty (CCC 2418 on animals).

frames.aligns: Humility and self-giving love against a man who wants to make himself a god; theosis is union with God by grace, not seized by power.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis) weighs the burned dog, the mother and baby, and the gore. A crucifix treated as powerless.

frames.aligns: Evil is plainly evil and defeated; a hero who lives by a moral code and dies for others; marriage honored.
frames.concerns: Phil 4:8 test: animal cruelty, cannibal horror, gore; vampires and zombies. Soul liberty: each family decides.

frames.aligns: Engaging culture: a redemptive-sacrifice shape (TV Tropes' "Messianic Archetype"); a clear moral universe; friendship across class (Speedwagon).
frames.concerns: Romans 14 conscience on gore and horror; human power (Hamon) saves, not God.

frames.aligns: Clear good and evil; a demonic-seeming figure destroyed.
frames.concerns: The "open door" concern: an Aztec sacrificial mask, vampirism, raising the dead as zombies, prophecy by Tonpetty (ch. 34), and Hamon as a spiritual-seeming energy from Tibetan monks. A crucifix shown as useless.

frames.aligns: Common grace lets families value the craft. Total depravity of the self-exalting will is vividly shown in Dio; Jonathan's goodness is costly. Westminster Larger Catechism Q139 concerns are light here (no lascivious content reported).
frames.concerns: Gore and animal cruelty; Araki's humanism, where people win "without relying on... divine beings" (ANN).

frames.aligns: Vocation: son, friend, husband; a father who dies for his son; sacrifice for the weak.
frames.concerns: Entertainment is adiaphora, but gore and horror call for conscience; LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Holiness of character (the gentleman ideal); social concern across class (Speedwagon, Ogre Street).
frames.concerns: General Rules on diversions; holiness churches more cautious than UMC about horror.

frames.aligns: Judged by framing (Lewis's tradition): a gothic tale where pride ruins and love sacrifices; the Victorian English setting echoes the tradition's own literary world.
frames.concerns: Clergy absent; gore and animal cruelty.

frames.aligns: Self-giving love, mercy to defeated enemies (Speedwagon, Bruford), mourning an enemy (ch. 42).
frames.concerns: Violence is the hero's main tool and is shown as heroic (Matthew 5:39); conservative groups avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Agency and choice: Dio chooses evil, Jonathan chooses good; eternal family and posterity (Erina's child); sacrifice.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth: gore and horror may not invite the Spirit for many families; vampires and undead.

frames.aligns: A poor boy's abuse shown as a cause of harm; cross-class friendship; care for the vulnerable.
frames.concerns: Thin female roles (ComicsAlliance via Wikipedia); a stereotyped Chinese character (jojowiki); animal cruelty.

frames.aligns: Great controversy between good and evil; pride and self-exaltation condemned (Isaiah 14).
frames.concerns: "By beholding we become changed" weighs gore and horror; the undead and vampires conflict with Fundamental Belief 26 on the state of the dead.

frames.aligns: A man who claims godhood is destroyed.
frames.concerns: jw.org counsel weighs violence (Psalm 11:5) and spiritism heavily: vampires, zombies, prophecy, a sacrificial mask; a crucifix appears (the cross is not used by Witnesses).

frames.aligns: Fear is mastered (Zeppeli, ch. 22); a breathing discipline over panic.
frames.concerns: Death, decay and bodily destruction shown as overwhelming and real; horror imagery.

frames.aligns: Honoring parents; marriage and children; humility against a man who makes himself a god; compassion for animals (tza'ar ba'alei chayim) is violated only by the villain.
frames.concerns: Many Haredi homes avoid such media; the gore and the undead; the forced kiss.

frames.aligns: Moral clarity; honoring parents; mourning even an enemy (compare Proverbs 24:17).
frames.concerns: Gore and horror. No antisemitic tropes reported.

frames.aligns: Ethical courage; protecting the vulnerable; class mobility through friendship.
frames.concerns: Violence; a stereotyped Chinese character. No antisemitic tropes reported.

frames.aligns: A man who calls himself "god" and seeks to live forever is destroyed, which echoes the Qur'an's accounts of tyrants (Pharaoh, 79:24); mercy and kindness to animals are honored by the hero.
frames.concerns: Images of living beings (scholars differ); gore; a forced kiss and lowering the gaze (24:30-31) are minor here.

frames.aligns: Dharma of the righteous warrior; breath discipline (Hamon) resembles pranayama; karma returns on Dio.
frames.concerns: Tamasic content (cruelty, gore); a guru's foretold death.

frames.aligns: Dio is a study in craving: for wealth, power and deathlessness, which brings only suffering. Breath as the root of strength echoes mindful breathing; Hamon from Tibetan monks.
frames.concerns: Non-harm (first precept) set against constant killing; animal cruelty.

frames.aligns: The five vices in Dio (ego, greed, anger, lust for power); a saint-soldier ideal of defending the weak.
frames.concerns: Violence; a villain who calls himself god.

frames.aligns: Noble character and service; unity across class (Speedwagon).
frames.concerns: Constant violence and horror ("chaste and holy life" applies more to sexuality, here light).

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) in Jonathan; gratitude and debt (George's debt, Speedwagon's loyalty); a mentor's spirit passed on.
Life-force energy tied to breath and sunlight; the Aztec past treated as mysterious rather than mocked.
frames.concerns: "Harm none" against constant violence; the Aztec sacrifice shown as horror.

frames.aligns: Self-determinism and personal responsibility; The Way to Happiness: "Do not murder," "honor and help your parents."
frames.concerns: Constant killing by heroes and villains.

frames.aligns: Shows how poverty and abuse can shape harm (Dio's childhood); cross-class friendship; animal cruelty condemned.
frames.concerns: A passive love interest and "bad or non-existent" female roles (ComicsAlliance via Wikipedia); a Chinese character with stereotyped looks and accent (jojowiki); an aristocratic gentleman ideal; Anime Feminist on DIO as a predatory-queer-villain trope (franchise-wide).

frames.aligns: Araki's stated theme: an "affirmation that humanity is wonderful" (Wikipedia) and people who win "without relying on machines and divine beings" (ANN). Human courage, learning and solidarity defeat a man who rejects humanity.
frames.concerns: Supernatural horror as fiction; prophecy accepted as true (ch. 34).

frames.aligns: The gentleman ideal, honor, duty to father and family, marriage, courage, legacy through children, and a clear moral order.
frames.concerns: Gore and animal cruelty for younger readers.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth (Speedwagon, the orphaned baby); compassion even for an enemy.
frames.concerns: Violence; a stereotyped character; a born-evil framing of Dio by some characters.

frames.aligns: Individual will and ambition are explored; the Satanic Temple's compassion tenet and the Church of Satan's Eleven Rules on harming animals both side against Dio's cruelty.
frames.concerns: Self-sacrifice for others is the story's highest value, which Church of Satan writings question; Dio's self-deification is punished.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Jonathan fights "to reclaim Erina's honor" (ch. 4); the gentleman's code (ch. 1); George's debt of honor to Dario (Wikipedia).

Order vs freedom.evidence: The ideal is an orderly gentleman's life; Dio's threat is lawless domination.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Family, lineage and personal loyalty drive the plot (ch. 11, 44); institutions barely appear.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: A landed-gentry ideal and master-disciple ranks (Zeppeli, Tonpetty), softened by Speedwagon's cross-class friendship.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Traditional code, marriage and inheritance celebrated; little religion shown.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival, duty and endurance over self-expression.

folkways.japan: The teacher-disciple bond, the debt of gratitude (on) that binds George to Dario and Speedwagon to Jonathan, and the acceptance of a foretold death (ch. 34) reflect Japanese norms as much as the story's English setting. The "gentleman" is a Japanese 1980s image of the English ideal, filtered through Western films that Araki cites (Wikipedia).

delivery.evidence: Araki calls Jonathan and Dio "good and evil, white and black"; Zeppeli states the moral aloud ("A hymn to humanity is a hymn to courage!").
delivery.note: The moral is spoken directly by heroes and mentors, while the villain gets a real backstory and charisma but no argument the story takes seriously.

personified.ideology: Ambition and domination; transcend humanity by any means
Gentleman's honor and self-sacrifice
Courage as mastering fear; humanity worth praising
Loyalty and honor across class

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (affirmed), Traditionalism (affirmed), Secular humanism (affirmed, per Araki), Might makes right and Transhumanism (critiqued through Dio).

series.title: The Eminence in Shadow
series.native: 陰の実力者になりたくて！

entry.heading: The Eminence in Shadow
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life, as Cid lives it, is pursuing your own dream with total dedication and on your own terms, whatever others think; the story also invites readers to laugh at how self-absorbed that dream is, while his followers find meaning in loyalty and in a cause bigger than themselves.

content.frequency: Frequent; nearly every volume has killing
content.framing: Mostly Endorsed or Neutral (Cid's and Shadow Garden's killings are played as cool or comic); Condemned for the Cult

frames.aligns: Real evil (the Cult's experiments on the sick, a plot to make itself immortal) is framed as evil and defeated; care for outcasts (the possessed girls); Cid protects his sister.
frames.concerns: Killing treated as sport and comedy (bandits, v1 and v7) makes violence attractive (Inter Mirifica 7); vengeance and private justice instead of legitimate authority (CCC 2263-2265, 2302); habitual lying; the Church shown as complicit; fan service against modesty (CCC 2521-2524); a suicide attempt (v6) shown as a dramatic beat.

frames.aligns: The demon Diablos and the Cult are enemies, not heroes; Aurora's suffering is met with compassion.
frames.concerns: Watchfulness (nepsis) over what one looks at: steady violence and fan service. Pride (Cid's craving to be the secret star) is the engine of the story and is played for laughs rather than repented of. A holy site and church tied to demonic power.

frames.aligns: Evil cult defeated; protection of the weak and of family.
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 test: casual killing, lies played as jokes, fan service, a church shown as corrupt. Soul liberty: each family decides.

frames.aligns: Depicting sin is not endorsing it, for many families; the story pokes fun at its hero's self-importance.
frames.concerns: Here the hero's vanity is also the source of his success; killing is part of the joke; the harem setup.

frames.aligns: The demonic (Diablos and his cult) is the enemy and is opposed.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": demon-cult, possession, a sacred site resting on a demon's arm, magic throughout, a witch's spirit living inside Claire (v8). Views vary by church.

frames.aligns: Common grace: discipline, craft, the folly of pride exposed by comedy (Proverbs 26).
frames.concerns: Private vengeance without lawful authority; lies; Westminster Larger Catechism Q139 concerns on lascivious pictures (fan service); church as complicit.

frames.aligns: Evil cult opposed; Cid's devotion to his sister; humor as adiaphora.
frames.concerns: Killing for sport; lying; fan service. LCMS and WELS families tend to be more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Rescue and healing of the outcast and sick (the possessed girls).
frames.concerns: Wesley's caution against diversions that cannot be used "in the name of the Lord Jesus": violence as fun, vanity, fan service. Holiness churches are stricter than UMC.

frames.aligns: A comic fantasy in which hidden evil is exposed; imaginative tradition (Lewis).
frames.concerns: How good and evil are framed: the hero is morally blank and the story rarely questions him.

frames.aligns: Rescue of outcasts; humility as an outward act (Cid as "background character").
frames.concerns: Violence shown as heroic and fun is the central concern, and here it is the main attraction (bandit-slaying, one-blow victories). Conservative groups avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Discipline and hard work; protecting family; evil cult defeated.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth asks whether media invites the Spirit: casual killing, lies, fan service, a suicide attempt. Members vary in strictness.

frames.aligns: Exposure of corrupt nobles and religious officials; care for the sick and outcast.
frames.concerns: Women as an adoring harem (Anime Feminist); fan service; vigilante violence.
"By beholding we become changed": violence as fun, fan service, spirits living in bodies (Aurora in Claire), conflicting with teaching on the state of the dead.

frames.aligns: Opposition to a cult and its immortality scheme.
frames.concerns: jw.org's questions on violence (Psalm 11:5) and spiritism (Galatians 5:19-21): killing is the hero's sport, and magic, demons and possession are everywhere; religious leaders shown as corrupt.

frames.aligns: The story mocks fear-mongering: Cid's invented threats are a game to him.
frames.concerns: Evil, disease (possession) and death shown as powerful and real; constant fear and violence.

frames.aligns: Exposure of hidden wrongdoing; saving the sick.
frames.concerns: Killing beyond self-defense (the law of the pursuer, rodef, ends when the threat ends); deception as a way of life; fan service and tzniut. Many Haredi homes restrict such media.

frames.aligns: Justice against hidden oppressors; protection of family.
frames.concerns: Vigilante killing and deception played for laughs; fan service.

frames.aligns: Exposure of corruption; rescuing the marginalized.
frames.concerns: Women as an adoring group around one man; vigilante justice.

frames.aligns: Opposition to injustice and to a demon-worshipping cult; loyalty; protecting family.
frames.concerns: Killing without just cause or due process; magic and spirits; fan service and lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31); a suicide attempt.

frames.aligns: Discipline (tapas) and dedication; good defeating demonic (asuric) forces.
frames.concerns: Ego (ahamkara) as the hero's motive; killing for sport; tamasic violence in Gita 17 terms.

frames.aligns: Discipline; rescue of the suffering; the comedy of a self that is only a role.
frames.concerns: Attachment to self-image is the hero's whole drive; killing breaks the first precept; no karmic reckoning.

frames.aligns: Defense of the oppressed against a cult; saint-soldier courage.
frames.concerns: Ego (ahankar) and anger (krodh) as admired traits; killing for sport.

frames.aligns: Exposure of corruption; rescue of outcasts.
frames.concerns: Secret violence instead of consultation and justice; fan service against a "chaste and holy life."

frames.aligns: Purity and sincerity valued by the heroines; spirits in the world.
frames.concerns: Blood and death (kegare) everywhere; insincerity (Cid's constant pretense) is the hero's method.

frames.aligns: Magic treated as natural; the "Witch of Calamity" Aurora is shown as a wronged woman, not a villain (v5); no stereotyping of witches.
frames.concerns: "Harm none": killing for practice and sport.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness: be industrious; the evil cult exposed.
frames.concerns: "Do not murder" and "Be worthy of trust" against Cid's habits.

frames.aligns: Corrupt nobles, churchmen and financiers exposed; outcast girls rescued.
frames.concerns: Anime Feminist (anime ep. 1): "sleazy, exploitative," "a ready-made harem of women ready to coo over his brilliance"; fan service; vigilante violence; Common Sense Media's sexual-assault content (anime).

frames.aligns: Reason and planning win (the counterfeit economic plot, v9-10); superstition and cult belief exposed; magic read as fiction.
frames.concerns: Cruelty played for laughs; no accountability; the hero lacks empathy (Silverman's "red flags").

frames.aligns: Discipline, family loyalty (Claire), defeat of a subversive cabal; dislike of corrupt elites.
frames.concerns: Self-glory as the hero's goal; vigilante killing; fan service; religion shown as compromised.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of the sick and outcast (the possessed girls); exposure of injustice.
frames.concerns: Worth of the bandits and enemies ignored; women as devotees; fan service.

frames.aligns: Self-determination and living by one's own will (Aizawa: Cid "stays true to his own dreams"); rejection of a corrupt church; mockery of grandiose pretension.
frames.concerns: The Satanic Temple's Tenets on compassion and justice weigh against killing for sport.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Justice is personal: Shadow kills the Cult's agents himself (Zenon v2, Lutheran v4, Crimson v8, Gettan v10); courts and knights are corrupt or absent.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Cid lives outside every rule and relishes a lawless city (v7); his order (Shadow Garden) has internal ranks, but the hero answers to no one.

Civic vs kin.evidence: He protects his sister Claire (v1, v15) and his own followers; he also rescues strangers (Yukime, Rose, a tavern girl, v10).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Shadow Garden is a ranked order revering one leader; royalty and nobility shape every arc.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Old institutions (church, crown) are compromised; Cid's modern-world knowledge and economic planning win (v9-10); magic and goddess-lore remain part of the world.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: The hero's whole life is self-expression and play; survival stakes are real for others.

folkways.japan: The chūnibyō ("eighth-grade syndrome") joke, the "mob character" (background extra) ideal of not standing out, and the isekai truck-death opening are Japanese pop-culture conventions; the ideal of quiet ordinariness reflects a Japanese norm of not drawing attention to oneself, which the story turns into comedy.

delivery.evidence: Reviewers read it as comic satire of chūnibyō power fantasies; Anime Café says it "became the anime it was trying to make fun of."
delivery.note: The story states almost no message aloud; its view emerges from the gap between Cid's narration and what really happens around him.

personified.ideology: Self-made identity; living one's fantasy whatever the cost
Loyal devotion to a leader and a cause

personified.character: The Cult of Diablos (Zenon and the Rounds)
personified.ideology: Power and immortality at others' expense

entry.dominant: Expressive individualism, Might makes right, Postmodernism (my framing), Pagan/occult.

entry.heading: Food Wars!: Shokugeki no Soma
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is spent getting better at a craft you love by cooking for real people, failing, learning from rivals and trying again. No one has the right to impose one "correct" taste on everyone else.

frames.aligns: Work as a vocation; humility and learning from failure; an abusive father is condemned and later reconciled; food as hospitality.
frames.concerns: Sexualized reactions of minors played as comedy, against the call for media that respects human dignity (Inter Mirifica 7; CCC 2523-2524 on modesty and permissiveness).

frames.aligns: Struggle against pride and gluttony-like craving (Azami's "True Gourmet," Erina's arrogance); reconciliation in the family.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis): repeated sensual imagery is the central concern. Pleasure in food shown as ecstasy can read as praise of the passions.

frames.aligns: Hard work, honesty, standing against corruption (Eizan) and abuse (Azami).
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 test fails on the fan service; immodest images of teens. Each family decides (soul liberty).

frames.aligns: Soma's identity rests on serving people, not winning; Beneath the Tangles links this to 2 Corinthians 12:9 ("power is perfected in weakness").
frames.concerns: Romans 14 freedom versus stumbling: the fan service is the main issue; "only the strong survive" ethos critiqued by the same writer.

frames.aligns: Clear moral arc against abusive control; perseverance.
frames.concerns: Holiness and modesty standards; sensual imagery as an "open door." No occult content, so the concern is moral, not spiritual.

frames.aligns: Common grace in craft and good food; vocation; exposure of pride.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 lists "lascivious... books, pictures" among sins against the seventh commandment; the reaction pages fit that concern.

frames.aligns: Vocation (Beruf): cooking for customers as service to neighbor; law and gospel echoes in failure and growth.
frames.concerns: Fan service; LCMS and WELS families usually more cautious than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Discipline, method and practice; social holiness in cooking for ordinary people.
frames.concerns: Wesley's rule against diversions that cannot be used "in the name of the Lord Jesus"; holiness churches would weigh the fan service heavily; UMC families vary.

frames.aligns: Imagination and craft valued; good and evil clearly framed in the Central arc.
frames.concerns: Fan service; the epilogue's half-sibling plot. Practice ranges widely.

frames.aligns: Nonviolent conflict: disputes are settled by cooking, not force; humility and community (Polar Star).
frames.concerns: Separation from worldly media; immodest imagery; competition and pride as a way of life.
For the Strength of Youth: entertainment that invites the Spirit; immodest imagery and sensual reactions conflict with that standard.

frames.aligns: Critique of elitism and gatekeeping; standing against an abusive parent and a controlling institution.
frames.concerns: How women are drawn (Anime Feminist); sexualized minors; the abuser's late sympathy.

frames.aligns: Diligence, health-adjacent interest in food, family.
frames.concerns: Fundamental Belief 22 and "by beholding we become changed"; the sensual reaction pages; heavy meat and alcohol in cooking may matter for some families (from general knowledge; to verify).

frames.aligns: Hard work, honesty, no spiritism or violence.
frames.concerns: "Uncleanness" and immorality (Galatians 5:19-21) in the reaction pages; immodest dress.

frames.aligns: Little fear or disease imagery; growth through effort; love outlasts an abusive father's control.
frames.concerns: Sensual imagery as a mental influence; Mana's "curse" of being unable to enjoy food.

frames.aligns: Diligence, honoring parents with limits (an abusive father opposed), community.
frames.concerns: Tzniut: frequent immodest imagery; many Haredi homes would not allow it. Non-kosher cooking throughout is setting, not message.

frames.aligns: Learning from failure; hospitality; justice against abusive authority.
frames.concerns: Modesty values applied by families; the fan service.

frames.aligns: Critique of elitism; standing up to unjust power; growth.
