frames.concerns: Sexualization of teenage characters; gender roles (Anime Feminist).

frames.aligns: Hard work, patience (sabr), justice against oppression, family reconciliation.
frames.concerns: Lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31): frequent immodest imagery. Pork and alcohol in cooking are part of the setting.

frames.aligns: Karma yoga echoes: dedicated work; guru-disciple learning; food as offering and hospitality.
frames.concerns: Some apply the Gita's rajasic and tamasic categories to sensual media; beef dishes may matter to some families.

frames.aligns: Learning from failure; non-attachment to winning is partly echoed (Soma's ease with losing).
frames.concerns: Craving for sensual pleasure drawn as ecstasy; the eight precepts' caution about shows.

frames.aligns: Seva-like service in cooking for others; langar echoes in the diner's hospitality; honest work (kirat karni).
frames.concerns: Lust (kaam), one of the five vices, played for laughs in the reaction pages.

frames.aligns: Work as worship when done in service; unity and friendship.
frames.concerns: "Chaste and holy life" counsel warns against degrading entertainment; the fan service.

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) in craft, gratitude for food, purity of ingredients.
frames.concerns: Little to raise in message; no disrespect to shrines or kami reported.

frames.aligns: Joy in the senses and the harvest; "harm none" in a story without violence.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; some may discuss consent in the reaction gags.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness: be industrious, be competent, honor parents (with limits), do not harm.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; the series has no psychiatry theme.

frames.aligns: Anti-elitism, critique of authoritarian control, women as major rivals.
frames.concerns: Sexualization of minors as comedy; women as reactors (Anime Feminist); Kotaku's "breast-to-food quotient"; the late sympathy for an abuser; the half-sibling marriage plot (ANN).

frames.aligns: Experiment, curiosity and learning from failure; freedom of inquiry against Central's single "truth."
frames.concerns: Objectification as comedy; the abuse arc's late sympathy.

frames.aligns: Hard work, small family business, merit, resisting central control; respect for craft and lineage.
frames.concerns: The fan service cuts against "the good, the true and the beautiful"; the incest-adjacent epilogue.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth (diner food is as worthy as elite cuisine); free search for truth versus Central.
frames.concerns: Stereotyped and sexualized depictions of girls.

frames.aligns: Individual excellence, defiance of illegitimate authority (Rebels against Azami), sensual pleasure without shame.
frames.concerns: Harm to children: Azami's abuse is condemned, which fits; sexualized minors may concern The Satanic Temple's tenets on bodily autonomy.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Formal duels settle disputes and pride is at stake in every shokugeki, but they follow rules and judges, and Soma takes losses lightly (ch. 274-275, Asahi's first win).

Order vs freedom.evidence: The free research societies and personal cooking styles are celebrated; Azami's enforced menu (Central, ch. 137-146 likely) is overthrown.

Civic vs kin.evidence: The family diner and the Nakiri family matter, but much of the loyalty is to the dorm and the Rebels, a chosen community.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: A commoner rises against elite gatekeeping, but the Elite Ten ranking remains and Soma ends as 1st seat; merit-based hierarchy, not birth.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No religion; innovation and testing beat fixed rules; Azami's "purity" is rejected.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: The dish should express the chef ("One's Own Taste," ch. 312, v36 likely); hard training and the 10% graduation rate keep a strong effort theme.

folkways.japan: The school's seniority, club culture, ranking lists and the shopping-street family diner reflect Japanese school and small-business norms; the honorific address and the formality of duels are setting more than message.

delivery.evidence: Dupree (ANN): Food Wars "evangelized how important a chef's personality is"; Central's members underdeveloped. No review in the entry calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The message about cooking for others and learning from failure is spoken by Soma and Joichiro and shown through duel outcomes, while the opposing elitist view gets a late sympathetic backstory but little development.

personified.ideology: Cooking for real customers; learning from failure
One enforced "True Gourmet" standard from the top
Elite palate that learns openness
Take others' skills; win at all costs

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Expressive individualism, Hedonism, Pragmatism; Collectivism/authoritarianism as the critiqued opposite.

series.title: Mushoku Tensei: Jobless Reincarnation
series.romaji: Mushoku Tensei: Isekai Ittara Honki Dasu
series.native: 無職転生 ～異世界行ったら本気だす～
series.warning: Sources document sexual misconduct by the protagonist toward child and teen characters, often played for comedy.

entry.heading: Mushoku Tensei: Jobless Reincarnation
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is a second chance taken seriously: face the fears and shame of a wasted past, work hard, protect and rebuild your family, and keep going after failure. The story says "everybody can make mistakes" (Wikipedia's summary of the author's message), but it gives little weight to the harm its hero's sexual misconduct does to others.

content.framing: Mixed: played as comedy early; the attempted assault on Eris is rebuffed; the sex scene is framed as romance; critics say there are few consequences

frames.aligns: A second chance and conversion of life; honoring parents; the dignity of the bullied and outcast (Ruijerd, Sylphie).
frames.concerns: Inter Mirifica 7: evil should not be made attractive, yet lust toward children is played as comedy; chastity (CCC 2337-2359); polygamy (CCC 2387); slavery left unexamined (CCC 2414).

frames.aligns: Struggle with the passions; reconciliation of father and son.
frames.concerns: Nepsis: the art invites the reader to look at children and teens through the hero's lust; a "god" speaking in dreams treated as normal; Roxy "worship" and a "Divine Artifact" gag.

frames.aligns: Redemption premise; hard work; family love.
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 fails on many pages; sexual misconduct toward minors is played for laughs; plural marriage. Families decide under soul liberty.

frames.aligns: A wasted life given a second chance; a shut-in who learns to go outside; a father and son reconciled.
frames.concerns: Depicting versus endorsing: the story itself depicts and often laughs; critics say the victims forgive with no repair (Anime Feminist).

frames.aligns: Overcoming fear and bondage to the past.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": a spirit-being directing a man through dreams; occult-style magic; lust as humor.

frames.aligns: Common grace in craft and family love; sin's lasting effects on a life.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 lists "lascivious... books, pictures" among sins against the seventh commandment; the series is a test case. Polygamy.

frames.aligns: Honoring father and mother (Fourth Commandment); vocation in study and family.
frames.concerns: Sixth Commandment: "lead a sexually pure and decent life"; humor at the expense of the neighbor. LCMS and WELS families stricter than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Growth and second chances; works of care for family.
frames.concerns: Wesley's rule against books that do not "tend to the knowledge or love of God"; "do no harm" is breached and joked about. UMC families vary.

frames.aligns: Judged by framing: the redemption arc and family love are real.
frames.concerns: The framing of the misconduct as comic; teen sex scene; polygamy. Episcopal and ACNA families weigh these differently.

frames.aligns: Humility learned; Ruijerd's protection of children; community and family.
frames.concerns: Separation from worldly media; lust and immodesty throughout; violence as the path to strength. MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Eternal-family echoes; a second chance; honoring parents.
frames.concerns: The law of chastity; For the Strength of Youth asks for media that invites the Spirit; plural marriage, which the Church no longer practices.

frames.aligns: Care for the bullied and the racially stigmatized (Ruijerd, Sylphie).
frames.concerns: Consent and the sexualization of children; victims made into partners; slavery shrugged off.
Fundamental Belief 22 on choosing pure entertainment; "by beholding we become changed" (2 Corinthians 3:18); spirit messages in dreams.
jw.org's test: immorality, violence and spiritism (Galatians 5:19-21) all present; magic is central.
Dwelling on lust and fear runs against "stand porter at the door of thought" (Science and Health 392).

frames.aligns: Honoring parents (Exodus 20:12); teshuvah as a theme.
frames.concerns: Tzniut and shemirat einayim: the content conflicts throughout; misconduct toward children; many Haredi homes would not have it.

frames.aligns: Teshuvah; family; resisting prejudice against an outcast people.
frames.concerns: Sexualization of minors; lashon hara-like mockery as humor.

frames.aligns: A second chance; standing against ethnic stigma (the Superd).
frames.concerns: Consent and harm to children; slavery left unexamined.

frames.aligns: Family duty; patience; plural marriage with the first wife's knowledge has a partial parallel.
frames.concerns: Lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31): the hero's gaze is the story's lens; sex outside marriage (zina); magic. Polygamy in Islam is conditioned on justice and marriage, not affairs.

frames.aligns: Reincarnation as a second chance; duty to family and teachers (Roxy as guru).
frames.concerns: Kama without dharma; the Gita's tamasic category for degrading content; rebirth without karmic moral weight.

frames.aligns: Rebirth; suffering rooted in a wasted life; right effort.
frames.concerns: Craving (tanha) is indulged and laughed at rather than seen as a cause of suffering; the third precept on sexual misconduct.

frames.aligns: Hard work, family, protection of the weak (Ruijerd).
frames.concerns: Lust (kaam), first of the five vices, is played as comic and largely unpunished.
Shoghi Effendi's call to a "chaste and holy life" (to verify wording); sex outside marriage; polygamy (prohibited for Bahá'ís).

frames.aligns: Sincerity and gratitude toward teachers; family continuity.
frames.concerns: Little on the sacred; the lack of sincerity (makoto) in the hero's early conduct; impurity themes.

frames.aligns: Magic as a craft learned through study; respect for a "demon" people.
frames.concerns: "Harm none": consent violations played for laughs.

frames.aligns: Self-improvement; The Way to Happiness precepts on honoring parents and industriousness.
frames.concerns: Precepts on being faithful to a sexual partner and not harming people of good will.

frames.aligns: Anti-bullying; racial prejudice condemned; a man working through trauma.
frames.concerns: Consent and sexualization of minors are the central concern: Anime Feminist says the story treats molesting and grooming as forgivable; Kotaku calls Rudeus a "groomer." Slavery shrugged off.

frames.aligns: Human growth without supernatural help; education; a deceptive "god" exposed.
frames.concerns: Cruelty and exploitation (slavery, molestation) treated lightly; the story's moral accounting is uneven.

frames.aligns: Family, hard work, honoring parents, a man growing up into responsibility as husband and father.
frames.concerns: Sexual immorality toward minors as comedy; polygamy; the hero's shut-in past.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of outcasts (Ruijerd, Sylphie); the free search for meaning.
Self-improvement and pursuit of one's desires; skepticism toward a manipulative god.
frames.concerns: The Eleven Rules forbid harming little children, and the Satanic Temple's tenets stress bodily autonomy; both are breached by the hero.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Swordsmanship and personal strength confer standing; Eris answers insult with her fists; Ruijerd's quest is to restore his people's honor (Wikipedia). Disputes are mostly settled by force, not courts.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Adventurers live by guild rules but mostly as free agents; Paul walks away from his noble house (Wikipedia).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Family is the center: the search for the scattered Greyrats after the disaster (vols. 3-10), Rudeus raising his sisters (ch. 87 onward, likely), and the household as the story's goal.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Noble houses and power rankings matter (Boreas family, Sword God, Dragon God), but the hero rises by talent, and Paul rejects rank.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Magic is learned like a science and Rudeus applies modern knowledge; religion is distrusted (the Man-God, Millis factions), though family custom is honored.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Much of the story is survival, work and saving money on a hostile continent; later volumes turn to domestic life and the hero's own pleasures.

folkways.japan: The hikikomori shut-in, school bullying, the reincarnation-isekai frame and the web-novel ranking culture (Shōsetsuka ni Narō) are Japanese contexts; the adult-mind-in-child-body sexual comedy is a known genre convention that Japanese and Western critics alike have questioned (Real Sound via Wikipedia; Anime Feminist).

delivery.evidence: Rudeus's narration states his resolve to live seriously; ScreenWise says the show "doesn't always excuse his behavior." No review found calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its message about second chances runs through Rudeus's inner monologue, while the harm he does to others is often left to comedy or quick forgiveness.

personified.ideology: Self-improvement and second chances
Fatherhood that recovers from failure
Honor and protecting children against prejudice
A deity who manipulates people for his own ends

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Hedonism, Pragmatism, Classical virtue ethics, Traditionalism. (Labels are my own framing unless a source is named.)

entry.heading: The Apothecary Diaries
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is a useful one: notice what is true, learn your craft, help the people in front of you, and keep your own mind free even when your body is not. Knowledge and quiet competence protect the vulnerable better than rank, rumor or superstition.

content.frequency: Frequent (as plot), brief on the page

content.framing: Neutral to endorsed (as medicine); harmful use shown with consequences

frames.aligns: Evil (poisoning, the late emperor's abuse of girls) is exposed, not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7); care for the sick and the poor; human dignity of servants and courtesans; the leads' "high regard for chastity" (traditional Catholic reviewer).
frames.concerns: Concubinage and a brothel are the normal setting and sex work is shown without moral judgment; drug self-testing (CCC 2290-2291).

frames.aligns: Exposure of hidden sin and corruption; humility and service in Maomao; mercy toward the sick.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis): innuendo, the brothel and court sensuality run throughout; no transcendent horizon.

frames.aligns: Clear exposure of wrongdoing; honesty; hard work; a heroine who refuses to be used.
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 test for the red-light setting and innuendo; alcohol and drug use. Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Depicts sin without endorsing it; justice for victims; compassion for the low-born.
frames.concerns: Sex work treated as ordinary labor (Common Sense Media) conflicts with biblical sexual ethics; Maomao's self-poisoning.

frames.aligns: Little occult content: ghosts and curses are usually explained away.
frames.concerns: Holiness standards: brothel setting, aphrodisiacs, innuendo. Views range between churches.

frames.aligns: Common grace: a careful, truth-seeking non-Christian work; total depravity echoed in court intrigue; justice served.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 ("lascivious... books, pictures") and the brothel setting; the court's sexual politics.

frames.aligns: Vocation (Maomao serves through her craft); lawful authority bears responsibility and is judged when it abuses power; adiaphora judged by conscience.
frames.concerns: Innuendo and substances; LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy: medicine for courtesans and the poor (ch. 49 "The Clinic," likely); honesty.
frames.concerns: Wesley's General Rules on diversions; alcohol and drug content. Holiness churches more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: Judged by framing: wrongdoing is exposed, the vulnerable are protected; a strong literary mystery tradition (Sayers).
frames.concerns: Innuendo and brothel setting; practice ranges from progressive to conservative.

frames.aligns: Little heroic violence; humility, simple service and care for the sick; suspicion of worldly power and luxury.
frames.concerns: Separation from the world: court luxury, sexual politics, alcohol; conservative groups avoid popular media; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Honesty, service, learning, chastity valued by the heroine.
frames.concerns: Word of Wisdom: frequent alcohol, tobacco and drug use; innuendo. For the Strength of Youth principles; members vary.

frames.aligns: Attention to the vulnerable: kidnapped servants, sex workers, discarded consorts (Anime Feminist); structural critique of court patriarchy.
frames.concerns: The male lead's pursuit of Maomao and power imbalance (FandomWire debate).

frames.aligns: Health and medicine valued; poisoners exposed; honesty.
frames.concerns: Alcohol, tobacco and drugs are frequent; Ellen White's caution about fiction that excites the passions; brothel setting.

frames.aligns: Spiritism is mostly absent or debunked; violence is not glorified; wrongdoers are exposed.
frames.concerns: Immorality (Galatians 5:19-21): concubinage and brothel setting; alcohol.

frames.aligns: Thought and attention as tools; calm, clear reasoning against fear and rumor.
frames.concerns: The story's answer to every illness is material medicine and chemistry, the opposite of healing through spiritual understanding; disease and poison are vividly real.

frames.aligns: Pursuit of truth and justice; care for the sick (pikuach nefesh echoes); exposure of a predatory ruler.
frames.concerns: Tzniut: brothel setting, innuendo, concubinage; many Haredi homes restrict such media altogether.

frames.aligns: Learning, healing, justice, the dignity of the low-born.
frames.concerns: Modesty values applied by families to the brothel setting and innuendo.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam echoes in protecting the vulnerable; informed autonomy; no antisemitic content reported.
frames.concerns: Power imbalance in the central romance; substances.

frames.aligns: Seeking knowledge and medicine (valued in Islamic tradition); justice against oppressors; the heroine's chastity.
frames.concerns: Alcohol and intoxicants (forbidden); lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) for the brothel and bath scenes; concubinage shown as normal.

frames.aligns: Ayurveda-like respect for plants and healing; dharma of one's role (Maomao's craft, Jinshi's duty); karma-like consequences for wrongdoers.
Compassion for the suffering; clear seeing against delusion and rumor; non-attachment to status.
frames.concerns: Fifth precept (intoxicants): drinking and Maomao's attachment to tasting poisons.

frames.aligns: Honest work (kirat karni), service to the sick, the vices of lust, greed and ego shown in the court and condemned.
frames.concerns: Alcohol and tobacco are forbidden for initiated Sikhs; brothel setting.

frames.aligns: Science and reason in harmony with the good; service; the equality of women and men as a hope.
frames.concerns: Alcohol and drugs (prohibited); a "chaste and holy life" and the brothel setting.

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto), purity and gratitude in care for others; rites shown without mockery.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; the court is Chinese-inspired, not Shinto.

frames.aligns: A respected herbalist "wise woman" figure; plant lore treated as real knowledge; "harm none" echoed in healing.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; Maomao's poison obsession shades into harm to herself.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness: "be temperate," "do not murder," honor and help others; poisoners condemned.
Women's survival inside patriarchy and class (Anime Feminist); sex workers shown with dignity; predatory power exposed.
frames.concerns: Debate over Jinshi's physical pursuit of Maomao and her youthful design (FandomWire); the system is survived rather than changed (Anime Feminist reading).

frames.aligns: Empiricism and skepticism: curses and ghosts are explained by lead, arsenic and human schemes; medicine and reason save lives.
frames.concerns: Self-experimentation with poisons needs real-world framing.

frames.aligns: Duty, loyalty (Gaoshun), competence, respect for elders (Luomen), chastity valued, order restored after rebellion.
frames.concerns: Sex work presented without moral judgment; skepticism of authority's virtue; the heroine's independence from marriage.

frames.aligns: Worth and dignity of servants and sex workers; free search for truth; justice.
frames.concerns: Power imbalance in the romance; substances.

frames.aligns: Skeptical, self-reliant heroine; reason over superstition; harm to children condemned (the late emperor).
frames.concerns: Deference to imperial hierarchy as the frame the heroes work within.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Face and reputation matter in court (consorts' rivalry, ch. 6-10), but the story celebrates truth-finding over avenging insults; Maomao ignores slights and avoids credit.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Court order is accepted and restored after the Shi rebellion (ch. 77-81), while Maomao's longing for freedom from servitude is sympathetic.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Found family (Luomen, the Verdigris House) matters deeply; birth kin (Lakan) is held at arm's length; service to the state drives Jinshi.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Hierarchy is the world's fact and is mostly respected, but a commoner earns respect by skill, and abuses of rank are exposed (ch. 55-58).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Rites are kept, but the story's heart is empirical: curses and ghosts are explained by chemistry and human schemes (ch. 1, 56-59, 67).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival in a harsh, unequal world comes first (kidnapping, trafficking, disease), though Maomao's quirky passions are celebrated.

folkways.japan: The setting borrows Chinese imperial institutions (the inner court, eunuchs, rites) seen through Japanese popular fiction; Hyūganatsu says she added "Japanese sensibilities." Workplace diligence, discretion and acceptance of rank reflect Japanese norms as much as the story's own message.

delivery.evidence: Reviews praise nuance; Anime Feminist calls its sex-work portrayal "arguably one of the best." No opened review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its views on women's lot, reason and power come through Maomao's dry inner monologue and the outcomes of each case rather than speeches.

personified.ideology: Empirical reason and self-reliance
Duty to the throne over personal desire
Genius that ignores social rules
A survivor hardened by an abusive system

entry.dominant: Pragmatism, Naturalism (empiricism), Secular humanism, Feminism, Classical virtue ethics, Confucian ethics.

series.title: Akira
series.adult_reason: Akira: Kodansha USA rates the 2009 paperback volumes and the 2017 35th Anniversary box set 18+ (the 2025 Hardcover Collection is listed 16+); deep entry scores 9 (violence), teen drug use, sexual captivity and attempted rape involving teen characters
series.warning: Includes sexual violence involving teenage characters.

entry.heading: Akira
entry.label: From summaries

content.framing: Shown with consequences (Tetsuo's captives); Neutral (Kaneda's early behavior)

frames.aligns: Evil is not made attractive: tyranny, drug control and experiments on children end in ruin (Inter Mirifica 7). Dignity of the vulnerable (the Espers). A Catholic writer, Philip Kosloski, found in the film "a divinity engaged in a real, messy world."
frames.concerns: No moral law or God; spirit mediumship shown positively (CCC 2116-2117); the hero's sexual exploitation is not clearly judged; sexual violence toward teen characters.

frames.aligns: The passions (pride, rage, lust) grow monstrous in Tetsuo, shown literally as his body mutates.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis) makes gore, drugs and sexual exploitation a strong concern; a worshipped child-emperor and mediumship.

frames.aligns: Corruption and pride are shown failing; drug dependence has costs.
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 test fails on violence, drugs and sexual content; spiritism (Kei as medium); no gospel or moral anchor. Each church decides; many families would avoid.

frames.aligns: Depicts sin without endorsing it; false religion (the drugged cult) is exposed; human power cannot save.
frames.concerns: The hero's early predation; mediumship and psychic power as salvation; no grace or redemption beyond human friendship.
Media as an "open door": spirit mediumship, precognition and meditation-based psychic power shown as good and decisive; a cult worshipping a child as divine; drugs. Views vary by church.

frames.aligns: Total depravity has an echo: power in human hands destroys. Common grace lets families value influential art.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 ("lascivious... books, pictures") for the sexual content; a child worshipped as emperor; no providence.

frames.aligns: Two kingdoms: rulers without justice become destroyers; the story shows what happens when authority fails. Entertainment as adiaphora judged by conscience.
frames.concerns: Violence, drugs and sexual exploitation; mediumship. LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Social holiness: exploitation of children and the poor is condemned by its results.
frames.concerns: Wesley's rule on books that do not tend to "the knowledge or love of God"; drugs and sexual content. Holiness churches more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: Judged by framing in the Lewis and Sayers literary tradition: power, pride and cults are framed as destructive; the Colonel atones.
frames.concerns: The hero's exploitation of women is not clearly judged; mediumship; drugs. Episcopal and ACNA families differ.

frames.aligns: Distrust of state and military power; the cost of violence shown on a massive scale.
frames.concerns: Violence is everywhere and the heroes fight with guns and bikes; separation from the world means conservative groups avoid it. MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Consequences of pride and drug use; friendship and community rebuilt.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth: does it invite the Spirit? Sexual content, drugs (Word of Wisdom) and gore weigh heavily.

frames.aligns: Critique of militarism, nuclear harm and state abuse of children; attention to the vulnerable (Espers).
frames.concerns: Treatment of women and sexual violence; the hero's predatory behavior (Loveridge, ANN).

frames.aligns: Drug dependence shown as destructive; pride brought low.
frames.concerns: "By beholding we become changed" (2 Corinthians 3:18) applied to gore and sexual content; Fundamental Belief 22; spiritism (mediumship) conflicts with teaching on the dead and spirits.

frames.aligns: Corrupt rulers and false worship fail.
frames.concerns: jw.org's test: violence (Psalm 11:5), immorality and spiritism (Galatians 5:19-21) are all central; Kei as a medium and Miyako's precognition are shown as good.
Matter, disease and destruction are shown as all-powerful; long body-horror passages.

frames.aligns: Protection of children and condemnation of those who experiment on them; idolatry (the Empire's worship) exposed.
frames.concerns: Tzniut and nivul peh make sexual content and language a concern; many Haredi homes restrict such media; mediumship (Deuteronomy 18:11).

frames.aligns: Critique of idolatry and abuse of power; the vulnerable defended.
Tikkun olam echoes in rebuilding after catastrophe; critique of militarism.
Tyranny and false worship (shirk) fail; intoxicants shown as destructive (Qur'an 5:90).
frames.concerns: Lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) for sexual content; drugs and alcohol; a child treated as divine; mediumship.

frames.aligns: Cosmic cycles of destruction and renewal echo in the ending; power without dharma destroys.
frames.concerns: Some families apply the Gita's tamasic category (chapter 17) to gore and intoxication.

frames.aligns: Craving and anger as the root of suffering (Tetsuo); meditation-trained monks (Miyako's temple); Thompson calls the ending "a moment of childhood Nirvana."
frames.concerns: Killing everywhere, against the first precept; intoxicants (fifth precept).

frames.aligns: The five vices (lust, anger, greed, attachment, ego) shown in Tetsuo and condemned by the outcome.
Critique of militarism and nuclear war; unity after catastrophe.
frames.concerns: The call to a "chaste and holy life"; drugs and alcohol forbidden; violence as normal.

frames.aligns: Sincerity and purity values are not mocked; a temple and spiritual discipline are respected.
frames.concerns: Blood and death as impurity throughout; little direct conflict.

frames.aligns: Spiritual practice (Miyako, Kei as medium) shown with respect; no stereotyping of witches or pagans.
The Way to Happiness precept against harmful drugs; government drugging and experiments on children framed as evil, in line with the Church's opposition to psychiatric control.
Anti-militarism, anti-nuclear and anti-authoritarian critique; abuse of children by the state condemned.
frames.concerns: The hero's sexual exploitation and treatment of Kei (Loveridge: "an irredeemably awful sexual predator"); sexual captivity and attempted rape of teen characters; women underused (MAL reviews).

frames.aligns: Free inquiry; distrust of pseudoscience-driven state programs; ordinary people rebuild without a god.
frames.concerns: Cruelty and exploitation shown at length; teen drug use.

frames.aligns: Corruption and tyranny exposed; the Colonel as an honorable soldier; the ending's stress on national sovereignty against foreign troops (EBSCO).
frames.concerns: Youth gangs, drugs and contempt for elders as the heroes' world; no family or faith anchor.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of the Espers and the vulnerable; justice against abusive power; free search for meaning.
frames.concerns: Sexual violence and treatment of women; violence as the default.

frames.aligns: Rebellion against corrupt authority is central; the Church of Satan's individualism echoes in the gang's self-rule.
frames.concerns: Harm to children (Eleven Rules) is extreme: the Espers' experiments, teen captives. The story condemns that harm.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Gang revenge and personal score-settling drive Kaneda (he seeks to end Tetsuo for Yamagata's murder, fan wiki; v1-2). Courts and rules play no role.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Biker freedom is the heroes' world; every attempt at order (military, parliament, Empire) fails (Thompson; Wikipedia).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Families are absent; loyalty goes to the gang and to chosen friends rather than to the city at large.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Rank is distrusted (Colonel, parliament, Tetsuo's Empire), though gangs keep leaders. The ending's self-governing state is youth-led.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Religious bodies are shown as manipulated (the drugged Empire) or mixed (Miyako), while science serving the state is also distrusted. Leans secular without trusting reason.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival in ruins dominates the second half; thrill-seeking self-expression dominates the first.

folkways.japan: The bosozoku biker gangs, the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, the 1960s student protests, the memory of Hiroshima and Nagasaki and the US military presence are Japanese postwar context (Loveridge; Gravett; Wikipedia), not a message aimed at other cultures.

delivery.evidence: Price (ANN): "an incredibly political – and an incredibly angry – work." No review found calls it preachy or its characters strawmen.
delivery.note: The story makes its case against controlling power through plot and catastrophe rather than speeches.

personified.ideology: Youthful freedom and loyalty against all control
Power as compensation; rule by force
State security and order
Spiritual leadership with mixed motives

entry.dominant: Collectivism / authoritarianism (critiqued), Might makes right (critiqued), Transhumanism (critiqued), Existentialism, Nihilism (explored).

entry.heading: All You Need Is Kill
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is earned through effort: you fail, learn and try again until you are strong enough to protect others. Love and comradeship give the struggle meaning, but victory may cost the person you love most, and the survivor must carry that cost forward.

content.framing: Neutral (war shown as tragic but necessary)
Shown with consequences (but one suicide test is played for laughs)

frames.aligns: Defense of others in a just cause (CCC 2265, 2309); self-giving love ("Greater love has no one than this," John 15:13, as Weber reads it); evil not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7).
frames.concerns: The gun-in-mouth test treats suicide lightly (CCC 2280-2283); a killing that both partners agree to is presented as the only way; heavy gore.

frames.aligns: Courage, endurance and self-sacrifice; grief shown honestly.
frames.concerns: Watchfulness over what one looks at (nepsis) weighs against hundreds of graphic deaths; killing even in war calls for repentance (St. Basil, canon 13), while Keiji's guilt has no outlet.

frames.aligns: Perseverance, protecting others, sacrifice; violence framed as tragic.
frames.concerns: Graphic violence and the crude nickname test Philippians 4:8; the suicide test is played for comedy. Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Weber, an evangelical apologist, reads it as a story about "our need for a savior" with "a whisper of John 15:13." Depicts war without glorying in it.
frames.concerns: Humanity saves itself through effort; no grace. Language and gore.

frames.aligns: Clear struggle against a destroying enemy; courage; no occult content.
frames.concerns: Graphic violence and the suicide gag; holiness standards on the nickname and fan service vary.

frames.aligns: Common grace: a well-built story about duty, vocation and sacrifice. The lawful sword against an aggressor.
frames.concerns: Self-murder (WLC Q136) used as an experiment; fatalism in the loop rather than providence.

frames.aligns: Vocation: the soldier's duty under lawful authority (two-kingdoms teaching); love of neighbor in protecting humanity.
frames.concerns: No gospel hope; confessional families may weigh the gore and the suicide gag more heavily.

frames.aligns: Growth through discipline, a picture of steady improvement; care for comrades.
frames.concerns: Holiness churches ask whether a book tends to the love of God; heavy violence; UMC peace emphasis.

frames.aligns: A literary tradition (Lewis, Sayers) that values imaginative war stories judged by their framing; sacrifice and grief taken seriously.
frames.concerns: The ending's logic of necessary killing; the light handling of suicide.

frames.aligns: Self-giving love; community of the squad; humility in Keiji's early fear.
frames.concerns: Violence shown as heroic is the central concern (nonresistance, Matthew 5:39); the whole story is training to kill better, and it ends with killing a loved one; conservative groups avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Defense in a just cause (Alma 43); perseverance; sacrifice for others.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth asks for entertainment that invites the Spirit; gore, the nickname and fan service weigh against that; the suicide test.

frames.aligns: A capable woman as the world's best soldier; grief and trauma taken seriously.
frames.concerns: Militarism and glorified competence in killing; the suicide gag; fan service.
"By beholding we become changed": constant gore and repeated death; historic noncombatant stance; the suicide gag.

frames.aligns: Love for comrades; no spiritism or magic.
frames.concerns: jw.org counsels avoiding entertainment that features violence (Psalm 11:5); the whole series centers on combat; political neutrality and no military service sit against a war hero story.

frames.aligns: Persistence against fear; Keiji's fear turns to courage.
frames.concerns: Repeated images of death, injury and fear are what members guard their thought against (Science and Health 392); death is made very real.

frames.aligns: Self-defense against an attacker is permitted; duty to protect life; mourning a friend.
frames.concerns: Haredi homes restrict secular media; the shower scene and fan service raise tzniut questions; the suicide test (suicide traditionally grave).

frames.aligns: Self-defense, courage, sacrifice; grief and memory.
frames.concerns: Gore and the light handling of suicide.

frames.aligns: Repairing the world through effort; a strong woman soldier.
Fighting only in a just, defensive cause; patience (sabr) and steadfastness; sacrifice for others.
frames.concerns: Suicide is forbidden and here is used as a test; immodest fan service and the shower scene for families who lower the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31); debates on images.

frames.aligns: Duty to fight in a righteous cause (Bhagavad Gita): Keiji, like Arjuna, must strike someone he loves for the greater good; effort without attachment.
frames.concerns: Ahimsa; rajasic and tamasic intensity in the gore.

frames.aligns: Repetition as a picture of samsara; letting go of fear; compassion to the dying (Rita's stories).
frames.concerns: First precept: violence creates suffering, and the story's only path is to kill better; no release except through killing.

frames.aligns: Defending the oppressed is righteous (Guru Gobind Singh); courage, discipline and service.
frames.concerns: Anger and ego in Keiji's berserk rampage; suicide test.

frames.aligns: Self-sacrifice for humanity; unity across nations in the army.
frames.concerns: Strong commitment to non-violence; the series is built on combat; suicide is forbidden.

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto), discipline and devotion to one's task; memory of the dead.
frames.concerns: Blood and death as impurity (kegare) throughout.

frames.aligns: Self-defense accepted; warrior virtues (Heathenry); the Valkyrie title.
frames.concerns: "Harm none" sits uneasily with the ending.

frames.aligns: Competence and industry (The Way to Happiness); persistence.
frames.concerns: "Do not murder" and concern about glorified violence.

frames.aligns: A small young woman as the best soldier; Rita's agency in choosing her own end; trauma taken seriously.
frames.concerns: Fan service of Rachel and the shower scene; a suicide method shown and played for laughs (safe-messaging guidelines); militarism; the crude nickname.

frames.aligns: Human effort, reason and learning from failure; meaning made in a single life; no supernatural rescue.
frames.concerns: Concern about glorified violence; the ending's "only way" logic, which critics dispute (Kotaku).

frames.aligns: Duty, discipline, courage, sacrifice, respect for rank and a sergeant who cares for his men.
frames.concerns: Gratuitous gore and the suicide gag; the crude nickname.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth: Rita's kindness to the dying; interdependence of the squad.
frames.concerns: Peace and justice emphasis against a story where killing is the only answer; glorified violence.

frames.aligns: Self-made strength through will and practice; Keiji masters his fate by his own effort.
frames.concerns: Self-sacrifice for the herd runs against Church of Satan individualism; The Satanic Temple's compassion tenet sits against the ending.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Warrior reputation matters: Rita's legend as the "Full Metal Bitch" and Valkyrie, Keiji's later name "Killer Cage" (TV Tropes); the ending is a duel. No insults are avenged.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Military drill and discipline are shown as good (Ferrell's push-ups, Mangapedia); everyone has a place in the chain of command.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Loyalty is to the squad and to humanity, not to family; Rita's parents are dead and Keiji's family is absent.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Rank is respected and sergeants revered, though skill (Rita, later Keiji) outranks title (Mangapedia).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No religion; the Mimics are explained scientifically; problem-solving is by experiment (Mangapedia; Weekly ASCII).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival is everything: training, ammunition, staying alive another day (Kotaku).

folkways.japan: The barracks hierarchy (senpai Yonabaru, three years senior, Mangapedia), stoic endurance, and green tea after a meal as an ordinary Japanese courtesy (TV Tropes) are Japanese context rather than the story's argument. Self-improvement through relentless repetition is a familiar Japanese ideal the story treats as true.

delivery.evidence: No reviewer found calls it preachy; Manga Bookshelf says the manga favors "spectacle, action, and battles" over the novel's commentary.
delivery.note: The story argues for perseverance and sacrifice through events rather than speeches, but the enemy is a faceless force, so no rival worldview gets a hearing.

personified.ideology: Growth through repeated failure and effort
Duty and self-sacrifice for humanity
Discipline and care for the men under him

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Utilitarianism, Pragmatism, Existentialism.

series.title: The Girl From the Other Side: Siúil, a Rún

entry.heading: The Girl From the Other Side: Siúil, a Rún
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is gentle: you care for someone who is not your own kind, without being able to hold them, and you keep loving them whatever they turn out to be. Fear of the different, enforced by walls, purges and religious authority, destroys more than the curse it tries to stop.

frames.aligns: Self-giving care for a child; refusing to kill another and laying down one's own life instead (v8); forgiveness at the end (v11). Evil (purging the innocent) is not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7).
frames.concerns: A church, "Holy Father" and "Heavenly Father" modeled on Christian forms are framed as the source of violence, and the god of light as a schemer.

frames.aligns: Patience, humility, watchfulness over a child; love that does not grasp (Teacher never touches her).
frames.concerns: Sacred titles and a god of light shown as a thief and a schemer; nepsis makes the devil-like hero and cosmic-horror imagery a point to discuss.

frames.aligns: Care for the fatherless (James 1:27); a critique of cruelty done in God's name.
frames.concerns: A Christian-like faith shown mostly as fear and control; dualism of two equal gods. Each congregation decides (soul liberty).

frames.aligns: Sacrificial love; mercy to the outsider; depicts religious violence without endorsing it.
frames.concerns: The god of light, called "Heavenly Father," is framed as scheming; no picture of a good God. Beneath the Tangles (a Christian anime site) praised the vol. 1 story but gave no spiritual reading.

frames.aligns: Love and protection of a child; evil done out of fear is exposed.
frames.concerns: A devil-looking hero (ANN: "a slight look of devils"), a dark "Mother" in a lake and gods as tricksters may be weighed as an "open door"; the church is cast as persecutor.

frames.aligns: Common grace: a beautiful work about mercy by a non-Christian author.
frames.concerns: A god of light who is a thief and schemer conflicts with God's goodness and sovereignty; two rival gods (dualism).

frames.aligns: Love of neighbor across boundaries; law without mercy (purges) shown as destructive.
frames.concerns: Christian-like church as persecutor; confessional families may weigh the "Heavenly Father" usage more than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy; care for the outcast and the sick; perfect love casting out fear (1 John 4:18).
frames.concerns: Christian-like faith shown as fear-driven; holiness churches may want discussion of the gods' portrayal.

frames.aligns: A fairy tale judged by its framing, in the line of MacDonald and Lewis; mercy and self-sacrifice.
frames.concerns: The god of light as schemer; an open ending some readers find unresolved.

frames.aligns: Teacher will not kill even to save Shiva and gives up his own life instead (v8); the story condemns persecution of the "unclean" by state and church, a history Anabaptists remember.
frames.concerns: A Christian-like church shown as persecutor; separation-minded families avoid most popular media regardless.

frames.aligns: Love of a parent for a child; a parent's love that survives death; forgiveness.
frames.concerns: A Christian-like "Heavenly Father" framed as a schemer; souls separated from bodies differ from LDS teaching.

frames.aligns: Critique of quarantine-driven exclusion and violence against the "unclean"; care for the outcast; dark-skinned, othered figure as the hero.
frames.concerns: The god of light as schemer; the open ending.

frames.aligns: Care for a child; health and quarantine themes; mercy.
frames.concerns: Souls separate from bodies and live on (v8, v11) conflicts with teaching on the state of the dead; dark "Mother" and trickster gods.

frames.aligns: Love, mercy, no glorified violence; a critique of religion allied with state power.
frames.concerns: Separable souls, gods and a spirit "Mother" are close to spiritism (Galatians 5:19-21); Christian-like god portrayed as a schemer.

frames.aligns: Love outlasts fear; the cursed hero remains good.
frames.concerns: A contagion that spreads by touch and fear of disease are the story's engine; dwelling on dread and loss of self.

frames.aligns: Care for the orphan; the dangers of fear-driven exclusion; no immodest content.
frames.concerns: A Christian-like church; two rival gods (against strict monotheism); a soul given away. Many Haredi homes restrict secular media regardless.

frames.aligns: Care for the stranger and orphan (Deuteronomy 10:18); critique of persecution; mourning and memory (Teacher's lost daughter).
Tikkun olam: protecting the vulnerable; critique of scapegoating the "infected."
Care for an orphan (Qur'an 93:9); mercy; no immodest content.
frames.concerns: Two rival gods and a god of light shown as a thief conflict with tawhid; a Christian-like church.

frames.aligns: Light and dark as complementary; the soul (atman) distinct from the body; selfless care (seva) and self-sacrifice.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; some may discuss the gods as thieves.

frames.aligns: Impermanence ("Everything eventually crumbles to dust," v11 blurb); compassion without grasping (never touching); forgiveness; loss of self.
frames.concerns: The soul as a fixed thing differs from anatta.

frames.aligns: Seva for a child; courage against oppression; ego and fear shown as roots of cruelty.
frames.concerns: Two rival gods differ from one Creator.

frames.aligns: The oneness of humanity: inner and outer peoples divided by fear; nonviolence; a "chaste and holy life" untouched.
Sincerity, gratitude for small things, nature spirits; purity and pollution (kegare) as themes.
frames.concerns: The story critiques exclusion in the name of purity, which some may weigh against purity customs.

frames.aligns: Dark is not evil; a great Mother in the lake; people becoming trees; a respectful folk-tale world; critique of witch-hunt-like purges (Beneath the Tangles).
The Way to Happiness: care for children, do not murder; the spirit distinct from the body.
Critique of fear-based exclusion, quarantine violence and religious authority; empathy for the othered.
frames.concerns: The open ending; abandonment of a child (framed as protective).

frames.aligns: Compassion without reward; critique of religious authority and fear; the gods' cosmology read as fable.
Protective fatherhood, duty, self-sacrifice; beauty in the old-tale style (Grimm, engravings).
frames.concerns: Authority (King, church) shown mainly as failing; the faith closest to Christianity is framed as cruel.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of the outsider; justice for the scapegoated; free search for meaning in an open ending.
Religious authority exposed as cruel; darkness associated with the gentle hero; compassion (TST Tenet 1).
frames.concerns: The story honors self-sacrifice over self-preservation.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Teacher never retaliates and will not kill even to save Shiva (v8 blurb); forgiveness closes the story (v11; WeekendNotes).

Order vs freedom.evidence: The Inside's order (walls, purges, revelation) is critiqued (TV Tropes; Comics Beat); the gentle life outside the rules is celebrated, though Teacher keeps one strict rule: no touching.

Civic vs kin.evidence: The bond of guardian and child outweighs the realm; even the King chooses one child over his kingdom (v10 blurb); Auntie abandons Shiva to save her (TV Tropes).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: King and Holy Father hold power and are framed as failing; the one hierarchy honored is a caring guardian's.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Institutional religion is critiqued and the gods are thieves, but the world is mythic and spirits are real; the story does not reason its way out.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: A survival setting (contagion, scarcity), but the story values tenderness, small joys (a puddle, Manga-News) and tolerance of the different.

folkways.japan: The Gothic European setting is a deliberate fairy-tale borrowing (Grimm, engravings, an Irish song), not Japanese custom. Readers may note an echo of Japanese purity and pollution ideas (kegare) in a curse spread by touch (from general knowledge; to verify); Nagabe says real-world references were avoided (pixivision).

delivery.evidence: ANN: "running on pure atmosphere"; Comics Beat: "much more nuanced than the premise implies." No reviewer opened calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The message is carried by images, silence and small domestic moments, and the Insiders' fear is shown as understandable even when its results are cruel.

personified.ideology: Gentleness and restrained, protective love

personified.character: The church and soldiers of the Inside
personified.ideology: Safety through purge and obedience to revelation
Duty to the many versus mercy to one
Protective love that must let go

entry.dominant: Secular humanism, Dharmic (Buddhist), Critical theory (critique of exclusion), Classical virtue ethics.

series.title: Bungo Stray Dogs
series.native: 文豪ストレイドッグス

entry.heading: Bungo Stray Dogs
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is found by belonging to people who take you in, and by choosing, whatever your past, to be "on the side that saves people." No one is worthless, and an old life of killing can be left behind, but the story is also honest that the people you love can be taken from you.

content.framing: Shown with consequences (deaths of heroes); Condemned (terror attacks)
Mixed: often played for comedy; sometimes shown with consequences

frames.aligns: Conversion and second chances (Dazai, Kyōka); the worth of an abandoned orphan; mercy joined to justice (Beneath the Tangles).
frames.concerns: Suicide made a running joke, against the gravity given it in CCC 2280-2283; Mori's predatory gag played for laughs; gang life glamorized (Inter Mirifica 7 on not making evil attractive).

frames.aligns: Repentance as a change of direction (metanoia) in Dazai and Kyōka; love that takes in outcasts.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis) against frequent violence; suicide humor; a villain who speaks of God and purifying sin.

frames.aligns: A new life after a sinful past; courage and loyalty; Atsushi's worth affirmed.
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 test on suicide jokes and gangster glamour; innuendo. Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Beneath the Tangles: the show's core is the longing "to be accepted and to belong," which Christ fills; justice must be used with "mercy, grace, and above all, love."
frames.concerns: Suicide played for comedy; a world where God is left out of the picture (Beneath the Tangles).

frames.aligns: Clear redemption arcs; protecting the weak.
frames.concerns: Supernatural powers, vampires, a cursed child and "Gods" (AniList spoiler tag) may raise "open door" concerns; suicide humor and a death-wish lead.

frames.aligns: Common grace: a non-Christian work that honors mercy and loyalty; total depravity echoed in Fyodor's view of humanity, though he draws the wrong conclusion.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 on lewd content applies lightly (innuendo); suicide humor; vigilante-style Agency work.

frames.aligns: Grace-like acceptance of Atsushi without merit; vocation (the Agency's work for the city).
frames.concerns: Fifth Commandment and the joking treatment of suicide. LCMS and WELS families tend to be stricter than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Social holiness: care for orphans and outcasts; transformation of character.
frames.concerns: Wesley's General Rules against diversions that cannot be used "in the name of the Lord Jesus"; suicide jokes; gangster glamour. Holiness churches more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: Judged by framing: evil framed as evil, villains humanized, redemption central; a literary work about literature.
frames.concerns: Suicide humor; Mori's gag; the Mafia's charm.

frames.aligns: Oda's refusal to kill (fan wiki, Mori page; Dark Era light novel) and Dazai's turn from killing echo a peace witness; love for outcasts.
frames.concerns: Armed conflict is the plot's engine; worldly entertainment (Schleitheim Art. 4).

frames.aligns: Repentance and new beginnings; loyalty; the worth of every soul.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth: suicide jokes and violence do not invite the Spirit; innuendo.

frames.aligns: Care for the abused and abandoned; critique of state frame-ups and a militarist hero.
frames.concerns: Suicide trivialized; a predatory joke about girls; homoerotic fan service sold to fans rather than portrayed honestly (ANN preview).
"By beholding we become changed" (2 Corinthians 3:18) weighs against suicide humor and violence; Fundamental Belief 22.
Violence (Psalm 11:5) is frequent; supernatural powers and vampires; suicide treated lightly; a villain who claims to act on God's will.
Constant images of death, suicide and fear as mental influences to be guarded against.

frames.aligns: Teshuvah-like turning from a criminal past; care for the orphan (Deuteronomy 10:18).
frames.concerns: Suicide is grave in halakha and here is a joke; nivul peh and tzniut on innuendo; many Haredi homes would not have it.

frames.aligns: Teshuvah and second chances; justice with mercy.
Tikkun olam in protecting the city; welcome of the outsider.
frames.concerns: Suicide humor; Mori's gag about girls.

frames.aligns: Care for orphans (a strong Qur'anic theme); repentance (tawbah); loyalty.
frames.concerns: Suicide is forbidden (Qur'an 4:29) and is joked about; innuendo and the gaze (24:30-31); violence.

frames.aligns: Dharma chosen after a past of wrong action; duty to protect; the self is more than its past (Atsushi).
frames.concerns: Tamasic content (Gita 17) in violence and death-wish humor.

frames.aligns: Suffering, attachment to past trauma and release; compassion for enemies (Kyōka spared and welcomed).
frames.concerns: Violence against the first precept; suicide humor; Fyodor's craving for a "pure" world.

frames.aligns: Protecting the weak; service (seva) in the Agency; the five vices shown in villains.
frames.concerns: Lust as a gag (Mori); suicide humor; anger and ego in gangsters.

frames.aligns: Unity across rival groups; the worth of every soul.
frames.concerns: Violence central; suicide treated lightly against a "chaste and holy life."

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) and loyalty; gratitude toward those who take you in.
frames.concerns: Death and blood as impurity; little sacred content either way.

frames.aligns: No stereotyped witches or pagans; respect for nature appears in Q's trauma from the trees' pain (fan wiki).
The Way to Happiness: help others, do not murder; criminals reform.
frames.concerns: A doctor (Mori) shown as a manipulator is neutral for this frame; suicide treated lightly.

frames.aligns: Found family; survivors of abuse finding worth; anti-authoritarian plot against frame-ups. Common Sense Media 15+.
frames.concerns: Suicide humor (ANN critics; Honey's Anime: the show makes Dazai's mental health a joke "rather than taking them seriously"); Mori's predatory gag and Naomi's behavior played as comedy; few women.

frames.aligns: Meaning found in human bonds, not cosmic answers; reason (Ranpo, Dazai) solves problems.
frames.concerns: Cruelty glamorized in the Mafia; suicide jokes.

frames.aligns: Duty, loyalty, courage, mentorship and respect for elders (Fukuzawa); celebrates a nation's literary heritage.
frames.concerns: Gangster glamour; suicide jokes; a state hero who becomes a terrorist (a critique of misused authority more than of authority).

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of every person, even a killer like Kyōka; justice with compassion.
Self-made identity; skepticism toward a "purifying" religious zealot (Fyodor) and a militarist state hero.
frames.concerns: Harm to children is a concern in the Eleven Rules (child assassins, Q, Mori's gag), though the story frames these as wrongs.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: The Agency works within law as licensed detectives and hands Fyodor to the authorities (ch. 53); the Port Mafia runs on honor, revenge and face, and Oda's revenge for his orphans is honored (Dark Era light novel).

Order vs freedom.evidence: The story values a stable Yokohama kept by a three-way balance among Agency, Mafia and government; it defends the Agency against a corrupt state unit (ch. 57-68) rather than celebrating freedom from order.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Loyalty to one's own group (the Agency "family," the Mafia) comes first, but the stated aim is to protect the city (Kyōka's sacrifice, ch. 36).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Respect for President Fukuzawa and the Mafia boss; mentor-pupil ranks (Dazai and Akutagawa); outcasts are still welcomed as equals.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Secular world; the one religious voice is a villain's (ch. 46); tradition appears as reverence for literary heritage, not faith.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Starvation and survival open the story (ch. 1); eccentric self-expression and personal meaning are prized later.

folkways.japan: Senpai-kohai and mentor-pupil bonds (Dazai and Akutagawa), loyalty to a company or "house" (the Agency, the Mafia) and reverence for the national literary canon reflect Japanese norms. The comic handling of suicide also draws on the real Dazai's public image in Japan; critics outside Japan found it hard to accept (ANN).

delivery.evidence: Asagiri wrote villains such as Fitzgerald and Sigma to be relatable (Wikipedia); ANN calls Fyodor an "appropriately threatening" villain.
delivery.note: Themes of belonging and second chances come through backstories and action, and the main villains are given real reasons for what they do.

personified.ideology: Searching for a reason to live; from nihilism toward saving others
Utilitarian "optimal solution"; people as pieces
Humanity is sinful and must be purified
Peace through one world military power

entry.dominant: Communitarianism, Existentialism, Utilitarianism (explored), Classical virtue ethics, Nihilism (critiqued).

entry.heading: Tomo-chan Is a Girl! (Fumita Yanagida)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is being loved and accepted as you already are, by friends and by the one you love, rather than reshaping yourself to fit what a "girl" or a "guy" is supposed to be; loyal friendship is the ground that love grows from.

content.framing: Neutral (gags); shown with consequences in places

frames.aligns: Faithful friendship; a romance that stays chaste and seeks a parent's blessing; Jun protects Tomo and reports the assault; apology and reconciliation.
frames.concerns: Fan service on Tomo's and Carol's bodies (anime bath scene; manga swimsuit); comic hitting. The story says nothing of marriage.

frames.aligns: Humility, loyalty, love expressed in patient faithfulness over years.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses applies to the fan service; anger and pride played as comedy.

frames.aligns: Loyal friendship, honesty, respect for a girl's father, protection of the vulnerable on the bus.
frames.concerns: Immodest art (Philippians 4:8 test); mild profanity; some families also raise gender-role questions. Soul liberty leaves the call to each family.

frames.aligns: "Man looks on the outward appearance, but the Lord looks on the heart" (1 Samuel 16:7) echoes the theme; friends who speak truth; forgiveness.
frames.concerns: Fan service; teasing that becomes cruel; a separatist minority would object to the tomboy heroine (see Holy Anime Wars).

frames.aligns: Courage, protecting others, joy and loyalty. No occult content.
frames.concerns: Holiness standards on modest dress vary by church; the fan service and short-skirt gags; comic violence.

frames.aligns: Common grace: a kind, funny story by a non-Christian; honest confession of fault (Jun's apology; Misuzu's admission).
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 on lascivious pictures applies to the fan service panels.

frames.aligns: Vocation and family (dojo, training), faithfulness in friendship, forgiveness.
frames.concerns: Fan service; LCMS and WELS families weigh it more than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy on a small scale; friendship as a means of grace; honest apology.
frames.concerns: Holiness churches more cautious about fan service and comic violence than the UMC.

frames.aligns: Kindness, loyalty, reconciliation; a story read for how it frames right and wrong, which it does clearly on the assault.
frames.concerns: Fan service; partial treatment of victim-blaming. Episcopal and ACNA families differ on gender roles.

frames.aligns: Humility, loyalty, peaceable resolution through talk and apology.
frames.concerns: Separation from popular media makes a secular comic a concern for Old Order families; violence as sport and comedy runs against nonresistance; fan service. MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Respect for parents in courtship; chaste romance; loyal friends; protecting others.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth counsel on modest dress and on dating as a young teen; fan service art.

frames.aligns: Welcome of a gender-nonconforming heroine; acceptance as you are; anti-harassment.
frames.concerns: Victim-blaming remark only partly answered (Anime Feminist); jokes misgendering Tomo; comic violence.
"By beholding we become changed": fan service and comic violence; romance-centered entertainment that excites the passions in Ellen White's sense.

frames.aligns: Honesty, apology, respect for a parent's authority.
frames.concerns: Dating as young teens without marriage in view (jw.org counsel); violence played for laughs (Psalm 11:5); immodest images. No spiritism.

frames.aligns: Love and honesty dissolve years of misunderstanding; no illness themes.
frames.concerns: Dwelling on the assault and on anger.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, honoring a father, kavod habriyot (dignity) for a teased girl, condemnation of the assault.
frames.concerns: Tzniut: mixed-sex teen dating, fan service, a girl in the boys' karate club; many Haredi homes would not have the series.

frames.aligns: Dignity of each person; friendship; protecting a victim.
frames.concerns: Modesty in the art; comic violence.

frames.aligns: Informed autonomy; acceptance of gender nonconformity; condemnation of harassment.
frames.concerns: Victim-blaming remark only partly answered; fan service.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, honesty, a father's consent sought before the relationship begins, condemnation of the assault.
frames.concerns: Unchaperoned dating; immodest art (lowering the gaze, Qur'an 24:30-31); Tomo dressing as a boy may raise the hadith on imitating the other sex for some families.

frames.aligns: Respect for the guru-father and the dojo's discipline; loyalty; dharma of protecting the weak.
frames.concerns: The student stage (brahmacharya) and romance focus; rajasic comedy and fan service for some families.

frames.aligns: Right speech grows through the story; suffering from wrong views (Jun's misreading) ends with honesty.
frames.concerns: Attachment and jealousy (Misuzu) played for laughs; comic violence; fan service for observant families.

frames.aligns: Seva, courage in protecting others, honest relationships.
frames.concerns: Krodh (anger) as a gag; kaam in fan service.

frames.aligns: Unity, friendship, parental consent to the relationship (a Bahá'í principle for marriage), honesty.
frames.concerns: The call to a "chaste and holy life" and degrading art applies to the fan service.

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto), harmony among friends, family dojo tradition; summer festival customs.
Self-acceptance, freedom of gender expression; harm to the victim condemned.
Way to Happiness precepts: be worthy of trust, honor parents, protect others; communication resolves conflict.
Gender nonconformity accepted in the end; harassment named and the harasser reported; Kotaku sees a look at "how antiquated gender norms get in the way of love."
frames.concerns: Critics split: Anime Feminist (premiere) and ANN's Hopper flag misgendering jokes, sexualized art and "toxic" romance ideas; victim-blaming answered only partly (Anime Feminist, 2023); violence against a boy played as comedy.

frames.aligns: Honesty, friendship and self-acceptance without religious framing; reason and talk resolve conflict.
frames.concerns: Gender gags and fan service; comic violence.

frames.aligns: A father's blessing sought before dating; discipline and martial tradition; loyalty and courage; chaste romance.
frames.concerns: Fan service; a heroine who rejects feminine norms reads as positive here, which some traditional families question while others see an old "tomboy" type.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth regardless of how one presents; justice for a harassment victim.
Self-determination; Tomo refuses to change for others; strength valued.
frames.concerns: The assault violates bodily autonomy (Satanic Temple Tenet 3) and the story condemns it, which aligns; Jun's demand that she change her clothes conflicts.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Physical strength and standing matter: Jun must face Gorou in a match to earn the right to date Tomo (vol. 8); Tomo answers insults with fists (TV Tropes). The assault is handled through police, not revenge (anime ep. 2).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Tomo is free to be a girl in the boys' karate club and to dress as she likes; dojo discipline and school life frame it.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Family dojo and two families who know each other well; the friend group is the main circle.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Friends are equals; a father's permission and dojo rank still count (vol. 8).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Secular daily life with customs lightly kept (summer festival, likely vol. 5); a traditional courtship ending.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Being accepted as yourself is the central value.

folkways.japan: The strict expectations about how a girl speaks and dresses (TV Tropes "Values Dissonance"), the family dojo, senpai-kohai relations, school clubs, the culture-festival play and summer yukata festivals are Japanese norms that frame the comedy more than they form its message. Groping on public transport is a recognized problem in Japan, which the bus episode reflects (Anime Feminist).

delivery.evidence: Silverman (ANN): "funny and still manages to make a point"; Kotaku: explores "how antiquated gender norms get in the way of love."
delivery.note: The gender theme comes through gags and the leads' misunderstandings, and the characters who push conformity are shown with sympathy but are proved wrong.

personified.ideology: Being loved as you are, without conforming
Girls must become feminine to be seen
Male reticence; friendship over romance
Paternal authority; strength earns the right to court

entry.dominant: Expressive individualism, Classical virtue ethics, Communitarianism.

entry.heading: Mieruko-chan
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is lived with steady nerve and quiet kindness: you keep your fear to yourself, protect the people you love, honor the dead, and find out that many "monsters", living or dead, are carrying pain.

frames.aligns: Care for the dead and for the suffering; abuse condemned; Godmother's self-offering for another (ch. 37). Evil spirits are not made attractive.
frames.concerns: Spiritism and mediums shown as genuine and helpful (CCC 2115-2117); a wish bargain with shrine gods; fan service of minors (CCC 2521-2524 on modesty).

frames.aligns: Remembrance of the dead; struggle with fear; compassion for the afflicted.
frames.concerns: Evil spirits are taken as real in the tradition, so a heroine who bargains with spirit "gods" and relies on mediums is a serious concern; nepsis (guarding the senses) weighs on both the horror and the fan service.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, courage, kindness to the weak; abuse shown as wrong.
frames.concerns: Spirits of the dead, mediums and shrine gods shown as real (Deuteronomy 18:10-12); fan service of teen girls. Views vary because each church is self-governing.

frames.aligns: Depicts spiritual danger without glamorizing it; compassion and sacrifice; abuse framed as harm.
frames.concerns: Spirit contact and folk rituals as the main tools; early sexualized framing of minors.

frames.aligns: Courage in the face of evil spirits; care for others.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": the whole series is spirit contact, shrine pacts and mediums, presented neutrally or positively; the "gods" demand a price. Fan service of teens.

frames.aligns: Common grace in friendship and self-giving; harm traced to sin (Zen's mother).
frames.concerns: Occult practice shown as effective; WLC Q139 names "lascivious... pictures" among sins, the test case for the anime's camera.

frames.aligns: Love of neighbor (Hana, Zen); honest grief for a father.
frames.concerns: Occult forbidden (Large Catechism, second commandment); mediums shown as genuine; fan service. LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy (freeing suffering spirits, protecting a friend); kindness to animals.
frames.concerns: Occult practice; fan service. Holiness churches more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: Judged by framing: the story sides with kindness and against abuse; a ghost-story tradition with English parallels (M.R. James).
frames.concerns: Spirits and mediums as real; the early camera framing of teen girls.

frames.aligns: Nonviolent heroine who endures rather than fights; humility, care for others.
frames.concerns: Conservative groups avoid such popular media; spirit contact; fan service. Violence is not central, so the usual main concern is low here.

frames.aligns: Families bound beyond death (the father's ghost at home, ch. 9); service and sacrifice.
frames.concerns: Occult and spirit contact avoided by members; fan service; For the Strength of Youth asks whether media invites the Spirit.

frames.aligns: Empathy for the lonely (Yuria) and abused (Zen, Michiru); compassion as strength.
frames.concerns: Exploitative fan service of girls (the guide's stated concern); critics' "male gaze" comments.
The dead are unconscious until the resurrection, so a dead father present in the home, ghost cats and spirits of the dead are a particular concern; fan service.

frames.aligns: Love of family and friends; abuse condemned.
frames.concerns: Spiritism and contact with spirits of the dead are the premise (Galatians 5:19-21); fan service.

frames.aligns: Love and compassion dissolve some evils (suffering cat spirits pass on once their pain is gone).
frames.concerns: Fear, ghosts and malevolent forces shown as real and powerful; dwelling on fear is what the tradition guards against.

frames.aligns: Honoring a parent after death; compassion for animals (tza'ar ba'alei chayim).
frames.concerns: Necromancy and spirit contact (Deuteronomy 18:10-11); shrine gods and offerings (avodah zarah); tzniut and the camera's focus on girls. Many Haredi homes restrict such media.

frames.aligns: Respect for parents and memory; kindness to animals; abuse condemned.
frames.concerns: Spirit contact and shrine gods; modesty values applied to the fan service.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam echoes in helping suffering beings; consent-minded criticism of fan service fits its ethics.
Patience (sabr) under trial; care for parents and animals; abuse condemned.
frames.concerns: Jinn are real in Islamic belief, so spirits are taken seriously; seeking help from shrine gods and mediums reads as shirk and sihr; lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) and the fan service.

frames.aligns: Spirits and deities as part of the world; honoring the departed (an echo of shraddha offerings); compassion.
frames.concerns: Little message conflict; modesty values for the fan service vary by community.

frames.aligns: Buddhist mantras and beads named; suffering spirits released when their pain ends; compassion for all beings including cats; equanimity under fear.
frames.concerns: Third precept and right mindfulness for the fan service; folk spirits are not usually a concern.

frames.aligns: Fearlessness (nirbhau) as an ideal; seva in protecting a friend.
frames.concerns: The Gurus rejected superstition, charms and spirit bargains, which drive the plot; lust (kaam) in the camera framing.
Spiritualism discouraged; "chaste and holy life" against degrading entertainment (fan service).

frames.aligns: Kami, spirits and shrines treated as real and powerful; offerings to the dead; purity and sincerity in Miko.
frames.concerns: Shrine gods portrayed as sinister and demanding a price (ch. 24, 27, vol. 6) could read as disrespect to kami; a shrine that "doesn't exist" (ch. 24).

frames.aligns: Spirits, protective practices and mediums shown with respect; Godmother as a genuine practitioner rather than a villain.
Helping others; the spirit as lasting beyond death.
frames.concerns: Little stated concern in the tradition.

frames.aligns: Empathy for the lonely and abused; animal cruelty condemned; a female-led cast.
frames.concerns: Sexualization of minors is the guide's stated concern, and critics (ANN, Beneath the Tangles) objected to the camera "ogling" a frightened teen girl.

frames.aligns: Human bonds, self-control, kindness; harm traced to human cruelty (Zen's mother, the cat killer).
frames.concerns: Supernatural presented as real (fine as fiction); exploitative framing of teens.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, a protective younger brother, honoring a dead father, self-sacrifice.
frames.concerns: Sexualized framing of teen girls; occult themes for some religious conservatives.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of the overlooked (Yuria, Zen, Michiru); free search for meaning; pagan practice treated respectfully.
Self-reliance; a heroine who solves problems herself; the cruelty of abusive parents and animal killers exposed (harm to children and animals condemned in the Eleven Rules).
frames.concerns: Gods demanding a price and mediums as authorities.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Miko never answers a threat or slight with confrontation; she endures and protects. Zen answers his mother only with a cold "I thought you left" (ANN ep. 12).

Order vs freedom.evidence: School rules frame daily life, but no rule system addresses the real danger; Miko acts on her own judgment.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Family (father, brother) and a few close friends come first; strangers' ghosts are avoided, though Miko helps Zen and the cats.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Godmother has a master and Rom defers to her (vol. 6 flashbacks), but authority in the story is earned by ability, not rank.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Shrines, offerings to the dead, charms and mediums are real and effective; skeptics are simply wrong.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival dominates the horror (keeping safe, keeping quiet), balanced by friendship, food and fan hobbies.

folkways.japan: Offerings to a dead parent, shrine visits, salt and Buddhist mantras, and the norm of not burdening others with one's troubles are everyday Japanese practices the story uses as background; readers from other cultures may read them as the setting's customs rather than a message.

delivery.evidence: Critics praise its "restraint in explaining its monsters" and its sentimentality (Steve Jones, ANN ep. 12); no review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its themes of compassion and grief come through scene and subtext, not speeches.

personified.ideology: Endure fear quietly; protect others
Spiritual craft as a paid service
Controlling, achievement-first parenting
Occult enthusiasm and exorcism

entry.dominant: Pagan / occult (Japanese folk religion), Classical virtue ethics, Stoicism, Pragmatism, Dharmic (Buddhist).

series.title: Smoking Behind the Supermarket with You
series.romaji: Super no Ura de Yani Suu Futari
series.native: スーパーの裏でヤニ吸うふたり

entry.heading: Smoking Behind the Supermarket with You
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is not won by success at work. It is made bearable, and even warm, by small daily rituals, by kindness to strangers and by one person who sees who you really are when the work mask comes off.

content.framing: Endorsed (mostly); one health scare shown with consequences, then reversed

frames.aligns: Kindness to the stranger (Sasaki defending a young worker, Smoke 0); chaste, respectful romance; dignity of work and critique of exploitative labor (Catholic social teaching).
frames.concerns: Tobacco is not forbidden in moderation, but CCC 2290 asks for temperance and avoiding excess in tobacco; the story makes a habit the center of intimacy. Deception between the leads.

frames.aligns: Humility and patience in Sasaki; love that grows slowly; care for the weary.
frames.concerns: Smoking is discouraged and forbidden for clergy in many places; the story treats a passion (habitual craving) as a source of comfort. Guarding the senses makes the constant smoking imagery worth discussing.

frames.aligns: Clean romance with no sexual content; hard work; kindness to strangers.
frames.concerns: Tobacco discouraged; the story presents smoking as the path to friendship and love, and the lung scare ends with Sasaki returning to cigarettes. Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Shows weariness and loneliness honestly; respectful romance; small kindnesses matter.
frames.concerns: Smoking discouraged; the story's comfort has no source beyond human company. Romans 14 freedom cuts both ways for families.

frames.aligns: Clean romance, kindness, no occult content beyond a played-for-laughs ghost story.
frames.concerns: Tobacco commonly rejected; holiness standards make the celebrated habit the main concern.

frames.aligns: Common grace: honest observation of ordinary life and work by a non-Christian author; Sasaki's restraint.
