frames.concerns: WLC Q136 lists "immoderate use of meat, drink, labour" among sins against the sixth commandment, which some apply to tobacco; the habit is never questioned.

frames.aligns: Entertainment as adiaphora; vocation in ordinary work (supermarket staff serving neighbors).
frames.concerns: Tobacco use is not addressed in the confessions; LCMS and WELS families may be more cautious about the glamorizing.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy (Smoke 0); patience and kindness.
frames.concerns: Tobacco discouraged in Wesleyan tradition and abstinence asked by holiness churches; the habit is framed as the source of comfort. UMC families are more open.

frames.aligns: Gentle, humane portrait of ordinary people; chaste romance; no mockery of faith.
frames.concerns: Glamorized smoking; deception. Episcopal and ACNA families differ little here.

frames.aligns: No violence; humility, simple kindness, quiet faithfulness to daily work.
frames.concerns: Tobacco discouraged (with some Old Order exceptions); the worldly night-time setting and the habit at the center. Conservative groups avoid most popular media; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Kindness, chastity, honest work, a romance that respects boundaries.
frames.concerns: The Word of Wisdom (D&C 89) rules out tobacco; here tobacco is the bond that drives the whole story and is never rejected, and the lung scare is reversed.

frames.aligns: Exploited workers and service staff treated with dignity; mutual, consensual adult romance; the younger woman's agency.
frames.concerns: Harm-reduction concern about addiction; age gap worth discussing.

Tobacco is not used by members, and the health message is central (Fundamental Belief 22); a story that frames smoking as comfort and love throughout, and reverses a health warning, runs against that message.

frames.aligns: Kindness, honesty valued (Yamada's guilt), no violence or spiritism.
frames.concerns: Tobacco is forbidden as defiling (2 Corinthians 7:1); the story treats it as the bond between the leads. Unchaperoned night meetings.

frames.aligns: Gentle, hopeful tone; fear and illness do not dominate; love and kindness prevail.
frames.concerns: Members abstain from tobacco; the habit is presented as a real comfort, and the X-ray scare puts disease at the center of a chapter.

frames.aligns: Honest work, kindness to a stranger (Smoke 0), restraint in romance.
frames.concerns: Many poskim now prohibit smoking under the duty to guard health (Deuteronomy 4:15); yichud and tzniut concerns about an unmarried man and woman meeting alone at night; mild teasing about bodies. Many Haredi homes avoid such media entirely.

frames.aligns: Kindness, dignity of workers, respectful romance between adults.
frames.concerns: The CJLS has ruled smoking prohibited; the story frames it as comfort and love.

frames.aligns: Consensual adult relationship; dignity of service workers; kindness to a stranger.
Patience (sabr), kindness, honest work, restraint and modesty in Sasaki's conduct.
frames.concerns: Tobacco is widely discouraged, and many scholars forbid it under the principle of not harming oneself (Qur'an 2:195); private night meetings between an unmarried man and woman (khalwa); mild jokes about the body.

frames.aligns: Duty to work done well, kindness, gentle romance; little to raise in message.
frames.concerns: Tobacco discouraged in many communities; some families apply the Gita's tamasic category (chapter 17) to the habit.

frames.aligns: Compassion for strangers, mindfulness of small moments, impermanence of comfort.
frames.concerns: The fifth precept covers intoxicants; tobacco is often read as a craving rather than an intoxicant. Craving (tanha) is the story's engine and is not questioned.

frames.aligns: Honest work (kirat karni), service to others, chaste conduct.
frames.concerns: Tobacco is one of the four kurahits (cardinal prohibitions) in the Rehat Maryada; the story celebrates it throughout as the bond of love.

frames.aligns: Service, kindness, chaste and honest courtship as an ideal.
frames.concerns: Tobacco is discouraged in the writings; the story treats it as the center of comfort. Deception before courtship.

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) and gratitude in ordinary work; harmony among the store staff.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; no codified teaching on tobacco.

frames.aligns: Consenting adults; small rituals that mark the day; no stereotyping of any faith.
frames.concerns: Harm-based judgment of tobacco under "harm none."

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness precepts: "Take care of yourself," "Be industrious," "Be worthy of trust"; kindness.
frames.concerns: The habit sits against "Take care of yourself"; deception against "Be worthy of trust."

frames.aligns: Critique of exploitative work; dignity of retail labor (Anime Feminist); female agency in the romance; consent is clear.
frames.concerns: Glamorized smoking with a reversed health scare (ScreenAnarchy, Tokyo Weekender); a 21-year age gap, which most reviewers here judge acceptable between adults.

frames.aligns: Meaning found in human connection, empathy and small daily goods; no supernatural framing.
frames.concerns: Evidence-based health concern: the X-ray chapter turns medical evidence into a punchline.

frames.aligns: Work ethic, decency, a chaste courtship, respect between generations, a man who behaves honorably.
frames.concerns: Concern if smoking is glamorized for minors; the publisher's Older Teen rating. Some read the overwork critique as neutral, not political.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of overlooked workers; consent and mutual care in the relationship.
Indulgence by consenting adults; bodily autonomy (Satanic Temple Tenet 3); Yamada's self-chosen identity.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: No one defends their honor; Sasaki absorbs his boss's criticism and resolves conflict by apology and patience. When a customer abuses young Yamada, Sasaki calmly intervenes (Smoke 0, end of v1).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Work rules and politeness are shown as heavy; the story celebrates the private space behind the store where people can be themselves and smoke freely (Tokyo Weekender on smokers' "rights").

Civic vs kin.evidence: Bonds are with co-workers and a stranger, not family: the store staff as found family, Sasaki's kindness to an unknown part-timer. Family appears only in the background (sister, Yamada's father).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Workplace rank is real (boss, manager, senior cashiers) and a harsh boss is shown unsympathetically; the leads meet as equals behind the store despite age and status (Anime Feminist: "equitable").

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No religion; life is ordered by work and personal choice. Chaste courtship and politeness are the only traditional notes.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Hard work and endurance are respected, but the story's center is quality of life: rest, small pleasures and being one's true self.

folkways.japan: The "black company," the mask of polite service (Yamada's cashier persona), senior-junior mentoring, unspoken feelings and Japan's recent turn against public smoking are Japanese settings the story takes as given; readers elsewhere may see the overwork and the smoking-area hunt as local color rather than a message aimed at them.

delivery.evidence: Reviewers call it low-key and "told through little scenes without words" (Tokyo Weekender); none calls it preachy; critics say it romanticizes smoking.
delivery.note: Its message about small comforts is shown through wordless routine, while the case against smoking appears mainly through a harsh boss and a health scare that is undone.

personified.ideology: Endure the grind through small comforts and decency
The true self hidden behind the work persona
Corporate authority over the worker (disapproves of smoking)

entry.dominant: Communitarianism, Hedonism (small pleasures), Expressive individualism, Existentialism. All four labels are my own framing, not a source's.

series.title: Jagaaan
series.warning: Includes the rape of a 16-year-old character and a backstory of childhood sexual abuse.

entry.heading: Jagaaan
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is not the comfortable script of job, marriage and family, nor the release of every hidden desire; it is finding out what you really want and answering for it. Desire indulged without restraint or connection turns people into monsters.

content.framing: Shown with consequences (sexual violence); otherwise neutral

frames.aligns: Disordered desire (concupiscence) shown as destructive; the rapist is punished; the hero moves toward justice.
frames.concerns: A hero who enjoys killing; evil often played for dark comedy, which risks making it attractive (Inter Mirifica 7); sexual violence against a minor in the plot; no mercy or repentance named.

frames.aligns: The passions shown as monsters that devour the person, close to the patristic picture of unchecked passions.
frames.concerns: Nepsis (guarding the senses) makes the gore and sexual violence a direct concern; no struggle toward God or repentance shown.

frames.aligns: Sin's consequences are visible; the rapist is judged.
frames.concerns: Fails the Philippians 4:8 test for most families: gore, nudity, rape. The hero's pleasure in violence is not condemned early on. Views vary because each congregation is self-governing.

frames.aligns: Depicts sin's fruit without endorsing the rapist; a dark mirror of the human heart.
frames.concerns: Little to redeem in the frame: no grace, no forgiveness named; heavy sexual content. Romans 14 freedom leaves the choice to conscience, but many would hold off.

Media as an "open door": a talking owl that grants power in exchange for killing, and a life-for-life bargain, may read as a spiritual transaction; holiness standards weigh the sexual content heavily.

frames.aligns: Total depravity has an echo: ordinary people become monsters once their hidden desire is fed.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 lists "lascivious ... pictures" among sins against the seventh commandment; no redemption outside the self.

frames.aligns: Law without gospel: the story shows desire's ruin clearly; the sword-bearer protects (late).
frames.concerns: No gospel: no forgiveness or grace from outside. LCMS and WELS families tend to be stricter than ELCA on the content.

frames.aligns: The hero changes over time, which echoes the hope that people can grow.
frames.concerns: Wesley's rule to avoid "diversions as cannot be used in the name of the Lord Jesus"; holiness churches would avoid it.

frames.aligns: Evil is shown as monstrous and self-consuming.
frames.concerns: Good and evil are blurred in the hero for much of the run; sexual violence against a teen.

frames.aligns: Desire and violence shown as destructive.
frames.concerns: Violence is the hero's pleasure and his solution throughout (Matthew 5:39). Conservative groups avoid such media.
For the Strength of Youth: content that drives away the Spirit (gore, nudity, sexual violence); marriage framed as dull.

frames.aligns: Social anxieties (bullying, abuse, voyeurism) made visible; abusers are punished.
frames.concerns: Sexual violence against a teen girl used in a shock-driven plot; women largely as victims; revenge as the victim's answer.
"By beholding we become changed" (2 Corinthians 3:18) applied to extreme gore and sexual content; Fundamental Belief 22.
Violence God hates (Psalm 11:5), sexual immorality, a talking animal that grants powers (spiritism concern).

frames.aligns: Hidden thoughts shape what a person becomes, which echoes the teaching that thought shapes experience.
frames.concerns: Fear, cruelty and sin shown as overwhelming realities; "Stand porter at the door of thought" (Science and Health 392).

frames.aligns: The yetzer hara (evil inclination) shown unchecked, with punishment.
frames.concerns: Tzniut makes nudity and sexual content a central concern; gore and nivul peh (crude speech); suicide themes. Many Haredi homes exclude such media.

frames.aligns: Same yetzer hara reading; justice for victims.
frames.concerns: Modesty, sexual violence against a minor, revenge framed as answer.

frames.aligns: Exposes abuse, bullying and voyeurism; tikkun olam echoes in the late turn to protecting others.
frames.concerns: Sexual violence used for shock; women as victims.

frames.aligns: Following one's whims (hawa) leads to ruin, close to Qur'an 45:23 and 25:43 (this entry's framing).
frames.concerns: Lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) makes nudity and sexual content central; suicide themes against Qur'an 4:29; a hero who enjoys killing.

frames.aligns: Kama and krodha (desire, anger) as gateways to ruin (Bhagavad Gita 3.37, 16.21; this entry's framing).
frames.concerns: Many would class the content as tamasic (Gita ch. 17).

frames.aligns: Craving (tanha) literally consumes its host; the hero's turn away from his first desire echoes the path.
frames.concerns: Killing is the solution (first precept); extreme imagery; no compassion for most of the infected.

frames.aligns: Four of the five vices (lust, anger, greed, ego) shown as monstrous and destroyed.
frames.concerns: Sexual violence and gore; little of the saint-soldier's restraint in the hero for most of the run.
Shoghi Effendi's call to a "chaste and holy life" warns against degrading art and literature (to verify wording); violence as the hero's path.

frames.aligns: Pollution (kegare) spreading through a town, with a need for purification, is a familiar frame.
frames.concerns: Little sincerity (makoto) in the hero at first; death and blood as impurity everywhere.

frames.aligns: Animals (frogs, owl) as carriers of power; consequences come back on the doer, echoing the threefold law.
frames.concerns: "Harm none" broken constantly, including by the hero.

frames.aligns: Way to Happiness precepts (do not murder; be worthy of trust) broken by villains who are punished.
frames.concerns: The hero kills as his job; no clear moral teaching.

frames.aligns: Exposes stalking, voyeurism, bullying and child sexual abuse; abusers are punished.
frames.concerns: Rape of a 16-year-old and childhood abuse used in a shock-driven horror plot; women mostly as victims; revenge castration as the victim's arc; no age rating from the publisher found.

frames.aligns: Desire, boredom and social pressure explained in human terms; no supernatural morality.
frames.concerns: Cruelty played for dark comedy; the suicide-related ending needs safe-messaging framing.

frames.aligns: Lust and aggression without restraint are shown destroying people; predators are punished.
frames.concerns: Ordinary marriage and family are framed as dull at the start; institutions (police, law) corrupt; gore and sexual content.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of victims; exposure of abuse.
frames.concerns: Sexual violence against a minor; the infected are killed rather than helped.

frames.aligns: Honesty about one's real desires; the predator who harms a child is punished (Eleven Rules on harming children).
frames.concerns: The story treats indulgence without responsibility as monstrous; a child is abused, against core Satanic Temple and Church of Satan rules.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Personal retribution is common and often succeeds: Moroha castrates her father and her rapist; the hero is a vigilante with his own gun (Japanese Wikipedia).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Police and law are weak or corrupt (half-monster chief, bullying lawyer); but freedom of desire is shown as monstrous, so neither side is celebrated cleanly.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Family ties are thin or abusive (fiancée killed, abusive father); the late hope lies in public heroism and a hero group (Triple H).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Rank gives no moral standing; a 16-year-old ends as Triple H's leader (Japanese Wikipedia).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No religion or custom guides anyone in the sources found; the supernatural (frogs, owl) is a mechanism, not sacred.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: The story is about self-expression of desire but treats it as dangerous; survival dominates the final arcs.

folkways.japan: The forced smile, the pressure toward a stable job and marriage, the neighborhood koban police box and the town mascot reflect Japanese everyday norms that the story satirizes; readers elsewhere may read these as setting rather than message.

delivery.evidence: No review calls it preachy; Gizmodo says the monsters' symbolism is left to readers; Anime Atelier finds no character likeable.
delivery.note: Its view of desire is shown through what each monster becomes rather than stated in speeches.

personified.ideology: Release of violent desire, later "justice"
Sexual desire as entitlement
Heroism as a public group project

entry.dominant: Hedonism (critiqued), Expressive individualism (critiqued), Existentialism, Dharmic (craving, this entry's framing).

entry.heading: Gokurakugai
entry.label: From summaries

frames.aligns: Evil (man-eating maga, serial killers) is not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7); human dignity is chosen and defended; adoption-like care (Tao for Alma).
frames.concerns: A counterfeit "family" and a villain who claims to be the source of life; suicide attempts and a suicide-pact chapter (CCC 2280-2283); smoking and drinking adults without comment.

frames.aligns: Struggle against the passions: Alma learning to master the hunger in his blood (ch. 11-12). Pity for the fallen.
frames.concerns: Corpses raised as monsters and a villain who claims power over death touch the sacredness of the body; guarding the senses (nepsis) makes the gore and fan service a concern.

frames.aligns: Clear evil; compassion for the outcast; a caring adult takes in a child.
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 test for the gore, the red-light setting and Tao's design; occult flavor of the maga. Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Depicts sin without endorsing it; redemption themes in Alma's choice; the counterfeit family exposed.
frames.concerns: No source beyond human care; occult monster lore.

frames.aligns: Good confronts evil; courage and sacrifice.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": monsters from corpses, gates from another realm, a hero powered by monster blood, a figure who claims to be where life returns.

frames.aligns: Total depravity has an echo in the hunger of the maga; common grace lets families value well-crafted art.
frames.concerns: Suicide-pact chapter and suicide attempts (WLC Q136); fan-service design (WLC Q139).

frames.aligns: Saragi as an order that bears the sword to protect the district; mercy to the fallen.
frames.concerns: Occult imagery; smoking and drinking left uncommented. LCMS and WELS families tend to be stricter than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy toward outcasts (beastmen, Kanata); growth in self-control.
frames.concerns: Holiness churches would weigh smoking, drinking and fan service.

frames.aligns: Judged by how it frames good and evil, and evil is framed as evil; strong monster-fantasy tradition.
frames.concerns: Suicide content; violence as the default solution.
Violence shown as heroic is the central concern, and every case ends in a kill (Matthew 5:39). Conservative groups avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Family as central; care for a child not one's own; hope of reunion with a lost brother.
frames.concerns: T+ violence and fan service; For the Strength of Youth asks whether media invites the Spirit.

frames.aligns: Attention to the marginalized: beastmen as a lower class; pity for monsters made by others.
frames.concerns: The beastman discrimination is raised but, per one reviewer, "never explored"; women's designs criticized.

frames.aligns: Clear good and evil; care for family.
frames.concerns: The dead raised and used by a villain conflicts with teaching on the state of the dead; smoking and drinking; Fundamental Belief 22 on entertainment.
Spiritism-like lore (the dead returned, other-realm gates); violence as the hero's calling (Psalm 11:5).

frames.aligns: Love outlasts evil; a child taught that he is more than his "nature".
frames.concerns: Death, disease-like hunger and fear shown as powerful realities.

frames.aligns: Protecting life; honoring parents and searching for a lost brother.
frames.concerns: Corpses desecrated by the villain (respect for the dead, kavod ha-met); a suicide-pact chapter; tzniut makes the red-light setting and Tao's design a concern. Many Haredi homes restrict such media.

frames.aligns: Protecting life; respect for the dead implied in the horror; repairing a broken district.
frames.concerns: Suicide content; modesty applied by families.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam echoes: protecting the vulnerable in a neglected district; prejudice against beastmen.
frames.concerns: Suicide content; violence as the default answer.

frames.aligns: Care for orphans (Tao raising Alma), justice for the oppressed, patience.
frames.concerns: Desecration of the dead; a villain claiming to be where life returns (a claim reserved to God); smoking and alcohol; suicide (Qur'an 4:29); lowering the gaze (24:30-31) for the fan service.

frames.aligns: Dharma of the protector; karma language (the "karmic restraint" stake); compassion for a being caught in a hungry state.
frames.concerns: Some apply the Gita's tamasic category to the gore and intoxicants.

frames.aligns: Gokuraku (Pure Land) in the title; craving as the root of suffering (the maga hunger); compassion for Kanata as karuna.
frames.concerns: Killing is the solution, against the first precept; the "paradise district" is a place of suffering, an irony that may be read as critique or as borrowing.

frames.aligns: Saint-soldier protection of the weak; mastery of anger and attachment.
frames.concerns: Intoxicants (alcohol, tobacco) shown routinely; tobacco is forbidden in the Rehat Maryada.

frames.aligns: Service, unity across races (humans and beastmen), care for a child.
frames.concerns: Violence as the heroes' path; alcohol and smoking.

frames.aligns: Yomi (the underworld) and torii-like gates are familiar mythic imagery; purity against corruption.
frames.concerns: Gates that resemble torii serve as monster portals and a shrine is a murder scene (vol. 4); blood and corpses are strong impurity (kegare).

frames.aligns: Respect for liminal beings; no stereotyping of witches or pagans; "harm none" echoed in protecting the district.
Way to Happiness precepts: help others, do not murder (murderers condemned); take care of the young.
frames.concerns: Killing as the main solution; drinking.

frames.aligns: Prejudice against beastmen shown; outsiders humanized; capable women.
frames.concerns: Fan-service design (Manga Test Drive); issues raised but "never explored" (MAL review); suicide content without safe-messaging; T+ violence.

frames.aligns: Humanity defined by choice and care, not origin; free inquiry into the maga's cause; no supernatural answer offered.
Duty, protection of the weak, a strong adult raising a child, hard training.
frames.concerns: Family breakdown everywhere; smoking and drinking; found family stands in for the natural family.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth even of a monster (Kanata); justice for the marginalized; free search for truth.
Self-determination: Alma defines himself against his origin; Tenet 1 compassion.
frames.concerns: Harm to children (Eleven Rules): teen characters as fighters and victims.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Personal grudges exist (Yoru vows to kill Tao personally, ch. 16; Shizuka tells Nei to kill him someday, ch. 26), but the heroes act out of protection and care, not to defend their name.

Order vs freedom.evidence: A "lawless" district (Viz) where private troubleshooters and a secret organization keep what order there is; the heroes value their independence.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Found family over blood family: Tao and Alma, against Yomi's blood "family" (ch. 7-9); Tao's loyalty to her brother Jin (vol. 4) pulls the other way.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Beastmen are a lower class, and that prejudice is shown, not celebrated (MAL); Saragi has trainers and seniors, but respect is earned.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No faith is practiced; Saragi does maga research and development (Wikipedia); religious names are setting only.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival in a poor, dangerous district, hard training and paid work come first; Alma's right to be himself is the counter-theme.

folkways.japan: The senpai-style training (Ryu, Nei), the restaurant as a community hub and the use of Buddhist and Shinto words for places are Japanese norms of the setting; the Chinatown backdrop draws on Yokohama.

delivery.evidence: MAL reviewer: issues like racism and suicide are raised but "never explored"; no review opened calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its message about chosen humanity comes through the cases and Alma's choices more than speeches, while the villains' views are sketched more than argued.

personified.ideology: Humanity is chosen by how you act
Family by blood; death as origin and return
Wanting to be human against one's nature
Weary realism that still guards a boy's humanity

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Communitarianism, Pragmatism, Dharmic (Buddhist) by imagery.

series.title: Seraph of the End: Vampire Reign

entry.heading: Seraph of the End: Vampire Reign
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is loyalty to the family you choose. You protect them, you refuse to trade any of them for a larger plan, and you stay human in a world where both rulers and rescuers use people as tools.

frames.aligns: Self-giving love among friends (John 15:13); exploitation of children condemned; reviving the dead by human power treated as a grave transgression with consequences.
frames.concerns: Seraphs and Abaddon reworked as weapons; heroes bound to demons (CCC 2115-2117 on occult practice, judged by framing); God appears mainly as a punishing force in the backstory.

frames.aligns: Struggle against the passions (Ferid's boredom, Guren's despair); repentance and confession of guilt (Guren, ch. 99).
frames.concerns: Angels and demons are spiritually real in the tradition, so heroes sealing demons into swords and angels used as bombs is a serious concern; guarding the senses (nepsis) weighs on the gore and the suggestive feeding scenes.

frames.aligns: Clear evil in Ferid and the experimenters; loyalty; refusal to sacrifice the innocent.
frames.concerns: Biblical terms (Seraph, Trumpets, Abaddon) used freely in a non-Christian myth; demon pacts as the heroes' power source. Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Sacrificial love; human institutions shown as fallen; consequences for playing God.
frames.concerns: Demons as allies; the sacred reworked as fantasy; God portrayed as hostile in the backstory (to verify as the ending lands).

frames.aligns: Courage and loyalty; evil named as evil.
frames.concerns: Spiritual warfare is real in this view: heroes making pacts with demons that live in their weapons and demon possession (Guren, Shinoa) are shown as normal tools; angels are weaponized. A major "open door" concern.

frames.aligns: Total depravity has an echo: every human institution is corrupt; common grace lets families value craft by non-Christians.
frames.concerns: God shown as wrathful but not gracious; reworking of Scripture's angels.

frames.aligns: Law exposes sin: every attempt at self-salvation (resurrection by force) makes things worse.
frames.concerns: Demon pacts; scripture names used as game mechanics. LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy and loyalty; social holiness in protecting children.
frames.concerns: Demon pacts; violence; suggestive feeding scenes. Holiness churches more cautious.

frames.aligns: Good and evil judged by framing in a long fantasy tradition; evil institutions exposed.
frames.concerns: Biblical angels and God recast in a punishing role.

frames.aligns: Refusal to sacrifice the innocent for a larger plan; suspicion of state and military power.
frames.concerns: The army, violence and demon pacts are the heroes' path throughout (Matthew 5:39).

frames.aligns: Family and loyalty central; consequences for tampering with life and death.
frames.concerns: Demon possession and pacts; angels recast as weapons; violence and fan service.

frames.aligns: Critique of institutions that exploit children; solidarity with the marginalized; same-sex devotion shown with warmth.
frames.concerns: Violence as the main solution; biblical imagery used loosely.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, self-sacrifice, consequences for reviving the dead.
frames.concerns: The dead revived by spells and a dream world with the dead's presence conflict with teaching on the state of the dead; demon pacts; Revelation imagery reworked.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, mercy, exposure of false religion (cults).
frames.concerns: Spiritism, demon contact and possession are central (Galatians 5:19-21); military violence; reworking of Revelation.
Evil, death, disease (the virus) and fear presented as overwhelming powers.

frames.aligns: Protecting life; honoring the bond of a family of choice; exposing idolatrous cults.
frames.concerns: Reviving the dead by sorcery and demon pacts (Deuteronomy 18:10-12); Abaddon and seraphs reworked; tzniut concerns about fan service; many Haredi homes avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Pikuach nefesh echoes in Yu's refusal to trade lives; exposure of cults.
frames.concerns: Necromancy and demonology as heroic tools; reworked angels.

frames.aligns: Protecting the vulnerable; critique of abusive institutions; moral agency over orders.
frames.concerns: Violence; loose use of Hebrew-Bible imagery (Babel, seraphim).

frames.aligns: Loyalty, patience in hardship, protecting orphans (a strong Qur'anic theme, Qur'an 93:9).
frames.concerns: Angels (mala'ika) obey God and are never weapons or rebels; demon pacts (jinn) and sorcery shown as power sources; necromancy; lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) for fan service.

frames.aligns: Dharma of protecting one's own; karma-like consequences for transgression; family duty.
frames.concerns: Little conflict with core message; tamasic content (gore, possession) some families limit.

frames.aligns: Attachment as the root of suffering: Guren cannot let his friends die, and the world ends; Ferid's fear of rebirth (fan wiki).
frames.concerns: Killing is the main solution, against the first precept.

frames.aligns: Courage to defend the oppressed; ego and attachment (moh) shown destroying the world.
Unity across enemy lines (Mika and Yu, vampires and humans cooperating).
frames.concerns: Violence as the path throughout; the sacred reworked.

frames.aligns: Purity and taboo: breaking the boundary between life and death brings disaster; torii and Mt. Fuji imagery (ch. 121).
frames.concerns: Defilement by blood and death throughout.

frames.aligns: Magic shown as a craft with costs; no stereotyping of witches; nature of life and death respected in the end.
frames.concerns: Magic cults exploit children; "harm none" is broken on every side.

frames.aligns: Exposure of drug-based experiments on children and of abusive institutions.
Critique of institutions that exploit children, of clan hierarchy and of blind obedience; same-sex devotion central and warm.
frames.concerns: The ANN-noted prostitution parallel and the sexually coded feeding of a teen by a child-looking adult vampire; fan service involving 16-year-olds; queer bond left ambiguous ("a matter of perspective").

frames.aligns: Human loyalty over divine or institutional schemes; accepting death as part of a human life; reason against cults.
frames.concerns: Gore; suicide pills (Code 284) need safe-messaging framing.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, courage, sacrifice, protecting the weak; consequences for hubris.
frames.concerns: Authority is nearly always corrupt; parents are abusers; heroes defy the chain of command.

frames.aligns: Rebellion against arbitrary authority (the Hiragi, the council, a punishing God in the backstory); compassion and justice for exploited children (Satanic Temple Tenets 1 and 2).
frames.concerns: The story still prizes self-sacrifice for others and a taboo on transgression, against Church of Satan individualism.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of every person, refusal to sacrifice anyone for a plan; justice for exploited children; unity across enemy lines.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Revenge drives Yu early (vow against vampires, ch. 1-3), but the story moves him from revenge to protecting family; honor and pride are not celebrated for their own sake.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Military discipline exists, but the story celebrates defying corrupt orders (Yu against Guren and Kureto, ch. 114-118).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Chosen family over humanity: Yu chooses Mika over a plan to save the world (ch. 115-120); loyalty is to "family", not the state.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Clan rank (Hiragi) and the vampire council are critiqued; the squad is close to flat, with friendly teasing of officers.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Taboos on life and death are treated as real and enforced by higher powers; but inherited clan ways and cults are rejected, and magic is treated as technology.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Post-apocalyptic survival; security of one's own comes first; little room for self-expression beyond loyalty.

folkways.japan: Military rank, clan (ie) hierarchy and the senpai-kohai banter of the squad reflect Japanese norms; the Shinto-style taboo on mixing life and death and the use of torii and Mt. Fuji imagery are Japanese settings, while the biblical names are Western borrowings used as atmosphere.

delivery.evidence: Kotaku says vampires are "more complex" than pure villains and the humans' actions are largely questionable; no review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its message about chosen family is stated in Yu's lines and tested through leaders who sacrifice others for larger plans.

personified.ideology: Chosen family above every plan
Ends justify means for those you love
Hierarchy and sacrificing the few for humanity
Nihilistic boredom, cruelty as play

entry.dominant: Communitarianism (chosen family), Classical virtue ethics, Utilitarianism (critiqued), Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued), Existentialism.

entry.heading: Bakuman。 (Tsugumi Ohba and Takeshi Obata)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is a dream chased with total effort, beside a loyal partner and honest rivals, inside a demanding system you learn to master, and crowned by a promise kept. Ohba's stated message: "If you have a dream and work hard for it, I don't think it's ever a waste" (Viz interview, 2012).

content.framing: Mixed: comic or shown as wrong
Mixed: endorsed as dedication, warned against as excess

frames.aligns: Work as a calling that develops the person (Laborem Exercens); talents used fully; friendship; a chaste promise that ends in a proposal; cheating (Nanamine) fails.
frames.concerns: Work and success crowd out rest, health and God; women judged by charm and loyalty; Sunday rest absent.

frames.aligns: Ascetic-style discipline and perseverance; faithfulness over years; repentance of rivals (Iwase, Fukuda's apology).
frames.concerns: Vainglory: the whole life aimed at rankings and fame; passions of envy and rivalry fuel the plot; no spiritual horizon.

frames.aligns: Diligence (Colossians 3:23); friendship; honesty rewarded; romance kept pure until a proposal; little to fail a Philippians 4:8 test.
frames.concerns: Career as idol; the uncle's death from overwork; dismissive lines about women. Soul liberty: each family decides.

frames.aligns: A clean, hopeful story of vocation and loyalty; a Christian reviewer calls it engaging with "great" competition moments (Beneath the Tangles).
frames.concerns: The same reviewer says it "objectifies its female cast" and that women "deserved better," citing Genesis 1:27 and Galatians 3:28. Success as the measure of worth.

frames.aligns: No occult content; diligence; chaste romance; deception exposed.
frames.concerns: Worldliness and ambition; overwork; holiness churches may question the fan-service talk.

frames.aligns: Vocation as calling in any field (common grace lets a non-Christian story honor faithful work); integrity rewarded.
frames.concerns: Work becomes the chief end of life; health and rest sacrificed, which WLC Q135-136 treats as a duty to preserve life; women's equal dignity.

frames.aligns: Luther's doctrine of vocation: ordinary daily work as service; partnership and neighbor-love among rivals.
frames.concerns: Works and achievement as the measure of a person; no rest. LCMS and WELS families may weigh the sexism and drinking more than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: "Gain all you can" through honest industry; friendship and mutual help among rivals.
frames.concerns: Wesley's same sermon limits gain to what does not hurt one's health; the uncle's death and Mashiro's surgery show that cost. Holiness churches stricter.

frames.aligns: A Sayers-style respect for the "work of the maker"; faithful love ending in marriage; honest craft.
frames.concerns: Gender roles; work idolized. ACNA families may be more cautious than Episcopal families on content, Episcopal families more on gender.

frames.aligns: Hard work, loyalty and community among rival artists; no glorified violence.
frames.concerns: Pursuit of fame and worldly success is the plot; competition over humility (Gelassenheit); popular entertainment itself avoided by Old Order groups; MC USA families more open.

frames.aligns: Hard work, goals and keeping covenant-like promises; chastity until marriage; marriage as the happy end.
frames.concerns: Health neglected (D&C 89 and 88:124 on rest); adult drinking; women's roles narrow but within family-centered norms many members share.

frames.aligns: Creative vocation; friendship across rivalry; critique of exploitation (an editor who keeps an artist in debt).
frames.concerns: Gender portrayal criticized as sexist by several reviewers; the industry's labor practices largely accepted.

frames.aligns: Diligence, temperance in story outcome (Mashiro cannot drink after liver damage), chaste romance.
frames.concerns: Health and rest sacrificed (the health message); adult drinking; no Sabbath; Ellen White's caution about absorbing fiction. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Honesty, diligence, chaste courtship toward marriage; no spiritism or violence of concern.
frames.concerns: A worldly career and fame put first; competition and pride; jw.org counsel cautions against making a secular career one's main goal. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Persistence and right thinking overcome setbacks; hope over fear.
frames.concerns: Long dwelling on illness, surgery, collapse and the uncle's death; anxiety over rankings.

frames.aligns: Diligence and partnership (chavruta-like); a promise kept; marriage as the goal of romance; cheating punished.
frames.concerns: Secular media in general for many Haredi homes; tzniut on fan-service talk and the gravure offer; work without Shabbat rest; lashon hara in the online rumor arc (shown as wrong).

frames.aligns: Hard work, learning a craft, loyalty, a kept promise; online slander shown as harmful.
frames.concerns: Rest and balance absent; egalitarian Conservative families may object to the gender attitudes.

frames.aligns: Creativity and effort; friendship; slander and exploitation shown as harms.
frames.concerns: Gender attitudes clash with Reform egalitarian commitments; success as identity.

frames.aligns: Striving (Qur'an 53:39), honesty, chaste courtship that ends in a proposal; cheating fails.
frames.concerns: Scholars differ on drawing living beings, the craft at the heart of the story; adult drinking (5:90); fan-service talk (24:30-31).

frames.aligns: Svadharma: each follows his own calling (Gita 3:35); dedicated work; respect for mentors and elders.
frames.concerns: The heroes work for the fruit (rankings, sales), the opposite of karma yoga's non-attachment (Gita 2:47).

frames.aligns: Right effort and right livelihood; friendship; impermanence (cancellations, the uncle's death).
frames.concerns: Craving (tanha) for success and recognition drives everyone; little middle way.

frames.aligns: Kirat karni (honest work); seva-like help among rivals; faithfulness.
frames.concerns: Haumai (ego) and pride in rankings; lust and anger in Nakai's arc are shown as faults.

frames.aligns: Work done well is worship; service and cooperation among rivals; chaste love ending in marriage.
frames.concerns: Equality of women and men is a core Bahá'í principle, and the female cast is criticized as unequal.

frames.aligns: Makoto (sincerity) and craftsmanship; gratitude to elders and mentors; harmony among rivals.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; overwork against purity and balance.

frames.aligns: Creative will and self-made path; no witches or pagans misportrayed.
frames.concerns: "Harm none" includes harm to self: the overwork theme; gender roles.

frames.aligns: Industriousness and competence (The Way to Happiness precepts); production as the basis of morale; persistence.
Creative ambition; satire of the industry; an exploitative editor shown as wrong; online harassment shown as harm.
frames.concerns: Multiple reviewers call it sexist (Thompson; Heroine Problem; Hooded Utilitarian; Beneath the Tangles); overwork glorified; industry labor norms accepted.

frames.aligns: Human creativity, effort and friendship give life meaning; no supernatural claims; honest work beats cheating.
frames.concerns: Narrow gender roles; career as the whole of life.

frames.aligns: Hard work, duty, loyalty, respect for elders and institutions, chastity and marriage; Thompson reads the series' stance as "conservative."
frames.concerns: The cost of overwork; a market-driven culture industry.

frames.aligns: Free and responsible search for one's path; creativity; mutual help.
frames.concerns: Inherent worth and equity: the female cast's treatment is the main concern; overwork.

frames.aligns: Vital existence; ambition and success by one's own effort; rivals as spur; the cheater fails.
frames.concerns: Submission to a large institution (the editor system); little else.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Worth is earned through work, not defended by force; punches are comic or shown as wrong (vols. 1, 15). Reputation still matters: the online smear of Miho (ch. 166) and the promise as a matter of honor (ch. 1, 176).

Order vs freedom.evidence: The leads choose their own path against parents (vol. 1), but within the strict order of editors, deadlines and rankings, which the story upholds (Nanamine's ban).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Partner, rivals, assistants and editors carry the heroes more than family; the uncle's legacy and grandfather's keys tie the dream to kin (vol. 1).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Editor and editor-in-chief authority, senpai-kohai and traditional gender roles; rivals are treated as equals and help one another.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No religion; decisions are made by reason, data (rankings) and craft. Traditional mores appear in gender and courtship.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: A dream of self-expression, pursued with survival-style grit; the mother's fear of poverty and the uncle's debts keep security in view.

folkways.japan: Weekly-magazine serialization, reader-survey rankings, the powerful editor (tantō), senpai-kohai manners, school-to-work pressure, overwork (karoshi) and the expectation of an office career are Japanese industry and social norms the story uses as its setting. The emphasis on effort (doryoku) and friendship is also Weekly Shonen Jump's long-standing editorial motto (from general knowledge; to verify).

delivery.evidence: ANN's Santos finds vol. 15's lessons "somewhat heavy-handed"; TV Tropes calls the anti-pandering message "not exactly subtle."
delivery.note: Characters state the creators' views on manga and work in long dialogue; rival methods get a hearing but are judged by the Jump system's results.

personified.ideology: Dream, effort and partnership inside the editor system
Crowd-sourced manga that bypasses editors
Security and a safe career over dreams
A woman's ambition driven by rivalry

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Pragmatism, Expressive individualism, Traditionalism, Communitarianism.

entry.heading: The Summer Hikaru Died
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life means facing what you cannot understand without forcing it into old categories, and choosing to stay with someone who is different, even when it frightens you. A community that hides its sins and forces people into roles harms those who do not fit.

frames.aligns: Evil is not made attractive: the head-for-wish bargain is a "sin" with mass death as its cost (vol. 5); repentance and apology (ch. 7, 16); mercy toward the outsider (Inter Mirifica 7).
frames.concerns: Sexual metaphor in scenes between teen boys (vol. 1); same-sex attraction treated sympathetically (CCC 2357-2359; CCC 2358 also asks respect); an attempted killing and a plea to be killed (ch. 16).

frames.aligns: Repentance and the weight of ancestral sin; compassion for the lonely.
frames.concerns: Nepsis: erotic-coded body horror with teens and constant dread; folk deity worship and spirits.

frames.aligns: Sin shown with consequences; loyalty; truth-telling at last (ch. 16).
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 test: horror and sexual metaphor; sympathetic queer framing against BF&M 2000 Article XVIII; a demonic-seeming being befriended. Each family decides (soul liberty).

frames.aligns: Depicts a pagan bargain as sin without endorsing it; sacrificial loyalty; mercy.
frames.concerns: A Christian anime site reads Yoshiki's silence as an implicit deal with the devil; sexual subtext; queer themes. Romans 14 freedom divides families.

frames.aligns: Evil spirits are real and dangerous in the story; sin has consequences.
frames.concerns: "Open door" concern: a possessing entity, spirits, a deity that took heads, and a teen who welcomes the being; erotic-coded body merging.

frames.aligns: Common grace in a well-made story; inherited sin and its effects are taken seriously.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 on lascivious pictures applied to the sexual metaphor; sympathetic framing of same-sex attraction; idolatry of a mountain god.

frames.aligns: Law without grace (penance rituals that "had no actual effect," fan wiki) shown as empty; repentance and forgiveness between friends.
frames.concerns: Sexual subtext with teens; sympathetic queer framing; confessional families more concerned than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Care for the outsider and the lonely; repentance.
frames.concerns: Wesley's rule on diversions; dread and erotic-coded scenes; UMC families now more open.

frames.aligns: Judged by framing: the monster's struggle for a soul, sin and penance, a refusal to destroy the outsider; literary horror in the line of Gothic fiction.
frames.concerns: Sexual subtext with teens; open questions about souls; practice ranges widely.

frames.aligns: Violence is not glorified: the stabbing is a breaking point, followed by apology (ch. 16); community sin exposed.
frames.concerns: Separation from worldly media; horror; sexual subtext; Old Order families avoid regardless.

frames.aligns: Family history and inherited obligations; repentance; loyal friendship.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth: dread and sexual metaphor do not invite the Spirit; the law of chastity and the Family Proclamation against the sympathetic queer framing.

frames.aligns: Welcome of the outsider; critique of a conformist village and of prejudice; queer youth seen with dignity.
frames.concerns: Teen codependency; the erotic-coded scenes and age-appropriateness; violence.
"By beholding we become changed": constant dread, body horror, spirits of the dead and a living mimic conflict with teaching on the state of the dead; sexual subtext; Fundamental Belief 22.
Spiritism and possession are central (Galatians 5:19-21); violence; sexual subtext; queer themes.

frames.aligns: Love outlasting fear in the end; the creature seeks to stop harming people (ch. 16).
frames.concerns: The whole engine is fear, disease ("impurities," plague of 1749), death and bodily horror, which this tradition guards against.

frames.aligns: Teshuvah: apology and repair (ch. 7, 16); ancestral wrongdoing reckoned with; human sacrifice framed as sin.
frames.concerns: Tzniut and the sexual metaphor; sympathetic queer framing against Leviticus 18:22; idolatry and necromancy themes; many Haredi homes restrict such media regardless.

frames.aligns: Care for the stranger; repair of communal sin; dignity of the outsider; the movement affirms LGBTQ members.
frames.concerns: Sexual subtext with teens; idolatry imagery; dread.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam; critique of scapegoating and conformity; dignity of queer youth.
frames.concerns: Age-appropriateness of the erotic-coded scenes; violence.

frames.aligns: Wrongdoing has consequences; loyalty, repentance, mercy.
frames.concerns: Shirk in the worship of a mountain deity; jinn-like possession; lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) applied to the storage-room scene; sympathetic queer framing against traditional teaching.

frames.aligns: Karma of ancestors; the soul as distinct from the body (ch. 16); compassion for a being trying to become human.
frames.concerns: Tamasic qualities (dread, gore, death); erotic-coded scenes with teens.

frames.aligns: Impermanence; grief and attachment; the creature is "outside the cycle of samsara" (fan wiki); compassion for a suffering being; questions of self (Swampman).
frames.concerns: Clinging is not resolved simply; erotic-coded scenes; violence.

frames.aligns: Courage, service, critique of empty ritual (the penance that did nothing); ego and attachment examined.
frames.concerns: Lust (kaam) as a vice and the erotic-coded scenes; superstition and folk deity worship.

frames.aligns: Overcoming prejudice; unity across difference; reason applied to superstition (Tanaka's investigation).
frames.concerns: "Chaste and holy life" and the sexual subtext; sympathetic queer framing against Bahá'í teaching on marriage; dread.

frames.aligns: Kami of mountains, shrine boundaries that protect (ch. 8), purity and impurity (kegare) as real forces; respect for traditional rural settings (Mokumokuren chose them "out of respect," ANN interview).
frames.concerns: A local deity shown as a head-taking horror; secret worship framed as sinful.

frames.aligns: Nature spirits and a living landscape; tolerance of the different; "harm none" broken by the old bargain and shown as wrong.
frames.concerns: Folk worship shown mainly as sinister (Endless Mode: "certified Wicker Man behavior").

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness: do not murder; be worthy of trust; the spirit distinct from the body.
Queer adolescence in a conservative town treated with depth (Reactor; Anime Feminist; PinkNews); critique of conformity and prejudice.
frames.concerns: Codependency and control (monitoring Yoshiki's contacts, TV Tropes); consent and age-appropriateness of the erotic-coded scenes with teens; CSM 14+.

frames.aligns: Free inquiry (library research, ch. 17-21 likely; Tanaka); old rites shown as useless or harmful; a person defined by relationships, not by origin.
frames.concerns: Violence and dread; supernatural premise as fiction.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, duty, responsibility for one's actions; reverence for rural heritage in the setting.
frames.concerns: The village, its elders and its traditions are framed as hiding sins and harming those who do not fit; sympathetic queer framing presented to teen readers; sexual metaphor with teens.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of the outsider; free search for meaning; justice for those a community excluded.
The "monster" as sympathetic outsider; challenge to a superstitious community; a deity's worship exposed as harmful.
frames.concerns: Harm to others, including children of the village, through the old bargain and the creature (Eleven Rules).

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Wrongs are answered with apology and repair, not revenge (ch. 7, 16); the one violent "answer" (the stabbing) is followed by remorse.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The village's order (rules, rites, gossip) is critiqued; Yoshiki wants to leave for the city (TV Tropes).

Civic vs kin.evidence: A private bond outweighs duty to the village; Indou family obligations are inherited (ch. 3; vol. 5).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Elders and family heads keep secrets that harm the young; trust goes to peers and one caring adult (Rie).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Old rites are shown as harmful or useless and investigated by reason, but the supernatural is real.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Identity, belonging and tolerance of the different are what the story values, in a declining rural setting.

folkways.japan: The rural village horror setting, shrine boundaries, kegare (impurity) and mountain deities are classic Japanese horror conventions the creator chose "out of respect" (ANN interview). Pressure to marry and village gossip reflect real rural Japanese norms as context, not the story's message.

delivery.evidence: Anime Feminist: "They're showing, not telling"; ANN vol. 1: subtext "just barely shy of text." No reviewer opened calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The message rides on mood, body horror and silence, and the village's views are shown mainly through gossip rather than voiced fully.

personified.ideology: Accepting the unknown other despite fear
A monster seeking belonging and a human heart
Conformity and hidden tradition
Pragmatic containment

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Pagan / occult (critiqued), Progressivism (queer identity), Critical theory (critique of conformity).

series.title: Domestic Girlfriend
series.native: ドメスティックな彼女
series.adult_reason: Domestic Girlfriend: Kodansha USA rates it 18+; sexual scenes involving high-school characters (deep entry held, sexuality 8)
series.warning: Depicts sex between characters under 18.

entry.heading: Domestic Girlfriend
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is following your heart and your calling through loss: love honestly even when society forbids it, work at the craft you were made for (writing, cooking, acting), and accept that love sometimes means sacrifice. The story lets forbidden love cost its lovers dearly, then rewards it with marriage.

content.framing: Mixed: teen sex is framed as romance; the teacher-student affair has career consequences but ends in marriage; assault is condemned

frames.aligns: Self-giving love (Hina's sacrifice); the dignity of victims (stalking, assault condemned); marriage as the closing goal.
frames.concerns: Inter Mirifica 7: evil should not be made attractive, yet teen sex and a teacher-student affair are framed as romance; chastity (CCC 2337-2359); fornication (CCC 2353); a child conceived outside marriage and raised apart (CCC 2201-2206).

frames.aligns: Struggle and suffering that purify; forgiveness between rivals and sisters.
frames.concerns: Nepsis: the art invites the reader to look at teen bodies through desire; passions treated as fate ("soulmates," ch. 275).

frames.aligns: Courage and self-sacrifice; consequences for secret sin (Hina loses her job).
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 test; sexual immorality endorsed as romance (1 Corinthians 6:18); an authority figure exploiting a minor.

frames.aligns: Consequences of deception are real; redemption themes (Alex forgiven, Natsuo grows).
frames.concerns: Many families would see the 18+ rating and teen sex as outside Romans 14 liberty; the ending blesses the affair.

frames.aligns: Perseverance through suffering; no occult content.
frames.concerns: Holiness standards on modesty and sexual purity; the "open door" of what one reads.

frames.aligns: Common grace in good craft and real emotion; sin has consequences.
frames.concerns: Westminster Larger Catechism Q139 names "lascivious... books, pictures" among sins against the seventh commandment; the teacher's abuse of her position.

frames.aligns: Honest portrait of sinners; grace and forgiveness between characters.
frames.concerns: Adiaphora judged by love and conscience: the 18+ sexual content and a minor's sexual relationship with his teacher weigh against it.

frames.aligns: Growth through discipline in a calling.
frames.concerns: Wesley's General Rules: avoid diversions that cannot be used "in the name of the Lord Jesus"; sexual content central.

frames.aligns: Works judged by how they frame good and evil: assault, stalking and exploitation are framed as evil; sacrifice as good.
frames.concerns: The teacher-student affair and teen sex are framed as love; marriage reached without repentance.

frames.aligns: Nonviolence admired in Natsuo shielding Hina; forgiveness.
frames.concerns: Separation from worldly media; sexual content and secrecy from parents.

frames.aligns: Marriage and family as the end goal; work and education valued.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth: entertainment that "invites the Spirit"; the law of chastity; a teacher's relationship with a student.

frames.aligns: Condemns stalking, assault and media exploitation of victims; LGBT characters present.
frames.concerns: How the vulnerable are treated: an adult teacher's relationship with a minor is framed as forbidden love (Anime Feminist); slut-shaming.

frames.aligns: Consequences for deception; recovery and perseverance.
frames.concerns: Fundamental Belief 22: entertainment "of the highest quality," avoiding the impure; "by beholding we become changed"; heavy drinking.
jw.org counsel against entertainment featuring immorality (Galatians 5:19-21); sexual immorality presented as love throughout.

frames.aligns: Recovery from injury and coma through love and persistence.
frames.concerns: "Stand porter at the door of thought" (Science and Health 392): fear, disease, lust and violence dwelt on at length.

frames.aligns: Family as central; consequences for a teacher who crosses a line.
frames.concerns: Tzniut and guarding the eyes; sex outside marriage; yichud (seclusion) rules broken constantly by the living arrangement.

frames.aligns: Honest portrayal of human failure; teshuvah-like growth in some characters.
frames.concerns: Modesty values; the teacher's misuse of her role; sex framed as romance among teens.

frames.aligns: Informed autonomy; care for victims; LGBT characters present.
frames.concerns: Power imbalance between teacher and student; the ending rewards it.

frames.aligns: Self-sacrifice; marriage as the goal; harm to others punished.
frames.concerns: Zina and its approaches (Qur'an 17:32); lowering the gaze (24:30-31); alcohol (5:90); seclusion between unrelated men and women.

frames.aligns: Dharma of work (Natsuo's writing, Rui's cooking); sacrifice; karma-like consequences for deception.
frames.concerns: Kama outside dharma; the teacher (guru) relationship misused, which tradition treats as grave; rajasic content (Gita 17).

frames.aligns: Suffering born of craving is shown vividly; impermanence (Tōgen's death, the coma).
frames.concerns: The third precept (sexual misconduct) broken without reflection; intoxicants (fifth precept).
Kaam (lust) among the five thieves, shown as the engine of the plot.

frames.aligns: Service through work; unity after conflict.
frames.concerns: A "chaste and holy life" (Shoghi Effendi; wording to verify); alcohol prohibited; sex outside marriage.

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) of feeling; gratitude; family bonds.
frames.concerns: Purity (harae) values; disorder in family relations.
"Harm none": real harm from a teacher's relationship with a minor and from deception.
The Way to Happiness: "Be faithful to your sexual partner"; drug use; the affair.

frames.aligns: Condemns stalking, assault, slut-shaming and media exploitation; LGBT characters.
frames.concerns: Consent and power: Anime Feminist calls Hina's relationship with her 17-year-old student "preying on a minor" and says the show treats it as forbidden love; others (Bubbleblabber) say it shows the consequences.

frames.aligns: Free inquiry, realistic consequences, self-directed meaning in work.
frames.concerns: Exploitation of a minor by an adult; the ending's message about it.

frames.aligns: Hard work, self-sacrifice, marriage as the goal.
frames.concerns: Undermines family order: secrecy from parents, step-sibling romance, teacher authority abused, a child raised outside the marriage.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of each person; justice for victims; diverse identities.
frames.concerns: Age-appropriateness; power imbalance between teacher and student.

frames.aligns: Personal freedom, sexuality without shame, self-determination.
frames.concerns: Church of Satan and Satanic Temple principles oppose harm to children: the adult-minor relationship.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Disputes go to police and courts (Tanabe, vol. 19-21); Hina protects Natsuo's reputation by leaving quietly (ch. 63-64), but the story celebrates personal feeling over family face.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The lovers break school and family rules, and the story sides with them; Rui chooses her own career.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Family is the stage and the final goal, but loyalty to one's love outranks family wishes.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Teacher-student hierarchy is collapsed into romance; parents' plans (Hina's blind date) are resisted.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No religion; sexual and family norms are set by feeling and choice.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Characters pursue creative callings: novelist, chef, actress (Japanese Wikipedia; TV Tropes).

folkways.japan: The step-sibling romance genre, adult children living with parents (ANN's McNulty), the Weekly Shōnen Magazine romance tradition and literary-prize culture (the amateur award Natsuo wins) are Japanese contexts. Japanese Wikipedia notes that its adult themes are unusual for a shōnen magazine.

delivery.evidence: Bubbleblabber says it doesn't romanticize the teacher-student relationship; Anime Feminist says it frames abuse as forbidden love. No review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its view that sincere love justifies its costs comes through plot outcomes, not speeches, and reviewers disagree on whether it critiques or excuses the teacher-student relationship.

personified.ideology: Romantic devotion and following one's heart
Love as self-sacrifice against social rules
Independence and love that lets go
Possessive, controlling desire

entry.dominant: Expressive individualism, Existentialism, Communitarianism, Hedonism. (Labels are my own framing unless a source is named.)

entry.heading: D.Gray-man
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is to keep walking forward through grief without trying to undo death, to love both friend and enemy as people who suffer, and to stay loyal to the people who make a home with you even when the institutions over you fail.

frames.aligns: Calling back the dead by a pact is condemned and punished (CCC 2116-2117 on necromancy); mercy toward enemies; self-giving friendship (John 15:13); evil in leaders is shown as evil, not glorified (Inter Mirifica 7).
frames.concerns: The Church itself, under the Pope and Vatican, is shown running child experiments and cover-ups; the first Akuma is a priest (to verify); God's character left ambiguous; Noah recast as the villains' forefather. Some families read this as a caricature of the Church, others as a fair picture of corruption that calls for reform.

frames.aligns: Grief, temptation and the passions (the Earl preys on despair); Allen's long-suffering love; repentance demanded of the Order (Alma, ch. 193).
frames.concerns: Holy things (God's crystal, priests, Noah) used inside a fictional cosmic war; a church army that tortures; nepsis weighs on body horror and fan service.

frames.aligns: Evil (the Earl, Lvellie's methods) framed as evil; compassion and loyalty; consequences for trading a soul.
frames.concerns: Biblical names (Noah, the Flood) reworked; a Catholic institution as backdrop; God's power treated as a weapon. Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Love for enemies (Matthew 5:44) in Allen's saving of Akuma souls; human institutions shown as fallen.
frames.concerns: Faith may be "an illusion" (ANN Hallow review reading); God shown as distant or vengeful; no grace message in the sources opened.

frames.aligns: Spiritual warfare is the premise: demons (Akuma) are fought by God's power; evil named as evil.
frames.concerns: Souls trapped and tormented; possession by Nea; dream-world torture; the "open door" concern with demonic imagery is high, though the heroes do not make demon pacts.

frames.aligns: Total depravity has an echo: no human institution is clean; the attempt to reverse death by human means brings ruin.
frames.concerns: God's sovereignty and goodness are not portrayed; second-commandment concerns are slight (no images of God reported).

frames.aligns: Law exposes sin: the Order's attempts to manufacture Exorcists make things worse; Allen's vocation to serve others.
frames.concerns: The church as a power structure with no gospel; violence. LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy; care for the soul of the enemy; social holiness in exposing abuse of children.
frames.concerns: Fan service; gore; God's role unclear. Holiness churches more cautious.

frames.aligns: Good and evil judged by framing in a Gothic fantasy tradition; corruption in a church exposed and condemned; grief and mercy central.
frames.concerns: Recasting of Noah and the Flood; vengeful picture of God in some readings.

frames.aligns: Suspicion of a militarized church allied with power (Schleitheim Article 4 tradition); Allen's mercy to enemies and his leaving an institution that betrays conscience (ch. 205).
frames.concerns: A "holy war" and an army of the church remain the setting; violence is the heroes' path.

frames.aligns: Families bound by love; consequences for tampering with death; service to others.
frames.concerns: Possession, torment of souls, fan service, violence.

frames.aligns: Critique of institutional abuse and cover-up; compassion for the outsider and the enemy; solidarity with exploited children.
frames.concerns: Violence as the main solution; Lenalee designed as fan service.

frames.aligns: Mercy, loyalty, consequences for calling back the dead.
frames.concerns: Souls of the dead conscious and trapped in machines, revived dead and visions of the dead conflict with teaching on the state of the dead; Flood and Noah reworked; holy war.

frames.aligns: The story's suspicion of a powerful church and its warfare; mercy and honesty.
frames.concerns: Spiritism, souls of the dead and possession are central (Galatians 5:19-21); violence; Noah and the Flood reworked.

frames.aligns: Love and perseverance outlast fear ("keep walking").
frames.concerns: Death, grief, fear and evil presented as overwhelming powers; body horror.

frames.aligns: Necromancy condemned (Deuteronomy 18:10-12); mourning that accepts death; protection of children.
frames.concerns: Noah, a righteous man in the Torah (Genesis 6:9), recast as the root of the villains; a Christian holy war as the frame; tzniut concerns about Lenalee's design. Many Haredi homes avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Mourning and moving forward (the Earl as a warning against refusing to let go); exposure of institutional abuse.
Moral agency over orders (Allen leaves the Order); tikkun olam in protecting the vulnerable.
frames.concerns: Loose use of Hebrew-Bible figures; violence.

frames.aligns: Patience in grief (sabr); mercy to the suffering; condemnation of sorcery and trading souls; care of orphans (Allen).
frames.concerns: Nuh is a prophet in Islam; the Noah lineage as the villains is a serious concern; God's power as a tool in a church army; lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) for fan service.

frames.aligns: Dharma of protecting others; karma-like consequences for calling back the dead; detachment from the dead.
frames.concerns: Tamasic content (gore, possession) that some families limit.

frames.aligns: Attachment as the root of suffering is the premise: clinging to the dead creates Akuma; compassion for every suffering being, even enemies; impermanence.
frames.concerns: Killing is the main solution, against the first precept.

frames.aligns: The saint-soldier ideal: fighting to protect the weak; moh (attachment) shown as destructive.
Unity across enemy lines (Allen's bonds with Road and Tyki are complicated; Allen sees Akuma as people); consultation over blind obedience.
frames.concerns: Religion as the cause and setting of a holy war; violence throughout.

frames.aligns: Purity and pollution: death and the dead kept separate; sincerity of Allen.
frames.concerns: Defilement by blood and corpses throughout.

frames.aligns: Grief and the cycle of life and death respected in the end; no stereotyping of witches.
Exposure of abusive experiments on children; perseverance.
Critique of institutional abuse, cover-up, surveillance and child soldiers; consent violated and condemned.
frames.concerns: Author-stated fan service of a teen heroine; Road's kiss with Allen; the possible ch. 232 abuse hint needs careful handling; fan-read adult-teen subtext.

frames.aligns: Accepting death; empathy for enemies; reason against an institution that lies.
frames.concerns: Gore; self-harm content (ch. 222 and a reported throat-cutting attempt) needs safe framing.

frames.aligns: Duty, loyalty, courage, sacrifice, protecting the weak; consequences for hubris over death.
frames.concerns: The Church and chain of command are often corrupt; the hero leaves his institution.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of every being, even Akuma; justice for exploited children; free search for truth (the Order's secrets).
Exposure of a corrupt church; justice for exploited children (Satanic Temple Tenets 1-2); rebellion against arbitrary authority (Allen leaves the Order).
frames.concerns: The story prizes self-sacrifice and mercy over self-interest; God's power remains real and good-intended in Allen's hands.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Allen answers cruelty with mercy rather than revenge (saving Akuma souls); Kanda drops his wish to kill Alma (ch. 199).

Order vs freedom.evidence: The Order's discipline is respected under Komui, but Central's control is condemned and Allen leaves (ch. 205-212).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Chosen family (Mana, friends, Komui and Lenalee) outranks the institution, but Allen still fights for the world and calls the Order home.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: The church hierarchy (Central, Pope's orders) is critiqued; Exorcists and staff treat each other as equals.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Faith and the taboo on raising the dead are taken seriously, while the church institution is critiqued and lore keeps being rewritten.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Wartime survival frames life; Allen's clowning and kindness are small acts of self-expression.

folkways.japan: The Western Catholic setting is a Gothic backdrop borrowed from Europe, as is common in Japanese popular culture; the emphasis on group bonds, the senpai-style relationship with Komui and the generals, and Kanda as a samurai-inspired figure (Wikipedia) reflect Japanese norms rather than the story's own argument.

delivery.evidence: Wikipedia notes the Order is later shown morally unclear and the Noah show hidden depths; no review found calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its message about grief and mercy rides on the premise itself, and both the Order and the Noah get sympathetic and cruel members.

personified.ideology: Mercy for every soul; keep walking
Institutional ends justify any means
Grief turned into war on God and the world
Exorcists destroy rather than save

entry.dominant: Christian (setting and reworked imagery), Dharmic-style non-attachment (my own framing), Classical virtue ethics, Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued), Existentialism.

series.title: Blue Exorcist
series.warning: Chapter 77 shows hypnotically forced sexual contact involving a 15-year-old; the story frames it as abuse.

entry.heading: Blue Exorcist
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is chosen, not inherited: you are not your father's blood. Loving the family that raised you, trusting your friends and protecting people, including the outcasts and the demons who do no harm, is what makes you human.

frames.aligns: Evil (Satan, the Blue Night) is framed as evil and resisted; a priest-father's self-giving love; mercy and acceptance for an outcast.
frames.concerns: The Church is fictionalized as a Vatican-run Order that hides crimes and clones bodies for demon kings; sacramentals and scripture work like spells; Satan is given a sympathetic origin; Fujimoto's death is self-inflicted (CCC 2280-2283, weighed against laying down one's life). The ch. 77 scene and fan service (CCC 2523-2525 on modesty).

frames.aligns: Struggle against inherited evil; repentance and reconciliation between brothers; a father's sacrifice.
frames.concerns: Holy things (holy water, crosses, scripture) used as weapons and holy water made from a demon (TV Tropes) touch the reverence owed to sacred things; evil spirits are real in the tradition, so a half-demon hero and friendly demons blur the line; nepsis makes the fan service and ch. 77 a concern.

frames.aligns: Clear good and evil; loyalty and sacrificial love; a hero who refuses his father's evil.
frames.concerns: Satan given sympathy and a love story; God absent from a Christian-imagery world; scripture as incantation. Views vary by congregation (soul liberty).

frames.aligns: Depicts evil without endorsing it; StoryScanner praises "Rin's choice of good despite his heritage" and "Shiro's sacrificial love."
frames.concerns: StoryScanner sees a "syncretic, relativistic outlook that treats different religious paths as equally valid" and a portrayal that "diverges from Christian theology."

frames.aligns: Spiritual warfare imagery; courage against evil.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": demon contracts, summoning familiars, magic circles, a hero who carries Satan's power, all shown as normal tools. Views range between churches.

frames.aligns: Common grace allows valuing a non-Christian's craft; inherited corruption that must be resisted.
frames.concerns: God's sovereignty absent; scripture used as magic; sympathetic Satan; suicide-adjacent scenes (WLC Q136); WLC Q139 on lascivious pictures for the fan service.

frames.aligns: Law and gospel echo: Rin cannot remove what he was born with but is accepted anyway; vocation of protecting others.
frames.concerns: Grace in the story comes only from people; sacraments treated as tools. LCMS and WELS families tend to be stricter than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Prevenient-grace echo: anyone, even a demon's son, can choose good; works of mercy for outcasts.
frames.concerns: Wesley's rule on "diversions" and books that do not lead toward God; fan service; the occult system. Holiness churches more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: Judged by its framing of good and evil, as in the Lewis and Sayers tradition; redemption shape; critique of hypocrisy in an institution.
frames.concerns: Sacred props as fantasy tools; sympathetic Satan; Fujimoto's self-killing; ch. 77.

frames.aligns: Distrust of a church allied with power and violence fits the critique of the Order; compassion for enemies.
frames.concerns: Violence is the heroes' main tool; a "church militant" with guns and swords; occult content. Old Order groups avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Family as central; a father's love; agency: Rin chooses who he becomes.
frames.concerns: Satan humanized and loved; occult system; fan service and ch. 77 against For the Strength of Youth.

frames.aligns: Critique of institutional abuse and cover-ups; scapegoating of a woman as "witch"; prejudice against Rin by "blood."

frames.concerns: Spirits and demons as allies and familiars; a sympathetic Satan conflicts with the Great Controversy view of Satan as the deceiver; "by beholding we become changed."

frames.aligns: Family love and loyalty; hypocrisy of a corrupt religious body exposed.
frames.concerns: Spiritism and demon contracts are central (Galatians 5:19-21); violence as the hero's path (Psalm 11:5).

frames.aligns: Love overcomes hatred; a father's love outlasts his death.
frames.concerns: Evil, possession and fear shown as real and powerful; suicide scenes.

frames.aligns: Protecting life and family; Section 13's unethical experiments condemned.
frames.concerns: Sorcery and spirit contracts (Deuteronomy 18:10-11); Christian ritual central to the setting; tzniut makes the fan service and ch. 77 a concern; suicide scenes. Many Haredi homes avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Compassion for the outsider; critique of persecution ("witch" branding); repair between brothers.
frames.concerns: Occult system; suicide scenes; modesty values.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam echo in coexistence; justice for the scapegoated; critique of unethical science.
frames.concerns: Ch. 77; suicide scenes. The villain group is called the Illuminati; no antisemitic coding was reported in sources opened, but families attentive to conspiracy tropes may note the name.

frames.aligns: Family loyalty, patience, protecting the weak; jinn-like demons that can be good or bad parallel Islamic teaching on jinn.
frames.concerns: Magic and demon pacts (sihr) treated as useful; Satan (Iblis's counterpart in name) given love and sympathy; suicide scenes (Qur'an 4:29); lowering the gaze (24:30-31) for the fan service.

frames.aligns: Dharma: doing one's duty despite birth; family duty; fighting evil forces.
frames.concerns: Few message conflicts; some apply the Gita's tamasic quality to the gore.

frames.aligns: The Kyoto temple's sutras and monks treated with respect; compassion for demons; Rin trains with a spirit named for a Buddhist wisdom king (Kongo Ucchusma, Wikipedia).
frames.concerns: Killing as the main solution; Buddhist deities classed as "demons."

frames.aligns: Saint-soldier echo: defending the weak; anger, ego and attachment shown in villains.
frames.concerns: Little in message; violence and fan service may be discussed.

frames.aligns: Oneness and unity: Yuri's dream of human-demon coexistence; prejudice condemned.
frames.concerns: Constant combat; the "chaste and holy life" standard for fan service.

frames.aligns: Inari shrine maidens and fox spirits treated with respect; Izumo's view that spirits are judged one by one (Game Rant).
frames.concerns: Kami and folk gods classed as "demons"; a local dragon god of lake legend (Hachirotaro) cast as an abuser.

frames.aligns: A woman branded "witch" by a church is shown as the wronged party (Anime Rants); nature spirits and familiars are allies.
frames.concerns: Pagan gods (Loki, Greco-Roman figures) recast as demons (TV Tropes).

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness precepts: honor parents, help others; cruelty condemned.
Prejudice by "blood" condemned; institutional abuse and bodily autonomy (Yuri) critiqued; strong women's arcs.
frames.concerns: Ch. 77 involving a minor, child Shura's flashback, adult fan service that Kato chose (TV Tropes), CSM's "sex objects" note.

frames.aligns: Identity by choice, not birth; critique of dogma, cover-ups and unethical science alike; the supernatural read as fantasy.
frames.concerns: Suicide scenes need safe-messaging talk; ch. 77.
