frames.aligns: A devoted father, brotherhood, duty, courage, discipline of training.
frames.concerns: A Christian institution shown as corrupt; a hero with Satan's power; religious conservatives may object to the premise.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth even of demons and outcasts; interfaith respect; free search for truth.
Hypocritical religious authority is challenged; bodily autonomy (Satanic Temple Tenet 3) is the wrong done to Yuri; compassion and justice (Tenets 1-2).
frames.concerns: Satan is a mass-murdering fantasy villain, not the symbol of rebellion and the self the Church of Satan uses; the hero's goal is to defeat him. No Satanists are stereotyped.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Rin answers insults with fists early on, but the story values earning trust over defending pride; Bon's anger at Rin is resolved by honesty, not a duel (ch. 26).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Training, exams and ranks are valued, but the Order's hidden rules are shown abusing people (Section 13; Rin's imprisonment, v7); heroes break orders to do right.

Civic vs kin.evidence: The twins and their foster father are the core; Satan's "blood" claim is rejected in favor of chosen family. Inclusion of outsiders (demons, Rin) keeps it from pure clan loyalty.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Ranks and Meister titles exist, but the top of the hierarchy (Grigori, Paladin) is shown as prejudiced or complicit; respect is earned.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Religious practice (Christian, Buddhist, Shinto) works and is respected, while religious institutions are critiqued; science is shown as powerful and dangerous.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Acceptance of difference and being yourself (Rin) are celebrated, within a world of constant danger and duty.

folkways.japan: Exorcist ranks, a cram-school setting, senpai-kohai respect and temple-family duty (Bon's line in Kyoto) reflect Japanese school and family norms; the Christian Vatican imagery is used as an exotic genre setting, as Kato noted that Japan is less sensitive to biblical references than Western countries (ANN, 2011).

delivery.evidence: Kato: "There isn't a 'high' message in it" (ANN, 2011). StoryScanner: it "does not overtly mock Christian faith." No review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its messages about choosing your own path and accepting outsiders come through character arcs, while each faction, including the Order and the Illuminati, has both sympathetic and cruel members.

personified.ideology: Identity by choice, not birth
Purity by force; hatred of demon blood
Immortality and a new order through science
Compassion and coexistence with demons

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Communitarianism, Classical virtue ethics, Pagan / occult, Christian (as setting).

series.title: Sun-Ken Rock
series.warning: Sources report a 16-year-old character having sex with an adult and a 15-year-old doing porn work; whether these are drawn is unconfirmed.

entry.heading: Sun-Ken Rock
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is to use your strength to protect the weak and keep faith with the people who follow you, to judge people by their souls rather than by what has been done to their bodies, and in the end to let go of revenge.

content.framing: Mixed: protective violence endorsed; cruelty condemned
Sexual violence condemned in the story; fan service endorsed

frames.aligns: Rape, trafficking and the abuse of the young are shown as evil (Inter Mirifica 7 allows depicting evil to show it as evil); Ken's claim that the victim keeps her dignity echoes the Church's teaching that dignity cannot be taken away; renouncing revenge.
frames.concerns: The hero's business includes prostitution and sex shops, presented as better-run rather than wrong; fornication and fan service treated as normal; violence as the answer; CCC 2523-2525 on modesty and permissiveness.

frames.aligns: Protection of the weak; mercy toward Yumin; letting go of revenge.
frames.concerns: Nepsis (guarding the senses) weighs heavily on constant fan service and sexual violence; sin is rarely named as sin.

frames.aligns: Evil acts are punished; loyalty and courage.
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 test fails on sexual content and gore; crime enterprise glamorized. Soul liberty: families decide; many would not choose it.

frames.aligns: Defending the oppressed (Psalm 82:3-4); Ken's teaching that the victim is not defiled resembles grace.
frames.concerns: No repentance from the crime life until the very end; women used as fan service; sexual violence as spectacle (ANN).
Holiness standards: pervasive nudity, sexual content and violence; no spiritual element to weigh beyond that.

frames.aligns: Human sin shown at every level of society (gangs, state, business); common grace in Ken's loyalty and mercy.
frames.concerns: Westminster Larger Catechism Q139 lists lascivious books and pictures; the hero's power grows by sin.

frames.aligns: Law exposes sin: abusers fall; vocation of protecting neighbors.
frames.concerns: Confessional families (LCMS, WELS) would weigh the sexual content heavily; ELCA readers less so.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy to the poor (the food-stall owner); exposure of exploitation of women.
frames.concerns: Wesley's rule against books that do not "tend to the knowledge or love of God"; holiness churches would avoid it.

frames.aligns: Good and evil are distinguished in what the story condemns (rape, trafficking, exploitation).
frames.concerns: Fan service and sexual violence as spectacle; a crime boss as role model.
Violence is heroic throughout; worldliness at its height.
For the Strength of Youth: the sexual content, nudity and violence are what the guide asks youth to avoid; chastity mocked in gags.

frames.aligns: Exposure of K-pop exploitation, trafficking, racism toward migrants, and Korea's Vietnam War record.
frames.concerns: Women as victims and fan service (ANN critics); an abuser (Yan) forgiven and kept in charge of the idols (TV Tropes).

frames.aligns: Ken gives up smoking and trains his body.
frames.concerns: Fundamental Belief 22 and "by beholding we become changed": constant violence and sexual content.
jw.org's test: violence (Psalm 11:5) and sexual immorality (Galatians 5:19-21) throughout.
Fear, violence and degradation are given great power over thought.

frames.aligns: Ken's teaching that a victim is not defiled; condemnation of abusers.
frames.concerns: Tzniut and nivul peh: pervasive immodesty and coarse humor; many Haredi homes would not admit it.
Immodesty and sexual violence as drama.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam themes: trafficking, migrants, war guilt.
Protection of the weak and of women's honor (in the story's own terms); justice against oppressors.
frames.concerns: Lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31): nudity and sexual content throughout; alcohol, gambling (the casino) and prostitution as the hero's businesses.

frames.aligns: Kshatriya-like duty to protect; consequences for adharma.
frames.concerns: Tamasic content (violence, lust) that many families limit.

frames.aligns: The ending renounces revenge; the monk-trainer; compassion for the poor.
frames.concerns: Killing and lust drive the plot, against the first and third precepts.

frames.aligns: Saint-soldier ideal of protecting the weak.
frames.concerns: Kaam (lust) and krodh (anger) shown as admirable or comic.

frames.aligns: Opposition to racism toward migrants; justice.
frames.concerns: Shoghi Effendi's call to a "chaste and holy life"; violence as the main tool.

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) of Ken; loyalty and gratitude.
frames.concerns: Blood and defilement throughout; yakuza culture.

frames.aligns: Way to Happiness precepts: protect the weak, be industrious, don't harm others of good will.
Exposure of K-pop exploitation, migrant trafficking and war crimes; victim not blamed (Miss Yoo).
frames.concerns: ANN's Friedman: violence against women as "flavoring" and "incel-friendly"; Silverman: sexual violence against most women is "not acceptable"; documented teen sexual backstories; an abuser forgiven.

frames.aligns: Reason over revenge (the ending, inspired by the Paris victim's family); human dignity apart from the body.
frames.concerns: Cruelty as spectacle; might as the means.

frames.aligns: Honor, loyalty, courage, protecting women and the weak; a man who keeps his word.
frames.concerns: The hero is a criminal; lawful authority (police, state) shown as corrupt; sexual libertinism.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of victims and migrants; justice.
Distrust of the state; self-made power; rebellion against corrupt authority.
frames.concerns: Harm to the vulnerable (Satanic Temple tenets) shown often; the story's ethic is self-sacrifice for others, not self-interest.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Insults and attacks are answered with fists; Ken repays kindness and avenges harm personally (fan wiki; TV Tropes).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Ken and the gang live outside the law and distrust the state, but keep strict internal discipline.

Civic vs kin.evidence: The gang as family; loyalty to Ken over the law (fan wiki).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Boss, right hand and henchmen; Ken lets members keep their own ambitions (fan wiki).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Little religion; honor codes and a monk's training sit beside a practical, money-minded world.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival, strength and security dominate; self-expression appears in comedy and the idol world.

folkways.japan: The boss-and-follower loyalty, the training ordeal and the yakuza codes draw on Japanese and Korean gang-fiction traditions; the Korean setting and its history (Vietnam War, migrants, K-pop) reflect the Korean-born author's own focus rather than Japanese norms.

delivery.evidence: Silverman says the Vietnam War discussions clash with the tone; reviewers quote "The state is just a gang that is legalized." No review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its ideas about the state, war guilt and protection come through speeches and backstories set inside a pulp gang story, and villains are given motives but abusers are drawn flatly.

personified.ideology: Strength exists to protect the weak
Gangs and countries are the same; pragmatic power
Revenge on a society that wronged the powerless
Law-and-order cop who becomes a yakuza heir

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (a warrior's code), Might makes right (explored), Communitarianism (gang as family), Pragmatism, Critical theory-style social critique (my own framing).

series.title: Tomodachi Game
series.warning: A 17-year-old is forced to strip and is photographed for blackmail, and her backstory includes sexual assault.

entry.heading: Tomodachi Game
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life puts friends before money and keeps trusting them even when every rule rewards betrayal, but the story also shows that the one who protects his friends best may be the most dangerous liar among them, and that he owes a full reckoning for what he has done.

content.framing: Mixed: exploitation condemned; fan service endorsed

frames.aligns: Love of money as a root of evil (1 Tim 6:10); the game that sells people is condemned; confession and the hope of forgiveness at the end; self-giving friendship (John 15:13).
frames.concerns: The hero lies, blackmails and threatens as standard method; the sexual exploitation of a minor is used as a plot "secret" and a reviewer says the show "leers" (ANN); underwear photos of a teen (CCC 2354, 2523 on modesty and the dignity of persons); gambling as a game (CCC 2413).

frames.aligns: Greed and betrayal as passions that destroy communion; confession of sin as the way back.
frames.concerns: Deceit is rewarded; nepsis (guarding the mind) weighs heavily on the sexual content involving teens.

frames.aligns: Money as an idol is named and rejected; friendship is honored; sin has consequences.
frames.concerns: The hero's manipulation is admired; sexual exploitation of a minor; teen fan service. Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Human nature is shown as fallen; every friend is capable of betrayal; the hero needs forgiveness.
frames.concerns: No grace or God in the answer; trust comes only through human cunning; sexualized content involving teens.

frames.aligns: Greed and deception exposed as destructive.
frames.concerns: The first game borrows Kokkuri-san, a spirit-calling practice, even if no spirit appears (ch. 1-3); sexual content involving teens.

frames.aligns: Total depravity has an echo: no one in the circle is innocent, the hero least of all.
frames.concerns: Cunning, not grace, is what saves; deceit is celebrated.

frames.aligns: Law exposes sin: each game reveals what the friends hid; confession of sin at the end.
frames.concerns: Lies used as the main tool of good; gambling; teen sexual content. LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Social holiness: exploitation of the poor and of children is condemned in the story's frame.
frames.concerns: Gambling (Methodist tradition opposes it); manipulation; teen sexual content.

frames.aligns: A dark morality play about greed and loyalty; the hero's guilt is faced.
frames.concerns: Admiration of cruelty; content involving teens.

frames.aligns: Simple living and mutual aid over money; the community of friends.
frames.concerns: Violence, gambling, deceit and revenge (Yuichi's finger-cutting threat on Kuroki, ch. 25) are the hero's path; worldly entertainment.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, honesty valued in the friends' best moments; repentance at the end.
frames.concerns: Gambling; sexual content involving teens; deceit rewarded; For the Strength of Youth guidance on media that is degrading.

frames.aligns: Critique of debt, poverty and a system that profits from the vulnerable.
frames.concerns: Misogyny critics see (ANN; Anime Feminist); exploitation of a girl used as plot spice; the hero's coercion of Yutori.

frames.aligns: Greed and betrayal shown as destructive.
frames.concerns: Gambling, violence, sexual content involving teens, spirit game in ch. 1-3.

frames.aligns: Honesty and loyalty praised in principle.
frames.concerns: Spiritism imagery (Kokkuri-san), gambling, violence, sexual content involving teens; the hero lies freely.

frames.aligns: Love and trust outlast fear in the friends' best moments.
frames.concerns: Fear, pain and evil presented as overwhelming and constant.

frames.aligns: Lashon hara (harmful speech) is literally the second game's mechanic (Backbiting Sugoroku) and shown as destructive; loyalty to friends.
frames.concerns: Tzniut concerns about teen fan service and underwear photos; gambling; deceit rewarded. Many Haredi homes avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Teshuvah (repentance) at the end; the harm of gossip and betrayal.
frames.concerns: Sexual exploitation of a minor as plot; deceit rewarded.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam in exposing a system that exploits the poor; moral agency.
Greed condemned; loyalty and keeping promises (Shiho keeps Yutori's secret).
frames.concerns: Gambling (maysir, Qur'an 5:90) is a game mechanic; backbiting (ghibah, Qur'an 49:12) is the second game; teen fan service and underwear photos (Qur'an 24:30-31).

frames.aligns: Karma: hidden deeds come back ("Karma Threads", ch. 113); dharma of friendship.
Craving for money as the root of suffering; the games make that visible.
frames.concerns: Right speech and right action are broken constantly by the hero; violence.

frames.aligns: Lobh (greed) shown as one of the five thieves; loyalty and sacrifice.
frames.concerns: Deceit and cruelty admired; content involving teens.

frames.aligns: Unity and trust among friends as the highest good.
frames.concerns: Backbiting, which Bahá'í writings call deeply destructive, is a game; gambling is forbidden; violence.

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) toward friends; Shibe's name means "sincerity" (fan wiki).
frames.concerns: Kokkuri-san treated as a game; defilement through blood and deceit.

frames.aligns: The threefold-return idea echoes in hidden deeds coming back.
frames.concerns: "Harm none" broken on every side; a folk spirit game used as a trap.

frames.aligns: Personal integrity and "be worthy of trust" as the stakes.
frames.concerns: The Way to Happiness precepts against deceit and harm are broken by the hero.

frames.aligns: Critique of debt, poverty and a system that profits from the vulnerable.
frames.concerns: Critics see misogyny, "weaponized rape accusations" and leering at a girl's exploitation (ANN; Anime Feminist); the hero's coercion of Yutori is admired; consent issues.

frames.aligns: Human bonds over money; reason and cunning against an exploitative system; confession and accountability at the end.
frames.concerns: Cruelty admired; content involving teens needs context.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, courage, sacrifice and keeping promises; money is not the highest good.
frames.concerns: Absent or criminal parents; the hero lies and blackmails; teen sexual content and fan service.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of every person against a game that prices them; justice for the exploited.
frames.concerns: Coercion of a teen girl by the hero; violence.

frames.aligns: Self-reliance and cunning against an arbitrary, exploitative authority (the game's management); personal responsibility.
frames.concerns: Harm to children (Eleven Rules) appears in Yutori's backstory and the hero's photos of her.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Yuichi answers attacks personally and repays Kuroki in kind with the finger-cutting game (ch. 25); disputes are never taken to police or courts except the staged trial.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The game's rules are imposed and the story celebrates beating them; but Yuichi keeps the rules exactly to win.

Civic vs kin.evidence: The circle of friends (chosen kin) comes before everyone else; Yuichi will harm outsiders freely (fan wiki).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: The friends act as equals; the hierarchy of management and wealthy watchers is condemned ("Humans Are Not Equal", ch. 49).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Calculation, psychology and reason guide the story; tradition and religion are nearly absent.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Debt, poverty and survival frame every choice.

folkways.japan: The school-class setting, the class trip fund, bullying ruled by group pressure, the shame attached to a girl's sexual past, and compensated dating (enjo kōsai) as a social problem reflect Japanese contexts; the "friends over money" motto and the reward for betrayal are the story's own argument.

delivery.evidence: ANN critics say villains' monologues constantly explain the plot ("tell-don't-show") and call the observers caricatures; no review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The friends-over-money motto is stated outright and repeated, while the game's cynical view of people is voiced at length by hosts and observers.

personified.ideology: Friends over money, by any means
Truth at any cost, even betrayal
People are products; despair is entertainment
Power through fear and pain

entry.dominant: Communitarianism (friends as the highest good), Consumerism (critiqued: money as the measure of people), Pragmatism (cunning as the way through), Might makes right (explored and critiqued), Utilitarianism (the games' logic).

series.title: I Am a Hero
series.warning: The 35-year-old lead has sex with a high-school girl.

entry.heading: I Am a Hero
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: The story questions the idea of the hero: an ordinary, fearful man survives a collapsing society mostly by luck, and what it holds up as good is small acts of care and empathy, including empathy for the infected, rather than heroic deeds. It leaves the reader asking whether surviving is the same as living well.

content.framing: Mixed: sexual slavery is shown as abuse; the lead's sexual acts with Oda and with Hiromi are framed as romance or comfort

frames.aligns: Dignity of victims; Oda's slavery shown as abuse; Hideo protecting Hiromi; empathy even for the infected.
frames.concerns: An adult's sexual act with a minor presented as romance; Inter Mirifica 7 asks that evil not be made attractive; CCC 2354 and 2389 on sexual abuse of minors; no hope beyond survival.

frames.aligns: Struggle with fear and despair is constant; small acts of care.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis) makes the gore and sexual content a heavy concern; the adult-teen relationship is not framed as sin.

frames.aligns: Clear evil in the outlet tyrants and Kurusu's cult.
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 fails for most families; the sexual act with a teen is not condemned within the story. Each congregation is self-governing, so views vary.

frames.aligns: Many distinguish depicting sin from endorsing it: slavery and cult violence are shown as evil.
frames.concerns: The adult-teen relationship is the line most families draw; Romans 14 conscience does not usually extend to it.

frames.aligns: Courage under terror; evil is visible.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": a prophet-cult, despair, and sexual content involving a minor. Holiness standards make it a strong concern.

frames.aligns: Depravity under pressure (the outlet rooftop, the cult) has a strong echo; common grace in Hiromi's empathy.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 lists "lascivious... books, pictures" among sins; the adult-teen act is unframed; providence is absent.

frames.aligns: Law without gospel: no one is saved by effort; neighbor-love in small acts.
frames.concerns: No gospel offered; LCMS and WELS families much more cautious than ELCA, but the minor's involvement is a concern across the range.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy; care for the weak.
frames.concerns: Wesley's rule against diversions not usable "in the name of the Lord Jesus"; the sexual content with a teen.

frames.aligns: A literary tradition that judges dark works by framing; tyranny and slavery framed as evil.
frames.concerns: The adult-teen act is framed as romance rather than as harm, which fails the framing test.

frames.aligns: Hiromi's empathy for the infected; the gun brings survival, not goodness.
frames.concerns: Violence as the way to survive; Old Order groups avoid such media entirely.

frames.aligns: Protecting the vulnerable; agency in chaos.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth asks for media that invites the Spirit; the 16+ rating, gore and sexual content with a teen put it far outside youth guidance.

frames.aligns: Critique of social failure, bullying, and the abuse of Oda.
frames.concerns: The vulnerable (a teenager) are not protected by the story's framing; power imbalance unexamined.
Fundamental Belief 22 and "by beholding we become changed" (2 Corinthians 3:18); impure content including a minor.
jw.org counsel on violence (Psalm 11:5) and immorality (Galatians 5:19-21); both are central.
The story dwells on fear, disease, bodily destruction and sensuality ("Stand porter at the door of thought," Science and Health 392).

frames.aligns: Saving life; protecting a young person from danger.
frames.concerns: Tzniut and nivul peh make the sexual content and gore a heavy concern; many Haredi homes restrict such media entirely.

frames.aligns: Dignity of victims; critique of tyranny.
frames.concerns: Degrading sexual content; an adult-minor relationship framed as romance.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam echoes in empathy for the infected; critique of cults.
frames.concerns: Exploitation of women and a minor shown without critique.

frames.aligns: Patience (sabr) under trial; protecting the weak.
frames.concerns: "Lowering the gaze" (Qur'an 24:30-31); zina; a minor involved; alcohol.
Tamasic qualities (Gita 17) in gore and sexual content; no path beyond survival.

frames.aligns: Suffering, impermanence and loss of self (the hive mind); compassion for the infected.
frames.concerns: The third precept against sexual misconduct, with a minor; killing as survival breaks the first precept.

frames.aligns: Courage for others; the five vices shown in the cult and the tyrants.
frames.concerns: Lust (kaam) involving a minor is presented without critique.
Shoghi Effendi's call to a "chaste and holy life" against degrading art.

frames.aligns: Aokigahara and Mount Fuji as settings; sincerity in small acts.
frames.concerns: Blood and death as kegare (impurity) throughout; harm to a young person. No doctrine on fiction.

frames.aligns: Nature reclaiming Tokyo in the epilogue; empathy for the infected.
frames.concerns: The Rede ("harm none"); sexual exploitation and a minor involved.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness precepts: "Do not murder"; tyranny and cult violence condemned.
frames.concerns: No content code for fiction; the minor's involvement conflicts with protecting children.

frames.aligns: Critique of social failure, bullying and sexual slavery.
frames.concerns: Consent, age and power imbalance: an adult-teen sexual act framed as a bond (Fandom Post: "underage sex").

frames.aligns: Meaning made without God; empathy across the human/ZQN line; no supernatural answer.
frames.concerns: Exploitation of a minor shown without critique; cruelty for shock.

frames.aligns: Courage, protection, critique of decadent and lawless groups.
frames.concerns: Undermines the protection of the young; contempt for order without a positive alternative.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of every person, even the infected; justice for Oda.
Distrust of prophets and cults (Kurusu); individuals make their own meaning.
frames.concerns: The Eleven Rules condemn harm to children and unwanted sexual advances; the adult-teen act fits the first.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Revenge and status are not celebrated; Kurusu's cult and Iura's rule run on fear and face, and both fall.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Every order built after the collapse becomes tyranny (outlet rooftop; Kuki Shogunate), while social order before it fails to react (Kotaku).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Small bonds (Hideo, Hiromi, Oda) matter most, but they are chosen companions rather than kin.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Hierarchies (Iura over the rooftop; the cult) are shown as abusive.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No faith or tradition offers an answer; religion appears only as a cult.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival is everything; the ending is a man hunting to live.

folkways.japan: The "loser" manga assistant, gun rarity, Aokigahara, NEETs and hikikomori, and Kotaku's reading of a society too bound to order and peace to react all reflect contemporary Japanese settings. The cluster match is loose (distance above 4 for all clusters), because the story's values are mostly defined by an extreme survival setting.

delivery.evidence: Dark Horse's editor says Hanazawa "played us" about who the hero is; no review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its themes come through irony and events rather than speeches, and the title's claim to heroism is left for the reader to judge.

personified.ideology: The ordinary man who imagines himself a hero
Empathy toward the other, even the infected
Nihilistic violence and cult worship
Order by force in a survivor community

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Absurdism, Nihilism, Collectivism / authoritarianism (critiqued), Might makes right (critiqued).

series.title: Kubo Won't Let Me Be Invisible
series.native: 久保さんは僕を許さない

entry.heading: Kubo Won't Let Me Be Invisible (Nene Yukimori)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life begins when someone truly sees you: being noticed and valued by one person can give a quiet, overlooked boy friends, joy and, in the end, the courage to say what he feels.

content.frequency: Romance central; mild fan service occasional

frames.aligns: The dignity of each person (CCC 1700) shown in seeing the one everyone overlooks; friendship and courtship as care for the other; honesty in confessing love; helping a lost child.
frames.concerns: Modesty and chastity (CCC 2521-2524) for the lap-sitting tease, the lingerie and swimsuit chapters; teasing that ignores the other's discomfort.

frames.aligns: Humility (Shiraishi), attentive love, a gentle path from loneliness to communion with others.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis) against even mild flirtatious imagery; romance as the main source of meaning.

frames.aligns: Kindness, patience, honesty, no sex shown; the overlooked person valued.
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 test for the lap scene, the swimsuit and lingerie chapters; an adult's drinking (ch. 30-31); teen dating as a family decision (soul liberty).

frames.aligns: Seeing the overlooked (Luke 14:13); not judging by appearances (John 7:24); courage to speak honestly.
frames.concerns: Mild fan service; romance as the answer to loneliness.

frames.aligns: Freedom from fear and timidity (2 Timothy 1:7 echo in Shiraishi's growing courage); no occult content beyond a shrine wish stone seen as sightseeing.
frames.concerns: Holiness standards on modesty and physical contact between unmarried teens.

frames.aligns: Common grace: a gentle, well-made story by a non-Christian; the worth of the ordinary person.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 on lascivious pictures applied to the lap-sitting tease and swimsuit chapter; teasing that tempts or embarrasses.

frames.aligns: Vocation in ordinary school life; the Eighth Commandment's "put the best construction on everything" in how Kubo reads Shiraishi.
frames.concerns: Mild flirtation; LCMS and WELS families may be more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: "Do good" to the excluded; social holiness in small acts (the lost child, the elderly person in Kyoto); welcome of the quiet person.
frames.concerns: Holiness churches more cautious about romance-centered entertainment, physical teasing and the picnic drinking.

frames.aligns: Kindness, belonging and honest courtship framed as good.
frames.concerns: Teasing that pushes past someone's comfort.

frames.aligns: Humility, gentleness, community and no violence at all.
frames.concerns: Separation from worldly media makes any secular manga a concern for Old Order families; flirtation, swimsuits and physical contact; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Ministering to the one; kindness; a chaste courtship with no kiss reported; warm family scenes.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth counsel on dating (group activities, waiting until 16), modesty (swimsuit and lingerie chapters) and the Word of Wisdom (adult drinking at the picnic).

frames.aligns: Inclusion of the overlooked; empathy for loneliness; a girl who takes the lead.
frames.concerns: Consent and boundaries: Shiraishi is "visibly unsettled" by some teasing (Anime Feminist); critics say Kubo exists only around him (But Why Tho).
Fundamental Belief 22 ("highest quality" entertainment) and "by beholding we become changed" applied to romance-centered teasing; temperance and the picnic drinking.

frames.aligns: Kindness, honesty, no violence, no spiritism in the plot.
frames.concerns: jw.org counsel that dating is for those ready to marry, so a high-school romance as the story's goal conflicts; physical teasing; shrine visits and a wish stone (ch. 133-134), even as sightseeing.

frames.aligns: Right thinking about oneself replaces the belief that one is "invisible"; love dissolves fear.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; dwelling on embarrassment.

frames.aligns: Kavod habriyot (dignity of each person), hesed, kind speech, not shaming others.
frames.concerns: Tzniut and the laws on touch between unmarried young men and women (lap scene, pinky-holding); swimsuit and lingerie chapters; mixed-sex dating as entertainment. Many Haredi homes would not have the series.
Modesty in the flirtatious scenes; families decide on teen dating.
Consent and boundaries in the teasing.

frames.aligns: Kindness, gentleness, honesty, warm family life, help to strangers.
frames.concerns: Free mixing and dating between unmarried teens; lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) for the swimsuit and lingerie chapters and physical contact (lap scene); alcohol at the picnic.

frames.aligns: Kindness, patience, gentle courage; family affection (Shiraishi and Seita).
frames.concerns: Some families apply the Gita's categories to romance-centered media; views on teen dating vary by community.

frames.aligns: Compassion and attention to others' suffering; right speech; gentle growth in confidence; Kiyomizu-dera shown as a place of kindness (helping an elderly person, ch. 138).
frames.concerns: Attachment to being noticed and to romance as the source of happiness.

frames.aligns: Sangat (good company) as a cure for isolation; humility; seva in small acts (Shiraishi caring for the school flower beds, ch. 33, 81).
frames.concerns: Kaam (lust) concerns in flirtatious scenes; teen dating against many families' practice; alcohol at the picnic.

frames.aligns: Unity, kindness to all, a chaste romance, truthfulness.
frames.concerns: The call to a "chaste and holy life" for the flirtatious teasing; parental consent and marriage norms versus casual teen dating; alcohol at the picnic.

frames.aligns: Harmony (wa), sincerity (makoto), gratitude; ordinary school and seasonal life; Fushimi Inari and its omokaru wish stone visited on the class trip (ch. 133-134).
frames.concerns: Little to raise; whether the shrine visit is shown with respect is unverified.

frames.aligns: "Harm none" in a gentle cast; acceptance of the quiet person.
Communication and affinity (the ARC triangle) grow between the leads; The Way to Happiness precepts (help others, be worthy of trust); no psychiatry.
Empathy for loneliness; a girl who takes the initiative; low-stakes kindness.
frames.concerns: Consent and boundaries: Anime Feminist says the teasing "feels mean-spirited" and that Shiraishi is "visibly unsettled"; critics call Kubo a "manic pixie dream girl" without her own wants (But Why Tho; Eisenbeis, ANN); mild fan service with teen characters.

frames.aligns: Human connection as the source of meaning; confidence grown through relationships; no supernatural framing.
frames.concerns: Teasing as a growth method without asking.

frames.aligns: Patience, manners, loyalty, a slow courtship ending in an honest confession, warm family life.
frames.concerns: Mild flirtatious fan service; teen dating presented as the goal.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth and dignity of the overlooked; community as healer.
Self-assertion: the "mob" learns to claim his place; empathy (Satanic Temple Tenet 1).
frames.concerns: Bodily autonomy (Tenet 3) in teasing that pushes past discomfort; Church of Satan readers may find the hero's dependence on another for self-worth weak.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Worth is inherent: the story insists the overlooked boy matters; no insults are avenged, and the rival suitor is simply turned down (ch. 115).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Characters live inside school routines, committees and group events without resisting them.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Friends and classmates matter as much as family; family scenes are warm (Seita, Yoshie) but secondary.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: The class's "invisible" member is raised to equal standing; ordinary school deference to teachers.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Secular daily life with school and seasonal customs (Valentine's Day, festival, class trip to shrines and temples); no religion guides choices.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Being seen, emotional honesty and quality of relationships are the core values.

folkways.japan: The fear of standing out and the comfort of blending in, school committees, sports day, the culture festival, Valentine's and White Day gift customs, the second-year class trip to Kyoto and Nara, and the confession (kokuhaku) as the formal start of a relationship are Japanese school norms that frame the story more than they form its message. The "mob" label comes from anime and game vocabulary for background extras.

delivery.evidence: Reviewers call it "pure fluff" and "dirt simple" (ANN); no opened review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The idea that everyone deserves to be seen is carried by sight gags and small daily moments rather than stated lessons.

personified.ideology: Every overlooked person deserves to be seen
Quiet humility growing into courage

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Communitarianism, Expressive individualism (all weak; my own framing).

series.title: Tomie
series.warning: In chapter 1 a 15-year-old is in a sexual relationship with her adult teacher (sourcing is thin).

entry.heading: Tomie
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: The story promotes no good life. It shows desire for beauty and possession as a force that turns people into murderers, and it offers no cure; the few who survive are those who are not drawn in, such as a boy who prefers a plain girl and a man still faithful to his dead girlfriend.

frames.aligns: Lust, envy and wrath lead to ruin, never to happiness; evil is not presented as good (Inter Mirifica 7).
frames.concerns: The abuse of a minor by a teacher and a child kissed ("Boy") are depicted without justice; despair as the ending; the body treated as disposable (CCC 2288-2291).

frames.aligns: Desire for a beautiful image as a passion that consumes the soul.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses: the book dwells on seduction and dismembered bodies; no repentance or light.

frames.aligns: Sin is shown with consequences; lust and jealousy lead to death (James 1:14-15).
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 fails on most pages; abuse of a minor; nudity. Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Can be engaged as a portrait of lust's power; nothing evil is called good. A Christian podcast (Cinematic Doctrine) engages it through the image of God in man and woman.
frames.concerns: Sexual exploitation of a teen and a child; no grace or hope; demonic "succubus" framing.

frames.aligns: Shows the destructive spiritual power of seduction.
frames.concerns: A succubus-like being that cannot be resisted or destroyed is the kind of content this tradition weighs most heavily ("open door"); sexual content involving minors.

frames.aligns: Depravity shown honestly; common grace allows valuing Ito's craft.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 on lascivious pictures; abuse of minors; no judgment or grace.
No gospel; abuse of minors; confessional (LCMS, WELS) families more cautious than ELCA.
Wesley's rule on books that do not "tend to the knowledge or love of God"; abuse of minors; holiness churches more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: The gothic and literary horror tradition judges by framing; lust and violence are never glamorized as good.
frames.concerns: Exploitation of a minor in story 1 and a child in "Boy"; misogyny debate; no redemption. Range across Episcopal and ACNA families.

frames.aligns: No heroic violence: killing is always shown as ruin.
frames.concerns: Separation from worldly media (Schleitheim 4); sexual content and abuse of minors. MC USA families vary.
For the Strength of Youth: media that does not invite the Spirit; sexualized minors and nudity weigh heavily.

frames.aligns: Attention to violence against women and the abuse of the vulnerable can be drawn out.
frames.concerns: Anime Feminist's and Berlatsky's charge that the stories blame the woman; abuse of a minor without justice.
"By beholding we become changed" applied to seduction and gore; Fundamental Belief 22.
jw.org: entertainment featuring what God hates (violence, immorality, the demonic): all three are central.
Fear, mortality and evil presented as unkillable powers, the reverse of the teaching that they are unreal.

frames.aligns: The yetzer hara (evil inclination) shown in full force.
frames.concerns: Tzniut and the nudity; sexual content involving minors; violence to the body; many Haredi homes avoid such media entirely.

frames.aligns: Jealousy and obsession lead to ruin.
frames.concerns: Abuse of a minor; nudity; no teshuvah (repentance).

frames.aligns: Informed autonomy; the gender critique can be engaged; no antisemitic stereotypes reported.
frames.concerns: Exploitation of a minor and a child needs context; misogyny debate.

frames.aligns: Desire and envy shown as destructive.
frames.concerns: Lowering the gaze (24:30-31) and the nudity; zina and its abuse of a minor; despair.

frames.aligns: Kama (desire), krodha (anger) and moha (delusion) shown as destroyers.
frames.concerns: Tamasic content under Gita 17; sexual content involving minors; no dharma or release.

frames.aligns: Craving for a beautiful form leads directly to suffering; the endless rebirth of Tomie mirrors samsara.
frames.concerns: What it feeds the mind (right mindfulness); sexual content involving minors; no path out.

frames.aligns: Lust (kaam), anger, attachment and ego (four of the five vices) shown as ruinous.
frames.concerns: Sexual content involving minors; no chardi kala.
A "chaste and holy life" against a story built on seduction; abuse of minors.

frames.aligns: A vengeful, unkillable spirit-like woman echoes onryō tales; pollution (kegare) of death and blood.
frames.concerns: Kegare without purification; no kami or shrine; sexual content involving minors.

frames.aligns: Female power feared by men can be read as a critique of how such power is demonized.
frames.concerns: "Harm none": harm is everywhere; Tomie as succubus stereotype of dangerous female power; harm to children.

frames.aligns: No psychiatry shown as a cure.
frames.concerns: Characters are helpless "effects" of her power; sexual content involving minors.

frames.aligns: The gender reading: possession and male violence exposed (Taylor via Wikipedia).
frames.concerns: Anime Feminist and Berlatsky: the stories excuse male violence by blaming the woman; exploitation of a 15-year-old and a child; consent.

frames.aligns: Shows how jealousy and obsession destroy rational people; read as fiction.
frames.concerns: Exploitation and cruelty with no human answer.

frames.aligns: Vanity and lust punished; marriage broken by temptation is shown as tragedy.
frames.concerns: The good, the true and the beautiful are absent; beauty is evil; adults who should protect children abuse them.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of each person, including Tomie, can be discussed.
Tomie's defiance and refusal to be owned; self-interest openly shown.
frames.concerns: The Eleven Rules oppose harm to children: the teacher-student abuse and the child in "Boy."

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Jealous rivalry and revenge drive the men ("Revenge," "Painter," "Top Model"), but the story never celebrates them; the vengeance always fails.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Neither order (teachers, doctors, family) nor Tomie's freedom is shown as good.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Families and classes both fail; brothers abuse their own ("Little Finger"); Tsukiko's father is a refuge ("Kiss").

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: The teacher's and doctors' authority is abused (stories 1-3); no hierarchy is honored or overturned.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Neither tradition nor science (the radiation and tissue experiments in "Basement" and "Mansion") helps.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Vanity and self-display (Tomie, Yukiko, the painter, the model) lead to ruin; survival comes from restraint and plain kindness (Fumihito).

folkways.japan: School trips, homeroom teachers, a sake brewery ("Moromi"), a mountain club ("Revenge") and the onryō (vengeful female spirit) tradition are Japanese settings and echoes; the onryō link is my own comparison. The values the story celebrates are few and not specifically Japanese.

delivery.evidence: Anime Feminist and Berlatsky say men's violence is framed sympathetically and Tomie is blamed; Taylor (via Wikipedia) reads it as critique.
delivery.note: The stories argue nothing outright; how fairly they treat women and men is the main point readers dispute.

personified.ideology: Beauty as power over others
Adult abuse of power
Loyalty and honesty

entry.dominant: Feminism (contested), Nihilism, Hedonism (critiqued).

entry.heading: Fly Me to the Moon (Kenjiro Hata)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is a faithful, everyday marriage: two people who commit first and then learn to love each other through small daily kindnesses, so that even an endless, lonely life can find a home.

content.frequency: Romance central; fan service and innuendo occasional
content.framing: Romance endorsed; fan service and innuendo comic

frames.aligns: Marriage as a lifelong covenant of mutual self-giving (CCC 1601, 1643); fidelity; suffering met with love; despair (Tsukasa's wish to die) shown as tragedy, not as a solution.
frames.concerns: Free and informed consent and maturity for marriage (CCC 1625-1628) when they marry after one meeting; modesty (CCC 2521-2524) in the bath, sauna and towel scenes; a 15-year-old's sexual jokes; the secret she keeps from her husband.

frames.aligns: Marriage as a path of mutual salvation; patience and humility; longing for an end to endless earthly life echoes the Christian hope beyond death.
frames.concerns: Nepsis (guarding the eyes) for fan service; immortality sought through an elixir rather than God.

frames.aligns: Marriage honored (Hebrews 13:4); a husband who works hard and cherishes his wife; no adultery.
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 test for innuendo and bath scenes; jokes about sex from a teenager; marrying in haste; a wife hiding the truth.

frames.aligns: Covenant commitment before feelings; sacrificial love (Ephesians 5:25).
frames.concerns: Fan service and innuendo; the folk-myth framing; romance as the whole answer to despair.

frames.aligns: Faithful marriage; despair turned to hope.
frames.concerns: An elixir of immortality and moon-princess myth as the story's supernatural frame; holiness standards on modesty for the many bath, sauna and towel chapters.

frames.aligns: Common grace: a non-Christian story that honors marriage as a covenant.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 on lascivious pictures and "light behavior" for the bath scenes and innuendo.

frames.aligns: Marriage as vocation; daily service to one's spouse.
frames.concerns: Fan service and a teenager's sexual jokes; LCMS and WELS families may be more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Holy love lived in the household; care for the sick spouse.
frames.concerns: Holiness churches' caution about romance-centered entertainment and innuendo.

frames.aligns: The prayer book's purposes of marriage (mutual comfort and help) played out in daily life.
frames.concerns: Haste of the marriage; secrecy; some bath-scene humor.

frames.aligns: Simple, frugal, faithful household life; violence in the backstory shown as horror.
frames.concerns: Separation from worldly media makes any secular manga a concern for Old Order families; fan service and innuendo; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Marriage and family at the center of the good life; fidelity; devotion.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth counsel on modesty and media for the bath, sauna and towel chapters and a teen's sexual jokes; marrying very young after one meeting; the secret.

frames.aligns: Mutual care; Tsukasa choosing her own path (Silverman's "agency" reading).
frames.concerns: A teen marriage and an "underage girl" (ANN's Dupree); sex talk from underage characters (But Why Tho); traditional gender roles.

frames.aligns: Faithful marriage; thrift; no substances reported.
frames.concerns: Fundamental Belief 22 ("highest quality" entertainment) and "by beholding we become changed" for innuendo and fan service; immortality myth versus the Adventist view of conditional immortality.

frames.aligns: Marriage honored; spouses caring for each other; no spiritism practiced.
frames.concerns: jw.org counsel to be "past the bloom of youth" and to know a partner well before marriage; an immortality elixir; bath scenes and sexual jokes; violence in flashback.

frames.aligns: Love casts out fear; healing of a damaged self-image.
frames.concerns: Dwelling on injury and despair in the backstory.

frames.aligns: Marriage and shalom bayit (peace in the home) as central goods; kindness between spouses.
frames.concerns: Tzniut for the bath, sauna and towel scenes; a marriage without family involvement; secular media in Haredi homes.
Age and haste of the marriage; secrecy.

frames.aligns: Marriage (nikah) as half of faith; mercy and affection between spouses (Qur'an 30:21); no premarital relationship.
frames.concerns: Lowering the gaze (24:30-31) for the bath, sauna and towel scenes; marriage without a guardian (wali) or family involvement; images of living beings for stricter families.

frames.aligns: Grihastha (householder stage) and dharma of spouses; devotion.
frames.concerns: Haste; some apply sattvic/tamasic categories to romance and fan service.

frames.aligns: Impermanence and suffering: an immortal who longs to end endless life is a vivid teaching image; compassion.
frames.concerns: Attachment to a beloved and to romance as the answer to suffering.

frames.aligns: Anand Karaj ideal of two bodies, one soul; householder life (grihasti) honored.
frames.concerns: Kaam (lust) in innuendo and fan service; marriage without family.

frames.aligns: Marriage as "a fortress for well-being"; fidelity; unity.
frames.concerns: Bahá'í law requires the consent of living parents for marriage, which the story treats lightly (Nasa tells his parents afterwards, fan wiki); the call to a "chaste and holy life" for fan service.

frames.aligns: Musubi (binding), sincerity (makoto) and gratitude in the marriage; Kaguya folklore and the Tsukuyomi name treated with affection, not mockery, as far as reported.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; confirm the shrine and kami references are respectful.

frames.aligns: Love and partnership; myth and moon imagery honored.
Communication and affinity grow between the spouses; The Way to Happiness precepts (be worthy of trust, fulfil obligations).
Mutual care; no domestic abuse; consent shown in slow intimacy.
frames.concerns: ANN critics on the teen marriage ("an underage girl he barely knows," Dupree); But Why Tho on sex talk from underage characters and youthful art; traditional roles.

frames.aligns: Meaning built through human love and work; Nasa treats the elixir as a system to analyze ("relay node" theory, ch. 268; ch. 279).
Commitment before romance; husband as provider; family blessing; fidelity.
frames.concerns: Marrying very young after one meeting; Nasa skipping school; fan service and a teen's sexual jokes.

frames.aligns: Self-determination: Tsukasa chooses her marriage and seeks her own release from immortality; enjoyment of life's pleasures.
frames.concerns: Bodily autonomy (Satanic Temple Tenet 3): she never chose immortality; youth of the marriage.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: No insults are avenged; Tsukasa's one massacre (vol. 16) is shown as trauma, not honor; worth is inherent (Nasa's mocked name, Wikipedia; Himari's apology, ch. 241).

Order vs freedom.evidence: The couple make an unconventional private choice but live inside ordinary routines and laws (ward-office registration).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Marriage and family come first: parents' blessing, Tsukasa's chosen family, Tokiko's lifelong guardianship and will.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Spouses are partners; Tokiko and Nasa's parents are respected but not obeyed.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Folk tale and myth frame the story, but life choices are secular, and Nasa approaches the myth with science (ch. 268, 279).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Quality of life, enjoyment and emotional security; also work and thrift (Nasa works instead of studying).

folkways.japan: Registering a marriage by form at the ward office, the former legal marriage ages (16 and 18), the public bathhouse (sentō) and hot-spring trips, the folk tale of Kaguya-hime and Mount Fuji, and the wife's role as household manager are Japanese norms that frame the story more than they form its message.

delivery.evidence: Critics call it cute, funny and slow ("sufficiently cute and funny," ANN; "charming and refreshing," Anime UK News); none calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The value of committed marriage is shown through daily comedy rather than stated, and Chitose's opposition is treated with sympathy before she changes her mind.

personified.ideology: Commitment first; devoted married love
Longing for home and for a mortal life
Family loyalty against the outsider

entry.dominant: Traditionalism (marriage-centered), Existentialism (immortality and meaning), Classical virtue ethics (all moderate or weak; my own framing).

series.title: Alice in Borderland
series.adult_reason: Alice in Borderland: shown with a warning; VIZ rates it Mature (18+, VIZ Signature); attempted sexual assault of a high-school girl and sexual relationships involving high-school characters (fan wiki, Japanese Wikipedia, Mangapedia); deep entry scores 9
series.warning: Includes two attempted sexual assaults on a high-school girl and an adult woman seducing a high-school boy; the teen leads also have sex.

entry.heading: Alice in Borderland
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is chosen, not found: Arisu goes from wanting to escape his life to fighting to keep it, carried first by the friends who died for him and then by his love for Usagi. The story treats the will to live as something people hand to each other, and treats despair, cynicism and the Beach's pleasure-seeking as dead ends.

content.framing: Assault condemned; consensual sex not critiqued

frames.aligns: Choosing life over despair; friends laying down their lives (John 15:13); predation and cruelty shown as evil, not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7); a world between life and death that points beyond itself.
frames.concerns: Sexual activity between unmarried teens shown without comment; assault of a young woman as plot; suicide shown repeatedly (CCC 2280-2283 on life as a gift).

frames.aligns: Struggle against despair (akedia) is the core of Arisu's arc; sacrifice for others.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis) against constant killing and sexual content; the afterlife shown without God.

frames.aligns: Clear moral contrast between sacrificial friends and predators; life worth choosing.
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 test fails on gore, assault and teen sex for most families; no reference to God in the answer to despair. Each congregation decides.

frames.aligns: Depicting sin is not endorsing it: the Beach's hedonism and Niragi's predation are shown as vile. Arisu's search for why he survived opens faith conversations.
frames.concerns: Hope rests on human bonds alone; sexual content involving high-school characters; some families favor separation.
Media as an "open door": a death-realm ruled by masked game masters and a Joker figure; graphic sexual and violent content.

frames.aligns: Human depravity is on full show at the Beach; common grace lets adults value serious work by non-Christians.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 on "lascivious... books, pictures"; teen sexual content; providence replaced by a game.

frames.aligns: No one wins by merit alone; Arisu lives because others gave themselves for him, which reads as a picture of grace.
frames.concerns: Explicitness is judged by conscience; LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy (Arisu seeks treatment for his enemies); social holiness against bullying and shaming.
frames.concerns: Wesley's rule on diversions that cannot be used "in the name of the Lord Jesus"; holiness churches would avoid it.

frames.aligns: Works judged by framing: evil framed as evil, death given weight, life chosen at the end.
frames.concerns: Sexual content involving teens; an afterlife without a word on God.

frames.aligns: Rejection of the Beach's armed regime; mercy toward enemies (Niragi).
frames.concerns: Survival by violence as the frame of every game (Matthew 5:39); Old Order families avoid such media entirely.

frames.aligns: Agency and choosing life; family restored in Retry (marriage, a child).
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth on media; Mature rating, teen sexual content and assault put it outside youth guidance.

frames.aligns: Sympathetic trans character (Kuina); critique of bullying, public shaming and coercion; mercy.
frames.concerns: Sexual violence against a young woman used as plot; teen sexual content.
An in-between realm of the dying conflicts with teaching on the state of the dead; "by beholding we become changed" weighs against the content.

frames.aligns: Love of friends, protecting the weak.
frames.concerns: Violence (Psalm 11:5) and immorality are central; an in-between realm of the dead conflicts with teaching on death.

frames.aligns: Mira's claim that "nothing is real" is resisted by love and clear thought.
frames.concerns: Constant fear, death, bodily destruction; members guard thought (Science and Health 392).

frames.aligns: Choosing life (Deuteronomy 30:19); memory of the dead; saving life.
frames.concerns: Tzniut and nivul peh: sexual content, assault and profanity weigh heavily; many Haredi homes restrict such media.

frames.aligns: Choosing life; critique of public shaming (lashon hara destroys Usagi's father).
frames.concerns: Sexual violence and teen sexual content.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam echoes in rebuilding after disaster; critique of bullying and coercion.
frames.concerns: Exploitation of a young woman as plot.

frames.aligns: Patience (sabr) under trial; saving life (Qur'an 5:32); the world as a test before the hereafter.
frames.concerns: "Lowering the gaze" (24:30-31) against swimsuit fan service and sexual content; suicide shown repeatedly; no reference to God.

frames.aligns: A realm between death and rebirth; duty and sacrifice; craving and cruelty lead to ruin (the Beach).
frames.concerns: Tamasic content (Gita 17) in gore and sexual content.

frames.aligns: Suffering, impermanence and attachment are the whole story; a liminal realm with the Sanzu River image (ch. 63) echoes Buddhist teaching on death; the bardo comparison is our framing; compassion toward enemies.
frames.concerns: Killing to survive breaks the first precept; mindfulness of what feeds the mind.

frames.aligns: The five vices (lust in Niragi, anger, greed in the Hatter's card hoarding, attachment, ego) lead to ruin; courage for others.
frames.concerns: Lust and violence shown at length; no reference to the divine.

frames.aligns: Service and sacrifice; unity of survivors from all walks of life.
frames.concerns: Call to a "chaste and holy life"; constant conflict.

frames.aligns: Life valued; sincerity (makoto) in Arisu and Usagi; grief and remembrance of the dead.
frames.concerns: Blood and death as kegare (impurity) throughout. No doctrine on fiction.

frames.aligns: Respect for life; a liminal realm between worlds.
frames.concerns: The Rede ("harm none") against constant killing; non-consensual sexual violence.

frames.aligns: Will to survive; precepts "Do not murder" and "Be worthy of trust."
frames.concerns: Mira, a psychiatrist, is the final manipulator who drugs Arisu, which fits the Church's distrust of psychiatry; graphic violence.

frames.aligns: Sympathetic trans character; critique of bullying, shaming and coercion.
frames.concerns: Consent and age: assault of a high-school girl used as plot; sexual relationships involving high-school characters.

frames.aligns: Meaning made by people in a world without a stated god; reason and cooperation; choosing life without supernatural rewards.
frames.concerns: Cruelty shown for shock; the afterlife framing is outside a naturalist view.

frames.aligns: Courage, loyalty, duty to friends; marriage and family in Retry; critique of the Beach's decadence.
frames.concerns: Gore, teen sexual content and assault; a trans character presented sympathetically (a concern for some, not all).

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of every person, including Niragi; free search for meaning.
Self-determination; rejection of arbitrary authority (game masters, the Hatter); this-life focus.
frames.concerns: The Eleven Rules condemn unwanted sexual advances and harm to the young, both shown.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Public shaming destroys Usagi's father (ch. 14); revenge-driven players (Niragi) are condemned; Arisu answers enemies with mercy.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The Beach's rigid order ends in executions and fire (ch. 16-29, v4-7); the story favors free association of survivors.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Loyalty to chosen friends rather than blood kin; Arisu also seeks to save strangers and enemies.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: The Hatter's rankings are condemned; leadership among survivors is informal.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Reason and observation win games; no religious practice; an afterlife setting without doctrine.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Staying alive is the whole frame; self-expression appears mainly as the Beach's hollow leisure.

folkways.japan: School settings, youth apathy, a father's pressure to match a gifted sibling, and the public shaming of a mountaineer reflect contemporary Japanese settings; the Sanzu River image draws on Japanese Buddhist folk belief; the card-game structure and empty Tokyo are the story's own. The cluster match is loose (nearest distance about 3.6).

delivery.evidence: AniList reviewers call it a reflection on "what is the meaning of life"; no opened review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Most of the theme comes through games and deaths, but ch. 43, ch. 62 and the final chapter state the argument openly, with Mira given a full case for giving up.

personified.ideology: Life is worth choosing for others' sake
Reality is meaningless; give up
Humans are predators; revel in it
Detached rational self-interest

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Nihilism (critiqued), Secular humanism, Communitarianism.

series.title: Dead Dead Demon's Dededede Destruction
series.native: デッドデッドデーモンズデデデデデストラクション

entry.heading: Dead Dead Demon's Dededede Destruction
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life holds onto one true bond and keeps seeing the human face in people others call enemies. Leaders, media and crowds that turn fear into hatred and profit are not to be trusted, and wanting to be the hero who saves the world can be more dangerous than choosing to save one person.

frames.aligns: Human dignity of the stranger and enemy; war and propaganda judged harshly; self-giving love for one person; evil is not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7).
frames.concerns: A teacher-student dynamic that turns sexual after graduation; premarital sex shown neutrally; no transcendence or grace; a child's suicide (CCC 2280-2283).

frames.aligns: Warnings against pride and the passions of fear and hatred; mercy toward the other.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis) makes the mass-death imagery and sexual scenes a concern; a nihilistic mood with no spiritual horizon.

frames.aligns: Exposes lies by leaders and media; shows the cost of hatred and revenge.
frames.concerns: Premarital sex and a teacher relationship shown without moral framing; no faith; suicide. Each congregation decides (soul liberty).

frames.aligns: "Engaging culture": a sharp critique of fear-driven politics and scapegoating; love for an outsider.
frames.concerns: Sexual ethics outside marriage; no gospel or hope beyond human bonds; suicide shown.

frames.aligns: Exposure of deception and hatred; care for the weak.

frames.concerns: Premarital sex; teacher relationship; despair. LCMS and WELS families tend to be more cautious than ELCA.

frames.concerns: Separation from worldly media makes the gore, sex and online culture a concern; conservative groups avoid such media; MC USA families vary.
Law of chastity: premarital sex and the teacher relationship; dark tone does not "invite the Spirit"; suicide.

frames.concerns: Power imbalance in the teacher relationship (called "grooming" by Anime Feminist); the girls "drawn very young" (TCJ; Manga Bookshelf).

frames.concerns: "By beholding we become changed": mass death, sexual scenes and a nihilistic mood; Fundamental Belief 22 on entertainment.

frames.aligns: Distrust of human governments and their wars fits Witness teaching on the world's political systems.
frames.concerns: Premarital sex (Galatians 5:19-21); violence (Psalm 11:5); body possession by aliens may be read near spiritism.
Fear, death and destruction presented as overwhelming realities; despair.

frames.aligns: Pikuach nefesh and the dignity of every life; condemnation of mass killing and incitement.
frames.concerns: Tzniut: sexual scenes, panty shot, swimsuit art; lashon hara and nivul peh in online banter; suicide. Many Haredi homes restrict such media.

frames.aligns: "Harm none" fits the critique of needless killing; no stereotyped witches or pagans.
The Way to Happiness: do not murder; be worthy of trust.

Critique of militarism, nationalism and media; empathy for refugee-like "others" (SF Encyclopedia: parallels with people "displaced and demonised by conflict"); queer-readable bond; a cross-dressing character accepted by friends.
frames.concerns: Teacher relationship called "grooming" (Anime Feminist); TCJ and Manga Bookshelf on girls drawn very young; panty shot; SHIP leader's motive "being jilted by a man" (Anime Feminist).

frames.aligns: Critical thinking about propaganda; human bonds as the source of meaning; no supernatural claims.
frames.concerns: Despair and suicide need mental-health framing; teacher relationship.

frames.concerns: Rearmament, the US alliance, nationalists and the government are satirized (TCJ; TV Tropes; a "Nippon!" rally shown as hollow, The Manga Critic); family and duty are mostly shown failing; premarital sex treated casually.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of every being, including the invaders; justice; free search for truth.
Rebellion against hypocritical authority; skepticism of crowds and the state; compassion and justice (Satanic Temple Tenets 1 and 2).
frames.concerns: Harm to children (bullying, a child's suicide, a teacher's interest in a student) is a stated concern of the Eleven Rules.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Revenge for a dead girlfriend (Kenichi) is shown as displaced and pathetic (ANN ep. 9; Anime Feminist); the story values seeing others' worth over answering insult.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Security measures, government messaging and military discipline are satirized (TCJ; TV Tropes); the girls' free, unscheduled lives are the warm center.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Loyalty to one chosen friend outranks wider duties: Ouran's choice to save one person (ANN ep. 13); blood family is mostly absent or failing.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Teachers, politicians and parents are shown as no wiser than the young; the prime minister is a "powerless figurehead" (ANN ep. 8).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No religion; time travel and science fiction explain events; traditions and national institutions appear hollow.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Games, humor and personal identity (Ouran's persona, Makoto's cross-dressing) matter more than security, even under the ship; LARB notes boredom with safety.

folkways.japan: The exam pressure, school-year structure, the Self-Defense Forces debate, Japan's postwar pacifism and the US alliance, and the memory of the 2011 disaster are Japanese contexts the story critiques from inside; readers elsewhere may take the satire as about their own countries (Solrad read it through COVID-19; Anime Feminist through Okinawa and Hiroshima), but its targets are specifically Japanese (TCJ; LARB; ANN manga guide; Asano 2014).

delivery.evidence: MAL reviewer: "a bit on the nose"; another says skip "the news talk and political pseudo-speech." No opened review calls it preachy; Solrad calls the politics "an undercurrent." Asano said in 2014 that after the 2011 earthquake "I decided that I didn't want to ever be preachy" (mangabrog translation). The Outer Haven (vol. 6) notes factions within the government, both protest camps and the invaders themselves.
delivery.note: The politics come through constant TV news, online chatter and protest scenes around the girls, while the leads themselves mostly joke about it.

personified.ideology: Revenge and anti-invader nationalism
Pro-invader activism
Wanting to save the world, believing in an "absolute"
Security state and profitable rearmament

entry.heading: Shikimori's Not Just a Cutie (Keigo Maki)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is a partnership in which each person protects, supports and openly accepts the other as they are: love does not erase weakness or bad luck, but shares it, and frees both people from narrow ideas of what a boy or a girl should be.

content.frequency: Romance central; mild fan service rare

frames.aligns: Love as willing the good of the other (CCC 1766); fidelity, self-gift and protection of the weaker; honest reconciliation with a rival.
frames.concerns: Chastity and modesty (CCC 2521-2524) for swimsuit scenes and Izumi's daydreams; an overnight trip alone as a couple (v20) and an epilogue plan to live together before marriage (CCC 2391), framed as a happy ending.

frames.aligns: Humility, mutual service, love that bears another's burdens.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis) against mild flirtatious imagery; romance as the main source of meaning; the overnight trip and cohabitation plan.

frames.aligns: Faithfulness, kindness, honesty, no sex shown, caring parents.
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 test for swimsuit scenes; some Southern Baptist families hold complementarian views (Baptist Faith and Message art. XVIII) and may discuss the role reversal; teen dating as a family decision; an unmarried couple's overnight trip and plan to live together, presented approvingly.

frames.aligns: Self-giving love, protecting the vulnerable, honest communication.
frames.concerns: Mild fan service; romance as the answer to life's troubles; views on gender roles vary by church; the overnight trip and cohabitation plan as discussion points.

frames.aligns: Courage and protection, joy, perseverance through misfortune; no occult content.
frames.concerns: Holiness standards on modesty and physical contact between unmarried couples; the overnight trip.

frames.aligns: Common grace in a well-made story; covenant-like faithfulness between the leads.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 on lascivious pictures applied to swimsuit scenes; complementarian churches (e.g. PCA) may discuss the reversed roles; cohabitation before marriage in the epilogue.

frames.aligns: Vocation in ordinary life (Izumi's cooking and care); mutual service.
frames.concerns: Mild flirtation; LCMS and WELS families may be more cautious than ELCA, including on gender roles and cohabitation.

frames.aligns: Love expressed in practical care; friendship and community.
frames.concerns: Holiness churches more cautious about romance-centered entertainment.
Little to raise beyond mild fan service.

frames.aligns: Gentleness, humility, service, no real violence.
frames.concerns: Separation from worldly media for Old Order families; flirtation, physical affection and the overnight trip; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Fidelity, kindness, warm families, a chaste-seeming relationship.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth counsel on dating and physical affection; an unchaperoned overnight trip (v20) and the epilogue plan to live together before marriage.

frames.aligns: Equal partnership, rejection of rigid gender roles (Anime Feminist), healthy communication (Eisenbeis, ANN), inclusion of the shy and lonely (Saruogi, Kamiya).
frames.concerns: Little to raise; the frame stays heterosexual.
Fundamental Belief 22 ("highest quality" entertainment) and "by beholding we become changed" for romance-centered stories; the overnight trip and cohabitation plan.

frames.aligns: Kindness, honesty, faithfulness, no spiritism reported.
frames.concerns: jw.org counsel that dating is for those ready to marry; a high-school romance as the story's core; the overnight trip and the plan to live together unmarried.

frames.aligns: Love and right thinking overcome fear; Izumi's "bad luck" never defines him.
Hesed, loyalty, kind speech, honoring parents.
frames.concerns: Tzniut and laws on touch between unmarried young people (yichud for the overnight trip); mixed-sex dating as entertainment; swimsuit scenes. Many Haredi homes would not have the series.
Modesty in swimsuit scenes; families decide on teen dating; the overnight trip.

frames.aligns: Equality between partners, emotional honesty, kindness.
Loyalty, kindness, protecting others, respect for parents.
frames.concerns: Dating and physical contact between unmarried young people; lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) and swimsuit scenes; khalwa (being alone together) on the overnight trip; the plan to live together unmarried.

frames.aligns: Devotion, duty to one another, family affection.
frames.concerns: Views on teen dating and living together vary by community; mild flirtation.

frames.aligns: Compassion, patience with misfortune, right speech in honest talk.
frames.concerns: Attachment to romance as the source of happiness.

frames.aligns: Seva, courage in protecting others, humility, equality of men and women (Guru Nanak's teaching on women).
frames.concerns: Kaam (lust) concerns in mild flirtatious scenes; teen dating and cohabitation against many families' practice.

frames.aligns: Equality of women and men, unity, truthfulness, kindness.
frames.concerns: The call to a "chaste and holy life" for flirtation and the overnight trip; marriage norms (parental consent) versus teen dating and the plan to live together.

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto), harmony, gratitude; the New Year's temple or shrine visit (v8; anime ep. 11) and the Kyoto trip shown as ordinary Japanese life.
"Harm none," mutual respect, strong woman as protector.
Communication and affinity (the ARC triangle) are strong between the leads; The Way to Happiness precepts (help others, be trustworthy).
Rejects many gender role expectations (Anime Feminist "Feminist Potential"); healthy, communicative couple (Eisenbeis, ANN); kind male friend (THEM).
frames.concerns: Cis-heterosexual frame only (Anime Feminist); Caitlin Moore (ANN) disliked the friends' advice that Shikimori go easy on Izumi to seem cute; Izumi called a "blank slate" (Dupree, ANN); some fans call the ending "too safe."

frames.aligns: Meaning through relationships and mutual support; no supernatural framing of the bad luck beyond the gag.
Loyalty, manners, steady courtship, caring families, diligence in exams, Izumi formally telling Shikimori's mother.
frames.concerns: The swapped gender roles invite discussion; mild flirtatious scenes; teen dating as the story's center; the overnight trip and the plan to live together before marriage.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth and dignity, equality in relationships, inclusion of the shy classmate.
Self-assertion (Shikimori claims both "cute" and "cool"); empathy and protecting the vulnerable (Satanic Temple Tenet 1).
frames.concerns: Church of Satan readers may find Izumi's dependence on a protector weak.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Threats to Izumi are met with protection, not revenge; Kamiya's rivalry ends in friendship (v5, v12 blurbs; ANN ep. 8).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Ordinary school order (tournaments, festivals, exams, class trip, dress code) is accepted; freedom lies in roles inside the couple.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Friends and classmates matter as much as family; families are warm but secondary (Silverman, ANN; v7-v8 blurbs).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: The couple are equals who swap roles; no ranks are celebrated.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Secular daily life with school and seasonal customs (New Year's temple visit, v8; Kyoto trip; graduation); no religion guides choices.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Emotional honesty, being accepted as oneself (ANN ep. 11) and relationship quality are the core values.

folkways.japan: The school calendar (ball-sports tournament, culture festival, sports fair, summer fireworks, New Year's hatsumōde temple visit, second-year Kyoto trip, Valentine's chocolates, university entrance exams, March graduation), the established "dating couple" (tsukiau) as a public status among classmates, and couples addressing each other by surname reflect Japanese norms rather than the story's own message. The contrast of kawaii (cute) and kakkoii (cool) is the Japanese frame for the title's play on words.

delivery.evidence: ANN says it is "having a conversation with gender norms"; Anime Feminist says it "explicitly addresses and rejects many gender role expectations."
delivery.note: The message about shared strength is carried by the comedy of role reversal and a few explicit talks, while Shikimori's wish to be cute and Kamiya's feelings are treated with sympathy rather than mocked.

personified.ideology: A woman can be both cute and strong; love as protection
Gentle, nurturing masculinity; accepting help
Competitive romantic rivalry

entry.dominant: Feminism (gender-role reversal), Classical virtue ethics, Communitarianism (all moderate or weak; partly my own framing).

entry.heading: Given
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is lived by facing loss honestly and turning it into something you can give others. Love and friendship carry a person through grief, and you cannot hold another person by force.

content.framing: Endorsed (romance); Condemned (the forced advance); Mixed (the vol. 7 scene)

frames.aligns: Grief honestly faced; suicide mourned, not glamorized; forgiveness; the forced advance treated as wrong.
frames.concerns: Same-sex romance presented as the good life (CCC 2357-2359); adult premarital and casual sex (CCC 2353); chastity teaching (CCC 2337-2359); the teen bed scene in vol. 7. The Church also calls for respect toward persons (CCC 2358).

frames.aligns: Mourning and memory of the dead; repentance-like change in Akihiko; humility.
frames.concerns: Traditional teaching on marriage and sexuality; romance and physical intimacy as the story's goal; guarding the senses (nepsis) weighs on the kissing, the teen bed scene and the adult sexual content.

frames.aligns: Perseverance, loyalty, honesty about pain, forgiveness.
frames.concerns: Same-sex romance affirmed (BF&M 2000, Article XVIII; usually a significant concern); adult premarital and casual sex; teen sexual content. Views vary by family under soul liberty.

frames.aligns: Honest grief, friendship that carries a hurting person, forgiveness.
frames.concerns: Most churches hold traditional sexual ethics, against the affirmed romances, the teen bed scene and adult sexual content; some affirming congregations read it differently.

frames.aligns: No occult or spiritual-warfare content; healing through music echoes worship's emotional power.

frames.concerns: LCMS and WELS hold traditional teaching on marriage and chastity; ELCA is affirming. Teen sexual content concerns the whole range.
