frames.concerns: UMC affirming since 2024; Global Methodist, Wesleyan and Nazarene traditional on sexuality. Teen sexual content concerns all.

frames.aligns: Judged by moral vision: grief, forgiveness and growth are taken seriously; wrongs are named.
frames.concerns: The Episcopal Church allows same-sex marriage; ACNA holds traditional teaching. Premarital and teen sexual content is a concern across the range.

frames.aligns: Almost no violence; community care for a grieving member; humility.
frames.concerns: Conservative groups hold traditional teaching on marriage and avoid most popular media; romance and band life as the goal. MC USA families vary.
Traditional teaching ("The Family: A Proclamation to the World") and the law of chastity against the affirmed romances, the teen bed scene and adult sexual content.

frames.aligns: Affirms same-sex love; grief, healing and community; the forced advance treated as wrong.
frames.concerns: The attempted assault and how quickly the couple moves past it; the vol. 7 scene's consent and the characters' ages; teen suicide for younger readers.
Marriage between one man and one woman (General Conference statements); same-sex romance usually a significant concern; adult premarital and casual sex.
jw.org counsel against entertainment featuring immorality (Galatians 5:19-21); homosexual acts considered sinful; casual sex shown.

frames.aligns: Thought shapes experience: Mafuyu moves from self-blame to expression; love over fear.
frames.concerns: Purity and marriage valued; adult and teen sexual content; dwelling on death and grief.

frames.aligns: Mourning and memory; guarding against despair; teshuvah-like change in Akihiko.
frames.concerns: Same-sex acts forbidden (Leviticus 18:22); tzniut and the kissing, the teen bed scene and adult content; many Haredi homes restrict such media.

frames.aligns: Dignity of each person (CJLS 2006 permitted same-sex commitment ceremonies; views vary); grief worked through in community.
frames.concerns: Casual sex, the forced advance and the teen bed scene; modesty values applied by families.

frames.aligns: LGBTQ inclusion; informed autonomy; healing after loss.
frames.concerns: Consent in the vol. 4 and vol. 7 scenes; teen sexual content; suicide for younger readers.
Traditional teaching on sexuality; same-sex romance as the central good; adult premarital and casual sex; lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31). Music is debated among scholars.

frames.aligns: Art evoking rasa (karuna, sorrow) and healing through music; duty to friends.
frames.concerns: Views on same-sex relationships vary, with traditional views common; adult and teen sexual content.

frames.aligns: Impermanence and grief; letting go of clinging (Mafuyu to Yuki, Akihiko to Ugetsu); compassion.
frames.concerns: Third precept: many traditions accept same-sex relationships, views vary; casual sex, the forced advance and the vol. 7 scene.

frames.aligns: Seva-like care for a friend; truthful living; the vice of attachment (moh) shown as harmful.
frames.concerns: Sex within marriage; Akal Takht opposed same-sex marriage (2005), though diaspora views vary.

frames.aligns: Rejection of prejudice; unity among friends; music praised.
frames.concerns: Teaching reserves sexual relations for marriage between a man and a woman; a "chaste and holy life."

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) in music and confession; respect for the dead.
frames.concerns: Little to raise in the message; no doctrine on same-sex relationships (practice varies, to verify). Teen sexual content raises the depiction concern.

frames.aligns: Love between consenting partners; LGBTQ-affirming; art as healing.
frames.concerns: The forced advance and the vol. 7 consent concern ("harm none"); minors.
The Way to Happiness asks faithfulness to one's partner; Akihiko's casual sex; teen sexual content.

frames.aligns: Positive same-sex relationships; supportive parents; a bisexual character; grief and mental health taken seriously; hurtful remarks about gay attraction shown as hurtful (vol. 6).
frames.concerns: The attempted assault and the forcer later becoming the partner (the BLog reviewer reads it as a twist on the "rape to love" trope; others may see it as softening it). Readers flag the vol. 7 confession as lacking clear consent between minors. Suicide content for younger readers. Age-appropriateness of sexual content in a Teen Plus book.

frames.aligns: Meaning made through art and relationships; grief faced without supernatural comfort.
frames.concerns: The forced advance; codependency; the vol. 7 scene.

frames.aligns: Perseverance, duty to the band, respect for seniors, work ethic.
frames.concerns: Same-sex romance presented to teen readers as the ideal, a concern for many families; adult casual sex; teen sexual content; parents largely absent.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth and dignity; welcoming LGBTQ people; compassion in grief.
frames.concerns: Consent in the vol. 4 and vol. 7 scenes; minors.

frames.aligns: Self-determination; rejection of guilt-driven dependence; LGBTQ-affirming.
frames.concerns: The forced advance and the vol. 7 consent concern (Satanic Temple Tenet 3, bodily autonomy); Church of Satan rules on minors.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Conflicts are handled by talk, music and apology; the one scuffle (code 6) is to stop a conversation, not defend a name.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Band discipline and rehearsal matter, but love and career are personal choices; parents and school rarely intervene.

Civic vs kin.evidence: The band and friends matter more than family; supportive mothers in the background; Akihiko's parents absent.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Haruki leads and senpai-kohai roles are kept (two students, two adults), but the band decides together and Mafuyu's talent overturns seniority.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No religious frame beyond an offstage funeral; same-sex relationships accepted without reference to custom; grief handled through art.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Self-expression through music is the cure and the goal; tolerance is assumed. Practical worries (money, jobs, going pro) are present but secondary.

folkways.japan: The senpai-kohai structure, school clubs, the live-house band scene and boys'-love genre conventions (beautiful young men, older-younger pairings) are Japanese settings and genre norms. The story's own message is about grief and honest expression.

delivery.evidence: Reviewers praise emotional resonance and realism (ANN; OutWrite; AIPT); no reviewer found calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Different views of love (possessive, patient, free) get fair voices. Hurtful straight views of gay attraction appear in vol. 6 as hurtful, and no religious or traditional objection is voiced.

personified.ideology: Grief expressed through art
Possessive devotion that must be outgrown
Love as freedom from obligation

entry.heading: Blue Flag
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is honest about who you are and whom you love, even when others' expectations and prejudice push you to hide; the choices you make at eighteen do not have to be final.

frames.aligns: Largely LGBTQ-affirming; "harm none" against exposure and cruelty.
The Way to Happiness: be worthy of trust, do not do harmful acts, respect others.

Multiple queer characters with full lives; prejudice and microaggressions shown as harmful (Mary Sue, But Why Tho); a critique of sexist double standards (Mami); read as feminist shonen in academic work (Lewis 2022).
frames.concerns: Masumi's marriage to a man (ANN calls it "a bit of a cop-out"); Futaba as "more catalyst than individual" (ANN); vol. 7 "more heavy-handed than it perhaps needs to be" (ANN); a rushed last chapter (But Why Tho).

frames.aligns: Meaning made through honest relationships; identity accepted rather than imposed; no supernatural claims.
Loyalty, self-sacrifice, respect for family, perseverance, condemning bullying.
frames.concerns: Same-sex romance presented to teen readers as normal and a same-sex marriage as the ideal ending, a concern for many when presented to children; questions traditional gender expectations.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth and dignity; welcoming LGBTQ people; honest search for meaning.
Self-determination; rejection of imposed identity; LGBTQ-affirming; personal autonomy.
frames.concerns: Exposure of Toma's feelings as a violation of autonomy (shown as wrong).

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Worth is inherent; the exposure and gossip (ch. 41-42) are framed as wrongs to a person, and conflicts are settled by talking (vol. 7). Fights lead to suspension, not respect.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Characters are celebrated for living as they choose against school and social expectations (Toma, Masumi, Mami).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Loyalty runs to chosen friends as much as family; Akiko's acceptance of Masumi (ch. 39) extends kin-like care outward.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: School status (Toma popular, Taichi at the bottom) is shown and quietly undone; the brother's authority over Toma's future is questioned (vols. 3-4).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No religion; inherited expectations about marriage and gender are questioned; personal choice guides life.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Tolerance and self-expression are the core values; exam pressure is shown as a burden.

folkways.japan: The final-year exam pressure, the Koshien baseball dream, the school sports and culture festivals, class hierarchy and the strong pull to fit in are Japanese school norms the story works within; Japanese reviewers framed its LGBTQ theme against Japanese social expectations (HuffPost Japan via Wikipedia).

delivery.evidence: ANN calls vol. 7 "more heavy-handed than it perhaps needs to be"; But Why Tho says the cringe-worthy prejudiced talk is there "because this is real."
delivery.note: The message is carried mostly by long conversations among the friends, becoming most direct after the confession (vols. 6-7).

personified.ideology: Being true to whom you love despite prejudice
Girls and boys can be friends; against sexist double standards
Rigid gender roles and anti-gay views
Conforming to hide one's orientation

entry.dominant: Expressive individualism (being true to yourself), Progressivism (critique of prejudice and gender norms), Existentialism (choosing a future).

entry.heading: Billy Bat
entry.label: From summaries

frames.aligns: Evil (murder, racism, Nazism) shown without being made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7); self-giving protection of children; Francis Xavier, a saint, is shown as a serious figure (a "child prodigy" who receives a revelation in a Basque cave; seen in Kevin's visions in vol. 8, Kodansha).
frames.concerns: Revelation reframed: Jesus points to the bat when asked about God's form, and the bat is said to stand behind the founding of the Church. That alternative account of the sacred is the main concern, judged by its framing on the page.

frames.aligns: Pride and the will to power (Kurosu, Hitler) end badly; sacrifice for others.
frames.concerns: Holy persons are venerated in icons, so a fictional Christ who reveals a different "form" of God touches the sacred directly; guarding the senses for murders and occult hallucinations.

frames.aligns: Courage and protecting the innocent; deceit and conspiracy exposed as destructive.
frames.concerns: A hidden spiritual entity presented as the source behind Jesus' teaching; drinking, prostitution settings. Views vary by congregation under soul liberty.

frames.aligns: A serious story about the power of images and stories, open to "engaging culture" discussion; sacrifice and protection of children.
frames.concerns: Jesus' teaching relocated to a non-Christian entity; Judas portrayed in a new backstory; the entity is ambiguous rather than good.

frames.aligns: Evil and manipulation are real in the story; the black bat is said to lead people to harm.
frames.concerns: A speaking spirit that guides chosen people, a cult around it and hallucinations are the "open door" content the tradition weighs most; it is called God or Devil and is never judged by Scripture. Views vary.

frames.aligns: Common grace in a well-made story; human depravity echoed in the bat's verdict that "humans are foolish."
frames.concerns: Many in the tradition object to images of Christ (Heidelberg Q96-98); here Christ also draws an image as God's form, the opposite of the second commandment as the tradition reads it.

frames.aligns: Entertainment as adiaphora, judged by love; vocation of the artist; sin and its consequences shown.
frames.concerns: The alternative account of Christ; confessional families (LCMS, WELS) stricter than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Social holiness: anti-racism, care for children, a lawyer suing a polluter; grace possible for flawed characters (Devivie's last act).
frames.concerns: Wesley's caution about diversions not "in the name of the Lord Jesus" applies most where Jesus himself is reframed; holiness churches more cautious.

frames.aligns: Judged by how good and evil are framed: murder, racism and Nazism are condemned; a literary work in the line of speculative fiction about history.
frames.concerns: The Christ scenes, read in context; the ambiguity of the bat.

frames.aligns: Heroes protect rather than kill; two enemy soldiers make peace in 2063; violence shown with cost.
frames.concerns: Assassinations, war and terror on the page; conservative groups avoid popular media; the reframed Christ.

frames.aligns: Warnings about secret combinations seeking power (Ether 8) map onto the scroll conspiracy; agency and choice between the black and white bat.
frames.concerns: Jesus reinterpreted; alcohol, prostitution settings; a dark mood. For the Strength of Youth asks whether media invites the Spirit.

frames.aligns: Critique of racism, Jim Crow violence, war, corporate abuse of artists and environmental harm; diverse cast.
frames.concerns: The Jesus scenes may still trouble some members; little else.

frames.aligns: Apocalyptic stakes and a world in ruin echo the tradition's prophecy themes; deception by powers exposed.
frames.concerns: A non-biblical entity as the source of prophecy; spiritism concerns; "by beholding we become changed" for the dark content. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Exposes political and corporate power as corrupt; warns against following leaders blindly.
frames.concerns: Spiritism: an unseen entity speaks to chosen people and guides history; a cult forms around it; Jesus is shown pointing to it. Violence and occult content are what jw.org counsels avoiding. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Truth exposing error drives the plot; fear is the villains' tool.
frames.concerns: The story dwells on fear, hallucination and catastrophe; an apocalyptic future. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Idolatry and the worship of a leader (the Tibet cult, Hitler) end in ruin; protecting life (pikuach nefesh) honored.
frames.concerns: An image treated as a path to God's form; Hitler on the page; a Jewish prisoner of war, spared and sent to America by Hitler, becomes a media magnate who has rival artists killed and wishes before his death that Billy Bat would "make the world unhappy" (Japanese Wikipedia; TV Tropes ch. 100; fan wiki). No reviewer has raised a stereotype concern, but families may want to check it on the page; secular entertainment generally restricted in Haredi homes.
The fake Chuck Culkin, identified as Jewish, as a Hitler-sent media mogul who kills rival artists (stereotype check, vols. 12-13 and 17); Hitler's portrayal (ch. 100-102).

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam in characters who warn and protect; critique of racism and corporate power.
frames.concerns: Same stereotype check on the fake Chuck Culkin (identified as Jewish); Hitler as a character (ch. 100-102).

frames.aligns: Condemns murder, terror and oppression; protecting children; humility before a power beyond human control.
frames.concerns: Depicting prophets, including Isa (Jesus), is widely forbidden; here Isa also gives an image as God's "form," which conflicts with tawhid; a spirit guiding history; alcohol and prostitution settings. Middle East terrorists who enforce the Islamic ban on images by punishing children's drawings and cut off the arms of the old artist who takes the blame (likely vol. 18; Japanese Wikipedia; how the page separates them from ordinary Muslims to verify).

frames.aligns: Karma-like consequences across ages; adharma of power-seekers; art as a sacred act (rasa).
frames.concerns: Mild; a divine figure reinterpreted may concern some.

frames.aligns: Craving for power (Kurosu, Hitler) brings suffering; Kurosu finally chooses not to make a wish and dies watching Earth from the Moon (Japanese Wikipedia). Kanbei, the Iga ninja, seals the scroll and spends his last years praying for the dead (菩提を弔う; Japanese Wikipedia, vols. 2-3).
frames.concerns: A cave cult in Tibet around Yamagata, raided by the People's Liberation Army (ch. 151-157, vol. 19; how Tibetan Buddhism is shown to verify); violence and alcohol.

frames.aligns: Ego (haumai) and greed condemned; protection of the weak.
frames.concerns: Little; depictions of sacred figures are a concern in the tradition, though not of the Gurus here.

frames.aligns: Unity of humankind across nations (enemy soldiers reconciled); independent investigation of truth; critique of racism.
frames.concerns: Bahá'í guidance discourages portraying Manifestations of God, including Christ, in drama (from general knowledge; to verify); here Christ's teaching is reframed.

frames.aligns: Sincerity in Yamagata; Japanese history (Iga, Akechi Mitsuhide, occupation) treated seriously; kami-like unseen beings are familiar in Japanese culture.
frames.concerns: Little; blood and death as impurity.

frames.aligns: No witches or pagans stereotyped; an animal spirit and a cave painting as ancient sources of meaning; "harm none" against murder.
frames.concerns: The bat can be manipulative; little else.

frames.aligns: Way to Happiness precepts (do not murder, safeguard the environment, be worthy of trust) align with the heroes.
frames.concerns: Hallucinations and a mind-influencing entity; a cult in Tibet. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Critique of racism, Jim Crow violence, war, corporate exploitation of creators and environmental damage; a Black protagonist, interracial couple, women lawyers and fighters (MangaUpdates; Japanese Wikipedia).
frames.concerns: Real tragedies (JFK, 9/11) used as plot devices; conspiracy theories as story material; a sex-worker character who is killed.

frames.aligns: Art, authorship and free inquiry as central values; power and fanaticism critiqued; the hope placed in a child's study.
frames.concerns: A supernatural entity is real in the story; popular conspiracy theories ("a faked Moon broadcast," JFK doubles) are woven in (Sammut, CBR: "blends popular conspiracy theories"), which the tradition watches as pseudohistory presented as fact.

frames.aligns: Courage, duty, loyalty, protection of children; the evils of Nazism and political conspiracy.
frames.concerns: Christian origins reframed; distrust of national institutions (CIA-type agents, a faked Moon landing).

frames.aligns: Free search for truth and meaning; inherent worth across race and nation; reconciliation of enemies.
Skepticism of authority; a "God" figure that manipulates people; the artist as a rebel who rewrites the story.
frames.concerns: Heroes act for others; the story does not exalt self-interest. Harm to children condemned, as the Eleven Rules also do. (from general knowledge; to verify)

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Heroes protect and warn rather than avenge; Yamagata answers violence by shielding a baby (Dallas, 1963) and children (vols. 18-20).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Secret state and corporate order is the threat; the artist's freedom to draw and rewrite is celebrated (Japanese Wikipedia).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Duties pass through chosen heirs and strangers (Yamagata to Goodman; Johnny and Sergei save a child not their own).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Racism and the Klan condemned (ch. 39-41, vol. 5); Tony and Diane Goodman's interracial marriage defended against family opposition (Japanese Wikipedia); ghostwriters against owners; a Black protagonist (MangaUpdates).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: History and sacred origins treated as stories open to revision; yet a supernatural entity is real and Japanese and Christian history are taken seriously.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Authorship, art and its credit are the core values (Sebsus; Kana editor), within a survival-thriller frame.

folkways.japan: The occupation era, the Shimoyama incident, Iga ninja and Akechi Mitsuhide, and Japanese American identity draw on Japanese history and memory; the story's view of America is that of a Japanese work looking at the occupying power and its pop culture.

delivery.evidence: An AniList reviewer calls it "a message to humanity"; ANN says it uses the thriller "to say something less conventional and more controversial." No review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The series argues through plot, history and the bat's direct speeches to its chosen artists rather than through narration.

personified.ideology: Artistic honesty and protection of the weak
A hidden "administrator" of history who judges humans foolish
Power through control of history
Ownership of stories for profit and power

entry.dominant: Postmodernism (metafiction), Pantheist / New Age (a cosmic guiding entity), Might makes right (critiqued), Consumerism (critiqued), Christian (reinterpreted).

series.title: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure Part 5: Golden Wind
series.romaji: JoJo no Kimyou na Bouken: Ougon no Kaze
series.native: ジョジョの奇妙な冒険 黄金の風

entry.heading: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure Part 5: Golden Wind
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: You cannot change your fate, but you can refuse to give up your sense of right: loyalty to friends who chose the same path, protection of the weak against those who prey on them, and the courage to walk that road to its end are what make a life golden, even inside a criminal world.

content.framing: Shown with consequences (heroes' killings largely endorsed)

frames.aligns: Evil is not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7): the drug trade and Diavolo's will to kill his daughter are condemned. Self-giving love (John 15:13) in Bucciarati and Narancia. Protecting the young from drugs fits CCC 2291.
frames.concerns: The way to good runs through a criminal organization, and the hero ends as its boss: the end seems to justify the means (CCC 1753, 1756). Vigilante killing; an endless-death punishment decided by a person, not God. Jokes about a 15-year-old girl's body (CCC 2354 on respect for persons).

frames.aligns: Courage and sacrificial love; a "devil" figure defeated.
frames.concerns: Watchfulness (nepsis) weighs the gore, the body horror and the fan-service gags; heroes as gangsters; a punishment like hell inflicted by a boy.

frames.aligns: Evil (drugs, a murderous father) framed as evil and defeated; loyalty and sacrifice.
frames.concerns: Phil 4:8 test: constant gore, gangs as heroes, a crime boss as the happy ending, groping jokes about a minor. Soul liberty: each family decides.

frames.aligns: Depicts without endorsing drug use; a hero who protects the vulnerable.
frames.concerns: The story's "good" stays inside the mafia; no repentance or redemption from crime is offered; fan service around a minor (Romans 14 conscience).

frames.aligns: Clear good and evil; a "devil" named Diavolo defeated.
frames.concerns: Souls pulled from bodies (Chariot Requiem), a walking corpse (Bucciarati), a Stand bred inside a woman (Baby Face), the son of a vampire as hero: many would see an "open door."

frames.aligns: A rich talking point: fate in the story is impersonal; the Westminster Confession (3.1) holds God's decree with creaturely freedom. Common grace lets families value the craft.
frames.concerns: Endorsed criminal ends; Larger Catechism Q139 on immodest images and jests (Trish's design and the gags about her); gore.

frames.aligns: Vocation and faithfulness in one's station read into Bucciarati's sacrifice; adiaphora: judged by love and conscience.
frames.concerns: The vocation here is crime; the story's hope rests on human righteousness alone; jokes at a girl's expense.

frames.aligns: Social holiness: concern for children harmed by drugs; Wesley's opposition to trades that harm neighbors.
frames.concerns: Gangs and killing as the path; General Rules caution about diversions; innuendo about a minor.

frames.aligns: Works judged by framing (Lewis's tradition): evil is clearly evil; sacrificial friendship.
frames.concerns: A crime boss as the happy ending; gore; fan service around a 15-year-old.

frames.aligns: Concern for the poor and for children harmed by drugs.
frames.concerns: Violence and a criminal hierarchy are the heroes' only tools; the ending crowns a new boss (Schleitheim Article 6; Matthew 5:39). Conservative groups avoid such media.

frames.aligns: The Word of Wisdom's rejection of harmful drugs matches the story's central cause; loyalty and sacrifice; agency.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth: gore, immodest design and crude jokes do not invite the Spirit for many families; heroes who are criminals.

frames.aligns: Attention to youth failed by families and institutions (ANN: "spurned and exploited and abused by those in power"); anti-drug-exploitation cause.
frames.concerns: Violence; gay-coded characters only as villains (ANN; Anime Feminist); the treatment of a 15-year-old girl's body as a joke.

frames.aligns: Anti-drug message fits the health message; good versus evil.
frames.concerns: Walking dead, departing souls and an afterlife meeting conflict with Fundamental Belief 26 on the state of the dead; "by beholding we become changed" weighs the gore.

frames.aligns: Drug use and a murderous father condemned.
frames.concerns: Constant violence (Psalm 11:5), spiritism-like content (souls, walking corpse), heroes who are criminals, sexual jokes; jw.org counsel weighs these heavily.

frames.aligns: Fear and death overcome by resolve.
frames.concerns: Decay, rot and aging made overwhelming and real (Grateful Dead, Green Day); body horror.

frames.aligns: Protecting the young from harm; pikuach nefesh in the drive to save Trish.
frames.concerns: Gangs and killing as heroic; tzniut and Trish's design and the jokes about her; gore. Many Haredi homes avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Friendship, courage and protection of the vulnerable.
frames.concerns: Criminal ends endorsed; gore; immodest design and innuendo about a minor. No antisemitic tropes reported.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam echoes in the fight against a drug trade that preys on youth.
frames.concerns: Violence; gay-coded villains (ANN); jokes about a 15-year-old's body. No antisemitic tropes reported.

frames.aligns: Belief in qadar (decree) with a duty to act righteously parallels Araki's theme; intoxicants (Qur'an 5:90) shown as a destroyer of the young.
frames.concerns: Gangs as heroes; vigilante killing; lowering the gaze (24:30-31) for Trish's design and the gags about her; gore.

frames.aligns: The Gita's call to act rightly without changing the result (2.47) is close to Araki's stated theme; karma returns Diavolo's deeds to him without end.
frames.concerns: Tamasic content (gore, cruelty, crude jokes); dharma pursued through a crime family.

frames.aligns: Karma and consequence (Diavolo); compassion for the young.
frames.concerns: Non-harm (first precept) against constant killing; craving for power is the villain's, but also drives the heroes' rise; the third precept and jokes about a girl's body.

frames.aligns: Hukam (divine order) accepted while living righteously; defense of the weak against oppressors.
frames.concerns: Violence; the five vices (including kaam, lust) in the villains and the gags; crime as a vehicle.

frames.aligns: Avoiding drugs is a Bahá'í law, and the story condemns the drug trade.
frames.concerns: Bahá'í teaching on obedience to just government and non-involvement in crime; violence; "chaste and holy life."

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) and loyalty; gratitude toward friends (Araki thanks his characters as "the golden wind").
frames.concerns: Death, blood and corpses (kegare) are constant; the gags about Trish.

frames.aligns: Personal will and fate as a thread (compare the Norns); protection of the vulnerable.
frames.concerns: "Harm none" set against constant violence; consent and the treatment of a 15-year-old's body.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness precept against harmful drugs matches the core cause.
frames.concerns: The same booklet's "Do not murder" against constant killing; a crime family as the path.

frames.aligns: Youth failed by families and institutions; anti-exploitation; Trish gains her own power.
frames.concerns: Gay-coded characters only as villains (ANN, Leach; Anime Feminist); Trish's design and groping jokes about her at 15 (TV Tropes; jojowiki); one female lead.

frames.aligns: Human loyalty and conscience against a tyrant; no supernatural moral authority needed.
frames.concerns: Fate presented as fixed; vigilante justice; heavy violence; a minor's body played for laughs.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, courage, sacrifice, anti-drug stance, evil punished.
frames.concerns: Gang life glamorized; the hero ends as a mafia boss; parents absent or abusive; crude jokes about a teen girl.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of outcasts; justice for the exploited.
frames.concerns: Violence; gay-coded villains; consent and a minor's body as a joke.

frames.aligns: Individual will against a hidden authority; outcasts take power for themselves; proportional retaliation against Diavolo.
frames.concerns: The Eleven Rules on children weigh the jokes about Trish and the drug trade aimed at the young; The Satanic Temple's Tenet 1 (compassion) against the cruelty of the punishment.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Disputes are settled personally and to the death; Giorno arranges Polpo's death (ch. 16); gang codes and betrayal drive the plot (Araki: "the beauty of betrayal").

Order vs freedom.evidence: The crew breaks from the Boss's order to save Trish (ch. 78-84), but values rank and discipline within the crew.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Loyalty is to the crew as family; courts and police are absent or corrupt.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Bucciarati explains Passione's ranks (ch. 17); Giorno ends at the top of the hierarchy, with Mista as his subordinate (jojowiki; Leach's "Godfather" reference).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Little religion; mafia codes and a bloodline balance secular practicality.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Street survival of outcasts comes first; style matters but security and loyalty dominate.

folkways.japan: The crew's loyalty to a superior and the gratitude Narancia and others owe Bucciarati for taking them in reflect Japanese norms of on (debt of gratitude) and vertical loyalty, applied to an Italian setting. Accepting a fixed fate while acting with sincerity echoes Japanese ideas of resolve and makoto (from general knowledge; to verify; no source links Araki to them).

delivery.evidence: MAL reviewers say Diavolo is "barely even shown"; TV Tropes says fans root for the rebel assassins.
delivery.note: The anti-drug and fate themes come through characters' choices and backstories rather than speeches, while the main villain's view is barely argued.

personified.ideology: Seize power within a corrupt order to make it just
Conscience over obedience to authority
Absolute power through secrecy; erase the past at any cost
Revolt against the Boss for a fair share

entry.dominant: Stoicism (affirmed, through Araki's fate theme), Classical virtue ethics (affirmed), Communitarianism (affirmed, the crew as family), Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued, through the Boss), Might makes right (explored).

series.title: The 100 Girlfriends Who Really, Really, Really, Really, Really Love You
series.romaji: Kimi no Koto ga Dai Dai Dai Dai Daisuki na 100-nin no Kanojo
series.native: 君のことが大大大大大好きな100人の彼女
series.adult_reason: The 100 Girlfriends: shown with a warning; Seven Seas publishes it as Mature-rated (Ghost Ship imprint, Seven Seas' Mature tier = 18+); BBFC and Australian MA 15+ describe sexualized focus on teen characters in the anime; adult principal and teachers date a high-school student
series.warning: Most of the cast are high-school and junior-high students (ages 12-16); the anime is officially classed as sexualizing teen girls, adult school staff are written as partners of the 15-year-old lead, and an adult's forced kissing of students is a running gag.

entry.heading: The 100 Girlfriends Who Really, Really, Really, Really, Really Love You (Rikito Nakamura, Yukiko Nozawa)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life means being honest with everyone you care about and making room for each person exactly as she is. Belonging is not scarce: a group grows stronger when no one is forced to compete or left out.

content.framing: Endorsed (the group arrangement); fan service played for comedy

frames.aligns: Honesty, self-giving protection of others, care for the outcast (Shizuka).
frames.concerns: Marriage as one man and one woman (CCC 1643-1645 on unity; CCC 2387 on polygamy); fan service with minors (CCC 2523 on modesty); adults in authority as partners of a student; forced kissing as comedy. Inter Mirifica 7: is wrong made attractive?

frames.aligns: Care for the lonely; Rentaro's sacrificial courage.
frames.concerns: Nepsis (guarding the senses) against fan service; marriage as one-flesh union; adults and minors.

frames.aligns: Truth-telling; kindness; standing up for the weak.
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 test on fan service; the Baptist Faith and Message on marriage as one man and one woman; adult staff and a student. Soul liberty leaves the call to families.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, honesty, a hero who never lets anyone be left out.
frames.concerns: The group arrangement affirmed as the good life; sexualized teens; drug-induced kissing; assault played as a joke. Engage-or-separate views differ.

frames.aligns: Restoration of wounded people (Shizuka, Nadeshiko, Chiyo).
frames.concerns: Holiness standards on modesty and sexual purity; a "god of love" deity running fate is a light spiritual concern.

frames.aligns: Common grace in kindness and honesty.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 lists "lascivious... pictures" and "books" and polygamy among sins against the seventh commandment (to verify wording); adult staff and a student.

frames.aligns: Care for the neighbor; daily faithfulness.
frames.concerns: Sixth Commandment ("sexually pure and decent life") against the premise and fan service; LCMS and WELS stricter than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy; welcome for the excluded.
frames.concerns: Wesley's rule against reading that does not "tend to the knowledge or love of God"; holiness churches would avoid it; UMC families vary.

frames.aligns: Judged by framing: honesty, consent-seeking among the main cast and kindness are real; the story knows it is a parody.
frames.concerns: The arrangement is endorsed, not explored; sexualized minors; adults with authority as partners; assault as a gag.
Separation from worldly media; sexualized content; the premise rejects covenant marriage throughout. MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Family as eternal ideal; kindness; developing talents.
frames.concerns: Law of chastity; For the Strength of Youth on entertainment; Official Declaration 1 ended plural marriage; dating before 16 discouraged; adults and a student.

frames.aligns: Inclusion, acceptance of difference, communication within the group.
frames.concerns: How the vulnerable are treated: adults in authority and a student; sexualized focus on teen and junior-high girls; assault as comedy.
Fundamental Belief 22 on entertainment; Fundamental Belief 23 on marriage; "by beholding we become changed." The premise rejects these throughout.
jw.org counsel against entertainment featuring immorality (Galatians 5:19-21); dating only with marriage in view, one partner; a "god of love" in a shrine.

frames.aligns: Love as the answer to fear and loneliness; Rentaro's refusal to accept "fate".
frames.concerns: Dwelling on sensual images as mental influences; drugs and potions; minors.

frames.aligns: Chesed (kindness) and truthfulness; care for the lonely.
frames.concerns: Tzniut and shmirat einayim against fan service; nivul peh in sexual humor; relationships outside the marriage framework; mother and daughter in one group; many families would not keep it at home.
Modesty; adults and minors; monogamous marriage as norm.
Consent and power between adults and minors; sexualized teens; assault as a joke.

frames.aligns: Honesty, fairness among partners (an echo of Qur'an 4:3's demand of justice), care for the weak.
frames.concerns: Lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) against fan service; intimacy outside marriage; same-sex elements; images of the body.

frames.aligns: Devotion and protection of the vulnerable; dharma of honesty.
frames.concerns: Kama outside dharma; rajasic and tamasic media (Gita 17); teachers as partners breaks guru-shishya respect.

frames.aligns: Boundless kindness for all as an image of metta; honest speech.
frames.concerns: Sensual imagery as feed for craving; a name joke on earthly desires; intoxicating potions (fifth precept); harm to minors (third precept).

frames.aligns: Seva and protection of the weak; truthful living.
frames.concerns: Kaam (lust) played for comedy; the Rehat Maryada's ideal of marriage (Anand Karaj) between one man and one woman.
Monogamy in Bahá'í law; call to a "chaste and holy life".

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) and gratitude; a kami of connection (en-musubi) as gentle comedy.
frames.concerns: Little doctrinal concern about the premise; purity concerns about minors; some may object to a deity as a comic bureaucrat.

frames.aligns: Relationships freely chosen and openly negotiated; acceptance of bisexual characters.
frames.concerns: Harm-none questions on adults and minors, on forced kissing and on drugging people with potions.
The Way to Happiness precepts on sexual fidelity, on drugs and on protecting children.

frames.aligns: Non-traditional relationship forms; communication and no forced competition (ANN; Gizmodo: "a surprisingly healthy polycule"); bisexual characters; disability care (Shizuka).
frames.concerns: Consent and age: sexualized focus on teen and junior-high characters; adult staff and a student; Anime Feminist on "sexual violence against minors (played for laughs)" and on ageist portrayal of an older woman.

frames.aligns: Meaning made through relationships; humane treatment of odd and lonely people.
frames.concerns: Exploitation questions (sexualized minors); drug use and assault as comedy.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, courage, a protective male lead.
frames.concerns: Rejects monogamous marriage throughout; sexual comedy; school authority inverted (ch. 213); mother and daughter in one group.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of every girl; acceptance; free search for love. UU has long hosted polyamory advocacy (from general knowledge; to verify).
frames.concerns: Age; power between adults and a student; stereotyped archetypes.

frames.aligns: Self-determined relationships, no religious guilt, candor about desire.
frames.concerns: The Eleven Rules of the Earth's prohibition on harming children; sexualized minors and adults with a student; non-consensual kissing.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Every girl's worth is inherent; conflicts end in talk and acceptance (ch. 14-19; Shizuka's mother, ch. 135), not vengeance.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Rules give way to feelings: the guidance counselor's "nothing precedes the rules" is overturned (ch. 213), and the class president's strictness is played for comedy (ch. 250). Rentaro's own rules (honesty, fairness) are the only order.

Civic vs kin.evidence: The "Rentarou Family" comes first and is treated as kin (ch. 14); members defend one another against parents and outsiders.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: All girlfriends are equal; age and rank (principal's family, teachers, maid, students) are flattened inside the group.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Customs of marriage and parental control are set aside; the god is comic.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Being accepted as one is is the celebrated goal.

folkways.japan: The shrine god and en-musubi (binding of fates), the seinen-magazine harem and ecchi conventions, senpai-kohai and school-club settings, a wealthy family with a maid, and the comic treatment of school staff as romantic characters are Japanese settings and genre conventions that frame the story rather than form its message.

delivery.evidence: Rentaro states the thesis in speeches (Guinness-record speech; ANN quotes "Who ever said that loving someone means your love for someone else is fake?").
delivery.note: The story states its case for shared love openly through Rentaro's speeches, but wraps it in absurdist parody, so readers differ on how seriously to take it.

personified.ideology: Shared, honest commitment to all
Objection to sharing, then acceptance
Shaming conformity
Rules before feelings

entry.dominant: Expressive individualism, Communitarianism, Hedonism.

entry.heading: orange
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is one where you speak up for the people you love before it is too late. Regret can be turned into care, friends can carry someone through despair, and a person in pain is worth staying alive for and with.

frames.aligns: Life as a gift worth protecting; self-giving love (Suwa); evil and despair shown, not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7).
frames.concerns: Suicide of a parent and of a teen for younger or vulnerable readers (CCC 2280-2283 treats life as entrusted to us, with judgment left to God). Hope comes from friends with no reference to God.

frames.aligns: Love that bears another's burden; humility and repentance in the regretful future selves.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis) in the despair scenes; no sacred dimension to healing.

frames.aligns: A life valued and rescued; friends who do not give up (Galatians 6:2, bearing burdens).
frames.concerns: Suicide content measured by Philippians 4:8; hope with no gospel source. Each congregation and family decides.

frames.aligns: Depicts despair without endorsing it; strong echoes of grace and sacrificial love (Beneath the Tangles).
frames.concerns: Heavy suicide themes; salvation through human effort and time travel.

frames.aligns: No occult or spirit content; the time travel is framed as science. Hope and healing of a hurting person.
frames.concerns: Despair as a spiritual as well as emotional battle; no prayer or spiritual help. A brief shrine visit.

frames.aligns: Common grace allows valuing a non-Christian work; the sixth commandment's duty to preserve life (WLC Q135) is close to the plot's whole aim.
frames.concerns: Suicide (WLC Q136 on self-murder, handled pastorally) for vulnerable readers; providence replaced by time travel.

frames.aligns: Kakeru cannot free himself of guilt over his mother; release comes from outside, through others. Entertainment as adiaphora, judged by love.
frames.concerns: Suicide content; LCMS and WELS families may be more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy; attentive friendship as a means of grace; growth in courage.
frames.concerns: Suicide content; holiness churches more cautious.

frames.aligns: Judged by framing: despair is named and answered by community.
Mutual aid and self-giving within a small community; nonviolence.
frames.concerns: Separation from popular media in conservative groups; romance as a focus. MC USA families more open.

frames.aligns: Worth of every soul; friends ministering to one in need; hope.
frames.concerns: Suicide content. For the Strength of Youth asks whether media invites the Spirit.

frames.aligns: Compassion, mental-health awareness, community care; vol. 7's message that asking for help is not weakness (Hakutaku).
frames.concerns: No professional help shown; the rescue rests on teenagers (Mage in a Barrel commenter; TV Tropes).

frames.aligns: Care for the vulnerable, hope, no spirits or occult.
frames.concerns: "By beholding we become changed" applied to the despair scenes; Fundamental Belief 22.

frames.aligns: No spiritism; love and loyalty among friends; life as precious.
frames.concerns: Romantic focus among teens; a shrine visit; letters from the future may raise questions about foretelling, though framed as science. Choices left to conscience.

frames.aligns: Love overcoming fear; healing of a despairing heart through love.
frames.concerns: Dwelling on death, illness and despair ("Stand porter at the door of thought," Science and Health 392).

frames.aligns: Saving a life (pikuach nefesh) is the whole plot; "whoever saves a single life, it is as if he saved an entire world" (Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5).
frames.concerns: Suicide traditionally grave; mixed-gender teen romance; many Haredi homes restrict secular media.

frames.aligns: Pikuach nefesh; care for those in distress; teshuvah in the future selves' regret.
Saving a life, mental-health awareness, community.
frames.concerns: Suicide content; no adults or professionals.

frames.aligns: Preserving life (hifz al-nafs); patience (sabr); hope against despair; friends as protectors.
frames.concerns: Suicide forbidden (Qur'an 4:29), here shown in one timeline as a tragedy and prevented in the other; teen dating and a kiss.

frames.aligns: Duty to friends; self-sacrifice; the value of a human life.
frames.concerns: Little to raise beyond the suicide themes and teen romance.

frames.aligns: Compassion (karuna); suffering from clinging to guilt; right speech as kind honesty.
frames.concerns: Suicide content; parallel worlds read through a non-Buddhist lens.

frames.aligns: Seva and selfless love; overcoming fear and ego; hope (chardi kala).
frames.concerns: Little to raise beyond the suicide themes.

frames.aligns: Unity, consultation among the friends, service to one in need.
Sincerity (makoto); harmony restored in a community; a respectful New Year's visit to Fukashi Shrine in Matsumoto (Japanese Wikipedia).
frames.concerns: Little religious content to align or conflict; the shrine is a setting, not a source of help.

frames.aligns: "Harm none"; healing through community; respect for life.
The Way to Happiness precepts: help others, be worthy of trust, do not harm.
frames.concerns: Despair handled by friends rather than by any method the Church endorses; no psychiatry shown.

frames.aligns: Mental-health awareness, empathy, dismantling the shame around depression; vol. 7's help-seeking message (Hakutaku).
frames.concerns: Teenagers carry a rescue no adult or professional joins (TV Tropes); "rescue fantasy" critique (Mage in a Barrel commenter); safe-messaging concerns about a completed suicide and an earlier attempt on the page.

frames.aligns: Human worth without earning it; responsibility for one another; reason-based science-fiction frame.
frames.concerns: No professional help shown (TV Tropes); safe-messaging care needed.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, self-sacrifice, a son's love for his mother, courage and honesty.
Inherent worth and dignity of every person; a caring community.
frames.concerns: Little to raise beyond the suicide themes.

frames.aligns: Compassion (Satanic Temple Tenet 1); bodily autonomy is not the story's frame, but care for a suffering friend is.
frames.concerns: Self-sacrificing ethics sit uneasily with Church of Satan individualism.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: No insult is answered with force; Ueda's harassment of Naho (likely v2) is answered by friends speaking up, not revenge. Worth is shown as inherent: Kakeru is worth saving regardless of his guilt.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Rules and institutions hardly appear; the story neither calls for stricter order nor celebrates freedom from it.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Kin are few (a grandmother, an absent father); a chosen circle of classmates does the saving (v1-v5).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: The six friends act as equals; teachers and seniors carry little authority.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No religious answer; the letters are explained by science (Letter 5 lecture; black holes in the Last Letter, per TV Tropes); a shrine visit is custom, not faith.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Expressing feelings, emotional honesty and quality of life are the goals; Naho's letters ask her to say what she feels.

folkways.japan: Reserve and not voicing one's feelings, school club and sports-festival life, New Year's shrine visits, the senior-junior gap (Ueda), and a regional city setting (Matsumoto) are Japanese norms the story uses as setting; its push toward speaking openly about pain is the story's own message.

delivery.evidence: ANN calls it "emotionally gripping throughout"; Mage in a Barrel says it "never fetishizes his struggle"; no review found calling it preachy.
delivery.note: The letters state the lesson directly at times, but the message mostly works through Naho's choices and Kakeru's inner chapter rather than speeches.

personified.ideology: His death would make amends to his mother
True love puts the other's happiness first
Speak now, or live with regret
Regret can be sent back as help

entry.dominant: Communitarianism, Secular humanism, Existentialism.

series.title: Neon Genesis Evangelion
series.native: 新世紀エヴァンゲリオン
series.warning: Includes nudity of 14-year-old Rei and a scene where 14-year-old Asuka undresses in front of an adult man, who turns her down; the story does not frame either as sexual approval.

entry.heading: Neon Genesis Evangelion (manga)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life means choosing to live among other people, with the pain that comes from being separate, rather than escaping into isolation or into a merged, painless collective. Facing others, and your own fear, is worth the hurt.

content.framing: Neutral (fan service); Condemned (Kaworu's advances; Kaji turns Asuka down)

frames.aligns: Despair is shown as a trap and Shinji chooses life; an adult (Kaji) refuses a minor's advance (stage 36); human attempts to seize godhood fail; dignity of each person over the collective; a father's late repentance.
frames.concerns: Sacred names and the Spear of Longinus used as props (respect for holy things); Angels as monsters; suicides (CCC 2280-2283); nudity of a minor (CCC 2521-2524 on modesty).

frames.aligns: Pride and the passions (Gendo's grief turned to will to power) lead to ruin; communion of persons rather than absorption.
frames.concerns: Holy names, the Spear and cross imagery used decoratively, which the tradition treats as serious; Angels shown as monsters; nepsis makes the nudity and gore a concern.

frames.aligns: Human schemes to become like God fail; honesty and responsibility grow in Shinji; adults who abuse children are condemned.
frames.concerns: Angels made into enemies and biblical names used loosely; Kabbalistic symbols; no Christ or gospel; suicides; nudity (Philippians 4:8). Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Depicts brokenness without endorsing it; Shinji chooses relationship over escape; pride (Seele, Gendo) fails.
frames.concerns: Biblical imagery without biblical meaning; Angels as enemies; minor nudity and an unwanted kiss.

frames.aligns: Clear failure of human attempts at godhood; endurance and courage.
frames.concerns: Angels as monstrous beings, souls inside machines, Kabbalistic and mystical imagery: the "open door" concern weighs heavily even though staff called it decorative.

frames.aligns: Pride and human sin drive the catastrophe (Second Impact is called human error, stage 71); common grace lets families value the craft.
frames.concerns: Sacred names used loosely; suicides (WLC Q136); nudity (WLC Q139).

frames.aligns: Law shows its limits: no one saves themselves by a project; grace has an echo in Rei helping Shinji back (stage 93).
frames.concerns: Sacred imagery as decoration; nudity. LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy (Rei's care), growth in responsibility, critique of adults who exploit children.
frames.concerns: Nudity; suicides; biblical names emptied of meaning. Holiness churches more cautious than the UMC.

frames.aligns: Judged by framing: despair and pride are shown as failures; strong literary tradition of reading dark myth.
frames.concerns: Sacred names and the Spear used for effect; suicides; nudity.

frames.aligns: Critique of adults who send children to fight; distrust of secret powers.
frames.concerns: Violence is the heroes' tool throughout; nudity; worldly media.

frames.aligns: Family as central: a father's love remembered (stage 92), a mother's soul watching over her son; choosing to live.
frames.concerns: Nudity of a minor, Asuka undressing before an adult (stage 36) and an unwanted kiss (For the Strength of Youth); suicides; sacred names used loosely.

frames.aligns: Critique of institutions that use the vulnerable; empathy for traumatized children.
frames.concerns: Fan-service nudity of a 14-year-old; Kaworu's advances framed as creepy; CBR contrasts the anime's "queer" Kaworu with the manga's "uncanny" one, which some may read as a negative same-sex portrayal.

frames.aligns: Human pride fails; endurance and care for others.
frames.concerns: Souls of dead mothers inside the Evas and Yui's soul visiting the dying Gendo (stage 92) conflict with teaching that the dead are unconscious; nudity; violence.

frames.aligns: Love of family, honesty, rejection of human schemes to remake the world.
frames.concerns: Spirits of the dead active among the living; Angels as monsters; violence (Psalm 11:5); nudity.

frames.aligns: Love outlasts fear: Shinji turns from despair to life.
frames.concerns: Fear, despair and death shown as overwhelming realities; long dwelling on trauma.

frames.aligns: Choosing life (Deuteronomy 30:19) over escape; honoring a parent despite failure.
frames.concerns: Kabbalistic symbols and the divine name used loosely; a rabbi quoted by the Forward notes errors such as the Tetragrammaton shown backwards (franchise imagery); Lilith as a giant being; tzniut makes the nudity a concern; suicides.

frames.aligns: Choosing life; repair of relationships; responsibility.
frames.concerns: Kabbalistic imagery used decoratively (Forward); nudity; suicides.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam echo in restoring a broken world; informed autonomy.
frames.concerns: Jewish mystical imagery used loosely (the Forward finds it mostly incidental); nudity of a minor.

frames.aligns: Patience through suffering, mercy, rejection of human attempts to play God (shirk-like ambition fails).
frames.concerns: Angels depicted as monsters (depicting angels is widely forbidden, and angels are honored servants of God); nudity (lowering the gaze, Qur'an 24:30-31); suicides (Qur'an 4:29).

frames.aligns: Duty under suffering; the self's struggle; merging and return echo ideas of the soul.
frames.concerns: Few message conflicts; tamasic gloom and nudity for some families.

frames.aligns: Suffering, attachment and craving (Gendo's grief) are the roots of harm; compassion (Rei); the "hedgehog's dilemma" of closeness and pain (from general knowledge; to verify in the manga).
frames.concerns: Killing as the main tool; the story rejects dissolving the self, which some Buddhist readers would read differently from no-self teaching.

frames.aligns: Facing fear, accepting hukam, the five vices (Gendo's attachment and ego, Seele's ego) shown as ruinous.
Unity is valued, but freely chosen unity of distinct souls rather than forced merger; the soul's progress after death.
Sincerity (makoto) in Shinji's choice; ancestors and mothers watching over; renewal of the world.
frames.concerns: Blood and death (kegare) everywhere; foreign religious imagery is not a concern.

frames.aligns: Lilith shown as a primal mother figure, not as a Satanic stereotype; life's cycle of death and return.
The individual spirit chooses its own existence; "do not murder" in the condemnation of Seele's killing.
frames.concerns: The series' heavy psychological framing of trauma (from general knowledge); violence.

frames.aligns: Critique of authority that exploits children; women professionals; trauma treated seriously.
frames.concerns: Fan-service nudity of a 14-year-old (stage 14); Asuka's undressing before Kaji (stage 36), though the adult refuses; a same-sex kiss framed as predatory (stage 67), which CBR's contrast with the anime's "queer boy" Kaworu makes a live question; suicides without safe-messaging framing.

frames.aligns: This-life focus: meaning comes from relationships and choice, not merger or escape; human error caused the catastrophe and human choice repairs it.
frames.concerns: Exploitative nudity of a minor; suicides need mental-health framing.

frames.aligns: Responsibility, courage, a son forgiving a father, the failure of utopian projects to remake humanity.
frames.concerns: Fathers and institutions are mostly failures; sacred symbols used as decoration; nudity.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of each person over the collective; free search for meaning; critique of secret power.
frames.concerns: Violence; nudity of a minor; the stage 67 kiss.

frames.aligns: The individual chooses his own existence over absorption into a collective; religion-flavored authority (Seele) is exposed as manipulation; harm to children condemned.
frames.concerns: Little in the message; some self-sacrifice framed as noble.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Worth is not a matter of personal honor; Asuka's pride is shown as a wound (stages 57-60), and the story values honesty about feelings over saving face.

Order vs freedom.evidence: NERV's discipline is shown as manipulative; Shinji's refusal of the imposed plan (stages 93-94) is celebrated, but duty to fight is also honored (Misato, stages 82-83).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Blood family is mostly broken (Gendo); a chosen household (Misato's apartment) and friends matter as much.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Command hierarchy (Gendo, Seele) is shown as corrupt; the restored world has no ranks shown.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Religion appears as imagery, not practice; science, human error and personal choice drive the story (stage 71, Final stage).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: The story's goal is emotional honesty and a life with others, not security; Instrumentality's "security" of merger is refused.

folkways.japan: School uniforms, obedience to a father and to one's post, reluctance to voice feelings, and the use of Christian symbols as exotic decoration (as Tsurumaki described it) reflect 1990s Japanese norms more than a message aimed at other cultures.

delivery.evidence: No review calls it preachy; CBR says Sadamoto gives "everything a concrete reason in-text"; Kotaku notes added inner thoughts.
delivery.note: Characters state the themes in dialogue and inner monologue, while the villains' plans are given motives.

personified.ideology: Choosing painful connection over escape
Grief turned into will to power
Engineered collective apotheosis
Death as release; possessive curiosity

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Secular humanism, Transhumanism (critiqued), Collectivism (critiqued).

series.title: My Love Story with Yamada-kun at Lv999
series.romaji: Yamada-kun to Lv999 no Koi wo Suru
series.native: 山田くんとLv999の恋をする

entry.heading: My Love Story with Yamada-kun at Lv999
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is found by getting back up after being hurt, letting people in, and choosing a partner who is quietly faithful and honest. Online friends can become real friends, but trust has to be earned.

frames.aligns: Infidelity is shown as a wound (ch. 1); faithful, self-giving care is made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7).
frames.concerns: Sex before marriage presented as a natural next step (ch. 69); an adult courting a high school student; drunkenness as comedy.

frames.aligns: Humility and quiet service in Yamada's care for Akane.
frames.concerns: Nepsis (watchfulness) and the bed scene; romance as the whole of life.

frames.aligns: Philippians 4:8 fits the loyalty and kindness; cheating is shown as wrong.
frames.concerns: Premarital sex endorsed; an adult dating a student; drunkenness (Ephesians 5:18). Each family decides (soul liberty).

frames.aligns: Faithfulness, care and forgiveness (Runa, Yui); caution about strangers. Beneath the Tangles' reviewer "highly recommend[s]" the anime.
frames.concerns: The romance's arc leads to sex outside marriage; a high school senior and a college student.

frames.aligns: No occult or spiritual content; kindness and loyalty.
frames.concerns: Holiness standards on sexual content and drinking.

frames.aligns: Common grace: honest craft on loyalty and recovery from hurt.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139's concern about "lascivious" books applies to ch. 69, though nothing explicit is shown.

frames.aligns: Adiaphora: a gentle comedy judged by love and conscience.
frames.concerns: Premarital sex; age gap. LCMS and WELS families likely more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Kindness, care for the sick, loyalty.
frames.concerns: Wesley's test of whether a book tends to the love of God; the sex scene; drinking.

frames.aligns: Good and evil framed clearly (cheating versus faithfulness); forgiveness offered.
frames.concerns: Premarital sex and the age gap; practice ranges widely.

frames.aligns: No heroic violence; humility, care, reconciliation after a quarrel (v6).
frames.concerns: Separation from the world makes popular romance media a concern; sexual content; drinking. MC USA families are more open.
The law of chastity; the Word of Wisdom and drinking; For the Strength of Youth counsel on dating; a youth dating an adult.

frames.aligns: Emotional honesty; a woman's recovery after betrayal; online safety; forgiveness.
frames.concerns: Power and life-stage imbalance between an adult and a high school student; consent and readiness at ch. 69.

frames.aligns: No violence, occult or gore; diligence and care.
frames.concerns: "By beholding we become changed": romance-centered fiction leading to premarital sex; alcohol as comedy.
jw.org counsels dating only when ready to marry; sexual immorality (Galatians 5:19) endorsed in ch. 69; drunkenness; a youth dating an adult.

frames.aligns: Love and kindness overcome hurt; little fear or illness dwelt on (one fever, ch. 28-29).

frames.concerns: Tzniut and shomer negiah: physical affection and sex outside marriage; yichud (the couple alone at his apartment, ch. 69). Haredi homes would avoid; Modern Orthodox families may read selectively.

frames.aligns: Kind speech; loyalty; caring for the sick (bikur cholim).
frames.concerns: Sexual ethics within committed relationships, applied by families; age gap.

frames.aligns: Informed autonomy; healthy relationship skills; online safety.
Loyalty, patience (sabr) after hurt, caution with strangers.
frames.concerns: Dating and sex outside marriage as the plot's direction; alcohol; lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31).

frames.aligns: Loyalty and care; Yamada's visit to Akane's family (v10) honors family ties.
frames.concerns: Love chosen without family involvement until late; premarital sex; rajasic attachment.

frames.aligns: Compassion; letting go of a past hurt; quiet, steady conduct.
frames.concerns: Third precept and craving; fifth precept and intoxication played for laughs.
Sex only within marriage; intoxicants; attachment (moh) as a theme.

frames.aligns: Service, kindness, the guild as a diverse community.
frames.concerns: Chastity before marriage; alcohol, which Bahá'í teaching forbids.

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto), gratitude and harmony in the guild.
"Harm none": cheating shown as harm, care shown as good; consenting adult partners.
frames.concerns: Concern about exploitation if the age gap is read as a power imbalance.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness: be faithful to your sexual partner; be worthy of trust.
A heroine's emotional recovery; honest communication; consent shown (she asks for the lights off, ch. 69); the couple waits while he is in school (Anime Corner vol. 6).
frames.concerns: An adult pursuing a high school student: Anime Feminist found her "imposing on him uncomfortable" (yellow flag) before recommending the show; ANN jokes she "should try waiting... after he turns 18!"

frames.aligns: Human relationships give meaning; online life treated critically.
frames.concerns: Age and life-stage gap; prank revenge on a neighbor.

frames.aligns: Faithfulness rewarded and cheating punished; Yamada meets her family (v10); marriage raised (v9).
frames.concerns: Premarital sex; an adult woman dating a high school boy; little parental presence.

frames.aligns: Worth and dignity of each person; consent; a diverse guild.
frames.concerns: Age gap and readiness, read through OWL's consent framework.

frames.aligns: Honest pursuit of one's desires; a consenting adult couple; indulgence without guilt.
frames.concerns: Harm to children is condemned in the Eleven Rules; the sources place Yamada at 18 by ch. 43 and ch. 69.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Insults and betrayals are mostly shrugged off or answered with comedy; Eita and Yamada break up the Ren confrontation rather than avenge (v6), and Akane makes up with Yui. The in-game campaign against the neighbor (v7) is a small honor-style payback.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Characters live by their own choices with little family or institutional oversight; Yamada lives alone (ch. 12); the guild is voluntary.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Loyalty runs to a chosen community met online, not to blood family; family appears late (v6, v10).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Age and school-year differences are noticed but do not set rank; the younger Yamada is the steadier partner. Senpai-kohai ties (Eita and Yamada, ch. 10) are light.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No religion or custom guides choices; life is guided by personal feeling and practical sense.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Hobbies, emotional honesty and quality of relationships are central; Yamada's work as a pro gamer is a form of self-expression.

folkways.japan: Guild "offline meetings," school cultural festivals, cram school and entrance exams (v4-6), graduation in March, the move to university in April, and homecoming visits to a rural hometown are Japanese norms that frame the story. Japan's age of majority is 18 (since April 2022; from general knowledge), and a romance between a college student and a final-year high school student is a familiar genre premise there.

delivery.evidence: Reviewers praise "mature communication" and genre comfort (Anime Corner; But Why Tho); none calls it preachy or moralizing.
delivery.note: Its points about faithfulness and online trust come through comic situations and Akane's inner monologue rather than speeches.

personified.ideology: Quiet loyalty and honesty over charm
Casual infidelity
Caution and care for others online
Controlling, unfaithful online "elite"

entry.dominant: Communitarianism (the guild as chosen family), Classical virtue ethics (faithfulness and care), Expressive individualism (following one's feelings across an age gap).

series.title: Black Butler
series.warning: Black Butler (vol. 27, ch. 135-136) depicts, non-explicitly, the sexual abuse of ten-year-old twins by a cult; the series also contains child trafficking, ritual child murder and suggestive framing of its 12-to-13-year-old protagonist.

entry.heading: Black Butler
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: The story honors a life lived by one's own word and pride to the bitter end. Ciel refuses pity and forgiveness, trades his soul for revenge, and keeps the bargain. The story admires his resolve, condemns the people who prey on children, and shows the price he pays in his own humanity.

content.framing: Shown with consequences (villains); ambiguous (Ciel's own orders)

frames.aligns: Abuse of children and trafficking are shown as grave evils; the cult is a parody of worship, not worship.
frames.concerns: A soul sold to a demon as the hero's foundation; revenge chosen over forgiveness; despair and loss of faith left unanswered; the demon made attractive (against Inter Mirifica 7). The ch. 135 imagery and the suggestive framing of a child concern CCC 2354 and 2525.

frames.aligns: Evil spirits are real and their bargains are deadly, which the story's fixed price echoes.
frames.concerns: Nepsis: the demonic presented as elegant and loyal; no repentance; a corrupted parody of liturgy (the cult's altar). The imagery of children's abuse is a serious matter of guarding the senses.

frames.aligns: Sin has wages: the contract ends in the loss of a soul. Evil men who harm children are punished.
frames.concerns: A demon as protector and near-hero; the protagonist rejects God; revenge drives him (Romans 12:19). Philippians 4:8 test fails often. Soul liberty means families decide; many would not choose it.

frames.aligns: Depicts evil (cult, trafficking) without endorsing it; shows the cost of a Faustian bargain.
frames.concerns: The demon is the reader's admired guide; no grace or redemption on offer; occult and demonic content central. Romans 14 freedom stops at content that sexualizes a child.

frames.aligns: The story agrees that demons are real and their pacts deadly.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": a demon pact, demon worship, ritual sacrifice and Grim Reapers are the premise, with the demon portrayed favorably. Ch. 135 and the sexualized child scenes add to the concern.

frames.aligns: Total depravity is visible in Victorian high society; judgment falls on predators.
frames.concerns: A hero who chooses damnation without the story calling it tragedy; no providence, only contract. WLC Q139 on "lascivious... pictures" bears on the suggestive child framing.

frames.aligns: Law without gospel: the story shows a world of contracts and debts with no grace, which Lutheran readers can name.
frames.concerns: Demonic pact as foundation; revenge; loss of faith; sexualized framing of a child. LCMS and WELS families would be more cautious than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Social holiness echoes: workhouses, trafficked children and the poor are shown as victims.
frames.concerns: Wesley's rule against diversions that cannot be used "in the name of the Lord Jesus": a demon-served revenge story with sexualized child imagery. No prevenient grace reaches Ciel.

frames.aligns: The Victorian Anglican world is drawn in detail; Faustian tales (Marlowe) are part of the English literary tradition and judged by framing.
frames.concerns: The framing admires Ciel's resolve and the demon's style more than it laments the bargain; suggestive framing of a child.

frames.aligns: Shows how violence and revenge consume a child.
frames.concerns: Revenge and killing are the hero's path; demonic service is admired; worldly aristocratic display is celebrated. Conservative groups avoid such media entirely.

frames.aligns: Families and servants who love Ciel; agency and its consequences.
frames.concerns: Covenant with a demon as the core; loss of faith; sexualized framing of a child; dark occult content. For the Strength of Youth asks whether media invites the Spirit.

frames.aligns: Exposes child trafficking, workhouses and predatory aristocrats; sympathy for an abuse survivor.
frames.concerns: Critics say the series aestheticizes the abused child and flirts with shotacon (Anime Feminist; Manga Bookshelf); revenge unquestioned; imperial setting.

frames.aligns: The wages of sin are shown.
frames.concerns: The state of the dead: Grim Reapers, revived corpses and a revived twin conflict with teaching that the dead are unconscious. Demons as helpers. "By beholding we become changed" weighs against the imagery. (from general knowledge; to verify)
Spiritism and demonism are the premise (Galatians 5:19-21); violence (Psalm 11:5); immorality. jw.org counsel would steer away. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Evil is shown as self-destroying in villains.
frames.concerns: Fear, cruelty, disease and evil are presented as overwhelming realities; the reader dwells on trauma. (from general knowledge; to verify)
Idolatrous and demonic practice central; revenge; tzniut concerns at the suggestive child framing; many Haredi homes would not admit such media. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Exposes abuse of children; questions of justice for the powerless.
frames.concerns: Revenge as purpose; occult pact; sexualized framing of a child.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam echoes: exposing trafficking and child labor; empathy for a survivor.
frames.concerns: Revenge unexamined; sexualized framing of a child; imperial setting.

frames.aligns: Oppressors of children are punished; loyalty and keeping one's word.
frames.concerns: A pact with a devil (shaytan) as the hero's foundation; sihr-like occult practice; revenge; lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) at the suggestive scenes.

frames.aligns: Karma visible: deeds bind, and every bargain bears fruit. Loyalty and duty of servants.
frames.concerns: Tamasic content (Gita ch. 17): cruelty, darkness and revenge; sexualized framing of a child.

frames.aligns: A clear picture of how hatred and attachment bind: Ciel's revenge costs his self.
frames.concerns: Revenge is honored more than released; right mindfulness of what feeds the mind.

frames.aligns: Defense of the helpless (circus children) is a duty the story touches.
frames.concerns: Anger and ego (two of the five vices) drive the hero and are admired; occult pact. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Exposure of cruelty to children; loyalty.
frames.concerns: Revenge, demonic pact, and degrading images clash with the call to a "chaste and holy life." (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Purity and impurity themes: the cult's defilement (the fan wiki says it aimed to "defile" the twins' souls). Grim Reapers draw on Japanese shinigami folklore.
frames.concerns: No shrine or kami disrespect; concern is the impurity of blood and death throughout. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Witches in the Emerald Witch arc are drawn as people with a history, not as cartoon villains (Sieglinde; TV Tropes).
frames.concerns: Demon worship conflated with child sacrifice; revenge against "harm none."

frames.aligns: Way to Happiness precepts: villains who harm children are condemned; competence valued.
frames.concerns: Revenge and killing; the hero's trauma left untreated.

frames.aligns: Exposes child trafficking and abuse by the powerful; LGBTQ-adjacent characters; creator supports same-sex romance stories (ANN).
frames.concerns: Critics say the series sexualizes its child protagonist: "not just BL but shota" (Manga Bookshelf); "dangerously close to shotacon" and "aestheticizing abuse" (Anime Feminist). Common Sense Media: "suggestive scenes between young teenage boys and older men."

frames.aligns: Critical eye on cults, aristocratic impunity and blind faith.
frames.concerns: Cruelty and child exploitation are aestheticized at times; revenge unexamined; supernatural treated as real.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, duty, manners, crown and household order; competence and composure.
frames.concerns: A demonic bargain at the center; sexualized framing of a child; revenge above law.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of exploited children; justice for the powerless.
frames.concerns: Revenge; sexualized framing of a child; violence as the main solution.

frames.aligns: Church of Satan individualism: a self-made boy who answers harm with vengeance and owes no god. Satanic Temple Tenet 1 (compassion) echoes in protecting children.
frames.concerns: A demon-worshipping cult that ritually abuses children repeats the "Satanic panic" stereotype both organizations reject; harm to children (Eleven Satanic Rules of the Earth).

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Harm to the Phantomhive name must be answered personally: Ciel refuses courts and pity and pursues revenge (premise; Wikipedia). Kelvin and the cult are killed, not tried (v7; ch. 140).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Household discipline, manners and the Queen's orders frame life; Ciel acts outside ordinary law but inside the crown's order.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Family, name and household come first; Ciel will let other people's children die to reach his goal (circus arc, TV Tropes).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Earl and butler, the Queen's Watchdog, Weston's prefects and fags (ch. 70-80, TV Tropes): rank shapes every relationship and is rarely questioned.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Aristocratic custom is honored, but faith is rejected and Ciel works as a rational detective; the supernatural is real but not sacred.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Revenge and survival come first; self-expression appears mainly in costume and comedy.

folkways.japan: The series is a Japanese view of Victorian England, so its aristocratic hierarchy and master-servant devotion reflect both the British setting and Japanese norms of loyalty to one's house; the "aesthetic of the perfect butler" is a Japanese pop-culture fascination more than a message about Britain.

delivery.evidence: No review calls it preachy. Beasi (Manga Bookshelf) finds "a deeper story" under a "fairly vapid" start; the OASG calls the darkness "not gratuitous."
delivery.note: The series rarely states a moral; its view emerges through Ciel's choices and the fates of villains, with the hero's revenge left largely unjudged.

personified.ideology: Revenge and pride over forgiveness
Demonic aesthetics and appetite
Aristocratic predation
Death and its reversal as entertainment
