series.title: Yokohama Kaidashi Kikou
series.native: ヨコハマ買い出し紀行

entry.heading: Yokohama Kaidashi Kikou (Yokohama Shopping Log)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is lived slowly and attentively: savoring small, everyday beauty, keeping friendships, and accepting that people, places and even humanity pass away.

frames.aligns: Beauty sought for its own sake (John Paul II, Letter to Artists); gratitude, hospitality, care for creation, honor of elders. Nothing evil made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7).
frames.concerns: Death met with acceptance but no hope of resurrection; the nude figures (Misago, Director Alpha) and the shared bath (ch. 31) against modesty (CCC 2521-2524).

frames.aligns: Stillness, attention and gratitude; a world seen as gift.
frames.concerns: Nepsis: guarding the eyes regarding the nude figures; mortality without resurrection.

frames.aligns: Kindness, contentment, honest work; nothing evil praised.
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 test for the nudity; robot "kissing"; no God in the world's end.

frames.aligns: Common beauty and friendship; depiction is not endorsement.
frames.concerns: No hope beyond death; the nude scenes; the girls'-love subtext.

frames.aligns: Peaceable community; no demonic content found.
frames.concerns: Unexplained spirit-like elements (Misago, "water god" mushrooms) are mild but noted; modesty standards for the nudity.

frames.aligns: Common grace in well-made art by a non-Christian; creation's goodness; vocation in ordinary work (the café).
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 on pictures that stir desire, applied to the nude figures, though sources call them non-sexual.

frames.aligns: Adiaphora; vocation and daily bread; love of neighbor.
frames.concerns: LCMS and WELS families more cautious about the nudity than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Kindness and hospitality; social holiness in small ways.
frames.concerns: Holiness churches more cautious about the nudity.

frames.aligns: A literary, contemplative work judged by its framing; wonder at creation.
frames.concerns: The nude figures; no faith horizon.

frames.aligns: Simple living, nonviolence, small community, contentment with little: close to Anabaptist ideals.
frames.concerns: Separation from worldly media for conservative groups; nudity.

frames.aligns: Kindness, family continuity (Takahiro and Makki's marriage and child), work.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth on modesty in media; no eternal family horizon.

frames.aligns: Care for creation, acceptance of the different (androids), quiet community.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; climate disaster is a setting rather than a call to act.
Fundamental Belief 22; the nudity; light drinking (ch. 54).

frames.aligns: Peaceful neighbors; no violence praised; no spiritism made central.
frames.concerns: Nudity; uncanny "water god" and Misago elements; robot "kissing."

frames.aligns: Calm, harmony and gratitude over fear; no illness dwelt on.
Kindness, hospitality (hachnasat orchim), honor for elders.
frames.concerns: Tzniut: the nude figures and the shared bath (ch. 31); many Haredi homes restrict such media.

frames.aligns: Chesed, hospitality, care for creation (bal tashchit).
Tikkun olam, kindness, acceptance of the other.

frames.concerns: Lowering the gaze (24:30-31) for the nudity and the shared bath; alcohol shown lightly (ch. 54); no akhirah.

frames.aligns: A sattvic, peaceful mood; impermanence and detachment; service to guests.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; some families note the nudity.

frames.aligns: Impermanence (anicca) is the core theme; mindfulness of small moments; equanimity in loss; non-harm throughout.

frames.concerns: Little to raise; modesty for the nude figures.

frames.aligns: Service, unity, harmony with nature, kindness.
frames.concerns: Chaste-life ideals and the nude figures; alcohol (forbidden to Baha'is) shown lightly.

frames.aligns: Reverence for nature, sea and seasons; purity and gratitude; mono no aware; uncanny presences (Misago, "water god" mushrooms) treated with respect.
The Way to Happiness: care for the planet, be industrious, respect others.
Climate-changed world, acceptance of the nonhuman other, queer subtext treated gently, no violence.
frames.concerns: The child Takahiro in a shared bath with an adult-presenting android (ch. 31) and his reaction to adult nudity are worth age-appropriateness review; the disaster is not examined politically.

frames.aligns: Meaning made in this life through friendship, craft and attention; mortality faced without supernatural comfort.
frames.concerns: Unexplained mysteries are left open rather than explained.

frames.aligns: Respect for elders, family continuity, hospitality, rootedness in place, beauty.
frames.concerns: Nudity; girls'-love subtext; humanity's decline met without striving.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth extended to androids; interdependent web of existence.
No harm to children or animals; personal pleasure in small things; no stereotyping.
frames.concerns: Gentle passivity sits apart from self-assertion ideals.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: No insults answered or feuds; the one drawn gun (ch. 60) is a startled mistake, not a quarrel (TV Tropes).

Order vs freedom.evidence: No authority structures; Alpha travels alone for a year (ch. 62-78); Takahiro leaves home to follow engines (Wikipedia).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Neighbors and friends matter as much as family: Ojisan and Takahiro, Sensei treating Alpha like a daughter (ch. 4).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Elders are honored but relations are easy and flat; humans and androids are friends.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Secular everyday life with a reverent mood toward nature and unexplained mysteries; no institutions or rites central.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Quality of life, art (Maruko, photography, the moon guitar), tolerance and contentment come before security in a declining world.

folkways.japan: The aesthetic of mono no aware, seasonal awareness, respect for elders and the iyashikei ("healing") genre's emphasis on calm reflect Japanese norms; the story's turn away from striving and economic growth is its own outlook rather than a general Japanese norm.

delivery.evidence: Nicoll: "more about savouring moments than answering questions"; Okazu calls it experiential with "no real plot." No review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The series has no antagonists or argued positions; its outlook is carried by mood, pacing and what it chooses to show.

personified.ideology: Contentment and attention to the present moment
Striving and going out into the world
Accepting age and death with grace

entry.dominant: Dharmic (Buddhist impermanence), Stoicism, Naturalism, Secular humanism.

series.title: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure Part 4: Diamond is Unbreakable
series.romaji: JoJo no Kimyou na Bouken: Diamond wa Kudakenai
series.native: ジョジョの奇妙な冒険 ダイヤモンドは砕けない

entry.heading: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure Part 4: Diamond Is Unbreakable
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is ordinary life shared with friends and neighbours, worth defending when evil hides behind a normal face. In Araki's words, "true strength is found in not doing bad things" (Wikipedia).

frames.aligns: Evil framed as evil and judged; justice for the dead (Reimi); a family that accepts an illegitimate son; neighbours protecting each other.
frames.concerns: Inter Mirifica 7: the killer is charismatic and popular with fans; stated sexual crimes against children; the hand fetish. CCC 2525 on permissiveness.

frames.aligns: Ordinary life as the place where good and evil meet; the dead are remembered.
frames.concerns: Nepsis weighs the fetish, the stated crimes against children and the body horror.

frames.aligns: Clear good and evil; the wicked face judgment (ch. 174).
frames.concerns: Phil 4:8 test: serial murder, sexual crimes against minors stated, the fetish; Ephesians 5:12 on speaking of such things. Soul liberty: each family decides.

frames.aligns: Community defends the weak; justice for victims; courage of a timid boy (Koichi).
frames.concerns: Romans 14 conscience on the fetish and stated sexual violence; ghosts and afterlife outside a biblical frame.

frames.aligns: Evil is overcome; the killer's soul faces judgment.
frames.concerns: The "open door" concern: ghosts who guide the living, a cursed arrow that gives powers, souls dragged away.

frames.aligns: Total depravity behind a respectable face; common grace in friendship and art (Rohan).
frames.concerns: WLC Q139: the stated sexual sins and the fetish; violence.

frames.aligns: Vocation: son, friend, neighbour, father (Hayato's family).
frames.concerns: Adiaphora, but conscience weighs the sexual crimes and fetish; LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Growth in character (Koichi, Okuyasu); social holiness: a town caring for its own.
frames.concerns: General Rules on diversions; holiness churches cautious about horror and sexual content.

frames.aligns: Judged by framing: evil exposed, victims vindicated, friendship honored.
frames.concerns: A charming villain; sexual crimes against children named in passing.

frames.aligns: Community, not a lone hero, overcomes evil; mercy and friendship.
frames.concerns: Violence is the means and is shown as heroic; Josuke fuses a man into a rock (ch. 8).

frames.aligns: Family across generations; a son accepted; the dead finding rest.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth: sexual content and horror may not invite the Spirit.

frames.aligns: Attention to victims: Reimi's justice; Shinobu and Hayato; a single mother respected.
frames.concerns: Women as the villain's victims; an abusive teen romance (Yukako) played partly as comedy.

frames.aligns: Evil is ended; the righteous protect the town.
frames.concerns: "By beholding we become changed"; ghosts conflict with Fundamental Belief 26 on the state of the dead.
jw.org counsel on violence (Psalm 11:5), immorality and spiritism: ghosts, souls dragged away, powers from an arrow.

frames.aligns: Fear and evil faced with courage.
frames.concerns: Murder, bodily destruction and fear presented as real and overwhelming.

frames.aligns: Justice for the murdered; honoring family; communal responsibility.
frames.concerns: Tzniut and nivul peh weigh the sexual crimes, fetish and fan service; many Haredi homes avoid such media; ghosts.
Sexual content and violence; the killer made charming.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam on a town scale; victims vindicated.
frames.concerns: Violence against women; an abusive teen romance played for laughs.

frames.aligns: Justice and accountability after death; protecting neighbours (a strong Islamic duty).
frames.concerns: Images of living beings (scholars differ); lowering the gaze (24:30-31) weighs the fetish and fan service; ghosts.

frames.aligns: Karma: the killer's deeds catch up with him; dharma of protecting the town.
Kira's craving for a "quiet life" without suffering produces suffering for others; the dead released when justice comes.
Protecting the weak (sant-sipahi ideal); lust (kaam) and ego shown in the villain and defeated.
frames.concerns: Violence; the five vices vividly shown.
"Chaste and holy life": the sexual crimes and fetish.

frames.aligns: A local town and its spirits; the unquiet dead pacified when wrongs are righted (Reimi); sincerity among friends.
frames.concerns: Death and corpses (kegare); the killer's ghost.

frames.aligns: Spirits of place; the dead guiding the living.
frames.concerns: "Harm none" against the violence; the arrow as a cursed relic.

frames.aligns: Competence and self-determination; The Way to Happiness on not harming others.
Ordinary people, a single mother and a child bring down a powerful man; victims remembered.
frames.concerns: Violence against women and a fetish turned into a fan-favorite villain; an abusive teen romance (Yukako) treated partly as comedy; stated sexual violence against boys; fan service of a teen (TV Tropes).

frames.aligns: Reason, observation and cooperation expose a hidden killer; Araki: "true strength is found in not doing bad things" (Wikipedia).
frames.concerns: Ghosts and afterlife judgment treated as real.

frames.aligns: Community, family, duty to protect the town; justice.
frames.concerns: An illegitimate son as the hero's origin; delinquent style; the sexual and violent content.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of every townsperson; justice for victims.
frames.concerns: Violence; a fetish made into a popular villain.

frames.aligns: Individualism (Rohan); a hypocritical "respectable" man exposed. The Satanic Temple's tenets on compassion and bodily autonomy side against Kira; the Eleven Rules oppose harm to children.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Josuke fights over insults to his hair (ch. 1-3), but the main fight is to protect neighbours, not avenge pride.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Teens act outside the law, yet the goal is to restore a peaceful town.

Civic vs kin.evidence: The town matters most (ch. 174), with family ties (Joseph, Josuke, the Nijimuras) close behind.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Friends of different ages and types cooperate; Rohan's arrogance is mocked.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Little religion, but ghosts and lineage matter.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Fashion, art (Rohan), food (Tonio), everyday pleasures; Araki's "feeling of everyday life" (Wikipedia).

folkways.japan: The town-as-community, the senpai-kohai ties among schoolmates, the delinquent pompadour, and the restless ghost who rests once a wrong is righted reflect Japanese norms; the salaryman villain reflects 1990s Japanese anxieties about the ordinary office worker (my own framing; to verify).

delivery.evidence: Viz calls it "a fun little murder mystery"; ANN's Hopper notes the arc lacks a "strong narrative throughline" (via Wikipedia).
delivery.note: The message comes through the town's slow discovery of the killer rather than speeches; Kira explains his "quiet life" philosophy in his own words, and the story answers it by his fate.

personified.ideology: Protect the town and the people in it
A quiet, private life at any cost to others
Art and curiosity above ordinary morality
Possessive, all-consuming love

entry.dominant: Communitarianism (affirmed), Classical virtue ethics (affirmed), Hedonism (critiqued through Kira), Expressive individualism (explored through Rohan and Josuke's style).

entry.heading: A Sign of Affection (Yubisaki to Renren)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is lived in honest connection: learning another person's language, saying what you feel, accepting help without being defined by it, and choosing a partner who widens your world. Disability is part of an ordinary, full life, not the whole of it.

frames.aligns: Dignity of a person with a disability; patient, attentive love; parents honored and consulted (CCC 2214-2220); good made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7).
frames.concerns: Cohabitation before marriage presented as a natural step (CCC 2390-2391); bar culture and drunkenness (CCC 2290).

frames.aligns: Love as attention to the other; humility; kindness to strangers.
frames.concerns: Living together before marriage; drinking. Nepsis for romance-centered media.

frames.aligns: Kindness, honesty, faithfulness within the couple; Oushi's possessiveness shown as wrong.
frames.concerns: Cohabitation and implied intimacy outside marriage (Hebrews 13:4; 1 Corinthians 6:18); drinking at a bar. Philippians 4:8 test; each family decides.

frames.aligns: Depicts care and sacrifice in a relationship; strong "love your neighbor" echo in learning sign language.
frames.concerns: Cohabitation endorsed by the story; drinking.

frames.aligns: No occult or spirit content; kindness and inclusion.
frames.concerns: Holiness standards on cohabitation and alcohol.

frames.aligns: Common grace: a non-Christian work that honors human dignity and faithful love.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 on the seventh commandment applied to cohabitation and implied intimacy; drunkenness.

frames.aligns: Vocation and love of neighbor in ordinary life; entertainment as adiaphora.
frames.concerns: Cohabitation; LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy and inclusion; growth in character.
frames.concerns: Holiness tradition caution on alcohol and on cohabitation; UMC families more open.

frames.aligns: Judged by framing: faults (jealousy, condescension) named and outgrown; love honors the other.
Nonviolence, community care, humility; inclusion of the disabled.
frames.concerns: Separation from popular media in conservative groups; worldly bar life; cohabitation. MC USA families more open.

frames.aligns: Family consulted; kindness; adult dating with commitment in view.
frames.concerns: Law of chastity and Word of Wisdom: cohabitation, implied intimacy and alcohol. For the Strength of Youth asks whether media invites the Spirit.

frames.aligns: Disability inclusion; d/Deaf representation praised by Anime Feminist; a partner who learns the other's language.
frames.concerns: Debate over hearing creators telling a Deaf story (Anime Feminist); lip-reading realism (ANN).

frames.aligns: Kindness, inclusion; no violence or occult.
frames.concerns: Alcohol (temperance teaching); cohabitation; Fundamental Belief 22 on entertainment and romance-centered fiction ("by beholding we become changed").

frames.aligns: No spiritism; kindness, honesty, peace-making among friends.
frames.concerns: Dating without marriage in view, then living together unmarried, runs against jw.org counsel; drunkenness (Galatians 5:19-21). Choices left to conscience.

frames.aligns: Love overcomes fear and limitation; Yuki is not defined by a disability.
frames.concerns: Dwelling on limitation and fear of being a burden (Sign 28).

frames.aligns: Kevod ha-briyot (human dignity) for a deaf woman; honoring parents; kind speech prized over cruel speech.
frames.concerns: Tzniut and shomer negiah: unmarried touch, kissing, a shared bed and cohabitation are central; bar scenes. Many Haredi homes restrict secular media.

frames.aligns: Dignity of persons with disabilities; honesty; family consulted.
frames.concerns: Cohabitation before marriage for more observant families.

frames.aligns: Inclusion, informed choice, respect for a minority culture (Deaf culture).
Good character (akhlaq), patience (sabr), care for others, consulting parents.
frames.concerns: Unmarried dating, kissing, a shared bed and cohabitation are the plot; alcohol is forbidden (Qur'an 5:90) and a bar is a main setting; lowering the gaze (24:30-31).

frames.aligns: Seva (service) and patience; duty to parents shown in seeking their blessing; love as devotion.
frames.concerns: Cohabitation for traditional families; alcohol for some.

frames.aligns: Right speech and attentive listening; compassion; looking at the person before you.
frames.concerns: The fifth precept (intoxicants) and the bar scenes; attachment in romance.

frames.aligns: Seva, humility, equality of all people; ego (haumai) in Oushi's possessiveness overcome.
frames.concerns: Alcohol is prohibited in Sikh practice and appears often; lust as one of the five vices is not a theme here.

frames.aligns: Unity, consultation (talking honestly as a couple), service.

Little religious content to align or conflict.

frames.aligns: "Harm none"; consensual, caring relationships; respect for difference.
Communication as the key to understanding (CSM's summary of the message) echoes the Church's emphasis on communication; Way to Happiness precepts on kindness.
frames.concerns: Alcohol use (The Way to Happiness counsels temperance); no psychiatry shown.

frames.aligns: Nuanced Deaf representation (CSM; Anime Feminist); autonomy without paternalism; consent and slow pace in intimacy (CSM; Sign 44).
frames.concerns: Hearing creators telling a Deaf story; Itsuomi patting Yuki's head on first meeting (Anime Feminist, anime ep. 1); optimistic lip reading (ANN).

frames.aligns: Human worth and capability; empathy built through effort; reason and honest talk solve problems.
Seeking parents' blessing; a man who shows respect (black hair for the meeting, Sign 29); work and responsibility.
frames.concerns: Cohabitation without marriage; bar culture; leaving one's home country for a personal dream.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth and dignity; justice and inclusion for Deaf people; free search for meaning.
Self-determination and pursuit of one's desires (Yuki and Itsuomi choose freely); consensual adult intimacy without guilt; bodily autonomy (Satanic Temple Tenet 3).

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Jealousy and slights are met with talk and patience, not retaliation; Oushi's sign insults are framed as a fault (TV Tropes).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Yuki moves from a curfewed home and a friend who polices her outings to choosing her own life and home (TV Tropes; v8-v10).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Parents are consulted (Sign 29), but a voluntary circle of friends and the couple carry most of the story.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Senior and junior students meet as equals; Itsuomi treats Yuki "like any other person" (Otaku USA). Courtesy to parents is kept.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No religion; modern urban university life; parents' blessing is a custom rather than a sacred rite.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Self-expression, tolerance of difference and pursuing dreams are celebrated (Itsuomi's plans abroad; Yuki's fashion and boldness).

folkways.japan: The parents' meeting (and Itsuomi dyeing his hair black to look respectable), the drinking age of 20, the university note-taker system and the contrast between Japanese Sign Language and Signed Japanese are Japanese settings the story works within; its own message is the inclusion of Deaf people in ordinary life.

delivery.evidence: ANN says it never defines Yuki "solely by her deafness"; Anime Feminist praises lettering that centers her view. No reviewer calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The inclusion message is carried by Yuki's point of view, lettering and everyday scenes rather than speeches, with Oushi's protective view given its own chapters.

personified.ideology: Openness: meet every person in their own language
Deaf people need to be protected from the hearing world
Disability is part of an ordinary, self-directed life

entry.dominant: Secular humanism, Progressivism (disability inclusion), Expressive individualism.

series.title: The Dangers in My Heart
series.romaji: Boku no Kokoro no Yabai Yatsu

entry.heading: The Dangers in My Heart
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life opens up when a person stops sneering at the world from a distance and lets others in. Seeing the good in other people, and learning to be kind and honest about one's own feelings, is shown as the way out of self-hatred and loneliness.

frames.aligns: Conversion of heart from contempt to love of neighbor; dignity of the outsider; families present and caring.
frames.concerns: Chastity and modesty (CCC 2521-2524): sexual jokes and suggestive art involving young teens; how far an early-teen couple's physical affection goes (vols. 9-13).

frames.aligns: Humility and repentance-like change; love that sees the other truly.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis): sexualized humor and suggestive panels of a minor.
Philippians 4:8 test: crude sexual talk and suggestive art; early-teen dating. Families decide under soul liberty.

frames.aligns: Depicts rather than endorses Kyotaro's dark fantasies, which he outgrows; seeing the good in others (Beneath the Tangles).
frames.concerns: Sexual talk among young teens; a dating relationship that tests physical limits.

frames.aligns: Transformation of a dark, isolated heart.
frames.concerns: Holiness standards on modesty; murder fantasies and sexual humor as "open doors."

frames.aligns: Common grace in a well-written story of growth; honesty and repair.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 on "lascivious... books, pictures": the suggestive art and erection/masturbation jokes are the test case.

frames.aligns: Vocation and planning a future (vol. 11); forgiveness and kindness among friends.
frames.concerns: Sixth Commandment: sexual purity in thought and word; LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Growth in love and kindness; friends who help.
frames.concerns: Wesley's rule on books that do not "tend to the knowledge or love of God"; sexual humor. Holiness churches would avoid; UMC families vary.

frames.aligns: Judged by framing: violent posing is outgrown, kindness and honest love win, adults are present.
frames.concerns: Sexual talk and suggestive art involving young teens.

frames.aligns: Humility, gentleness, a quiet young man who learns to love.
frames.concerns: Separation from worldly media; immodesty and crude talk; early-teen romance. MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Growth, kindness, planning a future; supportive families.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth: dating before 16 is discouraged; law of chastity in thought and speech; sexual humor.

frames.aligns: An outsider valued; boundaries respected (ANN); a girl with agency and a career.
frames.concerns: Early misogynistic monologues (Anime Feminist yellow flag); sexualized art of minors.

frames.aligns: Diligence and kindness; a mind renewed.
frames.concerns: Fundamental Belief 22 on entertainment "of the highest quality"; "by beholding we become changed"; crude talk and suggestive art.

frames.aligns: Kindness and honesty; a turn away from violent thoughts.
frames.concerns: jw.org counsel on entertainment with "uncleanness" (Galatians 5:19-21); dating by young teens; violent fantasies (Psalm 11:5).

frames.aligns: Thought shapes experience: Kyotaro's dark thoughts give way to love and the world changes with them.
frames.concerns: Dwelling on murder fantasies and sensual images.

frames.aligns: Teshuva-like change; kindness to the outsider.
frames.concerns: Tzniut: suggestive art and sexual talk; nivul peh (crude speech); unchaperoned teen romance.

frames.aligns: Repair of character; human dignity (kavod habriyot).
frames.concerns: Modesty; crude talk; sexualized humor about young teens.

frames.aligns: Emotional honesty, kindness, consent and boundaries.
frames.concerns: Sexualized art of minors; early misogynistic monologues.

frames.aligns: Kindness, mercy, character change; family respect.
frames.concerns: Lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31): suggestive art; unchaperoned dating between young teens; crude speech.

frames.aligns: Effort, kindness and a student turning toward his duties and future.
frames.concerns: Brahmacharya for students; rajasic sensual humor; tamasic violent fantasies early.

frames.aligns: Hatred and delusion giving way to loving-kindness (metta); right speech learned; seeing others clearly.
frames.concerns: Sensual imagery as feed for the mind; crude speech.
Kaam (lust) and krodh (anger) played for laughs early.

frames.aligns: Truthfulness, kindness and unity among friends.
frames.concerns: The call to a "chaste and holy life"; dating at a young age.

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) in the confession; harmony restored with classmates.
"Harm none" applied inwardly: violent fantasies are dropped; mutual care and consent.
frames.concerns: Little; some concern for how girls' bodies are drawn.

frames.aligns: Communication solves problems; a person improves his own condition.
frames.concerns: The Way to Happiness precepts on decency and good example.

frames.aligns: Anime Feminist: "sweet and accurate to the age group"; a girl with agency and a career; boundaries respected (ANN).
frames.concerns: Early monologues "too close to actual violent misogyny" (Anime Feminist); boys' sexual talk; suggestive art of a minor; handling of sex "hit-or-miss" (Anime Feminist via Wikipedia).

frames.aligns: Meaning from friendship, love and personal growth; empathy over contempt; no supernatural framing.
frames.concerns: Critical thinking about the sexualized art and jokes.

frames.aligns: A boy learning courage, kindness and responsibility; present, caring parents.
frames.concerns: Sexual humor and suggestive art involving young teens; dating at 14; early-teen physical affection.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of the loner; growth in respect and empathy.
frames.concerns: Age-appropriateness; how girls' bodies are drawn.

frames.aligns: Self-acceptance; a person defining himself; personal responsibility.
frames.concerns: The Eleven Rules' concern about harm to children applies to sexualized art of minors.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: The class status ladder is a source of shame that the story dissolves through kindness; Adachi stays a friend after the sports festival contest (Wikipedia); no face-saving revenge.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Parents are strict but loving (ANN); small rule-breaking is charming; school life is accepted, not resisted.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Peer friendships and family both matter; Anna's parents and Kyotaro's sister are present (ANN vols. 1-8).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: The "bottom of the class" versus "class idol" ranking is undone; the couple are equals and Anna often leads.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Secular outlook; no religious content reported.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Honesty about feelings, personal growth and career dreams are celebrated (vols. 9-12).

folkways.japan: The class "caste" (school hierarchy), chūnibyō posing, the middle school graduation as the natural end point, entrance exams and career paths, and the junior idol and model industry are Japanese school and media norms more than a message aimed at readers.

delivery.evidence: Eisenbeis (ANN) notes a "great message about growing up"; no review found calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The message grows out of Kyotaro's inner monologue and slow change rather than speeches, and rivals such as Adachi are treated as decent people.

personified.ideology: Contempt for the social world; violent edgy fantasy
Openness and seeing the good in others
Rivalry and status

entry.dominant: Secular humanism (empathy and growth), Classical virtue ethics (kindness, courage, honesty), Existentialism (self-making), with Nihilism and edgy misanthropy critiqued.

entry.heading: The Case Study of Vanitas
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life faces its own shortness honestly, refuses to treat anyone, human or vampire, as a thing, and lets itself be loved even when it does not feel deserving. Hatred, revenge and purity crusades on either side destroy the people they claim to protect.

content.framing: Mixed: the forced kiss is played as romantic comedy

frames.aligns: Human dignity violated by experimentation on children is condemned (Moreau). Memento mori in the title and earring. Mercy and restoration for the cursed. Evil is not made attractive in Moreau or the curse (Inter Mirifica 7).
frames.concerns: The Church as an institution is shown committing a massacre and feeding children to experiments, with its orders read as extremist (TV Tropes); eroticized blood-drinking and a forced kiss framed romantically (CBR); occult grimoire.

frames.aligns: Struggle with self-hatred and the passions; repentance and apology (vol. 10); the dead mourned.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis) makes the sensual blood scenes and body horror a concern; vampirism inverts the Eucharist's meaning of blood (from general knowledge; to verify); Western Church shown as violent.

frames.aligns: Sin has consequences; protection of the weak; friendship and honesty (Noé).
frames.concerns: Grimoire and occult names; church shown as persecutor; the forced kiss presented as romance. Each congregation and family decides (soul liberty).

frames.aligns: Depicts sin without endorsing it in Moreau and the curse; self-sacrifice (Jean-Jacques); confession and reconciliation between friends.
frames.concerns: Eroticized vampirism; occult framing; religious institutions as villains; the hero's forced kiss.

frames.aligns: Clear evil in Moreau and Charlatan; the cursed are freed.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": vampirism, a magic grimoire, true-name power, "witches," a sensual treatment of blood-drinking, all shown in a neutral or positive light; the Church cast as the extremist side.

frames.aligns: Total depravity has an echo: no faction, human or vampire, is innocent. Common grace lets families value well-made fiction.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 on "lascivious... pictures" applied to the blood scenes; the Church as persecutor; occult devices.

frames.aligns: Law and gospel: the cursed cannot restore themselves; restoration comes from outside. Honest picture of corrupt religious power (Lutheran history knows the theme).
frames.concerns: Sensual blood scenes; occult grimoire. LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy toward the outcast vampires; social holiness against exploitation and experiments on the poor.
frames.concerns: Wesley's General Rules on diversions; eroticized blood; forced kiss. Holiness churches more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: Gothic fiction in the tradition of judging works by framing; the story condemns cruelty and prejudice and seeks reconciliation.
frames.concerns: The Church shown mainly through its violent orders; the forced kiss. ACNA families more cautious on content.

frames.aligns: Critique of a state-aligned church that uses the sword (Gévaudan, the Paladins) echoes Anabaptist memory of persecution (from general knowledge; to verify).
frames.concerns: Violence and beheading are the main solutions; separation from popular media for conservative groups.

frames.aligns: Chosen family, sacrifice, forgiveness between friends.
frames.concerns: Sensual blood scenes and the forced kiss; occult. For the Strength of Youth asks whether media invites the Spirit.

frames.aligns: Attention to victims of institutional violence (Gévaudan, Moreau's orphans); prejudice between groups critiqued; queer subtext accepted.
frames.concerns: Consent problems (CBR); how a man of color is represented (Anime Feminist leaves it open).

frames.aligns: Care for the vulnerable; condemnation of cruelty.
frames.concerns: Vampires as undead and a grimoire conflict with teaching on the state of the dead and the occult; sensual blood scenes; FB 22 on entertainment.

frames.aligns: Loyalty and mercy; the false religious institution as violent may echo Witness views of Christendom (from general knowledge; to verify).
frames.concerns: Spiritism and magic are central devices (Galatians 5:19-21); violence (Psalm 11:5); blood is sacred and consuming it is forbidden (Acts 15:29), yet blood-drinking is eroticized.

frames.aligns: Restoration and healing of the afflicted; love outlasting hatred.
frames.concerns: Disease, curse, fear and death shown as powerful realities; body horror.

frames.aligns: Protecting life; condemnation of experiments on children; memory of the dead.
frames.concerns: Consuming blood is forbidden (Leviticus 17:10-14), and here it is eroticized; tzniut makes the fireplace and blood scenes a concern; many Haredi homes restrict such media.

frames.aligns: Human dignity, protecting the vulnerable, repair of harm.
frames.concerns: Blood consumption and sensual scenes; suicide attempts.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam: exposing institutional cruelty and prejudice against an outsider group; persecution by a church echoes Jewish historical memory.
Justice against oppressors, mercy to the afflicted, condemnation of cruelty to orphans (Qur'an 93:9).
frames.concerns: Consuming blood is forbidden (Qur'an 2:173), and here it is sensual; magic and grimoire; immodest scenes (24:30-31); suicide attempts (4:29).

frames.aligns: Dharma under pressure; impermanence; restoration of the afflicted; respect for the dead.
frames.concerns: Some families apply the Gita's tamasic category to gore and blood.

frames.aligns: The vanitas theme is close to impermanence (anicca); hatred and revenge shown as poisons; compassion for the cursed (karuna).
frames.concerns: Killing by beheading as routine; sensual craving in blood-drinking.

frames.aligns: The five vices (anger, lust, greed, attachment, ego) shown as destructive in Moreau, Astolfo's hatred and the curse; defending the oppressed.
Unity of peoples across a species divide; condemnation of religious fanaticism.
frames.concerns: Violence and sensual scenes; a "chaste and holy life" (to verify wording).

frames.aligns: Sincerity (Noé), purity versus corruption (the curse), gratitude between friends.
frames.concerns: Little in message; blood and death as impurity.

frames.aligns: Witches (the Hellfire Witch, the Silver Witch) are sympathetic; witch hunts after the Babel Incident are shown as persecution (TV Tropes).
frames.concerns: Little to raise; magic as fantasy device rather than practice.

frames.aligns: Moreau, a doctor experimenting on children's minds and bodies, is a clear villain; The Way to Happiness precepts on not harming others.
Critique of religious and aristocratic institutions; prejudice between groups; identity as a theme; queer subtext and an androgynous figure.
frames.concerns: The hero's forced kiss framed romantically (CBR: "unambiguous sexual assault"); Jeanne's muted response; race representation not examined (Anime Feminist).

frames.aligns: Human dignity against experimentation; empathy across groups; critique of fanaticism; mortality faced without supernatural comfort.
frames.concerns: Consent problems; occult devices treated as real in-world.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, honor, duty and protection of the vulnerable; aristocratic setting.
frames.concerns: Religious institutions shown as villains; gender ambiguity; sensual vampirism; family authority repeatedly fails.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of every being, human or vampire; justice against institutional cruelty; free search for identity.
Skepticism of a militant church; individual defiance (Vanitas); identity and self-definition; condemnation of harm to children (Eleven Rules).
frames.concerns: The forced kiss runs against Satanic Temple tenets on bodily autonomy (from general knowledge; to verify).

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Vampire nobility runs on honor and rank, but the story sides with individual worth: Jeanne will not kill Chloé on order (vol. 7-8), and consent is a stated vampire law (TV Tropes).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Institutions (senate, Church orders, family elders) are shown abusing power; the heroes act outside them.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Chosen family (Vanitas and Mikhail, Noé and Vanitas, Jean-Jacques and Chloé) matters more than civic duty; blood families often fail.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: The aristocratic world is rich and attractive, but the story values people across species and rank; Noé's equal friendship with a human is the core.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: The Church is treated critically and no faith is shown as true; the memento mori heritage is honored as art.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Identity, self-definition and an androgynous figure are treated with sympathy; Vanitas's flamboyance is his armor.

folkways.japan: The story is a Japanese author's romantic picture of 19th-century France. Its Catholic Church, aristocratic houses and witch hunts are borrowed European Gothic material, not a Japanese religious statement; readers in Japan, where Christianity is a small minority, may read the Church mainly as Gothic atmosphere (from general knowledge; to verify).

delivery.evidence: TV Tropes calls the Paladins an "extremist religious group"; CBR says the hero's forced kiss is framed "somewhat romantically." No review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its themes of identity and mortality come through plot and symbols, while the Church's orders appear mostly through violent members given sympathetic backstories.

personified.ideology: Self-hatred and mercy driven by revenge
Honesty and trust across species
Faith-driven hatred of vampires
Science without ethics

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Classical virtue ethics, Christian (as heritage, with the institution critiqued), Postmodernism, Communitarianism.

series.title: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure Part 3: Stardust Crusaders
series.romaji: JoJo no Kimyou na Bouken: Stardust Crusaders
series.native: ジョジョの奇妙な冒険スターダストクルセイダース

entry.heading: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure Part 3: Stardust Crusaders
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life protects its family and friends, faces evil without flinching, and is ready to give everything for others; the bloodline's "heritage for the future" is courage passed on, not power.

frames.aligns: Self-giving love: three companions die for others; a son's devotion to his mother; evil defeated.
frames.concerns: Inter Mirifica 7 on lurid violence; the shower scene with a young girl; divination and tarot as Stand names (CCC 2116).

frames.aligns: Struggle against an evil that feeds on others; the dead remembered by the living.
frames.concerns: Nepsis weighs the gore, the scene with Anne, and the occult names.

frames.aligns: Clear good and evil; evil destroyed; courage and loyalty.
frames.concerns: Phil 4:8: gore, toilet humor, a girl threatened in the shower; tarot and fortune-telling (Deut. 18:10). Soul liberty: each family decides.

frames.aligns: Sacrificial friendship; protecting the vulnerable (Holly, Anne).
frames.concerns: Romans 14 conscience on occult themes and gore; revenge as a hero's motive (Polnareff).

frames.aligns: Evil is overcome; spiritual warfare imagery.
frames.concerns: The "open door" concern: a fortune-teller hero, tarot, Egyptian gods, a vampire who gathers worshipful followers, souls gambled away.

frames.aligns: Depravity shown in Dio's lust for power; common grace in friendship and sacrifice.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 on lurid content; divination (WLC Q105) in the tarot framework.

frames.aligns: Vocation: son, grandfather, friend; love of neighbor in sacrifice.
frames.concerns: Adiaphora, but conscience weighs the occult names and gore; LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Growth in character (Iggy, Polnareff); social holiness in a band of friends.
frames.concerns: General Rules on diversions; holiness churches cautious about occult themes and gore.

frames.aligns: Judged by framing: evil exposed, sacrifice honored, a mother saved.
frames.concerns: Lurid gore; stereotyped foreign settings; tarot imagery.

frames.aligns: Mutual aid and self-sacrifice among companions.
frames.concerns: Violence is the only means and is heroic; the heroes kill (J. Geil, Dio).

frames.aligns: Family across generations; a son's love for his mother; sacrifice.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth: gore, sexual threat and teen smoking (Word of Wisdom).

frames.aligns: Friendship across nations (Japanese, American, Egyptian, French); compassion for victims.
frames.concerns: Racial and cultural stereotypes noted by ANN; women as victims or villains; a dark-skinned servant base for Dio.
"By beholding we become changed"; ghosts and souls conflict with Fundamental Belief 26; tarot and spiritualism.
jw.org counsel on violence (Psalm 11:5) and spiritism: fortune-telling, tarot, ghosts, a vampire.
Disease, death and bodily destruction presented as overwhelming realities.

frames.aligns: Kibbud em (honoring a mother); pikuach nefesh drives the journey; evil destroyed.
frames.concerns: Kishuf and divination (Deut. 18:10); tarot and idols named; nivul peh and tzniut weigh the gore and the shower scene.

frames.aligns: Saving a life, honoring a parent, friendship.
Friendship across peoples; standing up to a tyrant who rules by fear.
frames.concerns: Stereotyped portraits of Asian and Middle Eastern places; violence.

frames.aligns: Protecting and honoring a mother (a strong Islamic duty); justice against tyranny; sacrifice for companions. Shueisha and A.P.P.P. apologized to Muslims in 2008 and Shueisha redrew the mosque-like buildings (ANN; Wikipedia).
frames.concerns: Original printings showed fights on and destruction of buildings that "look like mosques" (ANN 2008; Wikipedia); a fortune-teller hero named Mohammed (divination, kahana, is forbidden); Stands named after Egyptian gods and tarot (shirk names); images of living beings (scholars differ); lowering the gaze (24:30-31) for the shower scene. The Qur'an pages and Al-Azhar's objection ("The scene depicts Muslims as terrorists," ANN) concerned the OVA, not the manga, whose scene showed "unintelligible scrawls" (ANN). Stricter families may grade C.

frames.aligns: Dharma of protecting family; good overcoming adharma; karma for villains.
frames.concerns: India shown through dirt, theft and danger (a MyAnimeList reviewer: "a personal grudge against the country"); tamasic gore.

frames.aligns: Dio's craving for immortality and power produces suffering; compassion in sacrifice.
Protecting the weak (sant-sipahi ideal); ego (haumai) and lust (kaam) in the villains, defeated.
frames.concerns: Violence; fortune-telling and tarot (Sikh teaching rejects astrology and omens).

frames.aligns: Purification by sunlight: Dio, a creature of darkness, is burned in the sunrise; sincerity among friends.
Tarot and Egyptian deities named with fascination rather than condemnation; spirits and divination as real; courage and loyalty.
frames.concerns: "Harm none" against constant killing; sacred symbols used as weapons for villains.

frames.aligns: Competence, self-determination, a group surviving by its ability.
A multinational band; a tyrant who rules by fear destroyed.
frames.concerns: Racial and cultural stereotypes (ANN); "every woman is a silly bimbo" (ANN); a girl threatened sexually; teen smoking; animal cruelty.

frames.aligns: Reason and observation win (Kakyoin's deduction); human solidarity.
frames.concerns: Fate, fortune-telling and tarot treated as real.

frames.aligns: Family, duty, honor, a son defending his mother, sacrifice for friends; evil named and defeated.
frames.concerns: A delinquent, smoking teen hero; gore; occult themes.

frames.aligns: Worth of each companion; friendship across nations.
Self-reliance and refusal to bow to Dio; The Satanic Temple's tenets on compassion side with the heroes; Dio as a cautionary tyrant.
frames.concerns: Self-sacrifice as an ideal; tarot as fate.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Polnareff hunts his sister's killer personally (ch. 14-32); insults and threats to family are answered by force; no court or police is involved.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The band acts outside every state's law across seven countries; their goal is to restore a family, not an order.

Civic vs kin.evidence: The mission is to save Holly (Wikipedia); the Joestar line matters; non-kin companions become family.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: The companions treat each other as equals despite age; Dio's hierarchy of servants is the evil.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Bloodline, fate and tarot matter, but no religion guides life; deduction wins.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: A fifty-day race to survive, told with style, fashion and humor.

folkways.japan: The stoic, few-words hero, the duty to a mother, and the delinquent (furyo) school uniform reflect Japanese norms of the 1980s; the view of Asia and the Middle East as exotic adventure routes reflects Japanese popular travel culture of the bubble era (my own framing; to verify).

delivery.evidence: ANN calls the anime "beautifully stupid" with "an ignorant and infectious glee"; reviewers praise fights, not messages.
delivery.note: The message comes through sacrifice and fights rather than speeches; Dio voices his view of fear and power in his own words, while most assassins are one-note hired killers.

personified.ideology: Quiet, stoic protection of family
Rule by fear; power to escape fear and death
Revenge for a murdered sister
Wisdom, loyalty and sacrifice

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (affirmed), Might makes right (critiqued through Dio), Pagan/occult (explored as imagery), Traditionalism (family lineage, affirmed).

entry.heading: Hajime no Ippo: Fighting Spirit!
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: Strength is not the power to hurt others but the courage to keep stepping forward. A bullied, gentle boy earns his place through relentless work, honors every opponent, and learns that the ring costs the body something real.

content.framing: Mostly Neutral (sport within rules); street violence and fouls Condemned; brain damage Shown with consequences
Played for comedy; Takamura's groping treated as a gag with an "inadequate" apology (TV Tropes)

content.frequency: Pervasive outside the book; rare inside

frames.aligns: Humility, perseverance, honoring one's mother (Fourth Commandment), a mentor who forms character; respect for opponents; violence within rules, not hatred.
frames.concerns: CCC 2288-2289 on care for health and against a "cult of the body" and sport at any cost; the brain damage arc tests this (from general knowledge; to verify). Takamura's groping played as a gag (TV Tropes); Inter Mirifica on depicting evil.

frames.aligns: Ascetic labor (podvig) in training; humility of the hero; endurance of suffering.
frames.concerns: Nepsis asks what pages of bloodshed and lecherous gags form in a reader; passions of anger and lust in side characters.

frames.aligns: Perseverance (Hebrews 12:1), honoring a widowed mother, humility, kindness; bully redeemed.
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 on Takamura's lewd gags and crude humor; mild profanity; soul liberty lets families decide on boxing.

frames.aligns: A clear underdog story with discipline, honesty and respect; a bullied boy grows in courage.
frames.concerns: Groping gag and lechery; drinking; violence as the center of every arc.

frames.aligns: Boldness, never quitting; no occult content found.
Common grace in a well-crafted story of vocation and hard work; consequences (brain damage) are shown.
frames.concerns: Sport as idol for the cast; Takamura's conduct.

frames.aligns: Vocation: Ippo's work on his mother's boat and in the gym; entertainment as adiaphora.
frames.concerns: LCMS and WELS families may weigh the crude gags more.

frames.aligns: Growth in character over time; accountability in a gym community.
frames.concerns: Wesley's test of diversions: does long, bloody combat build love of neighbor? Holiness churches may weigh drinking and lewd gags.

frames.aligns: Clear moral framing: fouls and bullying lose; kindness wins respect.
Humility, hard work, family business, gentleness of the hero.
frames.concerns: Nonresistance (Matthew 5:39): the whole series celebrates winning by striking another person, and violence is shown as heroic, the guide's central concern. Old Order groups avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Hard work, goal-setting, respect for parents and leaders.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth asks for entertainment that invites the Spirit: lecherous gags, groping, drinking; body as a temple vs. head trauma.

frames.aligns: An outsider and bullying victim finds dignity; respect across nations in many bouts.
frames.concerns: Women in support roles and as targets of gags; some foreign fighters shown poorly (Common Sense Media); head trauma in sport.
Health message: deliberate blows to the head and extreme weight cuts; Ellen White warned against amusements that excite the passions (from general knowledge; to verify); drinking.

frames.aligns: Respect for parents, hard work, no occult content.
frames.concerns: jw.org counsels avoiding entertainment featuring violence God hates (Psalm 11:5); here violence is the sport itself in every arc; competitive spirit (Galatians 5:26, from general knowledge; to verify).

frames.aligns: Overcoming fear and limitation; courage as right thinking.
frames.concerns: Injury, blood and brain damage are central; medical framing of the retirement differs from prayer-based healing. Members decide for themselves.

frames.aligns: Honoring one's mother (kibbud em); diligence (zerizut); respect for a teacher.
frames.concerns: Many Haredi homes restrict secular media; nivul peh and lewd gags; halakhic opinions on boxing differ because of the duty to guard health (Deuteronomy 4:15; from general knowledge; to verify).

frames.aligns: Kibbud em, mentorship, community at the gym.
Dignity of a bullied boy; repair of the bully relationship.
Sabr (patience) in loss; ihsan in training; honoring one's mother; humility.
frames.concerns: Hadith counsels avoiding the face when striking (Sahih Muslim; from general knowledge; to verify), and scholars differ on boxing for that reason; lewd gags and drinking; lowering the gaze (24:30-31).

frames.aligns: Svadharma: Ippo finds his calling; disciplined action (karma yoga); the guru who transforms a student.
frames.concerns: Rajasic anger and pride in rivals; lechery (kama) as comedy.

frames.aligns: Right effort; compassion for opponents; impermanence of titles; suffering after loss.
frames.concerns: First precept (non-harm): the story's core activity is striking others; craving to win drives the cast.

frames.aligns: The saint-soldier ideal: strength joined to humility and protection of the weak; chardi kala after loss; seva to the gym.
frames.concerns: Kam (lust) in Takamura's gags; krodh (anger) in rivals.

frames.aligns: Excellence and service; transformation of character; unity across nations in sport.
frames.concerns: Violence as entertainment; coarse humor against a "chaste and holy life" (to verify wording); alcohol.

frames.aligns: Makoto (sincerity) of effort; gratitude to mother and teacher; harmony of the gym; Ippo's fishing livelihood tied to the sea.

frames.concerns: "Harm none" vs. a consensual combat sport; lechery and the groping gag.

frames.aligns: "Be competent"; group dynamic of the gym; personal responsibility.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; medical brain-damage framing.

frames.aligns: Bullying victim finds confidence; emotional openness among men; respect for opponents from many countries.
frames.concerns: Women largely as support or gag targets; groping played for comedy (TV Tropes); some foreigners shown poorly (Common Sense Media); glorifying a sport with known brain-injury risk (from general knowledge; to verify).

frames.aligns: Human effort and reason, no supernatural help; real consequences of head trauma; growth after failure.
frames.concerns: Little to raise beyond the sport's risks.

frames.aligns: Discipline, respect for elders and a mentor, duty to mother, manly courage, hard work over shortcuts, sportsmanship.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; mild crude humor.

frames.aligns: Worth and dignity of a bullied boy; interdependence of the gym.
frames.concerns: Nonviolence values and the sport's harm; gender roles.

frames.aligns: Self-development, earned strength, no false piety; TST tenet on bodily autonomy fits the choice to box and the choice to retire.
frames.concerns: The series' humility and team spirit sit less easily with Church of Satan individualism. (Range: TST A; Church of Satan B.)

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Ippo does not answer insults with fists outside the ring (to verify), but rivalry, pride and payback shape many matches (Mashiba, Miyata's father).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Strict training regimes under Kamogawa; Takamura's freedom of appetite is comic, not a model.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Loyalty to the gym and to family; national and international bouts are sporting, not civic.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Deference to the trainer and seniors; but foreign and Japanese fighters meet as equals in the ring.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No faith shapes choices; training method and science of boxing win.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Endurance, hard work and making a living (family fishing business) are central.

folkways.japan: senpai-kohai deference in the gym, the trainer as a father figure, filial duty to a widowed mother, the family business on the sea, and the Japan title as a career ladder are Japanese norms shown as setting. The postwar occupation flashback reflects a Japanese memory of the period (to verify).

delivery.evidence: ANN's reviewer feels for opponents who "entered the ring with baggage"; Common Sense Media cites hard work and redemption themes.
delivery.note: The message comes through matches and training, and Takamura's harder view of strength is voiced by a beloved character rather than knocked down.

personified.ideology: Strength as courage and kindness
Win at world level by giving up "humanity"
Discipline and fundamentals
Winning by any means

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Communitarianism, Stoicism; Might makes right explored and partly affirmed in the ring, critiqued outside it.

series.title: Innocent
series.adult_reason: Innocent: Dark Horse rates all three omnibuses 18+ (Violence, nudity, language); graphic torture and executions; sources report sexual abuse of a girl under 10 (content warning); deep entry scores 9
series.warning: Includes the sexual abuse of a nine-year-old girl by an adult official (likely vols. 6-7) and a boy forced into sexual service by his father, alongside graphic torture and executions.

entry.heading: Innocent
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is to keep mercy and conscience alive inside a cruel duty you cannot escape: to see the condemned as human beings, to refuse cruelty for its own sake, and to hope for a justice that no longer kills.

content.framing: Abuse condemned; sex scenes neutral; eroticized suffering

frames.aligns: Charles's conviction that killing offends God mirrors the Church's current teaching that the death penalty is "inadmissible" (CCC 2267, revised 2018); abuse of children and cruelty are shown as evil (Inter Mirifica 7); atonement (the father's chapel).
frames.concerns: Reviewers call the eroticized suffering "very Catholic" and compare it to St. Sebastian and the Crucifixion (The Comics Journal; Manga Bookshelf); sexual content, including abuse of a child, beyond what CCC 2354 and 2523-2525 allow in media; fornication shown as normal.

frames.aligns: Compassion for the condemned; repentance and atonement.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis) weighs heavily against eroticized torture and child abuse.

frames.aligns: Evil (torture, abuse, corrupt nobles) is shown as evil; conscience.
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 test fails on sexual content and gore. Soul liberty: families decide; many would not choose it for teens.

frames.aligns: Charles's faith and his care for the poor (Matthew 25).
frames.concerns: Sexual content and sexualized suffering; little redemption shown in this title.
Holiness standards: pervasive gore, nudity, sexual abuse; spiritual themes are imagery rather than faith at work.

frames.aligns: A clear picture of human depravity at every level of society; lawful authority abused.
frames.concerns: Westminster Larger Catechism Q139 on lascivious pictures.

frames.aligns: Vocation: Charles serves in an office he did not choose, and suffers in it; the law exposes sin.
frames.concerns: Confessional families (LCMS, WELS) would weigh the sexual content heavily; ELCA readers less so.

frames.aligns: Social holiness: the poor, the condemned, prison cruelty.
frames.concerns: Wesley's rule on reading; holiness churches would avoid it.

frames.aligns: Moral seriousness about justice and mercy.
frames.concerns: Sexualized violence and abuse; Anglican Bible used as a frame-up (Japanese Wikipedia).

frames.aligns: Rejection of state killing is close to Anabaptist nonresistance; Charles's ideal of abolition.
frames.concerns: Violence and sexual content throughout; worldliness of the court.
For the Strength of Youth: sexual content, nudity and violence are what youth are asked to avoid; Dark Horse rates it 18+.

frames.aligns: Opposition to the death penalty and torture; class critique; a woman resisting patriarchy.
frames.concerns: Abuse of children used as plot; eroticized suffering.

frames.aligns: Care for the sick (the Sansons' medicine).
frames.concerns: "By beholding we become changed": constant gore and sexual content.
jw.org's test: violence (Psalm 11:5) and sexual immorality (Galatians 5:19-21) throughout.
Fear, pain and degradation given great power over thought.

frames.aligns: Talmudic reluctance to execute (Mishnah Makkot 1:10: a court that executes once in seventy years is "destructive").
frames.concerns: Tzniut: nudity and sexual content; many Haredi homes would not admit it.

frames.aligns: Same Mishnah tradition; dignity of the condemned (kavod ha-met).
Reform Judaism's opposition to the death penalty; justice for the poor.
Justice and mercy; condemnation of oppressors and child abuse.
frames.concerns: Lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31): nudity and sexual content; same-sex encounters.

frames.aligns: Duty (dharma) that conflicts with conscience, as in the Gita's opening.
Compassion for all who suffer; the first precept against killing is Charles's own instinct.
Justice and protection of the poor.
Unity, justice and the end of class prejudice.
frames.concerns: Shoghi Effendi's call to a "chaste and holy life"; cruelty as spectacle.

frames.aligns: Respect for bodies and the dead; a woman claiming power.
frames.concerns: "Harm none" broken constantly; abuse of children.

frames.aligns: Way to Happiness precepts: do not harm a person of good will; care for the young.
Abolition of the death penalty and torture as the ideal; class critique; Marie-Joseph's challenge to patriarchy; LGBTQ characters.
frames.concerns: Child sexual abuse; reviewers describe eroticized suffering of a young body (The Comics Journal) and call the father "cartoonishly evil" (Manga Bookshelf).

frames.aligns: Human dignity of the condemned; reason and medicine against cruelty and superstition; the arc toward abolition.
frames.concerns: Sexualized violence; little reasoning, much spectacle (Manga Bookshelf).

frames.aligns: Duty, family, faith and craftsmanship taken seriously.
frames.concerns: Inherited order shown as cruel; monarchy and nobility as decadent; sexual license.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of every person, including the condemned.
frames.concerns: Abuse of children; cruelty as spectacle.

frames.aligns: Marie-Joseph's defiance of God, King and the rule that "women must obey" (Japanese Wikipedia); critique of religious and royal authority.
frames.concerns: The Satanic Temple's tenets on bodily autonomy and compassion are violated by the abuse; Marie's pleasure in cruelty.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: The family's honor drives the plot, but the story sides with the dignity of the condemned and against honor-driven cruelty (Japanese Wikipedia; The Comics Journal).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Strict family and royal order is shown as crushing; Marie-Joseph's freedom is admired but ambiguous (Wikipedia).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Charles serves the family name, and the story honors his care for kin while questioning the cost (Dark Horse blurb).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Hierarchy is cruel (nobles escape justice; executioners despised); equality is the hoped-for future (Dark Horse blurb; Japanese Wikipedia).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Faith is sincere in Charles, but medicine, reason and reform point the way forward (Japanese Wikipedia).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival of the family weighs heavily, but self-expression (Marie-Joseph, gender, love) is celebrated.

folkways.japan: The story's fascination with 18th-century France follows a long Japanese tradition (The Rose of Versailles is the usual comparison; The Comics Journal; AniList review). The family-trade inheritance and the stigma of a hereditary "death" profession echo Japanese ideas of household (ie) succession and of outcast trades (from general knowledge; to verify), rather than the story's own message.

delivery.evidence: No review calls it preachy; Farris finds the symbolism "a bit too grandiose"; Dacey calls the father "cartoonishly evil", "a foil" for Charles.
delivery.note: Its case against cruelty and the death penalty comes through Charles's suffering and the image of the crowd rather than speeches, while the opposing view (duty and order) is voiced mainly by harsh relatives and corrupt nobles.

personified.ideology: Mercy, conscience, hope of abolition
Radical freedom; defiance of God, King and patriarchy
Duty to the family office above the self

personified.character: Count de Chartois / Count de Luxe
personified.ideology: Aristocratic privilege and impunity

entry.dominant: Existentialism (fate versus choice), Secular humanism (dignity of the condemned), Collectivism/authoritarianism (absolute monarchy, critiqued), Feminism (Marie-Joseph), Christian (Charles's faith and martyr imagery).

series.title: The Rising of the Shield Hero
series.native: 盾の勇者の成り上がり

entry.heading: The Rising of the Shield Hero
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is to protect the people in your care, endure injustice without becoming what wronged you, and rebuild trust one loyal companion at a time. The story pairs this with a strong appetite for public justice against those who abuse power, and it gives its hero the use of a slave system it does not fully examine.

content.framing: Mixed: the accusation is shown as a lie and punished; fan service and jokes are played as comedy

frames.aligns: False witness shown as grave wrong (CCC 2476-2477); care for an orphan; just authority restored; the former king's repentance.
frames.concerns: Slavery as a convenience (CCC 2414); vengeance and humiliating punishments; the only church shown is corrupt and its leader claims divinity, though the story calls it heretical.

frames.aligns: Patient endurance of injustice; protection of the orphan.
frames.concerns: Wrath as a passion the hero draws power from; a clergy portrayed as murderous; slavery.

frames.aligns: Honesty under persecution; providing for the orphan (James 1:27).
frames.concerns: Owning a child slave; revenge-flavored justice; coarse language ("Bitch," "Trash" as legal names). Families decide under soul liberty.

frames.aligns: Persecution of the innocent; loyalty; redemption offered to "Trash."
frames.concerns: Depicting versus endorsing: the slave purchase is framed as necessary and humane; the story enjoys its punishments.
A cursed weapon powered by rage as an "open door"; game-like magic; a self-proclaimed god.

frames.aligns: Common grace in craft and trade; lawful magistrate restoring justice (the queen).
frames.concerns: Slavery and the curse used to compel a child; WLC Q145 on false witness is shown well, but anger is rewarded with power.

frames.aligns: Eighth Commandment: "We should not tell lies about our neighbor"; vocation as protector and provider.
frames.concerns: The two kingdoms blur when the hero kills the High Priest himself; slavery. LCMS and WELS families stricter than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy to the poor and orphaned; Wesley's opposition to slavery gives a ready lens.
frames.concerns: Wesley's "Thoughts upon Slavery" stands against the hero's slave-holding, however kind.

frames.aligns: Judged by framing: false witness and abuse of power are condemned; the hero's protection of the weak is real; the king's repentance.
frames.concerns: Slavery and vengeance; anticlerical villain. Episcopal and ACNA families weigh these differently.

frames.aligns: Enduring injustice; care for the vulnerable.
frames.concerns: Nonresistance: the story's power is violence and righteous anger; killing a religious leader; slavery. MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Honesty, family-like care, a king given a chance to change.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth asks for uplifting media; coarse names; vengeance; slavery.

frames.aligns: Prejudice against demi-humans condemned; abuse of power exposed.
frames.concerns: The false-accusation premise and its use in debates about sexual assault; child slavery made sympathetic.

frames.aligns: Diligence, honesty, care for the orphan.
frames.concerns: Fundamental Belief 22 on choosing pure entertainment; magic, cursed power and rage as strength; corrupt religion with a self-made god.
jw.org's test: violence, spiritism and magic are central; coarse speech.

frames.aligns: Truth overcoming error (the lie is exposed).
frames.concerns: Dwelling on anger, fear and injury.

frames.aligns: Lashon hara and false testimony (Exodus 20:13 in Jewish numbering) shown as grave; care for the orphan.
frames.concerns: Tzniut concerns over fan service; magic; vengeance. Many Haredi homes would not have it.

frames.aligns: Due process and the duty to protect a reputation; prejudice against a minority people condemned.
frames.concerns: Slavery normalized as a plot device; humiliating punishments.

frames.aligns: Justice for the wrongly accused; stand against racial prejudice.
frames.concerns: The false-accusation trope and its real-world use; child slavery.

frames.aligns: Bearing witness truthfully (Qur'an 4:135); slander of the chaste condemned (24:4); care for the orphan.
frames.concerns: Magic shown as real power; fan service; a figure claiming divinity. Islamic teaching encourages freeing slaves.

frames.aligns: Dharma of the protector (kshatriya duty without aggression); truth vindicated.
Patience under abuse; compassion for a suffering child.
frames.concerns: Rage feeds power and is not let go; vengeance.

frames.aligns: Protecting the weak and standing against tyranny; honest labor (kirat karni).
frames.concerns: Krodh (anger) is one of the five vices and is the shield's fuel; slavery.
Slavery (abolished in Bahá'í teaching); backbiting and vengeance.

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) and purification of a stained name.
frames.concerns: Little on the sacred; a corrupt sect.

frames.aligns: Magic as craft; the threefold return on the accusers.
The Way to Happiness precepts on being trustworthy and not doing anything illegal or harmful.
Racial prejudice and abuse of power condemned.
frames.concerns: The premise centers a false rape accusation, which critics said echoes claims that false accusations are common; a child slave made sympathetic and romanticized; humiliation as justice (from general knowledge; critics not opened).

frames.aligns: Evidence and due process vindicate the innocent; a self-proclaimed god exposed.
A man endures injustice with honor, protects the weak, and is vindicated by lawful authority.
frames.concerns: Slavery; coarse language; the only church shown is villainous.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of demi-humans; justice in relations.
Skepticism toward a corrupt religious authority; personal responsibility; the wronged hero answers in kind.
frames.concerns: The Eleven Rules forbid harming little children, and the hero compels a child with a curse; bodily autonomy (Satanic Temple Tenet 3).

Dignity vs honor.evidence: The plot turns on a stolen reputation and its public restoration; punishment is public shaming by renaming (vol. 8, likely ch. 31-32).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Justice comes from the lawful queen, who outlaws the church and corrects the king (vol. 8; Wikipedia).

Civic vs kin.evidence: The found family (Raphtalia and Filo as daughters) comes before the kingdom that rejected him.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Monarchy, royal heirs (Melty, Raphtalia's heritage) and slave crests are accepted; prejudice against demi-humans is condemned.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Game-like systems and trade over faith; the one church shown is corrupt.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival against Waves, poverty and persecution dominates.

folkways.japan: The concern with public face and a stained name, the game-status isekai frame and the web-novel origin reflect Japanese contexts; the 2019 English-language controversy over the false-accusation premise was shaped by Western debates and was not a prominent issue in Japan (from general knowledge; to verify).

delivery.evidence: ANN calls the setup "enormously heavy-handed" railroading; Japan Powered: "there isn't much of an investigation." No review opened says strawman.
delivery.note: Its message about injustice and loyalty is stated through Naofumi's anger and the queen's verdict, while the villains are drawn with little inner life until the king's later redemption.

personified.ideology: Self-reliance after betrayal; protect your own
Manipulation for power

personified.character: High Priest of the Church of the Three Heroes
personified.ideology: Sectarian religion and self-deification
Prejudice born from grief

entry.heading: Dragon Ball Super (manga, 2015-present, on hiatus)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is joyful, unending striving: keep training past every limit, enjoy a worthy opponent, protect your family and friends, and give former enemies a seat at the table, even in a cosmos whose rulers can erase everything on a whim.

content.framing: Endorsed (fighting as joy and test), with mass death shown at a cosmic, mostly bloodless scale
Played for light romance or gag

frames.aligns: A god who despises mortals (Zamasu) is the villain; mercy to Frieza; Android 17's selfless wish restores all who were erased (ch. 42); a father protects his child (Gohan, ch. 93-99).
frames.concerns: A supreme being shown as a capricious child who erases worlds (ch. 26, 34); gods who can be trained by and surpassed; resurrection by wish.

frames.aligns: Repentance-like turns (Frieza as temporary ally, Vegeta owning Saiyan sins, ch. 69); self-giving.
frames.concerns: Fighting enjoyed for its own sake; "angels" serving gods of destruction and a childlike omnipotent ruler treat sacred categories lightly; nepsis (guarding the senses) applies to constant combat imagery.

frames.aligns: Courage, perseverance, loyalty, protecting the innocent; evil gods defeated.
frames.concerns: Many gods shown as real (John 14:6); the highest "god" erases life without moral reason; joy in fighting. Soul liberty means families differ.

frames.aligns: Self-sacrifice and selfless choices (17's wish); a corrupt "god" exposed as evil (Zamasu).
frames.concerns: Polytheistic worldbuilding as the frame of reality; omnipotence without goodness (Zeno); might as the final answer.

frames.aligns: Courage, protecting the weak, villains defeated.
frames.concerns: Gods, angels, a sorcerer who drains life (Moro), magic orbs and wishes are the real order of the world; media as an "open door" weighs this heavily; Plugged In (film) flags "mystical spirituality" and ki as "a magical life force."

frames.aligns: Common grace: real loyalty, sacrifice and mercy; a self-righteous god (Zamasu) judged.
frames.concerns: A sovereign who is arbitrary rather than holy; images of supreme and lesser gods (second commandment concern for many); salvation by strength.

frames.aligns: Fantasy as adiaphora; forgiveness and second chances; vocation (Gohan as scholar and father).
frames.concerns: Power earned by training reads as works; gods surpassed. Confessional (LCMS, WELS) families stricter than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Growth in character (Vegeta, Frieza's temporary cooperation); love of neighbor in 17's wish.
frames.concerns: Fighting as delight sits poorly with "do no harm"; diversions that cannot be used "in the name of the Lord Jesus." Holiness churches stricter than the UMC.

frames.aligns: Myth and fantasy have Anglican roots; good and evil clearly framed in Zamasu, Moro and Cell Max; mercy.
frames.concerns: Many gods; an amoral supreme being.

frames.aligns: Mercy to defeated enemies; 17's nonviolent wish ends the tournament well.
frames.concerns: Fighting is the core pleasure and solution, which nonresistance rejects at the level of message. Old Order families avoid such media; Mennonite Church USA families may be more open.

frames.aligns: Effort and eternal progression-like growth; fathers protecting children; enemies given chances. Little immodesty reported in the manga.
frames.concerns: Gods as fallible beings who can be surpassed may be read against Restoration teaching in different ways; constant violence; resurrection by wish. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Redemption over punishment; a god's contempt for mortals condemned; universal restoration through a selfless wish.
frames.concerns: Violence as the main solution; Goku's indifference to stakes (ICv2).

Living dead and resurrection by wish against the teaching that the dead sleep (Fundamental Belief 26); reincarnation (ch. 66); fighting as joy; "by beholding we become changed." (from general knowledge; to verify)
Loving violence (Psalm 11:5) is the story's engine; gods, angels and sorcery (spiritism); reincarnation. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Erased worlds restored; good overcomes destruction.
frames.concerns: Constant images of destruction and fear of annihilation; strength sought through matter. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Turning of former enemies; saving life; a god who wants to destroy humanity is the villain.
frames.concerns: Gods and a supreme deity as characters (avodah zarah concerns in an Orthodox reading); many Haredi homes avoid such media entirely; Modern Orthodox families selective. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Pikuach nefesh in heroes' protection of life; repair of past wrongs (ch. 69).
frames.concerns: Gods and a capricious supreme being as characters. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam: restoring erased universes; confronting genocide's legacy (Cerealians, Saiyans).
frames.concerns: Violence as the main solution. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Striving, discipline, protecting the weak, humility.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Saiyan pride drives Vegeta ("A Saiyan's Pride," ch. 12; "The Pride of an Entire Race," ch. 84); rivalries settled by fights; mercy also honored (ch. 42).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Goku follows his love of fighting over duty and even summons Zeno on his own (ch. 26), though he joins the Galactic Patrol (ch. 43).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Fighters protect their universe and others' (17's wish, ch. 42); family also central (Gohan and Pan, ch. 93-99).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: A strict cosmic hierarchy (Zeno, Great Priest, angels, gods, mortals) is accepted, though mortals rival gods in power.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Gods and rebirth are setting, not worship; technology and training solve problems.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Universes fight for survival in the Tournament, yet Goku fights mostly for joy.

folkways.japan: The master-and-disciple model (Whis, Piccolo), the Jump formula of friendship, effort and victory, and a pantheon drawn loosely from East Asian folk cosmology reflect Japanese boys' manga norms rather than the story's own argument.

entry.title: Parasyte

entry.premise: Worm-like Parasites arrive on Earth and take over human brains, then feed on other humans. One fails to reach 17-year-old Shinichi Izumi's brain and instead takes over his right hand, becoming Migi; the two keep separate minds and must cooperate to survive attacks from other Parasites. entry.title: Banana Fish
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: In 1980s New York, 17-year-old gang leader Ash Lynx, abused as a child by Corsican mafia boss Dino Golzine, chases the meaning of 'banana fish', a mind-controlling drug from the Vietnam War tied to his brother Griffin's breakdown. With Japanese photographer's assistant Eiji Okumura at his side, Ash wars against Golzine, rival gangs and government collaborators.
