entry.title: Sometimes Even Reality Is a Lie!
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: High schooler Kaoru Terazaki plays a female character in an online game and befriends a player he assumes is a man, until they meet and he learns Nami is Nanami Osaka, a reclusive girl who plays a male avatar. Her overprotective father won't allow male friends, so Kaoru dresses as a girl to visit her home. With his encouragement Nanami returns to school, and the two edge toward romance while her parents grow alongside her.
entry.life_message: It holds up friendship that sees the real person behind the avatar, and families that learn to trust.

content.note: Father's judo and kendo skills played as comic threat (Wikipedia).
Slow, chaste romance; no fan service noted (Wikipedia; MangaDex safe).
Nanami's social withdrawal and school avoidance gently resolved (Wikipedia).
Deceiving parents through a disguise; meeting online friends in person (Wikipedia).

entry.dominant: Online friendship made real; gentle romance; parents learning to let go

frames.aligns: Kaoru draws Nanami out of isolation; parents care deeply.
frames.concerns: Deceiving parents through cross-dressing is the central gag.

frames.aligns: Clean romance and a family that matters.
frames.concerns: Cross-dressing deception; Ephesians 6:1 on obeying parents.
Lying to her father; gaming focus.

frames.aligns: Fifth commandment honored as parents are won over.
Neighbor-love that brings Nanami back to school.

frames.concerns: Gaming culture and worldly media focus.

frames.aligns: Family involvement in a teen relationship.
Questions gender expectations kindly; inclusive warmth.
Parents' protectiveness is respected in the end.
Respect for parents grows on both sides.

frames.concerns: False speech as a running gag.

frames.aligns: Plays with gender roles and online identity sympathetically.
frames.concerns: Cross-dressing as joke could be discussed.

frames.aligns: Online and offline selves examined thoughtfully.
Strong father protecting daughter; family at the center.
Fear and isolation dissolve through love.
Each person seen in their true worth.
Equal friendship of boy and girl.
Communication and affinity across the screen.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Kaoru wins over the father through patience, not confrontation.

delivery.evidence: Trust theme carried by parents' gradual softening per entry summary; no review on delivery (to verify).

entry.title: Re:Monster
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Tomokui Kanata is murdered and reborn as a goblin with his memories and the power to gain abilities from whatever he eats. As Gobrou he devours monsters and enemies, rises to lead his tribe, takes several wives including human women the tribe abducted, and later founds a mixed-race mercenary company. The story follows his evolution through stronger monster forms and growing power.
entry.life_message: It holds up strength, appetite and building your own tribe as the way to thrive in a brutal world.

content.note: Constant lethal fights; elders beaten to death as example; hero eats defeated foes (Wikipedia; Suitable for Treatment review).
Grim tone but an unbeatable hero (review).
Abducted women held for breeding, a harem, and goblins allowed to rape drugged elves, told matter-of-factly (review; Wikipedia; AniList Female Harem; MangaDex suggestive).
Kidnapping and coercion within the tribe go unpunished (Wikipedia; review).

entry.dominant: Survival of the strongest; consuming to evolve; tribal expansion

frames.aligns: Gobrou's loyalty to his tribe members.
frames.concerns: Sexual violence against captives treated as normal; cannibalism; power as the only good.
Glorifies gluttony, lust and pride, the passions the tradition fights.
Rape, kidnapping, gore and harem without judgment.

frames.aligns: Some care for his own people.

frames.concerns: Monstrous hero, demons and gods, sexual violence.
Sin made attractive; no moral frame against cruelty.

frames.aligns: Duty to tribe as a kind of vocation.
frames.concerns: Fifth and sixth commandment violations celebrated.
Does harm; no mercy or holiness.
Frames evil as good when the strong do it.
Violence and conquest as the path to life.
Women as breeding captives; consent ignored.
Adharma of cruelty and lust unchallenged.

frames.aligns: Rebirth premise, though without karmic lesson.
frames.concerns: Killing, eating and sexual misconduct as progress.
Rape played flat; women as property.
Bodily appetite as the source of power.

frames.aligns: Tribal bonds and a natural cycle of eating and growth.

frames.concerns: Lust and violence against the weak.
Unwanted sexual advances break the Eleven Rules.
Gore, sexual violence and pagan deities.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Status is won by defeating rivals personally; challenges are answered with force.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Tribal law is whatever the strongest decides; Gobrou acts as he pleases.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Brood brothers, wives and children are Gobrou's whole world.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Rank in the tribe follows strength and evolution tier.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Pragmatic, game-like logic of leveling up; gods exist but guide little.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Eat or be eaten survival drives everything.

entry.title: Black Lagoon
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Japanese salaryman Rokuro 'Rock' Okajima is taken hostage by modern-day pirates, then abandoned by his company and joins them. The Lagoon Company, led by Dutch with gunfighter Revy and mechanic Benny, smuggles goods around Southeast Asia from Roanapur, a Thai port city run by Russian, Chinese, Italian and Colombian syndicates. Jobs spiral into gunfights, naval battles and gang wars, and Rock drifts deeper into the city's morality.
entry.life_message: It holds up no clear good life; it asks how far an ordinary person can sink into a world where violence is the only law.

content.note: Relentless gunfights, executions and gore across arcs (Wikipedia; AniList Gore, Assassins, Guns).
Child killers in the twins arc, cartel and Cold War backstories (Wikipedia; AniList Tragedy).
MangaUpdates lists Nudity and Rape; capped as not confirmed by a second kind of source (to verify; likely understated).
Profanity-heavy gangster dialogue widely reported; capped (to verify; likely understated).
Heavy drinking and smoking by Revy and others; capped (to verify; likely understated).
Revy's traumatic past and damaged child assassins; capped (to verify).
Smuggling, gun violence and crime as everyday work (Wikipedia; AniList Crime, Mafia, Triads, Yakuza).
Real firearms named and fetishized (to verify).

frames.aligns: Rock's lingering conscience and the twins' tragedy show what abuse does to children.
frames.concerns: Gratuitous violence, sexual violence and crime with little hope.

frames.aligns: Little to note beyond Rock's moral unease.

entry.title: Lucifer and the Biscuit Hammer
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Misanthropic college student Yuuhi Amamiya is pressed by a talking lizard into becoming one of twelve Beast Knights who must stop the mage Animus from smashing Earth with a moon-sized hammer. He swears loyalty to Princess Samidare, who secretly plans to destroy the planet herself once Animus is beaten. Through battles with golems, deaths among the knights and mentorship between them, Yuuhi moves from contempt for the world to finding reasons to live.
entry.life_message: It holds up finding meaning through bonds, mentors and protecting others, even for someone who began wanting the world to end.

content.note: Superpowered fights with golems; several knights die (Wikipedia; AniList Martial Arts, Super Power, Tragedy).
Light romance between Yuuhi and Samidare (AniList Heterosexual; MangaDex safe).
Yuuhi's nihilism shaped by a harsh grandfather; Samidare's wish to destroy everything (Wikipedia; Psychological genre).
Martial-arts training; early hostility to the world (Wikipedia).

entry.dominant: From nihilism to meaning; mentorship; found family among knights

frames.aligns: Yuuhi's conversion from despair to love; Tarou dies saving Hanako.
frames.concerns: Samidare's apocalyptic wish and battle deaths to talk through.

frames.concerns: Magic, violence and a cosmic war.

frames.aligns: Animal familiars and magic as allies.

Choosing life and repairing broken people.

entry.title: Yakuza Fiancé: Raise wa Tanin ga Ii
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Yoshino Somei, granddaughter of an Osaka yakuza boss, is sent to Tokyo to live with her arranged fiance Kirishima Miyama, grandson of a Kanto yakuza family. Kirishima is charming on the surface and violently unhinged beneath, and Yoshino, no pushover herself, sets out to outmaneuver him. Their dangerous, push-and-pull relationship plays out amid gang politics and brutal yakuza violence.
entry.life_message: It holds up refusing to be cowed: meeting a dangerous world on your own terms and with your own nerve.

content.note: Beatings, torture with a clamp, blood and threats (Common Sense Media on the anime; AniList Gore, Crime).
Menacing, unpredictable fiance and gang threats (Common Sense Media; AniList Yakuza, Criminal Organization).

entry.title: Elfen Lied
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Lucy, a horned mutant 'Diclonius' with invisible telekinetic arms, escapes a research lab in a massacre, is injured, and develops a childlike second personality called Nyu. Student Kouta and his cousin Yuka take her in, unaware of her past or their own buried connection to her, while government squads and other Diclonius hunt her. The story pairs harem romance and comedy with torture, experimentation, abuse and mass killing.
entry.life_message: It holds up love and acceptance as the only answer to cycles of cruelty, while showing how abuse breeds monsters.

content.note: Dismemberment, decapitations, torture, cruel experiments on children, a puppy beaten to death (Wikipedia; AniList Gore, Body Horror).
Sustained horror, child victims and tragedy (Wikipedia; AniList Tragedy, Body Horror; Horror genre).
Frequent female nudity and harem fan service; a child's rape by a stepfather and its aftermath (Wikipedia; AniList Nudity, Female Harem).

entry.title: Bocchi the Rock!
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Hitori 'Bocchi' Gotoh is a painfully anxious girl who has taught herself guitar at home but can barely speak to people. Drummer Nijika recruits her into Kessoku Band, which plays at the Starry live house in Shimokitazawa, alongside bassist Ryo and outgoing vocalist Kita. Four-panel gags follow Bocchi's surreal meltdowns and small steps as the band grows.
entry.life_message: It holds up finding your people and your voice through shared creative work, one awkward step at a time.

content.note: Stage fright played for surreal comedy.
Close friendships some read as yuri; no sexual content (AniList Yuri; MangaDex safe).

frames.concerns: Pursuit of performance and rock culture.

entry.title: Sasaki and Miyano
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: First-year Miyano is a self-conscious fan of boys' love (BL) manga who meets second-year Sasaki when Sasaki breaks up a schoolyard fight. Sasaki starts borrowing Miyano's BL manga, falls for him and is open about it, while Miyano slowly works out whether his own feelings are friendship or romance. A slow-burn high school romance focused on communication and consent.

entry.title: Marriage Toxin
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Hikaru Gero, heir to a clan of poison assassins, must produce an heir or his grandmother will force his little sister Akari into marriage. He enlists his would-be target, Mei Kinosaki, a male marriage swindler who poses as a woman, to coach him in dating. Their matchmaking jobs keep colliding with rival assassin clans, mixing romantic comedy and superpowered fights.
entry.life_message: It holds up protecting family and learning to love openly, even for someone raised to kill.

content.note: Assassinations, poison and hypnosis attacks, clan-master battles, a planned child sacrifice (Wikipedia; AniList Assassins, Crime).

entry.premise: In a near-future Japan, the government assigns every 16-year-old a marriage partner by compatibility to raise the birth rate, and refusing carries heavy penalties. entry.title: Basara

entry.premise: In a post-apocalyptic, feudal Japan ruled by the corrupt King Ukon and his sons, the prophesied 'child of destiny' Tatara is killed, and his twin sister Sarasa disguises herself as him to lead a rebellion and avenge him. She falls in love with Shuri without knowing he is the Red King, the son of the tyrant and her brother's killer; when the truth comes out midway, the two end up leading opposing armies. The rebellion aims to change society itself, and by the end few characters are simple villains (ANN House of 1000 Manga; VIZ blurb; MU Secret Identity, Revolution).

entry.title: Ultra Heaven

entry.premise: In a near future where mind-altering drugs are legal and served in 'pump bars' by medically licensed bartenders, the addict Kabu (Cub in the English edition) chases ever stronger highs, including near-death experiences. A mysterious pusher gives him a new hallucinogen he names 'Ultra Heaven', and the line between trip and reality collapses into nightmare, overdose and visions of paradise, while shadowy figures seem to be experimenting on him. The psychedelic, unfinished series asks what is real (Wikipedia; Last Gasp blurb; TCJ review).

entry.premise: Orphaned high schooler Ataru Kashiwagi lives in poverty with his younger sister Yuri and finds refuge in friends on the social network Real Account. He and about 10,000 users are pulled into a virtual version of the app, where the mascot Marble forces them into deadly games: a player who loses all followers dies, and when a player dies, so do their followers, while the world watches. Ataru teams up with his look-alike Yuuma to survive and find the masterminds; the series ends with the site destroyed and its creators dead (Wikipedia; ANN review).

entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: In the mid-4th century BC, as Philip II's Macedonia challenges Athens and Persia watches, a young man named Eumenes, who dresses like a barbarian but speaks fluent Greek, tries to cross the Hellespont and is drawn into the conflict; a long flashback tells his origins (Beneath the Tangles review). He will become a commander and secretary to Alexander the Great, rising by wit and talent rather than birth (K Manga blurb via AniList; MU).
entry.life_message: Intelligence, curiosity and self-command let an outsider make his own place in a violent, rank-bound world.

content.note: Review notes a gory opening scene and horror roots; War, Gore, Body Horror (AniList); Blood and Gore, Large Scale Battles, Murder (MU).

entry.premise: A one-volume anthology of nine horror stories chosen by Junji Ito with his own notes, plus one new story (VIZ blurb via AniList and MU). entry.title: Message to Adolf
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: In 1936 Japanese reporter Sohei Toge arrives in Berlin to find his brother murdered after claiming to hold a document that could topple Hitler; Toge is then hunted by the Gestapo and Japan's secret police (Experiments in Manga review; MU). In Kobe, two boys named Adolf, Kaufmann (son of a Nazi official and a Japanese mother) and Kamil (son of German Jews), are pulled into the affair, and Kaufmann is indoctrinated in the Hitler Youth as their friendship is tested (review; AniList).

Ten years later two Watch Guild sellswords, the devout Oczy and the cynical Gras, find the hidden research and must decide whether to pass it on at the risk of the stake (Seven Seas blurb via MangaUpdates; Comics Beat review).
entry.life_message: Seeking the truth about the universe, and its beauty, is worth more than safety, and the search is carried forward across generations.

entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Chakuro is the archivist of the Mud Whale, an exiled island-ship drifting on a sea of sand, where the emotion-powered 'Marked' die young and the 'Unmarked' rule. When he finds Lykos, an emotionless girl from outside, the ship is attacked by the Allied Empire, which sees emotion as the cause of war, and the islanders must fight to survive (Wikipedia; ANN; Viz blurb via AniList).
entry.life_message: Feeling fully, grief included, and choosing to live together freely is worth more than a safe life without emotion.

content.note: Invading soldiers massacre villagers; a sadistic enemy enjoys killing; friends die (Wikipedia; ANN 'violent invasion'; MU Mass Murder, Genocide).
Reviewers call it 'deceptively dark' and 'progressively darker' (ANN); AniList Tragedy 70.

entry.dominant: Emotion versus control; mortality and memory; resisting an empire

frames.concerns: Emotion-powered magic and creatures that feed on feelings; massacres.

entry.premise: Yogiri Takatou sleeps through his class being transported to another world, so he misses the 'Gifts' a mysterious Sage hands out. His classmates abandon him and Tomochika Dannoura as dragon bait, but Yogiri can kill anything with a thought and reluctantly protects her while turning the tables on the cruel classmates and the Sage. AniList and MangaUpdates tag it as satire of the isekai genre (J-Novel Club and Yen Press blurbs via AniList and MangaUpdates; ANN on the anime).
entry.life_message: Power is safest with someone who has no wish to use it, and those who abuse it get what they deserve.

content.note: Classmates impaled and killed on page; the hero kills enemies instantly (ANN; MU Blood and Gore, Death).

Revenge-style killing; sexual threats and fan service.

Enrolled after discovering she has a rare Alice of her own, Mikan finds that behind its grand facade the academy hides lies, manipulation and dangerous secrets tied to her own heritage. Friendship, especially with Hotaru and the prickly fire-user Natsume, carries her through growing trials.
entry.life_message: Loyal friendship and a cheerful, courageous heart can stand against powerful institutions that use children.

Plain classmate Tadano discovers this and pledges to help her reach her dream of making 100 friends, with help from the outgoing, nonbinary Najimi Osana. entry.title: Black Jack
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Osamu Tezuka's classic follows Black Jack, a genius surgeon without a license who charges enormous fees and is seen as a heartless rogue, in hundreds of self-contained stories. He often treats the poor for free or humbles the arrogant, and some tales end with good people facing death to save others. He lives with Pinoko, a girl he built from a removed teratoma, and clashes with Dr. Kiriko, a doctor who practices euthanasia.
entry.life_message: Life is precious and worth fighting for, and true healing comes from skill joined to conscience rather than status or rules.

entry.premise: Two thousand years after sacrificing himself to end a war between demons and humans, Demon King Anos (Anoth) is reincarnated to an ordinary couple. At the Demon King Academy his power is too great to measure, so he is labeled a misfit, and he finds his name forgotten and a society where royal 'pureblood' demons rule over hybrids. With his friend Misha, shunned by her own family, he sets out to unravel the false history. The manga ended after four volumes due to the artist's death.
entry.life_message: Worth is not set by bloodline, and real strength protects peace, friends and family.

Maid Shannon, taught that servants are mere furniture, has found love with grandson George through a bargain with the witch Beatrice; her brother Kanon distrusts the witch and refuses her offer. entry.title: Drama Queen
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Aliens who saved Earth from a meteor now live in Japan with special privileges. Nomamoto, a runaway factory worker with an abusive alien boss, befriends Kitami, whose family was killed in a crash caused by an alien; Kitami kills an alien and the two dispose of the body, and they set out to kill aliens. Later chapters complicate the story by giving alien characters, such as the twins Lily and Lally, sympathetic backstories.

entry.premise: Naota, a sixth grader who lives above the family bakery, is left behind with his older brother's 17-year-old ex-girlfriend Mamimi, who makes suggestive advances toward him, when an alien named Haruko runs him over on her Vespa and hits him with her bass guitar, making a horn grow from his head. The surreal two-volume manga, a tie-in to the anime, follows his chaotic passage toward growing up.
entry.life_message: Growing up is confusing and chaotic, and you become yourself by stopping pretending to be an adult.

content.note: Slapstick violence (guitar to the head); robot fights (AniList Slapstick, Robots).
17-year-old makes suggestive passes at a sixth-grade boy (AniList and MU descriptions; MU Older Female Younger Male; AniList Age Gap); frequent sexual imagery in the franchise (Wikipedia).
MU Mind Break (context unclear; to verify).
Hitting people with a guitar and reckless moped riding played for laughs.

entry.dominant: Surreal coming of age; adolescence and sexuality; absurdist humor

frames.aligns: Honest about the confusion of growing up.
frames.concerns: Older teen's sexual advances toward a child; chaotic morality.
Sexual imagery around a child; passions unchecked.

frames.aligns: Boy learns he is not yet an adult.

frames.concerns: Sexual innuendo with a sixth grader.
Violence played for fun; sexual content.
Sexual advances on a child violate the Eleven Rules.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Haruko's anarchic freedom upends a dull factory town.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Eccentric father and grandfather; brother's absence.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Adults are buffoons; little deference.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Modern, irreverent suburban setting.

folkways.japan: Naota's brother leaving to play baseball in America and the factory-town setting reflect Japanese suburban life and baseball culture.

delivery.evidence: Critics call the anime surreal and symbolic, a coming-of-age told impressionistically (Wikipedia; anime, not manga).
delivery.note: Meaning is left to symbolism and absurd events rather than stated.

entry.winners_losers: Naota moves a step toward maturity; no worldview is clearly rewarded.

How suggestive Mamimi's advances are drawn in the manga

Manga differs from the anime plot (MU Random Plot)

entry.title: Dolly Kill Kill
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: High-schooler Iruma Ikaruga loses his ordinary life when flesh-dissolving wasps and giant doll-like monsters called dollies invade and slaughter humanity. A year later he joins a group fighting the dollies after glimpsing the girl he liked, thought dead, held captive by them.
entry.life_message: Holding on to the people you love and refusing to give up is what keeps a person human in a collapsing world.

content.note: Reviewers call it ultraviolent, with limbs melting; AniList Gore and Body Horror, MU Massacre and Blood and Gore.
Survival horror with grotesque monsters; one reviewer calls it relentlessly bleak and cruel (ANN guide; MU Apocalypse).
Dolly scouts resemble giant pregnant schoolgirls and seem to capture only girls (ANN); no sexual content reported.
Iruma loses friends and everyone he cares about; reviewers note despair and characters who seem unhinged.
Teen fighting monsters with weapons; fantastical setting.

entry.title: Magilumiere Magical Girls Inc.
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: In a world where magical girl is a profession that exterminates monsters called kaii, struggling job-hunter Kana Sakuragi uses her excellent memory to help magical girl Hitomi Koshigaya and is hired by the small startup Magilumiere. The series treats magic as engineering and business, with rival firms, a government agency and industry politics.
entry.life_message: Diligent, careful work and good teammates give ordinary people a meaningful place in the world.

content.note: Monster-extermination action (AniList Kaiju, Superhero); MU has one vote for Character Death.
Kaii attacks such as one crashing a job interview; comedic tone (Wikipedia, AniList).
President Shigemoto dresses as a magical girl at work, played as comedy (Wikipedia; AniList Crossdressing); no romance reported.
Kana's repeated job-hunting rejections and self-doubt (Viz blurb).
Startup company life, business competition and industry politics are core (MU Business Competition, Capitalism; AniList Politics).

entry.title: Gon
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Gon, a tiny but unbeatably strong dinosaur living long after the dinosaur age, wanders the wilderness looking for food, sleep or solitude and gets tangled up in the lives of other animals. The stories are episodic and told entirely without dialogue or sound effects, in detailed naturalistic art.
entry.life_message: Living freely and boldly in nature, and standing up for smaller creatures against bullies, is a good life.

content.note: Encounters range from friendly to violent and Gon wins every fight against bigger foes (Wikipedia; Viz blurb on defending from the mean and hungry).
Predators and wilderness peril, played for comedy.

entry.title: WITCHRIV
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Nona, a mage hiding among humans, uses magic to fix her friend's glasses and draws the attention of the Bureau of Magic Surveillance, which persecutes mages. After the Bureau kills her friend's family she is jailed with another mage, Mira-Mira, and the story turns to escape and resistance.
entry.life_message: Refusing to submit to unjust persecution, and protecting those who share your fate, is the path to dignity.

entry.title: Somali and the Forest Spirit

entry.title: O Maidens in Your Savage Season
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Five girls in a high school literature club, written by Mari Okada, are thrown into confusion when classic novels and a club discussion turn their thoughts to sex. Kazusa struggles with feelings for childhood friend Izumi, Niina carries a past of grooming by an acting coach, Momoko realizes she is attracted to girls, club president Sonezaki wrestles with a strict upbringing, and writer Hitoha pursues a teacher she met in an adult chat room.
entry.life_message: Growing up means facing desire and love honestly, telling attraction from affection, and keeping faith with friends through it.

content.note: Emotional melodrama; Niina's grooming history (Wikipedia) is unsettling.
Sexual curiosity, masturbation and innuendo (MangaUpdates categories); a student pursues a teacher; anime reviewers list groping and grooming (Wikipedia). Anime-based reviews; manga detail to verify.
Frank sexual talk and euphemisms (publisher blurb); profanity level not confirmed.
Momoko's unrequited love causes deep depression (Wikipedia); no self-harm reported.
Hitoha meets an adult from an online adult chat room and blackmails a teacher (Wikipedia); reviewers say the teacher plot is not handled well.

entry.dominant: Feminism (female adolescence and desire); expressive individualism; critique of shame-based tradition

frames.aligns: Sonezaki learns love and lust differ; friendship loyalty is honored.
frames.concerns: Teen sexual exploration, masturbation and a student-teacher pursuit run against chastity teaching.

frames.concerns: Frank sexual material and affirmation of Momoko's queerness differ from most churches' ethics.

frames.aligns: Friendship and repentance-like reconciliations among the girls.
frames.concerns: Sexual themes throughout are weighed heavily under holiness standards.

frames.concerns: Lascivious content per Larger Catechism Q139; PC(USA) families may differ.

entry.title: Knights of the Zodiac
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Orphan Seiya earns the Pegasus Cloth, a constellation armor, and joins fellow Bronze Saints sworn to protect Saori Kido, the reincarnation of the goddess Athena. They fight through the Gold Saints' twelve temples to unseat a usurping Pope, then battle the gods Poseidon and Hades to save the world.
entry.life_message: True strength comes from friendship, self-sacrifice and fighting only to protect others and justice.

content.note: Continuous martial battles to the death through temples and the Underworld (Wikipedia); Thompson calls it combat-oriented; AniList and MangaUpdates tag tournaments and super powers.
Underworld journey, deaths of allies, Seiya mortally wounded at the end (Wikipedia); Athena sacrifices her life.
Little romance reported; Wikipedia notes a large fan pairing culture, which is outside the text.
Battle taunts; not otherwise reported (to verify).
Saga takes his own life after his good side returns (Wikipedia). Single-source detail, capped (to verify).
Heroic fighting and enduring injury for friends.
Toy-friendly armor designs and a large franchise; no in-story product placement reported.

frames.concerns: Greek gods shown as real and worshipped; Saga's suicide; constant violence.

frames.concerns: Pagan deities as protagonists' patrons; anger-fueled combat feeds passions.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, courage and good defeating evil.

frames.aligns: Laying down life for friends is a strong theme.
frames.concerns: Polytheistic cosmology presented as true within the story; violence level.

frames.aligns: Battle of good against evil gods.

frames.aligns: Righteous resistance to the tyrant Saga; common-grace appreciation of art.
frames.concerns: Worship of Athena as savior figure touches first-commandment concerns.

frames.concerns: Violence and a goddess-centered faith within the plot.

Violence, other gods and revived dead are major concerns.

frames.aligns: Pluralist myth-mixing and loyalty to friends.
Greek gods taken seriously; Athena as just protector goddess.
frames.concerns: Poseidon and Hades cast as villains; harm-none vs warrior virtues.

frames.aligns: Divine protectors, sacred armor and reverence for a goddess.
frames.concerns: Death and blood as kegare, but no disrespect to kami.

Unity of comrades from many lands.

Rebellion against a corrupt religious authority (the false Pope).

Avodah zarah: gods served and venerated by heroes.

entry.title: If It's for My Daughter, I'd Even Defeat a Demon Lord
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Dale, a young accomplished adventurer, finds Latina, a small devil girl near death in the forest, and adopts her. Raised among the regulars of the Dancing Tabby Cat tavern, with its owners Kenneth and Rita as extra parent figures, Latina grows up gentle and clever while Dale balances dangerous work with fatherhood.
entry.life_message: Love and protection of a child, whatever her origin, give life its meaning, and a caring community helps raise her.

content.note: Dale subdues demon beasts as an adventurer (Wikipedia); slice-of-life focus per AniList and MangaUpdates.
Latina is found nearly dead; mostly gentle tone.
Wikipedia says Latina later tells Dale she loves him and they marry, in the light novel; MangaUpdates lists Romance and a Loli tag. Whether the manga reaches this is unconfirmed (to verify).
Tavern setting (AniList Bar tag); drinking adults in background.

entry.dominant: Found family; communitarian care; acceptance of the outsider

frames.aligns: Adopting an abandoned child is a work of mercy; the tavern community shares her upbringing.

frames.concerns: Power imbalance if guardian becomes husband.

series.title: Saving 80,000 Gold in Another World for my Retirement
series.romaji: Rougo ni Sonaete Isekai de 8-manmai no Kinka wo Tamemasu
series.native: 老後に備えて異世界で８万枚の金貨を貯めます

entry.title: Saving 80,000 Gold in Another World for my Retirement
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Mitsuha, an orphaned eighteen-year-old who looks like a child, falls from a cliff and finds she can travel between modern Japan and a medieval fantasy world. She sells modern goods, wins a place with a local lord, opens a shop in the capital and trains with mercenaries on Earth while building toward a retirement fund of 80,000 gold coins.
entry.life_message: Security comes from shrewd planning, hard work and using one's advantages, while still protecting the people one comes to care about.

content.note: AniList tags War, Guns and Military-style conflict; ANN notes mercenary training and drift toward arms dealing. Graphic detail not confirmed (to verify).
Near death from a cliff fall and wolves (publisher blurb); grief over dead family (ANN).
MangaUpdates lists a Loli protagonist tag; ANN's reviewer is critical of the genre's focus on childlike heroines. No sexual content reported.
Mitsuha represses grief and hears her late brother's imagined voice (ANN).
Arms dealing, smuggling goods between worlds and manipulation of nobles shown as clever.
Profit and trading are the premise; AniList ranks the Economics tag highest; MangaUpdates lists merchants and trading.

entry.dominant: Pragmatism; market self-reliance; consumer goods as power

frames.aligns: Prudence and diligence, with Mitsuha protecting villagers she grows fond of.
frames.concerns: Wealth accumulation as life goal and arms dealing sit poorly with teaching on the common good.
Love of money and warfare as solutions.

frames.aligns: Hard work and planning for old age resemble Proverbs' wisdom.
frames.concerns: Deception of nobles and gun violence for profit.

frames.aligns: Honest trade and caring for orphans echo valued themes.
Artha (prosperity) as a legitimate life aim.

frames.concerns: Craving for wealth; wrong livelihood in arms dealing.

frames.aligns: Competent young woman succeeds on her own terms.

frames.aligns: Applies modern knowledge, medicine and agriculture rationally.
Thrift, self-reliance and planning for old age.
frames.concerns: Mercenary violence; deceit toward lawful authority.
Violence and military involvement; political entanglement.

frames.aligns: Memory of ancestors and family shapes her drive.
Kirat karni (honest work) and defending villagers.
Education and science brought to others.
Industry and care for her community.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Mitsuha talks her way into a lord's household rather than fighting, but later arms herself (ANN).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Self-directed entrepreneur working around rules of two worlds.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Driven by memory of her dead family, then by people around her shop.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Works within feudal nobility to gain status (ANN).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Modern goods, medicine and guns presented as superior to tradition (AniList tags).

folkways.japan: Reflects Japanese anxieties about retirement savings and the isekai convention of a modern Japanese person bringing knowledge to a premodern world.

delivery.evidence: ANN's review describes self-interest and ruthlessness through Mitsuha's choices, not lectures; no review calls it preachy.

personified.ideology: Shrewd self-interest and financial security

delivery.note: The profit-minded outlook is carried by the heroine's schemes and is rarely challenged by another worldview in the sources.

entry.winners_losers: Mitsuha prospers and rises in status; rivals and hostile forces lose to modern goods and weapons; pragmatic self-reliance gets the sympathy.

Whether war chapters show graphic deaths.

entry.title: The Yakuza's Guide to Babysitting
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Toru Kirishima, a violent enforcer known as the Demon of Sakuragi, is assigned by his boss Kazuhiko Sakuragi to look after the boss's quiet seven-year-old daughter Yaeka, whose mother has been in a coma since a car accident. As the two slowly bond, Kirishima learns patience and restraint, while a former acquaintance, Mashiro, tries to drag him back to his killer past.
entry.life_message: Caring for a child can soften even a hardened person, and family is built through patient daily attention.

content.note: Kirishima's past as a contract killer and a sadistic antagonist, Mashiro (Wikipedia); MangaUpdates lists a violent protagonist; the anime-era tone is mostly comedic.
Yaeka's mother in a coma; threats from Mashiro (Wikipedia); AniList Tragedy tag.
None reported; MangaDex rates it safe.
Gangster setting; level not confirmed (to verify).
Adult gangster milieu; smoking or drinking not confirmed (to verify).
Yaeka's withdrawn behavior after her mother's accident (Wikipedia).

frames.concerns: Organized crime presented as a loving family without clear judgment.

frames.aligns: Repentance of anger and learning patience.
Changed heart and responsibility for a child.
frames.concerns: Glamor of yakuza life; violence in Kirishima's past.

frames.concerns: Unlawful authority of the clan treated as legitimate.

entry.title: Boyish Girlfriend
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Akira and Daichi, friends since preschool, start dating when they go to different high schools. Akira is a tomboy who dislikes girly clothes, so when Daichi finds her in a cat-eared maid costume at her school festival and thinks it is adorable, much embarrassment follows. Short comedic chapters follow the couple's sweet, awkward moments.
entry.life_message: Loving someone means delighting in who they really are.

content.note: Teen dating couple; MangaDex rates it suggestive and MangaUpdates has a minor breasts tag. Publisher calls it wholesome.

entry.title: Kill Blue
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Juzo Ogami, a 39-year-old star hitman for the Z.O.O. syndicate, is stung by a genetically altered wasp and regresses to age 13. Sent to a middle school to vet it for his boss's daughter, the never-schooled Ogami finds he loves school life while juggling assassin rivals and Noren Mitsuoka, heiress of the pharmaceutical company that may hold his cure.
entry.life_message: It is never too late to experience the friendship and growth that an ordinary youth offers.

content.note: Hitman protagonist with guns and rival assassin groups (Wikipedia); AniList and MangaUpdates tag assassins and guns. An Otaku USA writer likens it to Case Closed with more violence.
Assassin fights and organized crime; comedic school tone balances.
A reviewer notes worrying potential for romance between adult-minded Ogami and Noren but says it is handled well (Wikipedia); a classmate has a crush on him.
Not reported; shonen action norms (to verify).
A classmate with a split personality (Wikipedia; AniList Dissociative Identities tag), presented comically.
Professional killer shown as cool and capable.

frames.aligns: Ogami discovers friendship, learning and the goodness of ordinary youth.
frames.concerns: A hired killer as hero without clear repentance.

frames.aligns: Renewal and humility in a hardened man.
Joy in learning and vocation as student.
Valuing simple school life over violence.

frames.concerns: Killing for hire; adult-minded hero with schoolgirls.

frames.aligns: Competence, loyalty and appreciation of schooling.

entry.title: My Room is a Dungeon Rest Stop
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Touru rents a suspiciously cheap apartment whose front door opens into a dungeon in another world. He rescues Ria, a poisoned knight separated from her party, and she mistakes him for a great sage because everyday things like running water and cola work like magic potions. A seven-volume comedy based on a novel, mixing dungeon adventure with apartment-sharing romance and fan service.
entry.life_message: Ordinary kindness and modern comforts can make an unremarkable young man a hero to someone else.

content.note: Poisoning and dungeon monsters such as slimes; ANN describes combat as mild.
Ecchi genre, Big Breasts and cohabitation (MangaUpdates), MangaDex suggestive; ANN vol. 1 notes a sexy design but no nudity; later volumes unknown (to verify).

Snack foods as potions are a running gag.

entry.title: Please Save My Earth
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Shy high-schooler Alice Sakaguchi, newly moved to Tokyo, babysits her bratty seven-year-old neighbor Rin. She and several classmates discover they share dreams of past lives as alien scientists who watched Earth from a moonbase, and what starts as a game turns dark as the memories reveal love triangles, jealousy and betrayal. After an accidental fall, Rin returns with adult maturity, psychic powers and an obsessive fixation on Alice. A 21-volume classic shoujo science-fiction series.
entry.life_message: The past can inform who you are, but you must choose to live in the present rather than repeat old wounds.

content.note: Psychic battles and a child's lethal powers (ANN); War and Revenge tags (AniList, MangaUpdates).
Tragic past lives and Rin's fall (Wikipedia: 'something darker'; ANN; AniList Tragedy).

entry.title: Defense Devil
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Kucabara, a demon prince banished and stripped of his powers, becomes a 'Defense Devil': a lawyer who proves the innocence of souls condemned to hell so he can collect their dark matter, though his soft heart keeps him spending it to save them. With the dragon demon Bichula and the exorcist nun Idamaria he returns to the demon world to stop his brother Legato, uncovers angels who rule hell, and ends recruited to defend God against angels who have betrayed Him. Ten volumes, written and drawn by Korean creators for a Japanese magazine.
entry.life_message: Mercy toward the condemned and loyalty to friends matter more than reclaiming power.

content.note: Battles with shinigami, demons and angels; a dragon family massacred (Wikipedia); Guns and Swordplay tags (AniList).

entry.title: Too Many Losing Heroines!
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Self-described background character Kazuhiko Nukumizu, a loner who reads light novels, overhears popular classmate Anna Yanami being turned down by her childhood friend. Soon he is entangled with several 'losing heroines', including track star Lemon Yakishio and shy literature-club member Chika Komari, each rejected by the boy she loved. He helps them move on, and in the process makes real friends for the first time. A manga adaptation of a light novel set in Toyohashi; ongoing.
entry.life_message: Heartbreak is survivable, and friendship can grow from shared loss.

content.note: Crushes and rejection; MangaDex suggestive, MangaUpdates Big Breasts (low votes).

entry.title: Laughing Under the Clouds
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: In early Meiji Japan, when samurai have lost their swords and crime is rising, the three Kumō brothers, heads of a shrine, ferry criminals to an inescapable prison on Lake Biwa. Eldest brother Tenka raises his siblings Soramaru and Chūtarō after their parents' murder, while the family's hidden duty is to find and destroy the vessel of the Orochi, a demon serpent reborn every 300 years. Betrayal by a trusted friend, a near loss of one brother to the serpent and a final battle follow over six volumes.
entry.life_message: Family bonds and shared duty can carry people through betrayal and darkness, and one should face fate with a smile.

entry.premise: In a world plagued by destructive monsters called mononoke, Dora Sasaki wants to join the Izanagi Force of anti-mononoke samurai to honor his mother, who was killed in an attack, but he has no supernatural energy. He teams up with Kusanagi, a weak, kind-hearted mononoke who shapeshifts into a katana and dreams of a gentle world. A short Weekly Shōnen Jump action series (five volumes) that ended early.

entry.title: Until Death Do Us Part
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Twelve-year-old Haruka Tōyama, whose precognition makes her a prize for criminal corporations, escapes her kidnappers by running to a blind swordsman, Mamoru Hijikata, and hiring him to protect her 'until death do us part.' Mamoru, who sees through special lenses, belongs to the Element Network, a secret vigilante group that punishes criminals the law cannot reach. Haruka helps the Network fight the mercenaries and assassins hunting her. A 26-volume seinen action thriller.
entry.life_message: Protecting the vulnerable justifies standing outside the law when the law fails.

content.note: Sword fights, explosions, assassins and mercenaries (ANN, Wikipedia); Assassins, Armed Combat (MangaUpdates); MangaUpdates genre Mature.

entry.title: Buddha
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Osamu Tezuka's retelling of the life of Siddhartha, from sickly prince to wandering ascetic to enlightened teacher, set in a turbulent ancient India of wars, bandits and caste oppression. Invented characters such as the animal-possessing bandit Tatta, the slave-caste woman Migaila and the wolf-raised Devadatta surround the historical story. Tezuka, described by his publisher as a humanist rather than a Buddhist, mixes philosophy with action, slapstick and anachronistic jokes. Eisner Award winner; eight volumes in English.

entry.premise: On a school trip to Tokyo Tower, three girls from different schools, Hikaru, Umi and Fuu, are pulled into Cephiro, a world shaped by will, where they are summoned to become the legendary Magic Knights. Guided by Guru Clef, they learn magic, gain weapons and giant guardian beings, and set out to rescue Princess Emeraude from High Priest Zagato. A three-volume CLAMP shoujo fantasy (first part of the saga).
entry.life_message: Friendship and a strong will can carry ordinary girls through a heavy duty.

entry.title: A Love Yet to Bloom

entry.premise: Hotori Arashiyama, a clumsy, mystery-loving high school girl, works at the Seaside cafe in the Maruko shopping district after its elderly owner, Uki, turns it into a makeshift maid cafe. Episodic chapters follow her friends, family, neighbors and shopkeepers, with occasional stories about aliens, ghosts and the paranormal. Ruby Crescent, who wants to be a treasure hunter like her father, teams up with Jio Freed, a lonely boy who trusts only money and wants to conquer the world, and who turns out to carry the demon called Satan inside him. entry.premise: Kou Ichinomiya, a rich young man raised never to owe anyone, is saved from the river by Nino, a homeless woman who says she is from Venus. To repay her he agrees to teach her about love, and he moves under the bridge as 'Recruit', joining an eccentric riverbank community that includes a mayor in a kappa costume, a star-helmeted musician and a gun-toting man in a nun's habit. Surreal comedy by Hikaru Nakamura; published in English by Vertical.
entry.life_message: A good life is found in mutual dependence and accepting others as they are, not in money, status or owing nothing.

content.note: Slapstick; Sister, a war veteran in a nun's habit, fires a machine gun and lays booby traps (Wikipedia; ANN).
Slow romance between Kou and Nino; a former yakuza wife and her lover in a comic affair; Kou's secretary implied to be infatuated with him (Wikipedia).
Hoshi buys cigarettes (Wikipedia); not a focus.
Kou has asthma attacks when indebted; a resident walks only on white lines out of fear (Wikipedia), played as comedy.
Living under a bridge shown as a happy choice.

entry.dominant: Community over money; absurd comedy; acceptance of eccentrics

frames.concerns: Parody church under an Orthodox cross; comic adultery subplot.

entry.title: Working for God in a Godless World
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Yukito Urabe, son of a cult leader, dies when his father sacrifices him to the cult's god Mitama, praying with his last breath for a world without religion. He wakes in a faithless world and settles in a village of outcasts, but when the empire begins executing them, Mitama appears and Urabe must build a following of believers, using his father's methods, to give her power to protect them. Seinen satire and fantasy by Aoi Akashiro and Hangetsuban Sonshou; published by Titan Manga.
entry.life_message: Belief is a powerful human tool that can manipulate or protect, and what matters is whether it is used to save people.

content.note: Reviewer calls violence graphic and brutal, citing hangings and executions; AniList Gore, MU Blood and Gore.

entry.title: Angel Sanctuary
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Setsuna, a troubled 16-year-old, is in love with his 15-year-old sister Sara and learns he is the reincarnation of Alexiel, an angel who rebelled against Heaven. He is drawn into a war among angels and demons that takes him through Hell and Heaven in search of Sara's soul, and ends in a confrontation with God himself. The author names 'forbidden love' as the theme, and the series also explores good and evil, nature versus science, and gender.
entry.life_message: Love, even a love the world forbids, is worth defying Heaven's order for, and good and evil are not sorted neatly by rank.

entry.premise: On rainy days, high-school girl Hina dreams of playing as a child with a boy in a garden she has never seen. entry.premise: Shino Oshima has a speech disorder that makes words starting with vowels, including her own surname, hard to say, and her first day of high school ends in laughter. series.title: Tokyo Ghoul
series.native: 東京喰種－トーキョーグール－

entry.heading: Tokyo Ghoul
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: Identity is a choice made under pressure: a person who belongs to two worlds can try to protect both, but the story counts the cost of that choice in pain and loss, and offers only a fragile hope that the two sides might one day live together.

content.framing: Neutral; predatory desire shown as menacing

frames.aligns: Dignity of every person, even the "monster"; critique of dehumanizing the outsider; evil (torture, revenge) shown as evil with consequences.
frames.concerns: Despair rather than hope dominates the original ending; revenge is pursued by several sympathetic characters; gratuitous gore in media is criticized by the Church ("Ethics in Communications").

frames.aligns: Struggle with the passions (hunger as a picture of a consuming passion); compassion for the enemy.
frames.concerns: Darkness without theosis or grace; strong concern about images that feed the passions; the church setting used for a cannibal scene (vol. 4-5) touches reverence for holy places.

frames.aligns: Clear depiction of sin's consequences; friendship and sacrifice.
frames.concerns: No saving answer, only human striving; graphic violence and strong language (Ephesians 4:29). Views vary by congregation, since each church is self-governing.

frames.aligns: Beneath the Tangles writers read Kaneki's arc as a search for redemption: "to be human means to feel pain." Evil framed as evil; mercy toward outsiders.
frames.concerns: The redemption remains unfinished; occasional nihilistic voices; gore and language.

frames.aligns: Clear battle between destructive and protective power.
frames.concerns: Ghouls are not demons, but the predatory, possession-like imagery (Rize "inside" Kaneki's mind, ch. 62-63, likely) can concern families attentive to spiritual warfare.

frames.aligns: Total depravity echoed: every faction, human and ghoul, is capable of atrocity; common grace lets families value a serious work by a non-Christian author.
frames.concerns: No providence or grace in view; vengeance taken into human hands (WLC on the sixth commandment).

frames.aligns: Law without gospel: the story shows people unable to save themselves. Two kingdoms: questions about the state's use of force.
frames.concerns: No gospel answer offered; confessional (LCMS, WELS) families more cautious than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Social holiness: concern for the outcast and the hunted; works of mercy (Anteiku feeding ghouls without killing).
frames.concerns: No grace named, and the hope of coexistence is left unfinished. Wesley's rule against diversions that cannot be used "in the name of the Lord Jesus" makes the graphic content a heavy depiction concern for holiness churches (Nazarene, Wesleyan), less for many UMC families.

frames.aligns: Respect for the outsider; just-war questions (Article 37) about the CCG's campaign.
frames.concerns: Despair at the end; revenge cycles. Episcopal and ACNA families differ more on gender than on this content.

frames.aligns: The cycle of violence is shown as destroying everyone; Anteiku's nonviolent ethic and Kaneki's mother's "better to be hurt" echo nonresistance.
frames.concerns: Kaneki abandons that ethic and the story makes his violence effective. Conservative groups avoid such media entirely; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Agency and the struggle of a divided nature; family love; service.
frames.concerns: A bleak ending with no hope beyond human effort; revenge pursued by sympathetic characters. For the Strength of Youth asks for media that invites the Spirit; the gore and language are the depiction issue. Members vary in strictness.

frames.aligns: Concern for the outcast; consequences of evil; the body treated as something that matters.
frames.concerns: Adventist teaching on media (drawn from Ellen G. White and the church's guidelines) warns against entertainment that dwells on violence and horror; the cannibal premise also clashes with the health message. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Prejudice shown as wrong; peace preferred to violence.
frames.concerns: Witness publications (Watchtower, jw.org guidance on entertainment) counsel avoiding media that features violence (Psalm 11:5); fighting is the main way the story's conflicts are settled, though it is framed as tragedy, and the horror imagery is a heavy depiction concern. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Compassion and the hope of reconciliation.
frames.concerns: Christian Science teaching stresses spiritual reality over material sense, so media that dwells on bodily horror, disease and death runs against the habit of thought it encourages. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Strong critique of prejudice and state violence against a minority; empathy for the marginalized; Ishida's majority/minority framing.
frames.concerns: Glorified fighting in places; little agency for some female characters; mental-health portrayal needs care.

frames.aligns: Respect for life; warning against dehumanizing a people; memory of the dead; revenge shown as a cycle that destroys (Leviticus 19:18).
frames.concerns: Eating human flesh and blood breaks food and purity law in its deepest form, though the story frames it as horror. Lashon hara and nivul peh make the language a concern; many Haredi homes avoid such media entirely.

frames.aligns: Respect for life; warning against dehumanizing a people; revenge rejected by the story's outcome.
frames.concerns: No turn toward repair at the end. Degrading content and vulgar speech are weighed by values of dignity; the cannibal premise is jarring for families who keep kosher.

frames.aligns: A plea against dehumanizing a minority, close to the prophetic call to justice; empathy for the hunted; cruelty shown as cruelty.
frames.concerns: Glorified fighting in places; few women with full arcs. Cruelty and exploitation are the ethical tests for the explicitness.

frames.aligns: Justice for the oppressed; mercy; patience under suffering (sabr).
frames.concerns: Revenge pursued by sympathetic characters; no turn to God or mercy beyond human effort; the premise breaks the deepest taboo, eating human flesh, which the Qur'an (49:12) uses as the image of backbiting, though the story frames it as horror. Foul language and graphic violence are a heavy depiction concern.

frames.aligns: Dharma under impossible duties; karma of violence returning on all sides.
frames.concerns: Ahimsa and vegetarian traditions find the premise especially repellent; despair at the end.

frames.aligns: Craving (hunger) as the root of suffering; compassion for all beings; cycles of harm.
frames.concerns: First precept: killing is central; no liberation shown.

frames.aligns: Harmony and the hope of coexistence.
frames.concerns: Blood, death and corpses are kegare (impurity), so a story built on them weighs as depiction; no shrines or kami are mocked, which is this tradition's main concern. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Equality of all people; standing against injustice (the sant-sipahi ideal); service.
frames.concerns: Violence for revenge rather than defense of the oppressed; Sikh codes forbid intoxicants and many Sikhs avoid meat, so the premise is jarring. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: The oneness of humanity and coexistence of opposed groups is the series' hope.
frames.concerns: Bahá'í writings counsel avoiding backbiting and degrading influences; heavy violence. (from general knowledge; to verify)

Scientology opposes psychiatry and psychiatric drugs; Kanou's surgical experiments and the CCG's medicalized control are framed as horrors, which fits concerns it raises, though the series' trauma framing differs. "Do not murder" (The Way to Happiness) and glorified violence in places. No public Scientology guidance on manga found. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Respect for nature and for beings unlike us; balance.
frames.concerns: The Wiccan Rede "an it harm none" is broken by every faction; revenge. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Critique of prejudice against a minority and of state violence; empathy for the hunted; Ishida's majority/minority statement.
frames.concerns: Few women with full arcs; Tsukiyama's coding mixes queer and predatory traits; safe-messaging concerns about self-harm and suicidal thinking.

frames.aligns: Reason, empathy and the value of a finite human life; refusal of easy good and evil.
frames.concerns: Glorified fighting; mental-health portrayal without support or recovery; bleak ending.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, protecting friends, a café that keeps order and restraint.
frames.concerns: Anti-authority strand (the CCG as oppressor); violence, language and moral grayness; no clear heroes.

frames.aligns: The Satanic Temple's tenets of compassion and justice, and the Church of Satan's focus on the individual, fit the story's sympathy for the outcast and its critique of the herd. (from general knowledge; to verify)
frames.concerns: Cruelty and non-consensual harm conflict with TST's tenets on bodily autonomy.

frames.aligns: First Principle, the inherent worth and dignity of every person, extended to the "other"; justice and compassion.
frames.concerns: Violence and despair; no community repair at the end. (from general knowledge; to verify)

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Revenge spreads harm: Mado's zeal and Touka's attacks (ch. 13-29) and Yamori repeating his own abuse (ch. 59-66). Kaneki's hardening to protect friends brings him no peace (ch. 80-94).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Authority on both sides, the CCG and Aogiri, uses violence as policy and is critiqued. Anteiku's quiet restraint, outside both systems, is the endorsed path.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Found family and protecting one's group come first (Anteiku, the Kirishima siblings, Hinami). Hide's friendship regardless of what Kaneki is, and the hope of coexistence, widen the circle.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: A hidden minority hunted by an organized majority; prejudice and state violence are critiqued. Aogiri's "strong eat the weak" creed is shown as hollow.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Christian imagery recurs ("Original Sin," ch. 126; the church fight, vol. 4-5) but is symbolic and offers no rescue. Kanou's lab science is shown as horror (ch. 95-111), so neither pole is celebrated.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival dominates a world of constant death, but the story's central value is tolerance across groups and the choice of one's own identity (life message).

folkways.japan: Ishida's sense of being "between the majority and minority groups" speaks to conformity pressure in Japanese society; Kaneki's mother's ethic, "better to be hurt than to hurt others," echoes Japanese ideals of self-effacement that the story tests and then breaks.

delivery.evidence: ANN's Silverman notes Kaneki's ruthlessness "doesn't look like it has brought him any more happiness"; no review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The story presents both ghouls and the CCG from the inside and lets events, not narration, weigh their views.

Righteous hatred of ghouls
Conscience inside the system
A monster can choose to shelter others

entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)

In the first, a British girl, Nicola, falls for Mimar, a young man at a bazaar in a small far-western Asian country, and years later returns with wealth and 'the secret of the world' to take deadly revenge. entry.heading: Death Note (Tsugumi Ohba and Takeshi Obata)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: The story shows a life spent claiming the power to judge others, and lets the reader watch where that leads. Ohba's own stated takeaway is: "Humans will all eventually die, so let's give it our all while we're alive" (Wikipedia, citing Ohba).

content.frequency: Constant (deaths every few chapters), mostly non-graphic

frames.aligns: The ruin of a proud man who makes himself judge of life and death; the innocent suffer from his "justice"; lawful authority prevails. Evil is shown in order to be understood, not made finally attractive (Inter Mirifica 7).
frames.concerns: No repentance or grace; the "Mu" rule denies judgment and afterlife; Light's glamor can invite admiration. Coerced suicides and death gods weigh as depiction; many parishes would treat it as older-teen reading.

frames.aligns: Light as a picture of the passions, above all pride, and of a man refusing repentance; an Orthodox writer at Geeks Under Grace reads it as "the throne without the Cross."
frames.concerns: No hope of resurrection in the story's rules; death gods taken seriously as spirits; guarding the senses (nepsis) weighs on the long dwelling with a killer's mind.

frames.aligns: Clear arc from sin to ruin (Galatians 6:7); deception exposed; a thoughtful teen can discuss justice and the death penalty.
frames.concerns: A human claiming divinity is punished, but no gospel answer is given; the "Mu" ending; death gods. Profanity in the Viz text and coerced suicide fail many families' Philippians 4:8 test. Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Plugged In praises the "compelling plot" and "conversations on morality and justice"; Christian reviewers read Light as a man seizing God's throne and falling.
frames.concerns: Plugged In warns of "spiritual themes, violence, and language" and apple and Eden imagery (anime). Range is broad, from churches that skip it to churches that use it for worldview talks.

frames.aligns: The man who takes a death god's power is destroyed by it.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": a supernatural death god who gives a human power to kill, and a notebook that works like a curse, are shown without any power of God against them.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Private judgment and killing are the story's target: Light's vigilante "justice" ends in exposure and death (ch. 103-107). Soichiro and the task force, who stand for rule of law, duty and honesty, are the moral center.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Law and due process are endorsed over one man's will. L's surveillance and confinement of suspects (Misa, ch. 33-35) are questioned, so order is honored but not without limits.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Rules are meant to apply to all, including family: Soichiro serves the investigation even as it points at his son. Light risks his father and sister (vols. 7-9), a betrayal of kin the story condemns as part of his corruption.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Light's claim to be "god of the new world" (ch. 1-2) is the root wrong; no person is above the law. The police chain of command and the Wammy's House succession (Near, Mello) are shown neutrally.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Religious language belongs to the villain and his cult (Mikami, ch. 83; the Kira worshippers, ch. 108). The "Mu" rule offers a naturalist note, and the duel is won by reason and investigation.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Crime, safety and deterrence are the central question; a frightened public accepts a killer who promises security (Pragmatic lens). Ohba's takeaway, "let's give it our all while we're alive," adds a modest self-expression note.

folkways.japan: Capital punishment, a powerful police bureaucracy and the public's quiet approval of Kira reflect debates in Japan, which keeps the death penalty; scholar Jolyon Baraka Thomas reads the cult elements against the 1995 Tokyo sarin attack. Soichiro's quiet devotion to duty echoes Japanese workplace norms.

delivery.evidence: ANN's Briana Lawrence: "two opposing sides that both believe in the same thing: justice." No review in the entry calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Light and L argue openly about justice, and the story ends with Light's fall rather than a stated lesson.

entry.heading: Black Clover
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is earned by effort, not birth: you refuse to give up, you lift up the people others look down on, and you build a family out of misfits.

frames.aligns: Dignity of the poor and the orphan; a church that shelters children; evil (the Dark Triad, Lucius) is never made attractive in the end (Inter Mirifica 7); reconciliation with enemies.
frames.concerns: The hero's power comes from a devil shown as a friend; angels and "holy war" imagery belong to the villain; a consecrated nun is the object of a running marriage-proposal gag.

frames.aligns: Humility and endurance; love for enemies; a church that raises orphans.
frames.concerns: Demons are real in the tradition, so a demon made sympathetic and fused with the hero (Devil Union, ch. 272-273, 326-327) blurs the line; angelic forms (halos, wings) given to the villain's creations. Guarding the senses (nepsis) applies to the steady combat.

frames.aligns: Hard work, perseverance, care for the outcast (James 2:1-9 on favoritism to the rich).
frames.concerns: Magic and devil power as the hero's tools; views vary by congregation because each church is self-governing.

frames.aligns: Clear good and evil; underdog grace; forgiveness of former enemies.
frames.concerns: The hero befriends and unites with a devil; spiritual realities in the story are not Christian ones. Engage-or-separate views differ.

frames.aligns: Courage, perseverance and a church shown kindly.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": devil contracts and hosting are the main source of power for heroes and villains alike, and the hero's union with a devil is celebrated (ch. 270, 326-327). Views range widely between churches.

frames.aligns: Common grace lets families value good art by non-Christians; human pride and lust for power (Lucius, the Dark Triad) shown as destructive.
frames.concerns: Devil alliance as the hero's strength; WLC Q139 concern for the fan service; images of angels and "holy war."

frames.aligns: Two kingdoms: Magic Knights bear the sword to protect the weak; vocation and faithful service in ordinary roles.
frames.concerns: Devil power and magic; LCMS and WELS families tend to be more cautious than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Social holiness: lifting up the poor and the excluded; works of mercy; prevenient grace has an echo in former enemies who turn.
frames.concerns: Wesley's General Rules caution about diversions; the devil alliance; drinking played for laughs. Holiness churches usually more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: Works judged by how they frame good and evil, in a fantasy tradition (Lewis; Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings is among Tabata's named influences, per Wikipedia); justice for the excluded.
frames.concerns: The devil alliance and inverted angel imagery; the nun gag. Episcopal and ACNA families differ mainly on gender, not on this content.

frames.aligns: Care for outsiders, community of misfits, forgiveness of enemies.
frames.concerns: Heroic violence is the hero's main tool throughout (Matthew 5:39); Old Order groups avoid such media; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Agency and effort; family (including adoptive family); service in a squad.
frames.concerns: Devil power and occult-style magic; fan service and drinking. Members vary in strictness.

frames.aligns: Strong critique of class, birth and ethnic prejudice; the excluded become heroes; a church that shelters children.
frames.concerns: The nun gag and early thin female cast (Anime Feminist; Fandom); violence as the means.

frames.aligns: Perseverance, care for orphans, clear defeat of devils.
frames.concerns: Magic, witches and devil hosting throughout; the dead brought back as Paladins conflicts with teaching on the state of the dead.

frames.aligns: Kindness to the poor, loyalty, hard work.
frames.concerns: Spiritism and magic are the basis of the whole world, and the hero's power comes from a demon (Galatians 5:19-21); fighting is the hero's calling (Psalm 11:5).

frames.aligns: Persistence, hope and love outlasting hatred.
frames.concerns: Evil, devils and fear are shown as real powers; magic as the source of strength.

frames.aligns: Care for the orphan and stranger (Deuteronomy 10:18-19); honoring those who raised you; persistence.
frames.concerns: Magic (kishuf) and demon alliances are central; Kabbalistic terms (Qliphoth, Sephira) used as fantasy labels; tzniut concerns with outfits and gags. Many Haredi homes restrict such media altogether.

frames.aligns: Love of the stranger, social justice, reconciliation after historic wrong (the elves).
frames.concerns: Magic and demons; Kabbalistic terms as fantasy; modesty values applied by families.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam: dismantling prejudice by birth and nation; outsiders included; historic injustice remembered and repaired.
frames.concerns: Kabbalistic terms used loosely; violence as the main tool.

frames.aligns: Justice for the poor, the orphan and the stranger; patience (sabr) and effort; family loyalty.
frames.concerns: Magic (sihr) is central; the hero allies with a devil (shaytan) and fuses with it; angelic imagery used by the villain. Lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) for outfits and gags.

frames.aligns: Effort and duty; a warrior who fights without hatred; reconciliation.
frames.concerns: Some families apply the Gita's tamasic category to the fighting; the birth-and-rank hierarchy story invites discussion that families approach in different ways.

frames.aligns: Compassion for outcasts and former enemies; Licht's hatred shown as suffering; craving for power (Lucius, Dark Triad) leads to ruin.
frames.concerns: Fighting is the main solution, against the first precept; ambition for the top rank is celebrated.

frames.aligns: Rejection of caste and birth-rank is a core Sikh value; courage to defend the oppressed; the five vices (ego, anger, greed) in the villains are condemned.
frames.concerns: Magic and devil power as a fantasy device; fan-service gags.

frames.aligns: Elimination of prejudice of every kind (race, class, nation) and the unity of peoples, as elves, humans and kingdoms are reconciled.
frames.concerns: Constant fighting; drinking played for laughs (alcohol is forbidden to Bahá'ís).

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) and gratitude; the Hino Country and the Ryuzen clan draw on Japanese setting.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; devils are a Western-style underworld rather than kami or yokai.

frames.aligns: Magic as part of nature; spirits of the elements (Undine, Sylph) aid the heroes; Vanessa, a witch, is a sympathetic hero.
frames.concerns: The Witch Queen is a manipulative ruler (likely ch. 90s; to verify); a stereotype check for "witch" villains.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness precepts: help others, be industrious, do not murder; self-determinism in Asta.
frames.concerns: Violence as the main solution; Lucius rewriting souls and minds is condemned, which fits the Church's concern about mind control.

frames.aligns: Anti-discrimination by class, ethnicity and ability is the core theme; disability-like "no magic" hero succeeds.
frames.concerns: The Sister Lily gag (Anime Feminist: a "refusal to respect a woman's wishes"; Fandom: "a kind of stalker"); fan service; Common Sense Media rates diverse representation "very little."

frames.aligns: Worth earned by effort and character, not birth or bloodline; human solidarity across peoples; magic read as fiction.
frames.concerns: Violence as the main tool; revivals lessen the weight of death.

frames.aligns: Hard work, self-reliance, loyalty, duty, protecting the weak, respect for good mentors and a legitimate elected leader.
frames.concerns: Inherited aristocracy is critiqued; blood family often fails while found family succeeds; some religious conservatives raise the devil alliance.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth and dignity of every person regardless of birth or power; justice for the excluded; reconciliation.
frames.concerns: Violence as the means; the nun gag.

frames.aligns: A devil reframed as a misunderstood outcast; defiance of unjust authority and false holiness (Lucius's "Archangels"); self-reliance; Satanic Temple tenets on compassion and justice.
frames.concerns: Most devils are still villains, so the stereotype check applies; loyalty and self-sacrifice for the group over the self.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Asta answers insults by proving himself, not by revenge; rivalry is a matter of pride, but vendetta (Licht's, the elves') is shown as manipulated and is reconciled (ch. 214).

Order vs freedom.evidence: The chaotic, rule-bending Black Bulls are celebrated (ANN: "the magical misfits"), but the Magic Knights and the elected Wizard King are upheld (ch. 392).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Found family over blood: an orphanage and a squad, while Noelle's blood family is cruel (ch. 5). Protecting the whole kingdom, and later former enemies, is the goal.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Rank by birth and magic is the main target (Noble, Common and Forsaken realms); merit, not lineage, earns rank. The story still celebrates reaching the top rank.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: The church is warm, but faith does not guide the plot; inherited aristocracy is critiqued; magic works like a natural force.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Hard work and endurance drive the hero (survival), joined to tolerance of outsiders and being oneself (expression).

folkways.japan: Senpai-style mentoring by captains, group loyalty to a squad and hard-work ("ganbaru") perseverance are common Japanese shonen norms. The church, nuns and the European-fantasy kingdom are borrowed Western settings, and the Hino Country (Yami's home) is a Japan-like land seen from outside.

delivery.evidence: Inferred from the entry's summaries; no review addresses preachiness. Trujillo (ANN) highlights its anti-discrimination themes.
delivery.note: Asta and his allies state the never-give-up and anti-discrimination themes aloud, while some snobbish rivals are later partly redeemed.

personified.ideology: Effort and loyalty can beat birth
Rank by birth and magic
Remaking everyone by eliminating flaws
